To help combat the debt the supervisors of the county voted to raise the income tax to 2% overall, and Luzerne County Court approved it.

headline: Gone but not forgotten
abstract: Mark Schweiker, former PA governor, is no longer mentioned in politics as it was three years ago. Schweiker began as lieutenant governor to PA Governor Tom Ridge and then took over as governor when Ridge left to take a national Cabinet position and after leaving office he was hired as the president of the Greater Philadelphia Chamber of Commerce. Many believe that he still has a future in politics if he wants it, but for now he is staying away from the political circle.

headline: Double oversight / It's all about saving Pittsburgh, remember?
abstract: The editorial criticizes the fighting between the two Pittsburgh-based recovery agencies, the Intergovernmental Cooperation Authority and the Act 47 recovery team.  Their main goals are to help Pittsburgh recover financially and rework the city's budget, but they have been fighting so much that ICA is suing the Act 47 team because it believes the team could have saved more taxpayer money.  However, the court fees associated with this battle is now costing the taxpayer $800,000.

headline: Nursing shortage prompts union to ask state for help
abstract: The Service Employees International Union District 1199P, which represents all nurses at state-run facilities in Pennsylvania is asking PA Governor Rendell and his administration to help advertise and recruit more nurses in state-run facilities. The Union believes Pennsylvania run prisons, hospitals, nursing homes and health departments are experiencing a shortage of nurses. The Rendell administration acknowledges a nursing shortage across the country, but does not feel Pennsylvania’s facilities are understaffed.

headline: Scott Twp. Supervisors Discuss Sewers, Decide to Hike Job Tax
abstract: The PA Environmental Hearing Board denied Dan Noll and Stephanie Clark of the group Concerned Lakeland Citizens a Petition to Reopen the Record in regards to their lawsuit against the township.  This denial ultimately means that Scott Township needs to only wait on the decision of the board on whether or not the PA Department of Environmental Protection and Scott Township have determined an accurate cost for a new sewer system.  The activist group, Concerned Lakeland Citizens, have protested that this system construction will bankrupt both the township and the residents.

headline: State office first sign of new downtown
abstract: This editorial compliments PA Governor Ed Rendell, Mayor Tom Leighton and the Greater Wilkes-Barre Chamber of Business and Industry for continuing progress in the development of the city of Wilkes-Barre.  Where there once was a massive hole in the ground because of a failed construction project, there is now a new state office building that will employ more than 250 people.  It also mentions the movie theater, shops, restaurants and renovations to Hotel Sterling that all will help bring development and activity to the area.

headline: Good work, good luck Rep. Kevin Blaum
abstract: This editorial wishes PA Representative Kevin Blaum well as he has decided to retire after 25 years in the state legislature in the 121st district and 5 years before that on Wilkes-Barre City Council.  It compliments his work on restoring Wilkes-Barre after the Agnes Flood as well as his role in constructing the Wilkes-Barre arena.

headline: Dover says no to Act 72
abstract: Dover Area School Board member Bill Buckingham, in stating why he was against opting in to Act 72, said he was not about to take a gift from Satan. The Board unanimously voted to opt out of the Act which was supposed to provide statewide property-tax relief. Allan Bonsell and Sheila Harkins were on the fence until the final vote, Harkins saying the board's decision was not whether to allow gambling in the state, but whether to allow people to benefit from it. Only 41 of 501 districts have opted in thus far.

headline: Were they kidding?
abstract: The authors think that comments made by PA state Representatives Bruce Smith and Mark McNaughton at a recent hearing on a proposal to raise hunting license fees are not right. The two legislators who supported the recent pay raise suggested that more public input is needed and the PA state Game Commission must demonstrate a real need.

headline: Pa. is $hunning stem-cell research
abstract: While many states such as New Jersey and New York are supporting stem-cell research, Pennsylvania maintains its reputation by providing zero funding whatsoever for embryonic-stem-cell research.  While PA Governor Ed Rendell claims he does support stem-cell research, he has not taken a stance on a proposal by PA Representative Mike Veon that calls for a $500 million bond initiative to fund research and create the PA Stem Cell Research Council.  Dr. Robert Young from the Fox Chase Cancer Center claims that states who fund any type of research gain a competitive advantage in that field.

headline: Scott Twp. Supervisors discuss sewers, decide to hike job tax
abstract: The PA state enviornmental hearing board denied a petition by local residents of Scott township, working under the interest group "Concerned Lakeland Citizens" that claims the township as well as the Department of Enviornmental Protection misled and manipulated local residents into approving a plan for a centralized sewage system that residents believe will economically starve their township. In other news, the supervisors plan to increase the job tax in the township passed, increasing the annual rate from $10 to $52. The township claims it will use the money for improving roads and the local fire department.

headline: Stay warm in PA summit
abstract: Governor Rendell is trying help Pennsylvanians when it gets cold this winter. He created the Stay Warm initiative which is meant to get people through what could be a cold, expensive winter. One of the more popular ideas was creating one point of contact so people would have one place to find information about heating help and safety. Governor Rendell is also trying to get more state and federal funding to the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Program.

headline: GOP caucus maps the road ahead
abstract: Republicans who control the state House of Representatives released their agenda for the next three months, but the repeal of the legislative pay raises did not make the cut. Property-tax cuts, a cap on state spending and reductions in state taxes are the main issues. Other smaller issues will be discussed time permitting.

headline: Easton Area tables Act 72 decision
abstract: After yet another turnout at the Easton Area School Board meeting to protest Act 72, board members again tabled the measure. The act would allot state slots revenue to school districts, allowing them to freeze or reduce property taxes. In exchange, income taxes would rise by .1 percent. Future school budgets would be subject to voter referendum. The board members appear to favor Act 72 four to two, but an official vote remains to be taken.

headline: West Ward cleanup draws few volunteers
abstract: Volunteer trash collectors were hard to come by Saturday morning in Easton's West Ward. Organizers believed the cold weather may have been partly to blame. This is an annual spring and fall event.

headline: Parents allege drug use at CD
abstract: Drug addicts, former addicts, and their parents testified at a Central Dauphin School board meeting about the reality of the drug epidemic in their high school. Students have claimed that they see other kids using heroin and prescription drugs pretty much freely in the bathrooms, hallways, and even cafeterias of the school.

headline: Sewer-link fight far from over
abstract: East Hanover township officials, including Supervisor Marie Beaudet, are fighting to change a PA Department of Environmental Protection's provision requiring Penn National Race Course to send it's sewage to East Hanover Township.  Solicitor Richard H. Wix questioned a provision forcing businesses to tie into township sewer, because the business operates a private sewer plant.

headline: Suburban sprawl reflects freedom of choice
abstract: The PA State Association of Township Supervisors, a group that is hoping to counter the call for government mergers that came from the Brookings Institution study, “Back to Prosperity: A Competitive Agenda for Renewing PA.” Some local leaders, including Allegheny County Chief Executive Dan Onorato and Pittsburgh Mayor Tom Murphy, have started to call for a merger of county and city governments that would do away with duplication of some services.

headline: GOP hopes to turn tide in Beaver County
abstract: Charlie Camp, the highest-ranking Republican in a Democratic Beaver County as County Commissioner, points out the phenomenon of higher numbers for registered Democrats in the region but more votes being cast for Republican candidates.  A good example is the Hopewell 21st Century Democrats led by Steve Plevel and Gary Hinkson who have crossed party lines many times in their posting of tickets of candidates in Hopewell commissioner races.  County Democratic Chairman Vince LaValle disagrees with this independent trend and says that each person will talk about a different trend taking place.

headline: Editorial didn't make the case for Wi-Fi
abstract: A woman writes to the editorial board saying that she doesn't believe they made a good case for the city providing wireless internet. She says that it isn't worth the money, that it will be an out-of-date technology soon, and that it won't benefit the poor.

headline: 'Brownout' ordered for grid
abstract: According to Ray Dotter, a spokesman for PJM Interconnection, most people would not notice a 5% reduction in electricity voltage, a measure taken as a result of record demand because of the heat.  Peco Energy reported peak demand and its spokesman, Michael Wood, referred to the voltage reduction as a "brownout."

headline: Philadelphia hospitals GET WELL
abstract: The Pennsylvania Health Care Cost Containment Council reported that while overall, hospital finances have improved, this does not necessarily constitute a trend. They warn that proposed Medicaid cuts by Governor Ed Rendell and President Bush could threaten health-care institutions.

headline: State Ag secretary supports ethanol
abstract: PA Secretary of Agriculture Dennis Wolff endorsed ethanol, although he stopped short of endorsing an ethanol plant proposed for Greene Township. The Franklin County Farm Bureau supports the plant, but hundreds of residents are challenging it. DeEtta Antoun, director of Citizens for a Quality Environment, says it is obvious Wolff has not researched ethanol, which is not economically viable. Scott Welsh, project manager for the potential Penn-Mar Ethanol LLC in Franklin County, hopes Wolff's support will help the Penn-Mar project.

headline: Street urges gentler way to get taxes
abstract: The nonprofit Community Legal Services of Philadelphia has accused the city's contractor, Linebarger Goggan Blaur and Sampson LLC of bullying poor and elderly homeowners into excessive payment plans, or not offering them at all in order to recoup over $200 million in delinquent taxes. Representatives of Philadelphia Mayor Street met with CLS to discuss the organization's suggestion to lower payment plans and grant partial amnesty to those who pay half their past-due balance within the year. Street wants to come up with a 'gentler' way to ensure taxes are recouped.

headline: GOP lawmaker announces run for lieutenant governor Michael Turzai of Allegheny County voted against legalizing slot machine gambling
abstract: PA Representative Mike Turzai has announced he will run for lieutenant governor this upcoming election in 2006 because of what he feels is the failure of PA Governor Ed Rendell.  He feels he would work with for his endorsement for governor, Republican William Scranton, because of their dedication to fiscal responsibility and focus on making the Pennsylvania competitive for employers.  Turzai also wants to reform medical malpractice by placing monetary limits on lawsuits against doctors.

headline: Ethics still get short shrift
abstract: The 2007 mayoral campaign is under way in the news media and city neighborhoods, Philadelphia Mayor Street is not out of the race. He has recently blocked a cut in the business-privilege tax and helped Philadelphia successfully hot Live 8 and Philadelphia Freedom concerts. The author believes that Philadelphia can be enhanced in its economic competitiveness by having meaningful ethics reform and Mayor Street can do this by providing the leadership that is necessary to create a permanent, independent and charter-sanctioned Board of Ethics for Philadelphia and fulfill his campaign promises by doing so.

headline: Cheap heat idea bubbling in deep fryer
abstract: Thomas Adams, from the University of Georgia, has promoted the use of cooking oil in place of heating oil and natural gas during the winter to save money as well as save the environment.  Philadelphia Fry-o-Diesel, an offshoot of the Energy Cooperative nonprofit organization, is currently using $369,696 to study the practicality of harvest trap grease, which is the waste poured down restaurant sinks.  Frank Palmarino recently made the switch to biodiesel for his truck and bioheat at his home heating system at a price of $2.27 a gallon rather than the $2.38-$2.50 for regular heating oil.

headline: Plans for medical center's cancer facility OK'd
abstract: The first piece of a planned $500 million expansion of the Penn State Milton S. Hershey Medical Center is on its way after the Derry Twp. Supervisors approved the development plan for an outpatient cancer treatment canter last night. The 7,800-square-foot building will sit between the hospital's south wing and parking garages. An enclosed corridor will connect it to the hospital. Officials said the center will centralize cancer serves and offer treatments not available currently.

headline: State cuts doe-hunting permits
abstract: The state's Board of Game Commissioners voted to reduce the number of doe permits that are given to hunters by 15.4% to slow the rapid decline in deer population. However, York County Commissioner Stephen Mohr and state Representative Ed Staback think that the number of permits allotted should be lowered even further.

headline: Streetscapes takin' shape
abstract: In Phoenixville the Streetscapes project is underway, and the project will reflect the past and rich history of the town. Early projections estimate that the project will cost $4.5 million and a Federal pass-through grant of 41 million was hand-delivered at borough hall by PA Governor Edward Rendell.

headline: GOP panel endorses Democrat
abstract: Derry Township Republicans are endorsing Donna Cronin, a Democrat, for the school board. The committee made their decsion after interviewing each candidate. Former school board member and Republican, John Grab, did not recieve an endorsement from the committee.

headline: Figures nixed, assessor rehired
abstract: Allegheny County Executive Dan Onorato rejected a consultant's work on property tax assessments as unfair in February, but that won't keep the consultant or her company from earning more of the county's money. The county has rehired Chief Assessment Officer Deborah Bunn for another year at $175,000. Onorato agreed to extend the services offered by Bunn and Tyler Technologies. City council is likely to approve a new system for calculating property values for 2006 taxes that Bunn would certify.

headline: Choice fizzles
abstract: Six years ago, PA embarked on an exciting and confusing journey into the world of electricity deregulation. There would be energy choice, competition! Well that is over now for individuals. Large commercial and industrial concerns will still be able to choose from competing energy suppliers. Community Energy is still an option for customers who feel strong enough about supporting renewable energy to pay an extra 2.5 cents per kilowatt hour. In the long run people are paying less though.

headline: Platts speaks out against tobacco
abstract: US Representative Todd Platts spoke on Capitol Hill in DC about his desire for tougher federal tobacco regulations.  He was joined by the Campaign for Tobacco-Free kids who placed 1200 shoes on the ground representing the number of lives lost to a tobacco related illness each day.

headline: State DEP approves Tamaqua pit plans
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Kathleen McGinty announced a modification to a mining permit for Lehigh Coal and Navigation Company that lets them use dredged sediment, coal ash and cement kiln dust in a reclamation project in Springdale Pit in Tamaqua.  Various officials and residents, such as PA Representative David Argall oppose the new permit's allowance for river sludge and other materials to be dropped into the mining pit.  McGinty along with PA Governor Ed Rendell both feel they kept constituents' opinions in mind but mentioned that their plan passed through the PA Cleanup Standards Scientific Advisory Board's tests.

headline: Taking sides on eminent domain
abstract: Residents from Ardmore, Westville and Haddon Township are rallying against eminent domain, what they call unfair practices between local governments and developers. Public officials counter that most redevelopment projects are necessary for revitalization. Louis Bezich, the leader of Public Solutions, a consulting firm, says redevelopment is not synonymous with eminent domain.

headline: GOP panel endorses Democrat
abstract: Derry Township's Democratic Committee hosted Governor Ed Rendell at a party workshop. Derry Township Republicans are endorsing Democrat Donna Cronin, a candidate for the school board, over her republican opponent John Grab. This is most likely because the school board, comprised entirely of Republicans, approved a 24% tax increase this year.

headline: Gov. Rendell should trust in elected officials
abstract: This editorial disapproves of PA Governor Ed Rendell and the Democrats' pushing for a referendum on Act 72, which was not enacted by most of the school districts throughout the state.  It sees this referendum as a lack of trust of elected school officials from the state government and feels that May 30th deadline for school districts to make the decision is arbitrary.  It does concede that Pennsylvania needs property tax relief, the purpose of Act 72, but it doesn't want property tax relief tied to gambling revenue.

headline: City gambling on gas prices
abstract: With gasoline prices wildly fluctuating because of hurricane and increasing worldwide demand, the city of Philadelphia has decided to roll the dice. The Street administration has entered the spot market in search of the best price to support its fleet of about 6,000 vehicles instead of locking in a price with a six-month contract, as it has done since early last year. Until last week, the city was paying as little as $1.77 per gallon for gas and $1.80 for diesel to Sunoco under a six-month contract. City officials declined a new contract when prices were raised.

headline: Prognosis looks good for supply of flu shots
abstract: Kristine Sheedy, spokeswoman for the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, reported that this year there will be an ample supply of flu shots ranging from 86 million to 94 million doses but recommends that young and healthy people wait until after October 24th to get a shot.  PA Department of Health spokesperson Richard McGarvey said the department ordered the same amount of shots last year, 150,000 doses.  He also said the state does not want to act as the main supplier of flu shots, rather that responsibility should be given to the hospitals and physicians.

headline: State DEP approves Tamaqua pit plans
abstract: The state department of enviornmental protection approved a modification to a mining permit for the Springdale pit in Tamaqua, PA. The modification allows Lehigh Coal and Navigation Co. to use dredged sediment, coal ash, and cement and lime kiln dust in Springdale's reclamation project. The decision has angered local officials and residents, who believe their opinions and needs have been disregarded by the department of enviornmental protection.

headline: The master plan
abstract: Highlights of Penn State Milton S Hershey Medical Center's 10 year expansion plans. Estimated cost is $500 million and additional jobs as many as 2,000. New buildings will add up to 1 million square feet extra.

headline: GOP rally brings out the faithful
abstract: Hundreds of Republicans gathered on Saturday for the Franklin County Republican Party's annual corn soup fund-raiser that has been taking place 50 years.  There was a table dedicated solely to supporting US Senator Rick Santorum, who is losing in polls for his re-election in November 2006.  PA Representative Rob Kauffman said that the gubernatorial race and the senatorial races are big events in the coming year, where Republicans hope to reprimand PA Governor Ed Rendell for his passing of Act 72.

headline: Governor's threats show desperation
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell and legislators should stop threatening to force school districts to participate in Act 72 and fix the seriously flawed act instead, according to editors. The Act proposes to use revenue from slots machines to subsidize property taxes which comprise school district budgets. Failing to convince most districts to sign on, Rendell announced to the PA Associated Press Broadcasters Association that legislators are likely to make the Act mandatory. Districts stand to lose a considerable amount of control in exchange for a relatively small amount of money.

headline: Coal to Fuel
abstract: null

headline: Rendell's health plan will put bite on Highmark
abstract: Governor Rendell’s Community Health Reinvestment Program calls for Pennsylvania’s four nonprofit Blue Cross carriers to fund $1 billion worth of charitable activity, mostly to expand state coverage for the uninsured. Highmark is expected to pay $90 million to the program because less of its business is subject to state income and premium taxes.

headline: State fines waste hauler
abstract: A waste hauler was fined $32,750 by the state on Friday for violations ranging from overweight and leaking loads to improper enclosures and failure to carry documentation. The Department of Environmental Protection said the condition of vehicles owned by Green Waste Services LLC of East Huntingdon, Westmoreland County, was particularly dangerous because of where he violation were found. Additional weight diminishes braking.

headline: Tobyhanna may add jobs, just not as many
abstract: The Defense Base Closure and Realignment Commission voted to realign rather than close the Red River Army Depot in Texas, which dashed hopes that a substantial number of its jobs would be transferred to Tobyhanna Depot in Monroe County.

headline: Governor considers distributor regulation
abstract: Legislation allowing beer distributors to pay an extra hundred dollars for a license to sell beer between noon and 5pm on Sundays is now on Governor Ed Rendell's desk.  Shawn march, a distributor, says it will be good for business, while Bob Spaziani says he doesn't know if he'll take advantage of the opportunity.  PA Senator Sean Logan, the bill's sponsor, said it was an issue of fairness.

headline: Group disputes property-tax law
abstract: The PA School Boards Association is considering either a court challenge or a campaign to change a new law that requires school districts to limit future tax increases if they accept gambling revenue to cut property taxes. The new law, known as Act 72, sets a May 30 deadline for schools boards to decide whether to take a share of the revenue from slot machines. Gov. Ed Rendell's administration projects slots will generate up to $1 billion.

headline: Coal to Fuel
abstract: John W. Rich, president of Waste Management and Processors, Inc. says he can use coal waste to make clean diesel fuel and sell it for as cheap as $1.25 a gallon. However, he needs a purchaser willing to make a twenty-five year commitment. The columnist suggests that Governor Ed Rendell's administration should invest in the company.

headline: Rendell's health plan would put a bite on Highmark
abstract: Highmark Inc, the region's largest health insurer, will pick up the biggest part of the tab for Gov. Ed Rendell's Community Health Reinvestment program, assuming the program holds up under fire from business interests, community activists and legislators. It calls for PA's four nonprofit Blue Cross carriers to fund $1 billion worth of charitable activity over the next 6 years.

headline: Township to fight landfill decision
abstract: The Broad Top Township supervisors are fighting a state decision allowing the amount of trash coming into a landfill in their municipality to more than double. They will appeal to the state Environmental Hearing Board because thy want reconsideration of last month's decision by the state Department of Environmental Protection to allow the daily trash trucked to the WSI Sandy Run landfill to increase from the current 300 tons to 750 tons. This would cut the life of the landfill, now estimated to have 10 years, to about four years.

headline: Trump Casino in Nicetown
abstract: A month after PA Governor Ed Rendell implored Donald Trump to invest in Philadelphia, the request seems to have drawn interest from Trump, who is shopping for property in the city's Nicetown section. It will have to wait until Trump's company emerges from Federal bankruptcy protection. Trump representatives met with Philadelphia Councilman Michael Nutter, whose district includes Nicetown. PA Rep. Jewel Williams also said he had been visited by Trump representatives. Ron Hinton, of the Allegheny West Foundation, said the location should be up to residents.

headline: Governor supports Democratic boost for National Guard
abstract: Days before PA House Speaker John Perzel was announce similar GOP legislation, PA Governor Ed Rendell, before the PA National Guard Association, announced initiatives of his own. Along with student loan interest forgiveness while on active duty, benefits would also include tax credits for employers to recoup the difference between active duty and regular pay. Almost three quarters of the state's National Guard has been deployed to Iraq and Afghanistan since 9/11.

headline: Group disputes property-tax law
abstract: The Pennsylvania School Board Association will legally challenge or campaign to amend Act 72, a law requiring school boards to decide whether they want to take a share in the revenue from slot machines. PSBA Executive Director Thomas Gentzel, questions why school boards have to make a decision to opt into the program so soon if homeowners will not experience tax cuts as a result of the slot machines revenue until the year 2007. With nearly sixty percent of PA homeowners applying for tax relief, Kate Phillips, PA Governor Rendell’s spokeswoman asserts that homeowners want school boards to opt into the program.

headline: Country's first soy fuel-injection facility opens in Pa.
abstract: A fuel-blending facility that is up and running in PA is the first in the nation that can inject soy-based additives into diesel or other fuels before they are put into tanker trucks. Fuel marketers typically combine soy-based additives with diesel or heating oil in taker trucks by sloshing them together. The new facility is more efficient, blending the fuels before they reach the pump, and spares marketers from having to buy store the additives, which are also known as biodiesel.

headline: Restaurant inspections tax
abstract: State auditors found that about 4,000 Pennsylvania restaurants outside the Philadelphia area have been licenses in recent years without the required inspections for sanitation and health. Auditor General Jack Wagner said the results show "systemic weakness" in the Agriculture Department's inspections process. He called for tougher penalties, more aggressive enforcement, and possible changes to he law that governs inspections.

headline: Trash-law violators to be fined
abstract: Last week, West Chester residents were hit with a flurry of warning stickers for not following the borough's in trash-disposal law. This week they could be hit with a blizzard of citations, with fines form $25 to $1,000. Last week's uncollected trash still lined several borough streets yesterday, though there was also a noticeable increase in the number to trash cans with lids.

headline: York Int'l vital to KIZ plan
abstract: Officials with the York County Economic Corp. are proposing a $100-million research and technology park that would include growing technology businesses. This is part of Governor Ed Rendell's Keystone Innovation Zones plan, which aims to keep college graduates in Pennsylvania by providing jobs. The PA Department of Community and Economic Development require that these zones are created around universities and must be partners of the universities and businesses in the area. York International Corp., a heating, ventilating, air-conditioning- and refrigeration business, will be included so that they can work with engineering graduates.

headline: Governor's fundraising a conflict of interest
abstract: J. Robert Lovett, chairman of the Lehigh County Republican Committee, complains about PA Governor Ed Rendell's fundraising trip to Las Vegas as the finance chair of the Democratic Governor's Association.  He cites Pennsylvania law that does not allow officials to accept contributions from gambling entities.  He does not think that Rendell's apology was enough and thinks he should resign as finance chair of the DGA.

headline: Group seeks Act 72 deadline
abstract: The Pennsylvania School Boards Association filed a law suit asking Commonwealth Court to allow school boards a year extension in deciding whether or not to opt into Act 72. Act 72 is the property tax relief plan championed by Governor Ed Rendell, that would lower property taxes using revenue from newly legalized slot machines.

headline: Energy provider to quit state
abstract: PA customers of Green Mountain Energy Co will have to switch to another electricity supplier because the company, one of the few choices outside local utilities, is dropping its service in the state. The company said rising market prices for electricity led to them move. Green Mountain's announcement follows a state Public Utility Commission report last week that, despite deregulation laws design to encourage competition, there are few choices outside local utilities when it comes to natural gas.

headline: Safety net threatened
abstract: Charles Debrunner, president of the Safety-Net Association of Pennsylvania Harrisburg, recognizes that PA Governor Rendell is concerned with the Medical Assistance program but disagrees with his proposed cutting Medical Assistance payments to hospitals by $350 million.  He cites the PA Health Care Cost Containment Council that 34% of hospitals lost money in 2004 and claims that cutting payments to hospitals by 15% is not an effective way to preserve the health care safety net.

headline: Trash-law violators to be fined
abstract: West Chester will issue citations, from $25 to $1,000, for violators of the new trash-disposal law. The law enforces rules on trash-can sizes, lids and placement. Borough Council President William J. Scott Jr. defended the new law saying it will ensure public health.

headline: Boyds Collection regroups
abstract: Boyds Collection Ltd. Based in Adams County announced last week that it does not meet the requirements for its stock to continue trading on the New York Stock Exchange. The beleaguered maker of Boyds bears and other collectibles said the NYSE notified Boyds on Sept. 21 that if failed t meet the listing requirements of $75 million in both market capitalization and net worth. In addition, its stock has been trading at less than $1 a share over a consecutive 30-day period.

headline: Governor's paying his own Super Bowl tab
abstract: PA Governor Rendell, criticized for his relationship with Comcast, will cover his and his family’s monetary expenses for their trip to the Super Bowl. Barry Kaufman, an executive director of Pennsylvania Common Cause, urges that Governor Rendell decline Comcast’s hotel offer in order to avoid distrust from citizens.

headline: Holding the line / The county can live with Onorato's frugal budget
abstract: Dan Onorato, the  Allegheny County chief executive, proposed a new $677.5 million budget. This includes funding to help increase the police force among other things. He did a good job with it and Council members should give the plan general support.

headline: Facing up to the cold winter
abstract: Letter to the editor praising Gov. Ed Rendell for taking the first initiative ever in proposing state LIHEAP funding, seeking PUC intervention for fair treatment of customers, along with the paper's plea for a national energy plan. The governor's proposal for remedying the shocking under-enrollment in the utilities' Customer Assistance Plan also deserves support.

headline: Senate passes ban on smoking
abstract: The New Jersey State Senate approved legislation due to prioritization from New Jersey Governor Richard J. Codey that bans smoking in all indoor public places except casino floors.  Barbara McConnell, a lobbyist with the New Jersey Licensed Beverage Association, said the organization is upset that the ban is unfair for smaller businesses.  Tom Duffy from the Eastern Division of the American Cancer Society, believes it was a step forward to protect many people from the dangers of second-hand smoke.

headline: Voters to decide May 17 if state should borrow $625 million for environmental programs
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell signed legislation that will allow voters to decide in the May 17th primary whether the state should borrow $625 million for environmental programs. Republicans and Democrats in the state House and Senate argued the amount of money for months before settling on $625 million. Andrew McElwaine, president of the Pennsylvania Environmental Council, said the state needs the money to preserve undeveloped spaces and keeping storm water from overwhelming sewage plants.

headline: $36.5 million bet at Presque Isle Downs
abstract: Gamblers wagered $36.5 million at Presque Isle Downs & Casino during May 7-13. The PA Gaming Control Board reported $33 million was returned to gamblers.

headline: Governor's paying own Super Bowl tab
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell will pay his way to fly south for the Super Bowl. He does get two nights hotel room from Comcast for being a football analyst. Some want the Governor to reject the hotel room and money for appearing on the show.

headline: Home owners need to learn frugality
abstract: The author does not think that the new homeowners in Berks County should be complaining about paying their taxes. They say that they weren’t forced to buy the new homes and there are thousands of other county taxpayers that own homes, pay taxes, save for their children’s education and save for retirement.

headline: First Place
abstract: The article is talking about how Pennsylvania is a state of firsts which include; the first in trash, the first state to put its website on its license plate and the first state to have a near meltdown at a commercial nuclear power plant (Three Mile Island Nuclear Power Station). The author believes that the state needs to return to its former prominence and it cannot do so right now with the officials in charge. The author criticizes PA Lieutenant Governor Catherine Baker Knoll who is head of the PA Emergency Management Agency.

headline: Senate passes legislation on mental hospital
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell instructed the Harrisburg State Hospital to close by the end of the year. However, a bill sponsored by state Senator Jeff Piccola and state Senator Patricia Vance passed the state Senate that prevents the hospital from closing without consideration by the Legislative Budget and Finance Committee. This bill will now be considered by the state House.

headline: Wade into deeper waters
abstract: This editorial criticizes PA Governor Ed Rendell for stalling the Delaware River Port Authority budget in order to convince the New Jersey delegation agrees to deepen the river channel from 40 to 45 feet.  It admits that Pennsylvania's argument that the deepening will attract more cargo ships and New Jersey's argument that the $300 million dredging project will deposit muck on its shores are valid.  It encourages both sides to stop arguing and studying various options and simply come together to complete the project before $200 million of federal funding disappears.

headline: $52 bite can 'hurt' workers
abstract: Many low wage employees in the Chambersburg area are complaining that the new $52 emergency municipal tax is too high, and Olympia Candy Kitchen owner Will Pananes even said that he had a worker quit as some of his employees' first pay checks were not high enough to pay the tax.  The Chambersburg Borough Council plans to exempt people making under $1,000 from the tax and a partial exemption for those between $1,000 and $5,200.  PA Governor Ed Rendell signed this tax into law to help municipalities with their finances.

headline: Great things come from...who knows? Casey Jones Opinion
abstract: Casey Jones supports Wilkes-Barre Mayor Tom Leighton for his development of the project that ex-Mayor Tom McGroaty failed to complete on South Washington Street.  Jones explains how McGroaty started a project but only left a hole in the ground where Leighton has now started the construction of an office building. The article attributes some of this success to McGroaty and encourages officials to take more chances and turn problems into opportunities.

headline: Homeowners get second chance at tax relief
abstract: Property owners from Lackawanna County have been or will be mailed applications to apply for a homestead exclusion and a property tax cut under the PA Homeowner Tax Relief Act.  This legislation directs some profits of the slot machine revenues to school districts in order to give property tax relief to eligible home and farm owners.  The state has predicted that an average homeowner's property tax bill will be cut by $333 a year if the slot machines' revenue reaches $1 billion.  However, to be able to participate in this tax relief program, each school district has to increase 0.1% the earned income tax.

headline: Home heating costs through the roof
abstract: Lehigh Valley residents can expect to pay more to heat their homes this winter, according to a government report. Home heating oil and natural gas customers will get hit the hardest, the US Energy Information Administration predicted in its annual winter fuels report. Oil customer will jump 30%. Natural gas will jump 31%. Electricity users will only increase by 2%.

headline: Sextuplets' mom seeks Medicaid help
abstract: Kate Gosselin, mother of sextuplets that are less than one year old and 4-year-old twins, will appeal for continued nursing help from Medicaid beyond a one-year-cutoff.

headline: Water loss draws many to site
abstract: The water level at Antietam Lake in Berks County continues to drop mysteriously. Authorities say that a shortage of rain could have caused three streams that feed the lake to be lower than normal and hot weather has likely increased the evaporation of the lake. The city-owned lake has dropped 8 feet in three weeks.

headline: ...But broad discussion, pro and con
abstract: Northampton County Council is considering whether or not to hold public forums on the proposed slot machine establishments to be built in Bethlehem, but the decision to license slot machine parlors is for the PA Gaming Control Board.  The editorial encourages the council to allow enough time during this forum to make sure all opinions are expressed.

headline: Greedy lawmakers should lose jobs
abstract: The author compares the pay increase of the PA state legislators to the Enron scandal and says that they showed arrogance and greed by voting for themselves. The author believes that the proper reward for the “self-serving bunch” is to not have them reelected in the future elections.

headline: How city got into budget mess
abstract: This article examines how Mayor Rick Filippi and City Council allowed the city of Erie to reach into a budgetary and financial crisis mode.  Filippi attributed the $2.6 million deficit he reported to an arbitration award that gave firefighters a pay raise higher than the budgeted amount as well as the Erie Bureau of Police being almost $1 million over budget.  Also, the city failed to collect a budgeted $1 million in municipal services from nonprofit authorities and colleges who are not required to pay taxes.

headline: Meet the Commission
abstract: This article gives a grading of each of the members of the Fairmount Park Commission with one of the criteria being his or her attendance at meetings.  The article rates E. Harris Baum, John Binswanger, Thomas Carter, Leon Tucker, Robert Nix III, Connie Little, Mary Mason, Marcia Makadon, Phil Price, Rosanne Pauciello, Doris Smith and Debra Wolf-Goldstein.  Wolf-Goldstein and Price received the highest ratings whereas Smith and Carter were given the worst ratings.

headline: Smokeless isn't harmless
abstract: PA is the only state that does not tax spit tobacco. Potential revenue from these taxes could be close to $100 million, an amount that could save some of the cuts proposed in the state's Medicaid health program. The reluctant cuts proposed by PA Governor Ed Rendell will most adversely affect the elderly, disabled, and those with chronic conditions. PA's failure to tax "other tobacco products" denies the state of revenue of has given youth financial incentive to switch to chewing tobacco and snuff, according to Jonathan Stein in his op-ed.

headline: TMI security upgrades in place
abstract: Three Mile Island nuclear power plant reported that it has invested $500,000 to enhance security on the south vehicle checkpoint, which serves as the first access point contractors must pass on their path to the plant's Unit 1 reactor.  Ralph DeSantis, spokesman for AmerGen Energy, claimed that opening access from the south gate will deal with parking overflows and security issues.  Since September 11, 2001, the plant has invested a total of $12 million on security, and next month, the US Nuclear Regulatory Commission will inspect the new security measures.

headline: 7 Pittsburgh neighborhoods in tourist campaign
abstract: Seven neighborhoods have teamed up to put a $60,000 state tourism grant to work for visitors who want more from Pittsburgh, according to Amy Camp of the South Side Local Development Company. Lenwood Sloan of the PA Tourism Office  said that collaboration if a condition of receiving the grants.

headline: Gubernatorial hopeful stumps in Somerset
abstract: Offering an upbeat message to reform state government, gubernatorial candidate Bill Scranton was the main speaker at the Somerset County Republican Fall Banquet. He is one of only three from the GOP hoping to unseat Democratic Gov. Ed Rendell. Scranton blamed Rendell for what he called a stagnant state economy. He would like small government and lower taxes.

headline: Inside the Capitol
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell spoke to township officials at the convention of the Pennsylvania State Association of Township Supervisors to encourage them to support Act 72. Act 72 is a property tax-reform plan that would require any school districts who sign onto it to not raise property taxes above the cost of inflation, and in return they would receive profits from newly legalized gambling. Under Act 72, taxes could only be increased above inflation through referendum. Rendell is also trying to win support for Growing Greener II. State Senator David "Chip" Brightbill sponsored legislation that makes adjustments to the State Report Card, a measure of how well schools are performing.

headline: More independent natural gas suppliers could have created lower prices
abstract: As the cost of heating a home on natural gas spikes nearly 50 percent this winter, state utility officials say better competition in the market in recent years could have helped lower long-term prices. A recent report released by the state Public Utility Commission concluded that six years after deregulation of the natural gas industry, there's still effectively no competition. Large utility companies dominate the market as always, setting prices. Yet the inclusion of more independent suppliers could have created lower overall prices, better customer service, and sign-on incentives that could have benefited consumers in the long run, as deregulation intended.

headline: State delays hospital closure
abstract: The Department of Public Welfare has reported the Harrisburg State Hospital will close a month later than expected at the end of January.  The state has moved 87 of the 260 residents to other hospitals as 5% were discharged to live at home or with family members.  Joan Erney, deputy secretary for the DPW, said the government funded the relocation of the hospital patients, the rebuilding of local infrastructure and Dauphin County's planned 16-bed residential care facility.

headline: Water utility seeks rate hike again
abstract: Residential water bills for most of Aqua Pennsylvania's 340,000 customers in the Philadelphia suburbs would rise about 14.4 percent next year, under a rate proposal under review by the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission. State Consumer Advocate Irwin Popowsky said he would challenge the plan, which would increase the typical residential customer's bill $6 a month. Aqua Pennsylvania is seeking the increase to help pay for $274.5 million in investments.

headline: 800 will be employed at Plains Casino
abstract: Pocono Downs Casino will consist of a shopping complex, a food court, a children's area and slot machines.  It's owned by Mohegan Tribal Gaming Authority and is located in Plains Township.  Steve Barrouk, president of the Greater Wilkes Barre Chamber of Business and Industry and State Representative Kevin Blaum were impressed by plans.

headline: Guv goes to court to save Willow Grove
abstract: PA Governor Edward Rendell and lawyers for the state went into a Philadelphia courtroom to press their case for saving jobs of more than 1,000 Air National Guard members at Willow Grove. Rendell contends a government proposal to close the entire base is unconstitutional by the federal government. The two PA US Senators Arlen Specter and Rick Santorum are also parties in the lawsuit and the hearing is before US District Judge John R. Padova.

headline: Leaders differ on fixing property-tax plan
abstract: A hearing on three bills to modify the state's property tax-reduction program revealed divisions over how the legislature should respond to the refusal of most PA school boards to participate. A key point in the dispute is whether the tax cuts should be made mandatory, as Gov. Ed Rendell proposes, or place din the hands of the voters. Homeowners would see about $300 in tax cuts a year.

headline: Pennsylvania should use more hybrid vehicles
abstract: The author likes that the administration of PA Governor Edward Rendell has agreed to increase the number of gas-electric hybrids in the state fleet, which should reduce costs. The author doesn’t like that gasoline prices fluctuate so much between towns that are so close together; they use the example of Chambersburg and Waynesboro being 11 miles apart and differing almost 20 cents. They also don’t like that US Representative Bud Shuster would not comment on the pay raises that PA legislators gave themselves.

headline: State Hospital
abstract: Locals are divided over the plan to close down the Harrisburg State Hospital. Some believe that the community is ready and able to handle the mentally ill patients that would be dispersed after the hospital closing, while others believe the state is rushing things and that the community does not have the necessary facilities and assistance to handle the patients. The Department of Public Welfare has announced they will hold two hearings concerning the issue.

headline: A blind spot on bus fatalities
abstract: The Southeastern PA Transit Authority blames bus drivers for two accidents in which pedestrian fatalities resulted during a left-hand turn, but members of Transport workers Union Local 234 say they have been complaining to management for months about the large side-view mirrors in SEPTA's fleet. The Union says because the mirrors make impossible to see pedestrians when making left-hand turns, SEPTA should take responsibility for the fatalities instead of scapegoating drivers. A reenactment of the second accident concluded that indeed, there is a blind spot.

headline: 9 sites, 11 scenarios
abstract: Mayor Street's 47 member Gaming Advisory Task Force has paired nine proposed slots parlor sites into 11 scenarios that it believes would maximize revenues.

headline: Habay faces 21st charge
abstract: State Representative Jeff Habay faces twenty criminal charges for falsely claiming a political opponent sent him a suspicious white powder, and for using his staff to campaign for him on state time. He now faces charges for intimidating a staffer who was cooperating in the county prosecutors' case against him.

headline: Keep Politicians ?Accountable?
abstract: According to the PA School Boards Association, 269 of the state's districts opted out of Act 72. Only 88 have opted in. The deadline is Monday. The act will distribute to slots revenue to participating districts which have chosen to reduce property taxes and raise income taxes instead. PA Sen. John Pippy and Rep. Mark Mustio introduced a bill to maintain the accountability of school and local government officials with regard to Act 72. The legislation would require tax rates to be decreases to produce a zero revenue increase, with a separate vote to raise taxes. Editors support this method.

headline: PUC says Met-Ed doesn't have to move utility poles
abstract: The state Public Utility Commission rejected a complaint by a Springettsbury Township man who asked them to force Met-Ed to remove six utility poles near Pleasant Valley Road. The man claimed the poles were a hazard for drivers, but the PUC determined that they were not.

headline: State hospital
abstract: While there are ambivalent feelings on the closing of the Harrisburg State Hospital, this editorial says the mental health and mental retardation services within Dauphin County are inadequate.  It cites statistics given by Dauphin County mental health and mental retardation services administrator Barry Wyrick that the county itself has 141 beds for community housing and a waiting list of 144 and those approved for a bed still have to wait 27 days to be admitted.  It claims the PA Department of Public Welfare should have had a hearing before closing the hospital to adequately set up a system that would efficiently deal with the needs of the community.

headline: Airline, local notables beam with possibilities ahead
abstract: Allegheny County Chief Executive Dan Onorato and chairman of the Allegheny County Airport Authority board Glenn Mahone were present at the opening of the Southwest Airlines services at Pittsburgh International Airport. Onorato noted the airport had rebounded from pre 9/11 sales, now hosting 7 low-fare carriers. Mahone avoided mentioning controversy with US Airways, saying that Southwest Airlines had kept its promise in coming to Pittsburgh.

headline: A new vehicle for arts funding
abstract: Many are in support of new legislation sponsored by PA Senator Jone Conti that would provide about $7.8 million a year to arts groups throughout Pennsylvania.  An amendment to the Johnstown Flood Tax, Conti's amendment would use revenues from tax increases by the PA Liquor Control Board to support arts and culture and another $5.2 million to promote tourism.  Conti also suggested that Rendell write this proposal into his next budget and then the necessary legislation would follow.

headline: Hats off to Santorum, he understands politics
abstract: The columnist criticizes United States Senator Rick Santorum for his manner of campaigning. Santorum was fundraising in Florida during the Terry Schiavo case and then was the lone Senator to visit the hospital the day she died.

headline: Law firm responds to Jill
abstract: Sharon Humble of Linebarger Goggan Blair and Sampson, a law firm, responds to a previous letter from Jill Porter that criticized tax lien sheriff's sales of abandoned homes on properties.  Humble claims that these sales have put abandoned homes into the hands of people who redevelop them  and put them back on the tax rolls.  She also says that the law firm itself has no power in setting the conditions of the sales and do not control the acceptance nor the refunding of deposits by the sheriff's office and has always acted responsibly.

headline: Rendell to kick off 'Stay Warm PA'
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell will announce a multi-point plan that could include the first-ever state contribution to help low-income households cope with winter heating bills. Rendell will kick off a Stay Warm PA program at LifeSpan Charities Senior Resource Center. Details remain unavailable.

headline: State hospital closing on track
abstract: The Harrisburg State Hospital, which opened in 1851, is the oldest of nine state hospitals in PA and is being closed. The PA state Department of Public Welfare has said that the hospital is being closed because it is more effective and humane to treat the mentally ill in community programs. Frank Kane, a spokesman for the PA state Department of General Services, said that nothing can be done to sell the property until the welfare office declares the property surplus.

headline: Airport eyes shorter wait for luggage
abstract: Allegheny County Airport Authority will now control baggage operations and Pittsburgh International Airport.

headline: A taste of Pennsylvania
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell wined and dined PA restaurateurs and food suppliers last week in attempts to forge business relationships and support PA products. Tastes of PA stations were set up around the rose garden of the governor's mansion in Harrisburg to showcase PA foods to encourage restaurant owners to buy state products. The event was part of the PA Preferred program.

headline: Health care compromise key to ending strike
abstract: After three teacher strikes, 39 grievances and hundreds of meetings, the unthinkable happened: The union and the board agreed. When teachers and officials signed a contract in March, Somerset Area shook off its title as the district with the longest-running teacher contract dispute in the state. That distinction now belongs to the Crestwood School District, where teachers have been working without a contract since 2002.

headline: Lawmaker working with schools on tax
abstract: In an effort to help stave off rising property taxes for senior citizens and those on fixed incomes, administrators in the Quakertown Community, Penn ridge and Palisades school districts are meeting with state Rep. Paul Clymer to come up with an alternative to Act 72. Penn ridge Superintendent Robert Kish met with about 15 of our residents in Quakertown and Paul Clymer to talk about the development of a legislative bill to either freeze taxes for seniors and those on fixed incomes, or to allow local school districts to implement or raise earned income taxes.

headline: Rendell unveils plan to help Pennsylvanians keep warm
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell unveiled a $30 million public-private initiative to help lower-income resident in the state stay warm and pay high heating bills this winter. It came amid mounting concerns about soaring prices for natural gas and other heating fuels and forecasts of a harsher-than-normal winter. The governor's Stay warm PA initiative includes a request to the Legislature for up to $15 million in state funds to supplement federal funds for the so-called Low Income Energy Assistance Program, which helped about 350,000 PA households pay their utility bills last year.

headline: State hospital closure bill passes Pa. senate
abstract: The Harrisburg State Hospital is planned to close, but a bill sponsored by state Senator Jeffrey Piccola that recently passed the state Senate prevents any state mental health facility from closing without it being studied by the Legislative Budget and Finance Committee. However, this bill is likely to be opposed by Governor Ed Rendell, and the state Department of Public Welfare.

headline: Airport reduces fees for airlines
abstract: Pittsburgh International Airport will cheapen its landing fees by approximately one-third and its ramp and terminal rates by one-fourth after recognizing that its revenues are higher than projected. JoAnn Jenny, airport spokeswoman, reported that the cheaper rates will save the airlines from $4 million to $5 million.  These cuts come despite US Airways announcing that it will remove about 14 flights from the airport by the end of the summer.

headline: Airline merger faces hurdles
abstract: U.S. Airways and  America West Airlines may merge. Allegheny County Airport Authority said that it would be difficult to accomplish.

headline: Holden not in favor of immediate troop pullout
abstract: U.S. T. Timothy Holden disagrees with his mentor Rep. John Murtha in regards to an immediate withdraw of troops from Iraq. He believes it is best to wait until after Iraqis choose their new government before setting up any timetable for withdraw. The Iraqis are scheduled to elect representatives to a new government on Dec. 15; the government will assume power in January.

headline: Lawmakers gear up study of finances of city schools
abstract: The PA legislature is set to launch an in-depth financial study of the Pittsburgh Public schools. The Legislative budget and financial committee will determine the scope of the study it will conduct in accordance with a Senate resolution sponsored by a bipartisan group of Allegheny state senators.

headline: Rendell: OK of rate was premature
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell said state utility regulators acted prematurely when they cleared Philadelphia to raise average residential natural gas bills by nearly 20 percent. The approval by the Public Utility Commission came at a time when the administration is trying to get additional federal funding to help low-income households pay their heating bills. The increase means the average PGW customer will pay about $172.20 a month, up from $144.28 as of Sept. PGW is the state's largest gas utility with 485,000 customers.

headline: State legislatures moving to address end-of-life issues
abstract: In response to the Terri Shaviavo case disputing end-of-life care, PA Sen. Stewart Greenleaf sponsored a bill establishing which person has priority in deciding care for a dying patient. The Shaviavo case prompted renewed interest in legislation over life or death decisions absent of an established living will or power of attorney. The bill es-tablishes a spouse as the principle authority over end-of-life decisions. A similar bill was vetoed by Gov. Ed Rendell in 2004, though it received broad support from physician’s accusations and the Pennsylvania Catholic Conference. Rendell initially supported the intent of the bill, but disagreed with some portions of the legislation. Similar bills across the United States have been introduced following the Florida decision in the Shaviavo case.

headline: As license requirements rise, 16-year-olds' fatal crashes fall
abstract: A nationwide study by the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety found that the number of fatal crashes involving 16-year-olds decreased substantially compared to other age groups once graduated licensing requirements were introduced. The Insurance Institute for Highway Safety recommends putting even more limitations on young drivers, but spokesperson for the state Department of Transportation Rich Kirkpatrick says that he knows of no proposals that would increase limitations on young drivers.

headline: Airline Union has little hope for deal
abstract: US airways entered Chapter 11 bankruptcy on Sept 12 and has said that it needs at least $1 billion in labor cost cuts in order to survive. Of the company's five labor unions, three have ratified pay and benefit cuts while two are still undergoing deliberations. The deadline for agreement is Thursday, when the US Bankruptcy court will rule on the airline's requests to abrogate collective-bargaining conrtacts and impose long-term pay and benefit cuts the company says it needs to survive.

headline: Home Again
abstract: After a year of lobbying, Philadelphia will join 350 localities in obtaining a Housing Trust Fund. The fund will bring in at least $10 million annually. The direct beneficiaries will be low and moderate-income households.

headline: Lawmakers mull changes to new $52 'EMS' tax
abstract: PA Representative Tim Solobay is proposing that the cities, boroughs and townships that currently collect the $52 emergency municipal tax to secure $5 solely for the local ambulance company.  Any town that does not impose the full $52 would be required to use 10% of the imposed tax in their area for the same purpose.  This legislation is in response to ambulance companies complaining that confusion about how the new "EMS" tax is used is hurting their fundraising efforts.

headline: Thousands face utility cut-offs after law change
abstract: After the PA Legislature passed Act 201, the Public Utility Commission can no longer stop utility terminations or negotiate better terms between the companies and the consumers.  As a result, Equitable Gas of Western PA has increased its gas shutoffs from 2 in 2004 to 3,287 in the first four months of 2005.  PA Senator Jim Ferlo reportedly plans to propose a bil that would restore the prohibition on winter shut-offs of utility service without the approval of the PA Public Utility Commission.

headline: State outlines medical cutbacks
abstract: Governor Rendell’s budget will affect Pennsylvanians that depend on medical assistance from the government and approximately 68,000 providers. According to Michael J. Masch, PA Secretary for Budget and Administration, the state’s budget could not have been balanced by leaving things unchanged. Administrative changes, limiting increases to health-care providers and limiting benefits to recipients will yield about $600 million in savings.

headline: Both parties need to get real about mass transit deal
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell is having the deal with the big mass transit agencies are in big fiscal trouble and they need more funding to avoid making them too expensive for low-income riders. State legislature members say they will oppose funding unless a companion bill raises the gas tax to fund construction and repairs for roads and bridges.

headline: Applebee's coming to township neighborhood
abstract: The Washington Township Board of Supervisors recently voted to allow a transfer of a liquor license from Greencastle, PA to a new Applebee's restaurant in Waynesboro, despite Supervisor Stewart McCleaf abstaining.  This transfer is yet to be approved by the PA Liquor Control Board, and Pittsburgh attorney Mark Kozar reported that the law allows one license for every 3,000 people.  Louis Cambeletta, director for the area for Applebee's, said the new restaurant will cost around $2 million to build and should be open by the end of 2006.

headline: Honorable politicians seem scarce these days
abstract: We live in an I generation, whether politician or citizen, today America is primarily interested in self-satisfaction rather than public service. Sadly, this means bad deals and bad laws and society pays the price. Those who can least afford it get stuck the most. We need to realize that self alone is not enough to make our society run the way it needs to.

headline: Lawmakers plan meeting on reform
abstract: Lawmakers and school board officials will meet tomorrow to fill in taxpayers on the myriad of ideas that have been proposed for delivering property tax relief. Along with broadening public understanding of the different reforms, the meeting's organizers, the PA School Boards Association and the legislative Local Tax Policy Caucus, are seeking input about the ideas garnering legislators' attention. The Local Tax Policy Caucus recently unveiled its revised tax reform plan that calls for putting the responsibility for funding special education entirely on the state through the use of revenue generated from a tax on slot machines

headline: City may use police funds to cover firefighter overtime costs
abstract: Pittsburgh City Council plans to vote on whether or not to use $2.58 million from the Police Bureau budget to cover the overtime costs in the Pittsburgh Fire Bureau due to severe understaffing.  Both the Fraternal Order of Police and the Firefighters Local 1 Union have expressed their frustration with the situation.  Local 1 President Joe King said the budget shifts are a result of the Act 47 recovery plan, which closed six fire stations.

headline: State should maintain reimbursement rates, emphasize cost containment
abstract: This editorial lists common misconceptions about PA Governor Ed Rendell's recent proposed Medicaid budget cuts and the truths that actually lie behind them.  It claims, among other things, that while Rendell says that he provides a 2% increase in Medicaid payments, his budget actually contains a 13% decrease in Medicaid payments to hospitals and creates a shortfall.  The editorial is extremely concerned that cuts to hospitals and limits on health care benefits to Medicaid patients will put the already suffering health care system in Pennsylvania in a worse position.

headline: Both parties need to get real about mass transit deal
abstract: Governor Rendell wants the state’s taxpayers to pay new taxes or fees so low-income people in Philadelphia, Pittsburgh and their surrounding suburbs can ride to and from work. Pennsylvania’s State GOP leaders want the state’s taxpayers to pay a gas tax road and bridge improvements their suburban and rural constituencies need. Pennsylvania’s state Democrats and Governor Rendell are having trouble developing a funding source for mass transit that the state GOP will agree with.

headline: Bar is no oasis; LCB should act
abstract: The editorial board encourages the Liquor Control Board to speed its process of review of a local bar which has been the site of acts of violence, and it's owner, Janine Laboranti, was charged with selling heroin from behind the bar.

headline: Hotel tax hike catches county by surprise
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell signed legislation authorizing Lehigh and Northampton to increase hotel taxes. Lehigh County sought an increase from 3.5% to 4%.  According to the amended state law, if the Northampton County Council wants to reenact the hotel tax, it must be at the Lehigh-decided 4%, according to Michael Stirshic of the Lehigh Valley Convention and Visitors Bureau.  Northampton County Council President J. Michael Dowd said he was surprised to learn that they had such little choice.

headline: Lawyer: Act 72 is 'defective'
abstract: School boards must decide by May 30th whether or not they want to sign onto the Homeowner Tax Relief Act, or Act 72, which would prevent school boards from making property tax increases, but would offset this with gambling revenue and a small income tax increase. However, homeowners might not receive as much property tax relief as Governor Ed Rendell predicts, and the president of the Carlisle Area school board opposes the law.

headline: City police force gets $1 million pay raise
abstract: A PA state arbitrator awarded a pay raise to the Reading police department which the mayor says may cause cutbacks in other areas The raises are part of a state arbitrator's award in the latest police contract that covers 2004-2006. Officials say the city's budget amounts to $53 million, with $19.9 million for the police department, but the award does not up wages for any other union employee.

headline: The Hot Zone
abstract: The editorial board seems to approve of the fact that the PA Health Care Cost Containment Council reported the number of infections caused by hospital practices.

headline: Bridge will be repaired
abstract: State engineers announced State Street Bridge in Hamburg, PA would have to be closed if it was not fixed soon, however the PA Department of Transportation has the bridge at the top of its list of priorities. However, residents and school district administrators will need to devise an alternate transportation route for the 18 month renovation period, PennDOT officials told the borough's road and safety committee.

headline: Beer distributors await Sunday sales
abstract: A bill passed be the PA State Senate allowing beer distributors to sell on Sundays is expected to be signed by Governor Ed Rendell .  Some distributors believe the bill will increase revenue and keep business from crossing state lines.  Others believe the required licenses will prove costly.

headline: House committee chairman vows to fight any plan to mandate Act 72
abstract: PA House Committee Chairman Brett Feese has vowed to block any attempt by PA Governor Ed Rendell to make good on a threat to force schools to elect to reduce property-taxes by accepting slot machine money. With just a month to go to sign on, only 10 of the state's 501 school districts have signed Act 72. The act would allow districts to raise income taxes rather than relying on property taxes for revenue. Rendell's threat was made before the PA Associated Press Broadcasters Association. A charge that legislators violated their own rules in approving slots stands before the PA Supreme Court.

headline: Let voters have referendum on Act 72
abstract: PA voters may get to vote on a referendum regarding Act 72.  Act 72 legalized slot machines with the condition that the profits go to school districts, which would be required to lower property taxes.  The Act gave the people a vote on major school district tax increases, leading many school districts to reject participation.  The propose of lower tax relief was a major campaign issue for Governor Ed Rendell.

headline: City police force gets $1 million pay raise
abstract: Mayor Tom McMahon reported that a $1 million pay raise for the city police force may need to make cuts in other department as this year's city budget of $53 million does not reflect any the wage increases.  The police union president, Barry L. Rambo, complained that the government knew the pay raises were coming but did not plan for them.  $500,000 of the total must be paid as a lump sum for retroactive increases according to the contract.

headline: US lists firms offering new drug benefit
abstract: The US Congress and President Bush have pushed through a bill that cover Medicare enrollees through the private insurance market and free market competition, and they named the private insurers that will cover millions of disabled and elderly people.  This expansion will cost approximately $70 billion next year and increase the total Medicare spending to $425 billion in 2006.  Medicare Administrator Mark McClellan reported that the idea of driving down costs with competition appears to be working as the average monthly premiums have been reduced from $32 to $37.

headline: Budget cuts will be no walk for city parks
abstract: In Pittsburgh, one of the biggest budget cuts comes from the maintenance of public parks. Mike Gable, deputy director of the Pittsburgh Public Works Department, reported that there was a drastic cut in funding from 2003 and 2004, but a small increase for 2005. The city is also spending $10 million to replace old playground equipment. However, the Pittsburgh Parks Conservancy found that $100 million is needed in park improvements.

headline: Bethlehem's gaming foes speak
abstract: At a townhall meeting many residents and councilmen in Bethlehem Township opposed turning a portion of the former Bethlehem Steel Corps into a casino.  Councilmen Gordon Mowrer and Joseph Leeson Jr. were expected to introduce a zoning ordinance change to ban gambling, but the council did not plan to vote on it.

headline: House GOP kills Dems' latest ethics move
abstract: United States House Republicans voted down Speaker of the House Nancy Pelosi's ethics proposal.

headline: Letters…Mayor Vader
abstract: A resident compares PA Governor Rendell to Yoda and Philadelphia Mayor Street to Darth Vader. He believes the city is going down the drain financially and crime wise.

headline: City police plan to increase downtown patrols
abstract: Hazleton police will increase patrols downtown and enlarge a narcotics unit in response to three shootings that occurred over four days last week. One of the shootings, a homicide, apparently committed because of a dispute about a car accident, occurred downtown Thursday afternoon, and another occurred Saturday night when a teenager allegedly shot and wounded a man who he said failed to pay for drugs. Extra patrols and more manpower are the latest efforts to fight crime in Hazelton. In the past year nine new police came and police began carrying semi-automatic weapons.

headline: Tuberculosis strikes at NCC
abstract: Officials at the Allentown Health Bureau informed Northampton Community College officials that a student there had contracted tuberculosis, but said it was unlikely anyone else would contract it. Officials at Allentown Health Bureau and the State Department of Health will be on campus Monday and Wednesday to provide students with TB tests as a precautionary measure. PA tuberculosis control program manager Donna Murray said TB is not contracted through casual contact as the student would have had with others in classes.

headline: Campus interchange would cost millions
abstract: The Harrisburg Area Transportation Study estimated that to route commercial and industrial traffic off the Penn State Harrisburg campus would cost $27.7 million, but the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation says the estimate is "way off". The Harrisburg Area Transportation study is proposing the connector road as part of PennDOT's Transportation Improvement Plan.

headline: Board to get help in checking out slots applicants
abstract: The PA state Gaming Control Board, under pressure to get slot machines running after a delay from failed PA state Supreme Court challenge, voted to outsource background checks for some potential applicants. The applicant, International Game Technology, submitted paperwork detailing its financial situation, SEC and IRS information, and insurance and litigation matters. The emergency procurement must be approved by PA state Department of General Services and will allow the board to collect the money and pay the investigators.

headline: House rejects cuts in Medicaid
abstract: The Republican-dominated PA House of Representatives unanimously voted against PA Governor Ed Rendell's proposal to make cuts to Medicaid, which is the state's fastest-growing expense.  Democrats voted against the Governor's plan because of claims that they created a plan months ago that they would rather use, but they accused the Republicans have trying to politically embarrass Rendell.  Lawmakers have been discussing how to use the $100 million surplus this year to compensate for some of Rendell's cuts and make Medicaid spending more responsible.

headline: Library branches to regain services
abstract: The city plans to restore full service this month 10 neighborhood library branches that saw their hours reduced because of budget cuts earlier this year. The money for the restoration of services comes from $3.5 million that Mayor Street and City Council agreed this year to add to the $35.27 million annual operating budget of the Free Liberty of Philadelphia. The Street Administration has said it would raise new money through a new billboard excise tax, higher billboard-licensing fees, a tax on valet-parking and other measures.

headline: City to study fire response times
abstract: The Pittsburgh City Council voted to scrutinize how quickly firefighters have responded to fires since six fire stations were shuttered. The investigation was led by Council President Gene Ricciardi. The state Fire Bureau keeps records of the response time to fires.

headline: UPMC unveils tech partnership
abstract: The University of Pittsburgh Medical Center and International Business Machines, Corp., are forging a $402 million partnership that will save the health care system up to $1 billion a year. The technology will allow for much greater efficiency. Such technology is included in the Bush Administration's budget.

headline: Council gives its Ok to $230M airport bond deal
abstract: Philadelphia's City Council approved a $230 million bond issue for the Philadelphia airport. Council members Michael Nutter and Brian O'Neill objected to its approval and asked Mayor John Street to renegotiate the fees with the lawyers and underwriters, but Council President Anna Verna said the airlines would be harmed if the bill wasn't passed.

headline: Casino's benefits touted
abstract: Representatives of Aztar Corp., owner of the Tropicana casinos, said that they will apply for a state slots license to build the $325 million attraction in Allentown. They plan to close in coming weeks n the purchase of 43 acres owned by Agere Systems Inc. Aztar is the third company to announce a proposal for a slots casino in the Lehigh Valley.

headline: How much...
abstract: This letter criticizes President Bush for claiming to be a compassionate conservative while he holds a very expensive gala for his inauguration while there is an Iraqi war and mass destruction from the tsunami.

headline: Mall plan worries Washington County neighbors
abstract: Developers from Continental Real Estate who are proposed the $40 million Union Highlands Shopping Center in Union Township claim that the shopping complex will create $850,000 in tax revenue to local, school, and county tax coffers and over 1,200 jobs.  However, many citizens in the area argue that the area cannot handle the traffic associated with the complex and that improvements on the infrastructure will cost the local government.  Marc Todd, Union Township zoning officer, says a study has been done on the potential effect on traffic, but the results are not finalized yet.

headline: Colleges use patrols and tough penalties as first steps
abstract: The Patriot news reports on various approaches taken by PA State Police and academic institutions to curb alcohol poisoning and incidents related to student binge drinking. Despite various approaches, many students say their intake and lifestyle has not changed. The PA Liquor Control Board does not record alcohol poisoning statistics. Steven Schmidt, director of the PLCB's Bureau of Alcohol Education noted it will take time to curb the kind of behavior that leads to alcohol poisoning and even death.

headline: Villa Teresa nursing home has license downgraded
abstract: The PA Department of Health has fined the Villa Teresa nursing home after finding 29 deficiencies in the home's care.
