Schools doing poorly are more likely to close than schools doing well. The displaced students would be assigned to either a higher achieving school or to one of seven to nine schools that would become "accelerated learning academies."

headline: State House security officers to be armed with handguns
abstract: The PA House of Representatives have allowed the uniformed officers who patrol the offices to carry handguns for what is called "terrorism prevention."  The director of security for the House, Phil Frederick, has consistently called for arming the guards after shootings in the US Capitol in 1998 killed two security officers.  The PA Department of General Services also endorsed the idea despite union officials claiming that the officers may not be properly trained.

headline: Willow Grove in limbo
abstract: The national base closure commission agreed to all but shut down Willow Grove Naval Air Station that separates pilots from their planes and creates an uncertain future for more than 1,000 men and women stationed there. The US District Court ruled that the Pentagon couldn’t strip Willow Grove of its 111th Fighter Wing but the BRAC did decide to retire six of the fighter wing’s A-10 aircraft and reallocate nine others to Air National Guard stations elsewhere; meaning the pilots can stay but their planes cannot.

headline: Spector vows he'll beat Hodgkins
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter, 75 disclosed that he is being treated for Hodgkin’s disease. Dr. John H. Glick, a cancer specialist, says Hodgkin’s patients have a 70 percent chance of survival. Senator Specter is optimistic that he will battle his condition and continue work on Capitol Hill for Pennsylvanians and America.

headline: Region's jobless rate up to 6.3%
abstract: In spite of increased hiring, the regional unemployment rate is up half a percent and is now 6.3%.

headline: Rendell approves school aid package
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell signed the $9.2 billion dollar educational budget at a ceremony, despite being heckled about Medicare after being introduced by state Representative Jennifer Mann.  In his remarks he focused on the $13 million set aside for the Temporary Special Assistance Supplement.

headline: State Police began 100 years ago, as strike breakers
abstract: The PA State Police, created by PA Gov. Samuel Pennypacker in 1905, is turning 100 years old. The force was originally created by Pennypacker in response to a commission which said the state's use of police in mining strikes violated that state's responsibility to protect its people. The independent statewide police force was the first of its kind in the country, notes PA Police Commissioner Jeffrey Miller.

headline: An advertising blitz targets city's changes
abstract: Atlantic City received more revenue from thousands of new casino hotel rooms and was able to increase marketing greatly in the form of advertisements: spending $326,000 for ads on cable television, $160,000 in newspapers and $137,000 on radio. They plan to increase marketing even more this year, including spending a half-million on Internet marketing to reach out to women and young visitors in order to change the perception of the city.

headline: Stark Contrast exists on raises
abstract: In stark contrast to the shameless display by the Pennsylvania General Assembly, the U.S. Senate by an overwhelming 92-6, voted to forgo an annual cost-of-living pay increase o 1.9 percent. This highlights the corrupt leadership of the state legislators; they should really start to follow in the federal governments foot steps.

headline: regressive shuffle
abstract: Republicans in Harrisburg called for cutting the personal net income tax without spelling out how the state could afford it. Members of the Commonwealth Caucus want to cut the sales tax and eliminate property taxes. It's clear who would bear the brunt of the charge: low-income Pennsylvanians. The plan takes from the poor and gives to the rich.

headline: Rendell: Schools can attach conditions to Act 72 approval
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell approved 2 conditions school districts may attach to Act 72. Pending the PA Supreme Court's approval of Act 71, which legalized slots gambling, some schools have said they will opt in. Other schools have said their opting in is conditional upon whether or not expected revenue, Rendell estimates $500 million at least, begins to flow by 2007-08. The act is supposed to provide homeowners with at least $330 in tax relief per year. However, still other schools have said they will opt in only if revenue is between $750 million and $1 billion. Rendell denied approval of this condition.

headline: State police need more troopers - and soon
abstract: Bruce Edwards, president of the Pennsylvania State Troopers Association, calls for the 2006-2007 state budget to include funding for 273 new state troopers.  He cites that 16% of officers within the state are state troopers, but they are in charge of controlling 65% of the state.  He also claims that because many municipalities are cutting their police forces to save money, much of the responsibility is being put on the already understaffed state troopers.

headline: Bliley technologies, Sunburst Electronics appoint Cline new chief executive officer
abstract: Two of Erie's most prominet high-tech manufacturing companies have a new leader in John Cline, 53. He comes in as Bliley technologies has received a $1.36 million package from PA governor Ed Rendell for the production of high performance quartz crystals.

headline: State considers next step for Act 72
abstract: Legislators are struggling to determine the next step should Act 72 fail as a solution to property tax relief. Statewide, 69 school boards have opted in, with 187 boards opting out. There are 501 districts in total. Several legislators have introduced proposals aimed at garnering public support, including referendums. PA House Minority Whip Michael Veon plans to introduce a bill to make the Act mandatory. However, such measures have yet to receive support by influential politicians, including PA Governor Ed Rendell. He threatened to use such measures in the past, but has backed off.

headline: Rendell asks agencies to limit spending
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell has asked state agencies to stabilize administrative spending for the following fiscal year in 2006-2007 on account of his wanting to increase spending for education, development and social services.  Budget Secretary Michael Masch reported that the revenue of the government is being surpassed by the number of low-income citizens and abused children.

headline: Roosevelt's bottom line; 'student achievement'
abstract: Mark Roosevelt is the new superintendent of Pittsburgh Public schools and he will be spending his first year trying to work on a new plan for educating students in the district that will pay off in three years. He has to present a plan to improve achievement across the district within six months, present a balanced 2006 budget and develop a plan for reorganizing and closing schools.

headline: State police, auditor agree on Megan's Law records
abstract: In a pact signed yesterday, the Pennsylvania state Police agreed to make available for limited review the records of convicted sex crime offenders so that the auditor general's office can complete a long-sought assessment of how well the state's version of Megan's Law is being enforced. The agreement is historic, say the parties involved, because it ends years of legal haggling between the auditor general's office and state police.

headline: Cable line bendable, breakable
abstract: It is unlikely that Comcast Corp will buy Susquehanna Cable, despite Comcast owning part of the company, according to Todd Mitchell, an analyst who covers Comcast for Kaufman Bros in New York.

headline: State Democrats gesture to pay raise repeal
abstract: PA Representative TJ Rooney presided over a meeting of the Democratic Senate Committee yesterday that attempted to repeal the recently controversial pay raise legislation.  The resolution, presented by Chuck Pascal, was passed by voice vote with no opposition despite many of these members voted for the pay raise.  The resolution, similar to one passed by the Republican State Committee, is only advisory and was weakened further by the fact that the meeting did not have a majority of the lawmakers present.

headline: Rendell budget plan will paint 'a grim picture'
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell has warned that it won't be pretty. When he unveils his $24 billion budget, he will try to make the case to legislators and Pennsylvanians that his spending plan makes the best of a bad situation. There will be very little increases and some cuts.

headline: Saucon Valley panel says no to Act 72
abstract: The Saucon Valley School Board recommended that the school district not opt into Act 72, a property tax-relief program that would disallow the school district to raise property taxes above the rate of inflation without a referendum, and in return would receive profits from newly legalized gambling. The board will vote on the matter May 23rd. State Senator Lisa Boscola supports Act 72. The school board also ruled that students most fully cover the $400 cost of driver education classes.

headline: State shirks duty to fund court system
abstract: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court ruled that in order for everyone to have equal protection under the law, it was necessary for the courts in all counties to be funded, so they ruled that Pennsylvania must fund the court system rather than individual counties. However, the state has not done this so far, and most likely will continue to neglect it because of the high cost.

headline: Comcast to buy Software Firm
abstract: Comcast corp said today that they will be buying Liberate Technologies, a California software firm. The purchase was made to boost interactive video services provided by Comcast, such as watching multiple programs at one time and checking your voicemail on your television.

headline: State doesn't need 253 lawmakers
abstract: The author is complaining about the 16 percent pay raise for PA legislators on top of the cost-of-living increase they received in January of the same year. The author believes that they are only serving themselves and don’t consider their voters. The author calls for the voters to prove the legislators wrong and vote them out of office.

headline: Rendell hopeful on tax cut
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell hopes that the PA Legislature will approve cuts to the property taxes especially if they are a larger reduction than the Senate approved last week.  While the Senate approved a bill that will reduce the taxes by 17% for all the 3,000,000 homeowners in the state, Rendell believes that the legislators can double that amount by removing exemptions from the state sales tax.  PA Senator David Brightbill said that  this cut is a building block and expanding the sales tax two years after it was raised is not particularly a good idea right now.

headline: School acting superintendent axes 3 top jobs
abstract: Less than a week after becoming the acting superintendent of Pittsburgh Public Schools, Andrew King is wasting no time in eliminating the positions of three top administrators who were allies of former superintendent John W Thompson. The positions of chief of staff, chief human resources officer and chief technology officer would be closed, forcing the demotion or termination of Philip Parr, Dwight Mosley, and Elbert Yaworsky, respectively, who are now filling them, according to board members and other district officials.

headline: State trooper charged in home break-in assault
abstract: PA State Trooper Glenn Whitney along with Clifford Grosvenor have turned themselves in to state police after they broke in the victim's house and assaulted him.  They are facing charges of burglary, criminal trespass, simple assault, harassment and conspiracy.  Whitney is suspended without pay pending the investigation results.

headline: Comcast to buy software firm
abstract: Comcast Corporation announced that it will buy a majority share of Liberate Technologies of California in order to speed up its development of software that will allow viewers to watch multiple programs and create more interactive television.  Comcast also stated that the sale would not be official until Liberate dropped its appeal of a bankruptcy court ruling that did not allow them bankruptcy protection, saying that Liberate had enough cash to cover its liabilities.

headline: State GOP begins watching 3 gubernatorial
abstract: The state GOP is excited about all three of its candidates for governor. They believe all three could make a good governor. Former Lt. Gov. Bill Scranton, Sen. Jeffrey Piccola and Lynn Swann are all discussed with their qualifications.

headline: Rendell to promote property tax reform
abstract: PA Revenue Secretary Greg Fajt has reported that PA Governor Ed Rendell would actually support a broader but decreased sales tax or a higher personal income tax in order to lower or get rid of school property taxes.  Rendell has consistently wanted to tax the slot machine revenues to reduce the property taxes on homeowners 20%.  While Rendell says he will entertain different ideas, the Commonwealth Caucus has proposed to lower the sales tax by 1% but broaden it to include food and clothing, something Rendell refuses to do.

headline: School acting superintendent axes 3 top jobs
abstract: The acting superintendent of Pittsburgh Public Schools, Andrew King, eliminated the positions of three top administrators who were formerly appointed by former superintendent John W. Thompson. The three administrators included, Phillip Parr, Dwight Mosley and Elbert Yaworsky. School board member, Theresa Colaizzi is supports King’s decision and the idea of eliminating costs in order to focus on the success of students.

headline: State-trooper charged in home break-in, assualt
abstract: Two state troopers from Susquehanna County turned themselves in to the Gibson barracks on charges of burglary, criminal trespass, simple assault, harassment, and conspiracy. The troopers assaulted an individual at his home on Saturday at 2a.m, only one has been suspended without pay as the investigation continues.

headline: Comcast's season for a rate hike
abstract: Comcast Corporation reported that it will raise the basic cable rates approximately 6% on average nationwide  for the coming year.  However, Comcast did say it would not raise the rates for digital cable or its high-speed Internet service.  A recent Federal Communications Commission study found that many customers might benefit if they bought channels individually as opposed to a packaged set of channels according to Kevin Martin, the commission chairman.

headline: State GOP begins watching 3 gubernatorial contenders
abstract: The chances of campaign success for 3 gubernatorial hopefuls, former PA Lt. Governor Bill Scranton, PA State Senator Jeffrey Piccola, and former Pittsburgh Steelers Hall of Fame wide receiver Lynn Swann, is being reviewed by the PA GOP.  The PA voters and PA GOP leaders view all of the contenders for the 2006 Republican gubernatorial nomination as not having an advantage yet. A Quinnipiac College poll shows all three losing to Governor Rendell by roughly similar margins.

headline: Sales tax bill fizzles
abstract: Lawmakers headed home for a Thanksgiving break without passage in either chamber of a bill to reduce property taxes, a goal Republican legislative leaders had hoped to achieve before the holiday. Democrats believe using revenue from a tax on slot-machine gambling would be the first step toward cutting property taxes.

headline: School board opts out of Act 72
abstract: Bellefonte Area, State College, Phillipsburg-Osceola and Penns Valley Area school districts have all voted this month to not use Act 72, which is a property tax relief program touted by PA Governor Ed Rendell.  The legislation plans to use the revenue from the slot machines within the state to reduce property taxes in the participating districts.  Justin Houser, school board member, claims there are too many questions left unanswered about the program, and many school directors do not support the effect on the school budget process and long-term financial planning for the schools.

headline: Suit: Home alarm sales crossed state's 'no call' line
abstract: Kenneth Broda, owner of Guardian Alert and Advanced Concepts, is being accused of breaking Pennsylvania's Do Not Call law, which protects those households whose number appears on a list that blocks telemarketers' calls.  The lawsuit in Monroe County Court will be seeking $1,000 per violation and $3,000 if the violation was against a consumer older than 59.

headline: Earthlink exec is sky-high on Philly
abstract: Donald Berryman has big dreams for Wireless Philadelphia. He sees a city where people can jump onto the Internet, anywhere, free in some spats and for a low price elsewhere, using a variety of different internet companies. Even where parking meters can tattle on drivers that failed to pay their quarters. EarthLink will be in charge of building a $10 million to $15 million high-speed wireless network throughout Philadelphia. EarthLink was selected to build, maintain and manage the network.

headline: State GOP joins critics of pay raise
abstract: PA Representative John Perzel spoke in front of the Republican State Committee to defend the legislative pay raises that have caused a lot of criticism from local officials and citizens alike.  He claimed that he was poor when he was first elected and that he is not ashamed to accept a pay raise to increase his salary to $145,000.  Both the Lebanon County Democratic Committee and the Lancaster County Republican Committee have passed resolutions that publicly condemn the pay raise.

headline: Sallie Mae gets cold shoulder
abstract: Legislators must soon allocate the 2005-06 PA budget, full of tough decisions because of an unexpected loss in federal aid. Sallie Mae has offered the State $500 million up front, with the rest, totaling $1 billion, over the next five years for the PA Higher Education Assistance Agency. PHEAA rejected the offer, saying it would reduce competition for loans and result in higher borrowing costs. The state faces millions in cuts to welfare, but even PA Governor Ed Rendell is not planning to push the deal. Talk has been quiet since the offer, leading many to believe it is no longer viable.

headline: School money in the wrong place
abstract: A person writes to the newspaper to complain about the tutoring program required by the federal No Child Left  Behind Act. Tutors are paid $45 an hour, are not required to have a college degree, work with only one student at a time, and are not required to pass a background check. Teachers do have college degrees, work with many students at a time, and are required to pass a background check, but only make about $30 an hour on average.

headline: Supreme Court ruling in child-welfare case gives primacy to wrong interests
abstract: The authors think that the lowers courts in PA were right and the state Supreme Court made a serious error when the PA Supreme Court denied the parents of a child who was killed by a babysitter in Allentown access to state records in the case. The Supreme Court reversed two earlier reviews by Lehigh County courts and the Commonwealth Court that said the parents of Andrew Jonathan Wagner should be able to see certain records.

headline: Radio Activity
abstract: KYW-AM 1060 has upgraded to digital radio, announcing it will let four engineers go this week.

headline: State House Leadership Pledges 'No New Taxes'
abstract: The Republicans who control the PA House of Representatives and the PA Senate got to work quickly after the swearing in of new legislators by addressing new legislation that does not necessarily coincide with the agenda laid out by Democratic PA Governor Ed Rendell.  House Majority Leader Sam Smith claims that he wants to phase out the Capital Stock and Franchise Tax, reform the civil justice system and deregulation.  He also reportedly wants to introduce educational, health care and environmental reforms in his program called Put Pennsylvania Back on Course.

headline: State budget blues ahead
abstract: PA Senator Ted Erickson warned of pressure on the legislative budget at a Delco Chamber of Commerce event. PA Rep. William Adolph joined him. Growing Greener, a ballot initiative, was discussed along with Act 72, a property tax reform act. School districts must decide by the end of the month whether or not to opt in to Act 72, under which property taxes may be reduced in favor of higher income taxes and slots revenue. Future property tax increases would be subject to voter referendum. PA Rep. Greg Vitali is against both bills, while PA Sen. Connie Williams supports them.

headline: School programs aim to give kids financial literacy
abstract: Banks and schools are starting programs to teach children about finances so that they can learn to be fiscally responsible.

headline: Tearful Rendell pays respects to slain soldiers
abstract: Nathaniel Detample  and three other Pennsylvania Army National Guard soldiers were killed when their armored patrol vehicle was attacked by insurgents in Bayji. PA Governor Edward Rendell ordered that state flags throughout PA be flown at half-staff until September 11th. State flags are typically flown at half-staff in countries in which fallen soldiers live but Rendell said that the number of deaths of Pennsylvania Guardsmen is “an enormous tragedy.”

headline: Santorum's bill could rain on National Weather Service
abstract: United States Senator Rick Santorum is proposing a bill that would prevent the National Weather Service from competing with private weather forecasting companies like State College's AccuWeather. United States Senator Bill Nelson said this would mean the end of websites that post weather forecasts.

headline: State House of Representatives Oks bill to sell former prison
abstract: Pa Representative William Deweese reported that the PA House of Representatives is allowing the sale of the State Correctional Institution at Waynesburg to a private company  for $990,000 who will reuse the former prison as a school for at-risk students.  He also claimed that it will now produce tax revenues for the local government and produce jobs as well.  The bill is now going to be voted on by the PA Senate and then sent to PA Governor Ed Rendell for his signature.

headline: State house leadership Pledges no new taxes
abstract: This article is about the new agenda of the Pennsylvania state assembly as senators and representatives came in for the swear-in ceremony. The legislature plans to reform the state's economic troubles, as well as advances in education and enviornmental protection. In addition to all of this, the legislature promises not to raise taxes and institute real health-care reform.

headline: School's Latino students to get mentors
abstract: Congreso de Latinos Unidos has received a three-year grant for $395,839 from the U.S. Department of Education to run the new mentoring programs for students in the Philadelphia School District. The program will pair about 70 mentors with students from Julia de Burgos School. The goal is to improve academic performance.

headline: Too many prison inmates, too few guards
abstract: The PA Senate and House have introduced identical bills proposing a minimum number of staff members to man every prison post.  Roy Pinto, Vice President of the PA Corrections Officers Association said prisons are overcrowded in PA, while Susan McNaughton, Press Secretary for the State Department of Corrections says they are fully staffed.  The state Department of Corrections opposes the bill, and the PSCOA finds that the legislation doesn't create new jobs, but ensures every position funded in the budget is filled.

headline: $52 bite can hurt workers
abstract: In Chambersburg, PA, local residents and workers are upset about the introduction of the new $52 municpal services tax to be taken out of worker's paychecks. Many workers are concerned that the amount is way too high and may actually do more harm than good because of consumers loss in buying power.

headline: State legislatures moving to address end-of-life issues
abstract: State Senator Stewart J. Greenleaf is trying to revive legislation previously vetoed by Governor Ed Rendell that would determine who has the right to make medical decisions for a dying patient who doesn't have a living will.

headline: State outlines medical cutbacks
abstract: Gov. Rendell's recently announced budget doesn't raise taxes, but it could still cost Luzerne County and many of its poorer residents more money, and will limit their access to 18 outpatient services and two inpatient procedures per year. Assuming the legislature approves the budget, the biggest changes will affect PA residents who get medical assistance from the government.

headline: Schools upbeat despite AYP drop
abstract: According to the PA Department of Education, only 2,311 schools in Philadelphia met the targets set by the No Child Left Behind act as compared to 2,388 schools from last year.  Ted Kirsch, president of the Philadelphia Federation of Teachers,  attributed the Annual Yearly Progress decline to an increase in the standards because he reported that test scores actually have gone up.  Amy Hodges Slamp of the PA Education Department claimed that more federal funding is needed for the state while the US Department of Education said federal funding is increased this year and should not be used as an excuse.

headline: Traffic Court's president judge to step down
abstract: Francis Kelly, president judge of Philadelphia Traffic Court, said that he planned to retire to join a lobbying and consulting firm in Plymouth Meeting. Gov. Rendell will choose a new president judge. Two traffic court judges. Thomasine Tynes and Bernice DeAngelis are considered the leading candidates.

headline: 200 rally against taxes at Capitol
abstract: An anti-tax rally was held at the Capitol. The main speaker was radio host Bob Durgin, who called Governor Ed Rendell a "socialist who hates capitalism". Several Pennsylvania lawmakers attended, and six spoke. Only one Democrat legislator spoke, state House Minority Whip Mike Veon. Durgin criticized Veon for the use of state taxes to fund public transportation.

headline: State Rep. Kotik joins race for Wagner's state Senate seat
abstract: Auditor General Jack Wagner vacated his South Hills Senate seat. PA state Representative Kotik will face County Councilman Wayne Fontana, Jeff Woodard, and Frank Oiglioui in a race for the Democratic nomination for the South Hills Senate seat. Winner will face state Representative Michael Diven, in a May 27 special election.

headline: Symphony still faces fiscal woes
abstract: The Pittsburgh Symphony announced an increase in 2004-5 subscription sales over 2003-4, but overall ticket sales did not meet budget projections for increased revenue. The difference between projected and actual ticket sales is contributing to possibly a $500,000 shortfall for the fiscal year.

headline: Scranton aims to close student achievement gap
abstract: Scranton High School is using an honors program for minorities and grade-level teacher teams to combat achievement gaps. High school teachers, district and school administrators, city officials and educators with the Northeastern Educational Intermediate Unit participated in a PA Achievement Gap Effort trip to a Florida high school to observe its methods. Now, the district is working on implementing some of these and others to close its own gap. Fred Rosetti, executive director of the NEIU, noted the school's four day week and remedial day on has improved performance.

headline: Traffic Court's president judge to step down
abstract: Francis Kelly, president of Philadelphia Traffic Court will retire, effective March 3, to join the Egan Bloom Consulting Group. Governor Rendell will choose a new president judge.

headline: 5 of 6 lawmakers return extra pay
abstract: PA Senators Noah Wenger, Gibson E. Armstrong and David Brightbill and PA Representatives Gibson C. Armstrong and Roy Baldwin have all returned the pay raises they received while PA Representative Michael Sturla has reported that his pay raise will be given to charities.  Sturla is a 14-year incumbent who possibly will have to run against Republican Keith Charles in the upcoming general election where the pay raise will be a major issue.  While Sturla claims other pay raises have not set off as much controversy, Charles said that by giving the money to charity Sturla is still able to use tax write-offs.

headline: State Rep. Kotik joins race for Wagner's state Senate seat
abstract: State Rep. Nick Kotik will face county Councilman Wayne Fontana and two other Democrats in the race for the Democratic nomination for he South Hills Senate seat vacated by Auditor General Jack Wagner. Kotik was a surprise entry as the filing deadline passed for the nomination which will be determined Sunday among Democratic committee members from the district.

headline: Survey: Employers remain cautious about hiring
abstract: According to a Manpower Employment Outlook Survey, 21% of employers plan to hire in the upcoming quarter, which is the same as the past two quarters of the year.  The survey is based off of 16,000 US companies, and the results display caution in the employers' hiring plans and outlook on the economy.

headline: Senators again want to rally around the flag
abstract: PA State Senators James Rhoades and Jeffrey Piccola have introduced legislation requiring the Pledge of Allegiance or singing of the national anthem in Pennsylvania’s public schools. This bill marks the third time such legislation was introduced since post September 11, 2001. The ACLU is opposed the bills. Larry Frankel, a spokesman for the ACLU questions the rights of teachers who under the mandate must lead their students in reciting the Pledge of Allegiance or singing of the national anthem.

headline: Troopers in Philadelphia
abstract: The editorial board approves of an agreement made during a budget session to deploy state troopers to patrol the interstate highways in Philadelphia.  The board hopes it will allow more local police to help prevent rising violent crime in the city.

headline: 500G in hand, consultant to continue to keep an eye on state police
abstract: Kroll Associates, an international security firm, will continue to oversee the PA State Police indefinitely as a consultant, Gov. Rendell said. Kate Philips, Rendell's spokeswoman, said Kroll's exact role or how much the firm will be paid has yet to be determined. The state police are welcoming Kroll's experience.

headline: State sues U.S. over Guard deactivation at Willow Grove
abstract: PA will sue the federal government to stop the Air National Guard Unit at Willow Grove Naval Air Station from being closed.  According to Governor Ed Rendell, he did not approve the closing, and the constitution mandates that the state governor consents to a closing of a National Guard unit.

headline: Take dramatic action in response to Act 72
abstract: A concerned resident applauds an opinion editorial by East Penn School Board member Chuck Ballard for his views against Act 72. In light of PA Governor Ed Rendell's recent threats to make the legislation mandatory, the resident urges voters to vote against him in the next election. He is certain the legacy of Rendell and the Legislature that enacted Act 72 will be higher property taxes and higher income taxes.

headline: Seven districts head back without teacher contracts
abstract: School boards in Cheltenham and six other school districts in PA suburbs have not reached accords with local unions and it is causing anxiety in school districts, because of the possibility of a strike.

headline: Vallas' brother pushes Ill. Race
abstract: Philadelphia schools chief Paul Vallas says he will not return to Chicago to make another run at the governorship in 2006, despite younger brother Dean Vallas' efforts to change residency requirements. Illinois law states that candidates must have been residents for three years prior to running, however Paul changed his legal residency to Philadelphia. He is committed to Philadelphia, saying he will fulfill his five year contract which runs out in 2007, and may even stay longer.

headline: 7 more judges sue to reinstate their pay raises
abstract: Seven lower court judges joined two other judges who are petitioning the PA Supreme Court to reinstate pay raises passed by the PA Legislature as they contend they violated the state constitution by voting to repeal the pay raise bill.    Chief Justice Ralph J. Cappy has removed himself from ruling on the issue as there is a conflict of interest.  Bruce Ledewitz, law expert at Duquesne University, contests that this obvious conflict of interest exists but there is no other way to decide the case.

headline: State watchdog
abstract: A legal dispute between then-State Auditor General Robert Casey Jr. and then-Treasurer Barbara Hafer has been settled. An independent consultant will review Pennsylvania's two largest pension funds and the Auditor General's Office will be allowed to review their various processes and the selection of investment managers.

headline: Tax breaks net some lawmakers thousands
abstract: A little-known tax break specifically for legislators can allow them to save thousands of dollars. The federal tax code allows legislators who live more than 50 miles from the Capitol a $141 tax deduction for each day they are in legislative session or attending a committee meeting. They also get a tax break when they are home, provided that no more the four days pass between legislative business days.

headline: smaller high school plan has its draws
abstract: Philadelphia students and education activists said they are big on small high schools, but they want to be more involved in school plans to create 28 scaled-down schools by 2008. School district officials envision that the schools will feature enhanced academic offerings such as college prep curriculums, honors, and advanced placements courses, smaller classes and university partners.

headline: Warrant signed for execution
abstract: PA Governor Edward Rendell signed a warrant for the execution by lethal injection of the Maryland man convicted in June 1996 shooting in Carlisle. The PA state Supreme Court upheld Antyane Robinson’s first-degree murder conviction and death sentence.

headline: 911th base argues against closing
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell is optimistic that the 911th Military Airlift Wing in Moon Township will make a convincing case to the Pentagon's Base Realignment and Closure Commission after he received briefings from Retired Air Force General Lloyd Newtown.  The Air Force estimates that the closing of this base will eliminate over 300 jobs and cost the local economy approximately $93.6 million a year.  Both Rendell and officials have criticized the Pentagon for miscalculating that the 911th only has room for 10 C-130s whereas it actually has enough room for up to 18.

headline: system not working, legislature raises show
abstract: The author is writing about the PA Legislature’s pay raise that was passed for the year. She uses the example of her husband, who works for the Philadelphia Fire Department, and how even after being injured he has not been given that kind of raise.

headline: Tax collectors
abstract: The effectiveness of the current PA tax collection system is questioned. Rather than outsource tax collection to several local agencies, a smaller more modern system could save more than $100 million. The use of state-of-the-art technology, including increased computerization and the internet, could make filing taxes easier and more cost efficient.

headline: Smaller high school plan has its draws
abstract: The Philadelphia School district plans to create 28 small high schools by 2008 in order to improve academic results, graduates and school management. The district plans to hire and partner with 4 companies that will provide technical assistance to the transitioning of high schools. Philadelphia students welcome smaller schools but are skeptical of the four companies role in the process. Meg Wise, of the nonprofit Philadelphia Education Fund says smaller schools can be a success, but its important that everyone involved in the process--students, parents, teachers and neighbors—work together.

headline: What to believe?
abstract: This editorial does not agree with Cumberland Valley High School's new discipline policy that is solely useful to deter drug use but not catch drug users.  It claims that teenagers need more consistent adult attitudes and influences to help teach good behavior rather than just suspensions from extracurricular activities.

headline: A plea to my brethren: Don't sell out our profession
abstract: John Baer, columnist for the Philadelphia Daily News, comments on the new trend of journalists who receive money from the federal government to promote their policies.  He feels these people, such as Armstrong Williams and Maggie Gallagher, are ruining the profession and committing a terrible crime.  The solution he says is to make sure every employee at the media outlets clearly review and sign a code of ethics for journalists to ensure they are clear about not accepting money from the government to write promotional articles.

headline: Street: Mariano should quit if convicted
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Street calls on Councilman Rick Mariano to resign from his position if  convicted of federal crimes.  The city is paying Mariano's attorney fees, but Street said it's up to City Solicitor Romulo Diaz to decide how long it lasts.  PA's Right to Know Act requires public agencies to make public any "account, voucher, or contract," involving tax payer money.

headline: Tax Collectors
abstract: The Governor's School for Local Government Services found that local taxes are collected in an inefficient manner that costs taxpayers up to $100 million, and that consolidated state tax collection is the most efficient and fair option. The editorial board urges Governor Ed Rendell to work with Republican state legislators to appoint a task force with the purpose of finding a solution.

headline: State approves district's plans
abstract: Superintendent of Shippensburg Area School District Jacqueline Lesney has reported that the PA Department of Education has approved the finances and design for three elementary school projects.  The three projects include renovating Nancy Grayson and James Burd elementary schools while constructing a new school for fourth and fifth-graders at a grand cost of $18 million.  The improvement plans for the middle and senior high schools of Shippensburg have to be submitted to the PA Department of Education because each school contains student groups who did not meet the No Student Left Behind requirements.

headline: Youth violence draws Senate's eye
abstract: US Senator Arlen Specter has publicly claimed the country, exemplified by Philadelphia, is in a crisis of youth and gang violence as the Senate Judiciary Committee will hold a field hearing in the city on Monday.  The hearing came from discussions between Specter and Philadelphia School District's chief executive Paul Vallas and will include law enforcement and other public officials.  Specter's main concern is to ensure that $160 million a year in federal funding for youth anti-violence programs is being put to the best use.

headline: A private tie for a powerful duo
abstract: A conversation between Delaware River Port Authority Chairman Manuel N. Stamatakis and lawyer Ronald A. White was picked up by an FBI bug placed in White's office.  It found that Stamatakis had been paying another DRPA commissioner and publisher of the Philadelphia Tribune, Bob Bogle, up to $10,000 a month.  He says the fees are paid for advice on "minority matters."  The fees raise questions regarding the fact that the men are on public boards but are dealing in private (DRPA's chairman, Governor Ed Rendell was unaware), the fact that Stamatakis has a city hall contract, and that Bogle must report his income on the State Ethics Commission forms, and he did not include this income.

headline: Street's response: 'Deeply saddened'
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Street said he was "deeply" saddened by the conviction of former city treasurer Corey Kemp for selling his public office. Street used the occasion to champion bills he introduced in City Council which would restrict outside employment by city officials and ban nepotism in city government. Street later attended a Democratic City Committee meeting celebrating the birthday of PA Rep. Bob Brady and upcoming primary elections. Executive Director of the Committee of 70, Zack Stalberg, said the convictions call for an overhaul of city contracting and campaign finance reform.

headline: Tax plan workable
abstract: PA State Representative Samuel Rohrer is writing about PA State Revenue Secretary Gregory Fajt seeing the deficiencies in the Commonwealth Caucus’ Plan for PA’s Future, but he believes that his concerns are unfounded. Rohrer says that two nationally recognized economics firms looked at the plan and they concluded that it does work and would produce significant gains for PA. He says that the plan will eliminate all school property taxes and that it will create something great for the people of PA.

headline: State approves district's plans
abstract: The PA department of education approved an $18 million school project for the Shippensburg area school district to construct and improve three elementary schools.

headline: 213th guard unit from Allentown gets down to business
abstract: 140 troops from the 213th Area Support Group Headquarters Company, a PA National Guard unit from Allentown, has been taking care of the citizens near St. Charles Parish in New Orleans after Hurricane Katrina has wiped out parts of the city.  The 213th is working with the Federal Emergency Management Agency among other groups to collect and distribute supplies such as ice, water, fuel and food to other neighboring parishes.  They are also are providing logistics to troops in an eight-county region called Zephyr Task Force.

headline: Baker Knoll opponents have baggage of their own
abstract: This is an article about the coming governor election in Pennsylvania. The office of governor is not under conversation but rather that of the Lt. Gov (equivalent of the vice president) which is now enjoyed by Catherine Baker Knoll. Despite her problems- frequent gaffes, her exclusion form government decisions, and her personal office choices relying heavily on her son who lives in Washington DC, the author believes there is a 60-40 chance she will stay on the ticket. The remainder of the article discusses other potential candidates and what they have to offer.

headline: Summer heat no match for Middle Smithfield race
abstract: Republican candidate for the Middle Smithfield supervisor seat, Scott Shaller, recently sent a pledge for his Democratic opponent, Joseph Rybandt, to sign to promise to run a clean election campaign based on the issues and free of personal attacks.  Rybant does not plan to sign it as he feels there is a hidden agenda behind the pledge.  Schaller defeated incumbent Fred May Republican nomination while Rybant ran unopposed for the Democratic seat.

headline: Tax reform
abstract: The PA Chamber of Business and Industry will create its own proposal for tax reform about 2 months after PA Governor Ed Rendell proposed cutting the corporate net income tax rate by 30%.  The corporate net income tax rate of 9.99% is the third-highest in the nation currently.  The chamber's proposal wants to cut government spending by eliminating redundancies and use the savings in order to lower business taxes.

headline: State College school district set to raise taxes by 5.6%
abstract: The State College Area School District is raising property taxes by 5.6%.

headline: A call for change echoes around the globe
abstract: Twenty years after the original Live Aid concert, organized by Bob Geldof, was held, the Live 8 concert was put on, to try to convince leaders at the G8 summit to aid Africa. Ten concerts went on around the world with performers such as Madonna, U2, Pink Floyd, and Paul McCartney.

headline: Base closings not always bad
abstract: The article cites a situation in Aurora, Colorado, in which two military bases closed down, but provided for the opening of new businesses and jobs.  Willow Grove, PA faces the same problems, and Governor Ed Rendell  with US Senators Arlen Specter and Rick Santorum are attempting to keep it open.

headline: Swann to declare candidacy after Sugar Bowl
abstract: Lynn Swann, former Pittsburgh Steeler and current college football commentator for ABC Sports, plans to declare his candidacy for governor on January 4th after the Sugar Bowl airs on television.  Many consider Swann and former Lieutenant Governor Bill Scranton the leaders for the Republican nomination despite other challengers including PA Senate Majority Whip Jeffrey Piccola and Jim Panyard, former CEO of the Pennsylvania Manufacturers' Association.

headline: Tax Tip
abstract: This editorial argues that the Pennsylvania government relies too heavily on raising taxes as a solution to a majority of its problems.  The Taxpayers Network ranked PA in 30th place as its residents paid $888.43 per capita in property taxes in 2001-2002.  The solution it proposes is to stop raising taxes to make the business environment more competitive and increase the leadership within Harrisburg.

headline: State defines Charter Schools
abstract: Charter Schools in Erie and Millcreek will be operating outside the intent of the state, according to a new document released by the PA Department of Education. The document specifies that charter school students must be educated in buildings separate from those used in the school district or in a completely separate part of an existing school building.

headline: Buck-passing
abstract: This editorial complains about every level of government's constant struggle to find more money for social service programs, especially in Pennsylvania where all of the social services are delivered through the county governments.  To worsen the problem, the editorial states how almost all areas of society are looking to cut taxes somehow, whether it be property tax, corporate tax or income tax.  Its solution is to restructure how social services are administered in the state so that the county and state are working more efficiently.

headline: Base panel starts its grueling process
abstract: The first of series of hearings to be conducted by the Base Realignment and Closure Commission was held yesterday. Based on its findings, the Pentagon will begin another round of base closures which many, including lobbyists and congressional aides, believe will include bases in the communities of Carlisle and Chambersburg. The Northeast-Midwest Institute noted those states have lost 41 percent of their military personal since 1988 due to base closings, PA being hit hardest. The Government Accountability Office revealed 85 percent of bases listed for closure actually survive.

headline: Tax reform plan deserves support
abstract: State Rep Samuel Rohrer and his allies need everyone's support in their effort to reform school property taxes across the state. Thursday evening. Rohrer explained a package of legislation he is sponsoring to a crowd of 375 gathered at the Blue Mountain Middle School. Although he is confident that his measures have enough support in the state House of Representatives to pass, he is less certain of the Senate and worried about Gov. Ed Rendell's opposition and his possession of the bully pulpit. He asks voters across the commonwealth to write their elected officials and press them to implement these changes.

headline: Unemployment rate increases slightly
abstract: The normal winter decline in construction and other outdoor jobs contributed to a .5% increase in the area's seasonally adjusted unemployment in December.

headline: State defines charter schools
abstract: The PA Department of Education have revised the Basic Education Circular, which in turn, has changed the definition of charter schools and affects the battle between Erie and Millcreek school districts.  The new change to the definition states that charter school students have to be educated in a separate building from the school district buildings, and out-of-district student tuition, $6,800 a year, has to be paid by the student's home district.  Erie School District will end up paying $1.5 million for its students attending the charter school in Millcreek Township School District and is challenging this law to Erie County Judge John A. Bozza.

headline: Care home closed for state probe into death
abstract: Annville Personal Care Home remains closed while the state Department of Public Welfare and law enforcement officials probe the death of a resident, Nancy Orlosky,  Oct. 17, as well as allegations regarding the home's operation. Her cause f death is unknown and is being thoroughly investigated.

headline: Beer drinkers hoist mugs to Sunday sales as some distributors offer boos
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell signed legislation allowing beer distributors to be open from noon to 5pm on Sundays.  Many consumers are pleased but some beer sellers, like Mike Gentis, aren't pleased with losing their only day off.

headline: Taxpayers to protest pay raises
abstract: Protestors are expected to arrive at the state Capitol today to protest the 16-54% pay raise that the legislators approved for themselves and another government officials.  Russ Diamond, who organized the event, said the goal of the rally is build support for bills that would repeal or reduce the pay raises as well as being symbolic - to show the strength of the anti-pay raise movement.  PA Representative Pete Daley and Mike Young, Harrisburg pollster, believe that if the turn out is low then it will be very disastrous for the movement.

headline: Unemployment rate increases slightly
abstract: The normal winter decline in jobs resulted in a .05% increase in the unemployment rate. According to Walter Nichols, an analyst with the Pennsylvania Department of Labor and Industry, the unemployment rate only increased by two-tenths of a percent, which could of resulted from the function of rounding.

headline: State looks into Santorum's case for good reason
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Education is scheduling a hearing to question if the U.S. Senator Rick Santorum should reimburse the Penn Hills School District $100,000 for the tuition they assumed was going towards Santorum’s 5 children’s cyber charter school education. Santorum owns a residence in the Penn Hills School District and believes his children are entitled to an education within the districts borders. Some within the District believe they should only have to pay if the children actually live within the districts borders.

headline: CareerLink helps victims of hurricane
abstract: Gulf Coast hurricane victims visiting the Keystone State can turn to PA's CareerLink offices for some relief. CareerLink offices throughout the state, including Pottsville and Tamaqua, are prepared to help displaced residents with some basic services, like finding food, shelter and medical benefits; along with filing unemployment claims and replacing Social Security cards or driver's license, just to name a few of the services offered. Last month, Gov. Ed Rendell designated the Department of Labor & Industry's statewide system of Career Link offices as a point of access for state agency services to aid Hurricane Katrina evacuees in PA.

headline: Best left alone / State contract bids should be opened in public
abstract: This editorial encourages PA Governor Ed Rendell and the PA Department of General Services to not award contracts behind closed doors because of potential problems such as degree of union labor, amount of campaign contributions and type of political connections.  It uses the construction for the Petersen Events Center as an example, where its initial price was $35 million but grew to $119 million despite state officials not being able to determine precisely why.  The editorial states that the administration's "Best Value" method is not the most ethical way and the public, lowest responsible bidder method should be applied for all projects.

headline: The legislative pay raise: A public shafting
abstract: The editorial board calls the legislative pay raise bill that was passed "despicable." It lists the House and Senate members who voted for the bill, dubbing it the "Roll Call of Shame."

headline: Unemployment tumbles
abstract: According to a report by the Center for Workforce Information and Analysis, Schuylkill County's unemployment rate fell from 6.4% to 5.4% from March to April.  The sectors that particularly benefited were construction, trade, transportation, professional and business services and educational and health services.  The unemployment rate nationally was 5.2% while Pennsylvania's state rate is 4.9%.

headline: State looks into Santorum's case for good reason
abstract: US Sen. Rick Santorum and his children are immersed  in controversial enrollment in a Pennsylvania cyber charter school. His situation raises questions that deserve answers.. The Dept. of Education is looking into whether or not Santorum should reimburse some or all of the $100,000 it paid to the cyber charter school that educated five of his children for years until November.

headline: Live 8 Redux
abstract: Joe Conclin was not granted ad lib opportunities at the Live 8 Concert, while Josh Groban visited Old City club 32 degrees.

headline: Blaum to move on
abstract: PA Representative Kevin Blaum, after 26 years in the PA House of Representatives, plans to retire from his post in order to dedicate more time to his wife and family.  His most prized accomplishment that people remember him for his ability to raise the funding and support for the construction of the Wachovia Arena in Casey Plaza.  His loss in the legislature will decrease the influence of the Wilkes-Barre area as he held a lot of influence with both PA Governor Ed Rendell and former Governor Robert Casey.

headline: The lt. gov.'s court-martial III
abstract: The writer of the letter stated that Lt. Governor Catherine-Baker Knoll handed out business cards at her father-in-law's funeral-home viewing, which the author found to be in very poor taste.

headline: 'We're gonna fire them'
abstract: Residents are angry that the PA Legislature has accumulated operating money that it doesn’t spend, but could have been used to offset shortages in the PA state budget when PA Governor Edward Rendell and the PA Legislature raised income taxes in 2004. This coupled with the high pay raises is making many angry with the PA Legislature because they are not handling the money well. The editors note that many would like to see the spending of the Department of Public Welfare go to schools or roads, this is why people elect representatives and senators, to make budget choices.

headline: State to rule on Santorum school costs
abstract: The PA Department of Education will hold a hearing to determine whether U.S. Senator Rick Santorum will have to repay the Penn Hills School District for the $100,000 tuition it spent on a cyber charter school for five of his children.

headline: Medicaid crucial for children
abstract: A woman writes in to the newspaper to criticize Governor Ed Rendell's proposed changes to how much financial assistance families with disabled children will receive. The legislature decided that the income of the parents should not determine how much of the child's medical care will be covered, but Rendell now wants to implement a sliding-scale system.

headline: Blood pressure rises along with lawmakers' pay
abstract: The author of the letter criticizes the legislative pay raise, while others suffer economically.

headline: The Meakem factor
abstract: The editorial board feels that former Lt. Governor Bill Scranton naming Free Markets founder Glen Meakem as his campaign manager was a wise decision and will help him beat Governor Ed Rendell in the upcoming election.

headline: A heated dispute
abstract: Liz Sessions, a moth o four-handicapped children, recently found out that she is responsible for a $2,000 UGI Utilities (a natural gas provider) bill, run up by her husband before he was sent to prison. Sessions points out that the UGI bill insert explaining a new state law, known as Chapter 14, said nothing about being held responsible for a boyfriends bill, incurred on his account, before she moved in with him. She wants to fight the new law.

headline: state to rule on Santorum school costs
abstract: The state Department of Education will hold a hearing to determine whether US Sen. Rick Santorum must repay a school district for tuition it spent on a cyber school for five of his children. He withdrew his children from the PA Cyber Charter school after officials in the Penn Hills School District questioned why they spent $100,000 on tuition for the senator's children since 2001, even though they spend most of the year in Santorum's Virginia home.

headline: Santorum seeks Social Security step
abstract: US Senator Rick Santorum plans to introduce the Social Security Act of 2005 this week, which would protect current benefits for those older than 2005.  He expressed concern for senior citizens who are worried that attempts to strengthen Social Security for younger workers could decrease their own benefits.  US Senator Charles Grassley, Finance Committee chairman, has not directly commented on the proposal.

headline: Campaign targets pay raise supporters
abstract: A conservative group, The Young Conservatives of Pennsylvania, are running radio ads targeting state Senate President Pro Tempore Robert c. Jubelirer because they are seeking repeal of lawmakers’ pay raises. The pay-raise backlash has prompted two more lawmakers to join about a dozen others who voted for it to reconsider collecting unvouchered expenses.

headline: The New Emmission Standards
abstract: Question and answer segment outlining the new standards. They take place 2008, only apply to new vehicles causing them to become more expensive.

headline: Bacteria blamed in deaths of 4 who used abortion pill
abstract: The US Food and Drug Administration as well as the New England Journal of Medicine are investigating the death of four young California women who were using the abortion pill Milfeprex also known as RU-486.  US Senator Jim DeMint introduced the RU-486 Suspension and Review Act in March after a California girl died of a sordelli infection due to the pill.  Scientists and doctors are unsure as to why certain girls are more susceptible to bacterial infections and others are not.

headline: Student loan money shouldn't go for bonuses
abstract: The Pennsylvania Higher education Assistance Agency is the latest organization to envy the private-sector because of the six-figure bonuses PHEAA administrators gave themselves. The PHEAA handles student loans and it manages a $120 million budget that includes upfront costs for student loans, covering loan forgiveness for members of armed forces and supplementing state money for student grants. The PA state House Appropriations Committee plans to investigate PHEAA’s finances and the author believes that this is good.

headline: To serve on council on aging
abstract: Mary Erwine, president of Erwin Health Services, was appointed o serve on the PA Council on Aging by PA Governor Edward Rendell and the state Senate. The PA Council on Aging acts as an advisor to the governor and the Department of Aging on planning, coordination and delivery of services to older people.

headline: Capitol Notes: Those lazy, crazy, fund-raisy days of summer, Pot vs. Kettle and more…
abstract: This article discusses the recent events and proposed legislation within the state government and lists the schedule for the rest of the month of June.  It also tells about the state felony charges against PA Representative Jeff Habay and the feud between PA Representative Mike Turzai and the group Citizens for Consumer Justice over Turzai's legislative package Empower PA, which makes it more difficult for consumers to sue manufacturers.  It also lists how PA Governor Ed Rendell named Reverend Loran Mann to the Pennsylvania Public Television Network commission and PA Agriculture Secretary Dennis Wolff's statement that the state reached 300,000 acres of preserved farmland.

headline: The political mixes with the personal
abstract: The release of Philadelphia Mayor Street and his family’s financial documents shows that Street is prone to mixing the political and personal with Philadelphia’s business. The newly released documents includes transcripts of wiretaps and e-mails between Mayor Street and Ronald D. White, Street’s chief fundraiser who died in November while awaiting trial.

headline: Black vendors outraged over Live 8 merchandising fees
abstract: 40 African-American men protested outside City Hall in Philadelphia over what they saw as Mayor Street's administration's lack of concern about the small amount of opportunities for black business owners.  Their main concern was the government's decision to tack on a $750 to $1,500 fee to sell Live 8 merchandise at the concert, and their not allowing vendors to use JFK Plaza for selling merchandise.  Joseph Grace, spokesman for the mayor, claimed that they don't see the fees as unfair and also need the plaza for crowd control during the event.

headline: Student loan rate will rise Friday
abstract: Keith New reported that the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency is busier than usual as interest rates on unsubsidized federal Stafford loans will increase from 3.36% to 5.3%, on Stafford loans for the in-school grace period from 2.77% to 4.7% and for the Parent Loans for Undergraduate Students from 4.17% to 6.1%.  New also said that the US Department of Education ruled that current students who borrowed can consolidate their loans now to capitalize on the lower rates.  Last year, PHEAA processed $3.1 billion in loan consolidation, and in this month of June alone, they have already processed $2 billion.

headline: United Way set to plead for funds
abstract: The United Way of Lackawanna County will make its case to state and federal officials as it pushes for additional government funding to help low-income residents pay their winter heating bills. Last week, Gov. Ed Rendell called on state lawmakers to add $15 million to the state's Low Income Heating Energy Assistance Program. 2

headline: Capitol pay raise is just part of a hefty package
abstract: The article outlines the recently passed legislative pay raise package.  The package benefits the legislature, Judges, and Governor Ed Rendell, along with some cabinet members.  The article goes on to describe lack of public support, and some lawmakers such as Representative Daryl Metcalfe voted against it.

headline: The political mixes with the personal
abstract: When the Eagles' new stadium opened in 2003, Mayor Street made sure two seats in the city's box were guaranteed for two of his sons before the rest were doled out for campaign contributions. He is now under investigation for corruption by the federal government.

headline: Cortes expected at Amani festival
abstract: PA Secretary of the Commonwealth, Pedro Cortes, PA’s first Latino Cabinet member, will attend the Amani Festival in Carlisle, PA. The festival celebrates multiculturalism and the elimination of racism.

headline: Study: City school has Pa.'s highest rate of violence
abstract: The PA Education Department has reported that the Fort Pitt Elementary School in Garfield has the highest rate of violence at 384.2 incidents per 1000 students, which is about 30 times the state average.  However, parents of students in the school feel the numbers don't tell the whole story, as Marion Ellis believes that its level of violence is at a typical level.  Ken Trump, president of the National School Safety and Security Services, claims that many schools adjust the numbers in order to protect their own reputation.

headline: A downside to Phila.'s development
abstract: The article uses the example of Bob Harvey to portray the downside to the residential development of Philadelphia as seven older properties adjacent to construction projects have been damaged or destroyed this year.  The Philadelphia Department of Licenses and Inspections has issued a warning in response that no building can proceed without an engineer signing a contract saying that they will support the foundations of adjacent buildings.  The article also uses Drew Dedo as an example, who refuses to let Universal Community Homes to continue construction without naming Dedo an insured party on their insurance carrier, paying engineering and legal fees and repairing the sidewalk and water damage in the basement.

headline: Casey ahead in poll; Santorum ahead at the bank
abstract: According to a recent Quinnipiac University poll, Bob Casey has a considerable lead over Rick Santorum in the US Senate race, while Santorum has a considerably larger sum of campaign money.

headline: The race to replace the lever
abstract: A steady stream of residents cast their votes for the electronic system they would like to see used next year in Lancaster county elections. Four companies are competing for a contract to replace the county's roughly 440 lever action voting machines. On Tuesday, company representatives demonstrated their products to the public at the former Armstrong Building. Three of the demonstration models were touch-screen systems and a fourth utilized a full ballot on top of an electronic display. The federal Help America Vote requires the county to replace its level voting machines with electronic ones by the May 2006 primary.

headline: Dover Teachers may present evolution alternative
abstract: Biology teachers at the Dover area school district may be required to read a four-paragraph statement containing an alternative theory to evolution in their next class. The statement reads that evolution is not a fact and that intelligent design is an alternative students could consider. The regional director of the ACLU, Witold Walczak, claims that the introduction of religion into the classroom is a fundamental violation of the Constitutional provision of separation of Church and State and is fighting the motion.

headline: Teaching intelligent design impedes learning
abstract: A leading science education expert, testifying in a federal court trial over teaching of evolution in a York County school district, said that introducing intelligent design into the science classroom is detrimental to learning. Brian Alters, a professor of science education at McGill University in Montreal, denounced a policy requiring a disclaimer on evolution be read in Dover Area School District high school biology classes, saying it engenders misconceptions about science. School biology teachers refused to read the statement that evolution is only a theory with gaps in it.

headline: Add beds for city's homeless
abstract: Calling it Philadelphia's moral and legal obligation, Mayor Street announced an ambitious plan to end homelessness in the next 10 years. Street said the goal would be achieved through better coordination of existing services, construction of 600 new units of subsidized housing for homeless people, and the addition of 100 beds for the chronically homeless. He has earmarked $10 million for the plan.

headline: Casey takes aim at Santorum
abstract: There was no question in anyone's mind who attended the Washington County Democrat Committee banquet Sunday night that Bob Casey Jr. is running for the US Senate in 2006. Casey, currently state treasurer and former auditor general, was the main speaker at the annual banquet. His opposition a year from now is expected to be incumbent US Sen. Rick Santorum. The theme of his campaign is going to be unite and prosper.

headline: The slush fund: Power and corruption
abstract: The author believes that it is no surprise that the auditor general of PA is prohibited from auditing $135 million slush fund controlled by the PA General Assembly’s leadership. The author believes that the lawmakers in PA are comfortable hiding from the public view since they have created one of the least transparent and accountable state assemblies in the nation.

headline: Immigrant Outreach Program Save a good thing
abstract: Thirteen-year-old Jacob Gray, who immigrated from Liberia, was nearly beaten to death by local African American teenagers. This event shows the hostility between African American young people and African immigrants in Philadelphia. Project Tamaa was started in 2002 to help the growing number of West African refugees who move to Philadelphia from war-torn lands.

headline: Teaching taking note - of how they teach
abstract: Haverford Middle School teachers have developed ways to receive student feedback - that way they can become the best teachers they can be. They have students hold up green cards if they understand the lesson, yellow if they are so-so, and red if they don’t at all. This helps teachers become more attuned to what is happening in class during instruction.

headline: Advocates and officials celebrate housing fund
abstract: About 200 housing advocates and politicians packed a room in City Hall to celebrate an agreement to create a multimillion dollar trust fund to build and repair low-income housing in Philadelphia. It’s the first kind in the city. The money would come from doubling the fees for deeds and mortgages. The mayor's Neighborhood Transformation Initiative also would provide the fund a one-time infusion of $1.5million.

headline: Casey's fund-raising in Texas brings in $18,000 post-Katrina
abstract: On the same day Sen. Rick Santorum canceled a fund-raising trip to Texas because of Hurricane Katrina, his leading Democratic opponent collected $18,000 in Austin and met with prospective donors in Houston. His campaign did not disclose when asked whether he planned to raise money outside the state before the close of the quarterly fund-raising period on Sept 30.

headline: The value of 'Race for the Cure'
abstract: A resident disagrees with the assessment that participating in Susan G. Komen's Race for the Cure is 'priceless.' It cost her $30 dollars and she had to miss Mother's Day. Friends should not ask friends for money--they should provide it themselves.

headline: 'Intelligent design' fails test
abstract: Most religious leaders and educators within Schulkill county were accepting of US District Judge John E. Jones III's decision against the Dover school board that the theory of intelligent design should be mentioned in schools.  Reverend Edward B. Connolly, a local pastor of two churches, said that religion teachers in public schools should not teach atheism nor intelligent design despite believing that the United States is a Christian country.  Pottsville Area Superintendent James Gallagher is in support of teaching evolution but would have no problem teaching intelligent design in a religion class, not a science class.

headline: The Santorums get a technicality
abstract: US Senator Rick Santorum used the address of a Penn Hills home he owns to require the Penn Hills School District to pay for his five children to go to cyber school, despite his permanent Virginia residence.  The State Education Secretary dismissed the district's request for reimbursement because a district only has seven days to challenge residence once a child is enrolled in cyber charter school.  The editorial board believes the Education Secretary should reach a settlement with the Santorums and alter the law.

headline: Advocates and officials celebrate housing fund
abstract: The Philadelphia Affordable Housing Coalition, housing advocates and politicians agreed to create The Housing Trust Fund. The first of its kind in Philadelphia, the multimillion dollar trust fund will be used to build and repair low-income housing in Philadelphia. PA state law currently does not allow Philadelphia to create such a fund. As a result, Philadelphia City Council members Jannie L. Blackwell and Blondell Reynolds Brown will introduce legislation to create the fund. In addition, PA State Senator Shirley M. Kitchen, PA State Representatives Louise Williams Bishop, John J. Taylor, and W. Curtis Thomas plan to sponsor state legislation to allow the creation of the fund.

headline: Castor mulls governor's race
abstract: Montgomery County District Attorney Bruce L. Castor is considering running against incumbent Governor Ed Rendell in 2006.

headline: The worst? Hardly
abstract: Time magazine named Mayor John Street one of America's worst mayors based on an investigation by the Federal Bureau of Investigation that uncovered corruption. The columnist objects, saying that former Philadelphia mayors Wilson Goode and Frank L. Rizzo were worse mayors, and that Mayor Street has made several positive changes in Philadelphia.

headline: Intelligent Design Might Be Meeting Its Maker
abstract: Despite President Bush encouraging schools to teach both evolution and intelligent design, the latter theory is facing more and more opposition from intellectuals and religious proponents alike.  Charles Harper Junior, senior vice president at the Templeton Foundation, said the organization was offering grants for proponents to submit actual research on intelligent design but nobody applied for the grants.  A pending case in Dover, Pennsylvania is waiting on a judge's decision to determine if intelligent design can be taught in a public school, as some claim that its theories advance certain religious beliefs.

headline: Tuition crunch breather
abstract: The Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency (PHEAA) is significantly increasing the amount of grant money it plans to provide college students.

headline: Allegheny County set to move on developing Mon Valley mill sites
abstract: Allegheny County received an $8 million federal financial package to help redevelop former steel mill site in Duquesne and McKeesport and the county has little more than five weeks to meet a deadline to claim the money or face losing it. The money will help finance about a dozen projects at two industrial sites that are owned by the Regional Industrial Development Corporation of Southwestern PA. PA Governor Edward Rendell visited early in the year and is the one who started the movement to complete these projects.

headline: Central Bucks board accepts new teachers contract
abstract: Teachers in the Central Bucks School District have a new contract. About 18 months of negotiations between the school board and union ended last night, when the board voted unanimously to accept a five-year contract proposed by a state mediator. The district's 1,300 teachers had already voted to accept the proposal. Negotiations resumed in January. The contract expired in June. Teachers will get raises but they will pay more for health care.

headline: They're setting an example
abstract: The Editorial Board admires US Senator Arlen Specter and Supreme Court Chief Justice William Rehnquist for continuing to be prominently involved in American Government, despite potentially fatal diseases.

headline: Man of the cloth
abstract: Maurice Jackson is President of Philadelphia Church Supply Inc which makes custom robes, baptismal gowns, and other clerical garments, mostly for African American churches in the Philadelphia region. He became President this past August. Robes cost $130 to $300 each and he will sell at least 1,000 of them this year.

headline: Tuition shock
abstract: Public colleges near Philadelphia have higher tuition rates than is seen nationally, however rates are rising faster nationally than locally.  Penn State President Graham Spanier says PA doesn't receive higher education funding like many other states.

headline: Allegheny County still has time to claim development aid
abstract: Allegheny County’s top economic development official told the County Council members that they have time to meet the deadline on an $8 million federal financial package for projects at two former steel mill site in Mon Valley. The package includes a $6 million loan and $2 million grant from the federal Department of Housing and Urban Development. The federal money will add to $4.5 million from PA Governor Edward Rendell’s economic redevelopment assistance plan.

headline: Chambers gets to 24-0 as he wins by decision
abstract: Eddie Chambers, of Philadelphia, won his 24th fight against Robert Hawking at the Blue Horizon last night and remained undefeated.  With this victory, Chambers won the Pennsylvania State and International Boxing Union Championships despites Chambers being upset that he did not finish the fight strong.  Both President Bush and PA Governor Ed Rendell were invited, but neither showed up although Rendell did send a citation.

headline: Third parties seek easier ballot access
abstract: A coalition of political third parties and independents has launched a campaign to make access to PA's ballot easier for their candidates. The coalition, including members of the Reform Party, Green Party, and Libertarian Party, is calling on state lawmakers to change the way third parties qualify to get on the ballot. The Poconos are a relative hotbed of third-party activity on PA due in part to the migration of New Yorkers where third parties enjoy greater prominence. Members say it's important to revamp ballot laws before elections next year.

headline: Valley Crest owner eyes new home
abstract: The CEO of Complete HealthCare Resources, which assumed ownership of the Valley Crest Nursing home is searching for a different site to build a replacement nursing home because Luzerne County is charging $200,000 per acre for land around the existing facility. County commissioners can't budge from the asking price due to state law. Complete HealthCare is planning on building a new home for around $12 million.

headline: State traffic fatalities rise
abstract: Traffic fatalities across Allegheny County jumped 35 percent last year, reversing a four year trend according to PennDOT. Officials attribute the increase to careless driving and a lack of seatbelt use among young drivers. Alcohol related deaths also increased this year.

headline: Settlement revealed in insurance case
abstract: Zurich American Insurance Company will pay $122 million to resolve claims of bid-rigging and price-fixing in the commercial insurance market under a nationwide settlement negotiated by Pennsylvania and 10 other states. Nearly 173,000 Pennsylvania policyholders are entitled to a portion of the settlement.

headline: Midstate voters show up angry at incumbents over pay raises
abstract: Voters were still very much upset with state lawmakers whom ten months ago voted without debate to raise their pay. This caused a lot of incumbents to lose in yesterday's primary elections.

headline: Valley-wide approach to public health has potential to be a role model for state
abstract: The Dorothy Rider Pool Health Care Trust and the Two Rivers Health and Wellness Foundation donated $58,000 which might enable Lehigh and Northampton counties to form a bi-county health department.
