The Board of Health supported the concept and will ask County Council to authorize approaching neighboring counties and hospitals about joining in.

headline: Township has gaming plan
abstract: Planning Director Howard Kulzer presented a draft of their new plan to have casinos and racetracks relegated to the northwest corner of the township under a new zoning law. This includes building the facility north of Route 22 and west of Route 191.

headline: Slot sites feature gambles for owners
abstract: Proposed slots sites in Bethlehem and Allentown have special circumstances related to them, which authorities say warrant additional review beyond securing a slots license and receiving local land-development approval. Las Vegas Sands LLC wants to build a casino on the eastern edge of the former Bethlehem Steel Corp.'s Bethlehem Works. PA Department of Environmental Protection spokesman Mark Carmon said everything the Sands proposes is considered nonresidential. Barry Gosin, a principal in the BethWorks Now team that bought the land in fall 2004, said he is confident in the company's cleanup effort. Aztar Corporation, the company vying for the slots license for Allentown, proposes a site that will require a signoff from the Federal Aviation Administration because it is less than two miles from the Lehigh Valley International Airport.

headline: Minimum wage issue confronts state lawmakers
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell and Democratic lawmakers have added an increase to the state's minimum wage to their agenda as the new legislative session approaches, part of a larger nationwide living-wage movement. Republican leaders oppose the shift as damaging to business interests and a matter of federal concern.

headline: W.Va. hospital sues Pa. for payment
abstract: West Virginia University Hospitals, Inc. has filed suit against PA, naming PA Governor Ed Rendell in the suit, seeking reimbursement for emergency services rendered to PA citizens on Medicaid. The hospital is located six miles across the border in West Virginia and treated more than 24,000 PA residents in 2004. In 2004, the PA General Assembly passed legislation enabling the PA Department of Public Welfare to reimburse hospitals for trauma services, payments which the West Virginia hospital is seeking.

headline: Traffic restricted on Derry bridge after inspections
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation restricted a bridge in Derry Township to one lane of traffic after inspections revealed deterioration to one of the bridge's beams. The inspections are part of statewide initiative after the collapse of the Lakeview Road bridge, with the state inspecting all state-owned bridges and requesting local government's do the same to locally-owned bridges. The Federal Highway Administration said 25% of bridges in PA are structurally deficient.

headline: Slots bill could turn tables on Mt. Airy, Pocono Manor owners
abstract: The PA Senate faces a vote today on a gambling reform bill that has the potential to change some ground rules for the slots license applicants from the Poconos. If the bill becomes law before the PA state Gaming control Board issues slot licenses for standalone casinos in late December. A new provision requires the board to review an applicant's felony record if it is more than 15 years old.

headline: Minimum wage should go up
abstract: The author supports the initiative to raise the minimum wage in PA, voicing approval of PA Governor Ed Rendell in the process.

headline: Where there's smoke...There's fire stoked by tobacco interests
abstract: Smokers often insist that it is no one else's business if they smoke in public but the surgeon general is saying otherwise. A recent survey found indisputable evidence that secondhand smoke is killing an estimated 50,000 people each year. In response Allegheny County is joining like many other counties in banning smoke in restaurants, taverns, and social clubs with 10 or more employees. Some establishments are suing because they think this is infringing on their rights

headline: Transportation center delayed again
abstract: Complications in Harrisburg has brought another delay to the $11 million intermodal transportation center planned for downtown Scranton. The final piece of the puzzle is legislative approval of a roughly $900,000  land swap between the Bus company COLTS and the state General Services Authority.

headline: slots' first week: $39M
abstract: Gamblers pumped $39.3 million into slot machines at the casino in the first week; the won back $35.3 million, as the machines have been paying out an average of 90 cents on every dollar waged. Of the $4.08 million left in the machines after all winnings were paid out, the state has taken $1.4 million for property tax relief, 163,000 for local government, $204,000 for economic development and tourism, and $490,000 for the state's horse racing industry.

headline: Mitman to endorse Rendell
abstract: Thirteen Republican mayors endorsed PA Governor Ed Rendell in his re-election bid, including Easton Mayor Phil Mitman over the Republican candidate, Lynn Swann

headline: Barbaro will be confined to his stall for months
abstract: Barbaro's home for months to come will be a stall in the University of Pennsylvania's George D. Widener Hospital for Large Animals. Barbaro needed 27 screws to put his right ankle back together. People continue to send the horse flowers and fruit baskets, hoping that he will get better.

headline: Transportation report triggers political carping
abstract: A study commission brought PA's transportation problems into sharper focus, saying the state will need an extra $2 billion to significantly help cash-strapped mass transit agencies and rebuild crumbling highways and bridges.  The issues is sure to bring up discussion of a tax increase.  Action in the legislature has waited on recommendations from the commission, established by PA Governor Ed Rendell in 2005.  The commission is schedule to deliver those recommendations after the election.

headline: Slots group fined $7k
abstract: The Gaming Control Board fined two of the owners of Crossroads Gaming Resort a combined $7,000 for making political contributions that violate the slots law. The two made contributions totaling $490 to political action committees and state Rep. Glen Grell; the law strictly prohibits them from making any.

headline: Mon Dieu!
abstract: The U.S. Senate passed a resolution stating that the national anthem and Pledge of Allegiance should be English. This is a ridiculous idea.

headline: Berks farmer urges lawmakers to protect farmland
abstract: Glenn Seidel, a beef farmer who owns a 118-acre farm along the Tulpehocken Creek appeared before the U.S. House Agriculture subcommittee to ask them to make farmland preservation and conservation funding a priority. Seidel said that unless something was done soon many prime farmland would be lost. Congress currently allots $168 billion for agriculture each year, but that program is set to expire in 2007.

headline: Troopers to set up sobriety checkpoint
abstract: PA state police from the Hamburg station will be conducting a sobriety check point for four days. They hope to decrease the number of accidents involving drunk driving.

headline: Slots group fined $7k
abstract: The PA Gaming Control Board fined two of the owners of Crossroads Gaming Resort a combined $7,000 for making political contributions that violate the slots law. The two made contributions totaling $490 to political action committees and PA Representative Glen Grell; the law strictly prohibits them from making any.

headline: Murphy has raised $502,000 in 2006 for Gerlach challenge
abstract: Lois Murphy, who is seeking the Democratic nomination to challenge Republican US Representative Jim Gerlach in the 2006 elections, raised $502,000 during the first three months of the year, 84 percent of which came from individuals and not political action committees. Mark Nevins, Murphy's spokesman, said the average contribution is less than $200, which Murphy positively views as a "mandate for change".  John Gentzel, campaign spokesman for Gerlach, said the campaign was still adding up the figures. In the 2004 elections, Gerlach raised about $2.2 million while Murphy raised $1.9 million, not including contributions from either party. The Rothenberg Political Report, a nonpartisan newsletter based in Washington, consider Murphy a legitimate contender, Political Editor Nathan Gonzales said.

headline: Chef kicks up recipe a notch
abstract: PA Secretary of Agriculture Dennis Wolff joined a chef at the PA Farm Show for a cooking exhibition. The article includes the recipe as well as a recap.

headline: Trucking industry undertaxed by state
abstract: The Pennsylvania secretary of transportation declared that the state's roads are in poor condition and the only way to fund the necessary repairs is a 12-cent tax on gasoline. However, massive trucks driving along our highways is the real problem. State Legislature won't go after them because the trucking industry has our state government in their pocket. Pennsylvania should add an additional tax for the trucking industry.

headline: Slots license seals return of Poconos as a destination
abstract: Mount Airy's used to be a very popular hotel in the Poconos; however, after years of bad business it closed in 2001. The PA Gaming Control Board recently voted in favor of it receiving a gambling license which should make the resort better than ever.

headline: Museum gets U.S. secretary on its side
abstract: U.S. Secretary of Interior Dirk Kempthorne wrote to Congress urging the proposed Revolutionary War museum in Valley Forge, which has been long stalled by bureaucratic wrangling. PA Governor Rendell and U.S. Senator Rick Santorum for PA appeared at a holiday parade in Glenside to make the announcement of Kempthorne's support.  The proposed museum will be the first in the country to tell the entire story of the American Revolution.

headline: Comments on wind-farm opponents draw fire
abstract: Kerry Campbell, a PA Department of Environmental Protection expert, blames growing opposition to wind farms in Pennsylvania on city residents who have moved into rural areas. She believes that people who grew up on the area are very welcoming of wind farms.

headline: Two transit tips
abstract: Pittsburgh could fix its public transportation problem by doing two things. First, they could raise money by making senior citizens pay a small monthly fee as opposed to riding for free. Second, making people pay when they got on the bus as opposed to when they get off the bus could cause things to run faster and more smoothly.

headline: Slots licensing: As much time as it takes
abstract: The PA Gaming Control Board is conducting intense investigations for slot licensing. Several hearings became contentious when board members challenged their gaming revenue projections. The board has compressed time frames for hearings, and the article proposes they move the hearings to different days to allow more time.

headline: Names may change, but game stays same
abstract: At least one-fifth of the Pennsylvania Legislature will change in Tuesday's election, but the way that legislators conduct business probably won't, say current and former legislators and staffers. Despite pledges by "government reform" candidates to change the system, the General Assembly is an institution driven by party leaders unlikely to cede power.

headline: County adds farmland for preservation
abstract: York County Agricultural Land Preservation is helping to preserve 30,000 acres of farm land in Pennsylvania. PA Secretary of Agriculture Dennis Wolff credited former governors and current Governor Ed Rendell for making agriculture a state priority. PA Senator Michael Waugh says that farmland preservation is vital to the health of the state.

headline: With fuel prices on the rise, saving rail passenger service makes sense
abstract: Amtrak has not been given the opportunity to die or to flourish in this country. It is given the minimal amount of funding to survive, $25 billion in its 35 years. In a time when gas prices are rising Congress should look to utilizing Amtrak more.

headline: Slots money no secret
abstract: David LeVan isn't secretive about how much he will own if Crossroads Gaming Resort and Spa is granted a license by the PA Gaming Control Board.  Chance Enterprises, a group of individual investors, announced in 2005 that it intended to apply for a license to build a slots parlor in Straban Township.  Both awaited the board released detailed list of ownership stake in all the slots proposals issued Monday. The list included in the article.

headline: National parties pour money into House races
abstract: The national campaign committees have spent a combined $18 million on a few tightly contested House races in Pennsylvania; democrats feel these are critical if they want to take control of the House. Some of the candidates include Iraq war veteran Patrick Murphy, Joe Sestak, and Jason Atmire. Altogether the Democrats must gain 15 seats to control the House.

headline: County adds farmland for preservation
abstract: York County Agricultural Land Preservation is helping to preserve 30,000 acres of farm land in Pennsylvania. Pennsylvania Secretary of Agriculture Dennis Wolff credited former governors and current Governor Ed Rendell for making agriculture a state priority. State Senator Michael Waugh says that farmland preservation is vital to the health of the state.

headline: 911 chief: 'Public counts on us'
abstract: A computer failure crashed Allegheny County's 911 system for six hours, causing 100 calls for help to be missed. A man's baby son died while he was trying to reach 911.

headline: Some uninsured adults to get coverage from Pa.
abstract: The PA Insurance Department announced received a surplus of insurance revenue, allowing them to expand coverage of the adult Basis program to an additional 30,000 uninsured Pennsylvanians. Non-profit insurance members of the Blue Cross organization are contributing the money as part of an agreement to reinvest funding.

headline: New voting machines face extensive checks
abstract: As Lackawanna County's voting machine consultant, Hugh Gallagher used a simple measure to determine how the county will use electronic voting in the May 16, 2006 primary election, he wants to make sure the results are accurate. The Voter Registration Office has been unpacking and testing the final 165 electronic voting machines ordered from Advanced Voting Solutions.

headline: Dairy Farmers need help and Gov. Ed Rendell says he wants to do something for them
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell has announced a Milk Marketing Board hearing to propose a new milk-pricing policy.

headline: A city like skyline on Cove Mountain
abstract: A New Jersey developer has submitted two sets of plans to build on 1,155 acres of Cove Mountain. The plans are being called the Preserve at the Mountainside with an east and west section. The east section would have three apartment complexes, one being 22 stories high. The west section calls for about 75 single-family houses.

headline: Split vote approves LCB post
abstract: Former PA State Senator Joe Contil will be appointed the first ever CEO of the Pennsylvania Liquor Control Board. He was approved by two of the three members of the LCB. His job will entail overseeing the day to day operations of the liquor control board, which is the nations largest buyer of wine and liquor.

headline: New voting system brings its share of problems for Luzerne County primary
abstract: Many poll workers were frustrated after the election was over. The new machines worked well during the day but after they had to wait up to a couple hours because the people working the machines didn't know how to take back the returns. Another man was angry because he got in line before 8:00 which means he is supposed to be allowed to vote, but he wasn't able to. This is because the machines shut off at 8:00 unless programmed otherwise, the poll workers didn't know how to do this.

headline: E. coli raises food fears
abstract: E. Coli was found in food purchases in Taco Bell restaurants across five states, including Pennsylvania. Officials believe that the bacteria was found in iceberg lettuce. Many people feel that the government needs to do a better job monitoring food throughout the country.

headline: A Fatal Case in Lower Merion
abstract: Stephen L. Meloni, a 19 year old Main Line student is charged with the vehicular homicide in the death of a 16 year old Jessica Easter. Easter was killed trying to get out of the car being driven by  Meloni, who had been under the influence of alcohol and marijuana.

headline: State an early winner in take from first casino
abstract: The first figures released by the PA Gaming Control Board showed that in the fisrt month $85 million were wagered and $76.3 million was won. The state's cut in this was nearly $5 million which will be used for the state's property tax relief and other purposes. The payouts, on average, where the lowest among casinos on the East Coast.

headline: Newcomer challenges House veteran
abstract: Peter Daley, a California Democrat is hoping to defeat Edward Angell to retain his seat for a 13th term. Daley, like many incumbent legislators, has come under fire for voting in favor of a controversial pay raise last summer. Daley did however, give the money to charitable organizations. Daley believes his record should enable him to win the election. Angell is running a campaign based on change, saying that Harrisburg needs to hear a new voice.

headline: Farm preservation program takes root
abstract: Southern Lehigh has become the first school district in the Lehigh Valley, and one of the first statewide to approve a measure designed to slow the sale of farmland for development. However, without support from municipalities within its borders the efforts will be meaningless. Under Act 4, farms enrolled in county agricultural preservation programs would get a break from rising, school, municipal, and county taxes under a mileage freeze, providing farm owners give up their development rights.

headline: Alliance aims to keep guns out of school
abstract: Adults who give or sell firearms to Philadelphia juveniles were given a stern warning by federal and local law enforcement officials and the head of the city school districts. If they get caught they could face 10 years in prison, as a new partnership of federal state and local law-enforcement and the school district plans a crackdown on firearms in and near schools.

headline: State board: No obstacles for Downs
abstract: PA Gaming Control Board has not found any issues that might prevent Mohegan Sun at Pocono Downs from getting slot machines.

headline: Newman leaving Supremes?...and by the end of this year?
abstract: Several PA Supreme Court sources and sources close to PA Supreme Court Justice Sandra Newman confirmed that she as said she is leaving after the elections are over this year.  Possible new employers include law firms based in Philadelphia, with some insiders saying Cozen & O'Connor are currently in the lead.

headline: FDA poised to approve food from cloned animals
abstract: The Food and Drug Administration concluded there is no difference between food from cloned animals and food from conventional livestock. This means that cloned animals are safe for human food supply and no special labels are needed for those products. The Consumer Federation of America is asking food companies and supermarkets to refuse to sell food from clones. Currently only about 150 of the 9 million total U.S. dairy cows are cloned.

headline: Amish school girls shot dead
abstract: Charles Carl Roberts IV entered an Amish schoolhouse with multiple weapons.  He told the boys and adults to leave, and lined girls up at the blackboard and shot them before killing himself. State and local police were at the scene.

headline: State cuts social services contract
abstract: The state of Texas is cutting an $899 million contract with Accentureby $356 million, the company operates call centers to determine benefits eligibility. Under the restructured contract the company will be largely relegated to data entry.

headline: News from the General Assembly
abstract: A breakdown of ongoing legislation in the PA General Assembly, including new drunk driving and child abuse regulations as well as teacher credential legislation.

headline: Giant stores to resume stocking spinach
abstract: Four grocery chains on the East Coast began restocking their produce shelves with fresh spinach yesterday as federal officials reassured the public the spinach was safe to eat. Signs in the stores will notify where the spinach was grown so customers can avoid spinach grown in the three counties in California where the other E. coli spinach was grown. So far 183 in 26 states have become ill from eating fresh spinach contaminated with E. coli. Stores are trying their best to gain back trust in their spinach.

headline: At 80, she's oldest female inmate in Pa.
abstract: At the age of 80, Lois Farquharson is the oldest female prison inmate in the state of Pennsylvania. She has been in jail since 1974 when she was convicted of masterminding the murder of Dr. Leon Weingrad. She would like to be free by the time she dies and is currently working on appeals to get her out.

headline: State House still has a vital agenda
abstract: The editorial board advocates the PA legislature passing three measures before it goes into recess for the election. They believe the state House should move the slots-casino reforms adopted in the Senate, and that the legislature should approve the expansion of the Children's Health Insurance Program proposed by the Rendell administration. They also believe a bill should be passed that would give tax credits to car companies that use clean-air technology.

headline: Newsmakers predict balanced budget, pie in sky in 2006
abstract: The newspaper staff asked PA politicians, local and state, to offer their predictions for PA politics in 2006 and includes the satirical responses in this article

headline: Gov. helps out Adams farm
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell presented at $279,250 loan to Irvin Orchard in Franklin Township as part of an effort to invest in family-owned agriculture through the state. The funds will be used by owner Harry Irvin to buy this brother's portion of the orchard and to buy machinery and equipment for the farm. The loan comes from the state's first $150 million First Industries Fund, which provides grants, loans and lean guarantees to businesses in the agriculture and tourism industries.

headline: Attorney general forms unit to combat elder abuse
abstract: At a news conference in Johnstown, PA Attorney General Tom Corbett announced he is forming a new elder-abuse unit designed to protect seniors and prosecute those who harm them.  The unit's goal is to make senior citizens safer. Elder abuse includes financial exploitation, physical abuse and sexual assault.

headline: Swann seeks support at county business expo
abstract: Republican gubernatorial candidate Lynn Swann was at the Centre county's Chamber of Business and Industry's 2006 Business and Industry Expo. He was asking questions, shaking hands, and posing for pictures. Swann said there are shortcomings in public education and that is a major concern of his.

headline: Next sheriff sees image problem
abstract: William Mullen will be replacing Dennis Skosnik as chief deputy of the Allegheny County Sheriff's Office. Mullen says that credibility in the Office will have to be restored after Skosnik resigned before pleading guilty to bribery, money laundering, witness tampering, and fraud charges. Governor Ed Rendell could allow Mullen to remain as acting Sheriff or appoint someone else after 90 days. In addition to Skosnik, former Lieutenant Captain Richard A. Stewart and former Captain Frank Schiralli were also convicted of crimes.

headline: Senate rejects GOP alternative on farm aid, risking Bush veto of bigger bill
abstract: U.S. Senate rejected a proposed $5.5 farm assistance bill because the amount of funding was seen as too low. Republicans and President Bush are not happy about the bill's failure to pass.

headline: Barletta: Illegals drain city
abstract: After two Hazelton officers were wounded in a shootout Mayor Louis Barletta reinforced his argument that the city's Illegal immigration Relief Act needs to be enforced. The man involved in the shooting wasn't an illegal immigrant but Barletta feels that they are draining the cities recourses. Enforcement of the relief act which punishes landlords and employers who house any illegal aliens, was put on hold by the courts pending the outcome of a lawsuit which declared in unconstitutional.

headline: Taxpayers may pay for promoting slots parlors
abstract: Taxpayers would pay for ads promoting PA's slots casinos, under a proposal released by the PA Tourism Office and related groups. The plan also says members of the PA Governor's Tourism Partnership, an advisory committee, should approach casino applicants now, before they are licensed - about help in promoting PA tourism.  That appears to contradict assertions by lawmakers and the PA Gaming Control Board that the board will award licenses based on the applicant's merits, without outside influence.

headline: Nigro's audacity
abstract: Russel Nigro, the first PA Supreme Court justice to lose a retention election is just as clueless as the magazines that wrote positive puff pieces about him. They blamed lack of party support and low turnout for his loss. They forgot to mention that he saw nothing wrong with Chief Justice Cappy conspiring with the Legislature behind close doors or his misuse of his expense account.

headline: SWAT puppy mills?
abstract: Awareness Day 2006 will be held in Intercourse to protest puppy mills with Chris DeRose, actor, and Rick Rockett, of Poison. PA Governor Rendell promised revision on state regulation of dog breeders, but has yet to act on the promise. Proposed changes are discussed.

headline: Bill would require larger towns to pay for state police
abstract: PA state Representative John Pallone unveiled legislation that would require municipalities with at least 9,000 residents without their own police departments to pay an annual $100 per resident for law enforcement provided by the PA State Police. Pallone said that some municipalities that do not have local police departments are large enough to support their own departments, yet rely on the state police for law enforcement.

headline: Thousands tricked into paying fees for discounts, state says
abstract: Two companies, Chase Bank USA and Trilegiant Corp, tricked hundreds of thousands of people into paying for membership in discount programs. The PA attorney general said those involved may be eligible for a refund. The companies are not admitting to any wrongdoing.

headline: No headline
abstract: Details campaign schedule for Lynn Swann who is running for PA Governor.

headline: Sweet news for growers: 'Stone fruit' ban is lifted
abstract: Adams County used to be among the biggest peach-producing counties in the country but  in 1999 the PA Department of Agriculture ordered a destruction of over 200,000 of its trees because they had the plum pox virus. Yesterday the department lifted its no replanting quarantine allowing the county to plant peaches on a previously banned 200 square mile area.

headline: Blurred words, unusual challenge
abstract: In a brochure about the PA Supreme Court, officials blurred the background of a photo because it showed a courtroom mural depicting the Ten Commandments. That 2004 brochure became a source of controversy at a confirmation hearing for Supreme Court nominee Cynthia A. Baldwin. According to a spokesman for the Administrative Office of Pennsylvania Courts, the decision to obscure the Ten Commandments was made by state court official while state and federal court challenges were pending regarding the public display of religious texts at courthouses. Baldwin was nominated by PA Governor Ed Rendell after Justice Russell Nigro was ousted by voters angry over a pay raise passed by the PA Legislature. After the hearing, Baldwin said she had not been aware of the photograph.

headline: US Airways center could locate here
abstract: Allegheny County lost a battle with Winston-Salem, NC two years ago for the call center of US Airways. Now Pittsburgh is competing for $25 Million flight operations center for US Airways. Proposals are to be submitted to US Airways by October 15 and a decision will be made by January or February.

headline: None of the above
abstract: Robert Syzpulski was very angry after reading a Tribune-Review editorial in which the board recommended "neither" in the race for Pennsylvania governor. He believed that too many people in this country sacrificed too much to allow us to vote and people should not give up that honor. Dimitri Vassilaros believes that voting for evil does not honor the fallen, however a principled vote does.

headline: Builders, workers bracing for strike
abstract: The Metropolitan Regional Council of Philadelphia and Vicinity and the General Building Contractors Association are warning their members to prepare for a strike on Monday if sides cannot reach an agreement before labor contracts expire on Sunday. A strike would affect major building projects such as the Comcast Center tower, Philadelphia School District projects and the Symphony House condominiums and theater. Edward Coryell, executive secretary and lead negotiator for the carpenter's union, could not be reached for comment, while Walter P. Palmer, president of the contractor's association, said Coryell had been unavailable to negotiate in the last few days. Palmer told contractor's association members that members of plasterer and cement mason and operating engineers unions would be on the job Monday.

headline: Candidates divided on gun control
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell and his opponent Lynn Swann differ on their opinions on gun control. Rendell supports a law that would limit the number of guns a person can purchase to one a month to prevent someone from buying many guns and selling them illegally. Lyn Swann doesn't support this law, though both agree an increase in the number of police is necessary. The state House is unlikely to pass a law limiting the number of guns a person can buy because Republicans have a majority in the House and gun laws are not popular in Pennsylvania.

headline: Veto Needed
abstract: The editorial board criticizes the state Legislature's decision to help Sovereign Bank in its battle with its major shareholder, Relational Investors LLC, following its acquisition of Waypoint Financial Corp. Touting the 3,500 jobs it provides the state, Sovereign came to the Legislature for a bill making it difficult to remove sitting directors. The PA Legislature passed the bill will no public hearings and with questionable following of procedural rules. Relational and investor advocacy groups, including the Council of Institutional Investors, said investor rights were being violated. Some legislators were upset that they didn't have an opportunity to present opposing viewpoints. Critics contend that there are political connections between Sovereign executives, PA Governor Ed Rendell and members of the General Assembly.

headline: Officials give vote of confidence to new machines
abstract: Despite the fact that most Pennsylvanian's will cast their ballots today on new voting machines, state officials do not anticipate major problems. All but one county will use either electronic touch-screens or optical scan systems. The changes are in response to Congress passing the Help America Vote act.

headline: Food workers' union endorses Evans for mayor
abstract: Local 1776 of the United Food and Commercial Workers, a union that represents thousands of supermarket and retail workers, threw its support behind Philadelphia State Representative Dwight Evans' mayoral campaign.

headline: Candidates divided on gun control
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell and his opponent Lynn Swann differ on their opinions on gun control. Rendell supports a law that would limit the number of guns a person can purchase to one a month to prevent someone from buying many guns and selling them illegally. Lyn Swann doesn't support this law, though both agree an increase in the number of police is necessary. The PA House is unlikely to pass a law limiting the number of guns a person can buy because Republicans have a majority in the House and gun laws are not popular in Pennsylvania.

headline: Vote on slots nears
abstract: The PA Gaming Control Board will award five licenses out of the 11 applicants to see who will get to open gambling halls. The slot law also requires the seven-member gaming board to have a "supermajority" of five members; this must include all four appointees of legislative leaders, plus one appointee of PA Governor Rendell. The supermajority rule was written to ensure a solid decision and to give more people a voice in the process.

headline: Oil, natural gas industries contribute $110,000 plus to Santorum's campaign
abstract: US Senator Rick Santorum received $110,050 for his campaign from Oil and natural gas industries. The two industries have given him more than $440,000 since 1991. State Treasurer Bob Casey Jr. is the likely candidate to run against Santorum in the upcoming election; he has received only 4,700 from the two industries.

headline: Jobless claims, indicators fall
abstract: As reported by the US Labor Department, new applications for unemployment insurance dropped by 10,000 to 303,000 last week, which is the best showing since the beginning of April. Before the report was released, the decline was expected to only be 5,000. However, the Conference Board, a private research group, said its Index of Leading Economic Indicators dropped to 138.4 in March from 138.5 in February, which suggests that economic activity could weaken later in the year. The Labor Department report also stated that the four-week moving average of new jobless claims fell be 2,250 last week bringing it to its lowest level since February. Although some reports indicate an improvement in the job market, the Federal Reserve will keep a close watch on wage growth and other inflation barometers.

headline: Care home owner's husband expected to plead guilty
abstract: Clifford Fake of Palmyra who is accused of abusing and neglecting residents in his wife's five personal care homes in Lebanon County is expected to plead guilty to federal fraud charges, attorney Gerald A. Lord, who represents Fake on the federal charges, said. Fake faces up to 20 years in prison if US Middle District Judge William W. Caldwell accepts the guilty plea. Prosecutors say that between 2000 and March 2005, Fake and his wife Tina M. Fake filed falsified paperwork with the PA Department of Aging. Tina Fake pleaded not guilty to the federal charges in November 2005 and is awaiting trial in federal court.

headline: With slots, the stakes are...secret
abstract: The PA Gaming Control Board knows how big a stake each potential owner of PA's slot parlors would own, but they aren't telling.  Its officials say the 2-year-old state law that both legalized slot-machine gambling in PA and created the gaming board to oversee the industry does not allow it to release the information publically. It is up to the applicants themselves to disclose who owns how much.

headline: One for the books
abstract: PA Representative Mark Cohen wants the Pennsylvania taxpayers to reimburse him for the $28,200 he has spent amassing his 800-book library because the reading, he says, makes him a "better legislator." The editorial board ridicules Cohen's request by noting fictitious books that legislators should read to increase their ability as representatives of PA citizens, including such titles as "Public Accountability for Dummies," "The Hitchhiker's Guide to Public Service" and "The Little Book of Hubris."

headline: Jobless rates dip; factory jobs slip
abstract: The PA Department of Labor and Industry released figures that show that unemployment id down in Erie and Crawford County. However, both counties are still losing manufacturing jobs. The decline in unemployment is likely due to an increase in service-sector jobs.

headline: Catchy code names give cases status
abstract: The PA Attorney General's Office uses catchy codenames for their projects. Most of the names begin with the word Operation, an example uses is Operation Bonecrusher. This makes it easier for people to associate it with something very important.

headline: Week in Review. Earnings reported.
abstract: Harsco Corp.'s stock hit record highs during the week after reporting record sales and earnings for the fourth quarter. The company also upgraded its earnings forecast for 2006. PPL Corp. upgraded its long-term earnings outlook after reporting its fourth quarter and full-year earnings. Tyco International Ltd. reported first quarter earnings of 39 cents a share. A division of the conglomerate reported revenue of $3 billion in the quarter.

headline: Onorato's pitches for Smith, Dermody credited
abstract: Allegheny County Chief Executive Dan Onorato's televised appeal to voters on behalf of state Rep. Frank Dermody and Matt Smith paid off. Dermody won with 51 percent of the vote and Smith won with 58 percent of the vote.

headline: Latrobe union OKs severance package
abstract: Union workers at Latrobe Brewing Company ratified a separation package with their former employer, InBev USA.  Union officials believe they're close to reaching a tentative contract with City Brewing Company, their prospective new employer. However, the tentative deal the union is negotiating with La Crosse, Wisconsin-based City Brewing Company will likely reduce pay and vacations for workers.

headline: City freed from police-sex suit
abstract: District Judge John Fullam criticized threw out a civil suit against the Philadelphia Police Department, saying the top commanders bore no blame for the 2002 sexual assault of a former stripper by two police officers. The two officers were fired after their arrests, pleaded guilty to sexual assault and were sentenced to probation.

headline: Week in Review. Executives retire.
abstract: Albert Boscov and his business partner Edwin Lakin announced their retirement from Boscov's Inc. Ken Lakin, Edwin's son, will be the new CEO and chairman of the department store chain. Mellon Financial Corp. named Robert P. Kelley as its new chairman, president and CEO, succeeding current chairman and CEO Martin McGuinn, who is retiring. John van Roden Jr., executive vice president and chief financial officer at Glatfelter in York, announced that he is stepping down as CFO. John Jacunski, currently vice president and corporate controller, will succeed him.

headline: Ordinary one moment, "heroes forever" the next
abstract: Hundreds of people gathered to remember Flight 93, the jetliner that fell on Sept. 11. 300 of the around 1000 people who attended were relatives of those lost in the crash. President Bush laid a wreath at the crash site in the ceremony.

headline: Letters: Minimum-wage boost is a good start
abstract: A Conshohocken resident says that the first increase in the minimum wage in nearly a decade will most certainly help 423,000 workers, and is disappointed it took so long.  PA Senator Christine Tartaglione, who joined the governor on the signing of the minimum-wage bill, made the point in her brief comments that the battle for helping the middle class is not over.  The author thanks Tartaglione for reminding everyone to stay focused.

headline: City police commander is demoted after memo
abstract: Catherine McNeily, a key figure in the controversy surrounding former city of Pittsburgh Operations Director Dennis Regan, was demoted to the rank of lieutenant yesterday. She has been a veteran of the force for 28 years.

headline: Week in Review. Sovereign Bancorp Inc.
abstract: In a controversial action, the PA State Legislature approved a bill that assists Sovereign Bancorp Inc.'s fight against its major shareholder that is mounting a proxy fight and is challenging Sovereign's sale of a stake in the company to a Spanish banking group. Shareholders immediately decried the legislation and urged PA Governor Ed Rendell to veto the measure.

headline: Our View: Lawmakers show they're out of touch
abstract: PA legislators repealed the July 2005 law that gave them generous pay increases only after a prolonged outcry from the public. But legislators still received a 3.64 percent increase with an automatic cost of living raise. The editorial board says that PA legislators are out of touch with the average voter and don't understand how much.

headline: Pa. Hearing on Immigration Marked by Heated Exchanges
abstract: The PA House Republican Policy Committee, a partisan caucus, directed pointed questions to two local institutions that minister to illegal immigrants, the Archdiocese of Philadelphia and the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania at a hearing. Senators questioned the two institutions asking them if was moral to help people break the law, while representatives from the two institutions said they do not ask people their immigration status when helping them.

headline: City seeks ways to cut inmates
abstract: With Philadelphia's prison population at record levels, the Mayor Street administration has been quietly meeting with key players in the criminal-justice system to find ways to reduce the burgeoning number of inmates. Proposed ideas are to make the courts work faster, expand pre-trial-release programs, build or rent more prison space, hire ore staff and so on.

headline: Wine-law chaos? It's a corker.
abstract: A recent federal court decision ruled that Pennsylvania's prohibitions against out-of-state wine shipments were unconstitutional. State regulators are now legally allowed to ship, but with no ruled for how to do so. Nationwide, state liquor laws are in flux, as long-accepted ways of doing business are challenged after a U.S. Supreme Court ruling that in-state and out-of-state wineries must be treated alike. A reporter's investigation found that many out-of-state wineries are wary of shipping to the state, either because they were unaware of the court ruling or because they were uncertain of tax regulations. PA Senator Jim Ferlo has sponsored a bill to permit direct shipping of wine to consumers and to require shippers to obtain a license, pay a $100 annual fee and pay state sales tax.

headline: Ousted Rep. Veon's pension about $60,000
abstract: Former PA Representative Mike Veon will receive a pension of close to $60,000 and free health insurance for the remainder of his life. Pensions are based on age, years of service, the average of the lawmakers' three highest annual salaries and a multiplier of 2 percent to 3 percent based on the retirement plan each legislator chose.

headline: Miners demand and get meeting with safety chief
abstract: Seventy coal miners picketed a meeting of the district managers of the U.S. Mine Safety and Health Administration. The acting administrator invited them inside to talk. The miners expressed their concerns with the quality of oxygen units and the need for more mine inspectors. Richard E. Stickler, the assistant secretary of mine safety and health, phoned in to promise to meet with the miners. Dennis O'Dell, administrator of occupational safety and health for the United Mine Workers of America, said he is optimistic that conditions will improve.

headline: City swears in new police chief
abstract: Nathan E. Harper was sworn in Tuesday as the first black police chief in Pittsburgh in more than a decade; Harper is a 29-year police veteran. Former chief Dominic Costa retired in September, citing medical problems.

headline: With a stroke, Ed can veto both booze bill & business as usual
abstract: Governor Rendell should veto the bill that will allow the slot parlors to serve unlimited liquor. It makes sense for reasons beyond allowing Pennsylvanians to consume more alcohol. Vetoing the bill would send a reform message to Harrisburg, telling them its time to change these late night voting sessions.

headline: Pa. governor's race at a glance
abstract: The article discusses the two candidates running for governor. Democrat incumbent Governor Ed Rendell is married to Marjorie O. Rendell, a judge on the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. He was the mayor of Philadelphia for eight years and, after that, the general chairman of the Democratic National Committee before becoming governor. He won approval from the Republican state legislature to legalize slot machines and use the gambling tax revenue to lower property taxes. He also slightly raised the income tax. Rendell received campaign donations from the Democratic Governors' Association and the PA State Education Association. Lynn Swann wants to overhaul the state property tax system but is not supported by the PA legislature. He received a campaign donation from the Republican Governors' Association.

headline: Rendell renews call to raise minimum wage
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell has renewed calls for the PA legislature to increase the minimum wage and join neighboring states who have taken the initiative in lieu of federal government action. PA Senate Majority Leader David Brightbill has promised to allow a vote on legislation that would increase the minimum wage.

headline: Cops: Alcohol involved in fatal 23-story plunge
abstract: According to Harrisburg police, a Scranton native and his fiancée had been drinking to celebrate their engagement, before he dropped her from his 23rd-story apartment window, killing her. The boyfriend, Kevin Eckenrode, was charged with criminal homicide and locked up in Dauphin County Prison without bail. Eckenrode was apparently under the influence of alcohol. Police also recovered a marijuana pipe from his apartment. Eckenrode was recently hired by the PA Gaming Control Board as a press aide.

headline: Area singer to perform at "Operation Salute"
abstract: Quittie Creek will have their biggest audience yet at the Bryce Jordan Center at Penn State at "Operation Salute" honoring 20,000 Air and Army National Guard troops. They sing gospel music, but include some pop and patriotic songs as well.

headline: Pa. needs a constitutional convention
abstract: A proposal to re-draft the PA Constitution, introduced by PA State Representative Craig Dally, R-Northampton, is awaiting action in the PA legislature. The authors argue for its passage, citing the need to update the Constitution due to confusing PA court decisions and recent law changes that included slots legalization and unfair reapportionment.

headline: States should lead on mine safety
abstract: The author cites the recent mine disaster in West Virginia as reason for the PA legislature and PA Governor Ed Rendell to enact stricter legislation on mine safety standards and to remove protocols that leave the matter to federal discretion. Additionally, the US congressional delegation from PA is urged to take up the matter at the federal level.

headline: Court lets innocent inmate sue
abstract: A federal appeals court is allowing former death row inmate Nicholas Yarris to sue Delaware County for allegedly destroying evidence pointing to the real killer, manufacturing evidence against him, and thwarting his attempts at DNA testing. Prosecutors tried to have the case dismissed on the grounds that prosecutors should be immune from lawsuits if they follow the law, but the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit ruled they do not have immunity in this case.

headline: Families, vets remember Pa. soldiers killed in 91 Scud attack
abstract: Families, friends and veterans gathered to remember 13 soldiers killed 15 years ago when an Iraqi Scud missile slammed into their barracks in Saudi Arabia during the first Gulf War. The ceremony took place at the Greensburg Memorial U.S. Army Reserve Center.

headline: Pa. passes bill limiting use of homes for polls
abstract: The PA state Legislature passed a bill stating that polling places were not allowed to be on private property, such as peoples homes. They have to be on non partisan public property. The fact that the bill was voted on so close to the primary election leaves some politicians believing this was done to hurt the democrats chances.

headline: Strikes more likely at forced-dues school districts
abstract: The opinion article written by Susan Staub, president of Pennsylvanians for Right to Work Inc., discusses that an underlying reason that some teachers have threatened to go on strike in PA is that they are in forced-dues contracts. Staub cites the March 21 "Strike Status Information" and the March 22 "Agency shop report" by the PA School Boards Association that says that 100 percent of the school districts in which teachers or "classified employees" have gone on strike so far this school year have forced dues contracts. Staub says the contracts force local taxpayers to fund the teachers' unions that educators must join or support, whether they agree with their policies or not. Staub provides support for the Open Workforce Initiative, which is a group of bills that would help return individual liberty to all PA citizens with respect to forced-dues contracts.

headline: Court orders Pa. loan agency to make public its spending records
abstract: The PA Commonwealth Court ordered the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Authority to disclose records and pay some legal fees of three newspapers which filed suit on the principle of the Right to Know Law. Judge Doris A. Smith-Ribner disagreed PHEAA could avoid disclosure of travel expenses because board members are legislators, or that it needed to keep financial information private to remain competitive.

headline: Fitzpatrick concedes to Murphy
abstract: Incumbent Republican U.S. Rep Mike Fitzpatrick conceded defeat on Wednesday to Democratic Iraq war veteran Patrick Murphy. Fitzpatrick lost by 1,500 votes, which is less than 1 percent, this is  the closest election in almost 25 years. Peoples distaste for the Iraq war was probably a large reason why Murphy won.

headline: Pa. politics foreign to them
abstract: PA Governor Rendell and US Senator Rick Santorum announced on July 4, 2006 a breakthrough on a proposed museum honoring the American Revolution.  The bipartisan moment about the nonpartisan project at Valley Forge was very important to Niu Zhen, a Washington-based reporter for China's Shanghai Wenhui Daily, because it was another puzzling piece of U.S.-style politics.

headline: Teamsters local feels railroaded out of jobs
abstract: The 12 employees at the Ameriport intermodal rail center in South Philadelphia are going to lose their job at the end of the month. They are members of the Teamsters Local 107 and their jobs are to load freight containers from ships onto trains headed to Canada or the Midwest. A new company bought their business and thought that they were earning too much and is thus going to replace them.

headline: Court rules in favor of homeowners' lawsuit
abstract: The PA supreme court overturned two lower court rulings that rejected a class action lawsuit filed by several Allegheny county property owners who claimed  appeals of property assessments were being handled illegally. Common Pleas Judge R. Stanton Wettick Jr. decided whether the Board of Property Assessment Appeals and Review was following its own rules when it rejected some appeals.

headline: Life after Iraq for guardsmen: Behind is hard part, but ahead isn't easy
abstract: The men and women of the Pennsylvania National Guard Brigade Combat Team's 28th MP Company returned from Iraq in June, a year after PA Governor Ed Rendell sent them off. The article discusses how difficult adjusting to civilian life can be for returning Guardsmen.

headline: Pa. will no longer make candidates take 'loyalty oath'
abstract: Candidates for public office in PA will no longer have to sign a McCarthy-era oath pledging that they are not "subversive," a change ordered by the PA Attorney General Tom Corbett after the requirement was challenged by John Staggs.  Staggs is a meatpacker that refused to sign the oath when he turned in nominating petitions earlier this year, and threatened to sue the state.  Corbett has told election officials to stop enforcing the requirement because it is unconstitutional.

headline: null
abstract: PA schools are not up to standards concerning asthma according to researcher at Penn State University. 1 in 8 children under 17 have asthma. One fifth of schools did not know what to do if a child was having a severe asthma attack and more than half did not allow students to carry their rescue inhaler medications. Schools are encouraged to have an "asthma action plan" for the future.

headline: Crime interrupted by violence
abstract: A man in Philadelphia who was in the process of robbing another man was shot in the shoulder by an unknown person before he could flee.

headline: Pa. Guard can volunteer to patrol border
abstract: The PA National Guard can allow as many as 500 soldiers and airmen to volunteer to patrol the Mexican border for as long as three months under authorization from PA Governor Ed Rendell.  The federal government will pay for the cost of them to participate in Operation Jump State, which is designed to stanch the flow of illegal immigrants over the southern border.

headline: Pay raise challenged again
abstract: Gene Stilp filed a motion for reconsideration that argued the high court lacked sufficient grounds to allow legislators to keep the money they collected in form of unvouchered expenses. The ruling issued a 5-1 ruling that dealt with challenges to the passage and repeal of a 2005 government pay-raise law. The ruling restored pay raises for about 1,000 judges.

headline: Board extends pact of system chancellor
abstract: The chancellor of the state-owned university system, Judy Hample, has had her contract extended by a year and will head the system through July 31, 2009.  The governing board of the PA State System of Higher Education unanimously approved the extension.

headline: Death toll rises to five in school shooting
abstract: The death toll has reached five in the massacre that took place in an Amish schoolhouse. Another five are in critical condition. Roberts' walked into the schoolhouse with weapons, allowed the boys and adults to leave, then lined up the girls and shot them. He then killed himself. Police believe his motive was grief over the death of his infant daughter nine years ago. He may have been planning to sexually abuse the girls before the police foiled his plans. Governor Rendell said that flags will fly at half staff at the state's capitol.

headline: Pa. Guard officer dies in Iraq
abstract: Michael McLaughlin of Mercer, PA, died in combat in Iraq, the first officer of the PA Army National Guard to die in action since World War II.

headline: 'Pay raise' pig visits Hamburg
abstract: Gene Stilp, who is protesting the legislative pay raise by carting around an inflatable pig he calls the "pay raise pig," visited Hamburg to protest four state general assembly members that have offices in borough hall - Republicans PA Representative David G. Argall, PA Senator David J. Brightbill, PA Senator James J. Rhoades and PA Representative Bob Allen. Stilp, a self-described "political activist," held a rally for about 50 people outside the offices. The rally has been a subject of contention between the Kutztown Area Democratic Club and the Borough of Hamburg, as borough council president Tammy Wilkinson denied the accusations that the council had stalled the rally out of sympathy for the legislators. Argall said he believed the rally was a Democratic rally disguised as a protest.

headline: Advocate, district expanding policing program
abstract: The Philadelphia safe schools advocate. Jack Stollsteimer, is teaming-up with the school district to expand a school-based community policing program to 40 of the city's most violent schools. He is also an advocate for families whose children have been victims of schools violence. He is trying to find ways around court consent decrees that make it harder for the Philadelphia school district to expel or transfer students than any other district in the state.

headline: Delay in repairs to Pier 34 is denied
abstract: Michael Asbell is on trial for involuntary manslaughter for allegedly not conducting the repairs on a pier that he was instructed to because of money problems. A section of the pier collapsed and killed three women. Asbell told the Common Pleas court that he repaired everything that he was told to repair.

headline: Penn State hosts National Guard salute
abstract: PA Army and Air National Guard are getting a show of gratitude at Operation Salute at Penn State's Bryce Jordan Center. It will be the largest one-day mobilization ever for the guard. There will be tailgates will free food, a ceremony, and musical performers including Craig Morgan and the Beach Boys.

headline: Pay raise political storm will continue to rain on 2006 statewide elections
abstract: The article recaps the major news in PA politics from 2005, specifically focusing on the approval and subsequent repeal of the unpopular pay raise that passed the PA legislature at the same time property tax reform efforts were failing,.

headline: Agency should put earnings into student loans, not bonuses
abstract: The PA Higher Education Assistance Agency is condemned by the author for justifying raises and bonuses for executives despite being a non-profit. The author contends the money should be reinvested for the benefit of student assistance.

headline: Democrats call for gun laws
abstract: A group of Democrat state legislators went to Montgomery County to announce new legislative initiative aimed at reducing gun violence. Polls show that suburban residents are concerned about gun violence. Democrats claim this issue crosses party lines. The article details the specifics of the gun control session.

headline: Pennsylvania reservists will be patrolling US-Mexico border
abstract: Reservists from the PA Army and Air National Guard units are being asked to volunteer for border patrol duty in Arizona.  The venture stems from a Memorandum of Understanding between Arizona and PA, which calls for reservists to volunteer to assist in US-Mexico border patrols as part of Operation Jump Start. Joan Nissley, spokeswoman for the PA Department of Military and Veterans Affairs, said the memorandum was put together by PA Governor Ed Rendell after President Bush stressed border patrol security in his State of Union Address.

headline: Payback too late
abstract: The author condemns the PA Legislature for the midnight pay raise, claiming the revocation of the raise can not erase the damage done. The author supports a constitutional convention to reorganize the PA government.

headline: Allentown schools evacuated after bomb threat
abstract: The Allentown School District evacuated all twenty-two of its schools after receiving bomb threats implying there were bombs in every school in the district. Parents were furious that they sent students back into the school only an hour after investigating. Superintendent Karen Angello, Mayor Ed Pawlowski and Lehigh County District Attorney James B. Martin held a news conference where they insisted that the maintenance staff of the schools and fire department were sufficient to search for bombs, but parents disagree.

headline: Deputy coroner says Amish school scene was 'horrible'
abstract: Deputy County Coroner Amanda Shelley called Charles Carl Roberts's massacre of girls in an Amish school "horrible". Shelley said that it appeared from the crime scene that Roberts had planned on staying in the school for a few hours, but panicked when police came and killed the girls and himself. His motive may have been anguish over the death of his infant daughter nine years prior.

headline: City reaches deal to provide wireless Internet
abstract: Philadelphia has reached a deal with Earthlink and Wireless Philadelphia to provide wireless internet access across the city, announced Philadelphia Chief Information Officer Dianah Neff. Philadelphia Mayor John Street will submit the proposal, which will be paid for by Earthlink, to Philadelphia City Council for approval.

headline: Pay-raise fails to dim interest in Pa. Supreme Court
abstract: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court remains a popular career destination for ambitious judges and lawyers despite the heat they are feeling from the state-government pay raises. Dozens of people are considering  running in the May primary.

headline: Allentown schools evacuated after bomb threat
abstract: The Allentown School District evacuated all twenty-two of its schools after receiving bomb threats implying there were bombs in every school in the district. Parents were furious that they sent students back into the school only an hour after investigating. Superintendent Karen Angello, Lehigh Mayor Ed Pawlowski and Lehigh County District Attorney James B. Martin held a news conference where they insisted that the maintenance staff of the schools and fire department were sufficient to search for bombs, but parents disagree.

headline: End secrecy and protect the children
abstract: The Department of Human Services told the Inquirer to "trust them" as a response to the death of children whose families at one time had cases with the department. City Solicitor Romulo Diaz Jr. has refused to release DHS reviews of the deaths of these children. This city can not have this type of secrecy, they must be held accountable.

headline: City, county connect/Joint purchase of phone service called largest ever
abstract: The Pittsburgh and Allegheny Counties have asked companies to compete for a deal to provide service on nearly 8,000 phone lines to the two governments with the hope to save millions of dollars over a few years and increase implementation of cutting-edge technology like use of Internet to carry voices.

headline: Pay-raise votes haunt incumbents
abstract: Nearly all the incumbents who lost in last weeks primary voted for the pay raise increase in 2005. In Erie County the House members who voted for the pay raise that have in opposition in November include Matthew Good and John Evans. The County's other two House members had no primary opposition and will have no general election opposition.

headline: Architect: Kimmel has itself to blame
abstract: In response to a suit filed by the Kimmel Center against Rafael Vinoly architects, the firm responded that the delays and increased costs of the project were caused by the Kimmel's failure to make timely, fixed and consistent programmatic and budgetary decisions required of it. The Kimmel is struggling with around $30 million in debt incurred during its construction. A solution to reduce or eliminate debt is being pondered from outside the Kimmel's leadership by a task force that includes community leaders and representatives of PA Governor Ed Rendell. The case has been assigned to U.S. District Judge Jan E. DuBois.

headline: Erie's low crime figures gratifying
abstract: In a study done by Morgan Quinto Press, Erie was rated as the 218 most dangerous, the 154th safest. However in 2005, Erie was 243rd most dangerous, the 127th safest. There are good figures but they are based on police crime reports, which can be unreliable.

headline: Contract deadline nears at Philly papers
abstract: Philadelphia Newspapers largest union, the Newspaper Guild of Greater Philadelphia, might strike at midnight tomorrow. Leaders of the union said they are most upset about company proposals to freeze and take over the pension plan,  disregard seniority when it comes to layoffs and cut sick pay. Analysts said a strike would hurt both the company and the employees. The Guild represents more than 900 editorial and other workers at the two papers.

headline: Pennsylvania bluestone the bedrock of northeast Pa. economy
abstract: There are more than 100 quarries in Susquehanna County extracting Pennsylvania bluestone, it has become part of the culture. For many struggling famers the bluestone is how they keep afloat financially.

headline: Arts in class, too
abstract: The author of the letter writes that it is a great thing that Philadelphia is being considered a cultural institution. Linda Fiore, the executive director of the nonprofit Youth Audiences of Eastern Pennsylvania, believes that the art influence should reach into the schools too.

headline: Film office chief to live, work in California
abstract: The Pittsburgh Film Office will establish a Los Angeles base next month when Direct Dawn Keezer relocates to California. Russ Streiner, chairman of the film offices board of trustees said they are expanding to Los Angeles but are not technically opening an office.

headline: Ex-official fined for taking bribes from high-tech firms
abstract: Thomas McGraw, a former PA state government official, received kickbacks for helping high-tech firms obtain money designed to help companies relocate or expand in PA, the State Ethics Commission said yesterday. McGraw was ordered to pay $403,000 in restitution and fines for misusing his authority as technology initiative manager with the Governor's Action Team within the PA Department of Community and Economic Development.

headline: Pension caps would benefit taxpayers
abstract: This opinion article addresses what the author, Richard C. Dreyfus, calls the "looming financial crisis" that Pennsylvania's public employee pension plans will face because taxpayer costs to fund the State Employees Retirement System and the Public School Employees Retirement System are expected to increase from $1 billion in 2007 to close to $4.2 billion in 2012. Dreyfus suggests that policymakers revert to the basics of pensions and evaluate a number of options including increase employee contributions, increase taxpayer contributions or increase investment earnings. However, Dreyfus says that all three options are unreasonable, impractical or prohibited, so he endorses a suggestion by budget secretary Michael Masch under PA Governor Edward G. Rendell that calls for caps on employer contributions that would prevent exorbitant payments toward pensions.

headline: Barnes art collection $150M closer to Philly
abstract: The move of the Barnes museum from its home in Merion to the Philadelphia took a giant step yesterday. It was announced that a $150 million fund-raising campaign had been completed to move the Barnes. Of the $150 million, 100 will go towards construction of a museum and $50 million would be used to establish an endowment for the collection's financial support.

headline: Fire, lockdown at SCI Dallas
abstract: Seven employees of the State Correctional Institution in Dallas, PA, were taken to the hospital to be treated for fire inhalation on Sunday. The fire began in a second floor cell of the Restricted Housing Unit, and all inmates were evacuated and were not hurt. Jackson Township volunteer Fire Company Chief Dan Manzoni said the institution's Fire Emergency Response Team and other staff members extinguished the fire and he was not allowed into the prison.

headline: Philadelphia Inquirer, Daily News staffers to launch competing online paper if workers strike
abstract: The Newspaper Guild of Greater Philadelphia which is the largest union at Philadelphia's two biggest newspapers (Philadelphia Inquirer and Philadelphia Daily News) is planning to launch an online newspaper to compete with the company Web site if workers go on strike after midnight on Thursday. About 200 people are expected to staff the site, which is going to include the normal array of news. Nearly 700 of the more than 900 Guild members have filled out strike eligibility forms.

headline: Perzel sees light, backs disclosure
abstract: PA House Speaker John Perzel, the legislator whom the editorial board calls "most responsible" for the state's lack of lobbying disclosure laws, now supports a lobbyist disclosure law. Pennsylvania is the only state to lack such laws. The stat Senate attempted to pass a disclosure law in April. Since then, it has languished in a state House committee, as Perzel has refused to allow the bill to emerge for a vote. Perzel has repeatedly argued that no one cares about disclosure except for "do-gooders and newspapers." The editorial board suggests that the controversy over the pay raise passed by the state Legislature has embarrassed Perzel into changing his opinion.

headline: Bethlehem Area School District eyes box to drop weapons
abstract: The Bethlehem Area School District is considering whether to place an amnesty box at the main entrance of secondary schools, Freedom and Liberty, for students who "inadvertently" bring a weapon onto school property. Superintendent Joseph Lewis said at a meeting with the school board's Human Resources Committee that the idea does not violate a PA Department of Education law that calls for the expulsion of students who bring who carry a weapon to school. The policy would allow students to voluntarily deposit dangerous objects in the amnesty box before an employee knows about it. School board directors Loretta Leeson and Diane Rowe said parents should be allowed to pick up the item depending on what it is, a decision that will be left up to the police that will be collecting the amnesty boxes.

headline: Forensic lab gets grant from state
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell announced that Berks County's forensic laboratory is one of the four county labs that will receive state grants, totaling $400,000. The lab is run by county detectives in the district attorney's office and serves forty-three municipal police departments.

headline: Talk to Iran, yes
abstract: Professor J. David Slocum did a good job in his essay on the advisability of President Bush opening talks with Iran. There is a lot of evil associated with Iran but the reality is they haven't done anything to harm our country.

headline: Political activist's lawsuit targets lawmakers' perks
abstract: Political activist Gene Stilp has filed a lawsuit in PA Commonwealth Court, attempting to deny lawmakers the perks they receive, including per diems, vehicles leases and walking-around money the legislators provide to their districts. Stilp was an integral component in the fight to rescind the pay raise passed in the previous year. PA Governor Ed Rendell and six of the leaders of the PA General Assembly, as well as the state itself and the legislature, are named in the suit.

headline: Bill gives dropout more attention
abstract: The PA state House has just passed a bill that is headed for the Senate looking to create more direct means of discouraging dropouts.  PA Representative James Roebuck proposed the bill, which would require school districts to conduct mandatory exit interview with students who are planning to withdraw or who have accumulated 10 unexcused absences in a school year.  The idea is to head off their outward trip through personal, curricular or vocational counseling, and track the students.

headline: Four killings put 2006 total over -05 top
abstract: During the weekend four men in Philadelphia were killed in gun fights, this brings the total number of homicide victims to 384. This is four more than last year and there is still 21 days left. Blame is being put on gun control laws and on the sense of desperation felt by impoverished young African American men, who are responsible for the majority of the shootings.

headline: null
abstract: Nearly 22,000 Pennsylvanian Republicans who voted for Lynn Swann as the GOP nominee for governor withheld their support from U.S. Senator Rick Santorum in the  primary. This, despite the fact that both were unopposed. Political strategists think this could be a bad omen for US Representative Santorum who is running against Bob Casey in the fall.

headline: Political games kicking into gear
abstract: The columnist ridicules Republican U.S. Congressman Curt Weldon for claiming that the FBI's investigation of him is politically motivated. She says that it is highly unlikely that it could be politically motivated when Republicans control most of the federal government. She also speculates that Joe Sestak Bob Casey, and Governor Ed Rendell will defeat their Republican opponents.

headline: Bill would give city schools' elected board greater voice
abstract: Legislation proposed by PA Representative Ron Buxton would allow two elected school board members to have full voting rights in the Harrisburg Board of Control.

headline: Franco Harris, Bettis' parents among those with piece of action
abstract: The ownership stakes of investors in three groups competing for Pittsburgh's lone casino license were released, and some well-known names, such as former Steelers running back Franco Harris, Detroit businessman Don Barden with Motown singer William "Smokey" Robinson, and the parents of Steelers running back Jerome Bettis, Johnnie and Gladys Bettis.

headline: null
abstract: Republican gubernatorial candidate Lynn Swann reported an adjusted gross income of more than $1 million last year; most of the income came from his broadcasting job for ABC. PA Governor Rendell and his wife reported an adjusted gross income of $618,560 for last year.

headline: Political newcomer Seip: Key issues are health care, property taxes, energy
abstract: Democrat Tim Seip hopes to replace state Representative Bob Allen in the 125th District seat in the state House of Representatives. Seip is a socially conservative Democrat, favoring gun ownership and is pro-life. His campaign is based on property-tax relief, health-care reform and alternative energy. He also thinks legalizing gambling could add necessary revenue to the state.

headline: Board solicits taxing advice
abstract: The editorial board writes that school board members and district administrators have an impossible task of educating every child, preparing him or her for responsible adulthood, and ensuring that none are left behind.  Because state and federal officials don't want to alienate their constituents, they won't take the unpopular step of asking the public to pay for all this, so local administrators and school board members have to.

headline: Funding emergency
abstract: Many volunteer-run fire companies throughout the state of Pennsylvania are facing the problem of underfunding and having to purchase some supplies out of pocket. Volunteer firefighter ranks dropped more than 50 percent statewide over the past 25 years for varied reasons, including having limited personal time, working outside the communities where volunteers live and having other volunteering options. Some PA municipalities have included funding for fire departments in their property taxes, such as Mt. Lebanon, Ohio Township and Monroeville. PA Senator Sean Logan, co-chairman of the Senate's fire and emergency caucus, said the state needs to make some incentives for people to volunteer. Currently, the state provides $115 million in grants and loans to emergency responders, plus an additional $25 million in grants.

headline: '05 Chesco meetings become an issue for state Senate seat
abstract: Two meetings that were held last year between Chester County's two Republican commissioners are becoming an important issues in the waning days of the campaign for an open Senate seat. This becoming an issue because the meetings were secret and did not include the third commissioner, Andy Dinniman. Now Dinniman is running against Alchele, who was one of the commissioners involved in the meeting.

headline: Politicians paying own way to Super Bowl this year.
abstract: Officials from the Pittsburgh Steelers and the National Football League will no longer offer local public officials free trips to the Super Bowl. The team has made game tickets available to some public officials, including PA Governor Ed Rendell and Pittsburgh Mayor Bob O'Connor, at the $600 face value, a perk not offered to the public. Those who do attend will have to pay for transportation and hotel accommodations. City Stadium Authority and sports authority board members have also been offered tickets at face value. The sports authority owns Heinz Field and PNC Park and the Stadium Authority controls the land between the two stadiums. Barry Kauffman, executive director of Common Cause/PA said the situation is an improvement over the former practice of offering free tickets.

headline: Bonuses for PHEAA execs equal to 189 college grants
abstract: The PA government's highest-paid employee, the chief executive of PA's college student loan agency, Richard Willey, made $489,900 in 2005, about 7 percent more than the previous year.  He was paid $290,00- in salary and earned a bonus of nearly $179,900 according to a story in the Patriot News of Harrisburg.  Willey's salary nearly triples that of PA Governor Ed Rendell, who suggests that the executive of the PA Higher Education Assistance Agency could be used better to help students pay their college tuition.

headline: Gaming board official's background wasn't checked
abstract: The PA Gaming Control Board's Bureau of Investigations and Enforcement was unaware of the employment history of deputy director of the board Thomas Sturgeon. Following an altercation, Sturgeon was removed from his position as Allegheny County police superintendent. Though all employees of the gaming board are supposed to pass background investigations by state police, only recently did state troopers appear at Allegheny County police headquarters to inquire about Sturgeon's employment history. Since his appointment to the gaming agency, Sturgeon has been questioned about allegations that he was involved in the 1999 fixing of a drunken driving case for William Slater II, a close acquaintance.

headline: 2 members join city oversight board
abstract: Two new members will join Pittsburgh's five-person financial oversight board. PA Governor Rendell named Sister Grace Ann Geibel, former president of Carlow University, will replace John E Murray, Duquesne University's chancellor.  PA Republican House Speaker John Perzel appointed Pittsburgh labor boss Richard Stanizzo, business manager for the Pittsburgh building and Construction Trades Council. Stanizzo will replace former Chairman William Lieberman.

headline: Poll: Affair, alleged abuse could cost GOP seat
abstract: Republican Pennsylvania Congressman Don Sherwood's extramarital affair and possible abuse of a woman will most likely cost him the election  in a district normally safe for Republicans. According to a poll, his opponent Chris Carney is favored by a large margin. In this same district, U.S. Senator Rick Santorum is expected to win.

headline: Broader teaching capabilities proposed
abstract: The PA Board of Education approved a set of rules for certified teachers and teacher preparation programs that will emphasize instructions for students with disabilities or with limited proficiency in English. The rule changes also emphasize diversity training for teachers.

headline: Going great guns
abstract: A Downingtown resident writes that we all wish we could do something to stoop the carnage in the black communities such as Philadelphia's 17th Police District.  Young black men are killing incident people, and the community has far worse problems than guns. The author writes that the present system isn't working and we should try something different
