abstract: The author addresses the debate between PA and New Jersey lawmakers over the deepening of the Delaware River, a problem that has recently ratcheted up as PA Governor Ed Rendell, as chairman of the Delaware River Port Authority, took issue with New Jersey. US Senators Arlen Specter and Rick Santorum, both of PA, have entered the fray as well as local lawmakers from either side of the river. The author advocates that representatives from each state return to more congenial deliberations.

headline: G.C. Murphy sale feeds Renaissance
abstract: Pittsburgh's Urban Redevelopment Authority sold the former G.C. Murphy store and six nearby buildings to Milcraft Industries, a Washington County developer, in an effort to fuel Downtown's residential renaissance with new apartments, stores and restaurants. In the last 11 months the corridor has attracted $40 million in renovation efforts.

headline: Dr. Berube: Professor the right loves to hate
abstract: Penn State professor Michael Berube was labeled one of America's 101 most-dangerous academics by conservative activist David Horowitz. Dr. Berube admits to sometimes being cheeky and snarky but claims he encourages open discussions in his classroom and does not try to pass his beliefs onto his students.

headline: Swann predicts budget shortfall
abstract: Republican gubernatorial candidate Lynn Swann took aim at PA Governor Ed Rendell and the 2006-07 budget he recently signed, claiming that the governor is going to train the state's Rainy Day Fund by 60 percent. The Rainy Day fund was created to ensure that lawmakers don't have to raise taxes if the economy takes a turn for the worse and the state's revenues aren't enough to cover expenses.

headline: Bumps in the road
abstract: The PA Senate Transportation Committee supported a bill preventing PA from adopting stricter auto-emissions standards, sending it the full Senate for vote. PA Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Kathleen McGivney supports the improved regulations, stricter than federal guidelines, as a means to promote cleaner air in state. PA State Senator Roger Madigan supports working with the US Environmental Protection Agency rather than adopting the standards as proposed, which were predominantly the same as those enacted in California.

headline: Grants will aid Chesco efforts to save land
abstract: Two new stretches along the Brandywine Creek in Chester County will soon be available or canoe and kayak launches thanks to state grants announced yesterday. The grants are the first round of open-space funding from the &625 million bond issue known as Growing Greener. This is in response to the fact that Pennsylvania ranks sixth in the nation in in acreage lost to development, despite being 48th in population growth.

headline: Electronic voting system opposed
abstract: A coalition of voting-rights advocates filed a lawsuit in PA court asking that the electronic voting machines bought by PA counties be decertified before the November election and replaced with systems that ensure a paper record of ballots. The 26 plaintiffs, a cross section of voters from the so-called voting integrity movement as well as members of the Philadelphia branches of the Black Clergy and the National Association for the Advancement of Colored People, are suing PA Secretary of State Pedro Cortes in Commonwealth Court. The plaintiffs worry about hacking and vulnerability of computer malfunctions.

headline: Swann puts his message, policy ideas in a book
abstract: Republican gubernatorial candidate Lynn Swann said that he wants to have a conversation with the people of PA, but the conversation may cost voters $10 each.  Swann wrote a book called "My Plan for a Better Pennsylvania" to try to give voters a better grasp of who he is and where he stand on major policy issues, but the book will only be distributed for free at campaign events between now and Election day and they are asking for a $10 donation for it.

headline: Clean air victory for Pennsylvanians
abstract: The PA legislature concluded its lame duck session without voting on measures that would have blocked the Pennsylvania Clean Vehicles Program and the Rendell administration's mercury reduction plan. Both programs help make Pennsylvania a cleaner state for all its citizens, and PennEnvironment applauds the state leaders for working to put us on the right track.

headline: Green space plan proposed for city of Pittsburgh
abstract: Swaths of woods in the city would be permanently off limits to development under legislation to be introduce in city council by Jim Motznik. He would make 524 acres into greenways or additions to existing parks. All of that land is owned by the city or its authorities. City council is not likely to vote until next week.

headline: Early poll puts Swann, Rendell in tight battle
abstract: Recent popular opinion polls reveal that Republican gubernatorial candidate Lynn Swann is nearly tied with Democratic incumbent PA Governor Ed Rendell. Swann recently won over former Lieutenant Governor Bill Scranton in the GOP primary race. Polls also reveal a tightening in the U.S. Senate race, where PA Treasurer Robert P. Casey Jr. shows a double-digit lead over U.S. Senator Rick Santorum. Issues such as unemployment, the stock market and the economy continue to rank as the top concern of about one fourth of polled residents. Around 82 percent of polled residents believe  that at least some members of Congress are corrupt, a finding that is troubling for incumbent Santorum's campaign.

headline: Swann sails through Slate Belt
abstract: Republican gubernatorial candidate Lynn Swann spoke with Pennsylvania voters in Bangor, PA, and asked them if they are unhappy with the current political situation in the state. Swann, while speaking with some small business owners, said the state needs a political outsider with a business-like approach to government. Swann also told voters he wants to bring jobs and economic development to towns across the state.

headline: Cleanup plan driven by concerns over water
abstract: PA state officials plan to move a million tons of acid-bearing rocks out of the Buffalo Run and Waddle Creek watersheds. No technology has been found that can successfully treat the acid rock to the levels required in the two watersheds. The state will instead truck the sandstone from the State College side of Skytop to the Port Matilda side.

headline: Group to showcase 3 Downtown structures
abstract: The Pittsburgh History & Landmarks Foundation views a $2 million-plus project to revitalize three old buildings in the heart of Fifth and Forbes corridor Downtown Pittsburgh as a symbol of a new attitude toward preservation.  The Foundation officials hope to showcase the project, which involves the reuse of three buildings at Fifth Avenue and Market Street, when preservationalists nationwide gather in Pittsburgh for the National Preservation Conference.

headline: Early Run
abstract: The Allegheny County Board of Elections ruled that the mayoral election will be held in 2007 instead of 2009 as previously scheduled. Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl, who took over after the death of Mayor Bob O'Connor, will run again. The editorial board of the newspaper agrees with the decision to hold the election in 2007.

headline: Swann to Rendell: Give a clue on slots laws
abstract: Lynn Swann called on PA Governor Ed Rendell to list specific gambling laws he favors so the legislature can act on them, but Rendell's camp said the governor had done that several days ago.  Rendell's campaign spokesman, Dan Fee, accused Republicans of stalling reform and $1 billion in property-tax relief tied to slots revenue by refusing to return to Harrisburg to work on that legislature during their summer recess.

headline: Comedy and cruelty combined in atlatl
abstract: Senior Vice President for Campaigns of the Human Society of United States in Washington, Heidi Prescott writes regarding the PA Game Commission board's decision to give preliminary approval to allow deer hunting with an atlatl. The atlatl was abandoned in most parts of the world, between 10,000 and 20,000 BC, with the introduction of the bow and arrow, a much more accurate and lethal means of hunting. Prescott argues that the atlatl will be the most inhumane hunting weapon ever allowed in the state. The atlatl has a very high wounding rate, but low accuracy, leaving animals to die slow and painful deaths. Prescott urges the board to reverse its decision.

headline: Groveton Village Tech Center Opens
abstract: For Lynn Bonner, the opening of the $1.1 million Groveton Village Technology Center was the realization of a dream because he is the president of the residents council at the Allegheny county Housing Authority development.  Allegheny County Chief Executive Dan Onorato cut the ribbon on the technology center, the fifth of 10 planned countywide.

headline: Editorial - Power politics
abstract: The editorial board writes that the U.S. Supreme Court has opened a Pandora's Box of gerrymandering after a top court ruled that starts are free to redraw congressional districts wherever they want.  The case involved the redistricting of congressional seats in Texas after Republicans gained control of the Texas House of Representatives in 2002, which was largely the work of the then-House Majority Leader Tom DeLay.  The editorial speaks of PA's redrawing of districts in 2002.

headline: Swann wants chance to 'Get things done'
abstract: As gubernatorial candidate Lynn Swann was giving a speech denouncing the governor for his role in approving the pay-raise legislation a small plane began to fire up its propellers, creating a sound that overpowered Swann's voice. This moment epitomized Swann's uphill campaign to unseat Governor Rendell. When Swann initially entered the campaign his blank slate worked as a positive but as the campaign continued many realized that he was not prepared to run the 6th largest state in the country.

headline: Counties look at big bills for gypsy-moth spraying
abstract: The Department of Conservation and Natural Resources told Pennsylvania counties that they will only have to pay $25 an acre to spray areas infested with gypsy moths, and the state will fund the rest. The cost that counties must pay may decrease if the federal government also offers funding.

headline: Haven chooses to get power through consortium
abstract: The Schuylkill Haven Borough Council is working on a deal with American Municipal Power-Ohio to buy electricity at the fixed rate of $47.41 per megawatt hour for 2008 through 2012, a much lower rate than projected for the upcoming years. Councilman Paul Bedway said the borough's engineering firm recommended that the council approve the plan, which was offered by AMP-Ohio during the consortium's meeting on March 30. The Council has only seven days from the meeting to make the decision. At the council meeting, the council also went over the plan to have all Cressona fire hydrants leased to Schuylkill Haven.

headline: Editorial: Delayed ethics board appointments
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Street still hasn't submitted his nominations to fill the Ethics Board. He claims it will be done shortly. The editorial is not happy that it is taking this long to name the appointees. He is defying City Charter, because the deadline came and went weeks ago.

headline: Swann, Rendell scrap over pay raise; Business taxes, medical malpractice also topics in debate
abstract: The first debate between PA Governor Ed Rendell and Lynn Swann started slow, but ended up a lively scrap about who should bear the blame for the infamous pay raise on July 2005. Rendell called Swann a hypocrite for faulting him on the pay raise but not others involved. The issues discussed in the debate are enumerated in the rest of the article.

headline: Couple severely injured in deer attack
abstract: PA state policemen Corporal Todd Brian and trooper Stephen E. Wilcox responded to a 911 call to find Linda Yost and Frank Rishel severely injured by a 6-point white tail buck. The officers were forced to shoot the buck, the carcass of which is now in custody of the PA State Game Commission to be checked for rabies and other diseases. Warren “Quig” Stump, Commission Northcentral Region Law Enforcement officer, says the officers saved the victims’ lives.

headline: Hundreds of houses planned for farm in growing township
abstract: Developers have purchased farmland outside of Carlisle, PA and are pursuing the construction of 300 to 400 homes on the land though they have yet to receive clearance from Middlesex Township.

headline: Editorial: Delco Democrats make the first leap
abstract: Bryan Lentz recently announced that he would leave his U.S. Congressional campaign while he would seek to unseat incumbent sate Representative Tom Gannon, leaving Joseph A. Sestak Jr. as the only opponent to U.S. Representative Curt Weldon. The truce was reportedly pushed by PA Governor Ed Rendell, who needs a united Democratic front if he is to win in the upcoming gubernatorial election. The editorial board commends the Democrats for refusing to engage in in-party fighting and instead presenting a unified front against their electoral opponents.

headline: Swann's celebrity not platform, draws crowd
abstract: Roughly 100 people gathered outside Agolino's restaurant Sunday hoping to meet Republican gubernatorial candidate Lynn Swann. Many of the fans said they were there to see him as a former Pittsburgh Steelers player and not as a candidate.  Swann is trying to unseat incumbent PA Governor Ed Rendell.  Swann wants to reduce the size of the legislature, cut taxes, preserve farmland and streamline farming regulations.

headline: Couple severely injured in deer attack
abstract: When state police responded to a call about an aggressive deer they found a six-point whitehall buck straddling a screaming woman in her back yard, repeatedly goring her face, neck and chest; a man lay near by with multiple wounds, in and out of consciousness. The local game officer was able to shoot the buck without causing additional harm to the woman.

headline: Ideas are sought on natural areas
abstract: Residents of Cambria, Somerset and Bedford counties will have the opportunity to offer ideas on how to utilize green spaces in the surrounding areas, Jeffrey Kloss, director of the Bedford County Planning Commission, said. The meetings are sponsored by the Southern Alleghenies Greenways and Open Space Network Project. Bradford Beigay, director of the Cambria County Planning Commission, said the effort to evaluate a region's park projects and potential improvements is the first of its kind in a state. The meetings are being held and open to the public because the commissions want to have the public's involvement, Fred Querry, assistant director of the Southern Alleghenies Planning and Development Commission, said.

headline: Editorial: O'Donnell in the 25th / A solid veteran must bow before winds of change
abstract: The editorial endorses Steve O'Donnell of Monroeville as the Democratic candidate for the 25th Legislative District. The editorial begins by remarking on how PA Representative Joseph F. Markosek, currently of the 25th district, apologized for voting for the pay raise legislation in July 2005 and returned the entire amount. Though the board comments on the positive developments Markosek has made for his district, it is disheartened that Marksosek did not now better judgment at the time of the pay raise. The editorial then describes the two candidates running against him in the Democratic primary, Daniel Mator and Steve O'Donnell, both of Monroeville.

headline: Swann's hour of crisis
abstract: The opinion article looks at the faults in Lynn Swann's campaign for governor in the 2006 election, the biggest of which is his campaign team. The author, Salena Zito, said that Swann's campaign team is too infatuated with him and his fame that it cannot focus on what is necessary for a victory and struggles to tell him how to handle himself. Zito said Swann is unprepared for the election season, especially with respect to his opponent, PA Governor Edward G. Rendell.

headline: Danger Lurks
abstract: Tom Rathbun, a spokesman for the PA Department of Environmental Protection says that PA's waterways have been made more perilous by the summer's flooding. Harmless looking water can lead to debilitating injuries or death for novice and experienced swimmers alike.

headline: Impact-fee bill would aid Poconos
abstract: PA Representatives Stephen Maitland, Pat Fleagle and Rob Kauffman have proposed legislation to give municipal officials in fast-growing counties authority to levy building excise fees of up to $13,000 per house in smaller new developments and up to $26,000 per house in large-scale new developments. Seventeen of Pennsylvania's 67 counties fit the bill's definition of fast-growth counties. The bill sponsors say local officials need "special powers" to address problems created by rapid growth, such as demands on public schools, police, emergency services, roads and water and sewage systems. The PA General Assembly has debated impact fee bills for 20 years but few have been specific as this.

headline: Editorial: Pay raise P.S./ Supreme Court looks venal approving its share
abstract: The decision by the PA Supreme Court to reinstate plump raises for itself and 1,200 judges across the state may seem just bad, but there's some good too. Justices finally give warning t state lawmakers that they've got to stop sneaking midterm pay raises through unvouchered expenses. The state's constitution prohibits diminishing judges' wages during their terms according to the Supreme Court, but the people do not like this decision and are trying to figure out a way to reverse it.

headline: Swann's run improving, analysts say
abstract: After several early missteps in the campaign and trailing PA Governor Ed Rendell by double-digits in the polls and millions of dollars in fundraising, Republican challenger Lynn Swann has just weeks to get it together.  Rob Carter of West Philadelphia says that Swann was being used by Republicans just to throw somebody out there.  Former New York Mayor Rudy Giuliani campaigned for Swann in King of Prussia.

headline: DEP outlines new guidelines for water alerts
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Protection will now require water companies to adopt new procedures to notify customers when there is a threat to drinking-water supplies. Water companies also will be required to work with local emergency management agencies, police departments and fire companies. The new regulations were issued in response to a fluoride leak that contaminated the water supply for about 34,000 homes and businesses on the West Shore. The PA state Public Utility Commission ordered an investigation into how effectively the company notified the public during emergencies. The PA Environmental Quality Board has responsibility for final approval of the regulations.

headline: Leader praises LVEDC
abstract: Jan Armfield was introduced as chairwoman of the Lehigh Valley Economic Development Corp. and expressed her belief that the Lehigh Valley will continue to express strong economic growth, encouraged by the group's impact.

headline: Editorial: State races offer plenty of interesting battles
abstract: The editorial board endorses state legislature candidates for the 2006 election. They endorse Ted Erickson, Thaddeus Kirkland, Steve Barrar, and Bryan Lentz.

headline: Sweet Valley resident eyes 117th
abstract: Ross Township supervisor Stanford Davis will run for the 117th seat that will be opened up by the departure of PA State Representative George Hasay. Davis said he would focus on job creation, tax reform and increased emergency services funding.

headline: DOT, DEP to answer questions at meeting
abstract: Representatives of the PA Department of Transportation and the PA Department of Environmental Protection will make public presentations and take questions on the state's $40 million plan for a permanent cleanup of the acid-rock drainage hazard at Skytop Mountain. These presentations will take place during the Patton Township supervisors' regularly scheduled meeting. Township supervisor chairman Elliot Abrams said supervisors decided to have the meeting for township residents who may want to express views on whether township money should be spent for the benefit of residents affected by acid drainage or for a ClearWater Conservancy campaign to preserve land from development.

headline: Latrobe brewery's boosters calling for boycott
abstract: InBev, a Belgeum Brewery recently sold Latrobe based Rolling Rock to Anheuser-Busch. In Response, leaders of 15 Westmoreland County union locals are tying to launch a nationwide boycott. They encourage all beer drinkers to drink as much Rolling Rock as possible until the end of July when the deal is complete; then they encourage everyone to boycott everything that both InBev and Anheuser-Busch produce.

headline: Ed's senior moment to forget
abstract: The writer thinks that U.S. Senate candidate Bob Casey should let PA Senator Rick Santorum "talk himself out of a job". The writer criticizes PA Governor Ed Rendell for his comment regarding seniors having "gray lives". He also mocks U.S. Senator Rick Santorum's analogy between Lord of the Rings and the war in Iraq. He criticizes Harrisburg Mayor Reed and the city council for concealing the $11 million budget deficit.

headline: Tainted spinach found in region
abstract: A bag of Dole brand baby spinach purchase din Indiana County was contaminated with the same strain E. coli that has sickened more than 175 people across the country. The person sickened by the spinach would not disclose where the spinach was purchased, but said it was bought September 8. So far eight PA residents had contracted the E. coli strain.

headline: Santorum gets favorable coverage
abstract: Letter to editor claims that York Daily record gave biased coverage to Santorum in the Santorum and Casey debate on Meet the Press.

headline: Dredging Delaware would waste time, money
abstract: The author disputes the paper's support for PA Governor Ed Rendell's support of dredging the Delaware River, finding the dredging unnecessary.

headline: Look down
abstract: The author of the letter writes that in all the praise of Philadelphia on the move, people forgot to discuss how dirty and disgusting our city was. It was much dirtier than such events in Chicago, L.A., and New York.

headline: Employee's suit claims sex bias in PHEAA pay
abstract: A PA Higher Education Assistant Agency employee claims men working for the agency receive higher pay than women for the same job.  Janet Johnson of Lower Paxton Twp, made the claim in a lawsuit filed in US Middle District Court.

headline: The minimum wage: Playing games
abstract: The editorial board asks the US House members to stop playing games with the state and federal minimum wage.  PA  Representatives Melissa Hart, Tim Murphy, Phil English and Bill Schuster voted for raising the federal wage by $2.10 to $7.25 over three years, and two Democrats, John Murtha and Mike Doyle, voted against the measure.  It passed.

headline: Santorum gets favorable coverage
abstract: Letter to editor claims that York Daily record gave biased coverage to US Senator Santorum in the Santorum and Casey debate on Meet the Press.

headline: Drought warning no worry in region
abstract: Though the PA Department of Environmental Protection has put the entire state under a drought watch, many farmers, like Harold V. Wiser from Girard, PA, are still planning on planting their harvests as usual. DEP Secretary Kathleen A. McGinty said precipitation levels were well below normal over the past two months in about two-thirds of the state's 67 counties. Freda Tarbell, spokeswoman for DEP's regional office in Meadville, said that the intention is that the DEP may be able to cut down on necessary action later if people make conscious changes to their water consumption now. Local Erie officials said they are not aware of any area waterways that are significantly lower than they should be at this time of year. The article then goes on to suggest conservation tips for citizens and describe Erie precipitation by the numbers.

headline: Mandalay official: No plans to move Triple A franchise
abstract: Richard Neumann, Mandalay Baseball Properties vice president of development, made it clear that he had no desire to move Triple A team from Luzerne county. Prior to this statement Luzerne county officials had fears that the team would move. Mandalay, will run the team under a management contract with Lackawanna County, will have the right to buy the team for between $13 million and $16.4 million, depending on when the purchase takes place.

headline: Ending the impasse over state troopers
abstract: There was a problem with limited state troopers because they were forced to do jobs that were not completely essential and they were not allowed to hire more troopers. The idea of hiring civilians to do those jobs did not go over well with some officials. Finally, Rendell signed a bill that allowed the hiring of 90 new troopers.

headline: The plot thickens in move of Barnes art
abstract: Montgomery County Judge Stanley R. Ott ruled that a collection of famous Post-Impressionist and early Modern paintings would be moved from its home in a wealthy Philadelphia suburb to a site downtown. It came to light that the PA legislature had already passed a bill allocating $100 million in funds to move the paintings, and PA Governor Ed Rendell signed the bill. When the appropriations appeared in the state budget, the state capitol was in the middle of a transition.Former Governor Tom Ridge left his position after being asked by President Bush to direct the Office of Homeland Security, and Lieutenant Governor Mark Schweiker took over. Governor Ed Rendell also announced that a $25 million state grant would go towards the relocation of the paintings.

headline: Santorum is desperate, Casey says
abstract: PA state treasurer and U.S. Senate candidate Bob Casey said to the union Teamsters Local 429  that Santorum's campaign ad implying that a victory for Casey could result in a nuclear attack proves that Santorum is desperate. The union is supporting Casey because of his promise to raise the minimum wage and lower health care costs. Casey also promised to help the state's seniors by fixing the Medicare prescription plan. Also speaking to the union was Lois Murphy, who is running for Congress against Representative James W. Gerlach.

headline: Family buries miner killed in explosion
abstract: A forty-three year old miner, Dale Reightler was killed by an explosion in a mine shaft. The U.S. Mine Safety and Health Administration, federal Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco and Firearms, and the PA Department of Environmental Protection's Bureau of Mine Safety are investigating the mine to see what caused the explosion.

headline: More condos planned in Easton
abstract: Ashley Development Corp. of Bethlehem proposed another condominium complex in downtown Easton; it consists of a $40 million plan to demolish the former Marquis Theatre and erect a nine-story high-rise with 143 condominiums. Ashley's received a $1.75 million check last week from PA Governor Rendell for the transformation of a department store into a condo.

headline: Erickson eludes Democratic shift
abstract: Despite the Democratic momentum and taint of last year's pay raise, state Senator Edwin Erickson was able to defeat Springfield attorney Michael Farrell in the 26th District. This was a seat that the Democrats thought they might be able to pick up. Erickson won by a 52-48 margin.

headline: The problem with Rendell: Gov. Sham Shaman
abstract: The editorial board ridicules PA Governor Edward G. Rendell in the tactics he uses in his gubernatorial campaign that take out parts of Pittsburgh Tribune-Review articles to twist the words so it seems that Lynn Swann, his Republican challenger and a Pittsburgh resident, is not supported by what would be his natural base. The editorial article cites the Manhattan Institute's City Journal in saying that during Rendell's time as mayor of Philadelphia, the city solved it's "age-old image problem" but barely addressed its "reality problem." The article also cites the tax raises Rendell has speared or enacted during his time as governor.

headline: Santorum keeps focus on defense
abstract: U.S. Senator Rick Santorum has been speaking on the issues of defense and the War on Terror in the weeks leading up to the election. He criticizes his opponent Bob Casey as being inexperienced and weak on these issues. Bob Casey recently accepted the endorsement of the Fire Fighters Union, Local 22.

headline: Game Commission could drown in sea of bills
abstract: Senate Bill 868 scares the PA Gaming Commission, it could potentially cost the agency $3.4 million by tripling annual in lieu of tax payments to counties, municipalities, and school districts. Currently the commission has to pay 40 cents per acre to the municipalities where the land is located but that fee could go to $1.20.

headline: More than just a pretty face needed to help Norristown
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell discussed the amount of grant money given to the state and asked why the money hasn’t been spent. A new parking garage will begin being built as a result of this. Starting the construction at the beginning of winter is just the beginning of the problems with the garage the editorial discusses. It also outlines the problems with subsidized housing.

headline: Ethics board raises campaign donor limits
abstract: The newly formed Philadelphia Board of Ethics jumped into the mayor's race by clarifying how much money contributors can donate to candidates. They raised the individual limit from $2,500 to $5,000 and the business limit from $10,000 to $20,000.

headline: The real scandal.
abstract: House of Representatives Majority Leader Sam Smith told the PA Newspaper Association's government affairs conference that multiple factors led him to conclude the House should consider lobbying legislation. Due to what the editorial board calls a "wrong-headed" Supreme Court ruling in 2002, PA is the only state in the nation that does not have a law covering lobbyists. The state Senate maintains a rule requiring lobbyists to register, but there is no mandatory disclosure in the House or executive branch. The editorial board suggests that the Washington scandal involving lobbyist Jack Abramoff has embarrassed state lawmakers into addressing the issue. The board believes that it is a "scandal" that residents can thank Ambramoff, not their lawmakers, for any future lobbyist reporting laws.

headline: Santorum keys on "Islamic fascism"
abstract: U.S. Senator Rick Santorum criticized Bush for refusing to paint the war in Iraq as part of a larger war against what Santorum calls "Islamic fascism". He says that Bush is afraid to offend the State Department or our allies in the Middle East. Santorum is most likely distancing himself from Bush in an effort to win the election against his opponent, state treasurer Bob Casey.

headline: Global warming poses dangers that don't convey easily to action
abstract: Global warming poses a greater threat than terrorism but it is more difficult to convey the same sense of urgency. A lot of Americans understand global warming but don’t do enough to counteract the problem. Global warming is evident when you see that 19 of the 20 hottest years have occurred since 1980.

headline: New environmental center offers varied views of Lake Erie
abstract: Erie's new Tom Ridge Environmental Center opens officially tomorrow morning. It will offer many new ways to view Lake Erie and the surrounding landscape. One is a 75 foot observation tower, another is an entire wing devoted to research. This is the first such center on any of the great lakes.

headline: Ethics board raises campaign donor limits
abstract: The newly formed Philadelphia Board of Ethics jumped into the mayor's race yesterday by clarifying how much money contributors can donate to candidates. They raised the individual limit from $2,500 to $5,000 and the business limit from $10,000 to $20,000.

headline: The real voting problem: third-party or independent candidates are shut out
abstract: The biggest problem with the 2006 Pennsylvania elections is that there were no third parties on the tickets. This is because they are required to get 67,000 ballot access signatures whereas many states only require 2,000. People need to show the legislature that they want to see this rule changed.

headline: Santorum kicks off final campaign push; Casey; rallies Dems
abstract: U.S Senator Rick Santorum returned to Johnstown, Pennsylvania, his parents hometown, to kick off his 22-county "Keep Up the Fight Tour." Former Pennsylvania Governor Tom Ridge was there urging the crowd to vote for Santorum, discussing how you need someone like Santorum out there since it’s such a dangerous world.

headline: Greene County wind turbine planned
abstract: Motorists traveling on Interstate 79 might notice something new on the horizon near the Waynesburg interchange in the coming months.  The Southwestern Pennsylvania Water Authority (SPWA) in Jefferson Borough has partnered up with the PA Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) to erect a small wind turbine on a hillside along the interstate to power communication systems in Green County and to try and spark people's interest in energy alternatives.

headline: New price tag: 165.5M
abstract: The Watt and Shand building is coming and down, and the cost of its replacement on Penn Square, a hotel and convention center, is expected to be $165.5 million, which is an increase of $10.1 million. Project developers said they did not need to find new revenue to cover the cost because the sources and uses match up and there hasn’t' been any increase in hard construction costs. A fall 2008 opening is planned for the meeting center and 300-room Marriott hotel.

headline: Evans chills firefighters' union
abstract: Elmer Money of the Northeast got a hankering to run next year as a Republican for an at-large seat on Philadelphia City Council after seeing block after block decay on a train ride to Suburban Station one day.

headline: Undemocratic Law
abstract: A resident from Shiremanstown writes that the U.S. Third Circuit Court of Appeals rules that PA election law does not "impose a severe burden" on third parties and independents, but the author feels that this is untrue due to the amount of signatures Independents and Third Parties need in comparison to Republicans and Democrats.  He thinks that PA has the most undemocratic election laws in the country.

headline: Santorum outpaces Casey in cash, but lags in polls
abstract: US Senator Rick Santorum continues to trail his Democratic opponent for the 2006 Senate election, PA Treasurer Robert P. Casey Jr. in the polls, but Santorum maintains a 2-1 cash advantage. The US Senate election is expected to be the top race in the country partly because Santorum is the number 3 Republican leader in the Senate and has close ties to US President George W. Bush. Santorum, with the help of Bush, Karl Rove and DC lobbyists, has raised $16 million thus far for the entire election cycle, while Casey's campaign, with support from former Secretary of State Madelina Albright, New York Senator Hillary Clinton and political consultant James Carville, has raised $8 million. Political analyst G. Terry Madonna said Casey does not have to match Santorum dollar for dollar as long as he can afford to campaign visibly on television and the radio.

headline: Group protests cleanup plan
abstract: Petitions signed by 1,124 people opposed to the state's plan to move massive piles of acid-generating rocks from Skytop into the Balk Eagle Valley have been sent to PA Governor Ed Rendell, leadings of a new grassroots group. The opponents say the rocks should be moved to a watershed near Philipsburg that's already polluted with acid mine drainage. Their quest for political support comes as the PA Departments of Transportation and Environmental Protection are putting finishing touches on plans PennDOT says must be in place before long-delayed construction of Interstate 99 at Skytop can resume.

headline: North Broad St. is looking up
abstract: The Philadelphia City Planning Commission unveiled a redevelopment scheme yesterday for North Broad Street. Streets Commissioner Clarena Tolson said one of the goals is to make North Broad Street safe for pedestrians and motorists and pleasing to the eye. A brochure displaying the new design described it as expanding and celebrating arts, culture and entertainment. Warren E. Huff, acting deputy executive director of the Planning Commission, said the project will improve Philadelphia's image as pedestrian-friendly. A significant portion of the project will be funded by private investors, Philadelphia City Councilman Darrell L. Clarke said. The goal is to have the redevelopment project completed within 10 years, Karen Lewis, executive director of Avenue of the Arts Inc., said.

headline: Evans chills firefighters' union
abstract: PA Representative Dwight Evans may have to count out the firefighters' union for help if he runs for mayor next year. That's because Evens isn't giving the union the support it wants in its effort to get Philadelphia Mayor Street to accept an arbitration award that would raise firefighters' pay by 10 percent.

headline: Under the Dome
abstract: The article talks about the upcoming gubernatorial race between incumbent PA Governor Ed Rendell and challenger Lynn Swann.  Rendell says that state lottery sales increased by 16 percent last year to nearly $3.1 billion, which could lead to the expansion of prescription and tax rebate programs for senior citizens.

headline: Santorum RV tour hits friendly central PA cities
abstract: US Representative has a RV tour of PA for a part family vacation, part political campaign. Polls show that the Democratic challenger PA Treasurer Bob Casey has a small lead over the two-term incumbent.  Santorum stopped in Johnstown and Tipton, towns outside of central PA, which usually votes Republican.

headline: Growing Greener funds to be rewarded
abstract: Lebanon County commissioners will award Growing Greener Environmental, a community group, funds that will be used for environmental projects. Lebanon Valley Conservancy, Rails to Trails and Union Canal Tunnel Park are other environmental groups vying for state aid.

headline: Ohio man exploring purchase of Penguins
abstract: Jim Renacci, the mayor of a small Ohio town, and a successful business man is thinking about buying the Pittsburgh Penguins. If he is the owner he plans to keep them in Pittsburgh, even though there are rumors about the team moving to another city. Isle of Capri Casinos inc. in partnership with the Penguins is pledging $290 million to build an area if it wins the city casino license, if that happens the Penguins would definitely stay in Pittsburgh. Governor Rendell has developed an alternative proposal called "Plan B" which would require the Penguins to contribute $4 million a year to the construction, the Penguins have not committed to this.

headline: Even brand name falls to celebrity
abstract: William Scranton III withdrew from the race for the Republican gubernatorial nomination. The editorial board argues that the race has taken as its primary focus not the well being of the commonwealth, but instead the celebrity of rival Lynn Swann. The board believes that the candidates have played to several key Republican State Committee members rather than to the electorate. The board argues that Swann has avoided not only policy debates but even statements about his political beliefs or governing philosophy due to the celebrity gained from his former professional athletic career.

headline: The view from the lowest political rung
abstract: The opinion article written by Stu Bykofsky pokes fun at the hierarchy of politics, especially in the city of Philadelphia. He explains his reasoning for running for committeeman, which he calls the "lowest rung on the political ladder."

headline: Santorum stresses security at rally
abstract: U.S. Senator Rick Santorum spoke at a Wyomissing Fire Department during his campaign tour, and discussed the threat of terrorism. He questioned the foreign policy judgment of his opponent Bob Casey. Casey is currently leading in the polls.

headline: Hearing slated for DEP permit
abstract: The PA state Department of Environmental Protection is going to hold a public hearing to hear comments on a proposed truck maintenance facility in Cass Township. The Minersville Water Authority has raised concerns that runoff from the site could harm its watershed and jeopardize the borough's water supply.

headline: Pier plan floated in Columbia
abstract: Bridge pilings that remind us of a silent testament to the fire that kept Confederate troops from crossing into Lancaster County might someday serve a new purpose becoming part of a pier for walking and fishing. This is just one of the plans for the revitalization of the region.

headline: Even Rendell has noticed Swann's candidacy
abstract: The author supports PA Republican gubernatorial candidate Lynn Swann against PA Governor Ed Rendell, citing Rendell's track record as reason for new leadership in the state's executive branch.

headline: They’ve gotta duke it out for victory
abstract: The author feels that the Republican candidates for PA Governor, Lynn Swann and former PA Lieutenant Governor Bill Scranton, are both facing a huge disadvantage in taking on sitting-PA Governor Ed Rendell but that both are strong candidates. The author feels the two, especially the underdog Scranton, would be best served by having a contentious, public primary race in order to attract attention.

headline: Santorum talks tough on dredging
abstract: US Senator Rick Santorum, R-PA, said he would block any legislation that could benefit New Jersey, the latest politician to enter the dispute between PA and NJ over the deepening of the Delaware River. PA Governor Ed Rendell has threatened to hold up the passage of the Delaware River Port Authority's budget if the plan to deepen the river by five feet is not passed, though NJ opposes the passage and questions the figures PA politicians have cited as the economic benefits.

headline: Is this what to expect?
abstract: The editorial speaks to a recent spillage of a trash truck near Rush Township that tipped over on the highway and spewed garbage across the roadway of I-80. The editorial board agrees with opponents of a landfill in Rush Township who warn that the landfill will increase traffic, accidents and pollution.

headline: PNC Firstside Park creates connections with labyrinthine landscape
abstract: With 101 trees chosen for the park, PNC Firstside Park will be an urban forest on a Downtown Pittsburgh block bounded by Boulevard of Allies, Grant Street, First Avenue, and Ross Street.  Construction has begun, and completion is expected in Spring 2007.  The lot is the former home of the Public Safety Building.

headline: Executives at PHEAA get raises totaling 6%
abstract: The executives of the PA Higher Education Assistance Agency received pay increases amounting to 6%, justifying the high salaries by pointing to the recent success of the agency.

headline: Tightening races boost state GOP's confidence
abstract: PA Republicans believe the political environment might be shifting in their favor before the November elections. Polls are tightening in the US Senate race and lower gas prices give them hope. Rick Santorum feels the media has been biased against him, but is feeling more hopeful. The governor's race is even hopeful for Swann.

headline: Santorum, Casey ply the name game during debate
abstract: US Senator Santorum and Robert Casey have been calling each other Bobby ad Rick to make the other appear less credible. The article discussions and reviews their debate strategies, but ultimately says the debate didn't matter much because not many people were watching.

headline: January is National Radon Action Month
abstract: With the nation marking National Radon Action Month, the author informs citizens that PA has the highest level of indoor radon in the nation, largely due to the state's geology. The US Environmental Protection Agency and the PA Department of Environmental Protection are urging citizens to buy testing kits and check their home levels.

headline: Probe the Pete / The auditor general is right to take a look
abstract: PA  General Jack Wagner may look into the cost overruns on the construction of the Petersen Events Center at the University of Pittsburgh. He wants to make sure that the public's $66 million spent on the project wasn't mishandled. It was originally going to cost $35 million but they made the building twice as big as originally planned.

headline: Ex-Fumo aides plead not guilty in federal probe
abstract: Two former PA Senate computer technicians, Leonard Luchko and Mark Eister pleaded not guilty to charges that they tried to thwart a federal probe of PA Senator Vincent Fumo in front of US Magistrate Judge L. Felipe Restrepo.  US District Judge William H Yohn Jr. filed an order scheduling the trial to begin January 8.

headline: To sine die or not...
abstract: Some Harrisburg groups have said the PA Senate is scuttling its post-election voting session this year, but top Senate aides say that's not the case. The confusion may be caused by the absence of the Senate schedule for November, which some groups have interpreted as the Senate doing away with its post-election, lame-duck session known as sine die. The calendar hasn't been released because they are unsure if they will use the one week in November available or not.

headline: Santorum's 10-debate offer is Casey trap, Sandals aide says
abstract: Alan Sandals, a possible Democratic opponent to US Senator Rick Santorum in the 2006 Congressional elections, said that Santorum's offer to debate his rivals is empty rhetoric and is aimed only at setting up Robert P. Casey Jr., the presumed Democratic candidate for Santorum's position. Sandals said he accepted an offer made by Santorum's campaign to debate the Democratic primary winner 10 times before the November elections, though he has received no correspondence back from Santorum's campaign. Virginia Davis, a campaign spokeswoman for Santorum, said the offer was made only to Casey. However, Santorum has since extended an offer to debate with any of the three Democrats running in the primary, including University of the Arts in Philadelphia professor Chuck Pennacchio, depending on who wins the primary.

headline: Kuchera wins $391,500 grant
abstract: Kathleen McGinty, secretary of the PA Department of Environmental Resources, issued a $391,500 grant to Kuchera Defense Systems that will be put towards developing a Center for Excellence for Advanced Energy Systems Manufacturing. The center will develop a pilot manufacturing facility for fuel cell assembly.

headline: Project will impact Perry
abstract: The editorial board suggests that, in light of a proposed 900-home development in eastern Perry County, the first thing Penn Township Board of Supervisors should do is to request professional assistance from the Governor's Center for Local Government Services. A New Jersey developer has bought over 1,000 sloped acres in the township and proposes to build a development that could nearly double the township's current population. The board believes that residential housing adds more service costs to a locality than it offsets with taxes. Traffic would be impacted heavily to the point of requiring significant upgrades. The board believes that this is a project that requires exceptional scrutiny from the planning, engineering and legal standpoints.

headline: Ex-treasurer, others eye Casey post
abstract: At least four candidates have expressed interest in filling the state Treasury position, which was left open when Bob Casey was elected to the Senate. Governor Rendell said he will only appoint someone who promises not to run again in 2008; he is doing this because the appointee will have to be confirmed by the Republican-controlled Senate, which would not want to give a Democratic candidate the advantage of incumbency in 2008.

headline: To win, Swann, heed this advice
abstract: In February of 2006 Gubernatorial Candidate Lynn Swann was only down to PA Governor Rendell by 3 points in the polls, now he is down by 14. There are two  major reasons for this; Rendell has utilized television commercials much more effectively and secondly, Swann's candidacy has been very week.

headline: Scarnati, Pileggi to lead state Senate
abstract: Senator Joe Scannati was nominated by Republicans as the Senate's first new president pro tempore in 12 years. Senator Dominic Pileggi was selected as Senate GOP floor leader, replacing David Brightbill.

headline: Mercury falling? / Environmental efforts weather the political storm
abstract: Pennsylvanians who care about environmental issues had reasons to be thankful on the last legislative session of the year. Firstly, the House adjourned without approving a Senate bill that would have blocked Pennsylvania from adopting tougher emissions standards for new cars and light trucks starting in model year 2008. Because the Senate failed to act, the second piece of good news is that Pennsylvania is poised to go beyond federal regulations in enforcing new regulations on mercury emissions from power plants.

headline: Public safety building for sale?
abstract: Harrisburg Mayor Stephen Reed is selling the city's public safety building in an effort to rescue the city from a multi-million-dollar deficit. The building currently is home for the city's police and fire officials, but Reed is proposing to sell the office building to another city agency - the Harrisburg Redevelopment Authority. Harrisburg would reap a $10.5 million purchase price from the authority.

headline: Ex-VA. Guv stumps for Dems here
abstract: Former Virginia Governor Mark Warner brought a little star power to the three local Democratic congressional candidates, while planting seeds that could his potential 2008 presidential bid.  Warner expressed his support of Patrick Murphy for Congress, as well as Lots Murphy and Joe Sestak .

headline: Tom Ferrick Jr.: Rendell tries best to woo heartland
abstract: PA Governor Rendell attending the 28th annual Oil Heritage Parade, handing out a $217,000 economic-development check to a small electronics firm in Tippery, PA.  Rendell is trying to get votes from the Republican town.  Rendell is doing his best to woo the folks in the heartland of PA to beat his rival Republican Lynn Swann.

headline: Scranton aide fired for remark
abstract: Republican gubernatorial candidate Bill Scranton's campaign manager James Seif was fired after remarking on the PA Cable Network that primary challenger Lynn Swann was "the rich white guy in the campaign." Seif admitted guilt and apologized. Seif was a former secretary of the PA Department of Environmental Protection. Scranton has been losing ground to Swann in the race for the Republican nomination. The article includes the text from the call-in show when the remark was made.

headline: Mine crisis evokes comparisons to Quecreek
abstract: As rescuers seek 13 miners trapped after an explosion in a West Virginia mine, some PA residents were reminded of the flood at the Quecreek mine in Somerset County in 2002, which trapped 9 miners.

headline: Region praised for readying sites for commercial use
abstract: When Chuck Henschel visited Pittsburgh region in 2002 he found a fragmented government, no regional focus, and very few shovel0ready sites for development. Four years later he says much of this has changed for the better. Henschel was part of the 2002 panel assembled by the Urban Land Institute a nonprofit real estate development and land use policy collaborative that urged local leaders to work together to jump start regional development.

headline: Fattah's run n not yet official
abstract: U.S. Representative Chaka Fattah screened three new promotional videos for volunteer members of his mayoral exploratory committee. He expects to receive the final findings in November.

headline: Tom Ridge helps Lynn Swann fundraise
abstract: Former Governor of Pennsylvania Tom Ridge through his weight behind Republican gubernatorial candidate Lynn Swann as he went campaigning with him. Swann will need the help, as of May 1 PA Governor Rendell had more than five times the amount of money on hand than Swann did.

headline: Scranton drops out of race for governor
abstract: Only days before the Republican State Committee's planned meeting to anoint a GOP candidate for the primary, former PA Lieutenant Governor Bill Scranton quit the governor's race, leaving former Pittsburgh Steeler Lynn Swann as the likely Republican nominee to challenge Democratic incumbent PA Governor Ed Rendell in the upcoming election. Swann appears to be uncontested for the state committee's endorsement and would be the first black candidate to receive either party's backing. Swann's campaign benefitted from a wave of publicity as the Steelers played in the 2006 Super Bowl. Swann's likely running mate would be Montgomery County Commissioner Jim Matthews.

headline: Mine Safety
abstract: West Virginia's governor and legislators, who quickly took steps to address mine safety following two deadly accidents in the state, want the federal government to move with similar dispatch. The editorial board argues that, instead of pushing premature legislation through Congress, it would be more prudent to take immediate action in smaller arenas and only then should legislators  propose a commission to devise broader proposals. The board argues also that it is important to end feuding between the United Mine Workers, politicians, and industry representatives. The board criticizes West Virginia U.S. Senators Robert Byrd and Jay Rockefeller for accepting campaign money from the mining industry and ignoring disregard for miner safety and unacceptable environmental practices.

headline: Rendell "ready and waiting" on school project
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell expressed support for Pottstown's $54 million Neighborhood Initiative. The project is a joint venture between the borough and the Pottstown school District and revolves around the construction of an $11 million early childhood education center in Washington Street neighborhood. The project also calls for housing revitalization and replacement affecting as many as 147 properties.

headline: Final thoughts on the 2006 election
abstract: Tony Phyrillas was disappointed that both Ed Rendell and Bob Casey won because he believes they are both bad for Pennsylvania. He wasn't surprised that the Democrats took back Congress because the Republicans have been lazy and greedy over the last few years. His biggest concern is that Bush won't be able to appoint a solid conservative to the Supreme Court should one of the aging liberals on the court die. His favorite candidate Jim Gerlach, defeated Lois Murphy who was favorited; they attributed his victory to a well run campaign.

headline: Top of Pennsylvania's ticket went solidly to Democrats' side
abstract: It was a Democratic blowout at the top of the ticket in Pennsylvania Tuesday. Governor Rendell defeated Lynn Swann; Bob Casey defeated incumbent Senator Rick Santorum. However, they fell short of capturing the sate House of Representatives; minority Whip Mike Veon, the 11-term incumbent, was defeated in an upset. More than one in four lawmakers next yea will be freshman.

headline: Scranton stumps in Delco
abstract: Republican gubernatorial candidate Bill Scranton made a stop in Delco on his campaign tour. Unofficial tallies put former Pittsburgh Steeler Lynn Swann ahead of Scranton in securing the Republican endorsement. Scranton, a former lieutenant governor, is asking the state committee to hold an open primary, though he has vowed to stay in the race regardless of which way the endorsement goes. If elected, Scranton said he would work to slow government growth, cut business and property taxes and modernize the state's education system. Scranton said his first priority in office would be reducing property tax. He then would make fundamental changes to the PA Legislature and push for lobbyist disclosure laws.

headline: New animal law will help to put bite on violators
abstract: Reading City Council revised the city's animal-control ordinance, expanding powers for the Humane Society of Berks County, which serves as the city's animal-control and enforcement agency. The new law will allow for officers to fine rogue pet owners as well as expanding violations which can result in incarceration.

headline: Revitalization expert to visit
abstract: Tom Leighton, former mayor of Indianapolis, is speaking in Wilkes-Barre about how they can revitalize and develop the urban areas of Wilkes-Barre. U.S. Economic Development Agency Regional Director Paul M. Raetsch will also be speaking. PA Governor Ed Rendell was invited to attend.

headline: Finally a win for Lynn Swann
abstract: A columnist declares gubernatorial candidate Lynn Swann to be the winner against a debate against PA Governor Rendell. He felt that they tied, but that Swann was the winner because he tied with a man known for his debating skills. Swann attacked Rendell for signing the legislative pay raise, while Rendell called Swann a hypocrite for supporting Senate President Pro Tempore Robert Julirer, who along with Rendell and PA Supreme Court Chief Justice Ralph Cappy, engineered the legislative pay raise. In spite of Swann's good performance, the columnist believes Rendell will still win the election.

headline: Torsella back as center president
abstract: Joseph Torsella was named the National Constitution Center's president and chief executive officer yesterday. This is Torsella's second reign as president; he is the man who got the center built. Torsella is only likely to serve for one or two years to get some initiatives passed. The organization is trying to help get the Olympics to come to Philadelphia in 2016.

headline: Scranton, Swann meet Republicans in Phila.
abstract: Republican gubernatorial candidates former Lieutenant Governor Bill Scranton and Lynn Swann courted Philadelphia's Young Republicans, each promising tax relief. Swann's campaign also released word they would not debate until after the Republican party makes an endorsement announcement.

headline: One man killed in mine accident
abstract: A man was killed in a mining accident in Schuylkill County. The state Department of Environmental Protection says that it is too early to know the cause of the disaster, but reports indicate it may have been an explosion. The U.S. Mine Safety and Health Administration reports that 41 people have died in mining accidents in 2006.

headline: Rock of ages/ The sale of a famous beer brand is hard to swallow
abstract: InBev, the Belgian brewer that owns Rolling Rock is planning to sell it to Anheuser-Busch. Currently Rolling Rock is brewed in Latrobe, the beer would not have nearly the same feel or taste if it was brewed in another city. 200 workers are in danger of losing their job.

headline: First case of political name recognition being used in wrong part of state
abstract: Eugene DePasquale, the grandson of famous Pittsburgh City Councilman Eugene "Jeep" DePasquale, is running on Tuesday for a seat in the state House. He was York's director of economic development until 2003, when he joined Democratic Governor Rendell's administration as a deputy secretary in the Department of Environmental Protection.

headline: Two Hazleton area voters file complaints about new machines
abstract: Two Hazelton residents filed official complaints concerning problems they encountered with Luzerne County's new electronic voting machines. One women said she was unable to vote for Senator Santorum and the other woman said she was unable to vote for gubernatorial candidate Lynn Swann. County officials said they will continue investigating all complaints, thought they have not found evidence of machine malfunctioning.

headline: Selling out the Pens
abstract: If Governor Rendell, county Chief Dan Onorato, and Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl let the Penguins be sold to another city it will be very bad. They can't afford to mess it up or else they will certainly face the repercussions when they are up for re-election.

headline: A tax cut that is well-cultured
abstract: In the 2007 budget approved by Pittsburgh's city government they will cut the amusement tax on nonprofit cultural groups to 1.25 percent; this will save the city's opera, symphony, and other performing arts institutions an estimated $300,000 to $500,000 total next year. None of the groups are expected to lower their ticket prices, instead using the tax cut to keep prices stable and help pad their budgets. There used to be a 10 percent amusement tax.

headline: Philadelphia greens up its act
abstract: Starting on July 10, 2006, the city will take another crack at boosting its recycling rate, which is next to last among the largest U.S. cities. The 123,000 households north of Cheltenham Avenue in Philadelphia - more than one-fifth of the city's total - will now be able to recycle plastic and corrugated cardboard at curbside.  Vita Legree, a Philadelphia Recycling Ambassador" has been going door-to-door education and awareness of the new program.

headline: Scranton seeks $44M to cover debt, projects
abstract: Scranton Mayor Chris Doherty wants to balance Scranton's budget and repay the $9.5 M in previous loans. It will cost the city $3M a year for the next 28 years. The tax increase has not yet been determined. The city will take out a loan from Standard & Porr's at the fixed interest rate of 6.5 %.

headline: For candidates, tomorrow's primary election took priority
abstract: Politicians involved in the primary election used mothers day as a way to garner some support. Mike O'Brien who is running for state representative in the 175th Legislative District handed out carnations and candy to mothers yesterday. He is running against Terry Graboyes, who is supported by PA Governor Rendell.

headline: U.S. needs real leaders, not rubber stamps
abstract: A man writes to the newspaper complaining that the newspaper has been biased in its coverage of the upcoming election. He expresses his dissatisfaction with President Bush's administration, and he says  U.S. Senator Rick Santorum and U.S. Representative Don Sherwood have been a "rubber stamp" on President Bush's policies. He asks readers to vote for Bob Casey and Chris Carney.

headline: Sen. Santorum panders to fringe element
abstract: Peter Senderowitz was pleasantly surprised by an October 29 editorial recommending Democrat Bob Casey for Senate, not so much because of what it said about Casey but rather what it said about Senator Santorum. Senator Santorum insults the intelligence of the electorate by pandering to the fringe element of our society when he gets very involved in issues such as Terri Schiavo. There are  more important problems in our society that need addressing.

headline: Behind Pa.'s increase: Costly services, lawmakers' wish lists
abstract: The PA legislature may approve a 5.8 percent state spending increase -- after more than a  year of Republican majority talking about forcing spending to rise no faster than inflation, or roughly 3 percent. Republican and Democratic legislative leaders who negotiated the budget offered two explanations. The first is the cost of welfare, public schools and prisons continue to rise faster than inflation in part because of health care costs and secondly that rank-and-file legislators submitted lists of items they wanted to see refunded.

headline: Proactive infrastructure planning is essential
abstract: Pennsylvania rural municipalities rely on the health of their water and wastewater systems to maintain the quality of life. However, challenges are threatening those systems and community leaders need to act now before problems arise. A study  done by the Center for Rural Pennsylvania outlined some of these challenges.

headline: Senate moves tax plan; House next
abstract: The PA state Senate approved property tax reforms that deal with older homeowners making up to $35,000 a year; the bill will allow them to receive rebates for this year's taxes. The House is supposed to approve the bill next. The bill is not what everyone wanted, but it was a compromise that served the interest of both parties.

headline: For Casey, fierce fight takes shape
abstract: US Senator Santorum's race against Bob Casey will be one of the most fiercely fought contest in the country. Santorum is the third ranking GOP in the senate and him losing would be a crucial blow to the party. Southeastern Pennsylvania will be a crucial vote because of all the swing voters.

headline: U.S. prof summoned in Korean stem-cell probe
abstract: The South Korean Supreme Prosecutors' Office has summed for questioning Dr. Gerald Schatten of the University of Pittsburgh who collaborated with disgraced scientist Hwang Woo-suk. Schatten was listed as a co-author of a 2005 paper in which Hwang claimed to have produced stem cells cloned to match patients. The paper was withdrawn after investigators from Seoul National University found the research results had been fabricated. State auditors questioned Hwang about possible misappropriation of state funds. It isn't yet clear if Hwang or any of his former collaborators could face charges of fraud. Before the scandal broke, Schatten said he was withdrawing his cooperation with Hwang due to ethical lapses.

headline: Budget boosts businesses
abstract: PA business's got a boost with the passage of the state's $26.1 billion budget, which included approximately $297 million in business tax breaks, helping to ease the burden on employers. Mark Vintner, senior economist for Wachovia, said that PA has not been a pro-business state.

headline: Rendell feels rock-debate heat
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell formerly expressed that he believed the acid-rock problem in Cambria and Indiana counties to be an issue that must be resolved by state agencies, not by the executive office. Rendell has recently taken more interest in resolving the matter, as residents and elected officials of Cambria and Indiana counties, who for the most part support Rendell, do not want to be the repository for a million tons of acid rock unearthed during Interstate 99 highway construction in Centre County. Residents of both counties fear danger on the roads, general wear and tear and possible environmental hazards.

headline: Slots bidder Barden promises aid for arena, Hill District
abstract: Detroit businessman Don Barden, head of PITG Gaming LLC, with the support of former Steelers star Jerome Bettis, has promised to help fund a new arena in Pittsburgh and has proposed a $350 million Hill District redevelopment project as part of his attempt at winning a slot machine casino license from the PA Gaming Control Board. Barden has answered both of his competitors, Isle of Capri Casinos and Forest City Enterprises, with his proposal. Barden agreed to provide $7.5 million a year for 30 years toward construction of an arena, which is a stipulation requested by PA Governor Edward G. Rendell in case Isle of Capri does not receive the license. The redevelopment of the Hill District is supported by both PA Representative Jake Wheatley and former Pittsburgh city Councilman Sala Udin.

headline: For Pa. officials, Super Bowl's a deal at full price
abstract: State officials, including PA Governor Ed Rendell, U.S. Senate hopeful Robert Casey, Pittsburgh Mayor Bob O'Connor and the Democratic leaders of the House and Senate will attend the 2006 Super Bowl, thanks to special access to a group of tickets from the Pittsburgh Steelers organization. The Pittsburgh Steelers and National Football League will no longer provide politicians with free tickets. Instead, they are being made available at face value. Many believe that this system still constitutes favored treatment, as tickets are otherwise being sold for $5,400 online and elsewhere. Barry Kauffman, executive director of Common Cause PA, said the team deserves credit for removing the free ticket system.

headline: U.S. suit on behalf of Latino voters gets mixed reaction
abstract: The federal Department of Justice is filing a lawsuit against the city of Philadelphia, charging that the city violates the voting rights of Spanish-speaking voters. The NAACP and Latino Advocacy Project claim that this lawsuit occurring so close to an election is a form of voter intimidation, while some Latinos welcome the support.

headline: Editorial: Benign budget/Pennsylvania sends help where it's needed
abstract: The editorial board writes that with the help of a $700 million surplus and an election year, it didn't take long for Democrats and Republicans in Harrisburg to overcome their differences and agree on a 2006-07 budget.  The $26 billion spending plan was passed by the PA legislature and signed by PA Governor Rendell about 26 hours into the new fiscal year. The board says that the package will focus attention on key human-service areas while managing to trim the business tax and are disappointed that the plan failed to shave the corporate net income tax, which at 9.99 percent, it’s the second-highest in the nation.

headline: Sewage backup turns fish belly up
abstract: Dead trout, suckers and other fish floated along the surface of the murky water, dead from untreated sewage that backed up Brush Creek in New Sewickley Township from a treatment plant in Cranberry Township.  Wes Hill, director of the Beaver County Emergency Services Center, issued an advisory saying that people and animals should stay out of the Brush and Connoquenessing creaks for the foreseeable future, until the raw sewage in flushed from the creeks.

headline: Small development firm making a big difference in Lawrenceville
abstract: Joe Edelstein of Wylie Holdings, LP, and his firm's partners are making a significant difference in the landscape of Lawrenceville, where they have restored and renovated about 25 buildings over the past four years. On May 5, the company will acquire three more building projects from Pittsburgh's Historic Review Commission. Most of the preservation projects are on Butler Street and Penn Avenue and 17 are corner buildings, which Edelstein said are the most visible type of building. Architect Jill Flannery Joyce has designed the facades for all of the firm's projects that have won awards from the Historic Review Commission, while civil engineer bill Volbrecht has designed all of the interiors.

headline: Former Pa. lawmaker alleges link between court rulings, funding
abstract: Former PA State Representative Ed Krebs submitted a written affidavit alleging that House Republican leaders won more court funding in 1999 to help ensure favorable rulings from the state Supreme Court in a federal lawsuit over last year's controversial pay raises. Common Cause of PA, a government watchdog group, put the affidavit in a revised copy of its suit. A spokeswoman for House Speaker John Perzel, who was then the majority leader, said Krebs' claim is "groundless and baseless." Krebs' affidavit references a court case considering workers' compensation legislation and an increase of the state's gas tax. The Common Cause suit seeks rulings that would ensure laws are passed constitutionally and ban improper discussions between lawmakers and judges.

headline: Unaffordable schools
abstract: Carlisle Area School District is again planning on raising property taxes in an effort to meet increase in teachers salaries, benefits, and debt service payments. Teachers must take responsibility for their own retirement and their own health care; they need to stop demanding salary increases. Citizens cannot afford to give them what they can never attain.

headline: Election-year budget fight expected to be fierce
abstract: PA Governor Edward G. Rendell proposed a $25.4 billion budget for fiscal year 2006-07, which has already been thrown out by PA Representative Sam Smith, House Majority Leader, and Pa Representative Brett Feese, Republican Appropriations Chairman. Both PA legislators are Republicans, while Rendell is a Democrat. The GOP has proposed the same $24.5 billion budget that was used for fiscal year 2005-06, pushing Rendell to justify the extra $1 billion in additional spending that he wants to use for increasing spending for welfare, basic education in public schools, special education programs and state prisons, among other things. Most PA legislators, including Rendell, are up for re-election this coming fall.

headline: Sinkhole called threat to water supply in township, Penn State
abstract: An expanding sinkhole near Houserville may threaten an underground water source that supplies residents of College Township and Penn State. The hole started in mid-October on a bank under the Mount Nittany Expressway overpass and it has expanded in recent weeks due to heavy rains. The township can draw on its other well to fulfill water needs.

headline: State funds will replace, improve downtown street lights
abstract: Street lamps in downtown Chambersburg will be replaced through the Home Town Streets Project; the borough secured $165,000 to fund the project from the state. The Home Town Streets Project is aimed to help redevelop downtown areas of Pennsylvania cities; there a total of 79 projects statewide totaling $52.8 million.

headline: Former Steelers line up in guv's race
abstract: The Pittsburgh Tribune-Review reports that the Philadelphia Inquirer asked former Steelers players their opinion about Lynn Swann running for governor. They include which players are voting for Swann and which are voting for Rendell.

headline: Vampire Senate: The public gets bitten when it comes out at night
abstract: The editorial board criticizes the state legislature for voting on a gambling and lobbyist disclosure bill late at night, which wound up containing errors, forcing them to vote on the bills again. They also criticize them for voting to award themselves pay-raises in the middle of the night.

headline: Job-tax gripes surface
abstract: Scranton City Council President Judy Gatelli said that she has received many phone calls from workers claiming that they employers are illegally deducting the new $52 Emergency Municipal Services Tax. Gatelli stressed that employers cannot legally deduct the tax from those workers earning less than $12,000. A state law enacted in 2004 allowed municipalities to increase the job tax to up to $52 if they money was earmarked for police, fire, emergency services, property tax reduction or road work.

headline: Split Season
abstract: A Harrisburg resident says he'd like to know why the Fish and Boat Commission is changing the opening of trout season in the southern part of the state.  The Commission says it was because the water in the trout streams there warm up at the end of May into June. But he says he knows that most fisherman stop fishing in the third week of May.  He does not like the split seasons.

headline: State questions city's use of grant money
abstract: According to Alison Everett, a spokeswoman for the PA Commission on Crime and Delinquency, the state is withholding a $17,392 grant that Wilkes-Barre Mayor Tom Leighton used to increase the salary of his assistant Greg Barrouk. The grant was part of a federal Weed and Seed crime prevention grant, and Barrouk was named the contact person for the new Community Action Team which is supposed to fulfill the requirements of the grant for a "community revitalization coordinator." City officials say the pay raise Barrouk received is justified because he sometimes works 70 hours per week and receives many calls about problem properties and inspections.

headline: Fresh faces to Harrisburg?
abstract: After the primary results it is obvious that there are going to be some fresh faces in Harrisburg. That includes 25 year old Jaret Gibbons who was only in high school when the incumbent he beat took his first term. Then there is PA Republican Greg Hopkins who is trying to take away the Green County legislative seat from PA House Leader William DeWeese; Hopkins has spent the last 11 years playing arena football.

headline: Vaughn: 2006 pivotal for county Democrats
abstract: New Chairwoman of the Chester County Democratic Committee, Michele Vaughn, sees 1006 as a pivotal year for county Democrats.  Coming off the recent election for PA senator Andrew Dinniman in the 19th District, Vaughn said its is crucial for the party to "leverage" that win for gains in the mid-term elections. By November 8, residents should know whether Dinniman's victory was a moment or a movement in the political makeover of Chester County.

headline: Letter to the editor - Blame GOP for tax inertia
abstract: The author of the letter criticizes a recent letter to the editor published in the Beaver County Times which placed blame for the lack property tax reform on PA Governor Ed Rendell. The author argues that the real blame rests with state Republican lawmakers, as Rendell has asked the GOP-controlled House and Senate to pass property tax reform, but they have failed to do so. The author states that Republican lawmakers should "be ashamed of themselves" for failing to keep their word on a vote on minimum wages by the end of January. The author argues that the state corporate income tax is too high, largely due to a tax exemption for most corporations in the state. Instead, companies transfer profits to Delaware through tax loopholes.

headline: State donates $25,000 to battle invasive garlic mustard weed
abstract: The state is giving $25,000 to the 15-acre Pine Hill Arboretum to help the Alliance for the Chesapeake Bay develop a program to get rid of invasive garlic mustard weed. Currently research is going on to find biological ways to prevent it from growing.

headline: Street budget to offer surplus of legacy
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor John Street will address Philadelphia City Council and the Philadelphia Chamber of Commerce in the coming days with a budget proposal that includes business-tax cuts and development plans with the end of his tenure as mayor in sight. Street is particularly concerned with his legacy dating back to his time with then-Mayor Governor Rendell when he sat on City Council and forged a partnership that began the reform of the city.

headline: Fresh-faced with fresh ideas
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl appeared on The Late Show with David Letterman to praise Pittsburgh, but Pittsburghers are still nervous about their young new mayor. He brings youth and energy to the Mayor's office and will run again when he has to, but that has not yet been determined. He might serve out the previous mayor's full term till 2009.

headline: Vote of confidence for new machines
abstract: Eligible voters that have physical disabilities will be able to vote more easily for the 2006 primary as new eSlate and eScan machines allow for them to cast a vote without assistance or without using an absentee ballot. Under the 2002 Help America Vote Act, Lancaster County must replace its old lever machines by the primary.
