abstract: Emilio Vazuez made history yesterday defeating Tony Payton 179th State House District; Vazquez was a write-in. Vazquez made rubber stamps with his name on it and had volunteers distribute them at the polls. Payton is contesting the results.

headline: 'They're selling the soul of Pittsburgh'
abstract: Critics claim that the construction of Fort Pitt to prepare for a $35 million renovation of Point State Park is getting destroying part of Pittsburgh's cherished past. The project would destroy seven oak trees planted about 50 years ago when the park was created. It would also destroy the "trench" that bisects the park, which has become an historic landmark.

headline: Council gives city smokers a holiday gift
abstract: Philadelphia City council tweaked the smoking ban yesterday. Previously only bars that derived less than 10 percent of their total income on sales of food and nonalcoholic drinks were allowed to have smoking; the new law increases that number to 20 percent.

headline: State gives Utilities Inc.-Westgate conditional approval for rate hike
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission granted conditional approval to Utilities Inc.-Westgate to increase their rates by $10 a month per customer. The rate hike the water company originally asked for was substantially higher, so they are still in the process of deciding whether to accept or reject the offer.

headline: Gaming inquiry looks for mob ties
abstract: PA State gaming board investigators are seeking to interview alleged Scranton mobster William D'Elia to determine whether he has or had ties to slots applicant Louis DeNaples. D'Elia was charged with conspiring to kill a witness while out on bail from a previous indictment on money laundering and other offenses. Character is a factor in awarding slots licenses in Pennsylvania, so if there are any ties it could really hurt DeNaples chances.

headline: Idiot? Maybe. But wrong? Nope.
abstract: Columnist Jill Porter received some negative feedback when she wrote that the slot parlors might be a good idea for the city. She admits that the people living close to the casinos have some reasons to be fearful but still believes it will be a positive for the city.

headline: Bethlehem Area misses goals again
abstract: Six out of eight Northhampton County school districts met PA academic performance goals for 2005- 2006, more than in any year since the state has been monitoring achievement. The county mirrors the state wide results as well. 95% of the commonwealth's school districts met their target. Bethlehem which did not make its goals tried to focus on the positives.

headline: Council majority still backs smoking ban
abstract: The Allegheny City Council may have enough votes to override an executive veto on a smoking ban. The ban would bar people from smoking in public places. However, they will make compromises if it becomes necessary in order to pass the bill.

headline: State orders safety checks of Pa.'s 77 mineral, coal mines
abstract: Under an order issued by PA Governor Ed Rendell, the state's 77 underground coal and mineral mines will undergo new inspections in the next 30 days. Spurred by the recent deaths of 16 coal miners in West Virginia, Rendell ordered inspectors from the PA Department of Environmental Protection to visit the mines and ensure compliance with regulations. Inspectors from the federal Mine Safety and Health Administration will conduct additional checks of conveyor belts used to carry coal or other products out of the state's mines. Rendell also asked state coal mine operators to participate in MSHA's "Stand Down for Safety," a voluntary educational initiative. According to George Ellis, president of the PA Coal Association, all coal mines in the state indicated they would participate.

headline: Gaming inquiry looks for mob ties
abstract: State gaming board investigators are seeking to interview alleged Scranton mobster William D'Elia to determine whether he has or had ties to slots applicant Louis DeNaples. D'Elia was charged with conspiring to kill a witness while out on bail from a previous indictment on money laundering and other offenses. Character is a factor in awarding slots licenses in Pennsylvania, so if there are any ties it could really hurt DeNaples chances.

headline: Illegal immigration has attention of state House GOP
abstract: In response to Hazleton City Council's discriminatory law against illegal immigrants, PA House Republican Policy Committee is holding a series of hearings on immigration policy. The committee has invited Hazleton Mayor Louis Barletta to testify regarding the unprecedented actions his city has taken, along with members of the Latino Community. PA Governor Rendell has recently vilified immigration reform efforts at the state and local level as "meanspiritedness."

headline: City group makes its bid for 2016 Olympics
abstract: Peter Ueberroth, the chairman of the U.S. Olympic Committee said that his organization would decide by the end of the year whether it would select Philadelphia as its bid for the 2016 Summer games. Philadelphia has been impressive with other large events it has hosted in the city. Other cities being included are Houston, Chicago, Los Angeles, and San Francisco.

headline: Declare war on infections
abstract: A groundbreaking report released by the Pennsylvania Health Care Cost Containment Council included good news for Northeastern Pennsylvania, in that patients in the region's hospitals collectively suffered infections at the lowest rate among the regions within the report. Overall the report makes the case for an all-out attack against hospital-acquired infections. According to the report, 12.2 of every 1,000 patients in Pennsylvania hospitals acquired an infection.

headline: Stop the dredging!
abstract: The author condemns the Delaware River dredging project as a means to help the oil industry using taxpayer money and staunchly opposes the project. PA Governor Ed Rendell is criticized by the author for misleading voters as the author believes the project will necessitate a tax increase and will not return economic benefits proportionate to it's costs.

headline: Good times roll in Philly; Chester is next
abstract: Residents of Northeast Philadelphia who have been going to the racetracks to gamble predict that people in Delaware County will love the addition of a casino. They believe that when Harrah's Chester Casino opens it will also help the town greatly.

headline: Impact of settlement details on campaigns unclear
abstract: U.S. Rep Don Sherwood remained silent Friday about a news report that stated he paid $500,000 to his former mistress in exchange for her silence in the months leading up to the election. Currently Sherwood, a four term Republican, is down by 8.6 points to Democratic challenger Chris Carney.

headline: City moves to privatize sludge treatment operations
abstract: Responding to changes in technology and warnings that the city is violating its own air-quality laws, Philadelphia Mayor John Street's administration is proposing to privatize the water department's biosolids recycling center. If Street convinces City Council to approve the contracts, the privatization will be the city's first major outsourcing in a decade. Water Commissioner Bernard Brunwasser said the proposal is not a reflection of the performance of union employees, but is instead a reflection of environmental issues and changes in the technology of biosolids handling. If City Council approves the contracts, Synagro will operate the current center on an interim basis while it builds its new facility.

headline: Declare War on Infections
abstract: The PA Healthcare Cost Containment Council released a report ranking Northeast PA among the lowest for number of patients contracting infectious diseases during hospital stays. Nonetheless, some hospital spokespersons questioned the methods of the study. The Hospital and Health Association of PA says progress is being made in number of patients infected. Editors would like to see insurance companies commission studies and the state government heed the advice of the Council.

headline: Utility workers racing the clock to restore power to Poconos
abstract: Workers for Met-Ed and PPL in PA were working around the clock in an effort to restore power to customers after high winds over the weekend knocked out power lines.

headline: Government needs to pay more attention to social ills of gambling, expert says
abstract: Professor Robert Goodman believes that the Pennsylvania government has become revenue-dependent promoters of the gambling industry instead of focusing on how to prevent and address social problems from the spread of casinos. He contended that newly legalized gambling could cost Pennsylvania $800 million annually if it leads to a 1 percent increase in compulsive gambling, at a social cost per person of $10,000.

headline: In 11th hour, Santorum pulling out all stops
abstract: US Senator Rick Santorum has been campaigning hard in the final stretch of the campaign. He has been making very persuasive speeches around the state. It seems to be working in his favor, but this is a democratic year. People are very upset with the way Republicans are handling the government. Despite this, Santorum is having President Bush fundraise for him. Casey's plan is to show his moderate stances and show Santorum's extremism. The article believes this plan could backfire.

headline: City to remain financially distressed
abstract: After an extensive review of Johnstown's finances, experts said they could not recommend that the city should emerge from the state's Act 47 program for distressed manipulates at least through 2009, further extending a slow recovery process that began in 1992.  Johnstown has not balanced its revenues and expenditures since 2001 and the city must now examine the possibility of cutting services, including personnel, in order to stabilize its budget.

headline: Doctors respond to emergency-care issues
abstract: The PA Chapter of the American College of Emergency Physicians announced they will seek better enforcement of the seat-belt law, a law requiring motorcyclists to wear helmets, and procedural changes to medical malpractice cases. The announcement coincided with the national chapter's release of a report, which listed PA as the seventh best in the nation for emergency care but as failing in the area of medical-malpractice.

headline: Tilting for windmills
abstract: Joe Green believes that turbines can help solve the region's energy problems. He is building 13 in Schuylkill County. They will be built on Locust Mountain which has an elevation of 2,950 feet; with such high elevation it is usually windy.

headline: Happy talk
abstract: The author contends the proposal to pay for the new Pittsburgh Penguins arena partially through slots revenue should be delayed until the slots are in place and  steady revenue received.

headline: In Delco, calm before the optical storm
abstract: It is surprising that more people in Delaware County didn't vote in the last primary, especially in the wake of last summer's legislative pay-grab. However, across the state people turned out to show their distaste, causing key legislators to lose their primaries. The editorial board writes that things will get a lot more interesting in November's election, with the Governor's seat and other key legislative seats being up for election.

headline: City to use fingerprints to track employee's hours
abstract: Pittsburgh's Department of Public Works plans to use a $70,000 fingerprinting reading system to track employees' work hours, but a union plans to fight it.  They system will keep employees from falsifying work hours or signing in for each other and will save money, said director Guy Costa.

headline: Don't cut Medicaid, officials say
abstract: A bush administration proposal to cut Medicaid spending could cause a $200 million hole in Governor Rendell's next budget. It could also cost Pennsylvania over $1 billion over the next 5 years. 60 to 65 percent of nursing home patients are on Medicaid which covers about 90 percent of the cost of care.

headline: Tunkhannock Twp. Erects windmill
abstract: Tunkhannock Township erected and started running a 35-foot windmill that will hopefully save hundreds of dollars a year in power bills. It was built with a grant form the PA state Energy Development Authority. Any unused electricity gets sent back through the building's electrical system. Turbine generates $840 worth of electricity a year.

headline: Harness racing panel member resigns
abstract: PA State Harness Racing Commission member Richard Bolte, Sr. resigned amidst criticism from PA State Representative Mike Veon after the panel declined both applications for the state's final harness racing license. Both decisions were appealed to the PA Commonwealth Court, with the applicants seeking the license and eligibility for a slots license.

headline: In the final days of campaigns, prospective voters will see stars
abstract: Political superstars began to descend on the region yesterday in hopes of rallying their party's faithful in the final days before the election. John Edwards came to center city; former New York City Mayor Rudolf Giulliani appeared in Wilkes-Barre last night alongside Senator Rick Santorum. Tomorrow, Senator John Mccain is schedule to be in Washington Crossing to help Rep. Mke Fitzpatrick. Al Gore will be in the three hotly contested suburban congressional districts with all three candidates.

headline: City wireless system set for full council
abstract: A pair of Philadelphia City Council committees approved a contract between the city and Wireless Philadelphia allowing citywide broadband service. The contract now has to be approved by the full Council. The service could be as little as 9.95 a month for low-income residents.

headline: Editorial: Lose the belly. It's time to rediscover fitness and lean foods
abstract: Americans got a little wider last year according to the Trust for America's Health. PA ranked 15th with 24.3 % of its adults being obese. The article discusses the health problems related to obesity. Under federal mandate schools began cutting calories in their meals. The editorial also offers ways to lose weight.

headline: Week in Review. Ohio utility proposes power line.
abstract: American Electric Power, a major utility company based in Columbus, Ohio, said it wants to build a 550-mile electric transmission line to connect AEP's power plants in West Virginia to the New Jersey market. The proposed placement of the line appears to cut a swath through south-central PA. AEP is allotting three years for the approval process and five years for construction. The project will cost $3 billion.

headline: Hill clergy lead effort to rebuff slots casino in Hill
abstract: A coalition of ministers and community supporters gathered at Freedom Corner to voice opposition to a casino in the Hill District. They believe that a casino would bring an increase in addiction, crime and poverty to the neighborhood. Isle of Capri Casinos Inc is the only one of three competing proposals that would put a slots parlor in the Lower Hill, on the site of Mellon Arena.

headline: Incumbents take major hit in primary aftermath
abstract: At least 14 incumbent legislators, 11 Republicans and three Democrats lost in Tuesday's primary. Of the 14 candidates who lost, 13 voted in favor of last July's pay-raise legislation. Among Delaware County representatives and senators, only Greg Viali of Haverford, voted against the pay hike.

headline: Councilman wants live backup 911 call center
abstract: Allegheny County Councilman Vince Gastgeb has introduced legislation that would enable a live backup 911 call center to take over within seconds if the county's primary system fails. They county's emergency dispatch center missed about 100 calls over six hours because of a computer failure and he does not want something like this happening again. In other news two Councilmen have reported progress in their effort to create a countywide riverfront park system.

headline: Editorial: Science, not ideology
abstract: The FDA has been in the mix of many controversies that are different than their mission of safeguarding food and drugs and enhancing public health.  Andrew von Eschenbach says that the agency should approve "Plan B" contraceptives and let the agency get out of the paralysis the controversy has set it in.  During the Bush Administration the FDA lost some approval when it approved the drug Vioxx, which was pulled off the market for not being marketed properly.

headline: Week in Review. United Water Co.
abstract: United Water Co. said that it is seeking approval from the PA Public Utility Commission for a 27.7 percent rate increase, the utility's first in eight years. Typically, requests like this are pared down by the PUC after a review process that can last six months or longer.

headline: Horse tracks first on agenda for casino panel
abstract: 27 months ago PA Governor Ed Rendell signed legislation authorizing up to 14 slot machines casinos around the state. The PA Gaming Control Board will start public hearings on the remaining 22 license applicants tomorrow including six licensed horse track operations. The projected profits for all 14 casinos is $1 billion a year giving tax breaks the homeowners and elderly.

headline: Inside the Capitol
abstract: The PA Senate yesterday voted to pass a bill intended to limit governmental property seizure powers that were expanded by a US Supreme Court ruling. PA Senator Jeff Piccola sponsored the bill that would bar local and state governments from taking property for use in future economic development projects until it is considered "blighted." The bill awaits approval by PA Governor Edward G. Rendell. The one opponent to PA Representative Ron Buxton in the Democratic primary, Dee Blount, lost her chance to get on the ballot when the PA Supreme Court denied her appeal of the ruling that was made by the Commonwealth Court that found that she had failed to obtain the 300 signatures necessary to gain a ballot spot. Republican Anthony J. Tezak will challenge Buxton for the seat in the fall.

headline: County Council strives for continued cooperation
abstract: Allegheny County Council President Rich Fitzgerald, a Democrat, praised the work of outgoing Republican council members Doug Price, Ed Kress, and Ron Francis in the Council's final meeting, capturing in his praise the partisan cooperation that marked the Council's time. Fitzgerald also praised Allegheny County Chief Executive Dan Onorato for his work with the Council, cooperation which had not existed under the previous regime. Onorato and the Council successfully implemented row office reductions and property assessment reforms.

headline: FDA says spinach tampering not suspected
abstract: Tampering is not suspected in an outbreak of E. coli linked to fresh spinach. The FDA has linked a California company's fresh spinach to the outbreak, which killed one person and sickened at least 109 others. There has been a recall on 34 brands of fresh spinach products. The FDA has warned people to not eat fresh spinach until further notice.

headline: 168 license plat for 1 state? That's nuts
abstract: The state of Pennsylvania used to have two different license plates, one gold with blue trim and one blue with gold trim. Now the state has four special-funded plates, 151 special organization plates, and 13 veteran plates, for a total of 168 different plates. The purpose of a license plate is to identify a vehicle, not be an advertisement for any personal platform; there are too many license plates in our state and it has become ridiculous.

headline: House shuffles gambling measure
abstract: The PA legislature failed to finalize a gambling-reform bill when an amendment added by the Senate accidentally used language from a former version of the bill.

headline: Inside the Capitol: Dixon Tribute ordered
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell has ordered state flags at the Capitol and in the five-county Philadelphia region to be flown at half-staff through Thursday in honor of the late F. Eugene Dixon, who chaired the State Horse Racing Commission and the PA state System of Higher Education Board of Governors.

headline: Cunningham sets goal to save millions
abstract: The first Democrat was appointed as Lehigh County Executive as Don Cunningham was sworn in, pledging to cut about $95 million in capital projects planned by predecessor Jane Ervin. One target for a funding cut is the planned County Courthouse, a proposal which could face opposition. Cunningham wishes to ease the burden of rising taxes by making the cuts, which would also include a restructuring of administrative duties.

headline: FDA says spinach tampering not suspected
abstract: Tampering is not suspected in an outbreak of E. coli linked to fresh spinach. The US Food and Drug Administration has linked a California company's fresh spinach to the outbreak, which killed one person and sickened at least 109 others. There has been a recall on 34 brands of fresh spinach products. The FDA has warned people to not eat fresh spinach until further notice.

headline: 7 counties seek state's help to tackle I-81 issues
abstract: In order to deal with traffic, noise, congestion and development along Interstate 81, the commissioners in seven counties have opted to shout with one voice rather than mutter with several small ones, so they are asking PA Governor Ed Rendell and the PA Department of Transportation to give them a voice.  In a joint letter, the commissioners from Cumberland, Dauphin, Franklin, Lackawanna, Luzerne, Schuylkill and Susquehanna Counties ask that Rendell form a planning group to address issues concerning the I-81 corridor.

headline: Indian tribe, Donald Trump pitch proposals for Philly slots
abstract: A number of competitors petitioned to members of the PA Gaming Control Board to vie for two licenses that would make Philadelphia one of the nation's biggest cities with casino-style gambling downtown. Donald Trump, proposing to build a casino on an unused industrial lot in the Nicetown neighborhood, said his proposal is the only one that will transform a neighborhood. Michael Thomas, chairman of the Connecticut-based Mashantucket Pequot Indian tribe, said 42 percent of the income from a casino his tribe will build along the Delaware River will go back to charities in Philadelphia. The other investors include Chicago real estate billionaire Neil Bluhm, several entertainers including Quincy Jones and politically connected lawyers and developers.

headline: Inside the Capitol: Lawmaker's votes reviewed
abstract: Ten representatives and four senators, all republicans, voted to raise their own pay a year ago, but voted against increasing the minimum wage. All fourteen lawmakers also voted to repeal their pay raise in response to public outrage.

headline: Cuts leave many feeling cross
abstract: Pittsburgh City Council President Doug Shields says that there are not enough school crossing guards, and that funding to hire crossing guards should not be cut from the city budget. He wants aides to Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl and the Pittsburgh public schools to determine where crossing guards are needed. Ravenstahl said he plans to hire more guards.

headline: Financial planner picks HAS to provide care for his family
abstract: Eric Beittel, a financial planner who sells Health savings accounts, insists families receive better and more affordable health care than they would with traditional insurance. HSA's put people back in contact with costs of health care, they are touted by supporters as a major step toward solving the nation's health care crisis. HSA's require families to be more careful and only use medicine or medical attention when it is truly necessary.

headline: A pitch to lease Pa. Turnpike
abstract: Governor Rendell and House Speaker John Perzel yesterday separately pitched the idea of leasing the Pennsylvania Turnpike to private investors to raise money for highways and mass-transit systems. Rendell said estimates of the value of such a long-term lease range from $2.5 billion to $10 billion. Perzel said the deal could be worth as much as $30 billion.

headline: Inside the Capitol: Gambling addiction alert
abstract: PA Representative Paul Clymer renewed his call for action on legislation to require all PA casinos to send out monthly win-loss statements to the households of any customers who have registered for "regular player" cards.  No other states with legalized gambling require such statements, but Clymer hopes his proposal can become part of a pack of reforms to the slots law that is expected to move later in the year.

headline: Inside the Capitol: Petitions' return awaited
abstract: Russ Diamond, the Annville businessman whose PACleanSweep group recruited more than 100 candidates to run for the Legislature, faced a daunting challenge of collecting 67,070 signatures to get his name on the fall ballot, but two weeks before the deadline he is still 47,000 signatures short.

headline: Decision favors homeowners
abstract: Only homeowners can request that recent sales prices be used in calculating adjustments to property assessments, an Allegheny County panel announced. This leaves out school districts and other taxing bodies. School districts are concerned about the decision and may end up suing the board.

headline: Flu-vaccine supply uneven so far
abstract: Area doctors say access to flu vaccines has been spotty so far; some have plenty while others don't have nearly enough. The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and vaccine makers say the supply will be plentiful eventually, some might just have to wait until December. Manufacturers said one strain of virus included in the shot was particularly slow growing, thus causing the initial shortage.

headline: Airport employee files suit over treatment
abstract: A public relations employee, Saul Ravitch, at Philadelphia International Airport has sued airport officials, saying they retaliated against him for criticizing airport operations and life-saving equipment.  Ravitch filed the suit in federal court in Philadelphia, arguing official violated his civil rights under the Constitution's free-speech and due-process provisions.

headline: Isle of Capri disputes low revenue projection
abstract: Isle of Capri Casinos Inc. is disputing a Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board report that shows it would generate the least revenue of the three competitors for the Pittsburgh slot machine license. They believe that they would produce more revenue than the others by its fifth year of operation, the board's benchmark. Isle of Capri is also considering purchasing the Pittsburgh Penguins.

headline: Inside the Capitol: Swann's not all ears
abstract: During an appearance on PCN's call-in program, Swann's earpiece kept falling out which he needed to hear the callers at PCN's Pittsburgh bureau.  He quipped that he has small ears.

headline: Desperately seeking ethics
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Street has thumbed his nose at the deadlines to fill the vacancies on boards and commissions. He still hasn't filled five slots on the city's new, more powerful Board of Ethics created in May when residents overwhelming voted to change the Home Rule Charter. The 90 day deadline was Sept. 3 but since City Council was out of session the names were expected by Sept. 14. There still aren't any names.

headline: Golf event ordered to pay PSU $4 million
abstract: The founder of an annual golf tournament for cancer research must turn over $4 million to Penn State under an agreement reached over the event's fundraising practices. The tournament claimed the contributions would go to the Jake Gittlen Cancer Research Institute at the Penn State Milton S. Hershey Medical Center, but not all of did. 20 percent of the funding comes from this tournament and it allows them to buy things grant don't cover.

headline: Airport unveils expansion plan
abstract: The Williamsport Municipal Airport Authority unveiled a 20 year plan that will enable the Williamsport Regional Airport to grow and meet the future needs of travelers and the aviation community. Major components of the plan call for extending the main runway, improving safety, constructing more hangers, and other tasks.

headline: It's official, racetrack wins slots approval
abstract: Penn National Gaming inc won a license for a slots parlor ending a 10 year quest to bring a casino to its racetrack in East Hanover Twp. The planned Hollywood Casino should be open by 2008. Penn National also became the first casino to be sanctione for unlawful contributions made by two of Penn National's directors. Penn National estimated its casino wil generate $160 million in the first year.

headline: Inside the Capitol: Third-party hopefuls OK'd
abstract: The signatures have been counted and three Green Party candidates running for statewide office, Carl Romanelli for US Senate, and  Marakay Rogers and Christine Valente for Governor, will appear on the November ballot.  The article lists other Green Party candidates running for PA state offices.

headline: Editorial: Imagine!/ Before Promoting city, Pittsburghers must believe
abstract: Marketing campaigns on Pittsburgh have failed in the past but a new one with the tagline "Pittsburgh. Imagine what you  can do here" has a chance of working if locals can support it. It comes at a perfect time because of Pittsburgh's 250th anniversary in 2008.

headline: Governors, Still Wrestling with Medicaid
abstract: The Nation's Governors discussed health care for their annual summer meeting and exploding costs and soaring populations remain a challenge. The article highlights steps governors are taking in their states regarding heath care plans and alternatives.

headline: Amtrak approval gives lift to HIA's train station plan
abstract: Plans for a train station at the airport have picked up steam. Amtrak has approved agreements giving Harrisburg International Airport clearance to seek more money to build a station. Amtrak reports it is ready to move forward, which is important because the airport could not move forward until Amtrak was officially on board. Amtrak will not be providing money though.

headline: Judge Oks brewery interim financing
abstract: The private equity firm United Growth Partners promise to give the struggling Pittsburgh Brewing Company more than $7 million so it can emerge from bankruptcy and expand operations. The firm will install a new management team for the brewery.

headline: Inside the Capitol:: Candidates offer opinions
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell and Republican challenger, Lynn Swann, have gone on record about what they think should be done to improve government accountability.  Rendell favors legislative term limits and having nonpartisan independent commissions, Swann supports a lobbyist measure that indicates what is being spend by whom and a strong penalty for those who don't comply.

headline: Editorial: State still needs property tax reform
abstract: A look at the week, the issues and people more made headlines. Property taxes, Hurricane Katrina, the Disney movie Invincible, schools, local businesses, among other hot issues are discussed.

headline: Grocers extend generic drug discounts
abstract: O'Hara-based grocer Giant Eagle yesterday began offering a 30 day supply of about 300 generic drugs for $4, just a day after Minnesota discounter Target said it would extend its own $4 generic prescription discounter program chain wide. Wal-Mart started this trend off but only includes 38 states, Pennsylvania not being one of them.

headline: Around the Fish Commission
abstract: Senate Bill 1262 was signed into law by Governor Rendell. The bill alters the Fish and Boat Code to say that a person is guilty of operating a boat under the influence of alcohol when their blood alcohol content is .08 percent, the same as drivers of vehicles.

headline: Lancaster firm hits jackpot in slots industry
abstract: Las Vegas-based International Games Technology Inc. picked PAP Security Printing Inc. of Lancaster to be its exclusive marketer of slot machines in PA.  The deal is a potential windfall for the local firm and would likely supply many of PA's 61,000 new slot machines. PA gambling law forbids slot makers from selling directly to casinos, therefore they must sell to a PA distributor that can resell the slot machines to PA casinos.

headline: Irey calls for ethics probe of Murtha
abstract: Washington County Commissioner Diana L Irey seized on a report Tuesday from Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington that targeted her opponent US Representative John Murtha. She is now calling for an ethics investigation to determine if Murtha violated federal law. CREW, a watchdog group, is investigating but is accused of being biased.

headline: Ending the violence
abstract: The next mayor of Philadelphia needs to address the 384 homicides that have happened so far this year. Each of the four democratic candidates have laid out their plans to help curb the cities problem.

headline: Health department wants patients to take control
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Health is co-sponsoring a symposium for all health care providers encouraging them to work with patients with diabetes and urge them to take care of their health and self-manage their disease.

headline: Bicycle lanes gain support on long stretch of Liberty Ave.
abstract: Pittsburgh is planning to install signs, adjust traffic patterns, and paint bike lanes on Liberty Avenue in the heart of Bloomfield on part of a bicycle route between Herron Avenue and Baum Boulevard.  Pittsburgh Planning Department presented the design strategy August 19, 2006 to a packed house at the West Penn Hospital's Wintergarden Auditorium.

headline: Latrobe beverage maker's future murky
abstract: Le-nature's court-appointed guardian yesterday recommended selling the bankrupt beverage maker's Latrobe plant, saying no one's willing to finance the millions of dollars it would take to bring back the idled operation. Evidence was found that the company's books had been manipulated and records destroyed. The scope of the fraud can be measured by the fact that the $275 million in annual revenue creditors and investors thought Le-Nature's was generating was really more like $32 million.

headline: Is Swann avoiding Pennsylvania media?
abstract: Lynn Swann, gubernatorial candidate for the Republican Party, has not yet done an in-depth interview with a major Pennsylvania news outlet, although he has talked with Sports Illustrated, The Washington Post and ESPN.com. Retired Penn State politics professor Michael Young said that Swann's lack of communication with PA news outlets raises questions about his preparedness for office. However, Swann has just hired Washington, DC, veterans Leonardo Alcivar, Amber Wilkerson and Mark Holman as communications director, deputy director and fund-raising operator, respectively. Experts believe that Swann's lack of defining himself and his platform should have given the opportunity to his opponent, PA Governor Edward G. Rendell, to define his campaign in negative terms.

headline: Free parking may lure city visitors
abstract: Pittsburgh's nation leading 50 percent parking tax will drop 5 percent January 1, but people who park in the city won't notice a difference because parking lot and garage owners plan to keep the rates the same and use the profits to cover rising employee costs. To compensate, Pittsburgh Mayor Ravenstahl and Pittsburgh Downtown Partnership President Michael Edwards want to give visitors five to 10 parking holidays next year to entice people to come out and shop.

headline: Holy Spirit Hospital to ban all smoking on site
abstract: Patients at Holy Spirit Hospital have complained about caregivers who smell like cigarettes, which is one reason the Cumberland County-based health care provider will ban smoking.  The ban won't stop at the end of the parking lot; Holy Spirit employees won't be allowed to smoke anywhere during work hours, even if they leave hospital property.

headline: Bids for light-rail tunnel to North Shore are too pricey once again
abstract: For the second time in six months, bids for the first construction contract to extend light-rail service in Pittsburgh came in so high that they may have put the project in jeopardy. To continue the work, the Port Authority has to convince federal officials it can cover the additional costs on its own. Extending the light-rail system from Downtown to the North Shore is considered a key to continuing development between PNC Park and Heinz Field. After the bids received in September were rejected because they were too high, authority officials deferred a proposed convention center in an effort to make the project affordable. The Authority has put contingency funds in the project budget, which includes $314.5 million from the Federal Transit Administration.

headline: Liquor law for casinos is far from done deal
abstract: Governor Rendell has not decided whether he will sign the last minute passage of a bill that would allow free booze to flow at Pennsylvania slots parlors. Lawmakers claimed the law was needed to help the state's parlors keep pace with those in neighboring states. Opponents of the bill fear that it could deal a financial blow to bars and restaurants near casinos.

headline: Issues are too large this time to lay down your right to vote
abstract: This election matters more than many elections in the past. There are a plethora of important issues ranging from the war in Iraq, to tax cuts, to the future of social security. It is important for every Pennsylvanian, despite their political affiliation, to come out and vote tomorrow.

headline: Give Pa. residents control of their lives
abstract: Nathan Benefield, a policy analyst for the Commonwealth Foundation, writes that rights belong to the people and limiting the powers of government is necessary to protect these rights.  In case of back-end referendums, however, these protections do not go far enough in the case of the recent property-tax-relief law (White House Bill 39).  He writes that PA needs absolute referendum over all school property-tax increases.

headline: Homeward Bound
abstract: There has been a new trend in nursing homes. In the past if someone was there for more than 3 months it became assumed that they would be there for life; however, people are now moving out of nursing homes when they feel they are better. Pennsylvania has developed the Nursing Home Transition program which helps people leave the homes.

headline: Bridges, tunnels and hills certain to make casino access complicated
abstract: Now that they agreed to build a casino in Pittsburgh they have to figure out how to solve the inevitable traffic problem it is going to create. The assumption is that nearly 90 percent of the traffic will come from Allegheny County, so they are planning according to that.

headline: Mellon name woven into the fabric of Pittsburgh
abstract: The name Mellon is certainly synonymous with Pittsburgh but the name lost some of its luster when in 2001Mellon bank was sold to Citizens Financial Group. Mellon is more to the city than a name though, the bank financed some very key enterprises in the city. The Mellon influences began 1869 when retired Judge Thomas Mellon opened Mellon and Sons' bank.

headline: Lead for Casey narrows in race against Santorum
abstract: The lead that PA Treasurer Bob Casey Jr., who is the favored Democratic challenger to US Senator Rick Santorum in the upcoming senatorial elections in November, had over Santorum has narrowed slightly over the last month and a half. A Quinnipiac University Poll found that forty-eight percent of voters preferred Casey, compared with 37 percent for Santorum. The 11-point spread was four points closer than the same poll in mid-February. Casey campaign spokesman Larry Smar said the poll reflects public dissatisfaction with developments in Washington and Santorum's support of the policies of US President George W. Bush. However, Virginia Davis, spokeswoman for Santorum, said it would be premature to draw many conclusions from polls this early in the campaign season.

headline: Hypocrite
abstract: A person writing to the newspaper criticizes U.S. Senator Rick Santorum for writing to Allegheny County and asking them to remove the homestead tax exemption on his Penn Hills residence, essentially giving him a property tax break if that residence were his primary residence. The writer of the letter claims that Santorum's primary residence is in Virginia and that he should not receive the tax break.

headline: Hospital infection data low; to low?
abstract: Philadelphia area hospitals only reported 149 hospital acquired infections compared to Pittsburgh's 2,054. Experts say that a number that low likely means many are not being reported. These same hospitals disclosed about 1/5 of the states serious events despite representing 2/5 of the care. One issue that drives underreporting is the fear of medical malpractice cases.

headline: Companies pitch turnpike plans
abstract: More than 40 companies from across the world met yesterday to offer their help to state policymakers who want to determine the value of leasing the Pennsylvania Turnpike. Governor Rendell wants to privatize the highway in effort to raise money for the state; he is looking for $2 billion to $30 billion.

headline: More than a token day
abstract: The first slot machine casino will open in Pennsylvania if it passes two tests run by the Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board. The casino will pay over half its winnings in state and local taxes, which will go towards improving local communities and bettering their economies.

headline: It's ready, aim, SPLAT
abstract: Only at the Pittston Festival would PA Governor Ed Rendell impress a crowd of nearly 5,000 about his knowledge of the world's heaviest tomato weighing seven pounds two ounces.  Rendell gave the festival committee a $5,000 grant that will be dispersed to Greater Pittston charities.

headline: Lawmakers eye property taxes
abstract: According to top legislative leaders, state lawmakers need to reconsider property tax reform in the session that begins in January. They believe that most taxpayers won't get substantial relief from House Bill 39 which was designed to help low-income senior citizens by expanding rebates for property tax and rent. The bill is not doing much to help residents who are under the age of 65. House Democratic Leader Bill DeWeese believes increasing the sales tax by either 1/2% or 1% could help fix the problem.

headline: Impact of UPMC, Mercy deal on coverage, costs uncertain
abstract: Patients covered by Aetna, HealthAmerica, and other insurance companies that provide full access to Mercy Hospital but not to UPMC Presbyterian and UPMC Shadyside are wondering what the merger means for their access to the county's only Catholic hospital. In he short term the answer is nothing. This could impact their ability to provide an attractive hospital network. It is also unsure how the merger will impact health care costs.

headline: Confiscated Airport Items Bring Cash
abstract: A man-sized artificial palm tree and a sausage grinder have shared space in a PA government warehouse with piles of Swiss Army knives and chain saws because people have had to give them up at airport security checkpoints.  PA turns a small profit by disposing of these castoff items, which it accepts from security contractors at 12 airports in five states, by selling them to the highest bidders at the online auction site, eBay.

headline: Mount Braddock company to add 30 jobs in next several years
abstract: The Dynamic Materials Corp. (DMC) facility in Mount Braddock is doubling its size and adding about 30 new jobs over several years.  DMC Clad Metal uses explosives to cold fuse metals of dissimilar nature together and the local company does its explosions in the former limestone mines in Dunbar. PA Governor Rendell's Action Team, under the PA Department of Community and Economic Development, serves point of contact for businesses that are interested in locating or expanding in PA.

headline: John Baer Despite numbers, it's too early to anoint Casey
abstract: Today's polls show Bob Casey in the lead against US Senator Rick Santorum and PA Governor Ed Rendell leading against opponent Lynn Swann. The author believes the governor's race has been long over, but the Senate race is still in play. Bush is slightly moving up in public opinion and this may help Santorum. Santorum is running negative ads and trying to get out the Republican vote to election year levels to win this election.

headline: Legislature to vote on tax cuts
abstract: A PA state legislative committee reached an agreement on a property tax relief bill aimed at helping senior citizens. The bill is a three-tiered plan that would more than double the number of senior citizens eligible for the state's property tax and rent rebate program. Many people are upset that the actions are being done so close to the election; citing that the politicians are only doing it to help themselves.

headline: Last gasp: Allegheny County bans most workplace smoking
abstract: Smoking in bars, restaurants and pubs has been snuffed out in Allegheny County. City council voted 14-1 to ban all workplace smoking. The bill now heads to County Chief Executive Dan Onorato, and if he signs it will go into law in 90 days. The consequences of the bill are discussed.

headline: Cost of carrying off carrion forces cuts
abstract: Stanley Bimline is paid by the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation for each road-kill deer they collect. However, he is not allowed to pick up every deer because the price for PennDot is too high. PennDOT typically spends $1.3 million a year on deer carcass removal, equating to a cost of $60,000 to $80,000.

headline: Museum has deal for Steel buildings
abstract: The National Museum of Industrial History has been given three years to raise the funds to turn part of the former Bethlehem Works site into a museum. The PA Gaming Control  Board is considering a slots license for the redevelopment of the site and the museum would work in conjunction with the casino.

headline: John Baer| Why didn't Dem try to slow rival?
abstract: Former PA Treasurer Bob Casey, Jr. should not be surprised that Rick Santorum, US Senator, erased the double-digit lead in the most watched Senate race in America, and now finds himself on the verge of survival.  Santorum as US Senate leader and therefore part architect of policies in place, should be - if reported state and national angst is real not doing as well, yet Santorum is beating case in ads.

headline: Letter to the Editor - Don't be fooled on tax cut
abstract: The letter author writes that after thirty years of property tax reform debate in Harrisburg the PA legislature did not do a good job. The legislation may benefit a small minority but most people will not really see any benefits. The only real way to see property tax reform is to eliminate it in Pennsylvania.

headline: Lawmakers grapple with children's health care
abstract: State lawmakers who approved PA Governor Ed Rendell's plan to increase the number of children covered by state-subsidized health insurance are still wrestling over how to implement the measure. Representatives from the Insurance industry, child-advocacy group and the Rendell administration testified before a Senate panel on legislation the would establish guidelines for Cover all Kids program. The program is hoping to get funding from not only the state, but the federal government. 15,000 kids are expected to enroll in the first year of the program and increase to nearly 70,000 within five years.

headline: Covered bridge closes for repairs
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation closed Saville and Adair's bridges as part of a rehabilitation project.

headline: Mylan Labs goes global with majority stake in India's Matrix Labs
abstract: Mylan Laboratories Inc. has agreed to buy a  major stake in the Indian company Matrix Laboratories Ltd, an acquisition that highlights a growing trend toward global expansion in the pharmaceutical industry. The Canonsburg, PA-based company has agreed to buy up to 71.5 percent of the Indian company, which makes drug ingredients, for $736 million.  Mylan chief executive Robert Coury said the deal would help it establish a global platform for its products.

headline: John Grogan| Time powerless to heal this hurt
abstract: Yvonne Reyes is still dealing with the death of her son, Gabriel Hanemann after he was shot in the chest when he refused to open his car door for a robber.  John Grognan says that this should be a reminder that gun violence is an American epidemic and we often forget that behind every homicide statistic is a human being and a family left behind.  Reyes supports gun-control advocacy groups and in 2000 participated in the Million Mom March to protest gun violence.

headline: Mayor endures setbacks
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Bob O'Connor remained acutely ill at UPMC Shadyside, but weathered several setbacks that a day earlier prompted doctors to downgrade his condition.  O'Connor stopped having seizures, and an infection in his spinal fluid and around a shunt in his brain was under control. O'Connor's doctors said nothing to address the mayor's overall condition.

headline: LVH may add children's hospital
abstract: Lehigh Valley Hospital is exploring if it should create a hospital within its system dedicated to newborn and pediatric care, as it already offers intensive car, trauma and burn care for children at its Salisbury Township medical complex. LVH's chief of pediatrics, Dr. John VanBrakle, wants to add a number of specialists to the pediatric unit at LVH so as to limit the amount of time and number of trips families would have to take to visit children in hospitals further away. There exist six free-standing children's hospitals in PA now according to the PA Department of Health, including Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, St. Christopher's Hospital for Children in Philadelphia, Temple University Children's Medical Center, Children's Hospital of Pittsburgh, Children's Home of Pittsburgh and Shriners Hospital for Children in Erie.

headline: Crash probe begins; airport reopens
abstract: Johnstown airport's main runway reopened around noon on Wednesday, while investigators are looking for the cause of Tuesday's crash that claimed the lives of two West Virginia women. Officials say a preliminary report will be used in a week to 10 days, followed by a report on the evidence in four to six months. The two women were flying to New jersey airport to pick up a patient and bring that person to West Virginia.

headline: New casino had no 'not in my back yard' problem in Chateau; there are no back yards
abstract: Contrary to previous reports, The North Shore is not getting Don Barden's Majestic Star Casino, Chateau is. Chateau is home to only five residences, four year round homes on the river and one on the "ward." Chateau became further isolated from residential tradition as neighborhood support businesses gave way to light industry, warehouses, and huge parking lots.

headline: John Kerry hits Fitzpatrick over 'Swift-boating"
abstract: John Kerry criticized U.S. Representative Mike Fitzpatrick for questioning his opponent Patrick Murphy's war record in Iraq. While criticizing Murphy's plan to withdraw troops from Iraq, he also claimed that Murphy exaggerated regarding his combat experience in Iraq, though Fizpatrick could cite no evidence of Murphy doing so.

headline: Mayor's public safety pick stalled
abstract: Mayor Luke Ravenstahl of Pittsburgh nominated Dennis Regan for public safety director, but the city council is challenging the nomination, arguing that the position of "public safety director" is no longer necessary due to changes in the city code.

headline: Mammograms are a necessity to beat disease
abstract: More than 200,000 women are diagnosed annually with breast in the United States and about 40,000 lose their lives. An easy way to help prevent this is to get a mammogram. However, the number of women forgoing this annual screening is increasing. A major reason is that many women are losing their health insurance benefits and can't afford the $250 to $300 cost. Women should find ways to get it done because it is very important for their health.

headline: Crews work to restore rail traffic through Pa. crash area
abstract: Tankers travelling in New Brighton jumped the rails while crossing a bridge and burst into flames. New Brighton Borough manager announced the fire was put out, and most evacuated families returned. The bridge temporarily reopened but will be closed again for further repairs.

headline: New smog reduction rules OK'd
abstract: New cars in Pennsylvania will be cleaner burning next year, now that a regulation pressed by Governor Rendell passed a final legal review yesterday by the attorney general's office. The new smog reduction rules are expected to have little or no impact on vehicle prices or performance.

headline: Judge extends time in Allentown pension fight
abstract: Judge Lawrence J. Brenner, a Lehigh County judge, granted Allentown and its police union two more weeks to settle their pension dispute, after attorneys for both sides said they'd agreed on the amount police pensions need to be reduced.  Gary Lightman, a Harrisburg attorney, is representing Queen City Lodge 10 of the Fraternal Order of Police.  Under the current contract, pensions for 53 retired officers, ranging from $32,000 to $92,000, are expected to cost the cash-strapped city's pension fund $3 million a year.

headline: Paisley's name resurfaces in probe of agencies' records
abstract: Beaver County Controller Rick Towicinak is investigating Legislative District candidate Jay Paisley because of financial discrepancies found in the Councils of Governments of Beaver and Butler Counties. Towicinak launched the investigation because COG, over a 10 year period had received $533,000 and HELP and about $1.3 million in federal money that passed through the county.

headline: Medicine same despite language
abstract: Two Chinese medical students, Tang Lujia and Wang Hulpeng, spend a day with American orthopedist Dr. Thomas Mutschler and watched him perform eight procedures. Lujia plans to become a cosmetic surgeon after she finishes her medical training in Shanghia, and Hulpeng plans to become an orthopedist. The two remarked that while the language is different, the same medical procedures need to be performed in both countries and they were glad to learn from another country.

headline: Driving under another influence; Pot
abstract: People are generally aware of the risks of driving under the influence of alcohol, but now kids are starting to drive under the influence of marijuana, which is very dangerous as well. In 2004, 9 percent of roughly 17,100 drivers tested positive for marijuana after being involved in a fatal crash.

headline: Now or never on slots reform
abstract: Time is running out for PA Governor Ed Rendell and PA lawmakers to get through slot supplier licenses, free drinks and rewards, before PA sees tougher ethics standards for regulators, stronger law enforcement powers for the state attorney general and a ban on investment by public officials. Rendell 's veto of a slots rewrite bill, Act 71, in late 2004 gives Republican lawmakers reason to put him at blame for their current situation.

headline: Judge not granted less pay
abstract: Superior Court Judge Joan Orie asked the Administrative Office of Pennsylvania if she could return the 11% pay raise given to her when the legislature granted themselves a pay raise. The pay raise was repealed by the legislature but reinstated by the PA Supreme Court. The Administrative Office of Pennsylvania told her she can not return the pay raise.

headline: Panel endorses earned-income tax hike
abstract: Under a recommendation from Bethlehem district's tax study commission people working within the Bethlehem Area School District would pay an additional 1 percent in earned income tax. Workers in the district already pay a 1 percent local earned income tax. There was a water-main break and a sewer gas leak at Freedom High School on Monday; both caused little disruption.

headline: Merck chief lauds area medical sites
abstract: Merck commended Windber Research Institute's preventative approach while discussing collaboration opportunities.  Johnstown native Richard Clark Jr. tour the institute while being honored as president a chief executive officer of pharmaceutical giant Merck & Co. Inc.

headline: Editorial: Land rush/Find funding first for the Mon-Fayette Expressway
abstract: The editors write that the PA Department of Transportation should find a way to finish the Mon-Fayette Expressway and Southern Beltway first, and worry about buying properties from residents later.  The PA Turnpike Commission, which is building the highways, said recently that it will be paying more money to acquire the properties, that is small consolation after a decade or more of living in limbo.

headline: Officials assessing area flood damage
abstract: Officials continued an evaluation of Lehigh Valley communities ravaged by flooding while President Bush considered declaring a disaster in four northwest New Jersey counties where a preliminary flood-damage assessment is complete. After the evaluation, Lehigh and Northampton County residents and business owners will find out if they're eligible for clean-up money or individual assistance from the Federal Emergency Management Agency, according to PA Emergency Management Agency spokeswoman Sandy Roderick.

headline: Kanjorski in a rout
abstract: Congressman Paul Kanjorski was elected to his seventh term in office for the 11th congressional District with a landslide victory over Republican challenger Stephen Urban on Tuesday.

headline: Panel says let County Council members stay while running
abstract: A Government Review Commission approved by Allegheny County Council members and Allegheny County Chief Executive Dan Onorato recommended that council members not be required to resign their seats if they run for higher office. Voters would have to approve a change to regulation meaning the four members of Council planning to challenge for positions in the PA legislature will still have to resign their positions on the council.

headline: Midweek Perspectives: Just a pinch? Tobacco is unsafe in any form
abstract: Dr. Howard Tolchinsky discusses how public smoking bans increase there is growing concern in the health-care community that smokers may be tempted to switch to smokeless tobacco products. The tobacco industry is promoting new flavored chew and spit-free products that they market as being more convenient and socially acceptable. Some advertisers try and say how these new products are healthier but that is not the case.

headline: E-Zpass ramps in Poconos garner support
abstract: Plans of the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission to build E-Zpass ramps at Route 903 in Penn Forest Township drew support from more than 200 people attending a public information session Thursday. Turnpike Commission spokesman Carl DeFebo said the commission estimates the project to cost $15 million and be finished by fall of 2010. The slip ramps would ease congestion and streamline access to tourist spots in the Poconos area of Carbon County. Kidder Township Supervisor Nick Pantages said the access will enhance the Pocono area. PA Representative Keith McCall of Carbon County told the crowd that he has been pushing the project for years. The next step is to get environmental clearance for the project.

headline: Pa. gaming board set to codify its ethics
abstract: The PA Gaming Control Board this week is expected to introduce its own ethics code. Republicans in the PA House of Representatives are working on a separate ethics bill for the control board which, in draft form, waters down a version already passed by the Senate. The draft House bill would also strip Philadelphia of the right to decide where two slots parlors will be located inside the city. A proposed version of the control board's own code would prohibit members from giving or soliciting contributions to political campaigns and asking casino companies to donate to charities. Slot opponents have warned about potential political influence in awarding lucrative slots contracts. Ultimately, what rules the board must follow may be determined by a combination of laws passed by the General Assembly and by policies adopted by the board itself.

headline: Keep Flaherty: Put his knowledge to work for the 30th district
abstract: The editorial board endorses Pennsylvania Representative Shawn Flaherty over his Republican challenger Randy Vulakovich. Both candidates support term limits, a smaller legislature, and funding for mass transit. However, Flaherty supports abortion rights while Vulakovich does not, Flaherty wants to ban smoking in all indoor workplaces while Vulakovich wants exceptions for bars and restaurants, and they differ on their positions on property taxes.

headline: Pittsburgh city hall lacks old hands, has fresh faces
abstract: The mayor of Pittsburgh, Bob O'Connor, passed away. The man who took his place as mayor, Luke Ravenstahl, is the youngest mayor in Pittsburgh's history at 26 years old. The nine-member city contains all young members with relatively little experience. Some argue that it is beneficial to have young members with new ideas, while others feel experience is more important. The city Board of Elections is in the process of determining whether Mayor Ravenstahl will be on the ballot in 2008 or 2009.

headline: New medications can help those with diabetes
abstract: Two groundbreaking medications, Byetta and Symlin, have been approved to aid diabetes management. Byetta imitates the body's natural glucose control by increasing insulin secretion only when blood sugars are high and decreases insulin release when blood sugars are normal or close to normal. Symlin assists with glucose control after meals and suppresses appetite.

headline: Fine finagling
abstract: Many cameras are being put up at intersections in an effort to deter people from running red lights. Many communities receive a lot of funding from these traffic violations. A better way to do this would just be to increase the fines given out and not set up the cameras in the first place.

headline: Pa. slots licenses to be awarded today
abstract: Today the Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board will decide who is awarded the 11 permanent slot licenses. Philadelphia could become the nation's largest city with a casino. So far, two racetracks already have opened slot parlors under conditional licenses.

headline: Kluko beats Kovach in late-night surge
abstract: Democratic primary Chad Kluko contestant overcame an earlier lead by Thomas Kovach thanks to his dominance in Allegheny County. He will now face incumbent U.S. Representative Tim Murphy. Kluko is a 44 year old, former television and telecommunications executive.

headline: Pittsburgh's youngest mayor, 26, starts job
abstract: Pittsburgh mayor Luke Ravenstahl is taking over after the death of Mayor Bob O'Connor. He previously was City Council president. He is currently familiarizing himself with the new responsibilities. The article discusses when the election officially selecting the replacement will be.

headline: No flu shot shortage
abstract: The Erie Center on Health and Aging will have plenty of flu vaccine to conduct its annual Regional Influenza and Pneumonia Vaccination Campaign. This is after two years of shortages. Between 5 to 20 percent of the US population gets flu shots each year. The article also lists what people should get the shot if possible.

headline: Governor signals end of line
abstract: Rising transportation costs have effectively killed a $2 billion mass transit rail project planned between Reading and Philadelphia, according PA Governor Ed Rendell.  The state's share for the rail project is $300 million,  The rest would come from the federal government or private investors.  Rendell said cost-cutting measures have been discussed.

headline: Pa.'s leaving money on casino-bids table
abstract: The authors contend that PA politicians should have insisted on an auction system to award slots licenses, citing revenue estimates which put the figure at over $2 billion. The state has opted to award the slots licenses for a flat $50 million fee, attracting bids from over 20 investors.

headline: Knoll declines to debate
abstract: PA Lieutenant Governor Katherine Baker Knoll will not debate her Republican challenger Jim Matthews before the upcoming election. The reason she will not debate him is because when PA Governor Ed Rendell debated his opponent Lynn Swann, they made an agreement to not use footage of the debate in campaign commercials, and Lynn Swann violated this agreement. Swann, however, claims there was no such agreement.

headline: Ravenstahl could fill in for mayor
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Bob O'Connor, who was diagnosed with cancer, were unable to return to office, the youngest member of the Pittsburgh City Council in Pittsburgh's history, Luke Ravenstahl, would be come acting mayor.  Ravenstahl is the City Council's President and is only 26 years old. Since O'Connor did not appoint and acting mayor, the city council president would fill in if needed.

headline: No shortage of flu vaccine this year
abstract: Guillermo Cole, spokesperson for the Allegheny County Health Department, announced there is an ample supply of flu vaccinations in the county. He said that 100 million doses were distributed nationwide, as opposed to the 80 million distributed a year before. The newspaper gives a list of what types of people should or should not be vaccinated.

headline: Haycock, PennDOT agree to land pact
abstract: Hayock Township and the PA Department of Transportation officials have struck a deal on a bridge reconstruction project that would have taken up more than 20,000 square feet of land adjacent to the road from homeowners. The number of transactions with homeowners has been reduced from six to three.

headline: Pathological gamblers
abstract: The editorial addresses a comment made by the PA Gaming Control Commission's executive director, Anne L. need, who said that there is "unwarranted fear about what happens when gaming comes to town," assuming that access to slots machines will not contribute to the habits of pathological gamblers. However, research from the National Gambling Impact Study Commission found that the location of a casino within 50 miles doubled the number of problem and pathological gamblers in the area. The editorial board states that it is disturbed at the thought that legislators and commission executives cannot grasp the true reality of gambling.

headline: Labor leader tapped for city oversight board
abstract: An influential Pittsburgh labor leader, Richard Stanizzo, may fill a vacancy on the Intergovernmental Cooperation Authority, a state-appointed agency that has overseen Pittsburgh's troubled finances since early 2004.  Stanizzo is a business manager for the Pittsburgh Building and construction Trades council. If he accepts, he would fill a vacancy created  when Pittsburgh businessman William Lieberman resigned.

headline: Referendum proposal to shrink council dead
abstract: Pittsburgh City Councilman Jim Motznik said that his plan to put a referendum question on the November ballot to shrink the council from nine to seven member is dead, because it would be too late for the August 8 deadline.  A group of political activists led by North Side resident David Tessitor submitted a petition to council asking for a public hearing on Motznik's proposal, which would have taken effect shortly after the 2010 US Census.

headline: No smoking: Street Oks, then rips ban
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Street signed legislation yesterday that bans smoking in bars and restaurants in Philadelphia. He did not use it as an opportunity for a photo shoot. Instead he signed it in private and notified a few people by e-mail. He drew praise from medical groups.

headline: High-speed rail to stop on county
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell announced that Amtrak will begin high-speed rail service between Philadelphia and Harrisburg late next month. This will reduce time from two hours to an hour and a half. Regular speed trains will continue to run as well. The main aim is to make commuting much easier.

headline: Penguins' sale reaches crucial stage
abstract: The Pittsburgh Penguins' have had four known bidders and a possible fifth to buy the hockey team. Allen and company, the New York firm brokering the sale of the hockey team is analyzing and verifying those bids and is expected to pare the number soon. The sale price is expected to top $150 million.

headline: Lawmakers' benefits add to the state budget
abstract: PA state lawmakers receive a starting salary of around $72,000 in addition to a pension plan and no-cost health care benefits and other perks. Political activist Gene Stilp recently filed a lawsuits challenging the legality of these benefits. The state's budget has grown by 48 percent over the past decade, while the overall legislative budget has grown by more than 70 percent. A spokesman for the House Majority Leader Sam Smith said the General Assembly has been hit with escalating costs for employee benefits, much like other public and private employers. A group of 42 House members recently introduced a resolution calling for a bipartisan commission to study the potential impact of a reduce Legislature, including assessing any cost savings.

headline: Resolution supports creation of tax-free zone for Westinghouse
abstract: A resolution adopted by Butler County commissioners supporting the possible creation of a tax-free zone in Cranberry was the result of a closed-door meeting between Westinhouse Electric executives at the company's Monroeville campus. Similar resolutions are expected from all the taxing bodies involved in Westinhouse's pending decision to expand in Cranberry.

headline: Nursing homes, Rendell duel over funds
abstract: The nursing home industry and the PA Governor Rendell administration are feuding over Pennsylvania's reimbursements for care of those patients who qualify for Medicaid coverage. The PA Department of Public Welfare plans to unveil a new funding formula that will change how it has paid the facilities for the past decade. Nursing home industry representatives feel that the state finds it easier to just penalize nursing homes than to plan strategically for their growing population.

headline: Hike in the gas tax needed but unlikely
abstract: A commission appointed by Rendell in February 2005, has called for a 60.5 percent increase in the gasoline tax as well as a hike in local realty taxes, wage taxes, and sales taxes. Many legislators accuse Rendell of ignoring Pennsylvania's deteriorating roads and bridges, for this reason many of them will probably not vote for the tax increase.

headline: Penguins say casino would keep them home
abstract: The Penguins hockey team will remain in Pittsburgh if the proposed casino near the city's Lower Hill District goes through, Penguins chief executive officer Ken Sawyer said. A new arena for the Penguins will be built no matter who wins the right to open a slot-machine parlor in Pittsburgh, according to a proposal by PA Governor Edward G. Rendell. Under Rendell's plan, financing for a new arena would come from a new slot-machine fund, an annual contribution by the company that wins Pittsburgh's casino license, money from the NHL team and money from naming rights and stadium revenues.

headline: Lawmakers get wealth of freebies
abstract: Pennsylvania is the only state that does not require lobbyists to disclose what they spend to influence legislation, and there is only a small amount of limits on legislative freebies. Last winter, about 75 Pennsylvania lawmakers collected 280 VIP season passes for themselves, their families or their staff courtesy of the Pennsylvania Ski Areas Association. Linda Irvin, executive director of the PA Ski Areas Association, said the purpose of distributing the passes is to let the Legislature know how much the ski areas contribute to the economy of the state. Other perks include theater tickets and Penn State football tickets. Barry Kauffman, executive director of Common Cause of Pennsylvania, a government watchdog group, said the only purpose of these gifts is to create a "preferred working relationship" when the contributors want specific legislation passed.

headline: Resolution supports creation of tax-free zone for Westinghouse
abstract: A resolution adopted yesterday by Butler County commissioners supporting the possible creation of a tax-free zone in Cranberry was the result of a closed-door meeting between Westinhouse Electric executives at the company's Monroeville campus. Similar resolutions are expected from all the taxing bodies involved in Westinhouse's pending decision to expand in Cranberry.

headline: O'Connor remains in ICU, shows gain
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Bob O'Connor, who has been hospitalized for more than a month while being treated for a rare form of brain cancer, is in stable condition and remains in intensive care, UPMC Shadyside doctors reported.  The mayor continues to be responsive, talking with family members and the mayor is expected to undergo another MRI scan this week, which may tell doctors whether O'Connor's condition is improving or declining.

headline: How much is too much for an expressway?
abstract: The Mon-Fayette Expressway and Southern Beltway  projects are growing more expensive, the cost of completing another 50 miles of the highways is going to be around $3.5 billion, more than double the estimate from a few years ago. The project costs $5.4 billion, which is the most expensive public works project in the United States.

headline: Penguins support casino in Pittsburgh
abstract: The Penguins reiterated their support for a proposed casino near Pittsburgh's Lower Hill District, Penguins chief executive officer Ken Sawyer said at a press conference. The speech was organized by Pittsburgh First, a coalition formed by the Penguins, Isle of Capri Casinos and Hill District community groups. Isle of Capri has pledged $290 million to a new arena if it is awarded the right to open a slot machine in Pittsburgh. The other two companies vying for the right are PITG Gambling and Forest City Enterprises Inc. Bob Oltmanns, spokesman for PITG, said PITG endorsed a proposal by PA Governor Edward G. Rendell to keep the Penguins in Pittsburgh regardless of who wins the casino contract. Isle of Capri has been endorsed by the Republican gubernatorial candidate, Lynn Swann.

headline: Lawmakers show signs of business as usual
abstract: Voters in Pennsylvania tossed out incumbents in this year's elections with hopes that they would change the way they do business in Harrisburg. Unfortunately, early signs indicate that not much will change, at least in the short term. House Reps, Perzel and DeWeese were both re-elected and they both have a history of abusing leadership power and not being open about their spending.

headline: Schuylkill Haven requests tax-abatement zone
abstract: Schuylkill Haven officials asked the county commissioners for a tax-abatement program to help attract businesses into the borough. The program proposed is the Local Economic Revitalization Tax Assistance, it would encompass about 600 acres of the borough land. New businesses established in the area wouldn't have to pay municipal, school and county real-state taxes for new businesses.

headline: Our View: Ban smoking in public places in Pa.
abstract: The editorial board expresses their support for a ban on smoking in public places because numerous medical studies report that smoking and second-hand smoke  is harmful. Even the PA Restaurant Association now supports such a ban, in part because second-hand smoke could become a growing liability issues.

headline: In Bethlehem Twp., fatality leads to traffic crusade
abstract: The Freemansburg Avenue Safety Team, formed after a fatal car accident involving a youth on the avenue in Bethlehem township, will have members meet with PA State Representatives and PA Department of Transportation officials. The group is seeking additional safety features on Freemansburg Avenue which may obtain funding through PA Governor Ed Rendell's Home Town Streets, Safe Routes to School program, part of the Growing Greener initiative.

headline: Penn National wins license
abstract: Slots are coming to Dauphin County's Penn National Race Course won a license Wednesday to open a slots parlor. Penn National projects it will bring in $300 million and create 1,000 new jobs. Before they got the license the issue of two sets of political contributions that violated slots law had to be resolved.

headline: Lawmakers stash hefty nest eggs
abstract: PA State legislature decided to lump themselves in with state troopers, allowing them to retire with full pensions at age 50, this is a decade earlier than most other state workers. This pension increase could cause problems for the state; in 2012 the cost of subsidizing pensions for state workers and school employees is expected to jump from less than $1 billion to more than $3 billion a year.

headline: Swann's Tax Plan
abstract: Gubernatorial candidate Lynn Swann's tax proposal does little to help public-school students; it would squeeze schools between capped revenue and rising cost. However, Swann is right in saying that Pennsylvanians rely too heavily on property taxes to pay for education. Swann's plan would also create a disincentive for people to move to Pennsylvania because new residents who purchase a home could get hit with a much higher property tax then their next door neighbors.

headline: Pa. slips in national health rankings
abstract: The annual report by United Health Foundation was released yesterday, putting Minnesota at the top of the health rankings for the fourth straight year. Pennsylvania was ranked 28th, down from 25 last year. The report is based on factors such as personal behaviors, the environment people live and work in, the quality of medical care, and decisions by public and elected officials.

headline: Inside the Capitol: Transportation plan Ok'd
abstract: The PA State Transportation Commission adopted a 12-year transportation program.  The $39.8 billion program prioritizes highway, aviation, rail freight, and public transit projects in three four-year segments.

headline: Pennsylvania pushes to become 'Wall Street West'
abstract: After the attacks on September 11th the federal government recommended that financial services companies create backup sites so that they will be able to continue business if there is another terrorist attack. Governor Ed Rendell pledged $30 million in funding for companies to create those backup sites in Pennsylvania. State Representative John Siptroth is a prime supporter of this as well.

headline: Lawmakers, others to see 2 percent pay raise
abstract: State lawmakers, top executive-branch officials and judges are expected to get cost-of-living pay increases of 1.98 percent for 2007, based on inflation statistics released by the federal government.
