This is the lowest cost-of-living adjustment for state officials since 2002, when salaries increased 1.6 percent. Pennsylvania has the nation's fourth-highest-paid legislature, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.

headline: Taxes, layoffs or debt must rise in '07
abstract: The process of passing Harrisburg's budget for 2007 could be a time of reckoning for the city's leaders; the city is burdened by a 6.8 million deficit from this year. Mayor Stephen Reed and the City Council have displayed disagreement over many issues but it might be time for them to lay aside their differences. Reed said part of his plan will call for a $10.5 million, 10-year loan to help erase the deficit and return the city to firmer financial footing. City Council has resisted borrowing beyond the original $7 million bailout loan.

headline: Philadelphia's Smoking Ban
abstract: A information box detailing the specifics of Philadelphia's smoking ban. Fines range from $25 to $300. There are exceptions for outdoor cafes. The ban goes into effect immediately.

headline: Many suggest routes to better transportation
abstract: The state should do whatever is needed to increase road safety, minimize traffic congestion, and find a dedicated source of money for mass transit locals told the state transportation committee. Many solutions were discussed, but most likely will only delay the problem. The highway and bridge money is short by $155 million.

headline: Philly group sues to stop state from awarding slot licenses
abstract: A dozen Philadelphia civic groups have sued Pennsylvania's highest court to halt the award of five slot-machine gambling licenses that are up for grabs around the state. The plaintiffs argued that the law did not give enough guidance to state gambling regulators to gauge the social impact that gambling would have on communities surrounding slot parlors.

headline: Lawyer: Green candidate's Senate petition is invalid
abstract: The Green Party candidate for US Senate, Carl Romanelli, has too few valid signatures to qualify for the November 7 ballot. After review of his petitions more than 29,000  signatures were deemed invalid. Judge James R Kelley heard 5 hours of testimony without issuing a ruling on whether or not Romanelli will be on the ballot. Both parties had to agree it was an invalid signature before it was claimed one.

headline: Why Allentown plan deserves casino license
abstract: Daniel McCarthy, a member of the Lehigh County Board of Commissioners discusses why Allentown plan deserves casino license. The residents and city council of Allentown are all behind the gaming license being awarded to the Tropicana in Allentown and that is not the case of Bethlehem residents who would get the Las Vegas Sands project. In addition to that, Allentown already has the perfect site for the casino.

headline: Pitt announces research center in Sicily
abstract: The University of Pittsburgh Medical Center has announced that it will partner with the Italian government to create a new $398 million Biomedical Research and Biotechnology Center in Sicily. Officials in Sicily and Italy's National Research Council will also partner in the project. Gianfranco Micciche, deputy minister for economic affairs and finance for Southern Italy, said the center could become a financial and scientific resource for the Mediterranean region. The goal of the center is to develop new drugs, vaccines, devices and other biomedical advances.

headline: Millions in transport improvements on way
abstract: The Lehigh Valley Planning Commission released their 2007 to 2010 Transportation Improvement Program which outlined the officials expectation of more than $280 million in state and federal funding for transportation projects in the region. The Commission also approved plan's for bridge replacement and rehabilitation in Lehigh and Northampton counties.

headline: Phoenix promises millions for US Airways center
abstract: In its opening bid to land US Airways' future 600-employee flight operations center, Phoenix has promised the airline $24.5 million in incentives; that is about $8 million more than the offer made by Pittsburgh. Charlotte, N.C. is also in the mix. U.S. airways wants to merge its two existing enters and that’s what the cities are bidding for.

headline: Legislative picks
abstract: In the 199th House district, incumbent Will Gabig faces Democratic challenger Bill Cobb; the editorial board is endorsing Cobb. In the 87th district incumbent Glen Grell is being challenged by Democrat Joseph Lombardi; the board is endorsing Grell. In the 88th district incumbent Jerry Nailor is being challenged by Democrat Margaret Stuski and Green Party Christopher Irvin; the board is endorsing Nailor.

headline: Why?  Because citizenry's unprepared
abstract: After spending more than $1 million to review all of the city's emergency-preparedness plans, Philadelphia Mayor Street says the city faces the huge task of teaching Philadelphians how to respond in a crisis.  Mayor Street wants to be trained to respond to an uncommon disaster.  The PA Emergency Preparedness Review Committee says that the city needs to engage its residents in a new way.

headline: Pitt researchers find test to detect ovarian cancer earlier
abstract: Researchers at the University of Pittsburgh Cancer Institute said Sunday at the annual meeting of the American Association for Cancer Research in Washington, DC, that they have identified a group of proteins that could detect ovarian cancer at an earlier and more treatable stage. Institute geneticist Anna Lokshin said there is no single protein that would recognize most of the people with early-stage ovarian cancer, so the researchers are looking to other markers to increase cancer sensitivity that would offer better diagnostic power. Ovarian cancer will strike and estimated 20,000 women this year in the US and account for about 15,300 deaths, according to the American Cancer Society.

headline: New vision for abandoned rail line
abstract: Since the R8 line which ran between Newton Borough and Fox Chase was canceled in 1983 by SEPTA many proposals have tried to get it back. Now the regional transportation planners are floating another idea; this would include paving over the heavily weeded railroad and then running a speedy bus line along the corridor.

headline: Pilgrim's Pride cutting 300 jobs
abstract: The Montgomery County Pilgrim's Pride plant, which was at the center of an outbreak of listeria that resulted in numerous deaths, will cease turkey processing operations and lay off 300 workers, a cutback the company attributes to the residual effects of the outbreak. The outbreak led to tougher regulations from the US Department of Agriculture and court cases are still pending against the company in New Jersey and federal courts.

headline: Legislator asking trustee to resign
abstract: With Judge Cynthia Brown's appointment to PA Supreme Court, PA State Senator Jeffrey Piccola asked her to resign as chairwoman of the Penn State board of trustees to prevent any conflicts of interest. Piccola also requested that PA Supreme Court Chief Justice Ralph Cappy resign from the University of Pittsburgh board. PA Governor Ed Rendell's office questioned Piccola's motives in making the requests.

headline: Former Gov. Shafer eulogized
abstract: Former Governor Raymond Shafer recently died at the age of 89; he served from 1967 to 1971. Roughly 250 people attended the service where he was described as a visionary leader and a compassionate man who dedicated his life to both his family and his state.

headline: Pitt scientist helps find secret to stable vision
abstract: Two neuroscientists have proven a Noble laureate's 56-year-old hypothesis about how our brains allow us to see the world as a steady whole, even though our eyes pick up images in jerky "snapshots." They discovered this by injecting monkeys with a drug that temporarily knocks out relay neurons in the thalamus, they than discovered that neurons in the visual cortex stopped adjusting to receive eye movement.

headline: PennDOT agrees to meet with tree protectors
abstract: Officials of the PA Department of Transportation have agreed to meet with residents of Jenner Township who are protesting the cutting down of 40 sycamore trees along Route 985. Roger Dodson, PennDOT's assistant district executive for construction, said he will meet with protest leader Larry Pearce to find a compromise. The trees are being cut down as part of PennDOT's $2.5 million project to upgrade pavement, shoulders and drainage on the highway. Officials say the trees are too close to the road and pose a hazard for drivers. Several hundred people have signed petitions against the project while others have found historical records for who planted the trees as a means of protest.

headline: Plan for profits-tax money from oil companies questioned
abstract: PA Governor Rendell is calling for a windfall profits tax on oil companies. He will probably do something negative with the revenue as he did by spending slots revenue on a new facility for the Pittsburgh Penguins.

headline: Legislature's secrecy may cover a multitude of sins
abstract: The author condemns the PA government for failing to have better lobbyist disclosure regulations, saying that the state has the most relaxed regulations in the country. Lobbyist's are required to give a total amount spent figure only for the PA Senate, with PA Governor Ed Rendell and members of the PA House of Representatives excluded from regulations requiring disclosure.

headline: Governors make prediction on Steelers-Colts game
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell and Indiana Governor Mitch Daniels each predicted a victory for their home state team in the upcoming football playoff game, with Daniels pushing Rendell to bet on the outcome.

headline: Program aims to raise awareness of HIV/AIDS
abstract: In an effort to raise awareness locally about AIDS, Penn State Mont Alto will host a community presentation next week. AIDS educator Jim Biddle will speak. As many as 117 million people could die from HIV/AIDS between now and 2030 some studies say.

headline: PennDOT Grants: HIA among 9 recipients
abstract: Harrisburg International Airport received $750,000 to clear a site at Crawford Station for future development.  The grant was part of a total of $3 million PA Governor Ed Rendell doled to nine airports in PA.  The funds, awarded by the PA Department of Transportation, are aimed at providing a more efficient and safer service for airport customers.

headline: Pocono resorts monitor Seven Springs' slots status
abstract: Resorts in the Pocono Mountains were eying closely the outcome of a potential block in Seven Springs; application for one of two 500-machine slots licenses designated for PA resorts by the PA Gaming Control Board.  Seven Springs Mountain Resort was recently bought by the Nuttings family of Wheeling, WV.  The Nuttings also hold a major stake in the Pittsburgh Pirates, which leads other resorts to think they may not apply for a slot license, since the Major League Baseball frowns on gambling.

headline: Letter to the Editor- Enough with he political ads
abstract: Letter points out the never ending cycle of political ads for the governor's race between PA Governor Ed Rendell and Lynn Swann. Whoever spends the most will probably get elected.

headline: High steaks: Senators bet a beefy lunch on Steelers-Broncos game
abstract: US Senator Rick Santorum, R-PA, has placed a friendly bet with a fellow US Senator over an upcoming playoff football game.

headline: Prostate-cancer study: Rethink watch, wait
abstract: A recent study done by researchers at Fox Chase Cancer Center and the University of Pennsylvania suggest that the previous belief that older men with early-stages, and low risk prostate cancer should "watch and wait" may be wrong. The new study suggests that the men may significantly benefit from surgery or radiation therapy.

headline: PennDOT overnight work on I-80, I-380
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation informs local drivers that Interstate 80 will have single lane conditions between Exit 293 and Exit 302 from Wednesday evening to Thursday morning due to road sign work. Delays should be expected on the Interstate 80 ramp from PA 940 as well as on Interstate 380 South.

headline: Poker, blackjack to follow slots?
abstract: Gaming table games like poker and blackjack may be the inevitable next step for the state's almost open slot parlors. It most likely won't happen anytime soon, but the Gaming Control board has already implied it might happen eventually. The state would be happy to have more gambling revenue stay in state instead of going to nearby states casinos.

headline: New pension law: Mostly good for Steel, other retirees
abstract: Forty-four million workers and retirees have their defined-benefits pensions insured by a federal agency, the Pension Benefit Guaranty Corp (PBGC).  About 75,000 Bethlehem Steel pensioners - hourly, salaried and surviving spouses - have received their monthly pension checks during the past three years from PBGC following Bethlehem's October 15, 2001 bankruptcy filing.  PBGC took over Bethlehem's pension plans in December 2002.

headline: Last night's games
abstract: The article notes all of the ice hockey games from 4/11/2006 and their winners and scores. According to the scores, the winners were the Devils, the Islanders, the Senators, the Red Wings, the Maple Leafs, the Thrashers, the Predators, the Wild, the Stars, the Avalanche and the Flames.

headline: Rapid Response program saving lives
abstract: The number of people going into cardiopulmonary arrest in Mount Nittany Medical Center's non-critical care areas dropped by 53% in nine months. This is due to the establishment of Rapid Response Teams, something that the National Institute of Healthcare Improvement encourages in all hospitals as part of its 100,000 Lives Campaign.

headline: PennDOT set to begin replacing bridges over I-80 today
abstract: PennDOT has announced that work to replace the Interstate 80 bridges over Tunkhannock Creek in Tobyhanna Township, Monroe County, and Kidder Township, Carbon County, will begin this week. On Monday through Thursday Drivers will face single lane restrictions for about two miles. The project is set to be completed by August 2008.

headline: Proposed Penn National casino a favorite at public hearing
abstract: As evident by the crowd at a public hearing on the proposed Penn National casino in front of the PA Gaming Control Board yesterday, officials from Penn National Gaming, Inc., are not facing much opposition to their proposal, unlike the proposed casino in the Gettysburg area that faces much opposition from the area. Penn National Gaming President and CEO Peter M. Carlino described the "Hollywood Casino" and said revenue is expected to reach $160 million in the first year of the casino. The casino is supported by the PA Restaurant Association, the African American Chamber of Commerce for Central PA and the PA Horse Breeders Association. The only opposing attendee was Henry Craven, a Camp Hill resident.

headline: Lobbyist 'reform'? Not here
abstract: PA has been unwilling to take a bold step on lobbyist reform measures.  The Keystone State maintains the only state in the union without a lobbyist registration and disclosure law. It has been without such a law since 2002, when a previous statue was struck down by the PA Supreme Court in a gambling bill.  Numerous measures are pending, from a Senate-approved measure sponsored by PA Senate President Pro Tempore Robert Jubelirer.

headline: Pittsburgh scored high with senior Olympians
abstract: The National Senior Games Association released results of a survey indicating widespread approval and appreciation for the job Pittsburgh did in hosting the Summer National Senior Games. The Pittsburgh Local Organizing Committee that conducted fundraising to attract the games has cease to exist.

headline: Remember the Pas
abstract: PA Governor Rendell would like nurse practitioners to have expanded responsibilities. He should also include physician assistants in that group. PAs are health professionals licensed to practice medicine with physician supervision.

headline: Peters Township School District adjusting bus schedule
abstract: Valley Brook Road between East McMurray Road and Route19 has been closed which has forced Peters Township School District to adjust starting  times to give buses more time to negotiate detours when school begins.

headline: Punxsutawney Phil sees his shadow, predicts more winter
abstract: This year's celebration of Groundhog Day in Punxsutawney turned into an impromptu pep rally for the Pittsburgh Steelers, who will play in the 2006 Super Bowl. The groundhog saw his shadow and predicted six more weeks of mild winter. The opportunity to celebrate Groundhog Day in the "weather capital of the world" draws people from around the globe. Bill Cooper, president of the Punxsutawney Groundhog Club's Inner Circle, estimated that around 5,000 people attended this year.

headline: Longtime lawmaker won't seek re-election
abstract: Republican PA state Representative Dennis E. Leh announced his retirement, frustrated by the state Legislature's inability to deliver property tax relief. With PA state Representative Sam Rohrer, Leh was a leading proponent of the Commonwealth Caucus Plan designed to eliminate property taxes by increasing the state sales tax slightly and expanding the sales tax to cover more items. Leh did not mention the July 7, 2005 legislative pay raise in the press release announcing his retirement. The pay raise decision led to an anti-incumbency movement that has prompted nearly 100 challengers to seek to oust incumbent legislators across the state.

headline: Private bus service set for casino
abstract: There are plans to open a privately operated bus service between Mohegan Sun Casino at Pocono Downs and several pick-up points in Northeastern Pennsylvania. The locations consist of Scranton, Wilkes-Barre, Hazelton, and Allentown. The buses are likely to run during mornings not during busy times such as Friday night.

headline: Rendell hints at broad health care plan
abstract: Governor Rendell said that reducing hospital infections, which increase costs for insurers and employees, will be a priority, as part of an effort to cut health care costs in Pennsylvania. A recent report showed that 1.2 percent of hospital patients in Pennsylvania got an infection after being hospitalized in 2005.

headline: Picture Perfect
abstract: This article discusses the daily life of an employee at the PA Department of Transportation's Drivers License Center. Diane Weidenheimer typically issues one new license about every four minutes.

headline: Reasons should come with slots ruling
abstract: On Wednesday the Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board will announce who landed casino licenses without explaining its reasons. This is not fair to the losing applicants who will obviously be looking for answers on why they didn't get it. It is understandable for them to not reveal the whole report but they should provide some type of cliff notes.

headline: Lopez to serve on state Latino advisory board
abstract: Dr. Agapito Lopez, a Hazelton physician, will serve on PA Governor Ed Rendell's Advisory Commission on Latino Affairs in a two-year term.  The governor also reappointed Anna Arias, who works with the family enrichment program at Catholic Social Services in Hazelton.  The Commission's task is to help Latinos continue to prosper in PA.

headline: Spanish speakers test Geno's
abstract: Gilbert Garcia, a North Jersey lawyer orchestrated an event to order a cheesesteak from Geno's Steaks in Spanish after Joey Vento claimed he has never refused service to anyone.  Vento had posted outside of his restaurant, "This is America. When ordering please 'speak English.'" Garcia watched as 30 people ordered cheesesteaks in Spanish.  No one was denied service. Local protesters were upset about Garcia's event because they felt that it was media stunt.

headline: Rendell keeps keen eye on voters as he unveils budget
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell's state budget includes spending increases for public education, higher education, bioscience research and public safety, as well as expansion of programs to provide health insurance to children in low-income families and prescription drug coverage. Some noted that this move was designed with the upcoming election in mind. Republican legislative leaders criticized the plan for its call for new spending and cuts in programs that help rural areas and provide job training and economic development. Republican lawmakers accused Rendell of not acting on commitments made in the previous budgets to the PA State Troopers Association to hire more state troopers for highway patrol duty. Rendell's plan includes no tax increases.

headline: Playing politics on bad roads
abstract: A quarter of PA bridges are structurally unsound, one-third of the PA's secondary highways are in poor condition, and mass transit agencies have cut routes, raised fares, reduced staff, and in Philadelphia and Pittsburgh alone, face an $81 million deficit for the first six months of 2007.  The editorial board writes that few if any responsible people seem to get elected and sent to Harrisburg, where legislators never allow their jobs -- public service -- to interfere with their politics to get things done.

headline: Reasons should come with slots ruling
abstract: The Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board will announce who landed casino licenses without explaining its reasons. This is not fair to the losing applicants who will obviously be looking for answers on why they didn't get it. It is understandable for them to not reveal the whole report but they should provide some type of cliff notes.

headline: Lt. governor hopeful uses Perzel for piggish prank
abstract: Gene Stilp, who has been a strict and loud opponent of the legislative pay raise in 2005, is running for lieutenant governor of Pennsylvania. Sltip called attention to the pay raise in a recent campaign effort by bringing a 10-foot-long blow up pig to one of the offices of PA Representative John Perzel, Speaker of the House, to emphasize the fact that although the pay raise was rescinded, Perzel has kept the money along with a number of other legislators. Stilp is running against current PA Lieutenant Governor Catherine Baker Knoll as well as Valerie McDonald Roberts, the recorder of deeds in Allegheny County, and William A. Hall, a builder in Northampton County. Roberts questions Knoll's ability to run the state and many accuse her of being elected on the coattails of PA Governor Edward G. Rendell.

headline: Rendell's plan insults doctors and their value
abstract: Governor Rendell is out of line when he thinks people can go to less-trained providers as opposed to doctors. If he really wanted to improve health-care delivery he could give the 93 percent of graduating family doctors that are fleeing the state a reason to stay.

headline: Police step up patrols, road work suspended for holiday weekend
abstract: Work will be suspended on the Parkway East and many other major state highways for the Memorial Day Weekend. In addition there will be extra cops out looking for motorists driving under the influence of alcohol or drugs.

headline: Rendell should have vetoed 'free drinks' bill
abstract: Governor Rendell signed a bill which allows casinos to serve alcohol for free for 19 hours a day. This shows that the state government has no concern for the local taverns and restaurants that could be affected. It is also ridiculous that the police can ticket us for not buckling up but then they abandon their concerns for safety when it comes to casinos and the almighty gambling dollar.

headline: Macungie resident bids to unseat Rendell
abstract: Former Macungie councilman and retired Lehigh Career and Technical Institute teacher Joe McAndrew has decided to challenge PA Governor Ed Rendell during the upcoming Democratic gubernatorial primary. McAndrew said that he's upset at how Rendell and state lawmakers handled last year's controversial pay raise and wants to return "honesty" to state government. McAndrew said he's not concerned about trying to match Rendell, who already has $12 million raised, in fund-raising.

headline: Rising costs for older people squeeze Pennsylvania
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell and other PA politicians are facing pressure to resolve issues with the state's long-term care strategy as costs for elderly care grow due to population growth and health-care cost increases. Rendell has expanded in-home care services during his time in office which has precipitated a doubling of expenses for the state's Medicaid funding. The state faces a short-term deficit of $120 million, which it expects to pay via an overall budget surplus fund, but also faces the need to revise the entire elder-care system in quick order.

headline: Pricey asphalt may mean rough roads ahead
abstract: The high price of oil is cutting miles of road-paving projects this year across the state.  PennDOT is on track to pay 60 percent more in 2006 than in 2005 for asphalt and diesel fuel because of price increases that hit during the projects.  Some municipalities are paving fewer roads or eliminating paving.

headline: Rendell should veto unlimited drink bill
abstract: State legislature passed a bill late Tuesday that would allow the slot-machine parlors to serve unlimited free alcohol beverages to players. This could potentially hurt local businesses who serve alcohol, for this reason Governor Rendell should veto the bill.

headline: Magazine ranks area among "Smart places to Live"
abstract: Klipinger's Personal Finance magazine ranked State College 19th on its 50 smart places to live, citing that it is a great place to retire. Nashville, Tenn topped the list

headline: Secondhand smoke is a definite hazard
abstract: A report from the U.S. Surgeon General Richard Carmona declares secondhand smoke to be a major health hazard for nonsmokers. The editorial board says that the report should add pressure on state lawmakers to pass a ban on smoking in the workplace. Philadelphia City Council recently approved a ban on smoking in workplaces, including restaurants and many bars, but the measure awaits Philadelphia Mayor John Street's signature.

headline: Privatize Turnpike?
abstract: Governor Rendell is considering privatizing the Pennsylvania Turnpike. He is looking to sell it for a price ranging from $2 billion to $30 billion.

headline: Rendell slots role eyed
abstract: According to a House Republican spokesman, a top lawyer for PA Governor Ed Rendell sent an e-mail to select state employees saying the administration must approve any state grants for slots casinos, a move that some say indicates that Rendell has a hand in the licensing process for casinos The PA Gaming Control Board was set up to independently award slots licenses and regulate the industry. A spokesman for the PA Department of Community and Economic Development said the e-mail in no way suggests grants are being lined up for license winners. Some state grant programs bar use of their money for anything related to gambling. By steering the grants through the governor's office, the administration could ensure the money does not go to casinos.

headline: Making his case
abstract: In an interview with the  Lancaster New Era, Governor Ed Rendell defended his previous actions and explained why he deserves another term as governor. He defended his gambling initiatives b y saying that it will bring financial benefits to Pennsylvania. He defended his support of the pay raise for Pennsylvania judges, saying that they were under-paid, though he agrees with the repeal of the pay raise for legislators. He said that his expansion of the property tax rebate program was "progress". He reiterated his promise to serve all four years if he wins the election, and expressed optimism that Democrats could win control of the state House.

headline: State patches drug-plan 'glitch'
abstract: PA officials announced they will intervene to resolve issues created by the switch to the Medicare Part D prescription drug plan which has left numerous dual-eligible patients with exorbitantly high co-payments. The state will pay pharmacies through the PA Medicaid program for dual-eligible's who have been overbilled. PA officials expect to be reimbursed by the providers and federal authorities.

headline: Public roads, private spirits
abstract: Over 40 companies from across the globe have expressed interest in leasing the Pennsylvania Turnpike. Governor Rendell would be better off privatizing the Pennsylvania Liquor Control Board, which earns more than $400 million a year for the government.

headline: Rendell to sign gambling, lobbyist reforms
abstract: A gambling and lobbyist disclosure bill were passed in the PA Senate and will be signed by PA Governor Ed Rendell. The bill requires the attorney general to establish a gambling crimes unit and allows law enforcement broader power to investigate gambling crimes. It also allows the Pittsburgh City Council to retain power over zoning decisions on where a casino is built rather than the PA Gaming Control Board.

headline: Mariano witness bought house for $1, chief of staff says
abstract: The chief of staff to City Councilman Rick Mariano said he had alerted the state's inspector general to ethics questions about a former aide expected to testify against Mariano at his federal corruption trial next month. City tax records show that the aide, Ana Davila, purchased her house for $1, raising chief of staff Jay McCalla's suspicions. Davila told FBI agents that Mariano berated her for not accepting gifts in exchange for helping a constituent. Mariano is charged with trading government favors to businessmen for nearly $30,000 in credit-card payments and membership dues in an exclusive health club.

headline: State-Federal combination drug plan for seniors begins today
abstract: Beginning today senior citizens with PA's low-cost pharmaceutical programs should bring their federal Medicare drug card when they get their prescriptions. This is the beginning of the new Medicare benefit "Part D" and the state programs Pace ad Pacenet, which fill in where federal Medicare does not cover. No one will pay more than they did before the new programs.

headline: Rendell to sing sad tune in talk with Parker
abstract: Governor Rendell said he plans to talk with the US Airways CEO in the next two weeks to see where Pittsburgh stands in the three-city competition for the airline's future flight operation. Pittsburgh's initial bid was $25 million which is about $8 million less that Phoenix offered. Charlotte, the third city in the mix, has not disclosed the details of its proposal.

headline: Rescue a horse
abstract: Kelly Young of Lost and Found Horse Rescue thinks that a proposed bill that would reduce horse slaughter has left people who think that they might not be able to easily unload unwanted equines to sell their horses for slaughter.

headline: Mayor O'Conner hospitalized
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Bob O'Connor was admitted to UPMC Shadyside after complaining of a sore throat and flu-like symptoms.  O'Conner, age 61, went to the emergency room because his doctor is out of town.

headline: State-Federal combination drug plan for seniors begins today
abstract: Senior citizens with PA's low-cost pharmaceutical programs should bring their federal Medicare drug card when they get their prescriptions. This is the beginning of the new Medicare benefit "Part D" and the state programs Pace ad Pacenet, which fill in where federal Medicare does not cover. No one will pay more than they did before the new programs.

headline: Rendell: Make an offer for Pa. Turnpike
abstract: Governor Rendell is trying to sell the Pennsylvania Turnpike to a private ownership. Rendell said it costs the city almost $2 billion each year to bolster its roads, bridges, and public transit system. Rendell is looking to sell it in the $2 billion to $30 billion range.

headline: Resort officials make pitch for slots license
abstract: Nemacolin Woodlands Resort and Spa presented an application for a 500-slot casino to Pennsylvania Gaming Control members. They plan to open the casino in April.

headline: Mayor places top officials on leave
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl put Director of Operations Dennis Regan on paid leave while lawyers investigate charges that he repeatedly used sick time to work side jobs. The allegations were levied by Commander Catherine McNeilly, who has also been put on paid leave for the duration of the investigation.

headline: Surgery centers expanding in Pennsylvania
abstract: The  Pennsylvania Health Care Cost Containment Council reported that twenty-five new surgery centers opened in Pennsylvania from June 2005 and May 2006 and that such centers are profiting. Some argue that this is increasing health care costs and hurting the profits of hospitals, but some disagree.

headline: Report gives state a 'B' for highway safety laws
abstract: Pennsylvania scored a seven of 10 on the association's inaugural Scorecard on State Highway Laws. The state's deficient areas include lack of a primary seat-belt law and a universal motorcycle-helmet law, as well as no passenger limitations on cars driven by teenagers. Primary seat-belt laws allow police to pull over drivers for not buckling up; in Pennsylvania and other states, officers may only issue motorists citations for not wearing seat belts when they are pulled over for another violation.

headline: Roddey/Miles-led group abandons its slots plans
abstract: New Century Entertainment received a license to distribute slot machines from the PA Gaming Control Board, which can be resold to PA casinos.  The company, along with 14 others that have been licensed are allowed to act as a middleman between the slots makers and the casinos that will ultimately put the machines into use.  New Century now says they don't want the license because gambling is not the business they want to be involved in.

headline: Mayoral players downplay election
abstract: Three of the potential top Democrat Philadelphia mayoral contenders, U.S. Reps Bob Brady and Chaka Fattah, and State Rep Dwight Evans, say that tomorrows election results will not play a part of their decision to run for Mayor. Former City Councilman Michael Nutter is the only announced Democratic mayoral candidate.

headline: Swann backs limits on medical liability
abstract: Republican candidate for governor Lynn Swann, with PA Senator Jeff Piccola, toured the maternity wing at Harrisburg Hospital yesterday and heard the complaints of doctors about the problems they face on the job because of the high costs associated with medical malpractice. Swann then held a joint press conference with Piccola to support the Fair Share Act, which would make defendants found liable for damages in a civil trial pay only the share of the damages that match their share of the fault, as decided by jurors. PA Governor Edward G. Rendell vetoed the bill last month saying it did not adequately protect the rights of victims in negligence cases.

headline: Residents pool for pool
abstract: Residents who use the Dormont Pool will have to wait until repairs can be made on the pool that will cost more than the initial expected amount of $30,000, Dormont Borough Councilman John Sparvero said during a council meeting. Dormont officials recently announced that $3 million in renovations are needed to make the pool safer. Dormont Mayor Thomas Lloyd said later this week a company would determine what can be done to seal the pool. PA Representative Tom Petrone and PA Senator Wayne Fontana have petitioned PA Governor Edward G. Rendell for the money needed for the renovations.

headline: Roddey's firm gets license to sell slot machines to casinos
abstract: Jim Roddey has recently become the slot machine mogul of his company New Century Entertainment.  His company was recently approved to get a state distributor license by the PA Gaming Control Board.

headline: Media on defense
abstract: The author condemns the media for failing to intelligently defend themselves against accusations of bias, contending that the media has become overwrought with opinion.

headline: Swann rejects running mate's smoking stance
abstract: Gubernatorial candidate Lynn Swann has rejected the smoking stance of his running mate, Jim Matthews. Matthews believes that Pennsylvania should adopt a smoking ban for bars, restaurants, and other public venues. Swann believes businesses should have the right to decide.

headline: Road solutions may miss the bus
abstract: There have been many accidents on the Roosevelt Boulevard despite efforts to help curb them. Rendell has proposed an idea of selling part of the Pennsylvania Turnpike which could help generate enough money to do sink part of the Boulevard which is what is really needed to make it safer.

headline: S. Africa radio listeners try to parse LCB system
abstract: Andrew Cassel, a columnist for the Philadelphia Inquirer, recalls his recent visit to South Africa. He was introduced to the most popular radio host there and he told him about Pennsylvania's liquor laws. The radio host was so surprised that a capitalist country could late a state control something as big as liquor sales. Cassel wonders what the host will think when he hears that they recently appointed a CEO to the Liquor Control Board.

headline: Medicaid payroll rider amounts to extortion
abstract: The author argues that legislation requiring companies with over 10,000 employees to invest a set percentage in employee health plans or contribute to the state Medicaid coffers amounts to socialism and is motivated solely by union lobbying. The author worries that legislation of this kind will destroy businesses and the US economy.

headline: The nation is facing a possible collapse in its health system because of a shortage of primary care physicians
abstract: The American College of Physicians said Thursday that the US is facing a possible collapse in its health system because of the shortage of internists, physicians that prevent, diagnose and treat illnesses in adults and are most people's primary care physicians. However, fewer and fewer medical students are shying away from internal medicine because of the relatively low pay, inadequate training and discourage from their superiors. Dr. C. Anderson Hedberg, president of the American College of Physicians, said the country is going to need more general internists as baby boomers age and if universal health care is enacted. A report from the college found that just 13 percent of first-year medical students in 2005 said they intended to pursue general internal medicine.

headline: State hopes to replace 12 country bridges in 12 years
abstract: The American Society of Civil Engineers reported that twelve of Schuylkill County's bridges need to be replaced. The closing of one bridge has caused local residents many problems, and Pottsville City Administrator Thomas A. Palamar said that residents have resigned themselves to the bridge staying closed.

headline: Safe bet
abstract: PA Governor Rendell announced that PA lottery sales for the 2005-06 fiscal year reached a record $3.07 billion.  In all, sales grew by $425 million, the largest dollar increase in the 34-year history, leaving the agency with a $400 million surplus.

headline: Meet the GOP's main mudslinger
abstract: A columnist criticizes the Republican State Committee of Pennsylvania for sending out e-mails insulting Democrats Governor Ed Rendell and U.S. Senate candidate and current PA State Treasurer Bob Casey.

headline: UPMC stretches out: Mercy Hospital merger makes health giant's footprint even bigger.
abstract: The proposed merger of the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center and Mercy Hospital of Pittsburgh means that the health care giant's footprint now goes significantly beyond its original Oakland home. This opens the door for redevelopment east along Forbes Avenue and promises to promote revitalization of Downtown.

headline: State readies compromise plan on park road closing
abstract: Officials of the Swatara State Park want to convert a four-mile stretch of Old State Road to nonmotorized use reserved for hikers, cyclists and horseback riders. Both Swatara and Bethel Townships had scheduled meetings to discuss the issue this week, but state officials said a compromise plan will not be ready until next month, Roger Fickes, director of the Bureau of State Parks, said. Most of the objections to closing the road have come from Swatara Township meetings, with some people arguing that elderly and disabled people will not be able to enjoy the scenery and wildlife viewing if the road were closed to motor vehicles.

headline: Sands selection sure bet when 'take' taken into consideration
abstract: Las Vegas Sands' in Bethlehem was awarded the gambling license over Allentown's Tropicana. This was the case because the Sands' is projected to take almost $100 million more in revenue each year. This will allow more of a reduction property taxes around the state.

headline: Meet the real subversives
abstract: The PA Loyalty Act was passed in 1951 that requires Commonwealth candidates to swear they are not subversives, still required by the PA Legislature although the act was ruled unconstitutional in Communist Party of Indiana v. Whitcomb (1974).  The Socialist Workers Party has now challenged the oath and PA State Attorney Tom Corbett rightly ordered the PA Department of State to discontinue the loyalty oath.

headline: Day of rest in Capitol before tough budget talks resume
abstract: The new fiscal year has begun for the PA state government with only limited spending powers due to an inability for Democrats and Republicans in the House of Representatives to agree on a $27 billion budget.  While necessary functions will continue, over 40,000 state workers are furloughed due to the limited ability to spend.  PA Governor Ed Rendell has refused to sign the budget without the Legislature first taking action on his proposals for cutting health care costs, promoting alternative energy, and raising funding for mass transit and road repair.

headline: The health-care triangle
abstract: It is widely assumed that when a new administration is installed in Washington, health insurance eventually will be made available to all Americans. But the author worries that the cost of universal insurance will be staggering unless we simultaneously address the many issues that have not only driven the cost of care to a record high, but also have given us inadequate bang for the buck. The other half of adult patients and a higher percentage of children are under- or over-treated, or treated inappropriately with respect to evidence gained in controlled clinical trials as to the safest and most effective course of action. Thus, we squander half of our payments for health care.

headline: Cell phones and driving don't mix
abstract: The author of editorial believes that the state should intervene and pass a law that bans hand-held cell phone use while driving, which is the largest distracter and leading cause of crashes and near-crashes. Two different bills are being considered but have not been passed; though confusion has arisen from emails that have been circulating that claim the bill was passed.

headline: Audit: Job grant effort needs more monitoring
abstract: PA Auditor General Jack Wagner released a five year audit report on the Department of Community and Economic Development’s Opportunity Creation Grant Program. He gave them a good score but did say that the department should monitor how each grant is used more closely, so it can be sure recipients are actually using the money to create or retain jobs. Some of his other suggestions are listed, which the department claims it will implement.

headline:
GOP cuts counsel's pay until a review
The Pa. House caucus will have an ethics panel look at a separate $95,000 contract given to a former legislator.
abstract: House Republican Leader Sam Smith has been criticized for giving a $95,000 a year government legal contract to Brett Feese, who served in the House last year and is now a legislative staffer. In light of the criticism, he submitted the contract to the state Ethics Commission to rule whether it violates a PA law that prohibits state officials and staffers from having separate government contracts. Smith claims that he didn’t think the contract violates his interpretation of the law; though several lawmakers and activists are surprised and angry over the contract.

headline: County, city team up for electric bargains
abstract: Allegheny County and the city of Pittsburgh will use the services of Co-exprise Inc. for an online electricity auction. The auction should get a number of electricity providers to drop their prices to compete for the large government contract. The city and county are also hoping to include some important government agencies in the auction.

headline: Despite negotiations, no end in sight for impasse
abstract: The PA budget impasse appears to be continuing despite constant negotiations between the legislative leaders, and the PA House of Representative Republicans are arguing to pass a "stopgap" budget that would send the furloughed state employees back to work.  Despite these calls for a "stopgap" budget, Speaker of the House Dennis O' Brien would move to a floor session.  PA Senator Mike Waugh is frustrated that PA Governor Ed Rendell is "bullying" the Legislature with his leverage on the budget.

headline: Thousands of children lack insurance
abstract: According to a survey by Market Decisions Limited Liability Company, more than 12% of children in Franklin County are uninsured making the county the sixth worst in the state.  This fact comes despite PA Governor Ed Rendell claiming that Pennsylvania's Child Health Insurance Program offers affordable health insurance to all children in the state.  Colleen Milligan, of Highmark, recently spoke to Franklin County of Governments about the CHIP program claiming that no child should go without health insurance.

headline: Commuters from area to big cities will hurt along with trucking companies if revenue-raising plan goes through.
abstract: Trucking companies will not be the only ones hit in the pocketbook if Interstate 80 becomes a toll road. Wilkes-Barre, Mountain Top and Hazleton residents commuting to work may be forced to pay an additional $2,000 in tolls per year, per driver to get to the state border, depending on the placement of toll collecting gantries along I-80. Stretching for 311 miles in the state, I-80 garners commuters from many surrounding local communities. A traffic study conducted by the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation shows that 306,060 workers from Northeast Pennsylvania commute to work , although it did not determine how many of those commuters utilized I-80 on a daily basis.

headline: Authority will foot convention center bill
abstract: The Pittsburgh city-county Sports Exhibition and Authority board have unanimously agreed to pay for the collapse at the David L. Lawrence Convention Center where repairs are estimated to cost $1.4 million.  The six-member board also plans to apply to the PA Department of Economic Development for a $10 million grant over 10 years to start construction of an outdoor music venue next to Heinz Field.  State spokesman Kevin Ortiz says the authority has not yet applied for the Infrastructure and Facilities Improvement grant and that the developers must meet annual tax revenue goals before receiving the grant.

headline: Gov. Rendell playing favorites
abstract: Scott Young writes to the editor to complain about PA Governor Ed Rendell's denial of state funds to Harrisburg to get rid of the incinerator deficit and calls his decision "irresponsible."  Young also accuses Rendell of playing favoritism with Philadelphia claiming that if Philadelphia needed money, he would use part of the $650 million dollar surplus.

headline: Do your Act 1 homework
abstract: Editors urge residents to think carefully about the proposed ballot question at the polls concerning whether residents want to shift school revenue from property taxes to earned income tax. Editors note only some are eligible for property tax reductions, while all will see an income tax increase. Property tax eligibility is expected to increase in the next few years. Act 1 is puzzling in itself, it seems to attempt to speed up property tax relief that was not to be instituted until gaming legislation brought in $500 million.

headline: Finally, a budget in place for Pennsylvania
abstract: The PA House of Representatives recently passed the 2007-2008 budget with a vote of 140-63, and PA Governor Ed Rendell is expected to sign the bill today.  PA Representative Dwight Evans claims that while the budget was two weeks late, it exemplified a successful bipartisan compromise that hasn't happened for a while.  Due to a $650 million surplus, Republicans were able to cut the proposed taxes from the budget, while Rendell was able to pass through educational and health care funding programs.

headline: Two Pittsburgh hospitals honored for protecting children's health
abstract: The Children’s Hospital of Pittsburgh and Magee-Womens Hospital will be honored by the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency for their efforts to protect children from environmental risks.

headline: Commuting cost crunch
abstract: With wallets as narrow as a bus seat, commuters watch gas prices skyrocket. The increase has caused a ripple effect for bus companies serving Pocono commuters. Fuel costs 85 cents a gallon more than last year at this time, according to Joe and Jan's Charter and Tours President Joseph Schoppy. Steele said mass transit may become more attractive to commuters as gas prices go up.

headline: Awaken city from its long planning nap
abstract: Much is made of William Penn's celebrated street grid, the Benjamin Franklin Parkway, and the making of Society Hill. Despite these landmark achievements, city planning has not been Philadelphia's strong suit for a long time. Philadelphia, meanwhile, wasted years praying over cursed tracts such as Penn's Landing. We starve our planning commission of funds and staff. Suddenly, Philadelphia is planning again: More than 1,000 people jammed the Convention Center for the recent unveiling of a new waterfront master plan. A new Zoning Code Commission has begun a rewrite of that tangled document. The city is at work on a bold GreenPlan for open space. Mayor-elect Nutter is strong on these issues.

headline: House, Senate may face open records showdown
abstract: The state House of Representatives and state Senate could be headed for a showdown over separate proposals intended to let Pennsylvania residents access government documents that have been shielded from the public for decades. The Senate voted 48-1 on Wednesday to pass a revamped version of the state open records law. The House State Government Committee later unanimously approved a measure similar to the Senate bill. A full House vote on that bill could occur as early as Tuesday.

headline: Fawcett: Assessment flaws forced drink tax
abstract: In his eight years as a member of County Council, Dave Fawcet considered himself a champion of small and efficient government. So Allegheny County political observers and restaurateurs opposed to the 10 percent drink tax were stunned when Mr. Fawcett cast a decisive vote for the tax, which is part of a new dedicated funding stream for the Port Authority. Mr. Fawcett, whose fights against the base year property assessment system and for the consolidation of county row offices established his credentials as one of council's fiscal conservatives, said he cast a vote for a new tax because of stark reality. Mr. Onorato had said a failure to enact the new taxes would force him to lay off up to 800 county employees.

headline: Governor got some increases he sought; much work remains
abstract: The editorial claims that the PA Governor Ed Rendell cannot be completely disappointed with the proposals he had to disclude in the recent budget impasse such as his seven tax hikes, ban on smoking in public buildings and his Energy Independence Fund.  Despite these losses, the editorial believes that Rendell's passing of his $945 million transportation funding, $200 million preschool and education funding and his increased roles for nurses and nurse practitioners are victories to celebrate.  The one lesson that the article stresses all areas of the state government needs to learn is to start the legislative process for the budget in March and April rather than June and July to avoid another budget impasse crisis.

headline: U.S. healthcare expensive, inefficient: report
abstract: A Commonwealth Fund report found Americans get the poorest health care but pay the most for it compared to Germany, Britain, Australia and Canada. President George W. Bush and Congress have agreed an overhaul of the US health care system is necessary. The US has the lowest percentage of physicians using electronic medical records or receiving electronic updates on recommended treatments.

headline: Conditions set for cargo airport aid
abstract: A Senate committee voted to put conditions on any release of state aid for the proposed cargo airport in the Hazleton area. In addition to adding dozens of projects to the House-passed capital projects bill, the Appropriations Committee stipulated that state and federal officials will have to sign off on various aspects of the airport project by Gladstone Partners LP.

headline: Boosting tourism funds spurs hot debate point
abstract: The PA House Urban Affairs Committee debated and passed a proposal sponsored by PA Representative Thomas Petrone that allows VisitPittsburgh, the Allegheny County tourism agency, to receive 2% of the funds that the Allegheny Regional Asset District receives each year from the county sales tax.  If Petrone's bill ultimately passed, many local organizations who typically receive funding such as  the Allegheny County Library Association, the Pittsburgh Opera and the Pittsburgh Zoo will be not receive as much.

headline: Governor's Goals
abstract: This list outlines the top priorities for PA Governor Ed Rendell as he proposes his spending plan to the Pennsylvania Legislature.

headline: Free these seniors from property tax
abstract: The Pennsylvania General Assembly has debated the best way to achieve property-tax relief for decades - but with little success. Ever since John Perzel was first elected to the legislature in 1978, property-tax relief for senior citizens has been always its top priority. Somewhere along the way, though, we legislators lost sight of our original goal. Instead of a focus on reducing the tax burden for senior citizens who can least afford to pay their property taxes, promises were made to the general population that many knew just could not be kept.

headline: House lawmakers pull pet projects
abstract: PA Rep. Dwight Evans convinced Democrats to withdraw earmarks from the budget proposed by PA Governor Ed Rendell, leaving the Legislature to consider passing Rendell's $27.3 billion proposal, or settling for a scaled down Republican version which maintains the current budget within 2 percent. The Republican proposal was defeated with Speaker Dennis O'Brien crossing party lines. A vote on Rendell's proposal is scheduled today. The budget is expected to go to a House Senate conference committee.

headline: Unions take closer look at health-care stories
abstract: The American Federation of Labor and Congress of Industrial Organizations have developed a new Web site named the "Health Care Hustle," which invites readers to submit it stories of the health care system failing in America.  The site also encourages viewers to send messages to the "greedy" corporations: the Pharmaceutical Research and Manufacturers of America, the insurance industry and the Bush administration.  The site follows a national trend that pushes for universal health care.

headline: Consumer group warns against private turnpike
abstract: The Pennsylvania Public Interest Research Group Education Fund has warned that the state will hinder its own ability to enact sensible transportation policies after privatizing the Pennsylvania Turnpike.  PA Governor Ed Rendell wants to find an investor to control and maintain the turnpike and the government would in turn receive a windfall of up to $13 billion.  PennPIRG believes the state should explore low-interest borrowing rather than privatization.

headline: Brookings Institution links nation's prosperity to urban areas
abstract: When it comes to jobs, population and the gross domestic product, Pennsylvania relies on its metropolitan areas. A study by the Brookings Institution has found that Pennsylvania is much like the rest of the country, with population, jobs and innovation clustered around metropolitan areas. The state's 16 metropolitan areas constitute 84 percent of the state's population and 87 percent of the state's jobs. As the report points out, though metropolitan areas take up only 12 percent of the land area of the United States, they are home to 65 percent of the country's population, provide 68 percent of the nation's jobs and develop 78 percent of the country's patents.

headline: Grand jury to have access to House Democratic records
abstract: The PA Supreme Court unanimously rejected an appeal from the House Democratic caucus over the seizure of 20 boxes of campaign and political documents. The material could be presented to a grand jury investigation into whether state employees received significant bonuses as payment for campaign work. Attorney General tom Corbett said that he is investigating all four caucuses.

headline: Income tax reform
abstract: Under a Rendell administration proposal to consolidate local earned income tax collection at the county level: The number of tax collectors statewide would be reduced from 560 to 66., municipalities and school districts would save $237 million annually, all municipalities and school districts in each county would meet and elect a single county tax collector, which could be a county government department, private third-party business or a nonprofit established solely to collect taxes and if enacted by the legislature, the reform would take effect in January 2011.

headline: In budget fight, isn't there some way to keep the casinos open? Ta-da!
abstract: John Baer of the Philadelphia Daily News writes on the closing of 5 slots casinos and furloughing of 26,000 state employees because of the budget impasse.  Baer believes that the PA Governor Ed Rendell should pass a stopgap budget, which would allow normal operations and state workers to continue working even through the impasse.  Bear cites Pennsylvania as the only state who have a late budget that are working without a stopgap budget and claims that everyday the casinos are closed the government loses $2.6 million a day in tax revenue.

headline: Universal health care provides everyone access
abstract: Domenick Buscemi of the Lehigh Valley Healthcare Reform Meetup Group disagrees with local op-ed columnist John Brinson's assertion that the US healthcare system is the best in the world  in his recent article about PA Governor Ed Rendell's "Prescription for Pennsylvania."  Buscemi believes a single-payer system would reduce administrative costs and create a more accountable program.  He cites studies by the World Health Organization that place US healthcare 15th out of 25 countries.

headline: County gets boost in fight against FAA airport plan
abstract: US Representative Joe Sestak is pleased that US Representative Jim Oberstar, chair of the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee has halted the Federal Aviation Administration's plan to redesign departing planes from Philadelphia International Airport.  Oberstar stated that the plan would not go into affect until a report by the Government Accountability Office is done.  PA Congressman Rob Andrews, like Sestak, is concerned about the plan and whether or not it is the best use of tax dollars.

headline: Casino's garage plan worries city
abstract: Mayor Luke Ravenstahl wants the owner of a planned North Shore casino to change the look of its garage and make the building environmentally friendly. Detroit businessman Don Barden initially said his Majestic Star Casino would have a soaring 110-foot glass drum as its signature design element. The slots parlor building would have nearly hidden the parking garage behind it. But in the latest designs, the garage has gotten slightly bigger while the drum stands at 87 feet. The garage would be nearly twice as tall as the 60-foot-high casino building. That's unacceptable, said Pat Ford, executive director of the city Urban Redevelopment Authority.

headline: Great debate: Strong public interest makes it a real mayor's race
abstract: Luke Ravenstahl became Pittsburgh’s Governor after the unfortunate death of Bob O’ Connor last year, and the county elections board decided that a mayoral election should be held this year, rather than 2009, in light of the circumstances. The author of the editorial was upset because it seemed like there wouldn’t be any competition for the election. However, a Republican candidate stepped up, and it appears that there will be a contested election, which the author believes is good for the city of Pittsburgh.

headline: It’s showtime
abstract: NBC "Today" show weatherman and co-host Al Roker, who is a huge fan of NBC’s television show "The Office," will be travelling to Scranton to kick off "The Office" convention at the University of Scranton. There are many planned activities, and at least nine cast members from the show will attend the festivities. Scranton Mayor Chris Doherty said that the show has brought the city a lot of good publicity, and big crowds are expected for the convention.

headline: It's the spending stupid
abstract: The defeat of Act 1 by voters shows they want tax cuts, not simply tax shifts as proposed by PA Governor Ed Rendell and passed along by the Legislature. This effort at shifting the burden of school funding from property taxes to income taxes was a failure. Seniors on fixed incomes are more inclined to support Act 1. However the Legislation HAD loopholes that allowed School Districts to raise property taxes above the inflation rate. The writer does not believe gambling revenue will offset property taxes as much as was promised.

headline: An unimaginable leap
abstract: Dmitri is a 380-pound Amur tiger, and as he lumbered across the grounds of his compound at the Philadelphia Zoo, it was difficult to imagine him leaping an 18-foot wall. But officials think that's what may have happened at the San Francisco Zoo on Christmas when a highly endangered tiger turned highly dangerous, escaping its pen to kill one person and maul two others. Yesterday, executives at some local zoos were bewildered that such a big cat was said to have leaped so high.

headline: County man suspended after accident in state vehicle
abstract: Norman Bristol-Colon, who serves as executive director of PA Governor Ed Rendell’s Advisory Commission on Latino Affairs was suspended with pay after an accident involving his state-issued vehicle on December 20, 2007. Bristol-Colon was a passenger in the vehicle when it veered off Route 283 near Elizabethtown. According to a police report, the car struck a highway sign and crashed into a parked tractor-trailer. The driver of the car, Adriana Malpica, told police she had two drinks at a Harrisburg nightclub earlier in the evening and might have fallen asleep at the wheel. A breath test indicated Malpica’s blood-alcohol level was 0.05 percent, below the state’s legal limit of 0.08 percent for drivers.

headline: Budget standoff stalls van service
abstract: The delay in the passing of the state budget in the PA House of Representatives have negatively affected the residents of the public housing community Prospect Terrace in East Pittsburgh.  The WorkLink Community Van is the only public transportation that these residents have access to get to work and the federal grant of $4 million that helps run the van cannot be used until the state commits the same amount of money to the program.  Residents such as Shiree Johnson and Reverend J.D. Middlebrook now have to walk 205 stairs to get to and from work.

headline: Green pastures: PHEAA execs need to get by on hefty salaries alone
abstract: The Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency, a public nonprofit chartered by the PA Legislature, has caused outrage among Pennsylvanians by granting its upper management lavish bonuses despite their already high salaries.  Chief executive Richardo Willey was granted a $180,857 bonus in addition to his $289,118 salary.  This editorial is skeptical about PA Senator Sean Logan's desire to change as he may just increase their salaries and decrease the bonuses, and the author also mentions if privatizing the agency would make it more responsible.

headline: New Phila. Tax bills will hit home
abstract: As part of one of the city's largest mass reappraisals, any day now they will be informed that their property-tax bills are about to go up - in some cases by more than $1,000 annually. In all, taxes are being readjusted on 413,000 parcels - better than 70 percent of the city's total. In each of the previous two years, the city reassessed fewer than 10 percent of the properties. The average residential increase would be $77, said Pete Peterson, a spokesman for the Board of Revision of Taxes (BRT). Only 6 percent of the new assessments would represent reductions; the rest, increases, mostly $200 or less.

headline: Legislators' budget mantra: cut (everyone else's) spending
abstract: Republican law makers in the PA House of Representatives disagree with PA Governor Ed Rendell's budget proposal because of his increased taxes and lack of spending cuts.  PA Representative Daryl Metcalfe speaks for many Republicans who feel the taxing increase limits the economic freedom of individual citizens, while Democrats largely feel the budget is sufficient but are hesitant about allowing the Governor to privatize the Pennsylvania Turnpike.  Lawmakers have until June 30 to pass the state budget.

headline: Clean & Green Acres
abstract: Columbia County claims state Agriculture Secretary Dennis Wolff owes $13,000 in taxes on his 117-acre farm. Tax assessors say he violated the state's Clean and Green farm and forest preservation program. Mr. Wolff's duties include statewide administration of Clean and Green. A milk store on Wolff's farm had been converted to nonagricultural uses like a minimart or to sell candles,

headline: Cross Valley overpass deemed structurally deficient
abstract: During a routine inspection earlier this year, the Bennett Street and Mercer Avenue overpass of the North Cross Valley Expressway was deemed structurally deficient. The bridge has a sufficiency rating of 79, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation. Bridges with a sufficiency rating of 80 or higher are not eligible for funding for repairs.

headline: Check it out: 1.5 million books in online library
abstract: Nearly a decade ago, computer scientists at Carnegie Mellon University embarked on a project with an astonishingly lofty goal: digitize the published works of humankind and make them freely available online. The architects of the project said they have surpassed their latest target, having scanned more than 1.5 million books -- many of them in Chinese -- and are continuing to scan thousands more daily. The latest phase in the development of the so-called Universal Library, called the Million Book Project, began in 2002 after Reddy's team successfully scanned 1,000 books.

headline: Group calls for fines for late budget
abstract: The watchdog group Common Cause of Pennsylvania have introduced a proposal that will apply stricter deadlines for approving the budget, a $100-a-day fine for all legislators for missing these deadlines and lawmakers forfeiting pay until the budget is completed.  PA Representatives Eugene DePasquale and Steven Nickol acknowledged the good intentions of the proposal but found flaws with how it was proposed.  However, PA Representative Bev Mackereth feels the fines punish lawmakers for standing up for their beliefs and would only endorse politicians caving in to the opposing party.

headline: Mayor vetoes council's freeze
abstract: Pittsburgh’s City Council froze the city’s parking tax at 45 percent because parking operators refused to lower rates after a previous drop, however, Mayor Luke Ravenstahl vetoed the decision. According to a state-mandated financial recovery plan, the tax had previously been increased, which angered downtown businesses,  but it was supposed to gradually lower to 35 percent by 2010. State Senator Jane Orie had threatened to withhold state funding if rates aren’t lowered,  Ravenstahl vowed to ensure that the rate reduction would benefit the public, and local businesses are pleased with Ravenstahl's decision.

headline: Local lawmakers oppose budget
abstract: Local PA Representatives Rob Kauffman, Todd Rock and Mark Keller all voted against the $27.2 billion that was recently passed because of the 5.3% spending increase over last year's budget.  Kauffman specifically opposes the fact the spending increase is more than twice the rate of inflation and provides $75 million in tax credits to the film industry.  The three representatives also publicly opposed the funding cuts to the PA Department of Agriculture, specifically the Crop Insurance Assistance Program.

headline: Dog bills
abstract: A bill, sponsored by PA Representative Mario Scavello, was approved by the House Judiciary Committee that prohibits the tethering of dogs between 10 p.m. and 6 a.m. and requires a specific length for leashes. A spokesman for The Humane Society of the United States said that it is a step in the right direction to protecting dogs.

headline: Debate Over Tolling I-80 Carries On
abstract: There is a pending amendment in a U.S. House transportation bill that is attempting to block state efforts to toll Interstate 80. However, Governor Rendell’s Deputy Chief of Staff Roy Kienitz believes that the state will be able to continue the process, but Rendell will also continue to pursue an alternative plan to pay for increasing transportation costs by leasing the turnpike to a private company.

headline: City plans second hotel near Capitol
abstract: Developers have proposed two plans for an 88-suite hotel for the stretch of State Street between the Capitol and the Susquehanna River. Developer Jules Patt of Hollidaysburg said the hotel would be geared to the higher-end luxury market. Last month, Harrisburg City Council approved plans for the $10 million, 183-room Starwood Aloft, which will be built at Second and State streets, a block from the Barto Building. Patt and Harrisburg Mayor Stephen R. Reed said construction on the Barto Building project will begin as soon as council approves the plans, with the hotel expected to open in summer 2008.

headline:
Groups propose redistricting plan for state lawmakers
The proposal would take the power of drawing state Senate and Assembly districts away from lawmakers.
abstract: The article is about a proposal from several California organizations that would require the state to change how legislative districts are drawn. If it were approved by voters, the proposal would create a commission made up of five Democrats, five Republicans and four others who would be chosen through a public application process which is described in the article. The commission would take power away from legislators.

headline: Mayor will eliminate amusement tax on arts
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl announced he would strike the 1.25 percent amusement tax on nonprofit arts organizations from the city's next budget. The cut is estimated to save organizations such as the Cultural Trust, Pittsburgh Symphony, Pittsburgh Opera, Pittsburgh CLO and Pittsburgh Public Theater almost half a million dollars. Mark Weinstein, arts council board chairman, says it will be difficult for any mayor ever to institute such a tax again.

headline: Mustio calls for state hiring freeze
abstract: PA Rep. Mark Mustio introduced a budget amendment to save $200 million through hiring freeze, passing on the savings to taxpayers in the form of tax cuts. PA Governor Ed Rendell has increased his budget proposal over last year's, to $27.3 billion. PA Majority Leader Bill DeWeese is proposing to increase the sales tax by a half a percentage point to offset property taxes. Rendell is posing a 1 percent sales tax increase. Minority Leader Sam Smith says all tax increases likely will fail.

headline: How to make next year's farmers markets even better
abstract: PA just completed its best farmers market season ever. The markets attracted thousands of customers who bought tons of apples, blueberries, lettuce, corn, zucchini and other fruits and vegetables from farms across the state. These markets are critical to keeping our farmers farming. Author requests some ways that the state can make next year even better.

headline: Don't put so much blame on trucking industry
abstract: Nolan Perin wrote this letter to the editor to criticize a local columnist, Paul Carpenter, who complained about the trucking industry. Mr. Perin sarcastically proposes levying thousands of dollars worth of taxes against the trucking industry to prove his point that Carpenter's claims were ridiculous. He argues that truckers are not "pampered" and feels that they will only raise their fees to compensate for any taxes that are levied against them.

headline: Commission delays hearing on casino design
abstract: Pittsburgh planning officials bowed to a legal complaint Thursday and agreed to delay a public hearing next week on designs for the $450 million Majestic Star Casino. The Pittsburgh Riverlife Task Force argued the city Planning Commission didn't give the 21-day notice required by law and that Majestic Star hasn't provided final plans for public review. The commission will now hold the hearing Jan. 14 or 15.

headline: Hampton teachers closer to strike
abstract: A bargaining session slated for Dec. 11 was canceled when the union officials left a meeting, said Arleen Starr, chief negotiator for the Pennsylvania State Education Association, which represents Hampton's 225 teachers. Talks began in January, and the teachers contract expired June 30. A general membership meeting is planned for Nov. 27, during which teachers will be informed about some 50 outstanding issues, Starr said. She said it is possible that a vote to authorize a strike could be taken at that time.

headline: Not a bad day's work
abstract: In almost all 498 school districts required to present the option of shifting from property taxes to income taxes to fund public schools, voters said no. PA Governor Ed Rendell supported the measure, which was proposed in light of expected income from slots machines. While it helps retirees, it hurt dual-income families and renters. Rendell's administration attributed the failure of the referendum to confusion rather than opposition. Mayor Luke Ravenstahl won the Democratic primary unopposed.

headline: Pa. budget fight brings partial shutdown
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell has ordered that 24,000 "non-essential" state workers to be furloughed as he and the PA Legislature cannot come to an agreement on the budget.  Despite this order, a Commonwealth Court judge has ordered that the casino slot parlors must remain open at least until Tuesday according to Doug Harbach of the PA Gaming Control Board.  The stalemate is in regards to Rendell's energy plan that he demands be passed before the budget, but Senate Majority Leader Dominic Pileggi claims that with a $650 million surplus, there is no reason that a budget cannot be passed.

headline: Neglected horses found in N. Phila. Stables
abstract: Officials found several neglected horses living in deplorable conditions in North Philadelphia stables. Officials from the city and the Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals went to the 2600 block of Fletcher Street in response to an anonymous tip. They said they had found tons of horse manure piled inside the stables, and the rotting carcass of one horse partly buried behind one of the buildings.

headline: DOT reversal spotlights problem
abstract: The state's top highway official reversed a decision his agency had made to withhold bridge safety ratings from the public. The House State Government Committee had requested testimony from the Department of Transportation on why it refused to release bridge safety ratings to a newspaper that had asked for them several months ago.

headline: Convention Center progress
abstract: The authors  represent the four organizations who are working together on the $700 million Philadelphia Convention Center expansion project. They believe the costly project is essential because of the economic benefits that it could bring to the city by keeping up with other cities on the east coast, creating thousands of construction and permanent jobs, and fueling tourism, which would be beneficial for local hotels, restaurants, shops, and historical sites. The authors claim that they have already booked over $1 billion worth of business for after the center’s completion and vow to cooperate to deliver on their promises.

headline: Harrisburg digging its way out of the muck
abstract: John Baer expresses his opinion on how the PA Legislature is finally beginning to devote itself to reform after much controversy in 2005.  He approves that the GOP-controlled Senate ended private vehicle leases, added co-pays for health insurance and ended secret employee bonuses.  PA Senate President Pro Tempore Joe Scarnati is also proposing to give $75 million of the Legislature's surplus to property-tax relief.  The Democratic House Denny O' Brien's Commission on Legislative Reform recommending changes to be voted on next week such as limiting hours, eliminating vehicle leases, and opening the process as a whole.

headline: Onorato presses County Council to OK new taxes
abstract: It seems that Allegheny County Chief Executive Dan Onorato is steeling himself for a budget showdown with County Council in 10 days over proposed new taxes on alcoholic drinks and car rentals. Mr. Onorato reiterated yesterday that he will veto any effort to raise property taxes instead of using the new taxes to pay the county's $30 million share of costs at the Port Authority. That would leave council with only one other option -- forcing the county to lay off an additional 800 workers and make more cuts in mass transit. Council will meet on Dec. 4, when the 15-member panel might adopt or reject Mr. Onorato's $727.5 million budget for 2008, in which he proposed a 10 percent tax on poured alcoholic drinks and a $2-a-day tax on car rentals.

headline: Pa. legislators close in on budget
abstract: After making a tentative deal on the spending plan of the 2007-2008 budget, the PA House of Representatives and the PA Senate are planning to vote on the final approval of the $27.2 billion spending package after a conference committee last night between six House and Senate leaders.  The state budget includes a 3.5% increase in health and welfare spending and a 5.8% increase in education spending.
