The Senate committee also passed a bill that will give funding for a $300 million Pittsburgh Penguins arena as well as other important Allegheny County projects.

headline: Pa. dog kennel inspection records available online
abstract: PA is the first state to post inspection records of kennels online, according to the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals, cutting down on paperwork and improving accuracy, said a PA Department of Agriculture spokesman. PA Governor Ed Rendell announced several measures to strengthen the laws for "puppy mills" which have earned the state a notorious reputation among animal lovers.

headline: Driver overtime busts transit agency's budget
abstract: Theresa Giurintano announced the County of Lebanon Transit Authority is in need of more drivers to make up for overtime paid to drivers filling in for absentees. The transit system also needs more riders. The system expects to be in a deficit this year. COLT and other transit authorities have lobbied PA Governor Ed Rendell and the Legislature to provide a designated funding source for mass transit.

headline: Council asks court to stop city casino A petition to the state Supreme Court seeks to halt SugarHouse from building on the riverbed.
abstract: The Philadelphia City Council has joined with a group of state legislators in an attempt to block SugarHouse Casino from being built over state-owned land underneath the Delaware River. The Council’s petition to the PA Supreme Court is similar to one that was filed by seven state legislators, which said that Mayor John F. Street’s Commerce Department improperly licensed SugarHouse to build on submerged state land and ass the court to stop it from being built. Mayor Street and PA Governor Edward Rendell want SugarHouse and a second casino, Foxwoods in South Philadelphia to be built.

headline: Health care, tax cuts, reform. Rendell winds up for an ambitious
abstract: The inauguration, concert and gala are over. Today, PA Governor Ed Rendell starts pursuing an ambitious second-term agenda that could define his legacy. Rendell's swearing-in drew a smaller-than-expected crowd, judging from all the empty chairs, but he outlined big goals in his 12-minute speech at the Capitol. He surprised some by pushing government reforms, noting the ousted lawmakers not attending his inauguration. "Voters believe that the political process needs reform," Rendell said. "I agree with the voters." Democrats and Republicans lauded Rendell's ideas.

headline: Onorato tax plan gets 2 endorsements
abstract: Kevin Joyce, chairman of the PA Restaurant Association, told the Allegheny County Council’s budget committee to consider alternatives to Chief Executive Dan Onorato’s proposal to add a 10 percent tax on poured drinks and a car rental tax to fund mass transit. He claims that it will hurt the hospitality business and drive many businesses out of the area. Despite these objections, the Allegheny Conference on Community Development and the Greater Pittsburgh Chamber of Commerce endorsed Onorato’s proposal if the Port Authority works out their financial issues.

headline: Pa.'s Budget Bickering - Knock it off
abstract: This editorial expresses frustration with the Pennsylvania lawmakers who cannot overcome party lines to agree on a budget for the next fiscal year.  The Democratic House approved a $27.3 billion budget that follows PA Governor Ed Rendell's plan to invest heavily in education and transportation, but the Republican Senate cut $330 million from the budget, specifically in education.  The author outlines what needs to be included in this year's budget:  investment in mass transit such as South Eastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority, Rendell's prekindergarten funding, and more funding for increasing health costs and the uninsured citizens.

headline: Amid anger and tears, difficult choices near
abstract: The Hershey Company has been criticized for local job cuts that will amount to 600 to 650.  Many of the workers who will lose their jobs do not have any options for new jobs and claim they cannot live on the severance packages.  Derry Township Supervisor August Memmi said elected officials do have the ability to make plans to help these workers to find jobs..

headline: Eachus: Airport limits aren’t ‘onerous’
abstract: Restrictions put on the proposed cargo airport by the state Senate Appropriations Committee on Tuesday are unusual, but not burdensome, according to its biggest legislative backer, state Rep. Todd Eachus.The committee attached four conditions before any state money is appropriated to it: the project must be approved by both the Federal Aviation Administration and the Bureau of Aviation Pennsylvania Department of Transportation, the in-progress study by the Legislative Budget and Finance Committee must result in a favorable recommendation for the airport, no other state and local funds can be used for it, the Department of Community and Economic Development must certify that at least 50 percent of project funding comes from private sources.

headline: Council backs proposal for ethanol storage tanks
abstract: The Steelton Borough Council recently passed a proposal to build 3 to 6 ethanol storage tanks to store the fuel until it is shipped away to be mixed with gasoline.  The facility will be built by Steelon Townships Corporation and is estimated to cost between $10 to $15 million to construct.  This project is a part of an initiative by PA Governor Ed Rendell to produce 900 million gallons of biofuels annually within the state in 10 years.

headline: Hearing on Corzine-girlfriend emails today
abstract: A New Jersey judge will listen to arguments and determine whether the state’s Governor, John Corzine, violated court orders. Tom Wilson, the state Republican chairman, claims that the Governor’s office disobeyed a court order requiring Corzine to produce e-mails and other communications dealing with Carla Katz, a union leader he used to date. Wilson believes the relationship affected Corzine’s role as Governor, and both Katz and Corzine argue that their communications should remain confidential.

headline:
Overseers approve city's budget
State pleased with progress, but skeptics see trouble on horizon
abstract: An outside agency approved Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl’s proposed budget, which will include lowering the parking tax, and it will be sent to the City Council for final approval. Pittsburgh has a serious debt problem that discourages investments, so Governor Rendell and State Budget Secretary Michael Masch are pleased that the city will have a budget surplus next year. However, some people are concerned about the final two years of the five year proposal because the city will again have a budget deficit due to projected rising costs in pensions and health insurance, which has prompted Mayor Ravenstahl to consider some reforms.

headline: Partial shutdown of Pa. government had little effect here
abstract: Local legislators in the Fay-West area report that despite the furlough of 626 Pennsylvania Department of Transportation workers, the budget impasse did not cause many notable problems.  PA State Representative Tim Mahoney reported that the deal struck between PA Governor Ed Rendell and the PA Legislature includes a provision that will pay the furloughed workers for the day that they missed.  Despite Rendell originally calling for seven tax hikes in his budget, the budget was passed without one of those tax hikes.

headline: Classes provide head start for tomorrow's miners
abstract: Coal mining industry analysts are projecting that 50,000 additional miners will be needed within the next 10 years to work in mines across the nation. The United Mine Workers of America Career Centers Inc., in conjunction with Penn State-Fayette, the Eberly campus, has started a school at the Greene Arc site near Ruff Creek to prepare men and women for careers in the mining industry. Steve Ziats said the program in Greene County is being funded through a three-year grant from U.S. Representative John Murtha.

headline: Erie planning to fix four bridges in next few years
abstract: The city plans to fix its four worst bridges over the next few years because federal and state money has recently become available. Three of the bridges are considered to be structurally deficient, meaning they need some level of repair but have been determined safe to use, city officials said. The fourth bridge does not have that designation. The city applied for federal and state money for the projects last year.

headline: Couple: Violent vagrants are destroying their neighborhood
abstract: Vgrants have been terrorizing a neighborhood, that was supposed to be developed by now, so they would move on. City government has been holding up on the rezoning that would allow it to become a part of the neighborhood. The community members would like to area to at least be fenced off and demolished until something else can be done with the site.

headline: Here come the experts
abstract: A panel set to work on picking the Eagles' best players ever included Gov. Rendell, Ron Jaworski, Mike Quick, Troy Vincent, Bill Bergey, Bill Mackrides, Jim Gallagher, Phil Sheridan, and Ashley Fox. Some of the best players were on the panel.

headline: Parking Authority says Dems blocking school $
abstract: Officials from the Philadelphia Parking Authority, including Republican mayoral candidate Al Taubenberger, tried to blame Governor Rendell and Mayor Street for agency’s measly contributions to the city’s public schools. They said that a profit-sharing agreement was forced on them by Rendell and Street, which forces them to pay the city $25 million a year. Since 2001, the Republican dominated agency has increased jobs, salaries and revenue, however, expenses have also increased substantially, and schools have been receiving very little money.

headline: Quotes about the new Pa. budget agreement
abstract: This article lists several quotes from stakeholders in the recent Pennsylvania budget agreement for the fiscal year 2007-2008.  PA Governor Ed Rendell and PA Senator Vince Fumo both are listed with positive quotes about the new budget as did Republican Senate Majority Leader Dominic Pileggi because of the Republicans ability to disclude the proposed tax hikes.  David Fillman, of the Council 13 American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees and Vince Donlevie, senior vice president of Harrah's Chester Casino expressed sorrow that state workers had to be furloughed but are happy that business can start as usual again.

headline: Courthouse workers go on strike
abstract: Beaver County officials are spending the weekend reviewing a proposal from the courthouse employees union that could settle a contract impasse that's lasted three years and prompted a one-day strike Friday. Commissioners Chairman Joe Spanik said the county would study the offer from Service Employees International Union Local 668 and return with an answer on Monday. With striking workers picketing in front of the courthouse, the two sides returned to the negotiating table early Friday. Shortly before 1 p.m., and with negotiations ended for the day, union officials asked Spanik whether striking employees could return to work. Spanik agreed, but said workers would not be paid for the hours they were on strike.

headline: Fairville Road bridge over I-81 to close for repair
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation plans to close the bridge that carries Fairville Road for six weeks beginning this Monday as they have contracted with HRI Incorporated of State College to repair it.  The repairs will be made to the bridge beams and expansion dams and will affect traffic patterns from 9 at night to 5 in the morning.

headline: Debt, delays shift project focus
abstract: The Koehler Brewery Square in Erie has been modified once again due to what W. John Knox III of Koehler Brewery Square reported as long-term commitment tenants backing out in the final days, such as Ion Health.  With PA Governor Ed Rendell threatening to pull out essential state funding, Koehler developers have changed the plans to renovate the Erie Brewing Company's office building into a $20 million retail, commercial, office space and light-industry complex.  While Kim Green, Erie'e director of economic and community development reported that Mayor Joe Sinnott is willing to give the developers another chance, Erie City Councilman Pat Cappabianca remains skeptical and believes Koehler developers should be held accountable for the money they have wasted.

headline: Hey, yo!  Don't tread on us!
abstract: A columnist for this newspaper writes an opinion in the form of the Declaration of Independence where he mockingly declares independence from the General Assembly of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania.  Among the grievances the author lists are an underfunded educational system as well as depriving the state's counties of more than $100 million dollars by not reimbursing them for the costs to maintain the Commonwealth's judicial officers and magistrates.  The article also complains about depriving Philadelphia representation on its mass transit agency and not allowing the local government to pass its own laws regarding gun ownership.

headline: Partial Pa. returns show voters largely rejecting tax shift
abstract: Unofficial results of a voters referendum on shifting the school burden from property taxes to income taxes by 25 to 50 percent, shows voters have rejected the proposal. Out of 72 districts reporting, only 3 appear to have accepted the referendum. PA Governor Ed Rendell supported the measure as a chance for homeowners to reduce property taxes in light of the introduction of slot machines. Senior Citizens would likely receive the greatest benefit from the shift, which would not tax Social Security or pensions. Scranton, Philadelphia, and Pittsburgh were exempted from presenting the proposal.

headline: Region’s Jobless rate Dips in 2006
abstract: The region's jobless rate edged up one-tenth of a percentage point in December to 4.7 percent and averaged 4.8 percent for all of last year, down from an average of 5.2 percent in 2005, according to preliminary estimates by the PA Department of Labor and Industry.  An expanding labor force combined with an increased number of employed residents and shrinking jobless ranks pointed to an improving regional economy, the department said. Significant job creation in education, health services, leisure, hospitality and government outweighed year-over-year cuts in manufacturing.

headline: Don't step back by cutting workplace program
abstract: The editorial supports the PA Governor Ed Rendell and his administration for starting the industry partnership program that works to train employees by companies in related industries.  The PA Department of Labor reports an average wage increase of 13% for workers involved in this program.  However, the editorial encourages lawmakers to not allow a massive funding cut to this program in the PA Senate because of its success and its good reviews from both employers and workers.

headline: Fears are raised on enforcing new mine-safety rule
abstract: The federal Mine Improvement and New Emergency Reponses Act, which increases penalties and fines for all infractions, passed by the US Mine Safety and Health Administration is considered to be meaningless by many within the administration.  MSHA director Richard Stickler claims that many citations are appealed and get reduced fines eventually but wants to focus on enforcement anyhow.

headline: Federal funds announced for Flight 93 site
abstract: Though officials have for years planned a permanent Flight 93 National Memorial, land acquisition for the sprawling tribute has been slow. That could change after Wednesday’s announcement of $4.9 million in federal funds for the Flight 93 project. The latest appropriation, along with $5 million in federal funds announced earlier this year, is expected to help the National Park Service buy more than 1,200 acres in Stonycreek Township, Somerset County.

headline: His run for judge cut short: He's given the job
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell last week nominated Dan Anders, an openly gay man, to fill a seat vacated by James J. Fitzgerald III on Philadelphia Court of Common Pleas. Anders, a lawyer with the Pepper Hamilton firm in Center City, must still be confirmed by the state Senate..With his nomination in hand, Anders yesterday said he would seek to withdraw his name from the May 15 primary ballot.

headline: People's choice: The state sheriffs should butt out of the May 15 vote
abstract: The author expresses the opinion that the Sheriff's Association of the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania should allow the citizens of Allegheny County vote for their own sheriff rather than have the position be appointed.  It is explained how Allegheny County has endured a lot of corruption within the police ranks with the conviction of four top officers, including Sheriff Pete DeFazio.  As a response, Allegheny County Council has decided to put a question on the May 15 primary ballot asking whether the citizens believe they should elect the sheriff or allow it to be appointed.

headline: Rendell expected to sign $27.2 billion budget today
abstract: Both the PA Senate and the PA House of Representatives have finally negotiated and signed a $27.2 billion budget that PA Governor Ed Rendell is expected to sign today.  The only two Senators who voted against the budget were freshman Republican Senators Mike Folmer and John Eichelberger.  The PA Senate is expected to vote as well on a $750 million transportation package for road repair and mass transit funding.

headline: Dueling data for teacher salaries
abstract: Stopteacherstrikes.org noted that Union President Barbara Zaborney earns "more than double what the median female worker earns." Yet union officials routinely argue such comparisons are a canard, a case of apples and oranges, and that teachers are underpaid compared to other professional workers with similar training. In the case of Zaborney, stopteacherstrikes.org is comparing a teacher who has hit the top of the current pay scale in the district, earning a master’s degree plus 60 credits and working for at least 20 years, with the median earnings of all female workers in Luzerne County, including high school dropouts in their first full-time job. It’s a stark comparison: $68,513 to $28,576.

headline: Fight brewing over reduction in parking tax
abstract: Pittsburgh City Councilman William Peduto has proposed to force the Pittsburgh Parking Authority to reduce parking rates by 12.5% over two years as City Councilman Jim Motznik has proposed to freeze the parking tax at 45%.  Peduto's plan is to lower rates to spur competition between the government-owned parking garages and private owners, which will ultimately lower rates across the city.  While Mayor Luke Ravenstahl claims that the Authority is actually lowering rates this year by allowing 6 free days of parking, PA Senator Jane Orie and PA Representative Mike Turzai are supportive of forcing a rate cut in order to help consumers save money.

headline: Filling in quarries worth considering
abstract: To the surprise of the US Army Corps of Engineers, the PA Department of Environmental Protection, and other agencies, two entrepreneurs are proposing to fill quarries in Northampton County to build houses and commercial buildings. The issue is controversial because the state was asked to award a $1.7 million Growing Greener grant. PA has no policy approach to the proposal, so the project would serve as a pilot. Residents at a Washington Township Zoning Hearing Board raised potential impacts on groundwater and settling. The editors think this is a great opportunity for reclamation.

headline: House bills seen as a way to control illegals
abstract: PA Representatives Darryl Metcalfe, Scott Perry, Mark Mustio and Tom Creighton are introducing a set of bills to help end what they see as an illegal immigrant invasion.  This legislation comes at a time when the US District Court in Scranton is currently reviewing Hazleton's ordinance that would penalize businesses and landlords that deal with illegal immigrants.  Estimates from the Immigration Control and Enforcement in Pennsylvania report that there are anywhere from 90,000 to 200,000 illegal immigrants in the state.

headline: Pittsburgh mayoral race pits charmer vs. reformer
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl will be facing two-term City Councilman Bill Peduto in the upcoming May 15th Democratic primary for Pittsburgh mayor.  Ravenstahl achieved a balanced budget in 2007 that will leave a $60 million dollar surplus despite Peduto's criticisms that Ravenstahl is not financially savvy.  Peduto is running as a reform politician who is older and has more experience in the political arena.

headline: Rendell fooled taxpayers again
abstract: A citizen expresses his frustration with PA Governor Ed Rendell as he feels he has fooled citizens again about how he will use his tax revenues.  He cites the example of the slot profits to reduce school taxes but a lot of that money will be used to build the new Pittsburgh arena.

headline: Expert lists immigrant statistics
abstract: In the trial addressing the legality of the Illegal Immigration Relief Act ordinance in Hazleton, Steven Camarota, director of research for the Center for Immigration Studies in Washington D.C., testified that between 1,500 and 3,400 illegal immigrants live in Hazleton.  He also estimated that these illegal immigrants consume more than $5,000 more in local and state services than they pay in taxes.  The ordinance in question would punish businesses for hiring illegal immigrants or landlords for renting to them.

headline: Funding a roadblock for bridge replacement efforts
abstract: Officials acted quickly last year to close the bridge in Lower Allen Township. However, when it gets repaired or replaced is anybody's guess. It took officials over a decade to cobble together the $2 million needed to replace the nearby Gilbert Bridge in Lower Allen Township.  The bridge collapse in Minnesota is prompting officials nationwide to renew calls for better funding and oversight of crumbling local bridges. Locally, Cumberland County officials have struggled for years to secure the necessary state and federal funding to replace some of its older bridges.

headline: Hearing on North Shore casino design delayed two weeks
abstract: A public hearing on the design of the North Shore casino has been pushed back two weeks because of the agreement reached Friday by developer Don Barden, Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl and Allegheny County Chief Executive Dan Onorato over issues relating to the casino's parking garage and smoking policies. The city planning commission had scheduled a briefing and a hearing Nov. 27 on the casino design and a controversial 3,800-space garage to be built behind it. That hearing now will be Dec. 11 to give officials time to incorporate the key points of the agreement into the design.

headline:
House committee OKs open records draft
Bill to amend state's open records law is reworked. PNA opposes changes.
abstract: Despite strong opposition from the PA Newspaper Association, the House State Government Committee approved a drastically revised version of a bill to change Pennsylvania’s open records law. The bill enacts some reforms, but opponents are disappointed that the revisions will not make pre-existing public records available if they weren’t available under the current law.

headline: Ravenstahl easily tops Peduto for party nod
abstract: Over 1,800 Democratic Party insiders from Allegheny County convened to vote to support candidates for the Pittsburgh Mayor, Pittsburgh City Council, city controller, Allegheny County Council, Pittsburgh Public Schools board, Common Pleas Court, and Sheriff.  Mayor Luke Ravenstahl celebrated a large victory of City Councilman Bill Peduto for the endorsement for mayor.  However, many incumbents in the Allegheny City Council were defeated despite the success of the incumbents in Pittsburgh's City Council.

headline: Rendell sacrifices 3 proposals for budget
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell was forced to sacrifice 3 of his main proposals in order to help move along the budgetary process.  Erik Arneson, a spokesman for the Republican Senate, claims that it is encouraging that Rendell dropped  his plans to lease the Pennsylvania Turnpike, raise the state sales tax, and tax oil company profits.  Rendell proposed a $27.3 billion budget that passed in the House, but the Republican-led Senate have tried to remove $400 million in spending and add $100 million of their own.

headline: Hershey Co. to shutter a 3rd plant
abstract: Hershey Company announced that they will close their Naugatuck, Conn plant by the end of the year and shit production to its Stuarts Draft, Va. Factory, which will benefit from a $25 million investment and 150 additional jobs. The 750 workers at the nonunion plant will be eligible to apply for jobs at Stuarts Draft; and those who don’t want to relocate will be offered severance pay for a minimum of eight weeks and a maximum of 65, depending on the length of employment.

headline: GOP state senator, congressman quarrel over I-80 tolls
abstract: PA Senator Joe Scarnati has publicly blamed US Representatives Phil English and John Peterson for not acquiring sufficient federal funding to fix the 6,000 bridges and 9,000 miles of road that are deficient.  Scarnati used the legislation introduced by English and Peterson that would halt putting tolls on a Pennsylvania interstate to raise revenue for road improvement.  These tolls were part of the $946 million transportation package over the next 10 years signed by PA Governor Ed Rendell to be funded by new tolls and various toll increases.

headline: Hockey arena deal criticized
abstract: Jim Schiffbauer claims that PA Governor Ed Rendell is wrong for claiming no tax money will be used in the construction of the new hockey arena.  He is upset that $7.5 million of funding from the state comes from the slot machine profits when these profits should be used to reduce property taxes.

headline: House Democrats' research office appears as focus of probe into legislative bonuses
abstract: A grand jury is investigating seven employees of the House Democratic caucus and the $3.6 million worth of tax funded bonuses to legislative staffers in 2005-2006.  PA Attorney General Tom Corbett searched the House Democrats' Office of Legislative Research and wants to determine if the payments were compensation to these staffers for working on an election campaign.  PA House Majority Leader H. William DeWeese denies any tie to the affair.  The article goes on to list the names of the staffers and the bonuses they received.

headline:
Reading to raise sewer rates for suburbs by 16 percent
Eleven municipalities will pay more. The largest are Muhlenberg, Spring and Cumru townships. City customers’ rates will not rise.
abstract: The city of Reading will charge outside municipalities that use the services of its Fritz’s Island sewage treatment plant more next year because of rising costs. Eleven municipalities will be affected and are determining the final rates that customers will be charged next year.

headline: Rendell's stance frustrated legislators
abstract: The state budget impasse finally ended on Monday night, but Republican area lawmakers have blamed the frustrating budget negotiations on PA Governor Ed Rendell's refusal to separate his health care and energy proposals from the $27 billion budget.  PA Representative Jim Cox expresses his desire to talk about these proposals in the fall but feels they have nothing to do with passing the budget on time.  PA Representative Dante Santoni Jr. blames the Republicans for not wanting to look at the energy proposal months ago so that the lawmakers can deal with property tax issues in the fall.

headline: Tama strikers approve contract
abstract: Unite Here, the workers’ union for Tama Manufacturing, announced that employees will return to work after a fifteen week strike, which grew bitter at times. Employees will pay less than a third of what the company had originally asked for towards health benefits, but they gave up wage increases for those in their first year of contract. The Lehigh County textile company is currently making uniforms for the Air Force and has downgraded in size substantially since 1996.

headline: Having transportation has made a difference
abstract: In this letter to the editor, a citizen writes in thanks to the PA Department of Transportation for the Rural Transportation for Persons with Disabilities program that granted her eligibility to ride the Franklin County Transport buses at a reduced fare.  She also thanks the citizens involved in Chambersburg Meals On Wheels and the Franklin County Integrated Transportation employees who are extremely considerate and empathetic.

headline: Homeless, not voteless, in the city
abstract: The Vote for Homes Coalition, run by the Project H.O.M.E. non-profit organization, has continued to canvass homeless shelters and soup kitchens in an attempt to register homeless or low-income voters for the upcoming May 15 primary for mayor.  Jennine Miller, coordinator of education and advocacy for the organization, reported that since 1999, this program has registered 9,600 people to vote.

headline: House prepares to take on open records litigation
abstract: A test of how reform politics fares in the wake of across-the-board judicial retention victories comes this week when the House takes up open records legislation again. The measure to make government records more accessible to the public has been the subject of hours of debate by House lawmakers already. After numerous changes were made to the bill during an Oct. 23 voting session, House leaders said they were giving the public time over the election recess to weigh in on the revised legislation. Bill provisions making e-mail off-limits to public inspection and establishing a process so citizens can appeal denials of open-records requests are drawing the most attention so far.

headline: Region soon to face key school tax votes
abstract: This editorial explains how registered voters in the Erie region will be facing a referendum on the upcoming May 15th primary that asks whether to shift part of their school-tax burden from property tax to income tax.  The author warns that only Erie homeowners who have less than $41,266 would see overall school-tax relief.  The referendum essentially asks whether to eliminate the district's .5% earned income tax and pay a new personal income tax of 1.1%.

headline: Rendell's tax plan was all talk, hardly a 'reform'
abstract: The author of the letter writes that we should hope PA Governor Rendell's plan for health-care reform works out better than his botched plan for property-tax reform.  The author is a senior citizen living on a retirement income. His property taxes are more than 11 percent of my income, but under the current legislation he will receive no benefit. A few have solid plans for truly reforming the way we pay for our educational system and doing away with the tax that increasingly threatens to force many out of their homes. He says most, however, would rather dance around the issue.

headline: UAW, General Motors reach tentative agreement
abstract: The President of the United Auto Workers union Ron Gettelfinger has reported that the UAW and General Motors Corporation tentatively agreed on a contract in order to end a national two-day strike.  The contract moves $51 billion of a health care obligation from General Motors to the a trust called Voluntary Employees Beneficiary Association, to be run by the union.  This shifts the responsibility for health care for over 340,000 employees and their spouses to the union.

headline: House OKs more local taxes to help pay for transit
abstract: Under a proposal passed by the PA House of Representatives last night, local governments in counties and municipalities would need to boost mass transit funding from 13%-20% by raising taxes if they want more state money.  The plan devised by PA House Majority Whip Keith McCall would total $450 million for highways and $268 million for transit in the first year and relies on the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission to borrow money and manage tolls on Interstate 80.  PA Governor Ed Rendell, however, stated that this plan is "inadequate" as he called for at least $1 billion.

headline: Investment fund to aid local startups
abstract:
Edward Engler, Steve Robinson and Robert Dickson, veterans of Pittsburgh's technology scene, have been tapped to build and manage a new investment fund charged with aiding local startups.
Selected from a pool of more than 50 candidates from across the country, the Pittsburgh Early Growth Partners' new management team, Engler, Robinson and Dickson, already has $2 million to work with from the local economic development groups and universities that joined forces to create the fund last year. Initially named the Pittsburgh Angel Fund, it was created to provide the difficult-to-find dollars that tech companies need to get going.

headline: House's open records bill still needs work, critics say
abstract: Dozens of changes were made this week to a 48-page House freedom of information bill, but critics say it still would do more harm than good if adopted into law. The bill advanced toward a final vote in the House, but opponents -- including the Pennsylvania Newspaper Association -- warn that its broad language and numerous loopholes would foreclose access to many records that are currently available. The bill would allow officials and agencies to keep secret their ''correspondence and related records,'' all e-mails to and from governmental entities, and any records that existed and were kept private before the law takes effect.

headline: Report faults pace of EMS response
abstract: Philadelphia's city controller - contending Mayor-elect Michael Nutter should be assessing city services before talking tax cuts - yesterday reported dangerously slow response times on emergency-medical calls. Nutter has pledged to enact tax reforms, including scaling back the business-privilege tax. The controller said the assumption behind the "tax-cutting craze" is that city services are up to snuff. But the performance by EMS ambulances is one example of a service that falls woefully short.

headline: Reps question total budget spending
abstract: The Republican lawmakers are wary of the tentative budget agreement between PA Governor Ed Rendell and the PA Legislature that ended the impasse.  With many details yet to be ironed out, PA Representative Rob Kauffman is concerned with the $27.49 billion spending plan that amounts to a 4.5% increase from the previous year.  PA Representative Will Gabig is particularly concerned with the large spending in the transportation plan that is still not specific with its funding proposals, but the vote will probably not come until the weekend.

headline: Union sends strike notice to Greater Alleghenies Red Cross
abstract: The Communications Workers of America union has threatened to strike an American Red Cross chapter that provides blood to parts of Pennsylvania and five other states. The Communications Workers of America filed a 20-day strike notice Monday that would enable blood collectors, phlebotomists and drivers to strike the Greater Alleghenies Blood Services Region of the Red Cross on Jan. 28 if their contract demands are not met. The key issue was how much workers will pay for their health benefits.

headline: How long can the elevated take us?
abstract:
A group of transportation and economic experts chose the Cira Centre to release a major study on how the city has failed to capitalize on transit-oriented development in building communities. 
Proponents of transit-oriented development maintain that investing in transit-line improvements and smart development near transit stops can stimulate economic growth in communities. These experts - which included Dr. Richard Voith, of Econsult, the author of the study - held their news conference at the Cira Centre because that complex, hovering over 30th Street Station, represents a good example of such development: a high-density, pedestrian-friendly hub of jobs, retail and transportation.

headline: Koehler project offers many lessons
abstract: Editors, after PA Governor Rendell announced the Koehler project failure that PA will no longer support projects not already backed and supported locally, that the region should get its act together. Rendell is partly to blame for the failure, as there was no local consensus before he supported it. During former Governor Tom Ridge's administration, the Erie County Civic Coordinating Committee vetted projects, however it has fractured. All levels of government and civic organizations should participate.

headline: How Nutter's win made history
abstract: Democrat Michael Nutter appears to have receive the largest percentage of white votes ever cast for an African American in a Philadelphia mayoral primary. Senior policy analyst David Bositis at the Joint Center for Political and Economic Studies, a Washington, DC think tank on African American affairs, says the five-way primary results indicate a movement beyond racial lines for voters. Other candidates included businessman Tom Knox, and US Reps. Chaka Fattah and Dwight Evans.

headline:
Residents will get tax bill estimates
New property assessments will come with before-and-after comparisons.
abstract: Due to the large number of public requests, Luzerne County will provide property owners with a before and after comparison of their school, county and local taxes; though they won't be broken down into specific categories. These comparison will allow property owners to compare current rates with estimates for 2009, which will change since the county will conduct its first reassessment of properties since 1965. Plans are also underway to explain a guide for residents to understand their new assessed values, and commissioners will look for residents who want to serve on three temporary assessment appeals boards.

headline: Senate administrator warns of government shutdown
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell and Republican lawmakers have already started to struggle over the administration's proposed $27.3 billion budget request for 2007-2008.  PA Senate Secretary Mark Corrigan, and independent employee of the Senate, has warned all employees that the proposed budget debate will last for the entire summer and vacations will not be allowed without exception.  Republican opponents of the plan are specifically opposed to the 3% payroll tax increase as well as an increase of the state sales tax to 7%.

headline: US Airways and union reach tentative contract
abstract: US Airways and union a tentative agreement that brings all 7,900 employees of the former American West Airlines and the old US Airways under one contract. It raises wages and boosts pensions. Both sides feel optimistic about the future official contract.

headline: I-80 toll battle heads to Congress
abstract: US Representatives Phil English and John Peterson have added an amendment to a federal transportation bill that would block tolls on Interstate 80 in Northern Pennsylvania and have also introduced the Free Highway Protection Act of 2007, which directs all toll money to be paid to the federal government as excise tax rather than the state using the tolls as revenue.  PA Governor Ed Rendell's spokesman, Chuck Ardo, responded that the proposition makes little sense because rather than looking for federal help, it sends the money to the federal government.  PA Representative Jay Moyer, despite being a Republican, supports Rendell's transportation funding plan with tolls and says the federal proposal will only create regional disputes.

headline: Las Vegas is latest stop as Penguins seek new home
abstract: Penguins owner Ron Burkle met with the mayor of Las Vegas Oscar B. Goodman in order to discuss the possibility of moving the team there amidst differences with government officials in Pennsylvania over the plans for a new arena in Pittsburgh.  PA Governor Rendell claims to be optimistic the team will remain in Pittsburgh despite the team receiving offers from Kansas City officials.  The article also reviews recent news throughout the NFL including scores and injuries.

headline: Hundreds of teachers protest
abstract: The Scranton Federation of Teachers wanted to show the School Board the faces of the people affected by a 34 percent health insurance rate increase for 2008.The board got to see more than 400 of those faces Wednesday. One hour before Wednesday night’s board meeting, more than 400 teachers, staff and family members marched from the union office on Wyoming Avenue to the district Administration Building. They walked around the building several times, almost single file, some holding candles, one holding a sign that read "Santa gave me a $2,225 pay cut for Christmas."

headline: State budget full of ups and downs for education in Cumberland County
abstract: Despite the Pennsylvania state budget increasing public education spending by 5.8% to $10.5 billion, Cumberland County school districts are not receiving many increases in funding because of the county's economic prosperity and low unemployment according to PA Senator Patricia Vance.  Jonelle Darr, the director of the Cumberland County Library System, is disappointed that PA Governor Ed Rendell has not increased library funding in the county despite his focus on education.  Lastly, Omar Shute, director of the Cumberland County Economic Development office, says that despite multiple business retention visits in the past years, the new state budget cuts funding in economic development in the business retention and expansion program.

headline: State budget impasse brings uncertain times for lawmakers, workers
abstract: This Monday morning, 25,000 state employees deemed "non-essential" will be furloughed, and they will be eligible to receive unemployment compensation.  PA Governor Ed Rendell is pursuing an aggressive spending budget as he enjoys a $650 million budget surplus, but the Republican-controlled Senate are adamantly opposing any fee and tax hikes included in his proposals.  The Republican Senate also just subpoenaed two officials to testify on how a shutdown will affect the casino industry.

headline: US Automaker Struck
abstract: 73,000 members of the United Auto Workers have begun a nationwide strike against General Motors Corporation in order to force GM to promise to keep production factories for the Chevrolet Cobalt and the Chevrolet Volt in America.  Ron Gettelfinger, president of the UAW, also reported that the union wants to discuss the Voluntary Employees Beneficiary Association, a trust that GM has requested to move $51 billion of health-care liabilities off their books.  Spokesman for General Motors Dan Flores expressed disappointment that the union is requesting such complicated demands.

headline: I-80 TOLL LAW: State senator not ready to repeal Act 44
abstract: PA Senator Jake Corman has publicly stated that the best option to fund the transportation package passed by PA Governor Ed Rendell is to lease to the turnpike to private investors but won't repeal the legislation that allows the tolling of Interstate 80 unless the Pennsylvania Turnpike is leased.  Corman feels that a $25 million deal in the leasing of the Turnpike is necessary to provide sufficient interest revenue to repair roads and improve mass transit.  Joe Brimmier, Chief Executive Officer of the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission, feels that leasing the turnpike will result in an even higher increase in tolls on Interstate-80.

headline: Lawmakers eye $700 million for Pa. Convention Center
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell has urged the PALegislature to pass a $700 million spending bill to expand the Pennsylvania Convention Center by the end of June.  The Philadelphia Redevelopment Authority has all but one of the 27 parcels of land needed to construct the expansion, which would increase the center's space by 60%.

headline: Improve system for higher courts
abstract: The newspaper says that it will not endorse candidates for appellate judicial seats because it believes the system is flawed because most PA voters don’t know anything about the candidates, and politics play too much of a role. The newspaper claims that appellate judges should be appointed based on merit and Senate confirmation; however, it believes voters should differentiate between local courts and appellate courts since there is a better opportunity for people to get to know local candidates. The paper also claims that the Judicial Evaluation Commission can be a fairly reliable source, and it provides the ratings of candidates for the Supreme, Superior and Commonwealth Courts, which were given by the commission.

headline: State rebate applications swell
abstract: The beginning of the article provides information on eligibility, income limits, how to apply, the deadline, and unclaimed checks for a state refund check program. Applications for the program that helps low-income senior citizens pay for property taxes with revenue from the lottery and slot machine have increased substantially, but there are still many who are eligible that have yet to apply. Some people, however, are not happy with the long waits to receive their checks and wonder why the state doesn’t just lower property taxes, rather than waste time and manpower sending rebates.

headline: State furlough notices going to 25,000 as stalemate persists
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell has publicly reported that he will be willing to freeze the budget and order furloughs in order to force the Legislature to act on his proposals for funding for transportation and alternative energy and a passage of measures to cut health care costs.  While the $750 million bill for fund mass transit and highway repair while increasing toll costs is close to being passed, the electricity surcharge in the alternative energy bill is staunchly opposed by Senate Republicans.  As the furlough begins, the nonessential workers selected for a leave of absence will be available for unemployment and keep health insurance.

headline: Workers make plans for life after Sony
abstract: Last month, officials at Sony Technology Center-Pittsburgh announced it would lay off up to 300 workers by the end of this month and as many as 600 more within the next year as the company moves production of rear-projection TVs to Mexico. Dislocated Sony workers received severance packages, which included one week's pay for every year worked, and 30-days paid health care benefits and related outplacement assistance.

headline: I-80 tolls the best of ideas...or the worst
abstract: This opinion criticizes the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission's recommendation to poll I-80 to the PA Legislature as the biggest problem the author sees with this plan is its legality.  The Federal Highway Administration has not approved the plan as of yet, and the PA House Transportation Committee Chairman Rick Geist has publicly doubted whether or not the FHA will allow the project to continue.  The author also cites the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation's study on the project that produced bleak results and did not recommend going on with the tolls.

headline: Library is given a $2 million donation
abstract: PA State Senator Vincent J. Fumo recently received extra $2 million from the state to fund the Philadelphia Phillies' project of a $175 million restoration of the Central Library of the Free Library of Philadelphia.  This extra $2 million was funded  by the PA Department of Community and Economic Development.  PA Governor Ed Rendell and PA Representative Dwight Evans both came up with money, $7.5 million and $2 million, respectively, to help fund this project.

headline: In backstretch, Nutter gallops to the lead
abstract: In the Democratic mayoral primary, former Philadelphia City Councilman Michael Nutter leads. His ratings are attributed to TV ads and media endorsements. Nutter leads over millionaire Tom Knox, US Rep. Chaka Fattah, US Rep. Bob Brady, and PA Rep. Dwight Evans. Voters list crime and violence as their top concerns. Knox, who was targeted by negative ads, saw his ratings drop slightly. The race is not over yet, there is room for another candidate to move up. Mayor Street's ratings continue to drop.

headline: State warns officials over parking lot
abstract: Judge Ronald C. Nagle has ruled for a temporary injunction to halt the construction of a parking lot as the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission's historical preservation officer Jean H. Cutler has written letters to the attorney Robert J. Sugarman.  In her letter to Sugarman, who represents two West Pikeland residents opposing the parking lot, she cites the Historic Burial Places Preservation Act and the state law that requires the township must have the approval of the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission to use this area, formerly a burial ground, as a parking lot.  Andrea Bowman, from the PA Office of General Council, also wrote similar letters citing the preservation act to Township Solicitor Guy Donatelli and Township Manager Jeri L. Liesinger.

headline: State House advances Rendell's budget plan
abstract: Democrats in the House approved PA Governor Ed Rendell's budget, sending it to the Senate but hoping changes are made before conference. PA Rep. Chris Sainato noted he would not approve the budget unless changes are made in the Senate. Senate Appropriations Chairman Dwight Evans noted the budget did not include a tax increase, though Republicans say it will lead to one. Rendell's February budget address called for tax and fee increases to fund mass transit and other programs.

headline: ‘No Child’ program is underfunded
abstract: A study released yesterday said the state of Pennsylvania would need to spend $22 billion on education to get all students up to speed in math and verbal skills. In fact, the total spending on Pennsylvania totals about $17 billion. That means the state would have to spend another $5 billion to meet the federal mandates. The $5 million question, of course, is where is the money going to come from? Taxpayers already feel they are squeezed to the max. And any state funding still comes from the taxpayers when all is said and done.

headline: If tolls aren't the answer, what is?
abstract: This article questions the opponents of the tolling of Interstate 80 by questioning what else the government can do about the massive infrastructure bill that needs funding.  PA Representative Steven Cappelli and Dave Hall of the Greater Susquehanna Valley Chamber of Commerce agree that some form of user fees need to be enacted in order to fund the repair of highways and bridges and mass transit programs.  However, US Representative John Peterson claims that these tolls will only finance inefficient transit systems and disagrees with the 3% increase every year after.

headline: Light emitting diodes aren't new, but their use is posed to "explode"
abstract: Jim Wassel of Perry Township has created a new prototype for municipal street lighting by way of light-emitting diodes (LEDs).  The PA State Department of Environmental Protection has reported that Ellwood City Borough, the proposed model for this type of municipal lighting, can save up to 80% to 90% a year on its lighting costs.  Domenic Vaccari, Ellwood City Borough manager, is hoping to acquire state funding for this project.

headline: In Harrisburg, "Year of Reform" comes up short
abstract: With more than 50 new lawmakers in the House and Senate vowing to bring change to the state Capitol, there was hope that 2007 would be the "Year of Reform": greater access to open records, tougher campaign-finance laws, and perhaps even a smaller legislature. Instead, lawmakers are poised to leave Harrisburg this week without having passed even the one government reform bill they believed could be sent to Gov. Rendell: the expanded open-records law.

headline: Tax-shift votes likely to divide communities
abstract: Under the state law known as Act 1, voters across Pennsylvania will be asked in the primary if they wish to raise their local income taxes in exchange for school property tax reductions. Retired seniors and homeowners with lower incomes would fare best under such a shift, while renters would lose because they would simply pay higher income taxes.

headline: State workers get layoff notices
abstract: Approximately 24,440 non-essential state workers will be furloughed this Monday unless the Pennsylvania lawmkaers are able to agree on a budget this Sunday night.  These workers will, however, receive health insurance and be eligible for unemployment compensation for two weeks.  PA House Representative Jerry Nailor feels that lawmakers are not working hard enough and should not recess for the 4th of July holiday as there has been no progress on the $300 million disparity between PA Governor Ed Rendell's budget and the Republican's budget.

headline: A U-TURN FOR KIDS ON THE WRONG ROAD
abstract: In the past year, more than 1,500 dropouts called a hot line to find out how they could re-enter school and earn their diplomas. Those 150 met the criteria for existing dropout programs, such as having eight credits from high school, and being able to read at a sixth-grade level. Project U-Turn's anniversary symposium Tuesday was billed as a celebration of progress in the organization's first year, and the $10 million that Philadelphia Youth Network has been able to raise for this project is impressive. But it also was a wake-up call signaling just how far we still need to go, especially when it comes to the city, state and school district working as a team.

headline: Immigration a tough issue that we must address now
abstract: A bus, which was headed for New York City when it crashed and nearly plunged into the Lehigh River, carried 22 Chinese nationals and one Mexican. U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents detained 23 of the 44 people on the bus for immigration violations. The author feels the federal government has failed to close our porous borders to illegal aliens, he feels they have not clarified the roles of the myriad of involved federal agencies, and have refused to spell out to states, cities and towns what they can and cannot do.

headline: Lights, camera, cash: Another Rendell crock
abstract: Hal Katersky, chairman of Pacifica Ventures, disputes accusations that a technology startup company he led defaulted on a multimillion-dollar lease in New Orleans. A later venture into studio management spurred a lawsuit alleging $1 million in misspending. Mr. Katersky insists none of this has any bearing on his Philly studio plans. Mr. Rendell, who supports the studio deal, "continues to believe that Mr. Katersky will be true to his word and that the project will go forward as planned," says spokesman Chuck Ardo.

headline: In solving the strike, Brady called a friend
abstract: Many Pennsylvania watchdog groups and legislators such as PA State Representative Dwight Evans are questioning whether PA Governor Ed Rendell's recent effort to help Bob Brady end a strike at Community College of Philadelphia was a subtle endorsement for his mayoral campaign. Both Rendell  and Brady have publicly said that Rendell is not endorsing anyone for the Democratic nomination for mayor.  Ted Kirsch, president of the PA American Federation of Teachers credits Brady with ending the strike, however, despite Rendell's pledge of $480,000.

headline: Turkeys
abstract: To the six members of Northampton County Council, three of whom were just re-elected, who couldn't make it to the council's annual budget review of human service expenses for the coming year. This is the single largest chunk of the county budget. Department heads are on the spot to justify their requests, and it's the only chance for the county's elected representatives to have a public discussion on the funding of these critical functions. Plus, the clock is ticking toward final budget approval. The committee members should sample the bitter taste of their good intentions before sending tax and fee hikes out to the full Assembly.

headline: State, local government needs modernized
abstract: Three reports coming from the Pennsylvania Economy League, the Brookings Institution, and the Pennsylvania State University are challenging the state's competitiveness and quality of life in relation to other states.  The Economy League claims that current public policy has not adapted to the changing way of life to citizens within the state.  The League continues to describe 5 pieces of legislation that would raise revenue, combat fiscal distress, manage expenses and increase economies of scale.

headline: Action on charter schools delayed
abstract: The approval of applications to open eleven new charter schools next fall has been postponed because the Philadelphia School Reform Commission is unsure of how to pay for them. Commission officials hoped for the eventual approval of these schools, they hired an outside agency to investigate school finances for the next several years and they also voted to construct a $44 million building at Kensington High School.

headline: In aftermath of Minn. collapse, Rendell says Pa. bridges safe
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell is not immediately concerned about the bridges in Pennsylvania after a truss bridge collapsed in Minnesota recently despite there being 25% of the 14,868 bridges listed as deficient by the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation.  A new state law is planned to bring in more than $500 million a year for highway and bridge repairs in the next 10 years, but both Rendell and US Senator Bob Casey believe that the Minnesota bridge collapse show that more federal funding is needed.

headline: Mayor, Pitt chancellor lead sweep of Oakland
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl and University of Pittsburgh Chancellor Mark Nordenburg, together with five city building inspectors, began combing the streets of Central Oakland in an effort to improve housing conditions in the student neighborhood. The city is making an effort to inform students of their rights as tenants. Ravenstahl is considering liens for landlords whose properties are in decline. 277 citations for code violations have been issued thus far.

headline: Inside the Capitol
abstract: Christmas tress bound for troops in Iraq. Democratic Rep. Tim Solobay has tapped the generosity of state growers to donate the trees and has encouraged state employees to donate holiday decorations. He also has the Pennsylvania mushroom industry’s commitment to pay for shipping costs. Elections are discussed. The state Supreme Court scrapped this year’s final round of oral arguments because of impending turnover in three of its seven seats, officials said Tuesday.

headline: Walkers enjoy Pittsburgh's vistas
abstract: StepTrek 2007 was recently held to encourage people to walk the steps in the city of Pittsburgh for fun, fitness and views of the city.

headline: Taxes, transit and energy drive debate
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell has hinted at tax increases to save his $27 billion budget proposal. Republicans and Democrats in the Legislature have vowed not to pass any. Rendell would like to raise the sales tax by a percentage point as well as to institute taxes to pay for health care and transportation. Rendell and Democrats want to place a surcharge on home and business energy consumption, with options for homeowners to conserve energy.

headline: All local school districts but 1 meet state target
abstract: Sharon City School District was the only Mercer County school district that did not meet the academic performance targets for 2007 as the Pennsylvania's Adequate Yearly Progress were released.  These targets are measured by graduation, attendance and Pennsylvania System of School Assessment text scores under the federal No Child Left Behind Act.  Sharon Superintendent John Sarandea is very concerned about not meeting the standards despite full-time math and reading tutors although he believes the lower graduation rate was simply an anomaly for that specific year.

headline:
Interest to lease turnpike is broad
Gov. Rendell has revived the idea. Thirty-four firms from the U.S. and abroad have offered qualifications.
abstract: Thirty-four companies, including a number of foreign firms, have submitted 14 different proposals over their qualifications to operate the PA Turnpike. Governor Rendell has proposed leasing the turnpike to a private company, which could raise $20 billion to pay for road projects. A law had previously been passed to avoid leasing the turnpike by increasing tolls and putting tolls on Interstate 80, however, the law has been criticized and may be repealed.

headline: Montco joins an end run to Kyoto
abstract: A Pennsylvania State University graduate student presented Montgomery County officials with a 145-page report on what it could do to reduce greenhouse gases - the culprits in global warming - Commissioner Thomas Jay Ellis was skeptical. Montgomery County, which emits more greenhouse gases than more than half the world's nations do individually, thereby joined a burgeoning list of cities, counties and states that have stopped waiting for federal direction on global-warming remediation. In Montgomery County, a new task force will begin meeting this month to consider options like switching to greener energy sources or vehicles for its buildings and fleet, expanding open space, planting trees, and making clogged roads flow faster.

headline: Inside the Capitol: Noteworthy
abstract: The state House passed a resolution that urges Major League Baseball to retire Roberto Clemente’s number.

headline: A growing sense of mission at home
abstract: null

headline: Two weeks late, $27.2 billion Pa. budget clears Senate
abstract: The PA Senate finally passed a $27.2 billion state budget two weeks late that focuses its spending on education and health services.  The Republicans in the Senate were able to cut out the various tax and fee increases originally proposed by PA Governor Ed Rendell, despite Rendell winning a massive transportation funding project.  The deal on the budget ended a one day furlough of 24,000 state employees.

headline: All on board budget at last
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell has signed the new budget for 2007-2008 17 days later than the fiscal year actually started due to what he blames as too much partisanship and political rhetoric.  The budget, totaling at $27.2 billion of spending, increased funding for education, public welfare and health care while decreasing funding to the PA Department of Labor and Industry's nursing shortage initiative and Self Employment Assistance program.  The PA House of Representatives also approved the provision that gives the authority to Education Secretary Gerald Zahorchak to reassigned students from the failed Duquesne High School to neighboring school districts.

headline: Its March; must be SEPTA crisis time again
abstract: The editorial encourages the PA Legislature to move forward on the current funding crisis with SEPTA as they face a $130 million deficit. Despite this, PA State Transportation Secretary Allen D. Biehler has proclaimed that there will be no last minute financial aid but rather a long-term solution to the financial problems.  SEPTA has proposed two solutions: an 11% fare increase with $100 million from the state or a 13% fare increase, service cuts, and 600 jobs lost, and the author still feels that PA Governor Rendell and the lawmakers need to pay more attention to the problem.

headline:
Mortgage holders put on hold
Judge gives OPFM until Nov. 2 to declare assets, identify creditors
abstract: Approximately 800 customers of Personal Financial Management Inc. (OPFM) found out that they were responsible for paying for mortgages worth thousands of dollars more than they had agreed upon due the owner's highly questionable ethics. OPFM recently went bankrupt, and a bankruptcy judge granted the owner more time to disclose its assets, which could be distributed as compensation; though many customers are outraged that an outside attorney will be paid with these same assets. The article also provides details of the investigation, specific law suits, and scheduled meetings pertaining to the OPFM bankruptcy.

headline: INSIDE THE CAPITOL: Public comment sought on diesel-idling proposal
abstract: The public can post comments about a proposed rule to limit idling trucks and the diesel exhaust that they produce on a website that’s listed in the article.

headline: A Presbyterian church
abstract: The author of the letter writes that in the Philadelphia Inquirers three and a half pages devoted to Prince Charles of England's recent visit, it should have been mentioned that he attended a Presbyterian church service instead of an Episcopal parish in the Philadelphia area.

headline: Updates in the Pa. budget stalemate
abstract: The Senate Community, Economic and Recreational Development Committee recently held a hearing on the effects of closing the slot-machine casinos.  The PA House of Representatives also unanimously rejected the PA Senate's education budget bill.

headline: Area schools among nation's best
abstract: Two Crawford County high schools have been placed on a nationwide listing of the best high schools, which analyzed data from thousands of U.S. public high schools. Cambridge Springs Junior-Senior High School and Maplewood Junior-Senior High School, both in PENNCREST School District, earned bronze awards from U.S. News & World Report, which ranked 18,790 U.S. public high schools in 40 states. Results from the magazine’s statistical analyses earned Northwestern Pennsylvania Collegiate Academy a silver award, one of 19 in the state.

headline: Lawmakers debate transit funding plans
abstract: The PA House of Representatives have begun debating a statewide transportation bill that includes higher tolls on the Pennsylvania Turnpike for drivers.  Other components of the bill include: a county government option of raising local taxes to increase mass transit funding, two more members on the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission, and giving Philadelphia six more seats on the South Eastern PA Transit Authority governing board.  Many county officials, especially from Bucks County, are concerned that they have to contribute more to mass transit by raising taxes.

headline: NHL - Pens declare impasse, may move
abstract: A breakdown in talks between Pittsburgh Penguins owners Mario Lemieux and Ron Burkle, PA Governor Ed Rendell, and other government officials increases the possibility that the Penguins will play in Kansas City next season.  The Penguins had an agreement with Isle of Capri Casinos for the building of the arena, but a state board chose Don Barden to fund the project instead.  Two losing casinos, including Ise of Capri, have filed appeals to the PA state Supreme Court, which delays the opening of the new stadium.

headline: Law would open files of state government
abstract: The Pennsylvania Legislature will vote today on PA Governor Ed Rendell's proposal to make expense records of the government more publicly accessible.  Rendell is working with the Pennsylvania Newspaper Association to help make these new rules apply to every level of government.  Currently, Pennsylvania is known for having one of the weaker public records laws in the nation.

headline: Area resorts back in business
abstract: Jack Frost/Big Boulder in Blakeslee had all of its 29 slopes open this weekend, and other ski resort officials say they should be following suit this weekend. Just in time, they say, to try and save a disastrous ski season so far. Big Boulder actually opened all of its slopes January 23. Jack Frost followed suit last weekend. The resort also was the first local ski area to open this year when it opened on Dec. 5.

headline: Watching the money
abstract: Former Lieutenant Governor Bill Scranton addressed the PA House Republican Policy Committee on the budget proposed by PA Governor Ed Rendell, which includes higher taxes. Scranton ran for a short time in the GOP primary for Governor. Amidst concerns over a costly energy independence proposal, an increased sales tax on cigarettes, a higher sales tax, and a payroll tax for employers that don't offer healthcare, Scranton also urged Republicans to pay more attention to public transportation systems, including the South Eastern PA Transit Authority.

headline: Attacking cyber schools
abstract: The author of the editorial criticizes the PA Legislature for its perceived efforts to contain cyber charter school enrollment throughout the state. The author essentially believes that the Legislature is trying to get rid of competition to public schools.

headline: Lawmakers seek halt to clear cutting along Interstate 81
abstract: PA Rep. Glen Grell and PA Sen. Pat Vance wrote a letter to the PA Department of Transportation concerning its practice of clearing land along roadways. Contrary to what the legislators believe, PennDOT spokesman Greg Penny said the agency's practice is not "slash and burn" but to maintain a 30-foot wide zone for clearance from the white line on the side of the road. State grants have supplemented the agency's tight budget.

headline: Officials weighing the impact of casino garage on city skyline
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl is committed to preserve the scenic views from Mount Washington and Fort Pitt Bridge after  a casino on the North Shore is planning to build a 10-story parking garage after Pat ford, co-chairman of the gaming implementation task force, has raised concerns about the potential awkward appearance of the skyline.  Pittsburgh's Contextual Design Advisory Panel have also objected to the 119-feet parking garage, but Lisa Schroeder, of the Riverlife Task Force, is confident that changes can be made to minimize the effect of the garage.  The city planning commission will hold a public hearing on Tuesday on the design.

headline: Leader tries to calm investigation frustration
abstract: PA House Majority Leader Bill DeWeese has defended the $3.6 million in bonuses that were paid to legislative aides despite the persistent investigation of PA Attorney General Tom Corbett.  The target of the investigation is to determine whether or not the bonuses were legally paid for legislative work or illegally given for campaign work.  House Democrats reportedly spent $700,000 more than the other three caucuses combined on bonuses for their workers.

headline: ESPN to back Maroons
abstract: The popularity of the "Breaker Boys: The NFL's Greatest Team and the Stolen 1925 Championship" has inspired ESPN to sponsor an online petition to try to convince the NFL to give the Pottsville Maroons their championship title back. The announcement was a highlight of Pottstown’s "Maroons Week," which celebrated the book's release. Book sales have been increasing, and many people are hopeful that ESPN’s support will convince the NFL to reconsider its position.

headline: 8 female professors claim bias in lawsuit
abstract: Eight female professors at Penn State Milton S. Hershey Medical Center’s medical school have filed a discrimination lawsuit, saying they were paid less than male colleagues. The women want back pay along with unspecified damages and legal expenses. They also want the medical school to be required to carry out a program to ensure equity for women.

headline: Avon Grove school officials discuss Act 1 tax payments
abstract: The Avon Grove School Board did not decide how to interpret Act 1, education reform legislation which gives qualified homeowners the option of paying their annual property taxes in installments. The PA School Board Association and the PA Department of Education agree that school districts must present the option to taxpayers, however attorneys statewide have differing opinions, noted district Business Manager James Asciutto. The public will be allowed to comment at the next meeting.

headline: Lawmaker says state should consider alternatives to tolls on I-80
abstract: The state's proposal to impose tolls on Interstate 80 to raise revenue for other road and bridge improvements is "in big trouble." It may take years before it begins making money. Gov. Ed Rendell also has proposed leasing the turnpike for an up-front fee and, in essence, living off of investment profits. Instead, the General Assembly passed Act 44 as a public-public partnership that directs the Turnpike Commission to toll I-80 and raise turnpike tolls by 25 percent in 2009, and 3 percent a year thereafter, to provide up to $116 billion to PennDOT for roads, bridges and public transit over the next 50 years. Mr. Rendell signed the bill in July as part of a state budget settlement.

headline: Orie says arena funding bill next
abstract: PA Republican State Senate Whip Jane Orie has reported that the bill essential to acquiring funding for the new Pittsburgh Penguins arena will be one of the first pieces of legislation to be brought up after PA Governor Ed Rendell broke the budget impasse.  The bill provides $7.5 million a year for 30 years to aid the construction costs.  This money is directly from the $1.6 billion fund for capital projects that is part of the 2004 legislation the legalized slot machines.

headline: JoePa's salary
abstract: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court for picked apart the defensive scheme of Penn State University, enabling the public to discover what the school was hiding. The court ruled the salaries of football coach Joe Paterno and some other Penn State officials are a matter of public record; it ordered the Pennsylvania State Employees' Retirement System to disclose their pay. The school chose to go to court rather than practice transparency. Penn State claimed the salaries are private because none is funded by the public. But taxpayers pay the pension benefits of the school's employees.

headline: Fancy this, Phillies fans
abstract: The article is about Nick Ferraro, who grew up in Philadelphia but moved to Lititz, PA. He opened up a store from the Philly Pretzel Factory franchise and came up with the idea of making P shaped pretzels to commemorate the Philadelphia Phillies National League East baseball championship. The article provides his store's hours and some personal information about his life.

headline: A conservative supports gay marriage
abstract: The announcement that Mayor Street has agreed to preside over a same-sex commitment ceremony is likely to please local liberals and anger local conservatives. The decision to accept the benefits and obligations of marriage is best left to the couple themselves. To let government restrict the selection of a spouse on the basis of race, religion, ethnicity or sexual orientation is to let government intrude on one of the most intimate decisions we can make. Conservatives should be the first to deny government that authority.

headline: Build upon success in public schools
abstract: It is hard to argue against the idea that increasing the amount of time students spend in school may advance their learning. The author is New Jersey high school biology teacher and who would love to have another semester for each of the courses I teach. However, additional school hours will require additional funding. Before advocating removal of needed funding, we should look at what is being successfully accomplished in public schools, and what else can be done to improve them.

headline: License, registration not easy to acquire
abstract: The author of the article describes the aggravation she and her husband felt towards the local Motor Vehicle Bureau over difficulties they faced while trying to obtain their PA licenses. However, at the end of the article she thanks them for sticking to the rules in light of New York, which is considering giving illegal immigrants licenses.

headline: Owners' words sound familiar
abstract: Harrisburg Mayor Stephen Reed is credited with keeping the city's baseball team, the Senators, from moving. Reed pled the city's case before the National Association, submitting a higher bid to retain the team. 11 years later, the team is being sold to Michael Reinsdorf, which will help the city out of debt. The contract is for 29 years, if renovations and upkeep are made by the city. PA Governor Rendell promised $18.3 million for renovations. The city will also contribute.

headline: John Baer | A new lawmaker sheds a rare light
abstract:
The columnist writes that PA's Legislature is nationally recognized for clandestine operations to protect its size, perks and gross spending - the largest, most expensive full-time legislature in America.
It's a body where costs continue to rise, up 9 percent last year, to $308 million, and fiscal stealth continues to rule.  PA Representative Eugene DePasquale partly answered that call by offering stunning transparency, creating a website that details each of his expenditures.

headline: Heinz Field pipes blamed in closure of restrooms during game
abstract: Pittsburgh Water and Sewer Authority crews yesterday determined that sediment in the plumbing system at Heinz Field was responsible for water pressure problems that caused the closing of some restrooms during Sunday night's preseason game. Early in the game, Heinz Field officials learned that flushometers on the urinals on the stadium's main concourse, club level and fifth level of seating were open and running continuously. Some restrooms were closed and stalls were closed in some men's rooms.

headline: ACLU wary of mayor's proposal
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl introduced an ordinance to the city council that would impose fines and possible misdemeanor charges against the owners of properties that are  the scene of frequent police or building inspection calls. The American Civil Liberties Union claims that the ordinance could violate the rights of property owners.

headline: Cal U to receive funds from Pa. LCB
abstract: California University of PA is one of 65 organizations in the state that will receive grants from the PA Liquor Control Board. The university was awarded $8,500, which it will put towards it Social Norms Campaign. The objective of the campaign is to change misperceptions that college students have about their peers’ drinking habits to help encourage students to drink in moderation or not at all.

headline:
Loans to fix roads begin
Turnpike borrows $532 million against tolls to pay PennDOT
abstract: The PA Turnpike Commission will borrow $532 million this week and could possibly receive up to $9.6 billion in loans based on legislation that was passed by the Legislature and signed by Governor Rendell to provide extra funds for various construction projects. The plan calls for the loans to be repaid by raising turnpike tolls in 2009 and adding tolls to Interstate 80 in 2011. The rest of the article provides more specifics about the loans; though ultimately the plan could be forced to change if U.S. Representative has his ways, and the Federal Highway Administration blocks the proposal for tolls on I-80.

headline: Penguins' lease can be rent free next season
