abstract: Lost in the discussion over Plan B is that the Penguins can exercise a short-term lease extension for Mellon Arena this summer that would give them more control over building revenues without paying any rent, perhaps while a new facility is constructed. Under the proposed extension, the Penguins would become master tenants of the arena in place of SMG, a property management group that specializes in running publicly owned facilities. SMG would become building manager.

headline: John Baer.. As state statewide , reform fizzles
abstract: PA's so-called "reform movement"  lost more of its tenuous grip on state politics as voters rejected reformers' calls to reject statewide judges. Supreme Court Justice Thomas Saylor easily won his yes/no retention election in the face of a "So long, Saylor" effort pushed by anti-pay-raise activists. And six other state judges on Superior and Commonwealth courts, including Commonwealth Court Judge Doris Smith-Ribner of Philadelphia, were headed to retention victories, too. The throw-them-all-out approach urged by groups such as PACleanSweep no doubt struck many voters as just too unreasonable.

headline: Local businesses report mixed results
abstract: The city of Scranton hosted a convention for NBC’s "The Office," which especially benefited local hotels, as well as restaurants and bars that have appeared on the show. However, some street vendors at a street festival were disappointed with crowds and sales, which they attributed to competition from convention events and bad weather. For the most part, businesses in Scranton saw increased sales because of the convention.

headline: An insider blasts Hazleton's leaders: A paid consultant said the mayor's immigration initiative has been "prejudiced and oppressive."
abstract: Zogby International, which was hired by the Greater Hazleton Civic Partnership and the mayor's office, released a report that criticizes Hazleton Mayor Lou Barletta’s ordinances aimed at cracking down on illegal immigrants. The report says that the ordinances are rooted in racism and challenges Barletta’s claims that illegal immigrants are the cause of many problems in the region. Barletta claims that the study is biased, and racism has played no role in the city's ordinances.

headline: California professor says university is "complicit"
abstract: William O' Donnell, professor of theater and dance at California University of Pennsylvania, has publicly claimed that the school is discriminating against gay and lesbian faculty and students.   The real problem, according to school president Angelo Armenti Jr., deals with domestic partner benefits which, according to Armenti, is under the control of the teacher's union and the PA State System of Higher Education.  During the same forum where O' Donnell made these claims, there were other controversies dealing with racial tensions between African-American and white students.

headline: Local bridges are safe, experts say
abstract: Dion Campell, Project Supervisor for RKR Hess Associates in East Stroudsburg has declared all bridges in Monroe County to be safe and efficient in the wake of the Minneapolis-St. Paul bridge collapse on Wednesday.  The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation, however, is responsible for all bridges on state roads and each municipality is responsible for the municipal bridges.  George Alexandris of the Delaware River Joint Toll Bridge Commission reports that they oversee 20 bridges and look specifically for section loss and deterioration when they inspect their bridges over the river.

headline: Penguins sign agreement to stay in city until 2040
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell and Allegheny County Chief Executive Dan Onorato publicly announced that they have signed an agreement with the Pittsburgh Penguins to keep them in Pittsburgh until 2040 as well as a lease for the new Penguins arena.  This agreement allows the Pittsburgh Sports and Exhibition Authority to close a $325 million bond to the Penguins, casino developer Don Barden and Pennsylvania's development fund to finance construction.  Mary Conturo, the director of the Sports and Exhibition Authority assured that there are no loopholes in the contract that the Penguins could use to leave the city.

headline: Judges appear to keep seats
abstract: Instead of ousting 68 judges facing "yes/no" retention votes, Pennsylvanians offered them job security for another 10 years by an overwhelming margin, based on unofficial results. They rejected the appeal of government reform groups that lodged a "vote no" campaign against 66 of the 68 judges. Democrats also clung to strong leads in incomplete results of elections to pick two new justices for the state Supreme Court. Democrats were leading in races for two of three seats on the state Superior Court.

headline: 'Office' aficionados grab convention tickets in Web sale
abstract: A convention dedicated to the NBC television series "The Office" had a very successful first day of online ticket sales as $63,900.74 of tickets were sold by 3:40 PM.  Although the series is based in Scranton, Pennsylvania, most of the tickets came from outside the region, even as far as Canada and Ireland.  Committee member Tim Holmes expects ticket sales in the area to increase as the convention draws nearer and news that cast members are attending spreads.

headline: Barletta: Figures don't tell the whole story
abstract: Mayor Lou Barletta claims that despite illegal immigrants in Hazelton only account for 30 of 8,600 crimes, the ordinance punishing employers and landlords in hiring or leasing to illegal immigrants is still necessary.  American Civil Liberties Attorney Witold J. Walczak questioned Barletta for over 3 hours in a case determining whether or not this city ordinance is legal.  He has argued the ordinance promotes discrimination against the 10,000 Hispanics within the city.

headline: Casey, Rendell support early-childhood education
abstract: This editorial encourages the PA General Assembly and the US Congress to support measures enacted by PA Governor Ed Rendell and US Senator Bob Casey that fund early-childhood education.  Rendell has proposed $25 million to add more all-day kindergartens in school districts as well as $75 million to making pre-kindergarten programs available to 11,000 more children.  Casey has proposed the Prepare All Kids Act of 2007 that gives $5 billion to all states to provide pre-K education and establishing higher standards for teachers, class sizes, and curriculum.

headline: Local restaurants balk at transit tab
abstract: The Allegheny County Council proposed taxing poured alcoholic drinks and rental cars in order to raise $27.7 million for the Port Authority’s annual budget, which the state requires in order to fund the other $184.4 million. Many restaurant and bar owners gathered to protest the proposal because they feel it will hurt slim profit margins and the young people who work in these establishments. Proponents of the tax, however, claim that it is necessary because there are no better alternatives, and a reliable public transit system is necessary for future development.

headline: Pens cool to arena deal
abstract: The Pittsburgh Penguins have been negotiating with the state for a new arena and incentives to help the team thrive financially going forward. Team owner Mario Lemieux toured a new arena in Kansas City in early January, and also is considering a look at a site in Houston.  While Lemieux said the negotiations have regressed, PA Governor Ed Rendell has said the state’s offer is so good that he might ask the NHL to intervene and block a move by the team, should Lemieux make that call.  The earliest a new Pittsburgh arena could be built is 2009, and the team’s Mellon Arena lease ends after this season.

headline: Kanjorski comments on bridge collapse spark fierce backlash
abstract: U.S. Rep. Paul E. Kanjorski from suggested Minnesota is trying to "screw" the rest of the country out of federal funding for its collapsed Interstate bridge, generating a firestorm among political bloggers. Comments the Nanticoke Democrat made Tuesday at a regional economic forum at the University of Scranton were posted on political blogs touching off the controversy.

headline: Other views
abstract: This article posts a hyperlink to an article on www.phoenixvillenews.com

headline: Council repeals 'pro-choice city' resolution
abstract: The Philadelphia City Council declared that its previous symbolic proclamation that the city is a "pro-choice city" has been rescinded.  Democratic Councilwoman Blondell Reynolds Brown sponsored this bill despite it not changing the actual policy of the city.  There is a definitive majority in the Philadelphia City Council that supports abortion rights but many members feel that the Council should not decide on a matter that is not actually in its jurisdiction.  The Council also approved more than 80 pieces of legislation in a pre-recess session that finds many legislators rapidly passing many new measures.

headline: Casino consultant an ex-aide to Vallas
abstract: SugarHouse Gaming, with plans to construct a $550 million casino on Delaware Avenue, has hired a new spokeswoman from the Philadelphia School District, Leigh Whitaker, the deputy chief of staff under Superintendent Paul Vallas.  Sugarhouse already employs John Miller from Channel 29 and KYW and Keny Snyder, who has worked for PA Governor Ed Rendell, US Representative Bob Brady and PA Senator Vince Fumo.

headline: Locally owned bridges scored
abstract: After the tragic bridge collapse in Minnesota on August 3rd, the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation has released ratings on the 6,400 bridges over 20 feet long in Pennsylvania with 1/3 of locally owned bridges being structurally deficient.  PennDOT also released gradings on the state-owned bridges with 1/4 of those being structurally deficient as well.  According to spokesman Rick Kirckpatrick, the new ratings should be reason to worry as the term "structurally deficient" only means that there is a higher level of deterioration.

headline: Performing arts group takes ownership of High St. building
abstract: The Pottstown Area Industrial Development Corp. signed over the title of 245 High St. to TriPAC on Tuesday. Funding for the building purchase and renovations is part of a $2.5 million capital campaign begun by TriPAC in September. The goal includes purchasing the three-story downtown building as well as the necessary renovations to make it a 180-seat performance and educational space for theater, music and dance, according to Kiesling.

headline: Knox defends hiring of felon at his Md. HMO
abstract: Philadelphia mayoral candidate Tom Knox yesterday defended his decision to hire a convicted embezzler David Fishbone, a bankruptcy lawyer in Philadelphia, at his Maryland health-insurance firm. Fishbone pleaded guilty in 1995 to looting six estates of more than $1 million. Knox said yesterday that he had moved Fishbone onto his own payroll as a personal assistant, but that he continued working at the Fidelity premises for about a month until he could relocate his family to Philadelphia.

headline: Phil's pantheon
abstract: Robinson was a darn good player for the Phillies and other teams. He was a good batting instructor, coach and a good person. Will his name be put on the wall? No! Will he get a big article? No! I'm tired of hearing about Darren Daulton, "The Dude" Dykstra, John Kruk, etc., from Harry Kalas. I'm sick of hearing about 1993. Let's talk abut Pete Rose and the 1980 team. Tug, Pete, etc., won a championship. We all know the Phillies were the last to integrate, but give other players their due who brought excitement here, Harry.

headline: Gay-rights speakers urge support for anti-discrimination bills
abstract: According to speakers at a forum at Lebanon Valley College, which was sponsored by the campus’s gay and lesbian group, PA is close to passing a law that would ban gays from being discriminated against. Dan Miller, a gay Harrisburg city councilman, spoke at the event and told the story of how he was fired from his job 15 years ago because he was gay. Over 100 people were urged to contact legislators to convince them to pass the bill, however, some anti-gay protesters were outside.

headline: Central Greene work to cost $1 million less than first estimated
abstract: The Waynesburg Central High School renovation project should cost over $1 million less than what was originally estimated, which is likely due to timely bidding on companies to do the work. The school board decided to use some of the extra money for alternate options, but most of the money will be put towards a new science wing. The school board voted 5-1 in favor of awarding the contract, while the dissenting vote thought it cost too much.

headline: Maglev's alive, but is it well?
abstract: The Federal Railroad Administration is in the process of releasing its final environmental impact statement, which could put Maglev Inc. into a leading position to develop the nation’s first magnetically levitated train system, which would take passengers between Pittsburgh’s airport and downtown at speeds of up to 240 mph. The company has already spent $27.6 million in federal and state funding for the project, but future funding remains uncertain. Several other nations have built or are in the process of building similar systems, however, the system’s construction is extremely expensive, and it remains unclear whether or not Maglev Inc.’s project or any similar projects will be approved in the U.S.

headline: Pucks for brains
abstract: Colin McNickle expresses frustration at the lack of government officials' toughness in their negotiations with Pittsburgh Penguins owner Mario Lemieux dealing with the funding of the new Penguisn hockey arena.  McNickle places much of the blame on the Pittsburgh-Allegheny County Sports and Exhibition Authority and their ownership of the facility on the public's behalf.  He also claims that taxpayers will cover twice as many costs as the Penguins, $225 million.

headline: Knox focuses on the future
abstract: Businessman Tom Knox is considering his next move after losing the Democratic Primary election to former Philadelphia City Councilman Michael Nutter. Some credit Knox's reform campaign with paving the way for Nutter after Knox's campaign came under attack. Knox said he hopes Nutter can remain independent from the Democratic party and believes he retain opponent and US Rep. Bob Brady as the party chairman. Knox praised candidates US Rep. Chaka Fattah, PA Rep. Dwight Evans, and even Brady.

headline: Pittsburgh roots gave 'Control' producer a leg up
abstract: One of just two Americans involved in the making of British-dominated "Control," producer Todd Eckert of North Side said his Pittsburgh connection earned him good will. The movie, which won the award for best European film earlier this year at the Cannes Film Festival, is the story of Ian Curtis, the lead singer of the British band Joy Division, which evolved from the Manchester music scene in the late 1970s. The connection earned credibility during Eckert's first conversation with Tony Wilson -- a Cambridge grad, TV presenter and owner of Factory Records who gave Joy Division its big break.

headline: High court backs Gannon
abstract: The nation's highest court won't revive a former Gannon University chaplain Lynette Petruska's  sexual-discrimination case against the school and its top officials. The Supreme Court let stand a ruling by a three-judge panel of the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals. It held in September that the courts cannot intervene in employment disputes between religious organizations and their ministers.

headline: Charter schools volunteer to take Duquesne students
abstract: Tim Daniels, of the Pennsylvania Charter Schools Coalition, reported that a group of charter schools including Northside Urban Pathways, PA Cyber Charter School and Propel Schools, have offered to take the 200 students in Duquesne High School that will be forced to move to new schools due to the district's financial failings.  However, the PA Education Secretary still wants to see if the Legislature will allow him to assign students to multiple school districts such as West Mifflin Area and East Allegheny.  Both of these school districts have opposed this proposal.

headline: Manufacturers’ association against tolling
abstract: The Manufactures Association of Central PA passed a resolution against the proposed tolling of Interstate 80 and sent letters to a number of state and national officials. It opposes the proposal because it believes that it will hurt businesses and economic growth along I-80, result in higher prices for consumers and could result in tractor-trailers congesting secondary roads.

headline: Rendell offers Pens revised plan
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell said a deal for a new Uptown arena for the Pittsburgh Penguins isn't quite finished, but he has given the Penguins a revised plan to keep the team in Pittsburgh. PA Senator Wayne Fontana, a Brookline Democrat on the board of the city-county Sports & Exhibition Authority, told the Pittsburgh Tribune-Review that negotiations between the Penguins and public officials were down to "just little things," and that he didn't know of any "major hurdles" remaining. Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl said he remains optimistic officials will reach an agreement with the team.

headline: Knox looks to deflect campaign attacks
abstract: Millionaire John Knox admits he is trying to buying City Hall in the five-way Democratic primary for Philadelphia Mayor, which includes US Reps. Bob Brady and Chaka Fattah, former city Councilman Michael Nutter, and PA Rep. Dwight Evans. The Committee of Seventy asked Knox to voluntarily cap his spending, which has funded ads credited for his massive gain in the polls, however he declined. Evans is fighting hard against Knox's "political outsider" image, pointing out that he has been a campaign contributor to both PA Governor Rendell and former Governor Casey.

headline: Sexy? Not so fast
abstract: Letter to the editor criticizing the paper's Sexy Singles who were not as sexy as advertised.

headline:
House bill on open records splits local representatives
But even supporters have reservations about measure
abstract: House Representatives are divided over a bill that would reform Pennsylvania’s open records laws; though the bill is expected to pass and be considered jointly with the Senate. Representative John Siptroth believes the bill has made improvements that make records more accessible; however, he, Representative Mario Scavello and Representative Mike Carroll are concerned about the number of exemptions that are in it. Kim de Bourbon, an advocate of the PA Freedom of Information Coalition, favors the Senate’s version of the bill, which doesn’t include as many exemptions, such as e-mail.

headline: City schools budget cut by $11.8 million
abstract: No Harrisburg teachers will lose their jobs because of budget cuts, but there will be fewer of them when classes resume next month.  Mayor Stephen R. Reed yesterday announced $11.8 million cuts from the Harrisburg School District's $140 million budget for 2007-08 but said every effort was made to spare teachers' jobs and maintain education and other services to the district's 9,750 students. The district will not fill 38 teaching vacancies, and that will reduce the total number of teachers to 740.

headline: Mean spirited
abstract: This editorial criticizes the justification that US Representatives John Peterson and Phil English used for including an amendment in a federal transportation bill that would block the Interstate 80 tolls that were proposed by PA Governor Ed Rendell and passed through the PA Legislature.  Their justification, according to the author, was sending the tax dollars from their rural districts to failing transit systems in urban areas.  The editorial goes on to point out that one-fifth of the counties (14 counties) such as Bucks, Philadelphia, and Montgomery are urban areas that make up 71% of the state's taxable income that is used for rural programs across the state.

headline: Rendell optimistic on Penguins deal
abstract: After a phone call with Penguins co-owner Ron Burkle, PA Governor Ed Rendell expressed renewed confidence about reaching an arena deal that will keep the team in Pittsburgh. A day after threatening to take his case directly to the National Hockey League if the Penguins try to relocate, Mr. Rendell disclosed that he had talked to Mr. Burkle about "some issues that need to be narrowed a little bit and we both agreed to work on them." He said Allegheny County Chief Executive Dan Onorato and Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl also had talked to Mr. Burkle this week.

headline: Lawmakers facing busy agenda in Harrisburg
abstract: The PA Legislature will reconvene this week after a summer recess and have a very ambitious agenda in front of them laid out by PA Governor Ed Rendell including more state-funded health coverage and clean energy projects.  Furthermore, PA Representatives Tom Quigley and Sam Rohrer, both Republicans, are trying to influence Democrats in the House of Representatives to support their proposed tax relief legislation, the Commonwealth Caucus Plan. The article highlights all the planned pieces of legislation and agendas for the upcoming year, but also mentions how Quigley claims that Rendell's proposal to give health insurance to all uninsured residents by putting a 3% surcharge on all employers.

headline: The Fairness Edition
abstract: KDKA-TV is the second news outlet to land that coveted ratings-booster, a Pittsburgh mayoral debate. Theirs is to be taped on Oct. 30 at Point Park University's GRW Theater, and broadcast that evening.  In its press release, the station noted that "Mayor Luke Ravenstahl and Republican challenger Mark DeSantis have agreed to participate." Others want more groups to join in. The conventional wisdom is that putting more candidates on the stage would benefit Mr. Ravenstahl, since it would reduce the amount of airtime Mr. DeSantis would get. Mr. Rauterkus, of course, argues otherwise.

headline: Interactive theater presents current issues for students
abstract: An interactive theater performance in Philadelphia is presenting young people with constitutional issues they hear or see every day in the media. Immigration, search and seizure, privacy, civil liberties and more. All are examined in a 20-minute interactive theater performance called Living News. It's geared toward student groups in grades seven through 12.

headline: City's newest floating classroom is on its way
abstract: RiverQuest, a non-profit science education organization, has launched the Explorer, an environmentally friendly floating classroom for students from Freeport, Florida to head to Pittsburgh's North Shore.  It is powered by a new hybrid diesel-electric propulsion system and built with environmentally friendly materials, windows, coatings, and paints.  Despite delays in acquiring certification from the US Coast Guard, it is expected to house 10,000 students a year for its ecosystem education program.

headline: Misrepresentation toll legislation
abstract: PA Senator Vincent Fumo writes an opinion article criticizing Philadelphia Inquirer journalist Kevin Ferris for sarcastically criticizing PA Governor Ed Rendell's plan to toll highway Interstate 80.  Fumo explains how tolling will prevent Rendell from raising taxes and also aids the financially strapped Southeastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority, which is more relevant to Philadelphia than the northwestern tier of Pennsylvania that Ferris sympathizes with.

headline: Rendell stops in Valley to promote turnpike plan
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell visited Lehigh Valley Thursday in a briefing sponsored by the Lehigh Valley Planning Commission to help promote his plan to lease the Pennsylvania Turnpike for $1.7 billion annually while increasing a tax on oil company profits.  The Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission argue that privatizing the road will lead to a high increase on tolls.  Rendell has visited 6 cities thus far on a 7-city bus tour.

headline: Lawmakers spend thousands on commercials
abstract: Pennsylvania lawmakers spent more than $6 million on public service announcements last term, while PA House members from Franklin County spent a total of $142,631.  Many critics of these advertisements claim that are used more so for self promotion than actually promoting the cause.  PA State Representative Rob Kauffman of Chambersburg cost the state $78,128 by running his ads but claims that he was surprised to learn how much he actually spent.

headline:
You've got a fiend in Pennsylvania
Or maybe just a bigfoot or 2
abstract: The PA Bigfoot Society is investigating photographs taken in Elk County that depict a strange creature; though some have speculated that the strange creature is bear. There have allegedly been over 800 sightings of "hairy wild man" in PA since 1830, but the Bigfoot Society isn’t jumping to any conclusions and will wait until experts view the photos to release an official statement. The article describes a number of these sightings, which have been reported in many different counties.

headline: Lawmakers can't duck vote
abstract: The author is disturbed at the decision of the PA legislature to delay voting on a bill that would give women who are raped emergency contraception to prevent pregnancy. She's also upset that opponents are trying to turn it into a pro-choice or pro-life debate. She claims that 85% of the population favors the bill, and legislators need to be bold enough to step up and pass it.

headline: Congress waits for Bush to sign enormous student aid increase
abstract: The US Congress passed the College Cost Reduction and Access Act, which is a $20.9 billion student aid package that will give Pennsylvania $1.17 billion in school loans and Pell Grant aid for the next five years.  US Representative George Miller wrote the legislation, and it is predicted that it will save every Pennsylvania college student with a loan $4,440 a year.  This bill comes at a time when the group Campaign for America's Future reported that college tuition has gone up 37% since 2000 but the median household income has dropped by 2%.

headline: More toll proposal opposition voiced
abstract: Area residents told the turnpike commission during a four-hour session at Milton Area High School that tolling Interstate 80 could adversely affect local economy, increase cost of living and negatively affect traffic patterns in the region. About 100 residents and business owners came to a public meeting, hosted by the commission, to ask questions and voice their opinions on tolling the 311-mile interstate that runs east and west though the state.

headline: Rendell threatens to jerk his support if Council, unions don't swiftly mend Convention Center hiring rift
abstract: Gov. Rendell has warned City Council that its squabble over work-force diversity and nonunion contractors on the planned expansion of the Convention Center could cause delays that scuttle the $700 million project. Rendell has convened a meeting to try to untangle the mess that Council's approval of the state-funded project has become. After a discussion last week of minority participation in construction unions, Council approved a provision designed to open the door to nonunion work on the project. The move infuriated labor leaders and their allies on Council, whose members met, caucused, and fumed all day yesterday but failed to approve the agreement needed to get the project moving.

headline: Lawyer: Ex-Rep. LaGrotta talks with prosecutors
abstract: Prosecutors on Wednesday accused former Democratic lawmaker Frank LaGrotta of placing two relatives on the state payroll as "ghost employees," the first criminal charges to result from a grand jury investigating legislative corruption. The sister and niece of the 20-year former legislator from Ellwood City collected about $25,000 for work that wasn't performed, said state Attorney General Tom Corbett, whose announcement was made one day after seven House Democratic staffers were let go or resigned in a staff shakeup. The two women face charges for allegedly lying to a grand jury, a misdemeanor.

headline: Ordinance revised
abstract: Hazelton City Council has changed the wording of the Illegal Immigration Relief Act so that complaints about possible illegal-immigration offenses cannot be based on national origin, ethnicity, nor race.  This change was in response to an argument many plaintiffs have been using in federal trials over the law according to solicitor Chris Slusser.

headline: Creating the urge to merge
abstract: PA State Representative Nick Kotik represents three small school districts, Carlynton, Cornell, and Sto-Rox, who are beginning to fail.  Kotik believes that the cash infusions and oversight boards that have traditionally kept these districts afloat  cannot address falling enrollment, aging schools, and weakening tax bases.  His recommendation is that smaller school districts, in order to succeed, must achieve economies of scale by merging with larger school districts.

headline: More toll trouble for Pennsylvania
abstract: The author of the editorial criticizes the passing of a PA state law that added tolls to I-80 and describes the uproar from local governments and industries near the interstate. The author also claims that several state and federal congressional members oppose the tolls. The author also questions several aspects of state spending and lawmaking, as well as other alternatives such as leasing the PA Turnpike.

headline: Rendell's remark about Warner Theatre stirs emotions
abstract: The author encourages PA Governor Rendell to be more sensitive after he insulted people in Erie by discounting the importance of the town's Warner Theatre. For many in the town, it is an important historic landmark and still a center of the community today. The Governor had said he did not think the theatre was worth more than $11 million in renovations, however after an outcry, he told local officials he would come through with $23 million needed for renovations.

headline: Legislation would be step in right direction
abstract: John Usalis encourages the PA House of Representatives to support a bill passed by the PA Senate that would eliminate the "lame duck" sessions that take place after an election and before the start of a new legislative year.  He cites the "lame duck" session that took place in 2005 where the legislators voted for their own pay increase, which angered all citizens.  He also quotes PA Senator James J. Rhoades who reported that these sessions are historically used to vote on controversial issues such as tax increases to avoid accountability.

headline: Is the obvious answer too obscure?
abstract: A number of recent public struggles are listed explaining its background and response by those in Harrisburg.  Costs to taxpayers are highlighted as well as conflicts of interest.

headline: Pa. sets post-rape rules for hospitals
abstract: According to new state regulations, hospitals throughout PA must provide emergency contraception for women who have been raped. However, supporters of emergency contraception and civil rights leaders are disappointed that hospitals can easily file for an exemption to the law; though they must still advise women that they can be transported to a different hospital for the pill. A current law that would get rid of these exemptions is pending but face a number of challenges.

headline: Despite missing federal benchmarks, city schools 'moving in right direction'
abstract: The Pittsburgh Public Schools missed federal achievement benchmarks for the fifth year in a row, thanks largely to low reading scores, giving the state the authority to impose tougher sanctions on the district, according to an analysis of 2006-07 test scores released yesterday. But tougher penalties, such as a state takeover of the district, aren't imminent. The state Education Department said it will continue to monitor Superintendent Mark Roosevelt's efforts to improve academics.

headline: New radar law is long overdue
abstract: Retired police officer applauds new radar and says they aren't trying to trap speeders. The law giving local municipalities the right to use radar in speed enforcement is long over due. The simple answer is pay attention to your driving and your speed and you won't need to worry about the radar.

headline: Report: City skimping on police, fire, rec-center repairs
abstract: Over the past eight years, Philadelphia has spent $850 million less than what was recommended by the City Planning Commission to maintain a number of city buildings and streets. The PA Intergovernmental Cooperation Authority released a review of 163 city buildings and found that a great deal of them require repairs. The report was released in hopes of encouraging the incoming administration to provide increased funding.

headline: Legislative reforms are long overdue
abstract: The opinion expressed in this article states that a package of legislative reforms will be in front of the PA state House of Representatives today; the most important being the curbing of the power of the Rules Committee is long overdue.  PA Representative and deputy Speaker of the House Josh Shapiro of Montgomery County claimed that the Rules Committee has an extreme amount of influence on the legislative process.  Other reforms would provide more openness in the legislative process, limiting House sessions to the day, and suspending public service announcements during election times.

headline: Highlights of Rendell health care proposal
abstract: The Rendell health care proposal will allow nurse practitioners to perform duties once limited to registered nurses.  It would broaden similar laws to apply to midwifes in prescribing of drugs.  It would require that insurance companies include nurse practitioners, specialists, physicians assistants and midwives in their listing.

headline: Pathetic measure
abstract: The author of the editorial argues that a measure to make Pennsylvania’s government records open to the public has far too many exceptions and is coded in secrecy.  In particular the author is disturbed that no public hearings were held, and officials’ e-mails are protected, which may actually  represent a step backward in attempts to open records to the public.

headline: District proposes tax increase
abstract: Harrisburg School District's first proposes property tax increase in five years weighs in at 5.2 percent, with plans to increase spending by 8.6 percent. The proposal depends heavily on state aid for specialized academic programs. District leaders are counting on PA Governor Ed Rendell in particular to push through funding for preschool education. A major cause of the tax increase is the surmounting debt facing the district after renovations.

headline: No more troubled bridge to Tatamy
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation will fill in a sinkhole that collapsed the Bushkill Street Bridge between Tatamy and Stockertown. It is up to the municipalities to determine whether they want the towns reconnected. Stocktown council is concerned a new bridge will increase traffic in the small borough. Stockertown Borough Councilman Paul Zaboy however, wants the bridge replaced in case of emergency. Tatamy Councilman Robert Fisher cited the risk of the sinkhole reopening as reason not to repair the bridge.

headline: Report: Pittsburgh arena in jeopardy if funding bill isn't approved
abstract: The PA Legislature is struggling to approve the budget before the summer recess, which puts the funding for the Pittsburgh Penguins hockey arena in trouble.  PA Governor Ed Rendell is encouraging legislators to act quickly on the legislation that would fund $7.5 million for 30 years towards this new arena.  The Pittsburgh-Allegheny Count Sports & Exhibition Authority would not be able to issue $325 million of bonds to finance the construction with any long delay in the budget approval.

headline: Legislature takes big step on open records
abstract: The Legislature should be applauded for steps it has taken towards a more transparent government. The most recent legislation made mandatory Internet disclosure of all names, job titles, and salaries of PA government employees on the state's payroll. The PA House is expected to follow the Senate's lead. Local government will also be subject to this legislation. The PA Newspaper Association and PA Governor Ed Rendell have made transparency a joint effort. Editors believe Harrisburg is finally headed in the right direction.

headline: Local lawmakers criticize Rendell
abstract: Conservative lawmakers are calling Rendell's spending plan "unacceptable."  The Republicans are opposed to new tax levies and an overall increase of spending they say is $1.3 billion.  House Rep Todd Rock of Waynesboro also comes out against the governor's plan to lease the Turnpike.

headline: Politicians fight against openness
abstract: The author criticizes a number of aspects of Pennsylvania’s Legislature but is particularly upset at recent amendments to a proposed open records reform bill. In the author’s opinion the original bill was promising and reversed the current law’s inadequacies by making most government information open to the public, however, the state House Government Committee betrayed these ideals by adding a number of exemptions. Any state agency would be able to not release public information if it is considered "burdensome," and e-mails, internal performance audits and previous records are not covered under the bill, which the author finds to be especially troublesome.

headline: Districts file suit challenging Duquesne plan
abstract: The West Mifflin Area and East Allegheny School Districts have filed suit in the Commonwealth Court that has placed high school students from the failing Duquesne District into their schools in future years according to Wester Mifflin Area solicitor John Cambest.  The Legislature passed a measure that allows PA Education Secretary Gerald Zahorchak to place the almost 200 Duquesne students into neighboring districts.  It is expected that a hearing and a ruling won't be finished for another 6-8 months.

headline: Our view: Don't delay Pa. 997 bridge any longer
abstract: This editorial expresses frustration with the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation has still not completed the renovation of Pennsylvania 997 bridge after a decade of delays.  PA Representative Rob Kauffman is urging PennDOT to open bids in October, as they had planned earlier, but PennDOT has moved back this date to December.  The author encourages all 5 legislators representing Franklin County to urge PennDOT to hurry the project along without any more delays.

headline: Rising costs may reduce size of Downtown hotel
abstract: The number of rooms at the proposed convention center hotel Downtown probably will be cut because of lengthy delays in getting the project started. Mary Conturo, executive director of city-county Sports & Exhibition Authority, said the hotel likely will end up at less than the 500 rooms envisioned when the $104 million budget was set in 2003. The authority is expected to meet with Cleveland developer Forest City Enterprises early next year to discuss possible alternatives in scaling back the size of the hotel.

headline: Letter to the Editor
abstract: A Newberry Township citizen writes in thanks to the Pennsylvania lawmakers who voted eliminate the $52 tax for those state taxpayers who make les than $12,000 per year.  She goes on to encourage lawmakers to adjust the taxes on utilities, cell phone bills, and gasoline.

headline: Port Authority OKs 15% cut
abstract: The Port Authority of Pittsburgh is threatening to cut service by 15% if the state does not come forward with needed funding.  The agency is also making cuts in payroll and increasing fares.  Riders and mass transit advocates have come forward vigorously against the draconian cuts.  The board that controls the transit agency has agreed to take a pay freeze.

headline: Protest at Comcast tower site
abstract: Bruce Crawley, former chairman of the African American Chamber of Commerce, led a group of about 25 demonstrators to the construction site of the Comcast tower yesterday, demanding greater inclusion of African-Americans in local construction. The Comcast tower was the site of an Oct. 1 incident in which a white construction worked allegedly waived a noose at a black worker. The white employee was fired, and prosecutors decided not to charge him with a crime. But Crawley charged that workplace intimidation is part of a pattern of mistreatment and exclusion of blacks in the industry.

headline: E. Allegheny to file suit over Duquesne transfers
abstract: East Allegheny School District Solicitor Daniel Beisler reports that the East Allegheny School District will file suit in Commonwealth Court in order to stop the reassignment of Duquesne High School students to the district.  PA Education Secretary Gerald Zahorchak passed a proposal through the PA Legislature that gave him the power to move 200 students from Duquesne to East Allegheny and West Mifflin Area schools.  West Mifflin Area has accepted the decision.

headline: Our view: Governor sets poor example
abstract: Unlike New Jersey Governor Tom Corzine, who apologized after a recent accident for not wearing his seatbelt and said he knows he set a bad example, PA Governor Ed Rendell continues to exceed the speed limit despite being cited for a traffic offense! When state troopers said they clocked his vehicle in excess of 100 mph several times recently, Rendell ordered a state investigation, even though he was in the car! Editors believe Rendell has an obligation to obey all the laws, not simply the ones he wants to.

headline: Save our parks
abstract: Andrew Loza writes to encourage PA Governor Ed Rendell says no the cuts to the Keystone Fund that are included in the current budget on the negotiating table after the PA Senate has proposed to cut conservation and recreation funding by $800 million over 20 years.  The Keystone Fund has funded thousands of community parks, athletic fields, community centers, playgrounds and pools, and Loza believes the indirect benefits of improving the livability of the communities and enhancing the lives of our children are far too important to forget about.

headline: Local reps big on earmarks
abstract: U.S. Rep. Chris Carney and Sen. Bob Casey ranked first and second among freshmen in the amount of federal funding they requested for special projects known as earmarks, according to a USA Today analysis this week. Three other freshman congressmen, Rep. Jason Altmire, of Pittsburgh, and Reps. Patrick Murphy and Joseph Sestak, who represent suburban Philadelphia districts, ranked third, fourth and fifth of the top 20 freshmen who had earmarks in federal appropriations bills, according to the report published Wednesday. All are Democrats. Mr. Carney, Mr. Altmire, Mr. Murphy and Mr. Sestak all won seats last year from Republicans and are considered vulnerable to defeat by Republican challengers in the election next year.

headline: Officials in Lawrence County back New Castle racetrack-casino
abstract: The State Supreme Court is set to decide which one of two racetrack/casinos will be allowed to proceed with construction in Western Pennsylvania.  The applicants are Bedford Downs located near the Ohio border and Valley View Downs in Beaver County.  It is the final license available for gambling in Pennsylvania.

headline: State leads the nation in black homicide rate
abstract: Pennsylvania leads the nation in the rate of black homicides, with nearly 30 deaths per 100,000 black residents annually, according to a study released by the Violence Policy Center. Firearms, especially handguns, were used in the overwhelming majority of the nation's 6,644 slayings with black victims. Eighty-five percent of black victims were male. Pennsylvania recorded 29.52 homicides per 100,000 black residents in 2004, the last year for which the FBI data was available, while Louisiana followed at 29.48 and Indiana was third with 29.3. The national rate was 18.71 per 100,000. The national homicide rate overall was 4.86 per 100,000 and the national rate for whites was 2.97 homicides per 100,000, the group reported.

headline: Educators mull financing alternatives
abstract: A public hearing, which was sponsored by three educational organizations, was held as part of a statewide campaign to develop a new system of state funding for education. One speaker said that schools are overly reliant on property taxes, and the state pays substantially less than the national average towards education. There will be six to eight public hearings throughout the state, and a report will be released in 2008.

headline: Our view: PennDOT, boro rulings show need to change law
abstract: When a major interstate highway in Minnesota recently tumbled into the river, many Pennsylvanians began to wonder about the safety of bridges in PA. After all, we've heard for years how tons of money will be needed to repair our bridges and highways. Of the 14,868 PennDOT-owned bridges that are longer than 20 feet, about one-quarter are considered to have a structural impairment -- more than any other state. But yet when a Beaver County newspaper asked to see inspection reports for Pennsylvania's bridges, a legitimate inquiry made long before the Minnesota bridge collapse, the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation said no. Releasing the reports would compromise public security and cause "undue alarm," PennDOT said.

headline: SEA gets $2M for shortfall
abstract: The Sports & Exhibition Authority again tapped Regional Asset District money to plug a gap in its annual budget. The city-county agency's board unanimously approved using $2 million from the RAD to create a pool of money to help maintain its sports venues and the David L. Lawrence Convention Center. The item is included in the agency's $14 million budget for 2008.  The authority, which owns local sports venues and parking garages, has failed to earn a profit at the Downtown convention center. Operating the building is projected to create a $3.8 million loss in 2008. Revenues are projected to reach $5.9 million, but expenses would be $9.8 million.

headline: Lots of passion among voters
abstract: Daniel Rubin found the black community is not as undecided as many newspapers are reporting over the Philadelphia Democratic Primary. Five democratic contenders include Chaka Fattah, Michael Nutter, and Tom Knox. Rubin discovered people are undecided because they are apathetic. Quite the contrary, people are very hungry for change.

headline: Treasures from Pa.'s past abound in rare books room
abstract: The rare book room of the Capitol in Harrisburg is explored.  The room is described as a dark, 30-90 foot closet.  A bound volume of the Pennsylvania Gazette is featured.  It dates back to 1752.

headline: "What's pushing medical costs?"
abstract: Patrick J. Geho, president of the Beaver County Chamber of Commerce, comments on PA Governor Ed Rendell's new health-care reform proposal by suggesting more focus should be placed on other drivers of health-care costs such as lawsuit abuse and mandated benefits.  He also feels insurance subsidies for lower-income families should come from general tax revenues rather than a payroll tax since a payroll tax adds the cost of each employee to a business.

headline: Educators not sold on bill to start school after Labor Day
abstract: Business leaders and educators are on opposite sides of a bill to be considered before the PA House Tourism and Recreational Development Committee. Erie School District Superintendent Robert Oliver says the proposal is not being considered from a legislative standpoint. Meanwhile president of the Erie Area Convention & Visitors Bureau, John Oliver, testified before the committee in support of the bill.

headline: Our view: Toughen penalties for boating while drunk
abstract: This editorial commends the PA Legislature for signing a bill that makes penalties for boating under the influence stricter while lowering the blood-alcohol content legal limit to 0.08 percent.  The editorial, by citing the tragedy of actress Natalie Wood, encourages PA Governor Ed Rendell to sign this bill into law.

headline: SEA ready to identify groups in collapse
abstract: The city-county Sports & Exhibition Authority will soon reveal the people or companies responsible for the February collapse at the David L. Lawrence Convention Center, Downtown. The authority plans to tell the unnamed companies that an ongoing investigation by its insurer has found them to be responsible for the partial collapse of the building's loading dock onto 10th Street. Officials did not say exactly when the parties will be identified. Once that happens, county Councilman James Burn Jr. plans to resume an investigation of the collapse and a nearby beam failure in 2005.

headline: Make them pay
abstract: This editorial attempts to remind citizens what to consider come the 2008 election.  According to the author, they should remember that PA Governor Ed Rendell and the state legislators are at fault for the furlough of 24,000 state employees who lost a total of $3.5 million in wages.

headline: State asked to investigate tax bureau
abstract: Cynicism is the theme in an article about asking the state to investigate a claim against the local tax bureau's office.  Local officials expect the issue to get lost in paperwork as there does not seem to be an office with the authority to handle their issue.

headline: $27 million marked to provide housing, services for the retarded
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell signed the state budget and with it, granted $27 million for adults with mental retardation that are on an emergency list for housing.  This money will reportedly to increase the full range of services to another 3,000 additional people.  Kevin Casey, deputy secretary for the office of developmental programs in the PA Department of Public Welfare, reports that the federal government with match the $27 million and as a result, will be sufficient to cover those adults in houses for 6 months.

headline: EUP faculty make preparations for possible strike
abstract: The faculty of Edinboro University of Pennsylvania are preparing for a strike of the Association of Pennsylvania State College and University Faculties as contract talks with the Pennsylvania State System of Higher Education are at their final round.  The contract between the two parties expires on June 30 and both parties report very slow progress.  The union wants a 20% wage increase over four years while the system has only given a one-time cash payment of $1,250 and a 7% increase over the rest of the contract.

headline: Pa. budget deadlock threatens county busline services
abstract: The Chester County Commissioners passed a loan that will keep the county's SCCOOT and Link bus lines in operation for at least 3 more months.  The Transportation Management Association of Chester County, who runs the bus lines, brought several community representatives to a meeting recently in order to convince the community leaders of the crisis in local transit funding.  Elaine DeRosa from the Holiday Inn Express, Tom DeMao from the Coatesville Veterans Administration and Eileen Glass from the Southern Chester County Chamber of Commerce were all present the $45,000 cost of running the lines is worth up keeping.

headline: State and elk foundation to build Pa. observation
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell reported he will give a $5 million grant at the Governor's Outdoor Conference on Tuesday to build an elk watching and education center near Elk State Forest in Benezette Township.  The center, which will include exhibits, trails and viewing areas, is expected to open in spring 2009.

headline: Martin-Roberts, Wilson triumph in Democratic race
abstract: Despite failing to be endorsed by Harrisburg Mayor Stephen Reed, Democratic City Council incumbents Gloria Martin-Roberts and Susan Brown Wilson have won nomination for second terms. Martin-Roberts and Wilson usually vote with a block which restrains Reed's spending and general powers. Brad Koplinksi, one of four Democratic nominees to gain Reed's endorsement, generally votes with a block of three seen to be "Reed friendly." The nominations came after last year's budget battles, which resulted in a 17 percent real estate tax hike.

headline: Pa. nursing homes chasing higher-paying rehab patients
abstract: As the market for long-term nursing patients reaches full saturation, the issue of more-short term facilities is explored.  Issues with Medicare reimbursement are discussed as well as the overall issues of cost and long-term viability of the industry.

headline: Alquippa hospital could face closure over state violations
abstract: The Aliquippa Community Hospital has been fined $62,000 despite being short on cash by inspectors and possibly may be shut down if it does not meet Pennsylvania health and licensing requirements.  Dan Miller says that if changes aren't made to the improper documentation and the prevention of the spread of communicable infections, they will have their license and revoked.

headline: Evans to receive national charter-school award
abstract: State Rep. Dwight Evans is scheduled to be presented with a national award tonight for his efforts to advance charter schools. The National Alliance for Public Charter Schools will present its Champion of Charters Award to Evans, an architect of the state's 1997 charter-school law who helped launch the West Oak Lane Charter School the next year. He is to receive the award from Nelson Smith, president of the Washington-based nonprofit organization, during 6 p.m. ceremonies at West Oak Lane Charter. Other 2007 winners of the award are U.S. Sen. Lamar Alexander, Georgia Lt. Gov. Casey Cagle, and Chicago Mayor Richard Daley.

headline: Pa. congressman says I-80 toll plan would hurt businesses
abstract: U.S. Representative John Peterson claims that plans to turn Interstate 80 into a toll road will hurt businesses along the highway and could stifle potential economic growth. Legislators approved the plan in July to generate money to pay for road improvements throughout the state. The Federal Highway Administration is reviewing the issue, and a series of public meeting will be held.

headline: State funding decision only a delay for stadium
abstract: Although the Major League Soccer stadium along the Chester waterfront has met a state funding bump, at least one official said the project is still alive and the franchise is still interested in the Delaware County city. Delaware County Council Chairman Andrew Reilly said an announcement would take place this week, although it may not be the ultimate stadium confirmation that had been expected. Delaware County has committed to spend $30 million to the project, although those funds are expected to come from the county’s share of gaming revenues from Harrah’s Chester Racetrack and Casino, which are required to be spent on economic development. Gaming revenues also cover a portion of the county’s debt service.

headline: Mayor Luke skittish about debates
abstract: The Pittsburgh Republican mayoral candidate Mark DeSantis reportedly wants four debates with his challenger, Democratic incumbent Luke Ravenstahl.  Ravenstahl has only agreed to two debates because of his claims that his commitments as mayor prevent him from participating in any more.  There is a lot of controversy over whether or not Ravenstahl is purposely avoiding these debates.

headline: Schools turn to voters for decisions on taxes
abstract: Voters are about to be asked to vote on comprehensive tax reform in Pennsylvania.  Voters seem to be more than confused with the implications of shifting the state's tax burdens.  Local income taxes, and property taxes are discussed along with their current and future impact.

headline: Becoming smoke-free
abstract: The editorial board writes that the perils of tobacco and secondhand smoke have been known for years. A key preventive measure included in PA Governor Ed Rendell's new health reform package is a ban on smoking in workplaces, restaurants and bars. But despite decades of litigation and squabbles over smoke-free environments, one practical step never taken is giving the Food and Drug Administration regulatory authority. Some Democrats want to use their newly acquired power in Congress to change that. Legislation was introduced in 2004, but Republican leadership at the time and the White House weren't exactly enthusiastic. The board hopes that a more addictive cigarette will not be produced.

headline: Faculty union alleges unfair labor practice by university system
abstract: The Association of Pennsylvania State College and University Faculties have sent a letter to 5,500 State System of Higher Education faculty members explaining what would happen to wages and benefits if the union members were to go on strike. Pat Heilman, president of the union, claims that this letter was used as to intimidate the teachers to not strike and incorrectly states that those who strike and teach summer school will not be paid for their sessions.

headline: Pa. House Democrats push new plan for transit, highways, bridges
abstract: The PA House of Representatives are debating on a transportation plan that is an alternative to Pa Minority Whip Keith McCall's plan as its goal is to bring in $720 million.  In the first year, this House plan would delegate $450 million to highways and bridges, whereas $35 million would be specifically for roads and bridges that local governments maintain.  However, PA Governor Ed Rendell refuses to sign the legislation if the package does not immediately generate $1 billion in funding.

headline: State funds mine training center
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell visited Greene County to announce a $9.3 million state grant that will construct a new coal miners' training center in Ruff Creek and assist in the building of the Waynesburg retail development project.  The new training center will train miners in a unique setting with modern equipment, technology and techniques in a curriculum approved by the US Mine Safety and Health Administration.  The funding was acquired through the PA Department of Community and Economic Development.

headline: Mayor wants officer's badge
abstract: Allentown Mayor Ed Pawlowski reported that officer Brett Guth has been suspended without pay until the hearing of the city council on Guth's traffic violation that caused the death of a 4-year-old boy, Daviay Legrand.  The PA State Police and the Lehigh County District Attorney have stated that Guth will be given a traffic ticket but no criminal charges for the crash.  Citizens in the area such as Ayana Johnson and Daysha Washington, seem to believe that Guth should be fired from his officer position despite the accident being unintentional.

headline: Pitt, CMU and WVU study ways to make coal less polluting
abstract: Local universities are looking for ways to make the region's vast reserves of coal more clean to be more marketable in the current political environment.  The hope is that coal may be able to help reduce the impact of foreign oil on our economy.  Much of the issue with deal with how to clean the local product, known for being particularly dirty.

headline: Belfanti named conferee on smoking law
abstract: Rep. Robert Belfanti was appointed Monday as one of three House conferees on a joint committee to find a compromise on a statewide smoking ban bill. Mr. Belfanti is a vocal supporter of smokers’ rights. House Speaker Dennis O’Brien also named Reps. Michael Gerber, D-Montgomery, and Ron Miller, R-York, to the conference committee. The conferees will try to craft a bill that reconciles differences between versions of smoking ban bills that passed each chamber earlier this year. The bills treat exemptions from a smoking ban differently.

headline: Feds try to build on No Child Left Behind Act
abstract: Five years after the signing of the No Child Left Behind Act, which raised the stakes for standardized testing, the Bush administration has released its plans for the next chapter. The administration's wish list includes keeping the hallmarks of the law, school accountability based on standardized tests in reading and math, and making changes to increase its reach, flexibility and ability to improve the lives of students in chronically low-performing schools.  In a conference call from Washington, U.S. Education Secretary Margaret Spellings announced the administration's priorities, called "Building on Results: A Blueprint for Strengthening the No Child Left Behind Act." The article outlines the proposed changes.

headline: Pa. Lawmakers Demand More Snowfighting Answers from PennDOT
abstract: Pennsylvania’s top highway, state police and emergency management officials spoke before the state Senate Transportation Committee to answer questions about what was learned from the failure of last year’s Valentine’s Day storm. Most committee members wanted to know how the agencies would communicate better with one another and with motorists when weather gets bad again.

headline: State lawmaker calls for building timeout
abstract: PA Representative Bob Freeman is hosting an open forum to debate whether municipalities can create development moratoriums while rewriting comprehensive plans or zoning and land use ordinances.  In 2001, the PA Supreme Court gave the ruling that municipalities did not possess this power, but Freeman has proposed that these municipalities could stop accepting development plans for up to a year while reviewing the ordinances.  Mark Mitman of the PA Builders Association Lehigh Valley chapter claims the law would restrict the third-largest economic contributor to the state.

headline: McCaffery, Krancer win shots at Supreme Court
abstract: In the Democratic judicial Primary for the PA Supreme Court, Seamus McCaffery, a PA Superior Court judge and a former cop, and PA Superior Court Judge Debra Todd were winners. Both were endorsed by the Democratic State Committee. In the GOP primary, the winners were Michael Krancer and PA Superior Court Judge Maureen Lally-Green. Philadelphia Common Pleas Court Judge Paul Panepinto, who was not endorsed by the party, pledge to support the winners. The Democratic victors won over Philadelphia Common Pleas Court Judge Darnell Jones II, whom PA Governor Ed Rendell supported.

headline: REWARDING JOBS
abstract: Public sector salaries are discussed with the amount of $100,000 salaried government officials there are.  That number is 3,042, and some are being paid upwards of $200,000.  The article compares their salaries to those of peers in other states.  The attractiveness and competitiveness of public sector work is discussed.

headline: Bill would help patients shop for health care
abstract: PA Representative Todd Eachus of Luzerne, with the support of PA Governor Ed Rendell, has introduced proposals that attempt to help consumers shop for health care services and find the lowest prices for prescription drugs.  The bill requires pharmacies to submit retail prices for the 150 most popular drugs to the PA Health Care Cost Containment Council to be posted on their website.  The Jewish Health Care Foundation and the Pittsburgh Regional Health Care Initiative both support the bill although they don't think it solves all of the health care problems.

headline: First ball caps, then cell phones, schools now banning iPods to stop cheating
abstract: Shana Kemp, spokeswoman for the National Association of Secondary School Principals, hopes each school will have in place a policy concerning digital media player use. A number of schools across the nation and around the world have begun banning digital media players. However, Duke University provides iPods for its students, one teacher noting that technology can corrupt but also can be productive.

headline: Pa. should test octane levels of gas
abstract: Kathy Leedy writes about how Pennsylvania drivers don't know if they're getting what they pay for, especially if they buy "premium" gasolines about Pennsylvania Auditor General Jack Wagner released a report on retail gas pump inspections in January. Wagner is recommending that the state Legislature require the testing of octane ratings.

headline: State mulls community revitalization grants
abstract: After PA Governor Ed Rendell and the PA General Assembly tentatively agreed on a 2007-2008 budget spending plan, local legislators are still debating on how to divide $360 million for the "walking around" money.  Last year, Pennsport School of Dance in Philadelphia received $10,000 for operation costs while the Friends of Monsignor Bonner Field of Dreams project in Upper Darby received up to $400,000.  PA Representative Nick Micozzie believes that the grants, which are paid through the PA Department of Community and Economic Development, are significant for the smaller communities and boroughs.

headline: McNaughton may not get gaming board post
abstract: Former PA state Representative Mark McNaughton's appointment to the PA Gaming Control Board, which carries a $145,000 annual salary, could be in jeopardy.  An opinion issued yesterday by Al Masland, chief counsel for PA's Department of State, raised several questions about the validity of the nomination of McNaughton, the former Susquehanna Township lawmaker who opted against seeking re-election in 2006.  It concluded by advising Secretary of Commonwealth Pedro Cortes not to swear McNaughton in yet as a member of the gaming board.

headline: Open-market health care the answer?
abstract: Interest in a single-payer health care system is gauged in this article.  Doctors and interest groups are asked their feelings on the subject and explain the differences in health care reform ideas.  While some go the single-payer route, others suggest high deductible plans and a more consumer oriented approach.

headline: Businesses a bit pessimistic
abstract: The PA Chamber of Business and Industry has released a report stating that more people are pessimistic than the business climate in Pennsylvania than there was last year.  The biggest concerns are increasing health-care costs but 60% of respondents opposed PA Governor Ed Rendell's health care plan that provided coverage for uninsured Pennsylvania citizens.  The businesses also disagree with his $850 million energy plan because of its funding through new taxes.

headline: Foreign student influx taxes school resources
abstract: The Scranton School District's enrollment is on the brink of reaching 10,000 students enrolled as more foreign students are moving into the area.  William King, the assistant superintendent is concerned about buildings that are nearing their capacity and an English as a Second Language program that is stressed as well.  Scranton Federation of Teachers President Rosemary Boland believes while the district is being pressured with more responsibility, more enrollment and an influx of students is a positive thing for the area.

headline: Pa. vows crackdown on aggressive drivers
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation has announced the expansion of the Smooth Operator program as it is now practiced by 175 local police departments and 15 state police troops across the state.  The program intends to target dangerous drivers who commit moving violations that would endanger other people.  PennDOT will expand the program by funding it with $2 million dollars.

headline: State offers assistance to help pay mortgages
abstract: The PA Housing Finance Agency, which already offers a program that helps Pennsylvanians who suffer a hardship pay for mortgages, announced two new programs over the summer. The Refinance to an Affordable Loan program is designed to help homeowners refinance into better fixed loans, and the Homeowner Equity Recovery Opportunity program is designed to help people who owe more on their mortgages than their homes are actually worth. PA is significantly better off in its foreclosure rate than many other states, which may account for why there haven’t been too many homeowners that have pursued these new programs.

headline: Mediators arrange sessions with Pittsburgh teachers
abstract: State mediators have arranged bargaining sessions with Pittsburgh Public Schools and its teachers union on Nov. 12 and 30. The contract for the district's 4,042 teachers, aides, counselors and other employees expired June 30. They authorized their union, the Pittsburgh Federation of Teachers, to call a strike if they consider it necessary. The main issues are pay and medical insurance. The average pay in the district for a teacher with a master's degree is $62,000 a year.

headline: More than meets the eye with lower jobless rate
abstract: The region's unemployment rate tumbled in February to 3.9 percent, its lowest level in 37 years.  Analysts dismiss the number as it reflects a number of hidden issues and could have been affected by weather or other unusual circumstances.  The new figure also reflects a drop in the labor force.

headline: Bush: SCHIP veto if tobacco tax rises
abstract: President Bush told Republican congressmen that he would veto any legislation expanding children’s health insurance if it includes an increase on the tobacco tax. He already vetoed a previous children’s health insurance bill, and Democrats are leading negotiating efforts to try to obtain the two-thirds majority that would be needed to override Bush’s potential veto.

headline: Former Temple student says his views cost him a master's degree
abstract: Christian Dejohn, a Temple University student is suing the university because he believes they denied him a master’s degree due to his political views. Lawyers for the school claim that the school denied him a master’s degree because he was a marginal student who turned in an awful thesis. DeJohn served in Bosnia for two years.

headline:
PennDot faulted on state plane use
An audit finds lapses in getting the required paperwork; the agency denies improprieties.
abstract: PA Auditor General Jack Wagner sent a letter to Governor Rendell that claims that PennDot has failed to live up to its oversight responsibilities over the use of state planes. Auditors found that PennDot failed to obtain the required pre-trip documents for a number of flights, and the agency didn’t obtain proof as to whether or not many passengers on state flights were travelling for official state business. PennDot has denied improper use of state aircraft.

headline: State Pledges $12M to RiverParc
abstract:
The Pittsburgh Cultural Trust landed a big-name donor in its multimillion-dollar plan to grow Downtown's Cultural District into a thriving residential neighborhood -- the state of Pennsylvania. 
PA Governor Ed Rendell pledged $12.3 million to the first phase of the group's $460 million RiverParc project, which will create 700 residences, 159,000 square feet of retail space and 1,500 parking spaces on six acres between Fort Duquesne Boulevard and Penn Avenue. Included will be environmentally friendly buildings, public parks, a cultural arts venue and, possibly, a four-star hotel.

headline: Mellow says bill will avert teachers’ strikes, protect taxpayers
abstract: Representative Robert Mellow is writing to garner support for his bill, which would end the practice of teacher’s strikes by allowing an impartial common pleas judge to make a final decision if negotiations stall for too long. He claims that 30,000 children were affected by strikes last year, and some contracts issues aren’t resolved for years, which can necessitate large property tax increases to compensate. He describes some details of his proposed settlement system and believes that it is air and will prevent students from being interrupted.

headline: Another first for Mohegan Sun: extradited fugitive
abstract: Police had to arrest a man at the Mohegan Sun at Pocono Downs on charges stemming from a gambling incident in Nevada.  Police at Pocono Downs say they got him on jaywalking of all things.  The man faces conspiracy and theft charges in Nevada.

headline: Care home licenses pulled
abstract: The operating licenses of two area personal care homes have been revoked by the state Department of Public Welfare, partly due to neglect charges against a Carbondale doctor who owns and operates the facilities. Birch Hills Residence in Simpson and Mallard Meadows Residential Healthcare Center in Waymart will be allowed to stay open, however, pending appeals.

headline: Free pre-K schooling starting, after school enrichment program growing
abstract: Pottstown has been getting recognition for early education programs and has received nearly one-tenth of the allotted state funds, which Mary Rieck, a local early education coordinator, attributes to Pottstown’s efforts to reach out to the community. A local after-school enrichment program offers children many different opportunities, and through state funding, Pottstown will provide free pre-K education to 100 students. The article details the efforts of Pottstown to get funding from local businesses and organizations, which has been successful and made Pottstown an example for the rest of the state to follow.

headline: PennDOT finds fix for recurring Rt. 28 landslides
abstract: PennDOT plans to cut away rock on a landslide-prone hillside over Route 28 and build a protective fence before the end of next year. Once PennDOT determines the cost, the local office might seek emergency highway money from its Harrisburg headquarters to pay for the work, although it might have to defer other local work to pay for the project. Several hundred tons of boulders and debris slid down the hillside in Harmar and O'Hara in October, crashing through a protective concrete barrier and causing a tractor-trailer to overturn as its driver tried to avoid the rocks. Other vehicles also were damaged.

headline: State-filed complaint could shut county down
abstract: Luzerne County commissioners have scheduled a closed session to discuss how to handle a state-filed complaint that could stop a plan to borrow up to $93.5 million and force layoffs or a government shutdown. Wilkes-Barre political gadfly Tim Grier filed a complaint with the state Department of Community and Economic Development to stop the borrowing plan. Janel Miller, spokeswoman for the state Department of Community and Economic Development, said the complaint shuts down the state review process, which typically lasts 20 days.

headline: Minor parties hurting in PA
abstract: Josh R. Zachmann wrote a letter to the editor describing how Pennsylvania is one of the worst offenders in undermining democracy in US politics, as claimed by the Helsinki Accords.  Zachmann cites the Green Party candidate for US Senate, Carl Romanelli, who needed to 67,000 signatures to become a candidate because of his minor party affiliation rather than the major parties, who need only 10,000.  The PA Superior Court ruled in an appeal by the Democratic Party that the signatures attained by Romanelli were not valid, despite Zachmann describing otherwise.

headline: Specter planning to hold hearing on Blues merger
abstract: The US Senate will examine the big merger of two insurance giants.  US Senator Arlen Spector (R-PA) is the ranking member on the Judiciary Committee and will preside over the hearing with Senator Leahy, chairman of the committee.  The new insurance giant will control half of the state's insurance market and collect up to $16,000,000 in premiums.

headline: Census' take on health, wealth
abstract: In a move sure to enliven the debate on health care, the U.S. Census Bureau released new data yesterday showing that the number of people without health insurance is continuing to rise. Forty-seven million people - 15.8 percent of the population - are now uninsured, up from 44.8 million, or 15.3 percent, in 2005.Congress and President Bush are wrangling over funding for the State Children's Health Insurance Program (SCHIP), which is aimed at children whose families are not quite poor enough to qualify for Medicaid.

headline: Funding education
abstract: The PA Legislature set aside $650,000 to analyze the state's education spending. Consultants hired by the state's leading educrats concluded the Keystone State should spend more on education -- about $5 billion more -- to reach state proficiency levels in math and reading. Never mind that the correlation between spending and academic performance is inherently flawed if not fundamentally fraudulent. Exactly how do higher salaries and sweetheart benefits for teachers and administrators translate into student performance? It's a lame horse beaten to death by the status quo.

headline: PennDOT inspecting Fort Pitt Tunnel ceiling tiles
abstract: PennDot was forced to close the Fort Pitt Tunnel in Pittsburgh in September due to falling ceiling tiles, which caused traffic jams since about 130,000 vehicles use the tunnel each day. It is investigating the problem but doesn’t know how much it will cost to fix yet.

headline: Street brought his skills to end Council deadlock
abstract: No one asked Mayor Street to help resolve last week the ongoing stalemate that threatened to scrap the planned $700 million expansion of the Convention Center. But the mayor decided to intervene anyway - and in doing so again showed his knack for settling crises, even on his way out the door. With three weeks left in office, the mayor also derailed whatever opportunity there may have been for a successor he doesn't much care for, Michael Nutter, to jump in and claim victory, and also thwarted Gov. Rendell's own ambition to broker a deal as well.

headline: More Joking Than Sparring Between Phila. Mayoral Candidates
abstract: Two Philadelphia mayoral candidates, Michael Nutter and Al Taubenberger, joked with one another during a debate, which the article describes.

headline: U.S. issues rules on chemical sites
abstract: New rules set to allow the government to control security at the nation's 15,000 chemical plants received mixed reviews from the nation's lawmakers.  Many of these facilities have been targetted by the Department of Homeland Security for needing special attention.  At the very least, plants will be required to meet certain standards for security regardless of the action the government takes on this issue.

headline: Cigarette smell is repugnant
abstract: Kelly McCurdy writes a letter to the editor to express her distaste for the bad odor and health effects of second-hand smoke.  She feels a tax should be placed on alcohol to make up for the loss of cigarette sales if a public smoking ban was passed, and she also proposes placing a "self-indulgence tax" on all fast food sales and junk food grocery items.

headline: Interest in agriculture grows at CV
abstract: It was 1952, and Judy Yohn Zimmerman and other Cumberland Valley School District students were to spend a year at Camp Hill High School while their own school was built along Route 11. Even after then-modern Cumberland Valley High School opened in 1954, it was known in the midstate as a rural school for farm kids. Senior Ryan Brown said students enrolled in agricultural science classes and the school's FFA chapter have been worried about district support for their program.
