The program is short-staffed, so students sometimes wait a year or more to enroll in such courses as animal husbandry and landscaping, he said.

headline: PennDOT investigates Bartonsville billboard
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation is investigating as to whether the digital billboard at the Crossroads Travel Center in Bartonsville is legal according to PennDOT's Digital Billboard and Changeable Message Display Policy.  Neighboring Stroud Township prohibits the digital signs, but Hamilton Township where the sign is located has no ordinance addressing digital billboards.

headline: Street's corridor money draws a Council crowd
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor John Street announced that $21 million in funding would be given to help improve the commercial sections in all of the city’s 10 council districts. The money will come from a $150 million bond that was sold by the city and will be distributed to various groups for various improvements. Eight city council members were in attendance for his announcement, and Mayor Street also spoke of some of his achievements while in office.

headline: Morganelli likely to run for state attorney general
abstract: Northampton County District Attorney John Morganelli said Monday that he's laying the groundwork for his third campaign for state attorney general, and expects to make an official announcement after Labor Day. And, unlike past years, the veteran prosecutor says he expects to have Gov. Ed Rendell, a fellow Democrat, in his corner.

headline: Don't dumb down the Legislature
abstract: This editorial by State Rep Daylin Leach (D-Montgomery County) is against citizens' plans to force the legislature to shrink and adopt term limits.  It would force out talented lawmakers, is anti-democratic, and will make elections more expensive and less competitive.  The effect on constitutient service would be dramatic.

headline: Clear up taxes
abstract: The author of the letter writes that he thought that he understood the Medicare Prescription Drug Plan, but he found it was written like tax tables and was too complicated. He agrees with the income-tax increase for all individuals, because this will involve all workers, homeowners and renters.  He also agree that the older troops, with no children in the schools, should get a percentage decrease in their property taxes. He writes that PA Governor Rendell should get this going by clearing up the language and numbers so that at least a high school graduate will understand it and  we need to lower our property taxes

headline: Interim schools chief Brady backs off, but remains available
abstract: Tom Brady, interim chief executive officer of the Philadelphia School District, has heard the will of the people and won't add his name to the pool of candidates seeking the job permanently. The deadline for applying to run the 169,000-student district was yesterday. At the same time, however, Brady said he is willing to stay in the post in case the School Reform Commission cannot reach an agreement with anyone on the formal list of candidates.

headline: PennDOT official admits snow removal problems
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell is waiting for a report on how the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation performed in removing snow from major highways on February 13th and 14th.  Despite Rendell's compliments, PennDOT Secretary Allen Biehler admitted to the operation encountering some problems, specifically in Luzerne County.  He claims that PennDOT does not have a strict protocol to properly close certain sections of highways in stormy weather.

headline: Study: States should do more for cities
abstract: The Brookings Institution's "Restoring Prosperity: The State Role in Revitalizing America's Older Industrial Cities" says states could do more for their cities, PA was cited as an example, with 9 major cities listed as distressed. But director of Brookings' Metropolitan Policy Program, Bruce Katz, noted PA was in a better position because of its Governor, Ed Rendell, formerly mayor of Philadelphia. The PA League of Cities and Municipalities praised PA Department of Community and Economic Development programs posed by Rendell.

headline: Move state's primary to an earlier date
abstract: Robert Speel brings up an excellent point about changing the date of the Pennsylvania primary to an earlier date. It has been discouraging at best to see how elections are played out before the primaries even begin. The last presidential election of 2004 is a prime example. By April, Pennsylvania voters were left with very few choices. I support a decision to move the primary so that the voters in our state can be more involved in the initial stages of the voting process. The current system provides an unfair advantage to other states.

headline: Pa. Supreme Court candidates rake in some big contributions
abstract: The war chests of a number of Supreme Court candidates are growing.  The varying amounts of funding and their sources are listed.

headline: PHEAA taps Preston as interim CEO
abstract: James Preston, an executive vice president for the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency, will serve as the interim president and CEO while the agency searches for a permanent replacement. Dick Willey, PHEEA’s former CEO, resigned amidst controversy over some of his spending practices. Preston said that he is committed to cutting costs and will do his best to calm the concerns of clients and employees in light of a new federal law and negative news coverage.

headline: It was just a matter of time before Edison raised more questions
abstract: Edison Schools Inc., the nation's largest for-profit manager of schools, seems to have sewn things up rather tightly.  Or, has it?  In Aug. 1, state Auditor General Bob Casey Jr. accused the state Department of Education of improperly awarding without competitive bidding a $2.7 million contract last summer to Edison to analyze the Philadelphia School District.  Further, he said, state education officials aren't cooperating with his constitutionally mandated work.

headline: PennDOT releases grip on bridge safety ratings
abstract: PennDOT on Tuesday released inspection ratings for 54 bridges similar to the span that fell earlier this month in Minnesota. The state highway agency published information for those bridges it is examining through October but has not yet made public inspection information for all of the state's 25,300 bridges. Until last week, PennDOT had refused to release the inspection ratings, saying the public might not accurately grasp their meaning. Gov. Ed Rendell decided to make the information public after state Rep. Babette Josephs, D-Philadelphia, criticized the agency's policy.

headline: Subsidies backlash
abstract: This editorial reviews the history of the state and local government officials' misuse of Pennsylvania taxpayers' money.  It uses the money given to Volkswagen of America Inc. in the mid-1970's to create an unsuccessful car, to a Sony factory who plans to cut 75% of their jobs as well as the recent example of the millions of taxpayer money given to entice the Pittsburgh Penguins to stay within the city.  The Allegheny Institute for Public Policy cites that the two older examples total to $334 million in taxpayer subsidies to wealthy corporations.

headline: Move up state primary date
abstract: The editorial encourages lawmakers to support a bill that will advance the date of the follow year's presidential primary election to February in order to prevent Democrats and Republicans from going through the motions but actually casting meaningful votes.  The County Commissioners Association of Pennsylvania is publicly opposed to this idea as are the state school boards association because of various laws that force them to make their budget too early to determine certain costs and funding levels.  The editorial acknowledges these concerns but feel that Pennsylvanians being able to cast meaningful votes in presidential primaries to be more important.

headline: Labor council withholds mayoral backing
abstract: Labor leaders in Philadelphia have spurned US Rep Bob Brady and have refused to endorse a candidate in the mayoral election.  Brady still has the most support from local unions in the election.  Union support is discussed as well as other candidates and their level of union support.

headline: Phila. University president resigns after 22 years
abstract: James P. Gallagher has resigned after 22 years as the president of Philadelphia University as well as a member of the School District of Philadelphia's School Reform Commission.  In the latter position, he has been openly critical of this district's chief executive, Paul Vallas.    Gallagher has also served as the Pennsylvania Commission for Higher Education as well as chaired the PA State Board of Education.

headline: It's a 'dream come true' for some students
abstract: For Rachael Welsh and Sarah Marince, the Lincoln Park Performing Arts Charter School in Midland is paving the way for teens to live their dreams to become musical theater performers. The girls reflect some of the many reasons parents and students have given local superintendents for why they want the ability to choose their school. Educators have heard some students want more class choices and the flexibility to work more and graduate sooner; others say school attendance is too demanding; others have disciplinary reasons for choosing an alternative school; some have physical limitations that make charter schools an inducement over traditional public schools.

headline: PennDOT unveils $19M overhaul for Route 32
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation held a town-hall meeting in Upper Bucks County to unveil a $19 million plan to repair parts of a state road along the Delaware River that was damaged two years ago in a flood.  Local citizens such as Barbara Faure expressed frustration that the road still has not been repaired and that the year-long construction and road closures can negatively impact business.  The town hall meeting was organized by PA Representative Marguertie Quinn in response to complaints about long-running road closures in her district.

headline: Tasty gets more than crumbs to aid move
abstract: Keystone Opportunity Improvement Zone tax breaks and $2.4 million in public assistance will help Tasty Baking Co. move to a new facility at the Philadelphia Navy Yard. PA Governor Rendell said the money was necessary to help the company clean up asbestos and other toxins left behind by the Navy. The move will result in a loss of 215 jobs. Rendell predicts more people will be working at the Yard by 2010 than when it was closed by the Pentagon.

headline: Negotiations underway on the Pennsylvania budget impasse
abstract: On the sixth day of the Pennsylvanian government not having a budget in place, PA Governor Ed Rendell met with leaders in the PA Senate and the PA House of Representatives of both political parties in the offices of House Majority Leader Bill DeWeese.  No great breakthroughs were reported as Rendell is determined that the General Assembly pass his transportation proposals, health care initiatives and a statewide smoking ban before he passes the budget.  Because of the budget impasse, the Rendell administration was forced to furlough 25,000 state employees for this coming Monday.

headline: Pa. DPW threatens to end agreement with Fayette County
abstract: The state Department of Public Welfare is threatening to end its agreement with the Fayette County Mental Health/Mental Retardation agency over a property issue in related contracts.  The contract issue may cause federal funding to be tied up as well as interrupting service for residents.

headline: Philadelphia teacher reports attack by eighth-grade girl
abstract: Joseph H. Smith III, a substitute teacher at Julia de Burgos School in West Kensington, Philadelphia, reports being attacked and choked by an eighth-grade girl.  The School District of Philadelphia's spokeswoman Felecia D. Ward has stated the student has been suspended and may be expelled pending a formal investigation.  The Philadelphia Federation of Teachers Union president Ted Kirsch said that officials may seek state legislation to make it easier to remove violent students under the support of School district head Paul Vallas.

headline: Jones' voice attracts, resonates
abstract: James Earl Jones, who does the voice of Darth Vader from "Star Wars" and Mufasa from "The Lion King,"  read a short story at Northland Public Library. He drew a large crowd of parents and children, who seemed to enjoy the event; though some felt it was too short. The library’s Executive Director was pleased with the turnout and believes that stars can highlight the importance of reading.

headline: PennDOT's new hiring try spurs ire
abstract: The York County Chamber of Commerce will send a letter to Gov. Ed Rendell protesting that the state is using driver's license information - which private companies don't have - to recruit workers. Officials with PennDOT recently sent brochures to 100,000 randomly selected commercial-driver-license holders in an effort to recruit them for part-time positions that could lead to permanent employment, said Rick Kirkpatrick. The state Department of Transportation's brochures mainly targeted CDL operators in the southeastern section of the state and Pittsburgh.

headline: URA seeks state help on Market Square asbestos project
abstract: Pittsburgh’s Urban Redevelopment Authority (URA) may contribute an additional $250,000 on top of the state’s $750,000 grant towards the removal of asbestos from a downtown building that will become a YMCA. The authority’s board will also seek the approval of an employment contract for the URA’s new director and a grant for a fitness center.

headline: New Interviews and Old Stories
abstract: This article on passopenrecords.org discuss the need for strengthening the Pennsylvania state government's Open Records Law by citing an opinion-editorial piece written by Senator Dominic Pileggi that names this legislation as his top priority. It also uses Jim Parsons as an example, who tried to get a hold of travel expenses for the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency but had to pay over $70,000 in legal costs before he could.  It also reports that PA Representative Josh Shapiro is announcing legislation to reform PHEAA to introduce spending restrictions, turnover of board members every 12 years and placing the agency under the Open Records Law.

headline: Lying to your physician can be dangerous
abstract: Patients are warned not to warn to their doctors as it has been shown to cause unnecessary complications that can endanger your health.  The different reasons people have to lie to doctors are discussed, including obtaining narcotics.

headline: Pitt seeks 8.5% increase in state funding
abstract: The University of Pittsburgh reported that it will increase its tuition for the following year at 4% of the current tuition, $12,000 if the state government increases its appropriation to the school by 8.5%.  The university is seeking a total appropriation of more than $200 million.

headline: Let the teachers teach
abstract: This editorial criticizes President Bush's attempt to change education policy with his No Child Left Behind Act and the lawmakers who are attempting to reauthorize it after its expiration this year.  While the author supports having standards and accountability, the article cites Joel Packer, policy manager for the National Education Association, who claims the curriculum is narrowed as a result of teachers only teaching students to pass the government's test.  The editorial's solution is to simply give teachers the freedom to teach.

headline: Pennsylvania needs to look at N.J.'s teen-driving laws
abstract: The editorial board writes that even the most experienced driver can be distracted by the whirlwind of noise and activity inside the passenger compartment. In this kind of pressure cooker, many young, inexperienced drivers lose their cool behind the wheel. A Saturday crash in Whitehall Township that claimed the lives of two Wilson Borough teens: Shea Picht, 17, and Jessica Irizarry, 16. The details remain sketchy. The board says PA can reduce these risks by adopting a tougher provisional license for 16- and 17-years olds to reduce the number of teens killed on our roads.

headline: Wal-Mart cancels Kilbuck project
abstract: Wal-Mart recently announced that it will not attempt redevelop the land where a landslide occurred last year to build a new superstore but will submit a new land stabilization plan to the PA Department of Environmental Protection in two weeks.  The new proposal will return the land to its original state with trees and vegetation included.  Bob Keir, leader of the watchdog grouped Communities First!, started the group to oppose the plan and is very pleased that Wal-Mart has cancelled its plans to develop the 75-acre site.

headline: New leader embraces role
abstract: According to the article, PA Representative Josh Shapiro has been an important voice as the co-chair of the legislative reform commission. He gave several recommendations from the commission, which included modernizing an open records law, reforming campaign financing, making the House ethics committee more independent, and reforming spending practices. He also said that he would call for a constitutional convention in 2009 if meaningful reforms weren’t enacted by the entire legislation, and the author of the article claims he "may be onto something" by incorporating a long term approach.

headline: Bids surpass $2 million: Companies seek contracts to build Agricultural Heritage Center
abstract: Local companies are bidding to build the Franklin County Agricultural Heritage Center.  They expect to award a bid on April 26.  The building should be completed by May 2008.  Franklin County is the number two producer of milk in Pennsylvania.

headline: Pittsburgh Public Schools budget still $18M short
abstract: The Pittsburgh Public Schools board will hold a public hearing Dec. 3 on the district's 2008 preliminary budget, which is leaner than this year's budget but still leaves a deficit of nearly $18 million. The budget projects revenues of $508 million and costs of $525.9 million, which is $3.1 million less than the 2007 budget. Superintendent Mark Roosevelt said the district has reduced operating expenses by $25 million in two years. The school board will conduct several hearings on the budget before a vote scheduled for Dec. 19.

headline: Linnaeus still matters
abstract: Tricia Davies of the American Swedish Historical Museum writes that as an educator in South Philadelphia, she read with great interest the recent article on Sweden's commemoration of Carolus (Carl) Linnaeus' 300th birthday. As an official part of this international celebration, ASHM is proud to present the special exhibition "Come into a New World: Linnaeus & America," opening Feb. 15. The opening reception at 6 p.m. is free to the public and features a panel discussion on "Why Linnaeus Matters Today." The exhibition at ASHM draws attention to unexpected links between Linnaeus and the Delaware Valley.

headline: Phila. Lawmakers seek hearings on end to transfers
abstract: The PA Legislature passed a bill that will stop any further fare increases for the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority, but PA Representative Jewel Williams met with SEPTA chairman Pasquale Deon to ensure that school children will not have to pay two full fares in place of the usual 60 cent transfer fee.  Representative Shirley Kitchen still demands hearings to address the low-income citizens who rely on SEPTA transportation and will have to pay the increase in transfer prices.

headline: West Philly merchants say they are taking a financial beating from SEPTA's reconstruction of the Market-Frankford El. Where's the promised $$ help?
abstract: Elected officials - city, state and federal - have come up with more than $2.5 million to help West Philadelphia merchants impacted by the massive project. But for every dollar of relief touted in press releases and photo opportunities with big blow-up checks, only a quarter has been spent so far, as the project enters its ninth and, hopefully, final year. More than half a million dollars in federal money is available right now, and not being spent by the Philadelphia Commercial Development Corp., the nonprofit in charge of dispersing all of the money to help merchants.

headline: New speaker has a sorry voting record
abstract: Dennis O’Brien was elevated from obscurity to one of the most powerful politicians in Pennsylvania overnight. He’s a Republican from Philadelphia just like his predecessor, John M. Perzel. We also know that O’Brien has held more press conferences (at least two) in his first month in office than Perzel did in four years as speaker. We already knew O’Brien voted yes for the Legislative pay raise in July 2005. That is a Scarlet Letter for all Pennsylvania politicians, including PA Governor Rendell, who signed the pay raise into law. The columnist writes that O’Brien has also voted the wrong way on just about every major bill to come before the House in the past couple of years and the article outlines those votes.

headline: U.S. Transportation secretary backs Rendell on turnpike lease plan
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell's plan to lease the Pennsylvania Turnpike is being supported by the Bush Administration's top transportation official.  They warn that the money is not available from the federal government to support the country's aging infrastructure and that creative financing will be needed to upgrade it.

headline: Plans for city schools aired
abstract: Due to an influx of enrollment the following changes were presented to Scranton area schools. Lincoln-Jackson Elementary, South Hyde Park Avenue, would close and most of its students would be sent to Sumner Elementary, where a two-story addition would be built at the North Summer Avenue location. John Marshall Elementary, Oram Street, would close and its students would attend a new school that would hold up to 700 students. Three locations are currently being evaluated by the design team, including one in West Scranton’s Tripp Park section.  A new Whittier Elementary would be built next to the current school on Orchard Street and the old one would then be demolished. Kennedy Elementary, Prospect Avenue, would be renovated.

headline: Local educators meet on state funding study
abstract: School board representatives sat in a room at the Allegheny Intermediate Unit in Homestead last night, listening to a presentation about the costing-out report commissioned by the state Legislature, and thinking exactly the same thing. The costing-out study, released last month, determined that Pennsylvania would need to spend $4.81 billion more than it does today for all school districts to meet state standards. Those standards include 100 percent proficiency in math and reading.

headline: Phone chat and driving don't mix
abstract: The author voices his opinion that while PA State Representative Craig Dally's proposed bill to ban junior drivers from using cell phones while driving is a good idea, it doesn't go far enough.  The author feels that cell phone use is the most common and most problematic distraction on the road.  The opinion article also criticizes PA State Representative Mario Scavello and State Representative John Siptroth for not supporting a total ban on cell phone use.

headline: null
abstract: Even as MTR Gaming Group Inc. transforms its flagship casino in West Virginia into a full casino with table games, Gov. Ed Rendell's caution about seeking expanded gambling in PA is somewhat understandable. But from a purely competitive standpoint, Rendell's caution could result in a costly missed opportunity. PA's existing casinos are already falling behind some of their competitors. Pennsylvania intends to make itself a viable option in the nation's gaming industry, and it has certainly made an impact already. Pennsylvania's racinos have cut into revenues in casinos in neighboring Atlantic City, N.J., West Virginia, New York and Ontario, industry reports indicate.

headline: New wrinkles in the old legislature
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell has proposed a $27.3 billion spending plan but is expected to face a lot of opposition from Senate Republicans and will take longer due to new legislation governing the way bills are passed into law. The bills must be read on the floor on 3 separate days before they become a law, but amendments must be added on the second day so third parties have substantial time to read the legislation.  PA Representative Steve Nickol claims that while it may seem Harrisburg is changing, the culture is more or less the same it has been.

headline: Rendell teams up with Cabinet member to push toll road plan
abstract: PA governor Ed Rendell stood shoulder-to-shoulder with US Secretary of Transportation Mary Peters on the subject of leasing the Pennsylvania Turnpike.  The leasing of the huge road will fund much of the state's transportation needs.  Other plans are discussed to fund the state's transportation needs.  Tolling I-80 is suggested.

headline: Pols to follow hot issue to Ag Progress Days
abstract: Both U.S. senators from Pennsylvania will address the government day luncheon at Ag Progress Days this year, raising the political profile of the annual event that also will include an address by Gov. Ed Rendell. The three-day outdoor agricultural exposition sponsored by Penn State's College of Agricultural Sciences will run Aug. 14-16 at the Russell E. Larson Agricultural Research Center at Rock Springs, nine miles southwest of State College on state Route 45.

headline:
Local rep tackles school funding
Rep. Bev Mackereth is calling for a special commission that would develop proposals for new school-funding formulas.
abstract: Representatives Bev Mackereth and John Siptroth joined to release a resolution that calls for a special commission that would draft at least two suggestions to overhaul what many feel is an outdated school-funding formula. Fast-growing districts in particular have complained about the current system, and the proposal, along with others, will be considered by House Education Committee Chairman James Roebuck.

headline: Plan to expand automated traffic citations in Philly troublesome for whole state
abstract: The author is against a proposal for the city of Philadelphia to expand its red-light camera programs and use devices to monitor vehicles and issue automated speeding tickets. He cites numerous examples for why the idea is unfair and won't improve safety at all.. He doesn’t believe that these devices will change drivers’ behavior and feels that it would be taking away from more just, less hypocritical programs that could improve traffic safety.

headline: $11 million only goes so far If big-ticket projects get big chunk of gaming revenue, what's left for others
abstract: Erie International Airport's runway extension project could move forward via a multimillion-dollar infusion of county gaming revenues. So could the county's plans to establish a community college. But some local officials want to make sure those two high-profile projects don't eat up too much of the $11 million in yearly slots revenues the county will receive from Presque Isle Downs & Casino.

headline: NHL | Rendell: Pens have good offer to stay
abstract: PA Governor Rendell says the arena deal that state, city and county officials are putting together for the Pittsburgh Penguins is the best offered to any National Hockey League team in recent years.  Rendell stayed in Pittsburgh overnight after meeting with Penguins officials and local politicians. No deal was struck, but a Rendell aide, Chuck Ardo, said he expected the deal to be completed in the next few weeks

headline: Off-duty fee for security riles Pittsburgh businesses
abstract: Local businesses who use off-duty officers as security for their properties are outraged by a new fee imposed by the city.  The fee is $3.85/hr for each officer.  The charge will net $400,000 for the city.  The city claims that the use of the off-duty officers can cost the city in unexpected ways such as lawsuits.

headline: Private firm hired to run school for disruptive students
abstract: The Pittsburgh school board voted 7-2 last night to bring in a Nashville company to open a school for disruptive students, hoping to address what Superintendent Mark Roosevelt has called the district's most pressing problem.  Community Education Partners, headed by former Tennessee GOP chairman Randle Richardson, will open the 432-student school next fall. Mr. Roosevelt proposed the six-year contract with CEP, saying disruptive students are a district wide impediment to academic improvement. The district hopes to get a $2 million state grant each year to help cover the cost. The district will pay CEP about $5.7 million a year to operate the school in the former Clayton Elementary building in Perry South.

headline: Many of these buildings retain value for educational purposes
abstract: This editorial explains how many very old school buildings are being left vacant or being torn down to make way for school megaplexes with the exception being Lebanon County, where six pre-1930 schools are still being used.  The author agrees with the work of the PA Historical and Museum Commission as they catalog old school buildings to highlight their historical values to communities.  The author also feels that renovation of these buildings is many times more viable than tearing them down.

headline: Planners give JARI project green light
abstract: Plans for the Phase II expansion of the Johnstown Area Regional Industries Business Park moved ahead as the Richland Township Planning Commission recommended that supervisors approve the project. Linda Thomson, head of Johnstown Area Regional Industries, breathed a sigh of relief as the commission recommended the six separate measures needed for the expansion to proceed. She and her staff have invested about four years in the Oakridge Drive project. The only concern raised by the commission dealt with road access.

headline: ... as casinos create jobs and funds for tax relief
abstract: It has now been one year since the first slot machine casino opened at Mohegan Downs in Wilkes-Barre. Since that historic occasion, this new industry has begun to deliver significant tax revenues and jobs, all of which will continue to increase in the months and years to come. Just this month, Gov. Edward G. Rendell announced that revenue from slots gaming helped provided property tax relief to over a half million Pennsylvania seniors under the Property Tax/Rent Rebate Program.

headline: No kiss-offs after Valentine's snafu
abstract: John Baer expresses opinion that the failed response to the storm on Valentine's Day should result in PA Governor Ed Rendell firing the department heads of the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation, the state police, and the Pennsylvania Emergency Management Authority.  He also criticizes the possibility of creating another government office and wasting money on consultants to assess the failing situation.

headline: Daily News/Keystone Poll: Brady up, Fattah down, but it's still anybody's race
abstract: Tom Knox has pulled into the lead in the Philadelphia mayoral race with US Rep Bob Brady, and US Rep Chaka Fattah are battling for second.  21 percent of voters remain undecided.  Former city Councilman Michael Nutter polled at 12 percent.

headline:
Reform the scandal-ridden PHEAA
The Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency needs a top-to-bottom overhaul
abstract: Ken Schaefer is displeased with the spending practices of the PA Higher Education Assistance Agency, and he believes that the agency should not only have forced out former CEO Dick Willey but should make him pay back some of the excessive bonuses he issued, lavish spending, and money he spent to cover up his actions. Schaefer also holds the board accountable and believes they should examine payments to lobbyists, require public disclosure of payments for outside services, require all providers of goods and services to compete for business and review the justification for the existence of three affiliated foundations. In addition, he believes the board should investigate its structure and purpose.

headline: Many schools no longer follow president's fitness standards
abstract: Laurie Shoemaker, a physical education teacher in the Easton School District, is considering dropping the standards of the President's Physical Fitness Test as childhood obesity is increasing throughout the country.  Shoemaker claims the standards are not based on any form of research and is considering switching to the Physical Best, a program that allows the children to pick their own goals.  Christine Spain, spokeswoman for the President's Council of Physical Fitness, reports that the fitness program has been modernized and still has plenty of positive aspects.

headline: Poll of Pa. voters supports plan to lease turnpike
abstract: A recent poll by Quinnipiac University of registered voters in Pennsylvania reported that they were in favor of a lease of the turnpike to a private investor by a 49-to-41 percent margin.  This opposed another recent poll by AAA, the automobile club, that found support for not privatizing the Pennsylvania Turnpike.  PA Governor Ed Rendell has proposed that the state privatize the turnpike while maintaining control of toll increase and maintenance schedules while using the $12 billion for road repairs and bridge construction.

headline: 2 events at casino site, one violent, one calm
abstract: Ed Verrall of Casino-Free Philadelphia has filed assault charges against Fishtown Action co-founder Donna Tomlinson after he screamed obscenities at her and pushed a female friend of hers at a picnic scheduled by her group and SugarHouse Casino supporting the project.  Philadelphia Police Department's Civil Affairs Unit was there to keep peace, and Lieutenant Frank Vanore has reported that detectives are investigating the assault complaint from Verrall.  Groups against the SugarHouse Casino are asking PA Attorney General Tom Corbett to acquire a court order to halt the casinos until the PA Department of Environmental Protection studies the impact of casinos on the environment.

headline: 'No' on Saylor
abstract: The author feels that Pennsylvania’s Supreme Court Justices ignored the PA Constitution by allowing legislators to give themselves lavish benefits. He believes the justices have not upheld the constitution on several occasions. In particular, he is displeased with Justice Tom Saylor and urges voters not to vote for him in the upcoming election.

headline: State seeks volunteers for future disaster duty
abstract: The state is joining a national registry of volunteeers ready if the need should arise in a crisis.  The state is looking for those that believe they have a service or skill that could be provided to those in need.  While the focus of the drive is to get health care professionals signed up, many states have broadened their efforts to include many different types of volunteers.

headline: Rendell knocks size of PHEAA bonuses, payroll
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell state a letter to the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency that criticized the size of the staff and extravagant spending on lavish bonuses and retreats.  Rendell cited the example of Dick Willey, who received a $181,000 bonus this year, which could have paid 35 students full tuition at a state-owned university.  Keith New, a spokesman for PHEAA claims Rendell is repeating old news from years before, but Rendell is still considering privatizing the agency to make it more efficient.

headline:
More teachers needed for Phila. schools
The district has 112 openings - 40 more than it did this time last year.
abstract: It is already seven weeks into the school year, and the Philadelphia School District still has 112 teaching vacancies. The Philadelphia Federation of Teachers says that thousands of students’ educations are being hindered, and it blames the district for trying to save money. District officials have denied these allegations and claim that teacher resignations and a decision by the School Reform Commission to add 130 teaching positions can explain why vacancies remain.

headline: Port Authority hearings scheduled
abstract: The first two public hearings on the Pittsburgh Port Authority's proposed service cuts and fare increases will be held today. The article gives the dates and places of the hearings.

headline: 6210. Rendell administration overrules consultant, blocks state police
abstract: This blog disagrees with PA Governor Ed Rendell and his administration's decision to allow the PA Gaming Control Board to issue casino licenses without criminal background checks and to block the state police from attempting any investigations on the matter.  The PA Department of Revenue hired Spectrum Gaming Group to write a blueprint for gaming within the state but fired the company after they recommended that the PA State Police control investigations.  The blog claims the result being that the state has awarded hundreds of licenses to casino owners without knowing any of the legal backgrounds of these businessmen.

headline: No second fiddle
abstract: Rendell for veep? Not likely. Gov. Ed Rendell is smart, charismatic and politically connected: just the kind of guy a president would want alongside him in the White House, right? Nope, says political analyst G. Terry Madonna. Mr. Rendell plays second fiddle to no one.

headline: RCN Corp. will lay off about 300 employees
abstract: 300 employees will lose their jobs at a call center in Plains Township.  The financial condition and recent struggles of RCN Corp are discussed.

headline: Responsibility
abstract: The editorial addresses the need for the PA Legislature and PA Governor Ed Rendell to act on the manner in which charter schools are funded, specifically the Lincoln Park Performing Arts Charter School.  The author disagrees neighboring school districts paying for their own students in the 4-year-old kindergarten at Lincoln Park despite not offering the same programs in their own districts.  It goes on to say that as charter schools are products of the state, the state should incur all the costs associated with their operation.

headline: N. Allegheny's Woten named state's Teacher of the Year
abstract: Governor Rendell selected David Woten, a North Allegheny middle school music teacher, as Pennsylvania’s 2008 Teacher of the Year. Southwestern PA had several finalists for the award, and it was the second year in a row that a teacher from Pittsburgh’s northern suburbs won. Mr. Woten, who has increased student participation in his elective course during his 16 year teaching career,  will represent the state for the National Teacher of the Year award.

headline: Port Authority seeks to lease park-n-ride lot
abstract: The Port Authority is giving up 28 acres to retail development, including its lighted park-n-ride lot behind Sheetz in the 9000 block of University Boulevard in Moon. Commuters who use the 600-space lot weekdays and ride the Route 28K Moon Express bus into Downtown and to Oakland will be relocated nearby to property controlled by the Allegheny Airport Authority. In exchange, the transit agency is to receive a long-term stream of income from leasing the park-n-ride property to a private developer, which plans "some type of retail, something like a strip mall," Port Authority Chief Executive Officer Steve Bland said.

headline: A champ is a champ: Barbaro's courageous battle comes to an end
abstract: Last May, Barbaro's dominance in winning the Kentucky Derby had horse racing enthusiasts making comparisons to the immortals of the track. Barbaro endured a number of surgeries, including the insertion of 27 screws to put his right hind leg back together and later the removal of 80 percent of his left rear hoof because of a painful condition called laminitis. Dr. Dean Richardson in Kennett Square, Pa., tried to relieve pressure on the right hind leg with another operation involving a plate, bars and screws. The editorial board expresses their remorse for the death or Barbaro and calls him a champ.

headline: None-of-the-above for mayor
abstract: Members of Pittsburgh's 14th Ward Independent Democratic Club are refusing to endorse Mayor Ravenstahl even though he is running unopposed. They support Mr. Lamb for controller and Rev. Burgess for council.

headline: New report predicts increased poverty, hunger, displacement of millions as temperatures rise
abstract: The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change projects worsening conditions for millions as temperatures rise on the planet.  Strong language was used in the report by the agency which is expected to be presented tomorrow in Brussels.  The editorial calls for increased political action in the face of the scientific findings.

headline: Right track
abstract: The PA State Education Association and the PA School Boards Association support legislation which requires the state to fund cyberschools and limit tuition charges. The bill is sponsored by Rep. Karen Beyer. The PA Department of Education would disburse funding and limit tuition to between $3,000 and $5,000. Tuition is currently limited to 75 percent of the cost of public schools per pupil, which varies statewide. Editors believe the state, not local property owners, should subsidize cyber charter schools.

headline: Nearly half of WSHS students stay home
abstract: Nearly half of West Scranton High’s students were absent from school amid rumors that a student was going to carry out an attack similar to Columbine. A male student was suspended and will likely be expelled; though there is no evidence that he had a "his list," which had been reported. School officials have used several measures to reassure parents and students that the school is safe, and attendance is expected to return to normal levels next week.

headline: Possible Amtrak strike is delayed
abstract: Forestalling a possible strike by Amtrak workers, President Bush yesterday created a five-member "presidential emergency board" to investigate the labor dispute between the passenger railroad and employees who have been without a contract for nearly eight years. Bush's action pushes back the start of any strike until at least Jan. 31. The president did not immediately announce the names of the board members. A strike, which would be the first by Amtrak workers, would also disrupt commuter railroads, including SEPTA and NJ Transit, which operate some of their trains on Amtrak tracks and rely on Amtrak dispatchers.

headline: A Majestic beginning on the North Shore
abstract: Majestic Star Casino owner Don Barden couldn't wait to make good on his promise to build a slice of the Las Vegas strip on the North Shore. The kickoff to what Barden has called the $450 million "flagship" of his six-casino empire received star treatment. Despite the pomp of the groundbreaking, Barden said last-minute attempts by the Pittsburgh Riverlife Task Force and Civic Design Coalition to delay the casino's construction overshadowed the day.

headline: Not on Ed’s ‘short list’
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell said he is not considering former PA Representative Gibson C. Armstrong for a position on the PA Public Utility Commission. Republican sources in Harrisburg said Armstrong’s name was on the governor’s "short list" for an open PUC commissioner post, but Rendell said that’s not the case. Rendell said Senate Republicans may nominate their own candidate for the post, but he hasn’t picked anyone yet.

headline: Hill leaders issue arena demands
abstract: Local business leaders want $10,000,000 for local redevelopment and guaranteed jobs for minorities as a part of a plan to build the NHL's  Pittsburgh Penguins a new venue.  Local leaders presented a plan to city leaders as a means to start negotiations.

headline: Safety factor
abstract: Editors believe the incident involving a high school math teacher who confiscated a student's iPod and was assaulted by two students for doing so. A judge sentenced one to a private reform school, but placed the other with the state, saying he was too dangerous for a private reform school. Editors do not understand how a student too dangerous for reform school was placed in private school.

headline: Nevels Resigns as SRC Chairman
abstract: Jim Nevels, the first and only chairman of the Philadelphia School District's School Reform Commission, announced Friday he will leave the board this fall. Nevels will leave a legacy of unprecedented academic achievement in the Philadelphia school system. Test scores in reading and math rose from average district proficiency levels in the teens when he arrived in 2001 to above 40 percent as he leaves.

headline: Prepare now for tolls' effect on Poconos
abstract: The author of the editorial claims that the newspaper has always opposed the proposal to toll Interstate 80 because it would divert a lot of traffic to inadequate local roads. However, the PA General Assembly approved the plan, and it has been submitted to the Federal Highway Administration for approval. In the author's opinion, there are a number of problematic questions that need to be addressed if the plan is approved, which should begin being considered now.

headline: Agency overreaches in effort to license online auctioneers
abstract: The move by the state Board of Auctioneer Examiners to compel online sellers -- those engaged in selling other people's wares -- to obtain an auctioneer's license is a classic case of mindless bureaucratic creep. But PA is by no means alone in this. The normal impulse of government, it seems, is to license and tax anything that might prove to be a fruitful source of revenue. It is driven to some extent by those individuals and enterprises that view the upstarts as competitors, and a possible drain on their own revenue. The Internet has allowed the development of a true "cottage industry" of people selling from their homes precisely because doing so is simple, easy and not constricted by the long arm of government regulation.

headline: Nutter looks at strategies for governing
abstract: Philadelphia Democratic mayoral candidate Michael Nutter traveled to Baltimore and has planned trips to other cities in the future to gain new ideas about how to govern a large city.  Nutter is considered by many to have an easy victory in the election as a Republican has not won the election in over 60 years.  The author compared Nutter's unassuming position to Ed Rendell's when Rendell was in his position and distinguished him the blatant Wilson Goode, who after winning the Democratic primary blatantly flaunted his easy victory.

headline: North Shore casino predicts smooth traffic
abstract: Traffic concerns are discussed as a new casino opens in Pittsburgh.  Officials say that traffic won't be a concern outside of rush hour and special events happening at nearby stadiums.  They say that the casino's nature allows for traffic to be spread out through the day.

headline: School districts paying for superintendents long after they have left
abstract: PA school superintendents will cost taxpayers millions when they leave their jobs because of contracts that include payment for unused sick days and free health care in retirement. An analysis of 447 contracts statewide shows that school boards promise superintendents compensation beyond publicly disclosed salaries, and that many costs occur after the superintendents leave, retire or die, the Altoona Mirror reported. PA school districts are not allowed to contract with a superintendent for more than five years, but there are no limits on payment or the method of compensation.

headline: No Child Left Behind law seen as losing favor
abstract: Parents and educators, including interim superintendent Dr. James Gilmartin, oppose the No Child Left Behind mandated testing. The tests are used to measure whether public schools are performing adequately. Dr. Paul Eaken, superintendent of the Fleetwood school district however, cautioned against significantly revised the law, but noted it cannot be used to accurately measure all students' knowledge.

headline: Privatization, not tolls, is the best route for roads
abstract:
Gov. Rendell recently proposed converting Interstate 80 into a toll road to raise money.
The author urges you to speak out against and work hard to defeat Gov. Rendell's ridiculous plan to add tolls to Interstate 80. This is a tax on everything we eat, drink, wear or burn, as every good consumed in this economy comes by truck. Transit will never succeed as long as it is government- run.

headline: Amounts being dropped in slot machines put tax-reduction picture in new light
abstract: Taxpayers ought to start paying attention to how much is being spent at slots casinos across the state. So far, six of the 14 planned casinos are open to gamblers. The amount of money being plunked into the slot machines, and what's being reported as gross revenue, are stunning. It has been a year since the first casino opened at Pocono Downs near Wilkes-Barre. Ever since, PA property owners have been wondering when they'd see the school property tax relief that slots gambling was supposed to provide. Gov. Ed Rendell said property owners would start getting that relief next year.

headline: Nutter's pitch for jobs brings 1,000 resumes
abstract: As of early Monday, more than 1,000 job seekers had forwarded resumes to Philadelphia Mayor-elect Michael Nutter, responding to a pitch he made last week encouraging young professionals and private-sector employees to join his administration in January. As mayor, he will have hiring power over several hundred civil-service-exempt positions.

headline: State police need to make a priority of probe to find out why trooper wasn't dispatched
abstract: This editorial calls for an investigation as to why a trooper wasn't properly dispatched when a Pennsylvania mother called to help her daughter being beaten by her boyfriend.

headline:
School study results called false
Erie district finds flaws in findings about Central Tech
abstract: A study was done for the Associated Press that cited Central Career and Technical School as one of 1,700 schools throughout the country that graduate less than 60 percent of its students. However, Erie School District officials are upset because they believe the high school achieved state graduation targets, and they blame the findings on poorly conducted research. The study only compared enrollment numbers from the freshman class to the numbers of seniors who graduate four years later, which school officials feel is unfair because it doesn’t account for students who leave to enroll at other high schools or students who graduate late.

headline:
No Child Left Behind
An upgrade
abstract: The author of the editorial believes that the No Child Left Behind Act, which will expire this year, isn’t perfect but has done a lot of good for the country’s education system. In particular, the author believes that an important part of the law is holding educators accountable and providing equal opportunities for all students. In the opinion of the author, the law should be renewed, however, some corrections are necessary, including increased funding and other measures.

headline: Public and private funds were always eyed for cargo airport, says Eachus
abstract: PA Representative Todd Eachus has thwarted the misconception that only private money would be involved with the proposed cargo airport in Luzerne County by reporting that the airport would be a combination of private and public funding.  PA Senator Ray Musto removed the $16.5 million for 30 years of public funding for the airport from the gaming capital budget because he feels there are too many questions to be answered about the project.  Eachus, however, still claims that he only looks for a state guarantee of $250 million worth of bonds paid for with gaming revenue.

headline: Anderson
abstract: Opinion by Eileen Anderson about at a hearing held by acting state insurance commissioner Joel Ario. Testimony was given by small business owners about difficulties encountered in maintaining health insurance coverage for employees. One of the problems small businesses face is medical underwriting. We should prohibit medical underwriting as a rating tool for small businesses. Medical underwriting is the tool used by for-profit insurers to evaluate employee's personal health histories and set insurance rates for small employers. PA is one of just two states that still allow insurers to increase small employers' premiums by unlimited amounts based on one employee's health history.

headline: Obama gets star treatment at Phila. Fund-raising trip
abstract: Democratic candidate for President Barack Obama campaigned in Philadelphia, hoping to net $500,000 in contributions. Obama denounced the war in Iraq as well as President Bush. Obama also met privately with the winner of the Democratic mayoral primary, Michael Nutter. Obama had endorsed US Rep. Chaka Fattah for president. Obama's overall PA contributions trail candidates Hillary Clinton and Joseph Biden.

headline: Strawberry Square to house university
abstract: Strawberry Square will become the new, though temporary, home of Harrisburg University of Science and Technology under a lease agreement announced yesterday.  The need for more space comes as the university awaits the completion of its new 16 story academic tower.

headline: Schools make grade in national rankings
abstract: A few midstate schools have earned a spot on a national magazine's honor roll. Hershey and Camp Hill high schools finished in the top 500 of more than 18,700 public schools ranked by U.S. News &World Report for its America's Best High Schools report, which hit newsstands Tuesday. Both earned a silver award. Cumberland Valley High School finished in the top 1,600, earning a bronze.

headline: No free ride for suburban students
abstract: Parents are speaking out saying that suburban families who must foot the bill for transportation to city schools should get the same TransPass that city dwellers get, since the passes are paid for mostly by state tax funds. The money isn't coming from property taxes but PA taxpayer money. Last August, Gov. Ed Rendell and state Sen. Vincent Fumo unveiled a new program to get Philadelphia middle and high school students to school for free. Until this year, Philadelphia was the only school district in the state that did not provide free transportation to students who live far from school, according to the governor's office.

headline: Public meeting Mon. on I-80 tolls
abstract: The Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission brings a traveling public meeting about tolling Interstate 80 to the Poconos. The meetings were advertised as a way to provide information and receive community input about the conversion of I-80 to a toll road. In July, PA lawmakers approved putting as many as 10 toll booths on I-80 and agreed to accelerate a toll increase on the Pennsylvania Turnpike. Tolling I-80 has been offered as an alternative to privatizing the turnpike. The plan, Act 44, would raise money for highway and bridge maintenance for the next 50 years. The money raised will not be used for mass transit.

headline: Another reason provided for ending the LCB
abstract: The author of the letter writes it was an obvious move to discredit Jonathan Newman, former chairman of the PA Liquor Control Board, the Inquirer Jan. 26 informed us about the members of the Liquor Control Board traveling lavishly on the backs of the taxpayers. In most cases their trips were to negotiate a purchase price for wine either already cheaper in other states or, as previously disclosed in The Inquirer, created for PA to look as if it were specially priced. Though we do not need additional justification to end this archaic, political and anti-competitive system in our state, we should be thankful to the PA LCB for giving us just one more.

headline: Official tries to explain voting-machine reasoning
abstract: The state government still wants to establish a paper trail for the state's touch-screen voting machines, Commonwealth Secretary Pedro Cortes said. But the paper-trail options that the state has reviewed could compromise voter privacy, Cortes told a lunch group at the Nittany Lion Inn. The printers that could be attached to the touch-screen machines, he said, would print votes in chronological order. And if those results were compared to chronological logs of voter signatures, Cortes said, each voter's choices could be identified. Under the federal Help America Vote Act of 2002, Pennsylvania was compelled to drop its punch-card and lever voting systems and adopt newer technology.

headline: Phipps to grow a 'green' parking lot out of recycled plastic
abstract: A new type of recycled plastic pavement is being used to convert a green space to an environmentally friendly parking space.  The pavement allows grass to grow beneath it.

headline:
State vows no repeat of winter I-78 fiasco
Better communication, more workers, faster snow removal are part of plan to avoid another botched snowstorm response.
abstract: An independent report blamed PennDOT, the PA Emergency Management Agency and PA State Police for the poor Valentine’s Day snowstorm response that stranded motorists for hours and closed parts of Interstates 78, 80 and 81. Transportation Secretary Allen Biehler said that PennDOT has learned from the experience, and he announced a number of changes that would be implemented, including posting more traffic condition signs, ensuring faster snow removal at certain spots and getting more tow trucks to remove stranded vehicles. The PA Emergency Management Agency and State Police also announced changes to prevent a similar event from occurring.

headline: No laughing matter
abstract: The Beaver County Times expresses concern over the future of the children in the Duquesne City School District, where enrollment and funding is spiraling downward.  The PA Education Secretary Gerald Zahorchak sought to move 200 of the Duquesne High School students to neighboring districts only for the legislation to be passed in the PA Senate and shot down in the PA House of Representatives.  As the editorial reports that similar situations are taking place in Alquippa, Clairton, Farrell, Monessen and Wilkinsburg Counties, it encourages urgency in the state government to pass legislation to solve these problems before school starts in 2 months.

headline: Rendell aide returns to work following investigation of crash
abstract: Norman Bristol-Colon, executive director of the Governor's Advisory Commission on Latino Affairs, has returned to his job under PA Governor Ed Rendell after being on paid suspension for 2 months.  Bristol-Colon was suspended for allowing a non-state employee, Adriana Malpica, drive a state vehicle after she crashed into a highway sign and a parked truck.

headline: Anti-casino movement: Wins, cash & questions
abstract: Casino-Free Philadelphia was able to get a referendum on the May 15 primary ballot asking whether or not casinos could be allowed along the Delaware River waterfront and then was able to influence City Solicitor Romulo Diaz that he was not able to remove that referendum.  Jethro Heiko, one of the group's founders, reports they have raised $30,000 while not taking money from corporations, law firms, or other casinos.  The non-profit group has been using The Gandhian Foundation to takes it donations so they can be considered tax-deductible.

headline: Official, unofficial vote counts overlap
abstract: In the latest twist in Lackawanna County’s star-crossed general election, officials started hand-counting 2,000 absentee ballots after the ballots could not be read by optical scan machines the county leased to do the job. It means the unofficial count will spill over into today, overlapping with the official count. The official count will get under way this morning at 9 at the Voter Registration Office on Jefferson Avenue. Most of the attention will be on the Mayfield Borough Council and North Pocono School Board races, where large numbers of still uncounted write-in votes could sway the outcome.

headline: Secretary Calamity
abstract: .The editorial slams the idea of PA Governor Ed Rendell serving in any capacity at the federal level terming his tenure as PA Governor "disastrous."  The editorial finds the Governor unfit for vice presidential duty as well.

headline: State-of-the-county talk centers on transit
abstract: Allegheny County requires major surgery if the system is to survive. That was the gist of comments made by county Chief Executive Dan Onorato, who used his annual state-of-the-county address to restate the problems and proposed remedy facing the debt-plagued Port Authority. On Jan. 3, 2007, Onorato and Port Authority officials, hoping to gain state help and stave off a projected $80 million budget deficit, proposed cutting the authority's bus and T light-rail service by 25 percent, increasing base fares by as much as 75 cents, and eliminating 400 union and managerial jobs.

headline: No new proposals at contract meeting
abstract: No new proposals were made at the recent negotiation meetings between the Downingtown Area School District School Board negotiating team and the Downingtown Area Education Association. Dr. Alice Johnson, school board president on the negotiating team, said Wednesday positive discussion occurred at the meetings held Nov. 1 and 6. Johnson said two more meetings have been set for Nov. 19 and 27.

headline: Rendell aide suspended over state-vehicle crash
abstract: The executive director of PA Governor Ed Rendell's Advisory Commission on Latino Affairs, Norman Bristol-Colon, was suspended with pay Friday after his supervisors learned of the crash of his state-issued vehicle just after midnight on December 20, 2007.  Bristol-Colon was a passenger in car when it veered off Interstate 283 near Elizabethtown, struck a highway sign and crashed into a parked tractor-trailer. The driver, Adriana Malpica, told police she had two drinks at a Harrisburg nightclub earlier in the evening and may have fallen asleep at the wheel. Malpica, who is not a state employee, was not allowed to be driving the state-owned vehicle.

headline: Atlantic City gaming revenue falls 10.6 percent in September
abstract: Atlantic City gaming revenue suffered its worst drop of the year, which can largely be explained by competition from Pennsylvania’s newly opened casinos.

headline: Open records legislation to governor by Wednesday
abstract: House Majority Leader Bill DeWeese said that he wants to send Gov. Ed Rendell a bill next that would give Pennsylvania residents more access to government documents. DeWeese, a Greene County Democrat who represents part of Fayette County, announced that goal after a clash between Republicans and Democrats during a House Appropriations Committee meeting. The dispute occurred over the Democrats’ new procedural strategy of placing open-records legislation on a fast track to a full House vote. The Appropriations Committee, in a party-line vote, agreed to send a state Senate version of the open-records legislation to the House floor.

headline: Report: Snowstorm caught Pa. off guard
abstract: Disaster response is discussed with former PA Governor Mark Schweiker in light of the recent     struggle Harrisburg had with winter weather.  An independent report showed that the state was caught off guard with the disaster in the state's northern tier that left motorists freezing and stranded for nearly a day.

headline: States are urged to require helmets
abstract: The National Transportation Safety Board has formally recommended that states require motorcyclists to wear helmets to prevent a motorcycle death.  Pennsylvania's helmet law was repealed in 2003, but the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation has reported that since this time, average annual motorcycle fatalities has risen to 183.  PA Governor Ed Rendell's office plans to study these recommendations but still maintains that riders should have their own choice to wear helmets.

headline: Online schools offer one-to-one advantage
abstract: Parents and teachers know that, like fingerprints, no one child is the same. It is why they are increasingly looking for more public education options and new ways to serve kids. One of the most innovative education models that emerged in the past decade are online public schools. Demand for online learning is skyrocketing across the country and enrollment in online public schools is among the fastest growing trends in education today. The Peak Group research firm estimated one million enrollments in K-12 online learning in 2007.

headline: Rendell claims Turnpike plan would protect capital projects
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell, in response to claims by head of the PA Turnpike Commission Joseph Brimmeier, said projects in the toll road's 10 year capital plan would be completed even if the road is privately leased, a plan legislators oppose. Rendell accused Turnpike officials of trying to scare the public. He noted that 2004 toll hikes would continue to go for capital improvements. PA Rep. Joe Markosek proposes phasing out the current commission in favor of legislative and gubernatorial appointees.

headline: Barden's casino was the 'best fit' for city, state
abstract: Businessman Don Barden won over the PA Gaming Control Board with a casino proposal that represented the "best fit" for Pittsburgh and a personal charisma that spoke volumes about his dedication to the project. In a 73-page opinion released, the gaming board said Mr. Barden and his company, PITG Gaming LLC, ended up winning the Pittsburgh slot machine license because his North Shore casino proved to be the "best overall project" for the city and the state. At the same time, the board said one of his competitors, Forest City Enterprises, was hurt by traffic concerns at its Station Square site.

headline: Open records reform scheduled for Wednesday vote
abstract: The House State Government Committee will be considering reform to make its records more open to the public, which is supported by the committee’s chairwoman, Babette Josephs and Senator Jim Ferlo.

headline: Freshmen legislators find House different than expected
abstract: Newcomers to Harrisburg are surprised to learn the realities of their jobs and the patience needed to be successful in Harrisburg.  Finding that they have to work within a 202-person body has proven to be a big adjustment for some.

headline: State's rural stretches carrying the banner against I-80 toll plan
abstract: Two US Republican Congressman, Phil English and John Peterson, are receiving compliments from the rural residents near highway I-80 for attempting to include a clause in a federal transportation bill that will stop the attempt to toll the interstate highway.  These tolls are part of a plan by PA Governor Ed Rendell to raise $950 million each year for 10 years to improve bridges, roads and public mass transit.  Peterson has received many calls since the measure passed in the PA Legislature and feels the tolling is a way for rural residents to pay for failing transit systems such as Southeastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority and roads in urban areas.

headline: Pa. falls way short on funding schools
abstract: Pennsylvania is woefully underfunding its schools if it hopes to meet state education standards, according to a state "costing-out" study. To enable students to reach 100 percent proficiency on reading and math, as well as master other academic standards, state and local governments would need to spend about $4.81 billion per year more on education than they do today, the study concluded. The state and school districts spent an average of about $9,512 per student during the 2005-06 school year, the most recent year for which the state has data. To meet state standards, they should have been spending an average of $12,057, according to the report. Of the state's 501 school districts, 474 spent less than the report estimates is required to meet state standards.

headline: Rendell pushes for more highway, transit money
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell has expressed his frustration with the slow pace of the PA Legislature in passing his transportation, health care, and energy initiatives.  Rendell's solution for mass transit funding is leasing the Pennsylvania Turnpike and increasing taxes on oil companies' profits but has not been overly popular with lawmakers.  A law firm, Drinker Biddle & Reath LLP, has claimed that a provision in the transportation bill, which prevents companies from passing costs of the tax to consumers, violates the commerce clause of the US Constitution.

headline: Beer buying should be easier to do
abstract: The author of the editorial is pleased with a bill that’s cosponsored by Representatives John Rafferty Jr. and Sean Logan that will loosen up restrictions on purchasing beer in PA. The author believes that old liquor laws are out of date, so the bill will pass, which should allow consumers more options and improve sales for PA breweries.

headline: 'Open-records lite' moves forward, lacks real means of enforcement
abstract: This could be the week that the General Assembly finally updates the state's ''keep-'em-in-the-dark'' open records law. The question is whether state lawmakers will actually approve meaningful reform that gives Pennsylvanians the power to learn about all their governments, from top to bottom. Last week, the Senate overwhelmingly passed Senate Bill 1. The House proposal, HB 2072, at least includes the General Assembly under what's known as the ''flip of presumption.'' Citizens would no longer have to prove that they have a right to access public records, although there are certain exemptions.

headline: Managing decline
abstract: New Orleans was the only metropolitan area to lose more population than Pittsburgh between 2000 and 2006.  Reasons for this are discussed.  Not all can be blamed on the state as a whole.

headline: Street leads call for transit funds
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Street led a rally of labor and management, businesses, and neighboring mayors to call attention to the need for public transit funding from the PA Legislature. The South Eastern PA Transit Authority, Street says, faces a 30 percent rate increase with a 20 decrease in service. It needs $129 million from the state to avoid a deficit. Street also advocates a dedicated funding mechanism for public transportation. President of the Philadelphia Chamber of Commerce Mark Schweiker and Pat Eiding, president of the Philadelphia Council AFL-CIO, were on hand for the rally.

headline: Pa. school kids like 'mystery fat'
abstract: And the kids in the Plum Borough School District have been eating "a mystery fat" and liking it. The secret ingredient is a plant-based fat substitute called Z Trim. It's been in the school's popular ranch dressing for months, quietly reducing the fat and calories students are getting when they load up their salads and chicken with it. The Plum Borough district in suburban Pittsburgh is believed to be the first school district in the country to use the fat substitute. School officials say the dressing's flavor is preserved, even though fat and calories are cut. Z Trim, which has no fat, is made from the hulls of corn, oats, soy, rice and barley. It was developed by a scientists at a U.S. Department of Agriculture lab in Illinois in the mid-1990s.

headline: Rendell refused Biehler's resignation over handling of Valentine's Day ice storm
abstract: State Transportation Secretary Allen Biehler said he offered his resignation to Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell after the February ice storm that left hundreds of motorists stranded on interstate highways, but Rendell refused the offer. Rendell's office hired a consulting firm run by former Federal Emergency Management Agency Director James Lee Witt, which issued a preliminary report March 27 blaming Pennsylvania Department of Transportation, state police and the Pennsylvania Emergency Management Agency.

headline: Belfanti bill would allow nonprofits to run poker games
abstract: State Representative Robert Belfanti Jr. is co-sponsoring a bill that would allow nonprofit organizations such as fire departments and veterans organization to use card games to raise money. Currently, these organizations are allowed to hold raffles or use other small games of chance, however, Belfanti believes this new law will provide them a better opportunity to raise their limited incomes.

headline: Our craving for 'realness'
abstract: Opinion on which politicians have authenticity. It takes discipline. Authentic leaders know who they are. They are comfortable in their own skin. Their own quiet, practiced belief in themselves is what moves them to inspire others. And they do that by first spending lots of time really listening to the people they hope to inspire. In a world full of cowards, genuine leaders are called on to chart new paths, take risks and even show a bit of old-fashioned courage now and then.

headline: Tests show no apparent threat
abstract: A cancer cluster amongst former college students has prompted testing to be done on a site near some off-campus housing.  Recent testing, however has not shown anything out of the ordinary.  Authorities say the investigation is worth the effort, but the whole thing may just be a coincidence.

headline: Supervisors turn to PennDOT to study stretch of Route
abstract: PennDOT will review a two mile section of Route 61 and look into a number of safety measures, including the placement of concrete road barriers. A woman died there in April, but according to PennDOT’s current evaluation system, it would be considered a low priority; though other factors could change this. A local project manager was pleased with the response and hopes that future lives can be saved with new safety measures.

headline: Pa. student-loan agency board hires interim CEO
abstract: James Preston, a current employee of the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency, was selected to become the interim CEO and president while the board searches for a replacement for Dick Willey, who resigned due to controversial spending.

headline: Rendell, Fumo: Foes of 1-80 tolls will fail
abstract: Efforts to block tolls on Interstate 80 are effectively dead, State Sen. Vincent Fumo and Gov. Rendell said yesterday. With state highway officials preparing an application to request the authority to put tolls on I-80, Fumo and Rendell said Pennsylvania Democrats in the U.S. House and Senate had assured them that two House Republicans from rural Pennsylvania would fail in their bid to stop the plan.

headline: Bickering goes on over smoking ban
abstract: The effort to ban most indoor smoking in public places in PA has entered its bell lap. Members of a House/Senate conference committee met to discuss a compromise that could leave most public places and workplaces off-limits to smokers. There are still pitched battles ahead. Conferees are debating on whether bus shelters and stadium concourses are covered by the "indoor" ban, or whether cities and towns should be able to pass local ordinances that are more restrictive than state law.

headline: Our view: Emergency response is inadequate
abstract: Provides a link to a website where the paper discusses its disappointment with the government's emergency response.

headline: More colleges adopt smoking bans for dorms
abstract: Eight Pennsylvania colleges, including Franklin & Marshall College, the University of Pennsylvania and Indiana University of Pennsylvania, have banned smoking in dorms.  Some students are against the bans, which require that students leave their rooms and smoke outside.  Littering and courtesy are discussed amongst the broader debate of the role of smoking on campuses.

headline: Taxes, tolls and transit: Lawmakers work to clear roadblock
abstract: The PA House of Representatives are working out a $900 million transportation package that is key to agreeing on the upcoming budget debate.  The current proposal would force drivers to pay higher tolls on the PA Turnpike and Interstate 80 and counties to increase funding by levying more local taxes to fund mass transit.  Republicans and Democrats are also negotiating whether or not Philadelphia should be granted two more seats on the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority.

headline: Parent sues Ambridge schools over teacher's sex with girl, 15
abstract: The mother of a 15-year-old girl who had sex with an Ambridge Area School District teacher says the district did nothing to stop the teacher from flirting with female students. The federal lawsuit was filed in Pittsburgh against the district, its administrators and 29-year-old David Costanza of Baden. Costanza is serving six months to two years in jail after pleading no contest to statutory sexual assault in July.

headline: Rendell: Show me the money and I'll pull plan for I-80 tolls
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell has stated that he will cancel his plans to toll the Interstate 80 highway if legislators can devise a plan to come up with at least $1 billion in funding a year for a decade to fund road and bridge repairs and mass transit improvements.  One of the options discussed among lawmakers is the privatization of the Turnpike, but that idea has not gained much traction among both parties in the PA Legislature.  Rendell is allowing bidders to submit formal offers to the government for the Turnpike, but at the same time, the government is applying to the US Department of Transportation to convert I-80 into a toll road as well.

headline: Bill would allow blackjack, poker in state casinos as early as this fall
abstract: A bill proposed by PA Rep. H. William DeWeese is opposed by PA Governor Ed Rendell. The bill would allow the 14 slots parlors recently licensed by the PA Gaming Control Board to begin offering table games a year after opening for business. Many lawmakers are reluctant to address the issue, as controversy over a legislative pay raise is still dying down. The bill would generate additional revenue for the state. DeWeese also wants to see income and sales taxes expanded to eliminate property taxes.

headline: Our View: Steel and Slag
abstract: The editorial staff gives "steels" to the good things and "slags" to the bad things that happened at the beginning of the year. Slag went to the PA House of Representatives for almost re-electing Republican John Perzel as the speaker and to PA Governor Rendell and the PA Liquor Control Board for their decision to appoint a new chief executive officer over the head of Chairman Jonathan Newman.  Steel praise went to Bill DeWeese, Democratic Speaker, who put aside his own claims in order to stop Perzel's re-election from happening.

headline: Put med school in downtown Project reaches milestone with appointment of dean
abstract: The Medical College of Northeastern Pennsylvania appointed Dr. Robert M. D’Alessandri dean of the new medical school.  They are looking at different measures regarding where to locate the school.  A downtown Scranton location is seen as favorable by some.

headline: Thanksgiving tops other holidays in alcohol-related crashes
