abstract: While plenty of people break out the bubbly for New Year's and enjoy their eggnog at Christmas, Thanksgiving is consistently the worst holiday in terms of drunken driving on Pennsylvania's roads. Nearly 2,400 alcohol-related crashes happened during major holidays last year, statistics from the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation show. Of those crashes, more than 10 percent -- 254 of them -- happened on Thanksgiving. There were an additional 398 alcohol-related crashes in the days just before or after the holiday.

headline: Parents challenge PPA
abstract: The Philadelphia Parking Authority needed some good public relations after what occurred yesterday in their headquarters' lobby. You can blame school district parents and child advocates who want the PPA to pay its fair share to the school district. They held a news conference in the rain, right outside the main door to the PPA headquarters, at 31st and Market streets. Several times, building security asked the parents and news crews to clear a path for people entering and leaving the building. However, someone who saw the 35-40 assembled people panicked and called the police. Seven cops arrived and found not a disturbance in the lobby.

headline: Require helmets, reduce carnage
abstract: This editorial cites a study by the National Transportation Safety Board that reports that since state lawmakers repealed the mandatory use of motorcycle helmets, fatalities on motorcycles have increased by 127%.  The author also claims that motorcyclists are less likely to be insured than car drivers and typically suffer far more serious injuries in accidents.  It continues to encourage the PA Legislature  to support PA Representative Dan Frankel's bill to reinstate the mandatory use of helmets on motorcycles.

headline: Casino should sweeten the pot
abstract: The editorial board writes that the operators of Philadelphia Park Casino in Bensalem must be testing just how little they can wager to win a jackpot of bad publicity. Even though a message on the Wheel of Fortune video screen Wilkinson was playing said he was $102,000 richer, the machine was designed to pay off a top prize of only $5,000. The jackpot limit was posted in the casino. They say that Wilkinson did the right thing by promptly filing a complaint with the PA Gaming Control Board. They write that Harrisburg officials are looking for gambling to provide millions of dollars in property-tax relief each year.

headline: PA widens probe into legislative bonuses
abstract: A total of at least 14 employees from the Democratic Party have now been subpoenaed to testify before a grand jury over the $1.9 million in year-end bonuses that were distributed. PA Attorney General Tom Corbett, a Republican, is leading an investigation into whether the bonuses were given for campaign work, however, he has been criticized by leading Democrats for not issuing any subpoenas to members of the Republican party, which also handed out substantial bonuses. Corbett denied allegations of playing favoritism, and investigators claim both parties are being investigated.

headline: If 2 wealthy senators did break the law, the question is why
abstract: A comparison between embattled legislators is made in this article.  The legislators are PA Senator Vince Fumo and NJ Senator Wayne Bryant.  Their crimes and motivations are compared and examined.

headline: The road to ruin
abstract: Toll roads such as the Pennsylvania and New Jersey Turnpikes were built on state lands with public funds and bonds. The expectation was that the tolls would fund the building and maintenance of these roads, with profit being a fine bonus. Now there is a move afoot among the politicians to lease toll roads to private firms, with the expectation that greater profit will result . Perhaps if we had good management of these enterprises, instead of filling the management ranks with political appointees, profits could match or beat what the private sector could do. A quasi-governmental enterprise could easily generate as much or more revenue than private industry if structured properly.

headline: Parents want say on schools CEO
abstract: Vice President of the Philadelphia Home and School Council echoes the sentiment of parents wanting to be involved and updated on the search for a new city schools chief to replace Paul Vallas, who is leaving to head the New Orleans Recovery School District. PA Governor Ed Rendell said an interim leader could fill the position for up to a year before a new leader is found. A School Reform Commission spokesman indicated it may not be possible for parents to give input, as the position may be filled within weeks.

headline: Richland native's shuttle launch today
abstract: After more than a year of frenetic training, space shuttle Atlantis astronauts finally got a break.  Mission commander Stephen Frick, a native of Richland, ate lunch with family members a little more than 24 hours before today's scheduled launch.  Frick was not available for comment. But fellow astronaut Dr. Robert L. Satcher Jr. said it was "a pretty relaxed day" for the seven-member crew. NASA officials projected launch temperature would be 71 degrees. They forecast scattered clouds with visibility of seven miles for the 4:31 p.m. launch. The probability of weather postponing lift-off was 10 percent, they said.

headline: Casino, arena, and other big projects will strain labor pool but that's a good thing
abstract: In 2004, Pennsylvania slow laws was enacted, and the state government believed that at the least a majority of the 14 casinos would be open by 2006 to help generate revenue for the surrounding communities and lower property taxes.  According to the Intergovernmental Cooperation Authority, which oversees Pittsburgh's finances, the delay of one casino's opening has cost the city $11 million.  Philadelphia is waiting the result of a referendum banning casinos near residential areas, and Pittsburgh is awaiting an appeal by the two losing bidders to the PA Supreme Court on the decision of the PA Gaming Board.

headline: Pa. ex-lawmakers back on public payroll following election losses
abstract: The PA legislators who were voted out of office after they voted for their own pay-raises have found jobs back in the state government or as lobbyists. Two prominent examples are former lawmakers Peter Zug who has become a licensing analyst for the PA Gaming Control Board and Fred Belardy who now makes 36% than he did as a lawmaker by managing personal matters for his former colleagues.  Matthew Brouillette, president of the Commonwealth Foundation, says this proves how corrupt and inefficient the state government has become.

headline: Krancer to stay on ballot as judge rejects challenge
abstract: A retired Philadelphia Family Court employee sought to have Krancer thrown off the May 15 primary ballot on the ground that he failed to report all his sources of income.  A state judge threw out the complaint.

headline: The Suitors
abstract: It is a list that was released by Governor Rendell, which provides the names of each company that submitted a proposal expressing interest in operating the PA Turnpike.

headline: Parents weigh in on 'fat letter'
abstract: Phelps, who is president of the Parent Teacher Association at her daughters' school, Westwood Elementary, got the letter last spring from the school nurse. Her girls, ages 7 and 9 years, are overweight, according to the Pittsburgh Public Schools. Barb Phelps called it "the fat letter." The PA state Department of Public Health requires school nurses to measure students' body mass index, or BMI, along with weight and height as part of its growth screening program. In 2005, Pennsylvania became the second state to require school nurses to measure students' body mass index and notify parents of the results.

headline: Roadblock to I-80 tolls in US bill is lifted
abstract: A joint U.S. House and Senate conference committee has stricken language from a massive transportation funding bill that would have forbidden the use of federal money to turn Interstate 80 into a toll road. The conference committee removed the language late Thursday night, said Reps. Phil English, R-3rd, and John Peterson, R-5th, who had it successfully inserted into the bill earlier this year.

headline: Casino-revenue tax to fund Pa. board.
abstract: State officials have come up with a new plan to raise more than $9 million to keep Pennsylvania's gambling regulatory agency operating through the end of the current fiscal year. The plan calls for the PA Department of Revenue to impose a 1.5 percent tax on the gross gaming revenues of three racetrack casinos currently operating and two others scheduled to open between now and May - raising $5.4 million by June 30. PA Revenue Secretary Greg Fajt and PA Gaming Control Board Chairman Tad Decker announced the plan during a Senate Community, Economic and Recreational Development Committee hearing.

headline: Pa. House closes in on rule changes
abstract: The PA state House of Representatives failed to reach a vote last night on various internal rule changes that planned to open up the legislative process.  These changes, recommended by the Speaker's Reform Commission, included banning late-night sessions, posting votes on the Internet, and limiting the ability of committees to radically alter bills before a vote.  The Commission did experience one defeat, as PA Representative Dwight Evans of Philadelphia was able to put through an amendment protecting the ability of the Appropriations Committee to amend nonfiscal bills.

headline: Profiling the city's gun violence
abstract: A panel of crime experts faced a panel in Harrisburg yesterday.  The testimony lasted three hours and was a sobering assessment of Philadelphia's gun crime issue.  The effect on health care and law enforcement is examined as well as the future of municipal gun control.

headline: Tolls for thee
abstract: Since few of the drivers who live in the area served by SEPTA are likely to use I-80 very often, I have an alternative to Gov. Rendell's plan to fund mass transit and road projects with I-80 tolls: How about toll booths on the Schuylkill and Blue Route? That way, Philadelphia-area motorists would be paying most of the freight for their own incompetent transit service. And a free Broad Street and Kelly Drive would be bumper-to-bumper.

headline: Paterno salary well behind highest-paid coaches
abstract: The State Employees' Retirement System said Paterno earned $427,220 through Oct. 31, putting him on pace to earn $512,000 for the year. His 2006 salary was $490,638. The retirement system released Paterno's salary information, along with that of two other Penn State administrators, in keeping with a state Supreme Court ruling last week. The Harrisburg Patriot-News requested this information in 2002, on the basis that Paterno and other employees participate in a taxpayer-supported retirement system.

headline: Senate nears $700M transportation deal
abstract: Despite the PA State Senate passing a transportation package that tolls Interstate 80 and raises $700 million through borrowing for mass transit and inadequate roads, a stalemate within the PA state government on a $27 billion budget for the following fiscal year still continues.  PA Governor Ed Rendell demanded at least $1 billion for the first year for funding for transportation and for legislative action on other proposals, such as a charge on electricity use to fund conservation efforts.  If the budget is not passed soon, an impasse will freeze government spending and furlough 25,000 state workers.

headline: Buying beer different ways
abstract: This editorial encourages the PA Legislature to accept the proposal of the new Wegmans store in Silver Spring Township to offer beer in the restaurant that has not drawn any opposition from residents.  The author although understands that the Malt Beverage Distributors Association is mobilizing to block this proposal, as many  of these beer distributors are smaller businesses within the communities and fear Wegmans being able to sell beer from their chain stores.  Finally, it is predicted that the state always treats these cases on a case-by-case basis, and there will not be much change in the laws.

headline: Pa. House Democrats report bonuses to staff of $2.4 million
abstract: PA House Democrats handed out more than $2 million in bonuses in the last two years, nearly tripling, to $3.7 million, the reported total amount of extra compensation awarded to legislative staffers. House Democrats announced yesterday that their payments totaled nearly $2.4 million, including more than $270,000 for staffers on the Appropriations Committee that was separately disclosed. On Wednesday, when the legislature's three other caucuses released lists of bonuses worth a combined $1.3 million, the House Democrats had estimated their bonuses at about $400,000 a year.

headline: Conspiracy or a paper tiger?
abstract: Dickson City Borough Council Vice President Paul Kwiec believes that bags of shredded documents contain the key to a $23,000 lawsuit complicated due to missing paperwork.

headline: TOUGH-TOWN TRILOGY: MEET THE 3 SCROOGES
abstract: If it is more blessed to give than receive, we may owe the Delaware River Port Authority a huge debt of gratitude this Christmas. How huge we won't know until the wise men of the DRPA decide how much more we must give to help offset their profligacy and mismanagement. They may decide to scrape by on what they collect on their bridges and from the PATCO High-Speed Line fare boxes. But there's a good chance they'll decide that they need more of our money to maintain and staff four bridges and a commuter railroad. That is, after all, what they're supposed to be doing.

headline: Schools may get some Parking Authority cash
abstract: It isn't the $20 million check parents of Philadelphia school students were hoping for, but the Philadelphia Parking Authority could soon send profits from its red-light camera program - expected to be $1.2 million to $1.4 million next fiscal year - to the city school district. Sponsored by Rep. William McGeehan, the authorizing legislation was approved by the House Appropriations Committee. It still awaits approval by the House and Senate, where at least some opposition is expected, as the bill essentially redirects the money out of a state transportation fund and into the school district.

headline: SEPTA expands senior discounts
abstract: Southeastern Pennsylvania Transit Authority, as a result of the new state transit bill signed by PA Governor Ed Rendell, will remove restrictions on senior discounts.  Because of this new policy, senior citizens will ride free on buses and the Regional Rail will cost only 1$.  However, the Street administration in Philadelphia has taken SEPTA to Common Pleas Court asking to remove the new transfer policy that makes riders pay a second full fare on a transfer.

headline:
Casino checks a roll of the dice?
GOP lawmakers want enforcement arm taken away from gaming board
abstract: The Bureau of Investigations and Enforcement, which investigates and conducts background checks on casinos and their personnel, reports directly to the state Gaming Control Board based on a PA law passed in 2004. However, controversy has arisen after reports surfaced that Louis DeNaples, who was awarded a license to open a casino, has ties to organized crime. Several legislators and a retired state police officer feel that the Gaming Control Board’s investigation branch should not be under its direct control and offered two main solutions.

headline: PA. House GOP will limit PSAs to only 3 per year
abstract: Republicans in the PA House of Representatives plan to decrease the costs of their frequent televised public-service announcements as they have decided to limit themselves to three per year.  House Republicans spent almost three times more than House Democrats, who spent $1.6 million for these advertisements.  Russ Diamond, a Lebanon businessman, is an outspoken critic of the Legislature who feels that they are unable to reform as they failed to pass a resolution that would ban these ads during election years.

headline: Casey says he will vote against bill to lift ban on funding stem-cell research
abstract: US Senator Bob Casey (D-PA) says that he will vote against legislation that would allow for more government funding of stem cell research.  This comes after he says he met with experts on both sides who have advised him.  The bill faces long odds of passage without the 67 votes needed to overule a veto by the White House.

headline: Transit agency to change surcharge policy
abstract: The Southeastern PA Transportation Authority began charging riders $1 extra if they bought a ticket on the train, however, they recently announced plans to begin offering same-day credits after many complaints were made.

headline: Schools report progress
abstract: While all school districts in Centre County made overall academic progress in 2007, an annual state achievement report released Wednesday shows some gains and losses for individual schools. For the first time in four years, State College Area High School was issued a warning for its Pennsylvania System of School Assessment scores for a particular group of students. Penns Valley, Bald Eagle and Bellefonte area high schools, all of which had received warnings last year, made progress. Only one school district in the county -- Philipsburg-Osceola -- has had adequate test scores in all of its schools since the passing of the federal No Child Left Behind Act five years ago.

headline: SEPTA granted transfer delay
abstract: SEPTA's effort to do away with the 60-cent bus and subway transfer was delayed until at least next Friday, as lawyers for SEPTA and the city yesterday asked for more time. Common Pleas Court Judge Gary F. DiVito, who had set a deadline of yesterday for filing briefs, agreed to the postponement at SEPTA's request. The city is attempting to block SEPTA's plan to eliminate the transfers, arguing the change would amount to a steep fare hike that would disproportionately affect poor and minority passengers.

headline: Casino developers expect to win final approval from city next week
abstract: Bethlehem’s planning commission will meet to consider the final approval of Sands BethWorks Gaming LLC’s estimated $635 million casino project, which will include 2,000 slot machines, a hotel, retail space, a garage and restaurants and bars.

headline: Pa. lawmakers take a break after a year of futility
abstract: Opinion on the Legislature recently. He says that they don't anything anyone cares about. A walkout by the Legislative Black Caucus to protest lack of action of guns, which, frankly could have been staged at any point in the last decade, and which, despite much chest-beating, got nothing done, apparently has a little back-story. Even the Governor is disappointed.

headline: Private Sector: Latest statistics show state workers continue to lose ground
abstract: Despite GDP growth, rising productivity and record profits, many feel financially insecure in the state.  Studies now show that in spite of the strong economy wages for most workers fell.  This included even college educated workers.  Advocates are seeking to restore the balance between economic growth and standard living increases for workers.

headline: Transit takes a toll
abstract: The PA House of Representatives recently passed a transportation funding bill that proposes raising almost $1 billion annually for roads, bridges, and mass transit systems by tolling Interstate 80 and bonding the Pennsylvania Turnpike.  The bill also requires municipalities to match 20% of state funding for the transit systems by levying income, sales, hotel room or vehicle rental taxes.  Most Democrats, such as PA Senator Lisa Boscola feel the municipalities need to pay their fair share while Republican PA Representative Douglas Reichley voted against the bill because of the taxes and the increased power of Philadelphia on the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority Board.

headline: Schools to pay exec while on new job
abstract: Lynn Spampinato, former Pittsburgh Public Schools deputy superintendent, has a new job but will continue to receive the remainder of a $213,333 consulting contract with Pittsburgh. Dr. Spampinato was nominated as commissioner of education in the U.S. Virgin Islands, a post that would put her at the helm of the territory's Department of Education.

headline: SEPTA releases budget wish list
abstract: The Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority plans to spend $426 million in the next fiscal year for new buses and railcars, reconstruction, and other various upgrades.  This budget makes the assumption the Pennsylvania Legislature passes PA Governor Ed Rendell's 6.17% tax on oil companies' gross profits to fund public transit agencies and President George Bush's planned budget requests for transit agencies.

headline:
Casino files suit on zoning
SugarHouse anxious to start building
abstract: Despite the state Gaming Control Board’s decision to award SugarHouse a casino license, the Philadelphia City Council has been delaying action on legislation that would allow construction to begin, which prompted its owners to ask the Supreme Court to force it to act. Several members argue that SugarHouse’s actions are an attempt to infringe upon the rights of the local government and the thousands of people who live on the Delaware riverfront and oppose the casino. Governor Rendell supports the developers, as does Mayor Street, who threatened to revoke the city's zoning control.

headline: Pa. lawmakers won't say and don't have to say where $360M went
abstract: In the passing of the 2007-2008 budget, the Pennsylvania legislators, as tradition usually goes, directed $360 million of the $27.2 billion budget into a "walking-around money" fund that is for legislators to use for local programs at their own discretion.  The PA Legislature, however, is not bound by the weak open-records law in Pennsylvania, and they are not required to tell the public where the money is spent.  Craig Staudenmaier, general counsel for the Pennsylvania Freedom of Information Coalition, claims that hiding the records only creates suspicion and mistrust of politicians from the citizens.

headline: Web media upstart caters to conservatives
abstract: Jeff Lord started QubeTV, web portal designed especially for conservatives. He is marketing the site as a place for conservatives to trade information and socialize with other like-minded people.

headline: Transportation authority anticipates state's budget, implements poetry program
abstract: The Luzerne County Transportation Authority have approved a $6.3 million budget for the next fiscal year as well as the power for Director Stanley Strelish to reduce expenses with anticipated state revenue is reduced.  Strelish is waiting to hear from PA Representative Mike Carroll about whether or not the Senate or PA Governor Ed Rendell have passed the mass transit funding bill.  The authority have also paired up with Lamar Advertising to display poetry on placards inside buses.

headline: Shaler teachers reject pact but don't strike
abstract: In a close vote, teachers in Shaler Area School District rejected a proposed contract yesterday, but they won't strike today as they had vowed. "We can't go out on strike with a vote this close," said Jo Ann Noble, president of the Shaler Area Education Association, who declined to reveal the vote tally. Teachers had reached a tentative agreement with the school board Nov. 19. As of yesterday, no school districts in Pennsylvania had teachers on strike.

headline: Shop gets national exposure
abstract: A local shop's bicycles will be featured in the national Bicycling Magazine. The owners are credited with having contributed to the city's downtown revitalization.

headline: Casino manager: W. Va. jockeying for advantage
abstract: West Virginia's Legislature recently passed legislation that allows for table games to be installed at its racetracks.  Mike Graninger, general manager at The Meadows Racetrack and Casino in North Strabane, claims this gives the neighboring state a huge competitive advantage over PA's slot machines.  Tad Decker, chairman of the PA Gaming Control Board, has stated new electronic simulations of table games are being reviewed whether or not to be considered slot machines, and PA State Representative Bill DeWeese of Waynesburg has proposed legislation that would legalize table games at the state's gambling halls.

headline: Purple Pennsylvania looking a little blue
abstract: Before President Bush was re-elected in 2004, Pennsylvania was considered a "purple state." For the uninitiated, that’s a mixture of a red state, with solidly Republican voters, and a blue state, solid Democratic. It’s a state that goes back and forth in voting for statewide candidates. The Republican president lost the state to Democratic Massachusetts Sen. John Kerry, leading to speculation that purple Pennsylvania was permanently shading bluer. After the latest election, it’s harder to call Penn’s Woods anything but blue and to wonder whether the toxic political climate for Republicans spawned by the president is hurting even their local candidates.

headline: State panel hammers out vital ethics reforms
abstract: A state commission wants to require all legislators to attend ethics training amongst other major reforms suggested by the body.  Legislators from both sides of the aisle seem to be interested in moving ethics reform as a whole forward.

headline: Transportation bill still faces long road
abstract: This article shows how the local legislators voted on the $720 million transportation funding plan  that recently was passed in the PA House of Representatives, 105-96.  The plan calls for $250 million for mass transit agencies and $450 million would be used to repair state highways and bridges.  Counties would need to contribute $18 million to the mass transit funding, and drivers would also see increased tolls by 25% on the Pennsylvania Turnpike.

headline: Shippensburg University's new president is William N. Ruud
abstract: Starting on February 19, 2007. Shippensburg University's new president will be William N. Ruud, a management professor and former college administrator who also has experience working with former Idaho Governor Dirk Kempthorne. Ruud was welcomed to the State System of Higher Education with a unanimous voice vote.

headline: Some won, some lost, in state budget deal
abstract: This article analyzes the winners and losers after the PA Governor Ed Rendell and the PA Legislature finally reached a deal on the budget on Monday night.  The winners were Rendell, who achieved his large transportation funding bill and early-childhood education funding, the Senate Republicans who halted all seven tax hikes originally proposed and the two urban centers, Philadelphia and Pittsburgh, who will see a new Pennsylvania Convention Center and Pittsburgh Penguins arena, respectively.  The loser were 24 state employees who were furloughed for a day without pay, motorists who couldn't take a road test or get a driver's license photo while having to pay higher tolls in 2009 and campers who couldn't camp in state parks during the furlough.

headline: City planners zero in on casino timetable
abstract: Don Barden, owner of PITG gaming LLC, is planning to start construction of the $435 million North Shore casino in Pittsburgh next month after his plans were delayed by appeals from losing bidders. Isle of Capri Casinos Incorporated and Station Square Gaming, who await the decision of the PA Supreme Court.  The casino also is in need of a building permit from the city and a storm water runoff permit from the PA Department of Environmental Protection before construction begins.  Barden claims that once construction begins, the casino will be finished in 14-16 months.

headline: Pursue the case: DeFazio's legacy should be an appointed sheriff
abstract: County sheriff Pete DeFazio pleaded guilty in a federal court to macing, the act of coercing an employee to give to a political candidate of a party. This is the reason that voters should abolish the election of county sheriff. From now on the position should be an appointed position, that way the sheriff needs no political contributions and his employees would serve without fear that their next promotion depends on how big a check they write to the boss's next campaign.

headline: VALLAS GOIN' SOUTH?
abstract: Philadelphia Schools Superintendent Paul Vallas confirmed that he is going to be leaving his position with the city to move south to New Orleans to take over the Hurricane Katrina-embattled school district.  A look-back at his career and what lies ahead for the city's schools is discussed later in the article.

headline: Transportation department launches new Web site
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation unveiled a new website, www.rideonpa.org, dedicated to keeping the public informed of proposed funding mechanisms and designated projects for revenue. PA Governor Ed Rendell proposed an approach which uses revenue from a new oil corporation gross profits tax and leverages the turnpike, though it will remain under state ownership. The details of various proposals are available via the website.

headline: SHS steps into future with state’s laptops
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell announced the state’s $200 million Classrooms for the Future initiative, 79 school districts in the program, including Scranton and North Pocono, have been preparing to receive the new equipment. The three-year state initiative is designed to improve learning and teaching in high schools with the use of technology-enriched curriculum.

headline: Southwest calls airport's fees a large concern
abstract: The Allegheny County Airport Authority authorized increases in landing, terminal and ramp fees to offset the revenue that Pittsburgh International Airport will lose due to US Airways cutbacks. The costs will be shared by all airlines, and officials from Southwest are concerned; though the price hikes aren’t likely to affect the airline’s intentions to add more flights next year. The authority is usually conservative with its cost estimates, so there is a good chance that money will be returned to the airlines, and money that the authority will receive from slot machine revenue could also bring down airline costs.

headline: Committee to study impact of casino
abstract: Northampton County Executive John Stoffa is creating a committee to study the possible effects of a Bethlehem casino on the county's human services, prison and court systems. Sands BethWorks Gaming LLC won a state casino license in December for the former Bethlehem Steel Corp. site. The company expects to open a 3,000-slot casino in mid-2008. County human services Director Ross Marcus said human service officials want to gauge possible effects on drug and alcohol abuse and the Division of Children, Youth and Families.

headline: Pa. Supreme Court race has implications for Philly
abstract: The control of Pennsylvania’s Supreme Court will be up for grabs in the upcoming elections, which will be very important according to Michael Nutter, who will likely be elected as Philadelphia’s mayor. A long list of important legal issues for Philadelphia have been decided by the Supreme Court in the past, and many more will be decided in the future, which would make its control desirable for both parties. The PA Bar Association released its evaluations of all candidates, and Judge Saylor was recommended for retention,  Candidates Todd and Lally-Green were given the highest ratings, and Candidates Krancer and McCaffery were given slightly lower rankings.

headline: State unveils personal care home plan
abstract: State Public Welfare Secretary Estelle Richman announced a plan to get started on the agency's backlog of inspections needed on 70% of the state's 1589 facilities.  These 70% are operating on expired licenses.  They are going to hire retired workers with experience in the matter to attack this backlog.  Advocates are hoping for improvements to safety and neglect accusations thorughout the system.

headline: Animal fight not over
abstract: Having spent much of the summer debating pet euthanasia, contracting procedures with shelters, and cat licensing, the city's nine legislators are scheduled to resume tomorrow a scrap over where to take wildlife for euthanization. Councilman Jim Motznik wants to contract with Triangle Pet Control Services of McKees Rocks, while Councilwoman Darlene Harris would like to continue efforts to train and equip city workers to end the days of captured raccoons, groundhogs and skunks.

headline: State universities approve 3% tuition increase
abstract: The finance committee of the PA State System of Higher Education has formally recommended a tuition increase of 2.75% for Pennsylvania's 14 state-owned universities.  The new rate for Pennsylvania residents will increase to $5,177 as the tuition for out-of-state students will increase to $7,766 to $12,944 depending on the major and the university.  After PA Governor Ed Rendell signed the most recent budget, the state's subsidy to these universities is increasing 3.5% as well to approximately $484 million, which falls short $12 million of what the universities' claimed to need.

headline: State likely to take its toll on I-80
abstract: There isn’t a lot of hope left to halt the tolling of Interstate 80 in Pennsylvania, U.S. Rep. Phil English said. English, Erie seemed resigned to the failure of his legislative attempt to stop the toll plan approved by state lawmakers but said he would still try to convince federal officials to reject the proposal. He introduced an amendment to a House spending bill to prevent federal funds from being used to set up tolls on the interstate. But English said House Speaker Nancy Pelosi will back an order to strip that amendment from the legislation.

headline: Despite problems at convention center, city's future as a destination may be bright
abstract: The nonprofit organization VisitPittsburgh's president Joseph McGrath is confident about the outlook of tourism for the city of Pittsburgh after a recent tourism convention in the David L. Lawrence Convention Center was a success.  McGrath did, however, express concerns about a lack of a headquarters hotel in the city, and as a result, the PA Sports and Exhibition Authority, developer Forest City, and revenues from the new casinos will all be funding an additional hotel next to the convention center.  The slots revenues are still not available after two losing casino bidders have appeal a PA Gaming Control Board decision to the PA State Supreme Court.

headline: Panel wants '08 primary held Feb. 12
abstract: The PA House State Government Committee have passed a proposal to move Pennsylvania's presidential primary forward to February 12 to increase its significance while reserving a day in May for referendums in school districts.  The PA House of Representatives have passed a bill to double the maximum fines for all criminal offenses to help pay for the salaries of the counties' district attorneys.  Lastly, PA Governor Ed Rendell signed legislation that collects the $52 municipal tax at one dollar a week rather than a lump sum while exempting people who make less than $12,000 a year.

headline: State allows districts leeway in Act 1 ballots
abstract: School districts will be able to add information to Act 1 ballot questions the state ruled.  The local officials want to be able to explain to voters the longer-term impact of the tax shift.

headline: Attempt to fast track bill to shrink state Legislature fails
abstract: The PA House voted against Representative Mark Mustio’s attempt to get his proposal to reduce the size of the General Assembly and its budget out of its committee for a full House vote. Mustio is disappointed, however, Majority Leader Bill DeWeese and State Government Committee Chairwoman Babette Josephs said hearings could be held throughout the state, so his proposal is still alive.

headline: State universities, faculty union avert strike with tentative 4-year contract
abstract: The PA System of Higher Education came to a tentative agreement with the union leaders of the Pennsylvania State College and University Faculties.  The system has offered a plan with a $1,250 cash payment for full-time faculty and annual raises of 2%, 2% and 3%, while the union claims to have sought raises of 4%, 5.5%, 5.5% and 5%.  This also squabbling over planned contributions towards health benefits, the use of temporary nonunion faculty members and distance education incentives.

headline: State official to visit deteriorating Murrysville bridge
abstract: PA Transportation Secretary Allen Biehler will visit Murrysville bridge during a statewide tour to bring attention to the infrastructure crisis. The PA Department of Transportation recently posted a list online of 800 bridges statewide in dire need of renovations. PA Governor Ed Rendell and legislators have been unable to agree on how to pay for the increasing costs of infrastructure improvements and mass transit.

headline: DiCicco to press today for more control over slots
abstract: Philadelphia Councilman Frank DiCicco today will introduce 10 proposed changes to how the city regulates the riverfront casinos approved by the state. The changes include banning casinos in the city, challenging the PA Gaming Control Board's choice of the local gaming sites and intensifying zoning controls for casinos. Asked about his legislation, DiCicco said he has heard from many neighbors of the casino sites who asked him to "try everything." He conceded that a total ban on gaming sites had little chance of passing. The Gaming Control Board is expected to soon release its written opinions on its site decisions, which will start a 30-day period when appeals can be filed with the PA Supreme Court.

headline: Pedoto's exit...Pittsburgh loses in a case of no guts, no glory
abstract: In the race for Democratic nomination for mayor in the May 15 primary, Pittsburgh City Councilman Bill Peduto has recently decided to drop out.  This leaves incumbent Mayor Luke Ravenstahl to be re-elected as there is no Republican contender for the office.  The editorial feels this is detrimental to the city of Pittsburgh because it is not an effective democratic process that would challenge the incumbent.

headline: Gov. Rendell targets Pa. health-care costs
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell is proposing a number of methods to keep costs related to hospital-acquired infections down.  This is in an effort to reduce costs and eventually insure every Pennsylvanian the governor says.

headline: Attorney general pursues removal of trust overseers
abstract: The trustees of a charitable trust created by the late labor leader Anthony F. Kane Jr. should be removed, state attorneys say, for lending most of the trust’s money to a business partner and friend of one of the trustees. The PA attorney general’s office, in a petition filed, asked Luzerne County Orphans’ Court Judge Michael Conahan to strip control of the trust from Gloria Bartnicki Riegel and her husband, Joel Riegel.  In 2005, the United Way and the state attorney general’s office challenged the Riegels’ handling of the trust in Orphans’ Court, questioning fees paid to lawyers, commissions paid to the trustees and investments in mortgages, which, they said, violated state laws governing investments by non-profits.

headline: State gaining on preschool education ranks
abstract: Pennsylvania has moved up on a list in a report by the National Institute for Early Education Research and Pew Charitable Trusts for spending on preschool education despite still lagging in school access for 4-year-old children.  Last month, PA Governor Ed Rendell proposed spending $75 million for block grants that would provide voluntary preschool programs for 11,100 more children.  PA State Education Secretary Gerald Zahorchak has stated that the Rendell administration has continuously pushed for more money in early learning.

headline: State officials will study potential downfalls to I-80 tolls
abstract: Even as several congressmen try to keep Interstate 80 toll-free, Pennsylvania officials are preparing to lessen the potentially negative consequences of tolling such as trucks taking a diversion off the interstate onto two-lane roads. The Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission will conduct periodic studies of the traffic leaving I-80 to escape tolls under a provision arranged by Senate Transportation Chairman Roger Madigan, R-Burlington Township.

headline: Gambling revenue brings bigger purses and bigger payouts to jockeys, trainers and horse owners, other changes ahead
abstract: Dyno Trevor won Wednesday night's fourth race at the Meadows. The prize was $15,400 50% higher than last year. The increase represents the boost the local horse-racing industry is drawing from the 1,738 slot machines running 24 hours a day. It has made horse racing bigger than ever.

headline: Pennsylvania Supreme Court: McCaffery wins; Todd jumps to lead in top court races
abstract: Superior Court Judge Seamus McCaffery won a seat on the state Supreme Court in yesterday's election. His Democratic running mate, Superior Court Judge Debra Todd, was hoping to join him in victory lane, but early this morning she was just narrowly ahead of one of her Republican challengers, Superior Court Judge Maureen Lally-Green. The two Democratic candidates jumped ahead early last night. .

headline: Rendell should open up the reform effort to the people
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell is encouraged to open up reform to the people instead of creating new positions and offices in Harrisburg.  Ideas such as citizen redistricting, larger legislature, and merit selection of judges.

headline: Audit: State agency paid $7.5 million in bonuses
abstract: Auditor General Jack Wagner released a report that claims the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency has given over $7.5 million in bonuses over the last three years. He is calling on the agency to permanently end the practice.

headline: State libraries: A great investment
abstract: Howard Sundwall, president of the Board of Trustees of the West Chester Library, writes an opinion that encourages funding of public libraries across the state of Pennsylvania.  He cites a study from the University of North Carolina called "Taxpayer Return on Investment in Pennsylvania Public Libraries" that reported that the citizens receive a 550% return on their investment as well as a total $1.4 billion boost from the libraries to the state economy.

headline: State should lease turnpike instead of tolling I-80
abstract: Pennsylvania lawmakers should reconsider the money they left on the table earlier this year after rejecting Gov. Rendell's initial plan to lease the Pennsylvania Turnpike to a private-sector partner. Such an agreement could generate billions of dollars needed for transportation infrastructure and transit systems without raising taxes, adding tolls or incurring more taxpayer debt. Amid increasing doubts about the viability of Act 44 of 2007, the law that permitted the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission to raise money by putting tolls on Interstate 80, the governor will soon announce a short list of teams that will make multi-billion-dollar bids for a potential turnpike lease.

headline: Drink tax still confounding foes
abstract: Tom Baron sees a "huge pain" when the new 10 percent tax on alcoholic drinks, which was approved by Allegheny County Council, takes effect in January. County Treasurer John Weinstein yesterday said the tax will apply to all retail liquor sales at bars and restaurants, except sales of six-packs. Pints of draft beer, glasses wine, shots of liquor, bottles of wine, bottles of beer, bottles of distilled spirits and mixed drinks sold at bars and restaurants will be subject to the tax, Mr. Weinstein said. He will soon draw up rules of how the tax will be implemented.

headline: People rally in support of immigration stance
abstract: Mayor Lou Barletta was given support by many local residents, including Arlene Thomas of White Haven, who are attending  over the Hazleton Illegal Immigration ordinance.  Many local citizens feel that they are living in fear and this ordinance will solve the crime issues that exacerbate this fear.

headline: Lawmaker health benefits abuse the public trust
abstract: Lawmaker health benefits are compared with the average citizen's health benefits in this editorial about health care costs.  While the average family's premiums are over $10,000, one US representative pays less than $1000 a year for their full coverage.  The editorial argues for reform of the practice of giving legislators lifetime health benefits at the expense of taxpayers.

headline: Ballot security stressed
abstract: Two judges serving as Lackawanna County’s Board of Elections gave a presentation that explained its security measures for the upcoming election and a how to fill out the new paper ballots that will be used. The judges spent most of the presentation outlining their security measures, which include a fleet of buses that will transport votes to be counted by optical scan machines operated by Premier Election Solutions. Representatives for both parties who attended the presentation seemed to agree that the safeguards would protect the integrity of each person’s vote.

headline: State official to meet with Duquesne High parents
abstract: PA Education Secretary Gerald Zahorchak plans to hold a private forum with parents of students of Duquesne High to address the closing of the school and the transferring of students to other schools.  Zahorchak has closed the meeting to the media and outside citizens so parents are able to speak candidly about their views on the topic.  Before any child can be reassigned or transferred, Zahorchak needs to pass legislation through the General Assembly.

headline: Transportation food for thought at dinner
abstract: PA Sen. Roger Madigan and Reps. Joseph Markosek and Richard Geist will speak at a dinner hosted by the Greater Lehigh Valley Chamber of Commerce in honor of National Transportation Week. They will address PA's transportation funding mechanism. Local officials say inadequate state subsidies are crippling the Lehigh and Northampton Transportation Authorities. PA Governor Rendell proposed leasing the PA Turnpike and taxing oil companies. Vice president of public policy for the chamber, Michelle Griffin, hopes to hear the speakers pitch policy alternatives to Rendell's.

headline: Ebay sellers pushed to get auctioneer licenses
abstract: Barry Fallon received a summon from Pennsylvania auction authorities after using eBay to sell other people’s possessions. Fallon, who ran a business called iSold It on eBay in Lower Paxton Twp., has been summoned to appear before the state Board of Auctioneer Examiners. He could face a fine of at least $1,000. The state claims that people like Fallon, those who accept things on consignment from other people and sell them using the California-based Web site eBay, are auctioneers and must obtain traditional state auctioneers’ licenses. The enforcement push means that online sellers would have to serve apprenticeships with traditional auctioneers or take college auctioneering courses

headline: Perzel to avoid House limelight
abstract: PA Representative John Perzel, who was just replaced as the PA House speaker, had crafted a deal that appeared to thwart Democratic leader Bill DeWeese's dream of returning to the speaker's rostrum and giving Perzel a leg up in his bid for a second full term as speaker. But DeWeese outmaneuvered him and nominated a hand-picked Republican PA Representative Dennis O'Brien, who went on to beat fellow Philadelphian Perzel by eight votes.

headline: Philadelphia Struggles to Quell an Epidemic of Gun Violence
abstract: The pace of killings in Philadelphia has worsened where 406 homicides took place last year.  Gun violence is becoming so common in certain neighborhoods, that people are no longer shocked by it, some experts say.  Efforts to control guns in the city are discussed.

headline: Barletta headed for stand
abstract: Hazelton Mayor Lou Barletta is expected to testify for multiple hours today in the case Lozano v. City of Hazelton.  American Civil Liberties Union attorney Witold J. Walczak, defending Lozano, already questioned Hazelton City Council President Joseph Yanuzzi for three hours.  The issue is determining the constitutionality of the Barlett's ordinance that punishes  landlords for renting to illegal immigrants or businesses for hiring illegal immigrants.

headline: State officials hope time will salvage Center-Monaca deal
abstract: State Rep. Vince Biancucci said that his actions may end up being the most important thing he ever does as a state legislator. Mr. Biancucci got state Education Secretary Gerald Zahorchak to send a letter promising the Center Area school board that it could have all the time it needed to assess a possible consolidation with the neighboring Monaca School District. Mr. Zahorchak's letter persuaded the board to change direction at its meeting and drop a proposal that would have withdrawn the merger application.

headline: Transportation secretary urges states to consider the weight of bridge during repair projects
abstract: The head of the nation's transportation system is cautioning states after the deadly bridge collapse here to consider the additional stress placed on bridges during construction projects. The warning from U.S. Transportation Secretary Mary Peters came after the National Transportation Safety Board said it found issues with Interstate 35W's gusset plates, the steel plates that tie steel beams together, and said they would look into reports of wobbling

headline: FEMA to end aid for flooding in new year
abstract: Starting Jan. 1, victims of the June 2006 flood might be paying a monthly fair market rent for living in Federal Emergency Management Agency housing. With the start of the new year, an 18-month period of assistance that began with a federal declaration of emergency will end, and 28 households in 12 counties will have to pay rent. In Schuylkill County, two FEMA emergency housing units remained as of Nov. 16 - a mobile home located in Ringtown and a travel trailer in Gilberton. FEMA External Affairs Specialist Josie Pritchard said how much local residents may pay after Jan. 1 will vary according to the type of emergency shelter.

headline: PHEAA chief may get raise by retiring
abstract: The author of the editorial criticizes the PA Higher Education Assistance Agency for the salaries and bonuses given to its top executives. In particular, the author is upset that the Dick Willey, who is retiring from PHEEA, will receive $61,000 per year more in retirement than his current base salary. Overall, the author believes PHEAA needs to be completely overhauled.

headline: Highmark spreads the wealth -- and influence
abstract: The influence of contributions made by Highmark is examined as regulators and lawmakers are going to review a huge merger between Highmark and Blue Cross.  They will need approval from a number of different agencies and levels of government.  Their campaign spending is examined further in depth.

headline: Be careful in casting votes in Lower Macungie
abstract: The author urges voters to be careful while voting in Lower Macungie. He says that if voters are serious about voting for a measure to obtain the first class township status that would give them five commissioners, they should vote no to a second question, which presents a trap that would maintain the status quo.

headline: State to city schools: No more money
abstract: Saying the state has been "extremely generous" in funding the Harrisburg School District, Education Secretary Gerald Zahorchak said today there would be no additional state money to help the city schools out of its budget crisis. City school officials said this week that as many as 100 jobs could be on the line as the 9,750-student district finalizes staff cuts in wake of a $10.5 million reduction in a certain type of state aid for 2007-08. Harrisburg had received a $13.5 million state demonstration grant for alternative education last school year. The funding has been reduced to just $3 million for this school year. The city school system had been seeking as much as $20 million in state demonstration grants for 2007-08.

headline: Travel costs will remain a problem
abstract: The options open to motorists, as indicated by a Morgan Stanley & Co. study commissioned by PA Governor Ed Rendell, include tolls on I-80, higher tolls on the PA Turnpike through a private lease, or a new "congestion tax" at an unspecified exit on the Northeast Extension in the Scranton/Wilkes-Barre area depending on which solutions are supported by the Governor and Legislators. Rendell supports private leasing.

headline: Fernwood Resort and Split Rock may seek resort slots license
abstract: Both Fernwood Resort and Split Rock Resort are potential applicants for two gaming licenses that would allow up to 500 slot machines as representatives from both resorts testified Tuesday in a PA Gaming Control Board hearing dealing with Category 3 resort licenses.  These licenses allow the 500 slow machines to be used by overnight guests or patrons of the resort.  According to Bub Uguccioni, director of the Pocono Mountains Visitors Bureau, there are five groups interested in the two licenses; the three others being Nemacolin Woodlands Resort, Valley Forge Hotel and Convention Center, and the fifth being undisclosed.

headline: PHEAA spent $409,413 on fight to shield expenses
abstract: Records released by the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency show it spent over $400,000 in legal fees in a court battle against The Patriot-News. The Patriot requested records of travel expenses by PHEAA employees and board members, however the Agency resisted all the way to the PA Supreme Court. For PA Education Secretary Gerald Zahorchak, the money spent equates to lost scholarships. Most of the expenses are from resort stays, where lawmakers were invited guests.

headline: Startup mentoring for tech firms blooming
abstract: Business owners will tell you that while the proverbial entrepreneurial basement or attic makes for a great story, formal working space is needed for more convincing success.  The Technology Council of Central Pennsylvania is going to be setting up incubators from rented space from other companies.  Entrepreneurs will have access to things missing from a basement, such as legal aid, accounting, office supplies and technology.

headline: Bill would let more use absentee ballot
abstract: Rep. Mark Cohen is proposing House Bill 1229, to allow voters to use absentee ballots regardless of their reason. Currently, exceptions to vote using an absentee ballot rather than at the polls are given only for very specific circumstances. Twenty-six states have adopted "no excuse" absentee voting according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. The League of Women Voters of PA and the PA Election Reform Task Force support Cohen's proposal. York County Director of Elections John Scott and Perry County's director Bonnie Delancey, however, do not.

headline: State-owned universities given $41.3 million
abstract: Private giving to the 14 state-owned universities totaled $41.3 million last year, with about half of that coming from alumni and individuals. Corporations, foundations and other organizations provided the remainder of the universities' support from July 1, 2005, to June 30, which fell shy of the $43.4 million raised the prior year. The system universities' combined endowments, however, continued their four-year climb to a record high $209.4 million, up 10 percent from the prior year. That is on par with the 10.7 percent average rate of return on university endowment investments nationally for the past fiscal year, according to the National Association of College and University Business Officers.

headline: Turnpike bridge project to break ground
abstract: The PA Turnpike Commission will begin a $190 million project of a new part of the PA Turnpike over the Allegheny River at the University of Pittsburgh Applied Research Center.  The highway will be widened to three lanes, and the plan is to rebuild the highway from Harmar to Oakmont.

headline: Former Bucknell President Named to Gaming Board
abstract: Former Bucknell President, Gary Sojka, is the newest appointee to the PA Gaming Control Board although his experience with casino gambling is limited to small wagers during recreational outings with family and friends. Sojka, who served as the university's president from 1984 to 1995 and is also a retired biology professor, said he has gambled on a cruise ship and at an Indian casino. Sojka was a decidedly nonpartisan choice for House Republicans, who reached far outside the political universe to avoid the kind of controversy that dogged their first pick.

headline: Pittsburgh school district, teachers to bargain again Nov. 20
abstract: Negotiators for Pittsburgh Public Schools and its teachers met Monday and have scheduled another bargaining session for Nov. 20. John Tarka, president of the Pittsburgh Federation of Teachers, declined to say how the talks went. The contract with the federation, which represents 4,042 teachers and other school employees, expired June 30. The union's members authorized it to call a strike if it considers it necessary. The two parties are trying to come to an agreement on issues such as pay and medical insurance.

headline: State should act quickly to reform constitution
abstract: The authors are advocating for a constitutional convention in Pennsylvania.  The last one was in 1873.  The authors favor a comprehensive look at state government and functions.  Term limits, session limits, legislature reduction, initiative and referendum, merit selection, and eminent domain reform are among the specific subjects that could be considered at such an event.

headline: Blowing a lot of hot hair
abstract: In this letter to the editor, Louise Diesing criticizes PA Governor Ed Rendell for not keeping to this campaign promises, specifically to senior citizen taxpayers. She also disagrees with the privatization of the Pennsylvania Turnpike and closing of the casino slots as she sees this as harming taxpayers.

headline: Student loan industry is rightly receiving a hard look from state and federal overseers
abstract: The author of this article discusses how congress is taking a hard look at the college student loan industry due to the investigations by New York attorney Andrew Cumo. The author suggests that these private lenders be required to put the disclaimer, is in no way associated with the Federal Government’ on the letters sent out to potential students up front in bold, large type. The author believes congress should look hard at better enforcement or necessary adjustments to truth-in-advertising laws and protecting the government's own official seals and Web sites.

headline: Turnpike Officials Pledge $1 billion for i-80 Work
abstract: State officials plan to spend more than $1 billion on improvements to Interstate 80 over the next few years under a plan to convert the 311-mile highway to a toll road. The improvements would focus on repairing bridges, adding climbing lanes for trucks, upgrading pavement and extending access ramps to the interstate, officials said. Last month, the state Legislature approved a plan to add tolls to raise money for road and bridge repairs across Pennsylvania, and also provide funding for cash-strapped mass-transit systems. Last month, the state Legislature approved a plan to add tolls to raise money for road and bridge repairs across Pennsylvania, and also provide funding for cash-strapped mass-transit systems.

headline: Foxwoods seeks casino site approval
abstract: The Philadelphia City Planning Commission will hold a hearing this month to overlook the site plan of the Foxwoods Philadelphia casino as it has drawn a lot of controversy from local citizens.  The other casino licensee, the SugarHouse Casino, has already passed its plan through the Commission and is awaiting the decision in the Philadelphia City Council.  The Foxwoods casino is also appealing to the PA Supreme Court to force the city to issue building permits.

headline: Pittsburgh unions decry oversight
abstract: City fire and police union bosses pleaded with a state Senate panel visiting Pittsburgh to remove the city from financial oversight and return some of their bargaining power. But the Senate Urban Affairs & Housing Committee convened its fourth in a series of five public hearings on financially distressed cities only to gather information -- not to chart Pittsburgh's course out of state receivership. Even so, state Sen. Jim Ferlo, D-Highland Park, used the occasion to call for an end to the city's five-member state oversight board, formally known as the Intergovernmental Cooperation Authority.

headline: Rendell’s pre-K plan worth consideration
abstract: The author comes out in favor of more pre-K funding as an alternative to State Rep. John Perzel's measure to hire 10,000 more policemen in the state.  The cost to that would be $225,000,000.  The investment in education is seen to be more impactful and more cost-effective.

headline: Both parties claim victories in wake of Tuesday's vote
abstract: Gov. Rendell and state GOP chairman Robert Gleason declared victory in Tuesday's general election, each claiming his political party seized the voter momentum heading into next year's presidential race. Rendell focused on two Democratic candidates who won seats on the state Supreme Court and 11 county commissions where Democrats took control. Gleason pointed to GOP wins in the lower courts and crowed that they had maintained control "in the governor's backyard" suburbs of Bucks, Montgomery, Chester and Delaware counties. Rendell, in a conference call with reporters, chuckled at the notion of a GOP victory.

headline: Student-loan agency cuts bonuses for leaders
abstract: The Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency has reported that it will freeze executive bonuses and cut $19 million in spending because it expects to lose $44 million in federal aid.  Dick Willey, president of the PHEAA, wrote a memo claiming there will be no bonuses, no new hires and no nonessential overtime or travel.  The agency also claims that the budget cuts are not related to PA Governor Ed Rendell's letter that criticized the agency's excessive bonuses.

headline: Turnpike panel says high cost imperil Mon-Fayette, Southern Beltway Projects
abstract: Rising cost estimates and lack of funding are jeopardizing completion of the Mon-Fayette Expressway and Southern Beltway. The Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission representatives disclosed just how serious the issue has become when an “executive committee” of elected, agency and planning officials held one of its infrequent meetings. Currently 1.3 billion has been spent on the two projects and about $526 million remains available.

headline: Fumo fights casino's court bid He comes out against SugarHouse's petition in Pa.'s Supreme Court. It's a ploy, says a challenger.
abstract: The state legislature's leading advocate of slot-machine gambling, facing a tough reelection campaign and under a federal indictment joined the legal fight against the casino owned in part by his friend and former lawyer. Sen. Vincent Fumo asked the state Supreme Court to deny SugarHouse Casino's bid to force city approval of zoning and land use for its $550 million project on North Delaware Avenue. SugarHouse last week petitioned the Supreme Court, which has jurisdiction over casino licensing and land-use appeals, to force City Council to act on a zoning change and site plan that SugarHouse submitted to the city.

headline: Political contributions by superintendent raise questions
abstract: The author claims that Merle Horowitz, the superintendant for Marple Newtown School District, told him on several occasions that she wanted to remain politically neutral, yet she contributed over $300 to the local Republican parties. He is upset that she said one thing but did another; especially in light of recent scandals at the Penn-Delco School District that involved political influence of the school board president and the superintendent. He questions Horowitz’s motives in the past and says that politics should be "left outside the schoolhouse door."

headline: Web site is useful open records tool
abstract: An editorial hailing the website www.openrecordspa.org which allows ordinary citizens to access information on public records, legislation, and general state and local government information.

headline: Brady's other issues
abstract: The author supports the decision of Senior Judge Patrick J. Toole of Luzerne County to not throw off US Representative Bob Brady off the ballot for the mayoral election of Philadelphia on the principle that voters should decide the elections, not judges.  Brady's rivals in the election, Tom Knox and PA State Representative Dwight Evans, attempted to get Brady thrown off the ballot because they claim he did not report $8,700-a-year government pension on his financial forms.  The author feels that a even the best candidates who claim to want to reform the city are more of the same political stereotype and give the few good politicians a bad name.

headline: Students want answers in cancer investigation
abstract: Many students of Susquehanna University are moving out of their apartments after the Patriot-News in Harrisburg has revealed a possible contamination of the soil near the "warehouse" apartments that may cause cancer.  The school recently held a meeting for students and parents to discuss what is going on and what may happen next.  Bob Yowell, Northcentral Regional office director of the PA Department of Environmental Protection said that results from the mobile labs will return tomorrow.

headline: US Airways drops Charleston to Pittsburgh flights
abstract: During a meeting of the Yeager Airport's governing board, it was announced that no more commercial flights will go between Charleston and Pittsburgh.  Yeager Director Rick Atkinson stated that Pittsburgh used to be a hub airport, but it has now been taken over by Atlanta for flights originating in Charleston.

headline: Gaming board member confirms budget impasse would close casinos
abstract: The PA Gaming Control Board decided that if a state budget negotiation arrives at a deadlock, they would be forced to suspend casino operations because of the state's decision to closely regulate gambling. The state legislators are in danger of not passing a budget by July 1, and the Rendell administration has reported that it give a temporary leave of absence to 26,000 of the state's employees, including 16 of the Revenue Department. The PGCB has interpreted the state's law that casinos must pass information on the slot machine's operation to the Revenue Department, and if these employees are not working, the casinos have to suspend operations.

headline: Political pay: House salary secrecy is no bonus to taxpayers
abstract: This editorial is skeptical of the Democratic leaders in the PA House of Representatives because of a report that showed a correlation between the size of bonuses from taxpayer dollars and the amount of political activity by state employees.  Those state employees who received the biggest bonuses either donated money or worked on the campaigns of PA Representative Bill DeWeese, PA Representative Mike Veon or the House Democratic Committee.  However, it does express optimism that the truth will be revealed after PA Attorney General Tom Corbett raided the Democratic Office of Legislative Research and found various boxes of files that will hopefully show the actual payments in question.

headline: Casino foes: We're not done yet
abstract: Opponents of casinos in Philadelphia say they will be collecting signatures for their referendum at polling stations.  They are forced to find another way to get on the ballot after a recent Supreme Court loss.  The referendum will ask if casinos should be put 1,500 feet away from homes, schools, churches, parks and other public spaces.

headline: Briefs: Voting stalls on animal euthanization procedure
abstract: This article reviews various local news stories in Pittsburgh and the surrounding area.  The main story is a Pittsburgh City Council debate on whether to contract Triangle Pet Control Services to euthanize wild animals that needs to be rushed according Councilwoman Tonya Payne, because the Animal Rescue League of Western Pennsylvania will stop accepting wild animals soon.  The article also discusses a contract won by a Democratic contributor, CLT Efficient Technologies Group, that will replace all of the city' traffic lights with more energy efficient light-emitting diodes.

headline: Survey: School nutrition falls short
abstract: While more than 3,100 Lackawanna County students eat breakfast at school every day, thousands more could benefit if local schools improved their breakfast programs, according to the 2006-07 School Breakfast Report Card, released this week by the Pennsylvania Hunger Action Center. The Riverside School District is the only Northeastern Pennsylvania school district to make the center’s "Failing the Children" list. The 18 districts on the list have no breakfast programs, despite having significant numbers of students who are classified as being "low income," meaning they would qualify for a free or reduced-price breakfast.

headline: US Airways transfers flight crews
abstract: Since 2001, the number of daily flights flown out of Pittsburgh International Airport by US Airways has dropped from 560 to 68 flights, which forced many of the company’s pilots and flight attendants to commute to work at other cities. The numbers will increase because US Airways announced that all of its remaining Pittsburgh based pilots and flight attendants will have to work out of Philadelphia, Charlotte or other airports. The announcement will put an even greater strain on the system of allocating commuter flights for employees.

headline: Good thing in small package
abstract: In the wake of the 2001 terrorist attacks a "Wall Street West" was proposed, where transactions at the major markets would be recorded and stored simultaneously in order to ensure their security in the event of a disaster. The "Wall Street West" has begun with SECCAS LLC, a major Wall Street data services firm, announced that it will open a secondary data center in the Diversified Information Technologies building in downtown Scranton.

headline:
Political trail: Bush visit + campaign $
IF THERE remains a place in America where President Bush can give a speech on controlling government spending without drawing horselaughs it is Lancaster County.
abstract: President Bush will give a speech in Lancaster County, which the author believes may have something to do with the fact that the county is notoriously Republican, and Bush has an extremely low national approval rating. The author also criticizes Bush’s plans to veto legislation that would expand a program for children’s health insurance despite broad Congressional support. The author questions how Bush can ask for billions of dollars towards foreign wars in Afghanistan and Iraq while allowing important domestic programs to suffer.

headline: Storms: Brewing of a 'bomb'
abstract: Weather forecasters described a recent storm as a "bomb" more intense than some tropical systems.  They say we should consider ourselves lucky to have dodged a bigger disaster.  NJ was in a state of emergency.  8 inches of snow fell in Chester County.

headline: Committee Approves Bonus Ban Bill
abstract: null

headline: Tactic puts Chester Upland under Rendell's authority
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell and his administration have used the Education Empowerment Act to dissolve the board of the Chester Upland School District and replace them with their own appointees.  The chairman of the new empowerment board is C. Marc Woolley with other new members being Juan Baughn of the Education Department and Kathy Schultz from the University of Pennsylvania faculty.  The PA State Education Secretary Gerald Zahorchak reported that the school district is projected to run a $2.3 million deficit this year and may be in a financial crisis.

headline:
US Airways turns profit 
of $177 million in third quarter
abstract: US Airways reported a $177 million net profit for the third quarter of the year, however, it lost $40 million in Pittsburgh during the last year. These losses prompted the company to eliminate 40 daily flights to the city, lay off 450 workers and close Pittsburgh’s flight-crew base. The company’s President expects pilots and flight attendants to commute to other airports and laid-off employees to accept layoff packages.

headline: High court says city must OK SugarHouse casino in Philadelphia
abstract: Pennsylvania's highest court sided with the owners of the planned SugarHouse Casino in Philadelphia and said they may sidestep obstacles that the City Council has placed in the path of the $600 million facility. Meanwhile, Foxwoods Casino Philadelphia announced an agreement with the city on development of the city's other casino on the Delaware River. In a 6-1 decision, the state Supreme Court said the city has no authority to interfere with the Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board's selection of the SugarHouse site along the Delaware River where the casino owner, HSP Gaming LP, plans to build.

headline: Poll shows Dems have chance to control county
abstract: Montgomery County Democrats this year have a real opportunity to wrest control of county government from the hands of Republicans who have been at the helm for more than 135 years, according to county Democratic Chairman Marcel L. Groen. Groen said his belief of a Democratic takeover of county government is based on the results of a recently completed poll commissioned by the party. Of the 400 likely county voters contacted, 34 percent said they would "definitely or probably" vote for unnamed Democratic county commissioner candidates compared to the 26 percent who responded that they would cast their fate with unnamed GOP candidates, with 40 percent undecided or mixed, according to the poll.

headline: Bill to set up review of Blues deal draws fire
abstract: Consumer advocates say that a recent law to allow the state to examine the proposed merger between Highmark and Blue Cross doesn't go far enough.  Along with looking at the merger, it extends the regulatory power of the Insurance Department to non-profit companies.  One PA lawmaker said that the bill does not adequately explain its benefits to the premium payers and uninsured of the state.

headline: Cadillac public bennies
abstract: The author of the editorial criticizes the benefits that retired state employees receive and feels that it is draining taxpayers’ money. The state expects to pay $600 million to former employees next year, and these retirees contribute an extremely small percent towards their health care.

headline: Taking Exception
abstract: The author defends the Education Empowerment Board in Chester Upland for establishing a maximum number of charter school slots, which equals 37 percent of the entire district. He claims that it allows any child going there to continue going, while also ensuring predictability for parents, as well as a quality education for children who attend both charter and public schools. He claims that a maximum number had to be set to avoid uncontrolled growth and spending.

headline: VERY IMPORTANT PART OF BRIDGE MAINTENANCE
abstract: One of the main causes for the deterioration of our bridges is drainage. Rarely is systematic drain-cleaning performed. All over the city, drains in viaducts and bridges have flowers and grass growing out of them. Pipes are too small in diameter, and are never flushed properly. Nobody wants to spend the extra money for new pipes.

headline: Horse racing's return yields success, hope
abstract: The author of the editorial is pleased with the results from the first season of horse racing at Erie’s Presque Isle Downs & Casino. The author does cite some problems, including a much higher rate for euthanizing injured horses than the national average; though horse protection officials feel it’s too soon to become alarmed. Overall, the author believes that problems can be corrected and expects higher levels of betting and attendance in the future.

headline: Polling places no longer secret
abstract: Governor Rendell rescinded a policy that kept the state’s list of polling place secret from public knowledge. The policy was put into place after consultation between several state agencies following the 2004 terrorist bombings in Spain. The author of the editorial thinks the policy was ridiculous, and he is glad that Rendell reversed it.

headline: Mystery donor's $15 million library challenge
abstract: The Free Library of Philadelphia's project to build a $175,000,000 expansion of its central library got an unexpected shot in the arm recently as an anonymous donor stepped forward with a $15,000,000 pledge.  The catch is that the pledge must be matched dollar for dollar from other sources.  The grant is by far the largest gift made to the library's fundraising campaign thus far.

headline: Campaign funding reform ideas aired at House panel hearing
abstract: Changing the way political campaigns are funded in Pennsylvania is a critical step toward renewing the public's trust in state government. Rep. David Levdansky, one of at least three lawmakers sponsoring bills to impose stricter limits on campaign fundraising and spending, acknowledged that such changes have been a tough sell over the last 20 years, mainly because leaders of both parties were satisfied with the current system.

headline: Talks continue on Shaler teachers contract
abstract: Shaler Area School District teachers and school board members held contract negotiations for the first time since teachers rejected a proposed contract in November. The two sides met with a state mediator for about three hours and agreed to meet again Jan. 28, said Jo Ann Noble, president of the Shaler Area Education Association. The school board is hoping the union will present new ideas at the next meeting, said Superintendent Don Lee.

headline: Viewing Harrisburg
abstract: Although historically the proposal of tolling Interstate 80 has never been able to pass through the PA Legislature, the idea is currently gaining momentum as it is being debated in the Capitol.  The truckers' magazine Overdrive rated the Interstate the worst highway in Pennsylvania next to the Pennsylvania Turnpike.  Previous PA Governor Tom Ridge suggested only tolling out-of-state drivers, which make up 75% of the users of the highway but to no avail.

headline: Iron City boss Piccirilli to leave company
abstract:
President Joseph R. Piccirilli, the man who brought Pittsburgh Brewing Co. out of bankruptcy in 1995, will leave it when the brewery emerges from bankruptcy, which is expected to happen this spring.
