abstract: The dumping of solid waste on a farm in East Brunswick, prompted a citation by the PA Department of Environmental Protection. Synargo was eventually allowed to spread the waste on an adjacent farm. However, the issue of using sewage sludge as fertilizer continues to be a volatile one, causing two township supervisors to resign. Several neighboring townships have passed ordinances to ban the practice, prompting the PA Attorney General's Office to consider a court challenge.

headline: Col. Jeffrey Miller speaks at press club luncheon
abstract: Colonel Jeffrey Miller, PA State Police Commissioner, addressed the Pennsylvania Press Club Luncheon. Miller highlighted the priorities for the PSP and recent initiatives to combat and prevent criminal activity in the state. First, he stated that quick, reliable information sharing is imperative in order for police to act quickly and have the ability to collaborate with other local, state, or federal agencies. In 2003, the PSP created a program to collaborate with 1,200 municipal police departments throughout Pennsylvania to share information in real-time, 24 hours a day. He also discussed other priorities they are focusing on currently.

headline: Rejected casino operators won't have to foot the bill
abstract: The PA State Supreme Court ruled that the casino operators who are appealing a PA Gaming Control Board decision to grant the contract to their competitors will not be responsible for the projected losses in state revenue if their appeals are rejected.  This motion filed by the gaming board was against four losing bidders: Riverwalk Casino in Philadelphia, two in Pittsburgh, and one in the Poconos.  The companies argued that this cost would discourage anyone from appealing a future decision.

headline: Republicans help former legislator
abstract: The author of the editorial is displeased with the $225,000 a year salary that former state Representative Brett Feese is making as the chief counsel to House Republicans and an in-house lawyer. The author doesn’t buy into justifications that he would be making more in the private sector and that he is actually saving the House money. The author ultimately believes that he is yet another example of House Republicans taking care of their own.

headline: DEP to hold hearing on landfill
abstract: The PA State Department of Environmental Protection is holding a public hearing with area residents of Pen Argyl to do a harms and benefits analysis of a proposed increase to Grand Central Sanitary Landfill.  Grand Central Landfill is owned by Waste Management Incorporated and wants to expand by 42 acres.  Lucy Eron, a representative of the Slate Belt Environmental Committee, has claimed that this expansion will only allow Grand Central to continue expanding in the future.

headline: Correction: Judge-Illegal Rentals story
abstract: The article is a correction of a previous published story that Common Pleas Judge Rayford Means did not obtain a city-required business-privilege license for landlords as the Philadelphia Department of License and Inspections recently reported that he did in fact obtain the license.

headline: Rendell names Oregon man insurance commissioner
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell appointed Joel Scott Ario as the state's new insurance commissioner to replace Diane Koken.  Ario was Oregon's chief insurance regulator and claims to want to review the new merger between Highmark and Independence Blue Cross to do what's best for the consumer.

headline: Reputable breeding community should be heeded for revisions
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell has proposed a system that would enforce uniform standards like crate sizes, exercise requirements and grass surfaces for all kennels in Pennsylvania.  The Independent Regulatory Review Commission has called Rendell's administration's proposal a "one-size-fits-all" approach that is "at odds with the recognition that not all kennels are alike." The state Agriculture Department, which has oversight for dog law enforcement, has estimated the costs of complying with the new regulations to be in the range of $5,000 to $20,000.

headline: Draw clean water from farm bill
abstract: The federal farm bill favors Midwestern states, but US Rep. Chris Carney and US Sen. Bob Casey Jr., both from PA, have proposed new legislation to more equitably distribute funds and provide cleaner water and air. The bill promotes the reduction of animal waste flow into the Chesapeake. The Chesapeake Health and Environmentally Sound Stewardship of Energy and Agriculture Act of 2007 also promotes additional conservation methods. Editors believe Congress should ensure cleaner water in the next version of the Farm Bill.

headline: Court says Pa. deputies lack power to investigate drug cases
abstract: PA's illegal-drug law does not permit sheriff's deputies to investigate crimes that occur outside their presence, the state Supreme Court said in the latest of a series of rulings delineating their powers. The 4-2 decision granted a request by the defendant in a Bradford County methamphetamine investigation that items seized in a 2003 search should not be used against him. Justice Max Baer wrote that the majority opinion should not "be read to suggest that the General Assembly lacks authority to grant broader investigatory powers to sheriffs."

headline: Rendell opposes panel to review insurance merger
abstract: Several bills have been introduced to grant authority to the PA Department of Insurance to review insurance mergers, now that Highmark Inc. and Independence Blue Cross are considering a merger. The companies would hold 53 of the state's insurance market. PA Governor Rendell opposes the legislation. PA Sen. Don White supports legislation to create a Senate appointed commission to review merger proposals. Rendell wants to keep the process apolitical.

headline: Return confusing
abstract: Frank Stearns of Dillsburg is confused on why PA Governor Ed Rendell is allowed to dedicate illegal donations he received to the charity of his choice.  He feels that this money should be given to reimburse the government or law enforcement agency that pursued the case in order to relieve taxpayers.

headline: Environmentalists oppose proposed change in mining rule
abstract: The U.S. Office of Surface Mining (OSM) was criticized by a number of people during a public hearing in Washington County over its proposal to change a rule that prohibits most mining activities within 100 feet of streams. The OSM claims that it would provide more clarity on guidelines, but many environmental groups argued that it would seriously damage streams and wildlife. A decision on the matter will be made next year.

headline: Crimes don't negate pension
abstract: Former Nitschmann Principal John Acerra, who is going to prison after being convicted of selling drugs at his school, will still be eligible for some benefits under the Public Employee Pension Forfeiture Act. He won’t receive full benefits because he doesn’t meet minimum age or service requirements, but his crimes won’t render him ineligible.

headline: Senate weakens smoking-ban bill
abstract: Certain private clubs and bars could possibly receive an exemption from the statewide ban on smoking in public places in a bill that PA Senate recently amended.  Whereas the bans would apply to places like malls, arenas, restaurants, stores, campuses, and convention centers, the full or partial exemptions would be given to slot-machine bars, cigar bars, private clubs, and nonprofit fundraisers among others.  The Pennsylvania Tavern Association has lobbied for exemptions as they are afraid they well lose business if they don't receive an exemption.

headline: Reynolds strike issues, competing claims are aired online
abstract: Since Reynolds teachers went on strike last week, the local school board and teachers’ union have been battling via the internet. Each side has been posting strikingly different claims and counterclaims over contract negotiations on their websites, which has made it difficult for some local residents to determine who to believe. Each side's website is listed at the end of the article.

headline: Ethics panel rules against Rendell's appointees
abstract: The PA Ethics Commission ruled that grants made by Secretary of the Department of Environmental Protection, Michael DiBerardinis, and Department of Conservation and Natural Resources Secretary, Kathleen McGinty, to the PA Environmental Council and the PA Horticultural Society, both which employ spouses of the secretaries, are conflicts of interest. The panel encouraged PA Governor Ed Rendell to direct disbursement in such cases to other authorities. The Senate was right to request an Ethics opinion before reconfirming the secretaries.

headline: Deadly stabbing adds to bloody weekend
abstract: Six people were murdered over the weekend in one of the city's bloodiest eruptions of violence this year. Shortly after 11 p.m. Friday, Diedra Burkett, 42, was stabbed multiple times in her home on Mercy Street near 20th in South Philadelphia during what police said was a domestic argument. A 15-year-old boy was injured.

headline: Sheetz wins beer battle
abstract:
For the first time ever, customers at a Sheetz Inc. store in Altoona were able to order a six-pack of beer along with their cheese nachos and made-to-order sub. Thousands of Pennsylvania beer drinkers are no doubt thinking it's about time. But others wonder where it might lead. This isn't the first time a Pennsylvania convenience store has been granted permission to sell beer. In the early 1990s, a Wawa store in Philadelphia was given the green light, but the store has since sold its license. 
 Sheetz has been fighting legal and logistical battles to get to this point since the PA Liquor Control Board granted it a provisional OK back in September 2004.

headline: Rove's political acumen was evident in Pa.
abstract: Beyond his Texas home, few states received more of Karl Rove's attention than Pennsylvania. In 2004, particularly, the state proved to be a laboratory demonstrating both the power and the limits of the political strategy that produced two presidential terms for George W. Bush. State Republicans who worked with Mr. Rove described him yesterday as a political genius whose planning had elicited unprecedented turnouts among core Republican voters.

headline: Federal action worsens Fayette mine acid flow
abstract: Greater Redstone Clearwater Initiative, an environmental group, is threatening to sue the U.S. Office of Surface Mining for tapping an abandoned mine in Fayette County and releasing up to 700 gallons of polluted water into a stream that eventually flows into the Monongahela River. The effects have seriously setback the watershed group’s cleanup efforts, and some members claim that the federal agency acted unlawfully; though they are seeking a compromise in order to fix the problem. In addition, Judy Silvis has refused to allow mining officials back onto her property and demands compensation for the government ruining the value of her property, which has been substantially flooded on a number of occasions.

headline: Death row inmates sue over Pa. lethal injection rules
abstract: Three death row inmates claim in the latest challenge to lethal injection that Pennsylvania's method of executing prisoners poses an "unnecessary risk of pain and suffering." The state has failed to make sure that executioners are adequately trained, and its procedures for administering the lethal cocktail are flawed, the inmates said in a federal lawsuit. State Department of Corrections spokeswoman Sue McNaughton said the department believes that lethal injections are administered properly in Pennsylvania.

headline: Slots licensing methods questioned
abstract: Representatives gathered to testify at a Senate hearing on whether the State Police and the PA Gaming Control Board’s Bureau of Investigation (BIE) shared important information while conducting background checks for slot-machine licenses. The issues became important due to Mount Airy Casino, which opened yesterday but was being investigated by a grand jury. The FBI refused to give the BIE information because it doesn’t consider it to be a law enforcement agency, which will necessitate changes in the BIE’s structure.

headline: Scandals bubbling up in Harrisburg could be toxic to spirit of reform
abstract: Last week, a former state lawmaker was indicted on charges of putting two relatives on the state payroll as ''ghost'' employees. A day earlier, seven key House Democratic aides were suddenly dismissed in what House Majority Leader H. William DeWeese, D-Greene, said was an effort ''in furthering my commitment to reform and change in the House Democratic Caucus.''

headline: Forget fluoride in water supply
abstract: The author is against a bill that would mandate adding fluoride to Pennsylvania’s water supply and cites evidence that it is wasteful, not effective and actually has some adverse side effects. The author believes that proper dental and health education will provide much better results.

headline: Deputy gets transfer after grand jury talk
abstract: Sheriff's Deputy Gim B. Yee was asked to turn in his radio and report for duty across the street in Allegheny County criminal court. The sheriff's department veteran was called to testify before a federal grand jury about a Common Pleas judge whose court he's worked in for 13 years. Two days later, the acting sheriff transferred him to juvenile court for an indeterminate time period, said John Bacharach, the department solicitor. The U.S. attorney called the deputy to testify about guns he received from the judge. Routinely, prosecutors submit requests to destroy firearms after criminal prosecutions involving guns and, routinely, judges approve these requests.

headline: Slots parlor will have view of rivers, city skyline
abstract: Pittsburgh North Shore's Majestic Star Casino plans to have a view of the cities three rivers and the city skyline when it opens next year.  Despite the Pittsburgh Planning Commission being briefed on the building's blueprints today, construction is delayed because two losing bidders for the slots license have appealed the PA Supreme Court to overturn the PA Gaming Control Board's decision.  Bob Oltmann, the casino's spokesman, reports the casino plans to have four themed restaurants, two nightclubs, and a martini bar on the top floor of the atrium.

headline: See Dick Run.  Bye Dick.
abstract: Dick Willey, the CEO of Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency, is quitting after five years and a series of controversies dealing with the agency's spending on bonuses and lavish retreats.  Willey's bonus of $180,857 last year exceeded PA Governor Ed Rendell's yearly salary, but he claims the bonuses were necessary to retain the best workers.

headline: Gamesa seeks to build more wind turbines in central Pa.
abstract: Officials at Gamesa Energy USA met with Snyder Township officials to seek preliminary reactions to the company's plans to lease land for wind turbines stretching from Blair to Centre County. Tyrone Mayor Jim Kilmartin said there is interest but approval is premature. A subdivision and land planner with the Centre County Planning office, Anson Burwell, said a few leases have been secured. A public meeting is scheduled to address concerns from residents.

headline: DeSantis, Ravenstahl differ on police policy
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl and Mark DeSantis, who will challenge Ravenstahl in the upcoming mayoral election, agreed that battling crime should be a key area of focus. However, DeSantis won the endorsement of the city’s police union by promising to eliminate residency requirements, increase the number of police officers, and update the department’s vehicles. Ravenstahl cited some successes while he was mayor, and he is against the elimination of the residency requirement and wants to enact legislation to keep officers from leaving Pittsburgh.

headline: Stakes raised in gaming probe
abstract: The owner of JC Vending Inc. and four bar owners were arrested on charges that stem from the alleged distribution and use of illegal gambling machines. According to investigators, JC Vending supplied illegal gambling machines to the four bars. The arrests are part of increased law enforcement efforts to target illegal gambling, and authorities are still looking into further arrests and hope that a message will be sent to others to stop illegal gambling.

headline: Senate bill offers hope in fight for open-records reform
abstract: The author of the editorial claims that PA has one of the worst open records laws in the country, and recent "reforms" would actually make public access to information even more difficult. The author was pleased with the original bill, which was proposed by Representative Tim Mahoney and supported by the PA Newspaper Association. However, the author criticizes the House State Government Committee for adding exemptions to the bill with no public input and hopes for better results from the Senate’s version of the bill.

headline: Guest Essay: Politicians shouldn't meddle with deer issues
abstract: The author finds PA Rep. Dan Moul's proposition to assign county officials the management of deer absurd. He believes PA Legislators should stay out of the Pa Game  Comission's business. The author agrees with executive director of the PA Federation of Sportsmen's Clubs, Melody Zullinger, that the meddling by politicians is about control of resources. Some legislators are attempting to force a merger with the PA Department of Conservation and Natural Resources and take the money that funds the Commission.  The author urges readers to insist on fee increases for hunting licenses.

headline: Dismayed at headlines
abstract: The author of the letter writes that they were dismayed at the choice of headlines for the horrific child-abuse case in Delaware County. In the Jan. 26 and Jan. 27 editions of the newspaper, the stories were headlined, "Three in Delco charged with child pornography," and "Calls, notes in child-porn case." He writes that the cases were not just a matter of "pornography," but allegedly of multiple and numerous sexual assaults and rapes of children.

headline: State gaming board grants target illegal slot gambling
abstract: Allegheny County law enforcement agencies received grants totaling nearly $600,000 Thursday to combat illegal slot machines, the State Gaming Control Board announced. The board awarded $5 million in grants this year statewide for training, education and enforcement, said board member Ken McCabe, who presented checks to Pittsburgh and Allegheny County police, and the county District Attorney's Office. Prosecutors in Erie, Lebanon and Montgomery counties, along with Susquehanna police, received grants and money will be awarded in coming months to law enforcement agencies in Washington County.

headline: Senate hearing to examine liquor board hire
abstract: For years, the PA Senate has confirmed gubernatorial nominees to the PA Liquor Control Board, which meets once a month and pays its members about $65,000 a year. But senators didn't have anything to say last month, when one of their own, retired PA Senator Joe Conti, was named to a $150,000 post called chief executive officer of the LCB. It's a hands-on position for day-to-day management of the $1.7 billion-a-year wine and spirits agency, a job that hasn't been filled for 20 years. The three-member board voted 2-1 to go along with PA Governor Ed Rendell's choice of Mr. Conti for the job. Board members Patrick Stapleton and Tom Goldsmith voted for Mr. Conti and then-board Chairman Jonathan Newman voted against.

headline: Gypsy moths return unopposed this year
abstract: Luzerne County chief of environment and recreation Andy Gegaris, was told there was no money available from the PA Department of Conservation and Natural Resources for spraying to protect against gypsy moths. Luzerne County did not submit a request for funding, which concerned DCNR Bureau of Forestry district forester Brad Elison as funding has become available. Because the county failed to apply for it, it is too late. Gegaris says the new funds available were allocated by the governor for state lands only. Neighboring counties have sprayed.

headline: Domestic violence group blasts Rendell
abstract: The PA Coalition Against Domestic Violence are angered that two-thirds of the long awaited $1.2 million budget increase for state domestic programs will go mostly to go to the city of Philadelphia as opposed to being spread evenly over the state.  Human services programs for the PA Department of Public Welfare also has an increase of $353,000.  Chuck Ardo, spokesman for PA Governor Ed Rendell, only reported that the details of this budget increase have not been finalized in the Legislature as of now.

headline: State panel's stance on slots award draws ire
abstract: Rep. Douglas Reichley said he was baffled that the Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board thinks it can "stiff-arm" the Legislature and refuse to answer questions about its awarding of Pittsburgh's casino license. He said he wants to ask the board about its process for conducting financial background investigations and how the agency evaluated gambling losses by Don Barden, owner of PITG Gaming, who won the Pittsburgh slots license in December.

headline: Sleepy old Harrisburg a happenin' place today
abstract: Downtown Improvement District Manager Jeff Murison notes how much Harrisburg has changed from 20 years ago. Mayor Stephen Reed, who is widely credited with the city's rebirth, hopes to eventually draw retail businesses to the downtown area. Harrisburg Young Professionals has also helped to make the city livable for the white collar crowd. Reed is determined to keep Harrisburg well positioned for the future.

headline: High lead levels detected at Highland Park's Farmhouse Playground
abstract: After a three year old boy was found to have a significant amount of lead in his blood, which could cause damage to the brain, central nervous system and kidneys, the Allegheny County Health Department inspected Highland Park playground and found an area of soil to contaminated with twice as much lead as is recommended by the federal Environmental Protection Agency. The city quickly scraped off old paint chips, but they didn’t post a warning about the site or remove contaminated soil, which has many parents up in arms. The city has hired an independent engineering firm to develop a long term solution but has said that there was no rush because it wasn’t an "imminent hazard."

headline: Domestic violence services funding attacked
abstract: Jacquie Albert, director of Fayette County's Domestic Violence Services, has recently criticized the Pennsylvania's government distribution of increased funding for domestic violence prevention and services.  Albert quoted statistics showing that Fayette had 1.35 deaths per 100,000 residents as opposed to Philadelphia's .79 deaths per 100,000, where 2/3 of the funding is going.  Albert has also reported gaining support from PA Representative Tim Mahoney and PA Senator Rich Kasunic.

headline: State slots have little effect on W.Va.clubs
abstract: In 2001 West Virginia Governor Bob Wise helped pass a law that created a state-run gambling industry that allowed bars, restaurants and fraternal organizations to operate slot machines. 605 of these businesses across northern West Virginia haven’t been significantly affected by competition from six casinos that have opened in PA. This is likely because most of these clubs cater to locals who don’t want to travel all the way to PA to gamble.

headline: Slots choice ill-advised
abstract: The author of the letter writes that Philadelphia citizens should not be proud to live there if "the ill-advised casinos" are placed on the water front.  He feels that his representatives from City Hall and Harrisburg have showed little regard for the long-term consequences of building two casinos near infrastructure that cannot handle present demand.

headline: Hunters shooting for safety
abstract: Statewide, hunting related shootings per sportsman have declined nearly 80 percent since 1959, when hunter education training began. Since the 1960s the number of shooting incidents fell to less than 10 per 100,000 from almost 50 per 100,000 hunter. The success of hunter education classes, which were made mandatory for first-time hunters in 1982 and expanded to all hunters in 1986. The classes have been extended from four to 10 hours over the years. The mandatory use of fluorescent orange clothing since 1988. Hunters must wear at least 250 square inches of orange on their head, chest and/or back during rifle season.

headline: Drug deal, gunshots - and some lucky cops
abstract: Officers Jeff Walker and Linwood Norman marched down a blighted block of North Philly, straight toward an alleged crack supplier and an alleged street dealer who were about to make a deal. Police officials said John Sullivan charged toward Walker and Norman and fired a shot from a .45-caliber semi-automatic pistol that he had hidden in his jacket sleeve. But the struggle ended in minutes, and the cops took Sullivan into custody. A few blocks away, Dmitrius Tolloiver, 20, also was apprehended, and officers recovered $5,200 worth of crack cocaine, police said.

headline: State Supreme Court upholds casino licenses in Philadelphia
abstract: The PA Supreme Court upheld the decision of the PA Gaming Control Board to allow SugarHouse Casino and Foxwoods Casino Philadelphia to build slot-machine casinos in Philadelphia.  The appeal was made by a losing applicant, Riverwalk Casino group, after losing the bidding contest.  Chief Justice Ralph Cappy wrote the decision that said the gaming board's decision followed all laws correctly.

headline: Smoking limit, utility shutoff lose to special interest influence
abstract: You don't have to be a political insider to figure out who really is represented by PA's representative government. In two key developments in the Legislature, it was Special Interests 2, The People 0. First, it became clear that a statewide smoking ban had become bogged down in the details, thanks to the tobacco, casino and tavern lobbies. Second, a move to reform how utili ties go about shut ting off service to households with overdue bills was overwhelmingly de feated, 24-5, in the House Consumer Affairs Committee, thanks to a full- court press by the utility lobby.

headline: Larger landfill planned for site
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Protection preliminarily granted approval for Allegheny Energy to expand its landfill in light of the increased amount of byproduct to be produced by the site's desulfurization scrubbers. The current rate of byproduct will fill the site within 2 years, and the new technology is expected to double the current rate. The expansion will allow the site to remain operational for the next 7 years. Surrounding municipalities have yet to file a response.

headline: Easton shooting victim recovering in hospital
abstract: The victim involved in yesterday's gunfight in Easton is recovering from his injuries after undergoing surgery at a local hospital. Easton police Lt. Scott Casterline said this morning the 21-year-old man, who lives in Easton, was able to speak to city detectives following the surgery last night. The investigation is progressing, Casterline said. Police had taken one person into custody last night and were questioning a second person about his possible involvement

headline: State's wine deals: Beyond compare?
abstract: Entering PAs wine and spirits stores, customers are often happily confronted with dozens of displays of Chairman's Selection wines at startling savings. The program is expected to survive the resignation of its creator, PA Liquor Control Board chairman Jonathan Newman, but his successor acknowledges criticism that the pricing of a few of those wines is "not portrayed correctly." In just over three years, Newman said before stepping down just after New Year's, the board has offered 500 wines as Chairman's Selections, selling more than five million bottles.

headline: Some may be happy about slots arrival
abstract: The author of the letter writes that he knows many people of modest means who enjoy playing slots with no expectation of retiring on their winnings, countering a previous letter to the editor claiming that "virtually the entire citizenry" is against slots.  The author writes that Philadelphia citizens shouldn't worry that slots will ruin the city's reputation since it known for 400 gun deaths a year and adult entertainment and for not doing anything progressive since the Declaration of Independence.

headline: Larva can devastate ash trees
abstract: Matthew Kern, a service forester for the PA Department of Conservation and Natural Resources in York and Adams counties, has reported that the destructive emerald ash borer bug originally from Asia could be found in south-central Pennsylvania.  As a result, the forestry officials are asking not to plant ash trees as these bugs destroyed over 10 million ash trees in Michigan.

headline:
Emergency declared at overcrowded jail
Minimal offender unit being fit with new fencing after other county prisons stop accepting local inmates.
abstract: After learning that other counties could no longer accept its excess prisoners, the Luzerne County Prison Board announced a state of emergency, which authorized Warden Fischi to award a contract to build additional fencing around a minimal-offenders unit in order to free up more prison space. The plan is only a temporary solution to the county’s overcrowded prison population and will cause some problems; though prison officials see not other alternatives. Long term solutions remain uncertain.

headline: Study: Arts generate $1.3 billion, 40,000 jobs in SE Pa.
abstract: A study by the Greater Philadelphia Cultural Alliance has reported that arts and cultural organizations in the southeastern Pennsylvania area create $1.3 billion in annual expenditures, 40,000 jobs and $158.5 million in state and local taxes.  Local governments also receive $5 in tax revenues for every dollar of funding for the groups, and the state receives $2.50 for every dollar in funding.  The report is a study of 177 organizations and 2,324 audience surveys.

headline: Specify disclosure in state ethics
abstract: Pennsylvania’s courts continue to deal with a host of challenges that were filed this year to primary candidates’ financial disclosure forms. Forms were challenged for offices ranging from county commissioner to mayor of Philadelphia to state Supreme Court. In 2006, the state Supreme Court made a ruling that the state Ethics Act is meant to boost public confidence in candidates and public officials by requiring certain financial disclosures. Most of the challenges deal with a "statement of financial interests,."

headline: Local businesses should go green
abstract: Edward Quinn, senior state executive for IBM in Pennsylvania, encourages businesses to go green in order to not only save money but combat pollution and global warming.  He cites the American Lung Association's statistic that Allegheny County is one of the top municipalities in the nation for smog, and Pennsylvania ranks third among all states in global warming emissions.  He continues that going green is possible by collaboration by industry, government, researchers and consumers to develop new and innovative technology.

headline: Ex-deputy attorney general says he was wrongly fired
abstract: A senior deputy attorney general, Thomas Eddy, has sued PA Attorney General Tom Corbett in federal court, saying he was fired for raising concerns that recently fired co-workers were terminated on political grounds. Corbett denies these allegations.

headline: SugarHouse gets a license to build
abstract: Philadelphia's commerce director awarded SugarHouse Casino a license yesterday to build on 12 acres of submerged state-owned land along the Delaware River. Stephanie Naidoff's ruling is yet another move in the chess game that pits Mayor Street and Gov. Rendell, who want to see two casinos built along the riverfront, against City Council, which has allied itself with neighborhood opponents and anti-casino activists. A lawsuit challenging Naidoff's decision is a foregone conclusion. The casinos in Philadelphia have thus far been blocked - first by appeals of the Gaming Control Board decision on casino locations, then by the city's refusal to grant zoning and building permits.

headline: Specter on immigration
abstract: US Senate Majority Leader Harry Reid is counting on moderate Republican Arlen Specter to convince his fellow Republicans overhaul the nation's immigration laws. Reid hopes to create a guest worker program before the upcoming campaign season further politicizes the issue. Specter is known for his moderate streak and helped negotiate a bipartisan bill last year which died in a conference committee between the House and Senate.

headline: Money woes squeeze recycling efforts
abstract: The commissioners of Cumberland have decided that they will not use tax revenue to maintain local recycling programs, which costs around $600,000.  Due to court battles last by various counties last year, the main source funding, administrative fess charged on each ton of trash dumped at facilities, has vanished.  PA Representative Mario Scavello has introduced legislation that would allow counties to impose administrative fees of $4 a ton in order to help save the recycling programs.

headline: Feeling the loss
abstract: At the Fraternal Order of Police's 14th annual memorial service for fallen officers, three PA officers who died in service were honored. They included members from the Philadelphia Police Department, the Reading Police Department, and Upper Saucon Township. The Pittsburgh Police Emerald Society Pipes and Drums were on hand for the service.

headline: SugarHouse says it's poised to start work
abstract: With a state Supreme Court ruling backing its bid to build in Philadelphia, SugarHouse Casino yesterday said it would break ground within three weeks even as casino opponents made plans to "occupy" the project's Delaware Avenue construction site. The Supreme Court overrode City Council and granted SugarHouse permission to build its $550 million facility in Fishtown/Northern Liberties, clearing most legal obstacles. SugarHouse announced its intention to complete the project by October 2009. The ruling may also clear a path for the city's other planned slots parlor, Foxwoods Casino, to build on Columbus Boulevard in the Pennsport neighborhood of South Philadelphia.

headline: Specter says he'll run in 2010 at age of 80
abstract: US Senator Arlen Specter of Pennsylvania has already decided to run for re-election in 2010  at the age of 80.  Specter would like to gain chairmanship of the Senate Judiciary Committee as well as rise in ranking in the Appropriations Committee.  Specter is considered a moderate Republican who begin his political career as a district attorney in Philadelphia.

headline: No three-peat
abstract: The editorial discusses the second time the Bruce Mansfield Power Plant spewed oily soot onto the houses of Shippingport residents in less than a year.  While the PA Department of Environmental Protection reports that the this does not pose a health risk to the residents, the author feels that two incidents is a serious problem.  Despite the editorial's reaction, Pat Lampe, the borough council president, claims that borough officials were pleased with the response.

headline: Firearms sense
abstract: Jay Rhine, a self-proclaimed gun owner and former member of the National Rifle Association, supports PA Governor Ed Rendell's proposal to limit gun sales to one per month.  While he supports law-abiding citizens purchasing guns for self-protection, he questions the financial motives of not supporting this bill.

headline: Table games in advance in W. Va.
abstract: West Virginia governor Joe Manchin signed legislation allowing the four racetrack counties to pursue casino table games at their tracks.  Machin signed the bill after ensuring it allowed a referendum on the issue as well as providing funding for in-home senior care.  West Virginia's new table games would increase out-of-state gamblers and have an advantage over the slots opening in Pennsylvania.

headline: Specter: Driven to crisscross Pa.
abstract: Political jousting in town hall meetings is a summer ritual for US Sen. Arlen Specter, who uses congressional recesses to visit all 67 counties in Pennsylvania - his version of a permanent campaign. Most politicians try to mingle with voters, but few are as methodical and intense about it. The tradition dates to mid-1980, when Specter trailed the Democratic candidate for Senate, former Pittsburgh Mayor Pete Flaherty, by 19 percentage points. Specter promised to go to every county, and the press loved the gimmick.

headline: One year later, no report on toxic spill
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Protection and the US Environmental Protection Agency have not finished an investigation of Merck & Corporation Incorporated after they admitted to spilling a cyanide-compound into Wissahickon Creek.  Maya van Rossum, the Delaware Riverkeeper, is frustrated that Merck, after acknowledging their mistake, has not been fined or punished yet after a year.  Bonnie Smith, EPA spokeswoman, has reported that 28 inspectors from both state and federal organizations are completing a thorough investigation, and because of the size of the facility, the report is taking a while to complete.

headline: Flawed Phila. formula: Arrest, release, repeat
abstract: Until eclipsed by the murder of Officer Chuck Cassidy, it was a jarring crime that rattled Center City - and seemed to signal a kind of open season on police. In an apparent hit attempt, a gunman fired into a parked car, wounding two men and a woman, then shot three times at a pursuing police officer. Trying to get away, Jerome Whitaker jumped into the Schuylkill and drowned. The killers criminal life is outlined.

headline: The "house" wins - again
abstract: Bruce Barron, the President of No Dice, expresses his frustration that certain government and public organizations are supporting the casinos' interests rather than the citizens' interests.  He cites the example of the four of the losing casino applicants who are not serving the state by costing a potential $100 million in taxes by appealing to the PA Supreme Court.  He also discusses his skepticism that the Philadelphia City Council will continue going against the casinos' interests, his anger at the Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board's working against the people's interests, and the Carnegie Science Center's double-speak on Pittsburgh's new casino.

headline: Stalemate emerges over state budget
abstract: Democrats in the PA House of Representatives rejected the Senate version of the $27 billion budget and in turn, forced a conference committee with the governor and caucus leaders to work out a compromise.  Approximately one week remains until state funding will run out and 45,000 or almost one half of the state employees will be furloughed and casinos will have to cease operations.  PA Governor Ed Rendell is demanding that his proposals for alternative energy, health care improvement and new biotech labs are dealt with before he signs the budget.

headline: Other Views
abstract: The editorial supports the smoking ban passed by Allegheny County despite it being struck down by the Commonwealth Court last month.  It also encourages other lawmakers to follow the lead of PA Senator Wayne Fontana of Brookline, who has publicly pushed for the passage of the Clean Indoor Air Act.  The article cites a study by Quinnipiac University that found that 60% of Pennsylvania voters favor a smoking ban in bars, restaurants, and public buildings.

headline: Free gun locks easy to obtain in Pa.
abstract: Project ChildSafe is a national program that gives police departments gun locks, which are given out for free to the public and could help prevent accidental shootings, such as a recent case involving a nine year old boy in Fayette County. The article describes the efforts of a number of police departments throughout PA to raise awareness and give away the free locks. Since 2003, the state has received about 1.4 million locks to give away, and a number of gun shops also provide them.

headline: This beer measure would hurt many businesses
abstract: The author of this letter to the editor is unhappy with a senate panel's plans to permit six-pack beer sales at beer distributors because the distributors could undercut prices and cause small businesses and restaurants to lose business. The author hopes the legislature votes down the bill and questions why the senate isn’t tackling more pressing issues.

headline: State authorities were tardy questions on the ground they don't understand.  That could send the issue back to the governor and the Legislature.
abstract: This editorial supports the school directors who feel that the state government has wasted their time by forcing them to write the referendum "property tax reform" question so that all people understand equally.  The PA Department of Education and the PA State Department have recently told the PA Bureau of Commissions, Elections and Legislation that the questions in the various districts' ballots must be uniform but will allow the county election officials to work it out.  The main concern is the disparity between questions in different counties could cause many legal problems.

headline: Pa. biologists head into bear dens to manage animal's comeback
abstract: Mark Ternent, information and education supervisor with the PA Game Commission, has been traveling throughout the state tagging and weighing of hibernating mother black bears and their cubs.  His job is to decide the optimal ratio of bears to people in order to determine how many bears need to be killed by hunters.  Steve Williams, president of the Wildlife Management Institute, thinks that increased interaction between humans and bears have created widespread concern and calls the Poconos the "epicenter" of this interaction.

headline: Fumo told he's target of probe
abstract: Federal prosecutors last year sent a formal warning to PA State Senator Vincent J. Fumo that he may be indicted. The issuance of a so-called target letter from prosecutors to Fumo  is a significant milestone in the four-year investigation, which appears to be in its final stages. The target letter was sent to Fumo last summer, around the time two of his computer aides were charged with destroying evidence to thwart the investigation, sources said.

headline: Top Pa. health insurers merging
abstract: The two biggest health insurers in Pennsylvania, Highmark Inc. and Independence Blue Cross, are merging to control more than 50 percent of the state's insurance market while still maintaining nonprofit status.  The PA Senate approved a bill to give the PA Department of Insurance more power over mergers out of concern that this merger will destroy competition within the state.  Both the US Justice Department and the state attorney's office are reviewing this merger to watch for potential antitrust and charitable trust problems.

headline: State budget battle could generate political casualties
abstract: The state of Pennsylvania may furlough 26,000 workers without pay this Monday if the two political parties within the Capitol do not reach an agreement on the 2007-2008 budget.  PA Governor Ed Rendell is insisting that the Legislature pass or at least act on other pieces of legislation including his energy, health care and transportation proposals while the Republicans would rather pass a less ambitious budget and wait to act on the other proposals.  PA Representative Dwight Evans feels that the citizens of the state voted so heavily in favor of Rendell for more ambitious plans while PA Representative Mike Turzai believes Rendell is misinterpreting the election results.

headline: Pollution cleanup needs funding to avoid layoffs
abstract: It won't be a happy new year for more than 100 state employees if lawmakers fail to find a way to continue paying for a cleanup of Pennsylvania's contaminated land and streams. Barring an accord, the state will send furlough notices on Dec. 14 to 130 employees of the hazardous sites cleanup program, said Pennsylvania Department of Environmental Protection spokesman Neil Weaver. The employees would work through December, Weaver said, but face layoffs early next year. It's unclear when the program's money will run out.

headline: Gaming investigator acquitted of falsification
abstract: Dauphin County Court Judge John F. Cherry acquitted Michael Ray Rosenberry, an investigator for the PA Gaming Control Board, of one count of false swearing and three counts of unsworn falsification.  Rosenberry was charged after state police discovered his college degree came from an online diploma mill.

headline: US Airways drops bid for Delta
abstract: US Airways Group might scout for another merger partner down the road, analysts say, after it dropped a hostile bid for bankrupt Delta Air Lines when creditors spurned the deal.  CEO Douglas Steenland said that Northwest, which plans to exit bankruptcy in the spring, will remain independent this year. US Airways mounted its $8 billion bid for Delta in mid-November, then raised the offer to $10.2 billion, including $5 billion in cash. But with Delta managers opposed and creditors cagey, US Airways set a Feb. 1 deadline for the offer to expire.

headline: State creates major self-inflicted wound
abstract: This editorial expresses frustration at the PA Legislature's and PA Governor Ed Rendell's inability to overcome the politics and pass a budget on time without furloughing state employees.  It also reports that the Pennsylvania government has meet the PA Constitution's deadline of July 1st with a new budget once in the past 5 years.  The author views this as another blotch on the Pennsylvania state government's record as there are no legitimate excuses for this to happen.

headline: Pa. seeks authority over nuclear materials
abstract: The US Nuclear Regulatory Commission is in the process of considering an appeal by PA Governor Ed Rendell to join 35 other states in having the authority to license, make and enforce rules and inspect businesses that work with radioactive materials.  This authority could allow the state to collect $2 million in fees while these fees would cost 30-40% lower than current federal fees.  Both the PA Department of Environmental Protection and PA Bureau of Radiation Protection would split oversight of the Commission's license.

headline: GOP renews push for limits on money awards by juries
abstract: PA Representative Mike Turzai and former Governor Dick Thornburgh support efforts to end what they consider to be excessive jury awards in civil cases. They argue that legislation would stabilize the cost for liability insurance for doctors and would prevent the cost of excessive jury awards from being passed onto consumers. The PA Trial Lawyers Association and a man who was awarded a settlement because doctors misdiagnosed his wife are against the bill.

headline: US Steel purchase no pipe dream
abstract: US Steel Corporation has purchased tubing maker Lone Star Technologies Incorporated for $2.1 billion cash and will become the largest producer of tubular products in North America.  The tubular industry has recently experienced a lot of mergers recently as energy explorers, such as Exxon-Mobil, are boosting their spending.  Lone Star employs 2,784, whereas 1,127 of these works are members of the United Steelworkers union.

headline: State fails to deliver
abstract: What does open-records reform and a smoking ban have in common? They are held hostage in the legislature, having passed both the House and Senate but needing work before becoming law. A smoking ban, you’ll recall, was approved in the waning session before summer recess, with the House passing a more complete ban than the Senate, which added all kinds of exceptions. It puffed out there, however; no action followed in the fall to pass a measure that would be supported by many state residents and municipal officials. The legislature, instead, spent the past few months concentrating on historic reform of the state’s 50-year-old open-records law.

headline: Pa. sees tougher laws on mining
abstract: Shortly after the Utah mine collapse on Aug. 6, Gov. Rendell issued a statement saying he would make passage of a new mining law a priority this fall, and the chief sponsor of a long-stalled mine bill is prepared to introduce a more comprehensive bill this fall. Meanwhile, mine operators and union negotiators, often at odds over regulations, say they are working toward agreement on controversial provisions contained in that phone-book-size bill. The Department of Environmental Protection said most of the key proposals being put forth by the Pennsylvania Coal Association, which represents the majority of the mine operators in the state, are unacceptable.

headline: Governor's gun proposals don't make sense
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell is wrong again about gun laws. So are the mayors around the state who agree with him. No country, state, or municipality ever lowered its crime rate by imposing new gun laws.  At his request, the House Judiciary Committee held a meeting to discuss anti-gun measures. Gov. Rendell urged members to pass some of the most onerous firearm restrictions in the state's history, including a ''one-gun-a-month'' scheme, a requirement that individuals report lost or stolen firearms and overturning Pennsylvania's pre-emption law, which forbids municipalities from adopting gun laws.

headline: Where is tax relief from gambling?
abstract: It's great to hear that $913 million was lost by Pennsylvania gamblers in the past year, half of the money to be split with the state. Shouldn't we be seeing our smiling governor on the news accepting one of those large fake checks and touting the benefits of tax relief to homeowners? Oh, that's right. I never received my tax relief, not even in the form of a bogus check.

headline: State gets bad grade on public information
abstract: The Center for Public Integrity released a report that grades how much information governors in each state must reveal about their private financial affairs and gave Pennsylvania's laws an "F."  Chuck Ardo, PA Governor Ed Rendell's spokesman, replied that Rendell voluntarily reveals his federal income tax return to the public in order to set an example to other Pennsylvania legislators and officials.  PA Representative David Steil, co-chairman on the legislative reform panel, supports opening the lawmakers' private financial records but not records of the spouses, as is recommended by the Center for Public Integrity.

headline: Panther Valley officials hope cleanup won't delay start of classes
abstract: At least 5,000 gallons of heating fuel leaked from a pipe leading from an underground tank to the new Panther Valley Middle School, seeping downhill toward the adjacent high school, threatening a nearby stream and drawing hazardous waste cleanup crews and specialists from the state Department of Environmental Protection. Classes, delayed a week so workers could finish paving the middle school parking lot, are scheduled to start. The DEP will continue to monitor it and groundwater. Officials said the fuel had not contaminated the stream.

headline: Gun bills blocked by Judiciary Committee
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell made a rare personal sales pitch to win support for three gun-control bills, but he still struck out. Rendell took the unusual step of testifying before the House Judiciary Committee on Tuesday. Saying the measures would reduce gun crimes, he asked state lawmakers to use their "common sense and backbone" to send the bills to the full House for a debate. The panel rejected two of the bills and tabled the third.

headline: Wagers remain in slump
abstract: Gambling at Mohegan Sun at Pocono Downs was down for the second week in a row. From Monday through Sunday, visitors played $33.3 million into the 1,203 slot machines in the Plains Township casino, down from $41.7 million the week before Mount Airy Casino Resort in neighboring Monroe County opened. It was the lowest weekly gambling total at the casino since March, when there were 100 fewer slot machines.

headline: State House steps forward (and slips a bit) on road to real reform
abstract: This article expresses an ambivalent opinion on the recent reforms made by the Pennsylvania House of Representatives in changing the legislative process.  While the author feels the House's new rules of prohibiting actions after 11 p.m. and released member and chamber expenses through email, it did not curb the Appropriations Committee's power to amend legislation as it sees fit.

headline: Paper ... or something that takes 20 years to degrade?
abstract:
"The best option in Pennsylvania is to use a canvas bag or to recycle your plastic bags at the local grocery store," said Jane C. Meeks, executive director of the Berks County Solid Waste Authority. 
San Francisco became the first U.S. city to outlaw the use of plastic bags at grocery stores. PA laws are also outlined along with grocer and shopper comments.

headline: Gun cultures clash and Pennsylvanians lose again
abstract: Pennsylvania's diversity showed itself again in votes against gun-control bills in a state of hunters, sportsmen and the National Rifle Association. Despite a reasoned, impassioned, at times accusatory 40-minute appeal by Gov. Ed Rendell in a rare appearance before a legislative committee, efforts to limit handgun sales, to give Philadelphia its own gun laws and to require owners to report lost or stolen handguns all failed.

headline: null
abstract: Family members of soldiers from the Allentown - based 213th Area Support Unit of the Pa. Army National Guard were invited to Gov. and Mrs. Rendell's tree lighting ceremony on Wednesday. The unit was televised from Camp Anaconda in Iraq.

headline: State judge accused of insurance fraud to run for retention
abstract: A Pennsylvania Superior Court judge indicted this week on charges of mail fraud and money laundering still plans to seek retention in November's election. Judge Michael Thomas Joyce was charged with nine separate counts stemming from two insurance claims he filed related to a car accident.

headline: Problems discovered on some turbine blades built at Games plant
abstract: The Allegheny Ridge Wind Farm project has discovered problems in seven blades that were manufactures at Gomes's Ebensburg-area plant.  Plant Manager Alberto Gross alerted officials of Portage and Washington townships, which are part of the wind farm at the Cambria-Blair border.  These problems were brought up at a meeting last Wednesday where Games and Washington and Portage townships signed an agreement about further development of the wind farm.

headline: Gun limits are needed
abstract: Why does anyone need more than 12 handguns a year? Some of those people could be selling them on the street or maybe planning a robbery, or terror attack, or maybe a school attack.  None of the laws proposed would have any negative effect on legitimate gun ownership or sales, but it just may hinder future gun crimes. The Second Amendment refers to guns for a citizen militia, and not about gun ownership in general. The Supreme Court will soon be speaking about the interpretation of gun ownership.

headline: Dems can derail troop increase, Murtha says
abstract: Democrats in Congress could derail President Bush's plan to send 21,500 more troops to Iraq by linking mandates for adequate soldier training and equipment outfitting to Defense appropriations, U.S. Representative John P. Murtha said. The Johnstown Democrat, who chairs the House subcommittee that controls the Defense budget, said adding the requirements to federal funding of the president's strategy could change the direction of the conflict. Last week, Murtha and members of the House, including Speaker Nancy Pelosi, of California, spent five days in Iraq, Afghanistan and Pakistan. Murtha said he continues to be disappointed with the situation on the ground.

headline: State officials to get pay boost
abstract: Starting with legislators’ Dec. 1 paycheck, they will receive an automatic 3.5 percent cost-of-living increase in base salary, according to the House and Senate chief clerk’s offices. That will set the base salary for state lawmakers at $76,163, a raise of $2,549. The automatic pay hike is provided for in a 1995 state law. The size of the increase is tied to the cost-of-living changes in the preceding 12 months in the Philadelphia-area Consumer Price Index, which is set by the U.S. Department of Labor’s Bureau of Labor Statistics.

headline: Region a showcase for power of wind
abstract: Lakeland School District, Tunkannock Township, and Westfall Township were among 15 Pennsylvania entities that were awarded 35-foot wind turbines from state grants.  The windmills generate 1.8 kilowatts of electricity but are being used more for the educational component according to Margaret Billings-Jones, the Lakeland School District superintendant.  While the state grants for windmills are not available, the PA Department of Environmental Protection is exploring other clean-energy projects.

headline: Handgun in backpack leads to North Phila. school lockdown
abstract: A gun in a backpack has led to a two-hour lockdown of a high school in north Philadelphia. School district spokesman Fernando Gallard says security guards using X-ray machines found the gun Wednesday at Strawberry Mansion High. Gallard says the student has been turned over to police and will be automatically expelled for bringing a firearm to school.

headline: Flight 93 bracelet fundraising campaign to resume
abstract: PA Senator Jane Orie, who started the "Hearts of Steel" campaign, has reported that the fundraising for the United Flight 93 memorial will resume as the Pittsburgh Foundation is taking over.  In August 2003, she was forced to put the $1 million collected into a trust and stopped taking donations as a part of federal reporting requirements.

headline: State probes Exeter Township mortgage business
abstract: Wesley A. Snyder is being investigated by the Pennsylvania Securities Commission for to see if he sold unregistered securities, which is a violation of state law.  Snyder is the president of an Exeter Township mortgage firm that recently filed for bankruptcy but according to courts, also owes $40 million to around 800 creditors.  If the commission finds fraud, they are obligated to turn the matter over to the state attorney general.

headline: Regulating wind farms still up in the air
abstract: PA's emerging wind energy industry presents a quandary for local government. Other state agencies can regulate or make recommendations for such projects, including the PA Game Commission, the PA Department of Environmental Protection, the PA Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, and the PA Department of Environmental Protection. However, decisions are usually left to residents. In Noxen Township, the board of supervisors is considering a nuisance ordinance to limit the size of wind turbines.

headline: Hazleton to test local laws against illegal immigrants
abstract: The town of Hazleton, Pennsylvania is going to trial before U.S. District Judge James M. Munley to determine the constitutionality of its ordinances that would punish landlords who rent to illegal immigrants and business owners who hire them.  There are many interest groups opposed to the town's ordinances such as the American Civil Liberties Union, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, and the Hazleton Hispanic Business Association, whose president said the ordinances have hurt the town's economy and made legal immigrants fearful.  However, Hazleton Mayor, Louis Barletta, pushed through the immigration laws after the murder of a Hazleton man by two illegal Dominican immigrants in May.

headline: Gronski promoted to brigadier general in National Guard
abstract: John L. Gronski was recently promoted to brigadier general in the Pennsylvania Army National Guard by Major General Jessica L. Wright.  Gronski currently is an assistant adjutant general at the Guard's Joint Force Headquarters at Indiantown Gap, and he previously commanded the 28th Infantry Division's 2nd Brigade Combat Team in Ramadi, Iraq.

headline: State school faculty bargaining to resume
abstract: The faculty members of 14 state-owned universities who are part of the Association of PA State College and University Faculties will resume contract talks with the State System of Higher Education today after talks ended early yesterday due to the system's latest offer.  While the union wants a wage increase of 20% over 4 years, the system only offered a $1,250 cash payment and a total of a 7% increase over the rest of the contract.  There is further dispute over contributions towards health benefits, the use of temporary faculty members and distance education incentives.

headline: Clearing the air
abstract: After a judge struck down Erie County's smoking ban in public restaurants and drinking establishments, many owners are going smoke-free on their own. Janet Vogt, tobacco-control program manager for the Erie County Department of Health says the county has seen more and more establishments impose self enforced bans. Chief executive of the PA Restaurant Association, Patrick Conway, said customers are demanding it.

headline: Report targets Pa.'s emissions
abstract: PA is one of three states that individually emit more global warming causing carbon dioxide than the combined emissions of 101 developing nations, according to a new report by the National Environmental Trust. The report highlighting the United States' role as the world's largest greenhouse gas emitter is part of an effort by environmental groups to rally public support for swift, mandatory, national and state policies to reduce those emissions. Pennsylvania utilities, industries and vehicles emit more greenhouse gases than Poland, a developed nation with three times the state's population.

headline: Head of police review board miffed
abstract: The Pittsburgh Citizen Police Review Board has requested that two officers that have had domestic problems in the past year, not be promoted.  Charles Rodriguez was promoted from sergeant to lieutenant despite having a pending criminal case of simple assault, and Eugene F. Hlavac was promoted from sergeant to patrolman is the subject of domestic abuse against his girlfriend.  A third officer, George Trosky has been promoted from homicide detective to commander despite multiple run-ins with law. The Pittsburgh City Council President Doug Shields feels the promotions are speculative, while Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl has not made a definitive public statement.

headline: History disappearing with WWII vets
abstract:
Vivid details of Dec. 7, 1941, when Pearl Harbor was attacked, live on in several veterans’ memories. 
But the number of World War II veterans is rapidly decreasing. Many military personnel were in their late teens or early 20s when the devastating attack occurred, but some 66 years later, many are in their early 80s. A thousand World War II veterans across the nation were expected to die today, according to the U.S. Department of Veterans Affairs Web site. The Luzerne County Veterans Affairs office helps handle funeral arrangements for 80 to 100 veterans a month. Many of those are World War II-era soldiers, said Richard Wren, Luzerne County Veterans Affairs director.

headline: State Senate Appropriations chief to retire
abstract: State Sen. Gib E. Armstrong, who chairs the Appropriations Committee and has served in the Legislature for more than 30 years, plans to retire at the end of next year and not seek a sixth term in the Senate. Armstrong said he wanted to retire eight years ago, but instead stayed on to help push through a convention center project now under construction in downtown Lancaster. Armstrong, who was elected chairman of the Appropriations Committee last year, said the strain of the leadership position played a role in his decision.

headline: Congress Passes Kids Health Bill Again
abstract: President Bush vowed to quickly veto legislation for the second time that would provide health insurance to 4 million more lower-income children whose families earn too much money to qualify for Medicaid and cannot afford to purchase their own health insurance. After Democrats failed to override President Bush’s first veto, they incorporated several changes and passed a new bill even though Bush vowed that he would not accept the proposal since it calls on raising the cigarette tax to fund it. Some Representatives remain hopeful that the bill will be passed, but the bill remains a source of tension and has become a highly complex political issues.

headline: Report: Ethanol plants can spark water pollution
abstract: The Chesapeake Bay Commission just released a report that the corn-based ethanol plants can spark more polluting runoff into water sources because corn uses more fertilizer than other crops.  The Northeast Ethanol and Renewable Resources Limited Chief Executive Officer Richard Scheller said that the proposed plant in Mayfield is for corn-based ethanol but can be switched to cellulose ethanol, which would use wood chips or grass.  However, the only reason that cellulose-based ethanol is lagging behind corn is because of the associated costs with its production.

headline: Here's an answer to gun violence
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell should be commended for bringing to light the issue of gun violence after the fatal shooting of a police officer in Philadelphia. However, it must be clear that the issue is gun violence and not law-abiding gun ownership. As a former New York City resident I lived under the most stringent gun restrictions in the country. They don't work. Law-abiding citizens suffer and criminals remain a threat. The answer begins with protecting constitutional rights of law-abiding citizens under the Second Amendment. They cannot be infringed.

headline: Officials say Pennsylvania Guard well-equipped and ready
abstract: The National Guard's struggle to respond to a tornado in Kansas left many concerned that deployment to Iraq and Afghanistan has stretched the force too thin. However, military officials say PA's National Guard is among the largest in the country. In equipment however, the state's National Guard could use more resources said Captain Cory Angell.

headline: State should flip on secrecy
abstract: This editorial encourages the PA House of Representatives and PA Senate to end a history of secrecy of state government records by supporting the House Speaker's Commission on Legislative Reform and PA Senator Dominic Pileggi's proposition that government records are to be open unless specifically exempted. The author continues to say the Commission should include an office to quickly resolve open-record disputes as well and that public officials' intercommunication should not be "cloaked" because they are indeed public discourse.

headline: Congressional Democrats vowed Wednesday to pressure Republican lawmakers to join them in an effort to override President Bush's veto of a bill that would expand a popular children's health insurance program.
abstract: President Bush vetoed a bill that would have allocated $35 billion over five years toward the State Children’s Health Program, which gives health care coverage for children whose parents make too much to qualify for Medicaid but cannot afford to purchase private insurance. Bush defended the veto by claiming that the bill is a step towards federalizing medicine and would miss its intended target. Democrats are trying to rally support to overturn the veto, and Congress will vote again on October 18th.

headline: Season's 1st day uneventful
abstract: The first day of deer season was certainly not ideal for hunting with rain most of the day and temperatures in the high 50s and low 60s. And as might be expected, it didn't encourage many hunters to take to the woods, at least in Greene County. Burns attributed the low turnout to the rainy weather but also to concerns about the late summer outbreak of epizootic hemorrhagic disease, or EHD.

headline: In last day of testimony, experts defend Hazleton's ordinance
abstract: Detectives Chris Orozco and Jason Zola testified in the final day of testimony in Hazleton's case regarding their Illegal Immigration Relief ordinance.  These two detectives claimed that illegal immigrants are a burden to the department as they are responsible for the increase in gang violence and drug deals.  US District Judge James M. Munley's decision for this case may not come for weeks or months.

headline: Soldiers struggle to get care
abstract: The article cites an example of Dean A. Nist of Glades Pike who returned from the war in Iraq with medical conditions and claims deplorable conditions in Walter Reed Army Medical Center.  Nist also states that veterans in rural areas have trouble finding access to the already crowded Veterans Administration medical centers throughout the country.  In response, Nist has started the Veterans Helping Veterans group in Somerset County.

headline: State, unions reach four-year agreement
abstract: The state has reached a tentative four-year agreement with a majority of its workers, offering pay raises in exchange for increased employee contributions to health benefits, PA Governor Ed Rendell said.  Under the agreement, which would take effect July 1, 2007, employees will receive a bonus of $1,250 in the first year, followed by pay increases of 3 percent, 3 percent and 4 percent in the second through fourth years. In exchange, employees would increase contributions toward their health-care costs from 1 percent to 3 percent of their pay, officials said. The deal, which will cost almost $2.1 billion over the life of the contract, would cover 45,000 of the state's 80,000 employees, said Joe Martz, PA Secretary of Administration.

headline: Costs can present screening obstacle
abstract: Although doctors say colorectal cancer screenings can save lives, many Pennsylvanians do not have insurance coverage for a colonoscopy, which can cost $1,500. "If we can catch this early, it’s a preventable disease," said state Rep. Jim Wansacz one of about four dozen legislators supporting a House bill to mandate that insurance companies cover colorectal screenings. The legislation, which would mandate that patient co-pays for colorectal cancer screenings cost no more than co-pays for similar tests, has passed in the House. A similar bill is pending in the Senate.

headline: Slow first day for state's bear hunters
abstract: Feature on bear hunting including personal stories from the first day of bear hunting season.

headline: Indicted Superior Court Judge
abstract: Facing federal insurance-fraud charges, Superior Court Judge Michael T. Joyce hung up his black robe rather than seek retention in November to another 10-year term spares voters an awkward decision, while also making a bow to political reality. Joyce's withdrawal follows swift, decisive action last week by the state Supreme Court, which suspended him from hearing cases until his own legal battles are concluded. The high court justices moved wisely, expressing the hope that Joyce's suspension would "protect and preserve the integrity" of the courts.

headline: The top priority is to support our troops
abstract: Letter to the editor calling for supporting the troops.

headline: Stevens headed for retention
abstract: State Superior Court Judge Correale Stevens sat in the office he occupied as a county judge at the Luzerne County Courthouse awaiting election returns. Judge Thomas Burke had kindly offered him his old office to see if voters across the state retained him for another 10-year term. He didn’t have to wait long for the local numbers, but statewide returns lagged slightly. With 76 percent of the statewide vote in, Stevens appeared to be set to retain his seat with 63.1 percent of voters casting "yes" votes for him, according to unofficial results.

headline: Court inaction leaves Allegheny County smoking ban hazy
abstract: Allegheny County Chief Executive Dan Onorato plans to institute a smoking ban in restaurants and bars pending a ruling by Commonwealth Court in a suit challenging the County. A spokesman from the Allegheny Health Department confirmed this attitude. A ban on smoking in the workplace was enforced on January 2, but Common Please Judge Michael Della Vecchia delayed enforcement in dining and drinking establishments. Bills for a statewide ban are circulating in the Legislature.

headline: State fines trash haulers
abstract: The state Department of Environmental Protection has fined three trash hauling companies $131,000 for violations involving their trucks. The agency says it fined Vogel Disposal Service, Tri-County Industries and Valley Waste Service, all subsidiaries of Vogel Holding. They operate in Beaver, Butler and Mercer counties. State officials say inspections last year and in June revealed Vogel Holding trash trucks with leaking loads and some without leakproof containers. Officials say waste could fall through the floors in other trucks.

headline: Inquest set Feb. 22 in shooting with Regola's gun
abstract: An inquest into a fatal shooting involving PA state Senator Bob Regola's gun will begin February 22, 2007. Westmoreland County Coroner Ken Bacha hired Pittsburgh attorney Thomas Farrell, a former federal prosecutor who now works as a defense attorney, to conduct the hearing. Bacha delayed the inquest so he could find a hearing officer with no ties to either Regola or the family of Louis Farrell, the 14-year-old boy found shot to death with the senator's gun last July 22. No charges have been filed in the shooting.

headline: Veterans, 'Stand Down' deserve out support
abstract: This editorial is outraged at the lack of care of approximately 200,000 veterans who are now homeless.  It also is frustrated with the awful conditions at Walter Reed Hospital for veterans in Washington D.C..   It finally encourages citizens to make sacrifices for the veterans such as Montgomery County Assistant District Attorney Robert Sander, who is a part of "Stand Down," an organization that helps homeless veterans by serving them meals, giving them clean clothes and providing them with employment counseling.

headline: Street to critics: Hold the phone!
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor John Street was waiting in line at 3:30 AM in Center City in order to be one the first people to purchase Apple's new iPhone.  Many citizens of Philadelphia, including a WYSP radio host, a retired Law Department clerk and Democrat Michael Nutter , criticized him in person for wasting his time in line when he should be working for the city.  The few times Street left the line he was replaced by city-paid members of his security team.

headline: Diabetes challenge: Finding pounds of cure in ounces of prevention
abstract: This article reviews the troubles and successes of a diabetes treatment center at the Veteran's Administration Pittsburgh Healthcare System and tells the story of a veteran, Robert Raubach.  Dr. R. Harsha Rao, the chief of endocrinology in the system, claims the biggest obstacle is working within a health care system that pays more for devastating complications rather using more funding for preventative care, specifically with diabetes.  However, a report released by the Annals of Internal Medicine found that this type of care was associated with more screening an testing, but these tests did not correlate with better results such as better cholesterol levels or blood pressure.

headline: State gets a C- on infrastructure
abstract: The New Jersey branch of the American Society of Civil Engineers released a report grading the condition of the infrastructure throughout the state as a C-.  The president of the New Jersey Sierra Club, Jeff Tittel, feels that the environmental issues addressed such as wastewater, parks and recreation, drinking water and energy are a good warning but do not reflect how dire the situation is.  New Jersey Governor Jon Corzine has now proposed to toll roads to pay off part of the state debt and finance infrastructure repairs and school construction.

headline: Law sets rules on end-of-life care
abstract: A new state law taking effect will determine how end-of-life decisions are made for Pennsylvanians who don't leave a living will or other instructions should they become incapacitated. Supporters of the law, which PA Governor Rendell signed in November, said an existing state statute on end-of-life care did little to help guide those decisions. Under the new law, if a person has not designated someone in advance, the decision-maker will generally be a spouse, adult child, parent, adult sibling, adult grandchild or close friend, in that order.

headline: What's on deck
abstract: Erie Shipbuilding LLC, which began operations in the former Litton shipyard facilities in late 2005, now has about 50 employees, Chief Executive Ned Smith said. That is fewer than expected because of the delay in a major project, the construction of an 840-foot integrated tug barge. The firm had hoped to have as many as 200 workers in its first year in operation, but it didn't reach that because of the delay in the barge project. Raymond Schreckengost, executive director of the Erie-Western Pennsylvania Port Authority, which leases the shipyard to Erie Shipbuilding, pointed to its spinoff business, such as robotics supplied through Erie Welders' Supply.

headline:
Students watch Democrats face off in Mandell Theatre
Candidates, minus Clinton, Dodd, greet students following debate
abstract: The Democratic Presidential candidates, minus Hillary Clinton and Chris Dodd, attended a debate at Drexel University, which focused on many issues; though education, student debt and health care seemed to draw the most audience interest. The article offers a number of opinions from students who attended the event, as well as some of the comments that were made by the five candidates who debated.

headline: Dispute leaves smoking ban smoldering till fall
abstract: The PA House of Representatives and the PA Senate have continued the debate on how strict a public smoking ban should be despite PA Governor Ed Rendell's insistence on a smoking ban and in attempt to lower health care costs.  According to PA Senate Majority Leader Dominic Pileggi, the Senate rejected a House version of the ban that contains less exceptions to the ban because he needed more time to answer questions.  Jim Christman, vice president of the Pennsylvania Tavern Association, said the patrons who he represents are all upset with the ban because of competitions in neighboring states.

headline: State health officials to review data on cancer cases
abstract: The PA State Health Department and the PA Department of Environmental Protection plan to conduct environmental tests around a former industrial site bordering Susquehanna University after the Patriot-News of Harrisburg questioned whether contamination could have caused the cancer of 18 alumni who attended the school between 1990 and 2001.  The University spokeswoman, Victoria Kidd, publicly announced that the university has called for these tests.
