Selinsgrove Borough Manager John Bickhart has stated that the borough's water checks have all come back negative for contamination.

headline: Law takes serious steps against police accused of abusing their family
abstract: Pittsburgh police accused of family abuse will get more scrutiny, face discipline and sometimes see their guns seized under legislation approved by City Council and signed by Mayor Luke Ravenstahl. The 10-page ordinance and a seven-page police policy now enshrined into law replace the ad hoc system in place in June, after three officers accused of family abuse were promoted, inciting women's advocates to anger and council to action. The legislation bars the hiring of police candidates with histories of violence and the promotion of those subject to active domestic abuse criminal cases or protection-from-abuse orders, known as PFAs.

headline: Private Sector: State needs to change outdated 'multiprime' approach to public building projects
abstract: William D. Clifford believes that the Pennsylvania Separation Act, which has required nearly all of the state’s public construction projects to utilize a multiprime bidding system that requires each public project to be split into at least four components for four different contractors. Clifford cites several examples that show this system is less efficient and more costly for taxpayers than the single-prime delivery system, which is traditionally used in the private sector and allows one main contractor to be accountable for the entire project and choose subcontractors at their own discretion. Clifford offers a compromise between the two systems to alleviate some legitimate concerns from subcontractors, but overall, he hopes that PA legislators repeal the Separation Act.

headline: Suburbs tighten up
abstract: Republicans triumphed Tuesday in races for control of the four county courthouses in the Pennsylvania suburbs, with a real scare only in Bucks County - despite poll indications and predictions that Democrats were poised for a historic victory in at least one contest. Democrats did do better than they did in 2003. The party also made some surprising gains lower on the ballot, including taking five of the nine row offices in Montgomery County for the first time in memory. Unique local twists influenced the outcome in each county, but analysts said the GOP victories shared characteristics that defied national and regional political trends favoring Democrats.

headline: Doctors want fewer limits on assistants
abstract: A lobbying group supports PA Governor Ed Rendell's desire to allow physician assistants to provide basic care as a way to decrease health care costs, increase access and improve quality. However, the PA Medical Society opposes eliminating a cap on the number of nurse practitioners a doctor may supervise. President, Dr. Mark A. Piasio, argues elimination of the cap would mean more medical errors, however Tine Hansen-Turton, head of the Nation Nursing Centers Consortium disagrees.

headline: States beat Feds on energy policy
abstract: Congress and the Bush administration still appear to be laboring under the notion that the United States does not need to drastically diversify its energy portfolio in order to sustain the economy, national security and the environment for the long haul.  Fortunately, the states are more aggressive. And, unlike Congress, many states, including Pennsylvania, have adopted policies that require substantial use of energy generated from clean domestic sources.

headline: Jobs instead of crime
abstract: Would the Philadelphia Re-entry Employment Program (PREP) have helped Jerome Whitaker? Police say that, on Oct. 30, Whitaker, out on parole, shot three people in a car near 15th and Sansom, then shot a Philadelphia police officer in the shoulder before jumping into the Schuylkill, where he drowned. PREP will provide tax incentives to employers who hire ex-offenders. City Council unanimously passed a bill that created the program two days after Whitaker's death. Sponsored by Wilson Goode Jr., it grants the employers a $10,000-a-job credit against city business-privilege taxes for three years. It also requires that the ex-offender be paid 150 percent of the federal minimum wage, and get tuition support.

headline:
Tripped by wireless
Phila. and other cities promising WiFi ignored obstacles.
abstract: Michael Balhoff acknowledges some legitimate goals behind a number of city leaders’ efforts to provide their communities with cheap or free government-sponsored wireless internet service. However, he feels that these leaders ignored many concerns and completely underestimated costs while overestimating demand, which has led to problems. Overall, he feels that mistakes were made but hopes that the government will learn from them, so it can work in its proper role by providing regulation, direction and incentives to the private sector.

headline: Taking Pennsylvania for a ride
abstract: Nearly three years ago, the Commonwealth Foundation joined a loose coalition of groups that spanned the political and ideological spectrum. The groups decided to set aside their policy differences to embark on a collaborative effort to promote more open, transparent, and accountable state government. Unfortunately backdoor deals continue. Examples of bills are given.

headline: Don't gamble with the flu
abstract: The PA Medical Society is disappointed with a poll that found that less than half of the adults surveyed planned to get a flu shot and claims that an average of 36,000 Americans die from the flu and complications each year. They urge Pennsylvanians to get the vaccination and provide a contact number for information.

headline: Throop official: EPA is ‘enemy’
abstract: Officials from the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency presented a report detailing a low risk of a mine fire at the Major battery recycling site and their intention to stay with a plan to place a protective cap over lead-contaminated waste at the site, now owned by Gould Electronics Inc. Borough officials want the waste materials moved off the site and away from residents. Councilman Joseph Barone said moving the material can be done safely, just as nuclear waste is transported by trucks.

headline: Judge delays ruling on legal bills
abstract: Judge James M, Munley of the US District Court for the Middle District of Pennsylvania in Scranton ruled that Mayor Lou Barletta and the City of Hazleton would not have pay legal bills for the plaintiffs' attorneys in the Illegal Immigration Relief Act case before an appeal is completed.  The attorneys, from the Puerto Rican Defense and Education Fund and the American Civil Liberties Union among others, will have to wait until after the Third Circuit Court of Appeals in Philadelphia to see if they will be paid the $2.4 million in legal fees from the city.  Mayor Lou Barletta was pleased at the news and expressed the need to focus on the appeal case.

headline: Rendell Embarks on European Trade Mission
abstract: null

headline: Tax shift leaves voters uneasy
abstract: If voters fail to pass the referendum on shifting property taxes to income to raise revenue for school districts, it is a message to legislators to come up with a real solution, some believe. Many voters outside mid-state polling locations voted no. A retiree said he voted yes because of the tax break he will get. Many missed the question on the ballot, voted no because the question was confusing, or calculated they would lose more by shifting the structure than maintaining it.

headline: Dr. Rendell wants you to feel better
abstract: This editorial is frustrated with the health care system in Pennsylvania as well as across the United States but applauds PA Governor Ed Rendell and his Health Care Reform director, Rosemary Greco, for addressing hospital staph infections and widening the responsibilities of nurse practitioners despite these improvements being overdue.  The article also scolded the Legislature for not passing a statewide public smoking ban in public buildings and President George Bush for not expanding the Children's Health Insurance Program.

headline: Toxin link not ruled out
abstract: A federal study confirmed 38 cases of polycythemia vera in three PA counties, and it has not ruled out environmental causes; though there are no known causes or environmental links. However, many people blame a former Superfund site that was closed in 1979 by the Environmental Protection Agency for releasing dangerous chemicals. There are possible connections, but in all likelihood the incidence of the disease cannot be explained by the site.

headline: Keep predators away from schools
abstract: Anne Reeves expresses the opinion that those who commit crimes against children should be released from their prison sentences completely unchecked.  She thinks they most importantly should be allowed to live in the surrounding areas of schools as well as being checked into a special treatment center funded by the state.  While it is expensive, she feels these centers, whether they completely cure the criminal or not, would protect children from these ex-criminals.

headline: State encourages exports to Europe
abstract: The weak dollar has made countries in central and eastern Europe more fertile ground for Pennsylvania exports, state economic development officials say. The state has invited companies to participate in a trade mission to Poland and the Czech Republic this spring. Such a trip to the two countries hasn't been offered since at least 2000, said Pete O'Neill, executive director of the Center for Trade Development in the state Department of Community and Economic Development. Early in his first term, Gov. Ed Rendell closed a state trade office in the Czech Republic.

headline: Technicalities may knock some candidates off the ballot
abstract: There are many candidates for county and municipal offices that may be taken off the ballot as there some challenges to the nominating petitions that the Common Pleas Court is reviewing.  The most prominent candidate in danger of being thrown off the ballot is Charles McCollough, a Republican candidate for the at-large seat on the Allegheny County Council, whose challenger has asked for him to be omitted because of omissions in his listing of sources of income.  Patrick Dowd, who is running for City Council in District 7, Rachel Cooper, a Democratic-endorsed candidate in District 9, and Rick Swartz, who is running for county Chief Executive, are all under scrutiny as well.

headline: Enrollment in CHIP on rise in state
abstract: Enrollment of Pennsylvania children in government-subsidized health insurance has increased 32 percent since 2003. There are now 166,151 Pennsylvania children covered by the Children's Health Insurance Program, known as CHIP. Arguing that health insurance has become too expensive even for many middle class families, Rendell expanded the state's version of CHIP so all children are eligible, no matter how much their parents earn. CHIP is for families who earn too much to qualify for Medicaid.

headline: Water authority awarded loan for line upgrades
abstract: Southwestern PA Water Authority Manager Joe Simatic thanked state Representative Bill DeWeese and state Senator J. Barry Stout for their support in getting a twenty year, $5.2 million low interest loan from the PA Infrastructure Investment Authority. The money will be used to replace 29,000 feet of deteriorating water lines in Jefferson and Waynesburg.

headline: Lawyers take final shots for, against Hazleton law
abstract: Two opposing lawyers both gave one final plea to Judge James M. Munley to close the controversial case determining the legality of the Illegal Immigrant Relief ordinance in the town of Hazleton.  American Civil Liberties Union lawyer Witold J. Walczak used an emotional appeal to the judge to attack the ordinance, while attorney for Hazleton Kris Kobach used a technical approach to appeal to the law.  Whoever loses this case is likely to appeal to the 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals in Philadelphia.

headline: A clear and present abuse
abstract: The editorial uses the corruption found within the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency as an example on why Pennsylvania needs better open-records laws.  After PHEAA was found spending close to $1 million on lavish retreats, PA Governor Ed Rendell and the Pennsylvania Newspaper Association are currently drafting legislation to consider all government records to be public.  The author expresses satisfaction that PA Representatives Tim Mahoney and Dominic Pileggi have both introduced legislation to include the legislature, the judiciary, and PHEAA in open-records requirements

headline: Tell your state legislators you want genuine open records
abstract: The author had been hopeful after Representative Tim Mahoney proposed a bill that would have changed Pennsylvania’s open records laws, which are among the worst in the nation. However, she is disappointed at the House State Government Committee for adding 21 pages of amendments with no public input. She feels that the public deserves open access to most government information, and she urges people to write to legislators to urge real open records reform.

headline: Faulty fridge might mean 350 have to be revaccinated in Pa.
abstract: Approximately 350 people may need to be revaccinated because of problems with Smethport Family Practice’s storage refrigerator. The temperature fluctuated in the refrigerator and may have compromised hepatitis A and B, tetanus, pneumonia, and meningitis vaccinations.

headline: Water bottling plant gets conditional approval
abstract: The Susquehanna River Basin Commission will approve drawing water from a tributary to Davis Run for a bottled water plant, but only for 79,000 gallons a day. Residents and representatives from the Pumping Station Dam Association asked about depletion of water sources. Studies were conducted with the PA Department of Environmental Protection and the PA Fish and Boat Commission. The host and surrounding townships and the Pumping Station Preservation Association oppose the application.

headline: Legislator seeks a probe of Capitol banner incident
abstract: Pennsylvania State Rep. Angel Cruz asked Harrisburg Police to investigate whether any laws were broken when two participants in a gun-rights rally held up a banner calling for him to be “hung from the tree of liberty.” At a news conference yesterday, Gov. Rendell decried the violent sentiment and racist overtones in the banner’s language, but said he did not support a state police investigation into the incident. Cruz is sponsoring a bill that would require gun registration and a $10-a-gun annual fee.

headline: 2 face investigation for Pa. film-lobbying role
abstract: PA Senator Jeffrey Piccola, chairman of the Senate State Government Committee will hire the private detective agency Cloud Feehery & Richter to investigate if Leslie Merrill McCombs, a former FOX TV reporter, and former PA Representative Mike Veon  exploited loopholes in the lobbying and ethics laws in Pennsylvania.  McCombs and Veon both lobbied on behalf of the Lionsgate production company for a $75 million tax credit for films made within the state; however, McCombs was not registered with the state as the company's lobbyist.  Both Rendell and Eric Epstein, founder of the watchdog group RocktheCapital.org, do not support the decision to hire detectives but do support tightening the lobby law.

headline: Tensions rising: 3 mayoral candidates launch attacks
abstract: After months of tepid exchanges in the mayor's race, open criticisms began to surface, most of them aimed at Tom Knox, the millionaire businessman who has bought a significant lead in the polls with $5 million in self-financed television. In a debated aired yester on WPI-TV (Channel 6), Congressman Bob Brad went after Knox charging that he had a history of "ripping off men and women" in his business venture". State Rep. Dwight Evans criticized both Knox and Fattah during the debate.

headline: Finances at state's hospitals grew in '06, though rural facilities still struggling
abstract: Many of the state's general hospitals are turning larger profits as smaller community hospitals continue to struggle to maintain operations according to the Pennsylvania Health Care Cost Containment Council.  Net patient revenue is up to 7.2% in the 2006 fiscal year, and the overall profit margin is up to 5.5%  in 2006 from 4.6% in 2005.  55 hospitals out of 170 in the study reported negative operating margins, and the main concern is that these hospitals are in rural areas where they are the only form of health care for the surrounding communities.

headline: Wind farms pushed for state parks
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell's administration will push to open PA's state forests and parks for wind farm development. Secretary of the PA Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, Michael DiBerardinis said the administration is close to making a decision. Legislative approval will be necessary. PA. Rep. Camille George, chairman of the House Environmental Resources and Energy Committee. Although the PA Game Commission does not prohibit building wind turbines, it has seen none of those posed through.

headline: Lobbyist receives 18-month jail term
abstract: John J. O'Connell's 18-month prison term for embezzlement closes a shocking chapter for the high-powered Harrisburg lobbyist, but his sentence kicked off fresh speculation over whether he turned investigators onto other crimes. O'Connell was sentenced yesterday by U.S. District Judge Sylvia Rambo for embezzling more than $226,000 from a client. The sentence was based in part on a motion filed by Assistant U.S. Attorney Kim Daniel acknowledging O'Connell provided "information that did launch an investigation" that has gone before a grand jury.

headline: 210 cited in crackdown on drag racing on York
abstract: 210 people were charged with summary citations for illegal drag racing on U.S Route 30. Authorities claim that most people there were charged with trespassing.

headline: The best of times and worst of times
abstract: The editorial staff writes the best and worse of PA Governor Ed Rendell's first term.  They list the following as the best: raising the state's minimum wage, which rises to $7.15 on July 1, investing in preschool for the first time in state history, expanding state programs that provide low-cost prescriptions to senior citizens. Moments to forget: signing the law to raise pay of legislators and state officials, letting his state police drivers fly down the Pennsylvania Turnpike at speeds of more than 100 mph, suggesting funding for black fly spraying be cut, failing to visit Campbelltown, Lebanon County, to inspect tornado-ravaged neighborhoods in 2004.

headline: Former nursing home aide says she misled Pa. inspectors
abstract: Bonnie Janney, a former nursing home aide, testified that she misled state inspectors about staffing when they arrived unannounced in the middle of the night because she didn't want to get former administrator Martha F. Bell in trouble. Janney testified  that she was working alone in a 30-bed unit at the Ronald Reagan Atrium I Nursing, Research and Rehabilitation Center in Robinson when a PA Health Department team arrived in March 2002. That visit followed the death of Atrium resident Mabel Taylor, on October 26, 2001, after she was trapped overnight in a locked outdoor courtyard.

headline: null
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell is promoting his $850 million proposal that would invest in new technology for renewable energy in his attempt to make Pennsylvania less dependent on foreign oil and a producer of renewable energy for a thriving market.  There are two other, less expensive proposals by legislators that Rendell has to compete with.

headline: Man fatally shot on Christmas
abstract: A man was found shot to death in West Philadelphia on Christmas night, police said. The body of Shawn McKnight, 35, was found between a car and a cherry-picker truck. He had been shot multiple times in the chest. McKnight was taken to the Hospital of the University of Pennsylvania, where he was pronounced dead just after 8 p.m., police said. Police believe that McKnight may have been a victim of an attempted robbery turned deadly.

headline: A 3-way heat but no sure thing in Fourth District
abstract: Councilwoman Carol Campbell says she has not put much energy into her campaign to retain her seat over Curtis Jones Jr. and Matt McClure. The fight is over former councilman Michael Nutter's seat, to which Campbell was appointed. Several political action committees with ties to Campbell are being investigated by the city's Ethics Board, which Campbell says is an attempt to discredit her and the Democratic party. Jones favors increased property taxes to better education. McClure ranks second in fundraising behind Campbell.

headline: The Cappy retirement
abstract: This editorial criticizes PA Supreme Court Chief Justice Ralph Cappy for not remaining nonpolitical, as judges should, by endorsing the 2005 pay-raise of the PA Legislature.  The author also was frustrated with Cappy's argument for higher judicial salaries and his describing raising salaries as showing "prudent courage."  Cappy is stepping down from the court but the article encourages citizens to keep his misguided deeds in mind for the future.

headline: Fresh blood revives faltering AGH heart transplant program
abstract:
The heart transplant program at Allegheny General Hospital is on the upswing after a steep decline in the number of transplants over the past five years. Surgeons at the North Side hospital have performed 12 heart transplants in the past nine months, compared to four in all of 2005, officials said. 
Officials at AGH, where a liver transplant program also is in the works, attributed the program's resurgence to the recruitment of Dr. Srinivas Murali as director of cardiovascular medicine and two heart surgeons, Drs. David Dean and Stephen Bailey.

headline: $18,000 in grants awarded
abstract: Three businesses in Luzerne County received almost $18,000 in grants from the state and Department of Environmental Protection to improve energy efficiency for small businesses. With the cost of energy soaring, the state announced that 89 small businesses statewide will share in $521,000 meant to conserve energy and improve the bottom line. Gov. Edward Rendell said the grants will allow small business to conserve energy and reduce pollution through the use of innovative technology.

headline: Marchers' message: 'Stop the violence!'
abstract: A march in Philadelphia was organized to send a message to City Council members, PA Representatives, and the mayor to do something about violence and homicides on the city streets.

headline: A constitutional convention is required
abstract: Mark P. Widoff, interim chair of Democracy Rising PA, believes that the small reformed changes in the PA House of Representatives and the ongoing discussion of meaningful reform in the Capitol in Harrisburg is extremely heartening.  He goes further to call on citizens, who he feels have done well in recent times to oust corrupt or inadequate leaders, to help clean up state government.  He feels the PA Supreme Court is particularly undemocratic and feels a constitutional convention is the only way to reform the PA state government.

headline: The City's Campaign-Finance Law
abstract: This editorial believes the Pennsylvania House of Representatives should support a bill proposed by PA State Representative Dwight Evans would allow Philadelphia officials to set donor limits and set up publicly financed city elections.  Former City Councilman Michael Nutter also supports this bill because of it decreases big-money influence on city politics.  However, this law is has been challenged and brought to the Commonwealth Court to determine if Philadelphia has overstepped its authority.

headline: Half of region non-drinkers but smoking's on the upswing here, latest report shows
abstract: Bats Clever, executive director of Carlisle Area Health and Wellness Foundation, has reported in the Foundation's recent report that up to half of the surrounding area are non-drinkers.  While binge drinking remains a problem on college campuses, only 8% of adults of the area were classified as binge drinkers.  The survey also discovered that smoking is rising in the region as the PA Legislature debates a public smoking pan throughout the state.

headline: ACOG examines use of bio-fuel
abstract: The Abington Council of Governments held a meeting to discuss the implications of using bio-fuel instead of gas fuel for vehicles. Brian Singer, a Kutztown graduate with a degree in Environmental Science, said he would volunteer to assist with ACOG’s efforts to locate information regarding bio-fuel. Hatala noted that Lackawanna County differs from other counties concerning agriculture.

headline: Merger proposal for city housing police and city force stirs union concern
abstract: An emerging plan to merge the Pittsburgh Housing Authority's 30 police officers with the city's 840-man force has aroused the ire of the Fraternal Order of Police. FOP President James Malloy sent a letter yesterday to his union members outlining his opposition to the move, which would allow authority police to join the bureau even if they don't meet requirements like the 60-college-credit minimum for city applicants.

headline: A Council record of accomplishment
abstract: Michael Nutter is a city councilman who is running for Mayor of Philadelphia. He has said that current Mayor Street was one of the inspirations for him to enter the political realm; this is ironic because the two are currently bitter enemies. Nutter is an interesting man with many qualities that make him unique.

headline: The contenders
abstract: A list of candidates for Luzerne County's upcoming elections is posted, including the positions for Commissioner, Recorder of Deeds, Clerk of Courts, Sheriff, Treasurer, District Attorney, Court of Common Pleas Judge, and Coroner.

headline: Health care expansion for kids would be the right thing to do
abstract: This editorial disagrees with President Bush's decision to increase funding for the Children's Health Insurance Program by $4.9 billion to only cover children who are already a part of the system.  On the other hand, the author also supports US Senators Bob Casey and Arlen Specter and their avocation to expand this program to cover all children for $50 billion over 5 years.  The article also explains how Democrats are accusing the US Department of Health and Human Services of purposely underestimating the number of uninsured children at 6 million rather than the actual number at 9 million.

headline: Aqua Pa. eyes 14 percent water rate hike
abstract: About 145,000 Delaware County households may have to pay $5.72 more a month for water if the latest rate increase requested by Aqua Pennsylvania Inc. is approved by the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission. If approved, the 14 percent rate increase would bring a typical monthly residential bill to $46.90 and an annual bill to $562.80, up from $495. Aqua executives have requested the rate increase go into effect Jan. 21, 2008, but the Public Utility Commission typically takes up to nine months to complete an investigation and analysis of the request.

headline: Nearly 4,000 Guard troops may go to Iraq
abstract: Nearly 4,000 PA National Guard members have been notified that they could be sent to serve in Iraq within a year. It would be the state’s largest guard deployment and would be the first time that the guard’s Stryker vehicles would see combat. These vehicles can perform a number of tasks and move at speeds of up to 75 mph.

headline: A House reformed plans more work
abstract: The PA House of Representatives have passed  32 recommended changes to how they operate from the Speaker's Commission on Legislative Reform.  The two co-chairman of this commission, Representative David Steil and Representative Joshua Shapiro plan to meet with House Speaker Dennis O' Brien soon to create a timeline for the second phase of work for the panel.  They claim that although the newer changes were passed, the commission is not finished opening the legislative process to the citizens.

headline: The Issue is Crime
abstract: Crime is still the biggest issue in the Philadelphia mayor's race, but voters are also looking for the next mayor to improve public schools and fight corruption in City Hall, according to the latest Daily News Keystone Poll.

headline: Health care proposal still alive
abstract: Rosemarie Greco, PA Governor Ed Rendell's top health care official, has reported that Rendell is confident that his health care proposal will become law in a few days and has become victim to insurance companies and businesses spreading false information.  The measures will include: dependent children on family health plans until the age of 29, changing premiums set by insurers on businesses, banning smoking in public places and requiring the use of electronic surveillance to eliminate infections in hospital patients.  There is a lot of controversy on the 3% payroll tax on businesses that don't provide health coverage as it is opposed by the PA Chamber of Business and Industry and the Insurance Federation of Pennsylvania.

headline: Big oil pushes its interests, not Alaska's or environment
abstract: The author feels that the public has been fed biased news on the part of corporate development in the problem over drilling on a 1.5 million-acre area of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge.  He explains that the US does not have enough oil and drilling in the refuge will not relieve the country of oil dependence.  He also feels that the refuge has too much natural value in beauty and wildlife that drilling here for a small percentage of our total oil consumption is not worth ruining the area.

headline: New device to help ID impaired drivers
abstract: Police in Blair County arrest hundreds of impaired drivers annually, mostly for alcohol abuse. That number could increase in the months ahead because of a new instrument called a pupilometer, which will be used to detect drivers using drugs. PennDOT, state police and several local law enforcement officers introduced the pupilometer to Blair County Monday.

headline: A man with a vision for Whitehall Township
abstract: The author endorses Ed Hozza Jr. for Whitehall Township’s next executive in the upcoming election, and he criticizes his two opponents, Dan McNeill and Edward Koren. He says that he has known Hozza for over 25 years, and he is qualified to lead them into the future.

headline: The mayor's five-figure fans
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl has $695,906 in the bank with no opponent in the Democratic primary now that Councilman William Peduto dropped out. Most of the funds are from large checks from PACS and Unions, including the International Brotherhood of Electrical Workers Local 5, the Buchanan Ingersoll Political Action Committee and others. Contributions in such amounts are illegal in other states and federally, but not in PA. The money will be kept for the general election and future years.

headline: Health insurance crisis addressed
abstract: The head of the Pennsylvania Department of Insurance was in Chambersburg, outlining plans for health care insurance reform that he said are long overdue. Joel Ario, acting commissioner of the Pennsylvania Department of Insurance, told leaders of local chambers of commerce and business owners that small businesses are especially feeling the burden of rising health care costs. Insurance providers can use factors like gender and past medical history in setting premiums. Because small businesses have a smaller employee pool to draw from, a few employees can have a dramatic effect on health care costs for the business.

headline: Biodiesel offers promise for farmers, consumers and a cleaner environment
abstract: Carl Shaffer, President of the PA Farm Bureau, believes that biodiesel energy is a key part of the renewable energy solution because it would reduce pollution and the reliance on foreign oil.  However, he claims that PA biodiesel producers are struggling because they are being undercut by out of state companies that receive better incentives from their state governments. He urges Governor Rendell and the General Assembly to pass a three-year biodiesel production incentive plan, which would allow local companies to survive and supply biodiesel fuel to Pennsylvanians.

headline: Now off-air Philly TV anchor called governor after arrest
abstract: A TV news anchor accused of punching a New York police officer in the face has started a scheduled vacation early so she can deal with her legal problems. Alycia Lane was arrested in Manhattan on a felony charge of assaulting a police officer. Lane, who co-anchors evening newscasts at KYW-TV, the CBS affiliate in Philadelphia, had been scheduled to start a two-week vacation next week. Given the circumstances, a station spokeswoman said, Lane began that time off Monday and will remain off the air for now.

headline: A new rathole
abstract: Legislative leaders in Harrisburg certainly think taxpayers are fools.  The latest outrage in a long string of "public purpose" outrages is reported by The Philadelphia Inquirer: Legislative leaders have paid $466,000 this year to conduct focus groups and public-opinion polls whose purposes smack of politics and not public policy. State Attorney General Tom Corbett would be wise to add this outrage to his public corruption probe.

headline: The Ravenstahl win: Past is prologue
abstract: Accidental Democrat Mayor Luke Ravenstahl was elected in his own right on Tuesday, handily defeating Republican challenger Mark DeSantis, 64-35 percent. "Close election" is a relative term in Pittsburgh politics. Mr. Ravenstahl, the nation's youngest big city mayor at 27, campaigned on the "Republicans are baaaaad" platform. Democrat voters, with a 5-to-1 registration edge, chose to follow the bleating sheep like lemmings over a cliff.

headline: Hearing to focus on nursing homes
abstract: Following the recent death of an elderly woman, PA legislators have drafted several amendments to laws that govern nursing and personal care homes. The House Aging and Older Adult Services Committee will hold a public meeting to get feedback on these proposals; some of which are described in the article.

headline: Bond funding may stall Rendell's energy initiative
abstract: The PA Governor Ed Rendell has proposed a $850 million bond issue to fund the implementation of his Energy Independence Strategy, but according to John Hanger of watchdog PennFuture, the slow actions of the PA Legislature are to be blamed on traditional partisanship and lobbying by utility companies such as Allegheny Energy Incorporated.  The bill in question forces these companies to maximize conservation  and the use of smart meters.

headline: NRA, GOP stance quite lame
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell's crusade to bring common sense to the state's gun laws continues to create a butting-heads battle with the National Rifle Association, and the Pennsylvania Republican Party. Case in point: state House Republican majority caucus spokesman Steve Miskin, who upon hearing of the governor's plan -- in the GOP's case, any plan regarding guns -- termed it just another Rendell plan to prohibit something. That includes the administration's call for changes that would allow great municipal control of gun laws, a restriction on handgun purchases to once a month and the establishment of a database for stolen weapons.

headline: A 'novel' concept to grasp
abstract: The author of this opinion piece writes that ignorance and arrogance emboldens Public Officials & Acolytes Inc. to conclude state or federal constitutions do not apply to them. PA Governor Ed Rendell offers a pretty expansive case study in such behavior. Witness all of his "economic development initiatives," never mind that they are in direct violation of Article VIII, Section 8, of the Pennsylvania Constitution. The author writes Rendell repeatedly violates the state Constitution and his oath of office by transferring millions of taxpayer dollars to private corporations

headline: Too much Knox
abstract: The author of the letter asks "Is Philadelphia mayoral candidate Tom Knox running for mayor or sainthood?"  She doesn't believe he can attain either. She writes that he has put out too many TV ads in an effort to gain name recognition. She writes that spending millions can buy a lot of media time, but not the votes. Voters are already sick of his ads and self-proclaimed goodness. By election time Knox may have name recognition, but for the wrong reason.

headline: Highmark disputes heart surgery report
abstract: The Pennsylvania Health Care Cost Containment council released recently that showed disparities that Highmark Inc., primary insurer in southwestern Pennsylvania, paid to different area hospitals for cardiac surgeries.  Darren Macioce, Highmark Senior Vice President, claims that the costs do not reflect the risk-adjusted scores developed by Highmark to determine the cost of the procedure.  The West Penn Allegheny Health System has continuously alleged that Highmark uses favoritism with reimbursements  do not agree with one claim made by the insurer.

headline: City chosen to participate in solar power initiative
abstract: The US Department of Energy named Pittsburgh one of 12 Solar America cities while giving the city part of a $2.5 million funding package along with federal expertise to develop plans to use solar power in government, boost its use by private citizens, and promote large-scale solar installations. Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl attributed it to the city's hard work behind the grant application.  The Department of Energy's plan is to make solar energy cost-competitive by 2015.

headline: Officer who detained mayor is transferred
abstract: The Pittsburgh police officer who handcuffed Mayor Luke Ravenstahl before a 2005 Steelers game,, Mark A. Hoehn, was transferred Monday to the bureau's Special Deployment Division. Hoehn is not being rewarded for releasing Ravenstahl without arresting him, said James Malloy, president of Fraternal Order of Police Fort Pitt Lodge No. 1. Ravenstahl acknowledged the incident at an Oct. 31, 2005, game after an account of his run-in with the police appeared on a blog run by a former talk radio host.

headline: A pugilist's sensibilities score a KO
abstract: The writer notes that there are a number of reasons why now top contender for Philadelphia Mayor in the Democratic Primary Michael Nutter was ignored during the campaign. US Representatives Bill Brady and Chaka Fattah had bigger names. Other campaigns had more money. Nutter's luck started to change with a TV spot by his 12 year old daughter, bad publicity for his rivals, and media endorsements. The biggest factor working in Nutter's favor is that other campaigns underestimated him.

headline:
Under GOP, Parking Authority balloons
But city schools profit little from Republican takeover
abstract: Since the Republicans took over control of Philadelphia’s Parking Authority in 2001, the number of employees and six figure salaries has increased substantially. The agency’s revenue reached a record high of nearly $198 million last fiscal year, which can be attributed to an expansion in the authority’s duties, however, increased expenses ate up most of the new revenue, and Philadelphia’s schools haven’t received as much money as expected. Employees are allowed to remain active in politics, and there has been some controversy over high salaries and campaign contributions from employees.

headline: Highmark donation to help build children's hospital
abstract: Pennsylvania State Milton S. Hershey Medical Center will receive $25 million as the result of a donation by Highmark Incorporated while Highmark will receive 60,000 new insurance customers from Penn State University and the medical center. $20 million of this donation will go towards developing a new children's hospital in the medical center.  Cliff Shannon, an outspoken critic of Highmark Inc.'s policies, raises the concern that Highmark is using its surplus donations to continue its market dominance in Pennsylvania.

headline: Clear the air: Relicense nuke plants
abstract:
Forrest Remick, professor of nuclear engineering emeritus and associate vice president for research emeritus at the Pennsylvania State University and a former commissioner of the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, writes that as the economic and environmental value of nuclear-generated electricity has become more evident, the renewal of nuclear plant licenses has taken on increasing importance, and it offers grounds for optimism about nuclear power’s growth in Pennsylvania. 
The Nuclear Regulatory Commission is considering whether to extend for another 20 years the operating license of the Susquehanna nuclear plant, the first of Pennsylvania’s nuclear plants to seek license renewal.

headline: Officials, police rally for gun controls
abstract: Until recently, Mercedes Raye hadn't participated in the community forums, street marches or other anti-violence efforts around Harrisburg. But with her 12-year-old daughter recuperating from being shot in both legs outside a teen dance party in the city last month, Raye has become an instant gun control advocate. Elected officials, police officers and advocates who feel like Raye rallied at the Capitol Monday in what some termed a push for "common-sense gun safety" laws.

headline: A stench in Beaver
abstract: The editorial is encouraging federal and state investigators to look into the nonprofit agency Voluntary Action Center and its president, wife of PA Senator Gerald LaValle, Darla LaValle.  She reportedly was paid $619,000 in an 8-year period when the group's income was $1.6 million, where half of the income was from state grants.  Senator LaValle claims to have played no role in the her securing state grants, and Board president Bernadette Matsook reported that she doesn't know who is the advocate within the Legislature for the nonprofit.

headline: The Votes
abstract: This short article shows how the Pennsylvania House of Representatives voted on amendments to the changes proposed by the Speaker's Commission on Legislative Reform including the Appropriations Committee power, term limits for a chairman, private vehicle leases, and the creation of an equal opportunity officer.

headline: Highmark offers the ultimate get-well card
abstract: Highmark Inc. is now offering its new Healthcare Gift Card, which could only be used at places that Highmark’s partner, Visa, has categorized as a health-related location. Highmark’s intended target will be seniors and college students, who are usually reluctant to spend their money on health-related expenses. There are some issues that Highmark would like to fine tune; however they believe the card will be a success by forcing recipients of the gift card to use the funds on health-related expenses.

headline: Cow manure to power Crawford County dairy farm
abstract: One of Crawford County's largest dairy farms is moving forward with plans to turn cow manure into electricity to power the operation. Don and Jack Bortnick's plan got a boost recently when they received a $600,000 state grant to build a manure-to-gas operation at their farm. Their proposed system breaks down the carbon in manure into methane gas. The gas then powers a generator to make electricity, said Tom Wilson, agricultural engineer for the Crawford County Cooperative Extension.

headline: On the Web - Witness List
abstract: This article gives the witness list for Tuesday and Wednesday in the trial regarding the Illegal Immigration Relief Act.

headline: A tight race in a district that meanders
abstract: Philadelphia's Seventh Council District is called the most heavily gerrymandered in the nation. Its most recent councilman Rick Mariano is in federal prison and predecessor Harry Jannotti was involved with the Abscam scandal. The election race is a tight, with community activists Maria Quinones Sanchez and Marnie Aument Loughrey considered top contenders over incumbent Daniel Savage. Sanchez is the only Council candidate endorsed by PA Governor Rendell. Savage is endorsed by District Attorney Lynn Abraham and a number of unions.

headline: These weren't junkets
abstract: The author of the letter writes that he does not know Jonathan Newman, former chairman of the PA Liquor Control Board, but is outraged at the attack on his travel expenses. The author writes to implicate that Newman's expenses were extravagant and lavish is just plain political. The author praises Newman for a miraculous turnaround of product availability and, more important, a huge increase in the quality of service and employee knowledge of the products. He writes that the politicos should have left this one alone, and P.J. Stapleton, who replaced Newman, should keep his mouth shut and make sure he doesn't ruin what Newman created.

headline: Hispanic growth in rural towns creates health-care challenges
abstract: As more Hispanic migrant workers have moved into rural areas throughout the country, many health care providers and hospitals are struggling to overcome language and culture barriers that prevent them giving suitable care.  The US Department of Agriculture estimates the Hispanic has doubled from 1980 to 2000 and will be the largest minority by 2025.  Dr. Carol Vidal, a Spanish psychiatrist, reported that language barriers, lack of transportation, long work hours, perceived discrimination and deportation fears are the main obstacles blocking access to basic health care.

headline: Crazy days: Don't fail the public on energy and transportation
abstract: This editorial encourages the Pennsylvania state government to support two "critical items" before adjourning on recess.  Firstly, it asks the legislators to pass a mediocre transportation package that would toll Interstate 80 and allow for various local taxes to fund mass transit systems throughout the state.  The second legislation is an energy independence plan for the state that would allow business to enter into long-term contracts with utilities, encourage the use of smart meters on houses, and incentives for environmental policies all to be paid for by a small charge on the monthly electric bill.  It also accuses Republicans in both the US Congress and the State Senate of being the main problems in energy independence.

headline: Ordinance could cost Hazleton $2.4M
abstract: American Civil Liberties Union attorney Witold Walczak, who successfully challenged a Hazleton city ordinance against illegal immigrants, has asked the federal judge, US District Judge James M. Munley, to force the city of Hazleton and Mayor Lou Barletta to pay the $2.4 million in court fees.  Barletta claims the number is absurd, as the city's annual budget is only $7.9 million and has appealed Munley's decision to the 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals.  Walczak feels that the fees are actually very reasonable as he requested $500,000 less than the actual fees but has vowed, along with Barletta, to appeal to the case up to the US Supreme Court.

headline: A tough Act to follow
abstract: PA Legislators will reconsider property taxes after an attempt to shift the burden to income taxes failed via voter referendum in the primary. In Lancaster County, all 16 districts defeated the proposal. PA Governor Ed Rendell blamed the failure on school districts, saying they did not properly explain the benefits, especially for seniors. Rendell suggested raising the sales tax to fill a hole in the state's budget from less federal funds. Lancaster city police Sergeant Michael Branner faces Janice Jiminez, a university police sergeant for district judge in the election.

headline: Thornburgh tells House Wecht's prosecution is political
abstract: Former U.S. Attorney General and PA Governor Dick Thornburgh exchanged heated remarks with U.S. House members over the federal prosecution of former Allegheny County Coroner Dr. Cyril H. Wecht, who is being represented by Thornburgh’s law firm. The meeting was held because of allegations that political motivations have played a role in federal prosecutions of some local officials in light of the recent controversial firings of nine U.S. attorneys. Thornburgh tried to link Wecht’s case to these allegations; though he had no actual proof.

headline: Hitting the most vulnerable
abstract: The author criticizes President Bush for his veto of the State Children’s Health Insurance Program. In the author’s opinion, the President and congressmen who support him failed to address middle class concerns and should be ashamed that such a rich country like the U.S. cannot take care of its children.

headline: DEP says conservation key to avoiding electric rate spikes
abstract: Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Kathleen McGinty told members of the House that PA could be facing an "economic train wreck" because electricity rate caps will expire at the end of 2010, which could drastically increase prices for consumers. She also used the opportunity to promote Governor Rendell’s Energy Independence Strategy, which would require utilities to provide services at the lowest possible cost and invest in cost saving measures and alternative renewable energy sources. The plan would also allow Pennsylvanians to have electric meters in their homes that monitor electricity usage and costs.

headline: Our nation has gone overboard with alarm
abstract: Gerard Vaerewyck makes a comparison between the communist state of East Germany 20 years ago to Pennsylvania today under the threat of terrorism, as both states do not allow unauthorized photographs to be taken.  Vaerewyck feels that the arrest by state police of two men taking photographs in a public place is illegal and extremely unnecessary.  He also says that the turnpike service plaza is not a likely target for a terrorist attack and therefore, should not be so heavily guarded.

headline: A.G. offers tips to avoid holiday shopping rip-offs
abstract: Attorney General Tom Corbett Thursday released a list of tips for the holiday season, to help consumers avoid common problems and fraud."The joy of the holiday season can quickly be spoiled by crimes like identity theft or disputes involving gift purchases," Corbett said. "Consumers should carefully consider all their purchases and charitable gifts, and not allow the excitement of the season to rush them into hasty decisions that can be regretful and costly."

headline: Today in Harrisburg
abstract: A bill will be unveiled to make teacher strikes unconstitutional, and Representative Mark Mustio will propose reducing the size of the legislature by 20 percent. In addition, the PA Newspaper Association will call for action on a new open records bill, and Representative Scott Boyd will argue against Governor Rendell’s health insurance plan.

headline: Hospitals join race for care
abstract:
Hospitals are vowing to see patients within a half-hour of showing up in the emergency room and others are scheduling patients for doctors' appointments within three days, instead of three weeks. 
Dr. Jonathan Landis, medical director of the emergency department at Canonsburg General Hospital in Washington County says they know the patients time is critical and timeliness often can help prevent complications, unnecessary hospitalizations and more serious outcomes.

headline: DEP suspects gas well in fire, contamination
abstract: A family in Cumberland Township had their water well ignite, so the family had  to leave their homes and live in a hotel. Eastern American Energy Corp. drilled a gas well across the street a few weeks ago, and ever since, the family has encountered problems. The PA Department of Environmental Protection didn’t find gas in any of the area’s surrounding homes, but it did find gas in another nearby well, which it believes was probably caused by the gas drilling; though more tests are needed to be conclusive.

headline: Pa. among 8 states seeking sex offender list
abstract: PA Attorney General Tom Corbett, together with several Attorney Generals from other states, asked MySpace.com to turn over a list of registered sex offenders using the database. The site partnered with Sentinel Tech Holding Corp. in December to find and root out sex offenders using the database. The Attorney Generals want to know by May 29 the steps that have been taken to remove the profiles in question and warn users about sex offenders.

headline: Abington teachers, board OK contract
abstract: It took seven minutes for the Abington Heights School Board to ease more than 20 years of rancor over teachers’ contracts. With a unanimous vote, the board approved a three-year contract that will raise teachers’ salaries by 3.8 percent annually and reduce health care costs by 3 percent annually. It was the first time since 1985 the board and teachers’ union agreed on a contract without resorting to strikes and often-public animosity. The meeting ended with loud applause by the two dozen teachers in the audience. Some hugged and others fought back tears of relief.

headline: Tutu's visit this week first to city
abstract: Archbishop Emeritus Desmond Tutu, the 1984 Nobel Peace Prize winner, will visit with a convicted murder, be honored at a reception dinner and hold an interfaith service during his first ever visit to Pittsburgh.

headline: House OKs health bill under veto threat
abstract: The U.S. House passed a revised bill that would add $35 billion to the State Children’s Health Insurance Program, however, they did not obtain the two-thirds margin of supporters that will be necessary to overcome a veto, which Bush enacted on the original version and will almost certainly do again. Democratic leaders said they made changes to the bill to address concerns about participation by adults, illegal immigrants and families able to afford health insurance; though critics remain unconvinced, which makes it highly unlikely that the bill will pass. Democrats have argued that the bill is supported by most Americans, and both sides have accused one another of turning the bill into a political game.

headline: DOE considers rehearing of powerline policy
abstract: Local officials said they are pleased the U.S. Department of Energy might be taking a second look at its designation of two massive electric transmission corridors, which could allow a federal agency to approve a proposed high-voltage power line through Greene and Washington counties. The DOE announced that it will review requests for a rehearing of its Oct. 2nd designation of the Mid-Atlantic and Southwest Area National Interest Electric Transmission Corridors. Interested parties had 30 days after the designations were made to request a review.

headline: Pa. judge to stand trial on charges
abstract: PA Superior Court Judge Michael T. Joyce was rear-ended by a vehicle going 5 mph and claimed that he suffered an injury that prevented him from exercising for over a year. He received $440,000 from two insurance companies, however, his indictment claims that he was actually engaging in a number of physical activities during the time he claimed to be injured. He was suspended by the state Supreme Court, decided to not seek a second term and will stand trial on federal money laundering and mail fraud charges.

headline: Advocates debate how to restore trust
abstract: A recent PA Senate State Government Committee held hearings yesterday to decide how to reform the state constitution for the first time in 40 years in an attempt to regain trust from the public after recent scandals have plagued the government.  A reform group, PACleanSweep, supported a constitutional convention and claims there is a crisis in the in public confidence.  PA Governor Ed Rendell also supports a convention as he thinks that the lawmakers have failed to create reforms in the past years.

headline: Two Rendell nominees pass the test
abstract: PA Governor Rendell's cabinet nominees, up for reconfirmation by the PA Senate, passed. Secretary of the Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, Michael DiBerardinis and Secretary of the Department of Environmental Protection, Kathleen McGinty were under investigation for awarding grants to nonprofits where their spouses worked. McGinty is known for supporting policies even more stringent than federal ones. PA Sen. Connie Williams voted against McGinty for comments about Public Utility Commission chairman Wendell Holland.

headline: INSIDE THE CAPITOL: House seeks consensus on smoking ban legislation
abstract: The PA House is expected to try to push legislation that would impose a statewide indoor smoking ban into the House-Senate conference committee for compromise on some issues.

headline: Electric buildings
abstract: Would it be possible to build an entire structure - house, commercial building, skyscraper - out of material that would generate electricity when exposed to sunlight? Would it be possible to store some of the power in a storage battery for use at night or on a rainy day? If it's possible, it would save a lot of power-grid electricity.

headline: Pa. Killer Still Missing; Hid in Trash
abstract: A convicted murderer remained at large Tuesday, two days after he escaped from a medium-security prison by hiding in a garbage can. The inmate, Malcolm Kysor, 53, has been serving a life sentence since 1988 for an early 1980s murder in Erie County. He was discovered missing from the State Correctional Institution-Albion during a routine check Sunday. Surveillance camera video showed that after Kysor hid in the garbage can, another inmate, John Gromer, helped Kysor escape by placing a box and plastic bag over him for concealment, then pushed the can off a loading dock and into the back of a pickup truck.

headline: After leading Democrats to control of state House, DeWeese a focus of bonus probe
abstract: The PA state grand jury is investigating bonuses of $3.7 million were given to staff members and Democrat Bill DeWeese is cooperating with the attorney general in order to save his political career. DeWeese  has been able to change House rules in 2007, changes that he describes as the most dramatic and fundamental modification to the House chambers. If DeWeese is not absolved of wrongdoing his political career can be jeopardized.

headline: Union: Money at root of Crestwood contract dispute
abstract: Crestwood School Board member and Luzerne County Commissioner candidate Bill Jones was criticized by union members for saying that the district support staff contract dispute is "not about salary." The union, which represents workers such as custodians, secretaries and aides, also criticized the school boards’ unwillingness to negotiate. However, the school board responded by providing examples of four partial agreements that had been reached, and Jones took an opportunity to criticize current County Commissioner Stephen Urban for his plans to support the union.

headline: Insurance problems aired at hearing
abstract: Eight central Pennsylvania businesses gathered for a hearing before Joel Ario, the state’s acting insurance commissioner, to highlight problems faced by small businesses and garner support for Governor Rendell’s proposal to enact health care reforms. Rendell’s proposal would give the state the authority to review premiums and prevent insurers from rejecting or overcharging women of childbearing age or people who are older or have preexisting conditions. State Representative Scott Boyd disagrees with the proposal and feels that the lack of competition among health insurers is causing most of the problems described at the hearing.

headline: Energy bill offers reason to go green
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell in his $850 million Energy Independence Strategy has offered tax credits and rebates to homes that install solar-energy units, buy a "smart meter" and those who replace appliances with more enviro-friendly appliances.  While the bill costs $6 per person a year in taxes, Rendell claims it will save money when energy regulation caps in 2010.  He has expressed a need to pass a bill before the PA Legislature's recess specifically because the potential of utility bills to climb at least 50%.

headline: Pa.'s flawed system of death
abstract: The author believes that Pennsylvania’s death penalty system is flawed based on a study by the American Bar Association, and she feels nobody should be put to death until it is fixed. In the author’s opinion PA doesn’t require biological evidence to be saved after convictions, relies on outdated eyewitness testimony practices, doesn’t properly inform juries of procedural rules, and has the second highest percentage of African Americans on death row in the nation.

headline: All quiet on the political front
abstract: Elections for eight public offices in Luzerne County will be conducted in only a month, however, candidates have remained surprisingly quiet. Two races have already essentially been determined since both Democrats and Republicans have endorsed the same candidates, which may explain some of the inactivity. In the article, a number of consultants and candidates offer their explanations, and one consultant believes that it’s getting close enough to elections that the introduction of negative campaign advertisements could backfire.

headline: University contract up in the air
abstract: Pat Heilman, the president of the Association of Pennsylvania State College and University Faculties, reported that the 7 council members have reversed its support for the tentative agreement with the Pennsylvania State System of Higher Education that was reached last month due to a misunderstanding in the language of the agreement.  This deal called for an immediate $1,750 cash bonus for all union members, with raises of 3%, 3% and 4% in successive years.  A vote is not expected until after Labor Day.

headline: Investigation sought in cancer cases near university
abstract: In 2002, four alumni from Susquehanna University died of aggressive cancers after possibly being exposed to hazardous fuel that leaked into the soil close to the campus.  Clifford Weisel, a contamination specialist at the School of Public Health at the University of Medicine and Dentistry of New Jersey, and Steven Browning, an environmental epidemiologist at the University of Kentucky both feel that a thorough investigation is necessary.  The PA Department of Health, however, refused to comment citing insufficient information.

headline: Energy bills short-circuit negotiations
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell's energy proposal is a big reason why the government has stalled as Republicans vehemently oppose the small tax on energy usage that they feel would hurt small businesses.  Rendell claims this 0.0005 cents per kilowatt hour charge would cost a residential consumer $6 a year, would be capped for industrial users at $10,000 and would save consumers $10 billion over 10 years.  The governor wants to invest the money from this fee to develop alternative energy supplies and businesses.

headline: Perjury charges in death of teen by senator's gun
abstract: PA State Senator Robert Regola was charged yesterday with improperly storing a handgun and lying to authorities trying to determine about how a 14-year-old neighbor, Louis Farrell, used it in his suicide.  Regola is scheduled to turn himself in at a Greensburg magisterial district judge's office today.  Westmoreland County Coroner Ken Bacha has ruled the death a suicide, but the Farrell family disagrees and believes Regola's son, Bobby Regola, was present at the time of his death.

headline: Almost $17 million worth of good news for NEPA
abstract: U.S. Rep. Paul Kanjorski was understandably pleased to announce that nearly $17 million in funding for 21 local projects throughout Northeast Pennsylvania is a mere signature away. The Senate passed the 2008 Omnibus Appropriations Act by a 76-17 vote, sending it to the House where it received approval by a 272-142 vote. For the 11th Congressional District in PA "which includes parts of Luzerne and Lackawanna counties, and all of Carbon, Columbia and Monroe counties" the bill’s passage could mean a slew of developments ranging from agriculture and defense to education and transportation.

headline: Upper Darby top cop considers run for D-7
abstract: Michael Chitwood, Upper Darby Police Superintendent, will be debating whether to run against US Representative Joseph Sestak in the 2008 elections after Upper Darby Republican Chairman John McNichol asked him to consider running.  Chitwood was turned down an offer to run for governor in Maine where he was once police chief in Portland, but Sestak is a former 3-star Navy admiral who has over $1 million saved for his upcoming campaign.  John McMeekin II, president of Radnor School District Board, and Stephen Elliott, deputy assistant secretary at the US State Department, are two other Republican candidates that have expressed interest in running.

headline: Ironing out a health-care question
abstract: Harry Gross gives advice on insurance companies and getting them to put promises in writing. Keep a careful record of the date and time of the call and the full name of the person you speak with. Then send that person a letter certified mail with a return receipt requested. And help on retirement savings and bankruptcy.

headline: Energy policy in play
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell has introduced an energy plan to attempt to make Pennsylvania more independent with energy and less dependent on foreign petroleum by developing alternative sources of energy such as ethanol.  Rendell proposed to charge 0.05 cents per kilowatt hour to help pay for his plan and the Energy Independence Fund.  Irwin Popowsky, PA Consumer Advocate, claimed at a hearing of the Senate Environmental Resources, and Energy and Consumer Protection Committees that the policies the state decides on today will determine whether or not Pennsylvania has a "crash landing" in regards to its energy policy.

headline: Phila. Faces down state, passes gun law
abstract: In violation of its authority, Philadelphia City Council unanimously passed eight gun control bills sponsored by Councilman Darrell Clarke and Councilwoman Donna Reed Miller. The city will also file a lawsuit in Common Pleas Court to gain the authority to pass its own firearms legislation. PA House Speaker Dennis O'Brien confirmed that the House opposes giving the city authority in the area of gun control legislation. Mayor John Street is expected to support the City Council's legislation.

headline: Altmire to duel with TV's Colbert
abstract: Unrepresentative Jason Altmire is just a few weeks into his new job as a Pennsylvania congressman, but the McCandless Democrat already has made a career move that many of his colleagues wouldn't dare to consider. He's a guest tonight on the hit Comedy Central show, "The Colbert Report," which is exceptionally adept at poking fun at lawmakers. In past episodes, host Stephen Colbert convinced a Florida congressman to jokingly admit to having a cocaine habit; he told a black representative that he couldn't see the color of her skin; and he asked US Representative Barney Frank about his wife.

headline: Urban Warrior| Have state stores come far enough?
abstract: The author of the opinion piece shares a story about a bad experience shopping in a Wine & Spirits Store, or state store.  He writes that since LCB Chairman Jonathan Newman stepped down last week after leading an effort to reform the system and urges them to become more friendly.  He writes that it may be a good time to privatize them, but he know that will not happen while PA Governor Rendell holds office since he opposes it.

headline: Keep studying area's cancers, Specter urges
abstract: U.S. Senator Arlen Specter released a letter urging state and federal health officials to continue monitoring cases of a rare type of blood cancer after a two-year survey found higher than average cases in Schuylkill, Carbon and Luzerne Counties. He also vowed to get money for the study.

headline: Fast Eddie's farce
abstract: This editorial criticizes PA Governor Ed Rendell's call for a $850 million bond issue to promote biodiesel and ethanol plants and production within the state.  The author cites the rising cost of food and fuel due to biodiesel production and the lack of efficiency of the production of ethanol as major problems with the plan.  It finally states that taxing residents for this plan is way out of line with the common interests of the citizens.

headline: Pittsburgh sues landlords over nuisance house
abstract: The city of Pittsburgh is suing landlords over a house that police claim has attracted drug and gang violence continuously.  Mayor Luke Ravenstahl said the home was one of the worst properties in the city and other homes like it will be shut down and boarded up or torn down.  The city lawyers have filed a civil lawsuit against Mary P. Ware and Robert J. Branch-Ware in an attempt to have them close down the rental home.

headline: Cashing out: The Legislature could use some per-diem reform
abstract: The editorial board writes that three departing legislators remind PA citizens some members of the General Assembly have been greedy. While heading for the exits, former PA Senate Majority Leader David Brightbill and former PA Representatives Mark McNaughton and Peter Zug helped themselves to a combined $37,000 in per diems going back 18 months. Despite his $105,000 salary last year, Mr. Brightbill applied for $17,724 in per diems. Mr. McNaughton was given $10,436 and Mr. Zug $9,164. Each of them had a salary last year of $72,187. The kicker is that all three politicos live within 30 miles of the Capitol; one of them lives in Harrisburg.

headline: Voters to cast ballot for one candidate, not seven
abstract: Residents of Wilkes-Barre will vote for only one city council candidate in the upcoming elections instead of seven, which they have done in the past. One council member from each of the city’s five voting districts will be elected. The article describes what territory is included for each district, and it provides information about each candidate's background and campaign platform.

headline: Lawmaker wants more drug label information
abstract: State Sen. Sean Logan takes Lipitor to keep his cholesterol in check, but has no idea where the drug is made. The country where Logan's Lipitor was made would have to be printed on the bottle or in accompanying literature under legislation the Monroeville Democrat plans to introduce in January. Several residents called Logan's offices and complained that local pharmacies and drug manufacturers were not helpful in supplying information about where their drugs were made. That's when Logan decided to draft the legislation.

headline: Feds order electric corridor review
abstract: At least one state representative approved of the U.S. Department of Energy's decision to review its designation of two electric transmission corridors, including one that involves York County. The DOE has issued a rehearing order that will allow the federal agency to consider the concerns raised in requests about both the Mid-Atlantic Area National Corridor and the Southwest Area National Corridor. In October, the DOE designated the Mid-Atlantic Area National Interest Electric Transmission Corridor to identify areas where significant electric transmission congestion exists.

headline: Police commander wins injunction in suit against city on whistleblowing
abstract: Catherine McNeilly, who was demoted from that senior rank in the Pittsburgh Police Bureau last month, was reinstated yesterday after a federal district judge found that Commander McNeilly acted in good faith by going to City Council with her concerns about the nomination of Dennis Regan to the position of public safety director back in October. Commander. McNeilly filed a federal lawsuit Dec. 21 against the city, its police chief and mayor, citing the state's whistleblower law and claiming that her First Amendment rights were violated.

headline: Choosing judges: Rendell's snout slap
abstract: PA Government Ed Rendell says ordinary Pennsylvanians should not be allowed to choose their appeals court judges. The editorial board writes that judges should get their jobs through merit-based selection, not politics. Instead, a coterie of political appointees would submit names to the political governor. He would send a nominee over to the political Senate for approval. Voters will lose the right to elect their appeals court judges only if they approve a constitutional amendment that first must pass two consecutive sessions of the PA Legislature. The editors suggestion to the public: Don't vote away that right. You're not as dumb as the powers that be would have you think.

headline: Votes show Dems' clash
abstract: Councilman Bill Peduto of Point Breeze has a dozen years of experience in city government. He's challenging Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl has spent most of his life in the North Side and has worked three years for the city.  An analysis of their votes when the two served together on City Council reveals stark political and philosophical differences. Although most City Council votes are unanimous, Ravenstahl and Peduto clashed on several key issues from 2004 to 2006, including how to best manage the city's financial recovery and how to rein in wasteful spending by their colleagues. Peduto announced last week he would run against Ravenstahl in a campaign that could cost each candidate about $1 million.

headline: Lawmakers want faster results in Muhlenberg Township cancer study
abstract: PA Sens. John Rafferty Jr. and Michael O'Pake introduced a bill to create an Office of Illness Monitoring in the PA Department of Health, saying the slow progress of a community cancer study proves the department does not have adequate personnel. Initial results found no elevated cancer rate in Muhlenberg Township, but included data from parts of Reading. A second review was requested but has not been released. O'Pake aims to make the bill a part of budget negotiations to get it passed quickly.

headline: Gas prices expected to soar
abstract: According to a report released by The Lundberg Survey, gas prices nationwide will increase from 5 to 10 cents a gallon depending on the price of crude oil.  Many of the predictions that see an increase in prices are concerned with tropical storms in the Gulf of Mexico region.  Bevi Powell, spokeswoman for the Pittsburgh American Automobile Association reported that prices in the region were 3 cents higher than the national average but usually remain stable.

headline: POLICE UNVEIL SQUAD TO HELP NEIGHBORHOODS; C-TIPS CAN BE REACHED VIA CITY'S 311 CONTACT LINE
abstract: The Community's Technical Investigative and Preparedness Section, or C-TIPS, has a broad mandate to improve communication and collaboration between the bureau and a variety of organizations, Chief of Pittsburgh Police Nate Harper said. It helped out, for instance, after a Jan. 12 bomb scare forced the evacuation of the Children's Hospital construction site in Lawrenceville, costing some $250,000 in lost productivity. C-TIPS Officers Andre Henderson and Sheldon Williams went to the site, and trained employees on how to identify dangerous objects and respond to threats.

headline: City council forum
abstract: 28 candidates for Wilkes-Barre city council are invited to attend a forum moderated by WILK radio host Sue Henry. 17 candidates, including incumbents Councilman Bill Barrett and Tony Thomas have said they will attend. The invitation was extended by editor of the LuLac Political Letter blog, David Yonki.

headline: Voting 'no' on judges lets pols pick them …
abstract: The authors of the article feel that Operation Clean Sweep, a Pennsylvania reform group that is advocating voting no to the retention of 67 judges throughout the state, is a serious possibility in light of public anger towards the current political environment. However, the authors are against the idea because they believe it sends a message that the state’s reform movement has become desperate and run out of ideas. They also argue that it won’t solve any of the state’s political problems, and replacement judges will be appointed with no voter input by Governor Rendell, which would only serve to diminish the influence of voters.

headline: Legislators ought to act on smoking
abstract: Editors hope legislators will address smoking ban legislation soon, as 16 other states have banned smoking in public and work places. PA Governor Ed Rendell supports a ban. In Erie and Allegheny Counties, legislation passed by the counties to ban smoking is being held up in the courts. The PA Restaurant Association now also encourages a ban on smoking in work and public places. The Legislature should get on board!

headline: House, Senate at odds over role of ethanol
abstract: PA Governor Edward Rendell and PA lawmakers are working to develop a statewide energy policy because energy bills passed during the year by the Republican-controlled Senate and Democratic-controlled House stake out different positions requiring the use of ethanol in fuels sold in PA. The disagreement is over whether ethanol can emerge as a viable alternative fuel in PA, the best way for the state government toe encourage ethanol production and the impact of a new federal law requiring more ethanol in PA’s energy strategy. Michael Smith, spokesman for the PA Department of Environmental Protection stated that Governor Rendell thinks that the use of ethanol requirement is a way to reduce the US’s dependence on foreign oil.

headline: Positive guidance needed to stem violence
abstract: On Monday, the shooting death of a 42-year-old West End resident near his Engle Street home marked the 25th homicide this year in Chester, the 22nd as a result of gunfire. His murder came one day after an 18-year-old man died of a gunshot wound to the chest about a block from his Elson Road home in the Toby Farms section of Chester Township. While the victim may not have been a gang member, Chester Township police maintain he was a casualty of violence between gangs in Chester Township and the city of Chester.

headline: City GOP: Alive but not kicking
abstract: Al Taubenberger, who is involved in the least competitive Philadelphia mayoral campaign in over 50 years, basically received the Republican nomination by default because party leaders couldn’t find anybody else to run. The city’s Republican Party has been struggling to remain competitive, and registration has been dropping substantially, which prompted Kevin Kelly, an emerging Republican leader, to issue a manifesto calling for reform to rebuild the party. Michael Meehan, the current party leader, has been criticized by some party members; though he attributes the city’s struggles to national party misfortunes.

headline: Voting system "just totally antiquated"
abstract: Reaction to Lackawanna County’s vote-count debacle ranged from sarcasm to diplomacy as the count of paper ballots stretched to the end of a second day. Voters leaving polling places joked that poll workers were like proctors at college entrance exams, hoarding pens voters used to fill out ballots.
