Before the election, Mr. Washo, who, with Mr. O’Brien cruised to an apparent victory in the Lackawanna County Commissioners’ race, repeatedly pointed out the county could have rented touch-screen voting machines for $300,000, instead of the system of paper ballots read by optical scanners for $155,000.

headline: Nonsmokers have rights, too
abstract: Letter to the editor outlining the healthy problems associated with second hand smoke along with the costs that it demands on the state. Author recommends smokers smoke outside.

headline: House votes against amendment that would stop power lines
abstract: The US House of Representatives have not passed the attempt to block the government from placing new major power lines in local communities that oppose them.  The supporters of the new power lines claim that they will help keep up with growth and prevent the major blackouts that took place in 2003.  The corridors were designed by the US Energy Department and have pushed aside local rights according to the opponents of the bill.

headline: POW camp marker missing
abstract: A marker that described the historical significance of Camp Security is gone. Friends of Camp Security say the sign marked the location of the only Revolutionary prisoner-of-war camp still known to be intact. The group wants the sign returned to its home, which is for a now-topless pole on East Market Street in Springettsbury Township.

headline: City's new campaign law called a winner
abstract: Philadelphia's campaign reform law weathered its first test and set a record for funds raised in a mayoral campaign. Michael Nutter is the winner of the Democratic primary. The reform prevented contractors from contributing, prompting ordinary citizens to contribute in higher numbers. The rules did not prevent nonprofit organizations from contributing without revealing their donors. Their role is being investigated by the city's Board of Ethics. The Committee of Seventy, a watchdog organization, approves the reform laws.

headline: Wagner calls for state nominees on transit agency board
abstract: PA State Auditor General Jack Wagner has requested that the board of the Port Authority of Allegheny County be restructured with more state officials because the state government provides about 60% of the operating revenue.  Furthermore, Wagner insists that the historically lavish perks and pensions for the top executives are excessive and harming the authority.  Wagner wants the nine-member board to have two appointees from the governor.

headline: Local health care provider gives Carney crash course
abstract: A local health care provider is concerned pending federal legislation could impact how it provides oxygen treatment to approximately 1,600 people in Northeastern Pennsylvania. As a result, representatives of Apria Healthcare invited U.S. Rep. Chris Carney, D-Dimock Township, to tour their facility in the Hanover Industrial Estates on Monday. Carney got a crash course in how the facility’s 100 local employees deliver and process medical services, specifically the delivery of oxygen and liquid oxygen.

headline: Illinois gets Pa.'s support in quest for high-tech coal project
abstract: Governor Rendell sent a letter to FutureGen to voice his support for Illinois over Texas to become the site of FutureGen's prototype coal electricity plant. The plant would  produce virtually no carbon dioxide emissions by pumping it underground. Illinois gave a number of reasons for why it should be chosen, and Rendell endorsed it because PA is a coal rich state and could harness the technology.

headline: Probe tests Pa. casino oversight
abstract: The Dauphin County Court is investigating the allegations that Louis A. DeNaples misled investigators from the PA Gaming Control Board that he had no connection with William D'Elia, an infamous mob boss, in the process of winning a $412 million bid for a slots casino in the Poconos.  The state police are not entirely cooperating with the grand jury as they won't share negative information obtained about DeNaples in previous investigations because of a privacy law.  Besides D'Elia, investigators are also looking into DeNaples' connections with a jailed and connected Muslim cleric, Shamsud-din Ali, a life-term prisoner Louis Covello and James Decker, former Lackawanna County chief clerk who was convicted for defrauding the government.

headline: Cleanup bill passed by State Senate
abstract: Would not pull up online

headline: Wagner: PHEAA spent $7.5 million on staff bonuses
abstract: Auditor General Jack Wagner released a report that claims the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency spent $7.5 million in bonuses and paid $108,000 to entertain employees at Hersheypark. Wagner claims that the agency reneged on promises to cut back spending in order to help more students pay for college. A spokesman for PHEAA defended the agency and cited some errors in the audit.

headline:
Malpractice fund payouts drop again
$191 million in claims represents amounts awarded above doctors' insurance.
abstract: The Medical Care Availability and Reduction of Error fund, which helps pay the costs of malpractice claims that rise above the minimum state requirements for coverage, will pay half the amount it did last year, which Governor Rendell claimed is evidence that recent reforms are improving malpractice problems in PA. The President of the PA Medical Society said that reforms have helped, but PA still compares poorly to other states.

headline: Keep it clean
abstract: Carolyn Pengidore, president of Comperio Energy, writes her positive opinion on the Governor's Energy Independence Strategy that will go to vote in the PA Legislature.  She believes that clean energy is the industry of the future, especially with the research facilities available within Pennsylvania such as the National Energy Technology Laboratory.  Pengidore encourages the community leaders and legislators to support this new energy strategy because it will economically support this industry, benefit the environment and create new jobs in the state.

headline: Protect Lehigh County with Anthony as judge
abstract: The author believes that Jim Anthony will be the solution to Lehigh County’s crime problem. He believes Anthony has strong track record and urges voters to vote for him in the upcoming election.

headline: Closing phone records
abstract: The day-to-day legislative maneuvering in Harrisburg over an open records bill makes it impossible to predict the details of what will ultimately emerge - if anything actually does. We hope the finished product will be a law that guarantees public access to all government documents, save for a few necessary exceptions, and puts the burden of demonstrating that a record should be closed on the agency that wants to deny access. Although the county refused to release the records and court intervention was necessary to find out about the calls, which in most respects is considered one of the most deficient in the country. It would be ironic if that law were to be replaced with a "reform" in which knowledge of such phone calls would be off-limits to the public.

headline: Washington County: GOP's Toprani stuns Pettit in DA race
abstract: In one of the most competitive races in years for Washington County's top law enforcement post, Republican newcomer Steven M. Toprani scored a stunning victory over embattled District Attorney John C. Pettit. The race that promised to be the most exciting in the county last night did not disappoint, with Mr. Toprani, 28, of Carroll, running away with a 2-1 lead over Mr. Pettit, 72, of Washington, for most of the night.

headline: Many Eligible for Child Health Plan Have No Idea
abstract: It was only in May that Ms. Hall learned that her family qualified for the State Children’s Health Insurance Program, which provides subsidized insurance to children of the working poor. That she had never heard of the joint state and federal program made her typical of countless parents of the estimated eight million uninsured children. Despite a decade of marketing efforts by governments and private foundations, nearly 30 percent of children who are eligible for the health insurance program and are not covered by private plans have yet to enroll, according to a new government study.

headline: Letter to the Editor
abstract: A citizen writes in protest of the corporate power that he feels influenced some of the US Representatives vote when they denied an amendment to block the creation of electric transmission corridors that would cover most of Pennsylvania.  These corridors will allow the utility companies to build transmission lines without the consent of state officials or the citizens.  The author of the letter reports that the average amount of money given to the 6 state representatives who voted against the amendment was $35,816.

headline: Putting officials through the fire
abstract: The International Association of Firefighters Fire Operations 101 program are inviting firefighters from across the area to help out to take participants into a building where a controlled fire will be burning in one room.  The participants will be local and state government officials such as PA Governor Ed Rendell, US Representative Charlie Dent and Easton Mayor Phil Mitman.  While some of the officials, who are all carrying their own equipment, will be focusing on putting out the fire and others  working on rescuing a mannequin, they will also learn how to use the Jaws of Life and how to perform Cardiopulmonary Resuscitation.

headline: Coddling killers
abstract: The author is angry that Mayor Street called the shooter of Officer Cassidy a troubled person, and she believes that criminals should be dealt with more harshly.

headline: Wasteful reimbursements
abstract: As PA Governor Rendell called for legislative reforms at his second inauguration, the editorial board writes that there was fresh evidence that such action is sorely needed. It was reported that before leaving office late last year, three lawmakers from central Pennsylvania cashed in a total of $37,000 in meal and lodging expenses paid by taxpayers. Some of the "per diem" expenses dated all the way back to 2003.  Former PA Senate Majority Leader David "Chip" Brightbill was reimbursed $17,724 in per diems, intended for legislators who stay in Harrisburg while the General Assembly is in session. Brightbill lives about 20 miles from the capital.

headline: Moral meddling
abstract: Most Americans agree that all of us deserve the opportunity to make such decisions on what measures the hospital should take to prolong the patient's life in the event of a catastrophic illness or injury, within the bounds of the law, without interference from meddling politicians or hospital administrators. Pennsylvania's Independent Regulatory Review Commission approved regulations that would allow health-care facilities with religious affiliations or moral objections to claim an exemption from a laudable new rule that requires hospitals to inform rape victims of their right to emergency contraception, and to provide the contraceptive pills to the raped woman if she wants them.

headline: Limits to expire; lawmakers fear 30% increase
abstract: An executive for PPL told PA senators that an extension of rate caps on electricity, which are set to expire by the end of 2009, would negatively affect the company’s plans to build a third nuclear reactor for its Susquehanna plant. Senator Lisa Boscola is torn because of her support for the development of nuclear power, which supplies a third of the state’s electricity, and her desire to prevent price hikes after the caps expire. In addition, security issues were a big area of focus in light of the recent events at Peach Bottom nuclear plant.

headline: Ramsey sees crime emergency
abstract: Expect Michael Nutter's new police commissioner to start out of the gate next month at a sprint. Charles H. Ramsey, Nutter's choice to replace Sylvester M. Johnson, fully agrees with the incoming mayor's promise to declare a crime emergency in some parts of the city on his first day in office, Jan. 7. How Ramsey will carry out the emergency response is less certain. He spent much of last week getting his bearings in his new city - meeting with Johnson and the department's command staff as well as attending several district roll calls to introduce himself to the rank and file.

headline: Committee sends presidential primary bill to House
abstract: The PA House State Government Committee have supported a plan to advance the state's presidential primary to February 12th to increase the significance of the votes as well as to reserve a day in May for referendums dealing with property tax increases in school districts.  PA Governor Ed Rendell has chosen the 2008 primary to be held on February 5 to maximize the influence of the state's voters.  The separate school tax referendum date was proposed by Representative Sean Ramaley to respond to the calls by Pennsylvania School Boards Association to a later date to ease the budget-making process.

headline: Watchdogs say budget process still needs work
abstract: Despite the Pennsylvania lawmakers insisting that the legislative process has been improved and opened up since the pay raise scandal in 2005, many watchdog groups, including Rock The Capital, still feel that the public still does not have enough time to vote on legislation in the final hours of voting.  Spokesman for PA House of Representatives Speaker Dennis O' Brien reported that this year, legislators have 24 hours to overlook 300-page budget bills rather than less than an hour.  Russ Diamond of PA CleanSweep asserted that the lawmakers do deserve credit for ending late night sessions.

headline: NFIB predicts Pa. job loss
abstract: The National Federation of Independent Business (NFIB) released data that predicts that Governor Rendell’s plan to levy a three percent payroll tax against businesses that don’t provide health insurance to employees will cost a total of $19.2 billion, as well as the loss of 167,000 jobs. A spokeswoman for Governor Rendell said that the plan will gradually be implemented over a six-year period and is absolutely necessary in light of the continual rise in health care costs that leaves 767,000 PA workers uninsured . Rendell travelled to State College to promote his Cover All Pennsylvanians health care plan, but Representative Scott Conklin and members of the NFIB have vowed not to support his call to tax businesses.

headline:
Natural gas rates going up this year
All 3 utilities file increase notices for next 3 months
abstract: All three of Pittsburgh’s natural gas utilities gave notice to the Public Utility Commission that they would be increasing their rates from a year ago, however, the prices will be considerably lower than two years ago when Hurricanes Katrina and Wilma affected production. The article also provides information pertaining to the current and expected prices of crude oil, and the U.S. Department of Energy reported growing inventories in natural gas, as well as crude, gasoline and heating oil, which could eventually depress prices.

headline: Register of wills sued over visa arrest
abstract: An Egyptian man jailed after the Cumberland County register of wills staff questioned a visa he tried using to get a marriage license is suing the county office.  Mehany Mousa and his fiancée, Kendra Vernon, both of Camp Hill, are suing Register of Wills Glenda Farner Strasbaugh in federal court, claiming her staff overstepped its authority when they called immigration authorities about the visa. A visa is not an adequate gauge of an immigrant's residency status, Shagin said, because it only shows the holder was allowed into the U.S. legally.

headline: Controlling interests
abstract: With eight days before the Democratic primary, the article reports on the fundraising totals filed by candidates with the Allegheny County Elections Division. In the lead are Allegheny County Prothonotary Lamb and City Council President Doug Shields. At the back of the pack is DaMon Macklin, a Highland Park businessman.

headline: Westmoreland officials want aid if voting system nixed
abstract: Government officials from Westmoreland County are requesting some form of state and federal government pay for new voting machines after US Congress passed the Help America Vote Act of 2002.  This act requires that each computerized voting machine have a printer to produce a paper trail of the votes.  In 2005, Westmoreland County used a federal grant and paid $3 million to purchase new touch screen machines and find it too expensive to update their machines already.

headline: Nursing home off provisional status despite deficiencies
abstract: Laurel Crest nursing home in Cambria County has been given a one-year operating license after being fined in March $8,750 for failing to correct deficiencies.  There was also fear that all Medicaid and Medicare reimbursements would be stopped, which in turn would force the closure of the nursing home.  Despite giving the home a full operating license, the PA Department of Health will return in September for a follow-up inspection to see if there is progress on 13 deficiencies, 2 of which are classified as constituting "actual harm."

headline: Live-Blogging the Governor
abstract: This is a live blog that follows PA Governor Ed Rendell's speech to both the PA Senate and the PA House of Representatives promoting his energy independence plan, which he views as a national security issue as well as an environmental issue.  In his speech, he also mentions that he wants Pennsylvania to produce its own energy, and he also claims that he has spoken with many people who want to build biodiesel and ethanol plants within the state.  The blog also follows his proposals of a $850 million bond issue to fund the project and a call for smart meters on every residential home in the state to save money and electricity.

headline: Regola surrenders in gun case
abstract: PA State Senator Robert Regola has surrendered on charges that he improperly stored a handgun and allowed it to fall into the hands of a 14-year-old, Louis Farrell, who fatally shot himself, and then lied about it at a coroner's hearing.  Westmoreland County District Attorney John Peck claims Regola has contradicted himself in official statements given to police previously.  Magisterial District Judge James Albert released the senator on $25,000 unsecured bond until his hearing on April 5.

headline: Convert state pensions to defined contribution
abstract: Pennsylvania's defined pension benefit program is facing significant funding shortfalls: $10 billion-plus in unfunded liabilities in the state defined-benefit plans, and pension plans in Pittsburgh and Philadelphia in near-crisis status. These issues, if left unaddressed, could severely impact our state's economy and taxpayers will end up paying the costs. It is critical both to taxpayers and civil servants that our governments adopt a comparable retirement benefits package that is predictable and affordable, as well as free from political manipulations.

headline: What They're Promising: Police
abstract: A look at the latest proposals of major candidates in Philadelphia mayoral primary examines Tom Knox, who has promised to hire 1,000 more police at a cost of $52 million, according to the PA Intergovernmental Cooperation Authority. Knox would also implement aggressive recycling, a streamlined development review process, and call centers. However, Knox has not said where he will find the revenue to fund these proposals, or which departments might lose funds and jobs as a result.

headline: Ohio smokers head for the border
abstract: Business and restaurant owners near the PA and West Virginia border in Ohio are concerned they will lose smoking clients to neighboring states where smoking bans are not in effect in establishments. In Allegheny County, PA, a smoking ban was stayed by a Commonwealth Court judge until the Court rules on whether or not the county has the authority to enforce such an ordinance for bars and restaurants.

headline: Making the switch: Rendell touts area wind farm, change to alternative energy
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell celebrated the opening of a new wind turbine at Locust Ridge Wind Farm in Mahanoy Township that will produce 68,238 megawatt hours of energy per year.  According to the PA Department of Environmental Protection, this will power more than 6,500 homes. Wind power is a significant part of the Governor's $850 million Energy Independence Strategy which focuses on clean energy industries, stabilizing electricity rates, and reducing dependence on foreign oil.

headline: Rendell says casinos stay; neighbors vow to fight on
abstract: Governor Rendell sent a letter to a local activist who is trying to force Foxwoods and SugarHouse to move their proposed casino locations. In the letter Rendell says he asked the casinos to reconsider, however, they both refused, and he has no authority to force their hands. He offered to meet with residents of the proposed locations to discuss traffic, parking and crime concerns, but the Casino Free Philadelphia group and City Councilman Frank DiCicco are disappointed with Rendell and vow to continue their fight.

headline: Costs balanced for professors and students
abstract: The author is pleased that a contract was worked out for the faculty of the State System of Higher Education, which is composed of the 14 state owned universities. The four-year contract is described in the editorial, and the author feels the contract is fair for both sides and served the best interests of students.

headline: What's good for the goose
abstract: Pittsburgh mayor Ravenstahl may not see his proposal to get a 10-year tax abatement for residents in new housing Downtown passed. Councilman Jim Motznik opposes the proposal unless it is expanded to include neighborhoods citywide. Motznik and three other council members face re-election next week.

headline: Other views
abstract: This editorial explains how there is a projected need of doctors in Pennsylvania and that recent legislation by PA Representative Josh Shapiro to create a medical school loan-forgiveness plan for doctors who practice in the state for 10 years is essential.  However, the article does also agree with PA Governor Ed Rendell who feels the legislation should be changed to require that some of the doctors to practice in low medical service areas.  The article blames the state's medical-malpractice environment and rising costs of medical school for the current crisis.

headline: Modest rate hike for energy program feasible
abstract: The editorial encourage Pennsylvania legislators to deny certain proposals by PA Governor Ed Rendell including an increase in sales tax to 7%, a tax on oil companies' profits, and taxes on companies who don't provide health care.  Despite these disagreements, the author also supports some of Rendell's proposals such as leasing the Pennsylvania Turnpike and the fee on electric bills to help increase the Energy Independence Fund.  They feel this small increase will save homeowners money as it will be invested in energy saving programs.

headline: Rendell touts gun plan as police chiefs meet
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell spoke the Pennsylvania Chiefs of Police Association in Lancaster County about his new gun control proposal that will limit handgun purchases to 1 per month and increase penalties for owning a stolen firearm.  Republicans in the Legislature, including Republican PA Senator Mike Brubajer, are very wary of the proposal and generally do not support additional controls.  However, Bill Howatt, the president of the Police Association, spoke highly of the governor and his new proposal.

headline: Council's Tasco is incoming president
abstract: null

headline: Where's Earll on smoking ban?
abstract: State Sen. Jane Earll has been the champion of many good issues throughout her career, with the exception of her endorsement of then-U.S. Sen. Rick Santorum. However, there is one issue that Earll has been relatively quiet on, and that is the state Legislature's attempt to pass a smoking ban. Could it be that Earll's own smoking habit is clouding her judgment and the health concerns of her constituents?

headline: Outdoor smoking bans start Thursday at 5 hospitals
abstract: Geisinger Medical Center has given employees nearly a full year's notice and now the Danville facility is ready to ban smoking outdoors as well as indoors. Geisinger is one of five central Pennsylvania facilities cracking down on the outside-the-door smoking crowds. No smoking, even in cars on hospital property, will also be the rule at Berwick Hospital Center, Evangelical Community Hospital in Lewisburg, and at Shamokin and Sunbury hospitals.

headline: New energy policy would aid state businesses, homeowners
abstract: The research on nanotechnology at Penn State will contribute in a big way to the development of solar energy technology. However, so will local government projects like the one in Media Borough in Delaware Company. PA Secretary of Environmental Protection Kathleen McGinty presented the borough with the Governor's Award for Environmental Excellence. Five buildings have been outfitted with solar panels, with more in the works. The PA Legislature should approve PA Governor Ed Rendell's Energy Independence Strategy, which taxes kilowatt hours of electricity consumption.

headline: Rendell wrong on gun control
abstract: Author writes in response to your editorial about Gov. Ed Rendell's recent testimony before the state House Judiciary Committee in support of four gun control measures. The sad state of affairs in Washington, D.C., New York City and other cities, which severely restrict firearms ownership, provides strong evidence of the failure of gun control in this country. It is illegal to even possess a handgun in Washington, D.C., yet the city's murder rate is one of the nation's highest. Perhaps this is because criminals, by definition, don't obey laws, and so laws that restrict firearms ownership deter them no more than laws against murder do.

headline: County council picks up another Democrat
abstract: Democrats strengthened their grip on Allegheny County government Tuesday as Chief Executive Dan Onorato coasted unopposed into a second term and his party picked up a seat on County Council. Democrat Nick Futules, a Verona councilman, knocked Councilwoman Susan Caldwell, R-Plum, out of office with a margin of 56 percent to 43 percent to represent the northeastern suburbs, according to unofficial returns.

headline: Why gun control has no shot
abstract: State Rep. Dan Frankel took note of the e-mails he received last week concerning a package of gun control bills emotionally endorsed by Gov. Ed Rendell. Unofficially, the count was about 1,000 to 10, with the gun-rights lobby winning that grassroots campaign just as it succeeded in rebuffing Mr. Rendell's efforts to sway the House Judiciary Committee. In nine years, he's yet to be on the winning side of any significant legislation opposed by the National Rifle Association and other gun-rights lobbyists. And, with their continued strength in hunting-happy Pennsylvania, there's no telling when -- or even if -- he'll ever be.

headline: Pa. House passes bill to cover autism care
abstract: PA Speaker of the House Dennis O' Brien introduced a bill that passed through the PA House of Representatives unopposed that requires private insurers to provide an annual amount of $36,000 for autism care, with the government providing the rest.  The PA House also approved a bill that requires health care providers to create infection control plans and insurers to cover infection screenings.  The House also delivered a bill to PA Governor Ed Rendell that expands the duties of nurse practitioners under a specialty certification.

headline: New York Senate stands against powerline rules
abstract: The Pennsylvania House of Representatives passed a resolution that disallows the federal authority to site electric transmission lines on the same day as the New York Senate.  The resolutions reaffirm the rights of states and criticize the fact that the US Department of Energy hearings regarding this issue were held too far away from the impacted area.

headline: Rendell's Gun-Control Showdown
abstract: The murder of a Philadelphia police officer should be an influential moment in the fight against the illegal trafficking in handguns in Pennsylvania. Gov. Rendell is right to seize on the tragic Halloween shooting of Officer Chuck Cassidy. While city prosecutors pursue Cassidy's accused killer through the courts, Rendell today plans to demand accountability from Harrisburg lawmakers over lax handgun laws. The showdown is planned at a Pennsylvania House committee hearing, where Rendell will speak up for several commonsense gun proposals. It drives home the point that the state faces a crisis in the rise of gun violence.

headline: County Dems make history
abstract: Five Democrats have cracked through the Republican wall around Montgomery County’s government. While all eyes were focused on the heated county commissioners’ battle, five of the nine Democratic row office (elected department heads) candidates defeated their Republican counterparts in Tuesday’s elections. Montgomery County Democrats have not had an elected row officer, other than the jury commissioner that is required by law, since as far back as the Civil War.

headline: Why is Rendell back?
abstract: The author of the letter addresses all PA citizens who reelected PA Governor Ed Rendell and says it is hard to understand why they would reelect a man who used your taxpayer dollars to keep his powerful friends in the medical, insurance and gambling communities happy in his first term.

headline: Pa. law on methadone clinic sites struck down
abstract: The 3rd US Circuit Court of Appeals ruled that a Pennsylvania law that restricts methadone clinics within 500 feet of parks, places of worship and residential neighborhoods violates the federal Americans with Disabilities Act.  The lawsuit is the result of a Reading clinic that wanted to open a new location but could not because City Council would not approve the location of the clinic.  The plaintiffs' lawyers of the Public Interest Law Center of Philadelphia report that this ruling will effect everyone statewide.

headline: Opening way for new corridors creates a number of problems
abstract: The author understands why U.S. Energy Secretary Samuel Bodman wants to address concerns over future blackouts because electricity is crucial for a modern society to operate. However, in the author’s opinion, his decision to approve the construction of new transmission lines that would run through a large portion of PA is a bad idea. The author believes it will be harmful to the environment in the long run and may not even prevent future blackouts.

headline: Report: College substance abuse taking on dangerous forms
abstract: According to a report by the National Center on Addiction and Substance Abuse at Columbia University, a particular culture of excessive consumption of drugs and alcohol has flourished in recent years on college campuses across the country.  The frequency of binge drinking has increased since 1993 and hundreds of thousands more students are abusing prescription drugs as well.  Joseph Califano, president of the center, dispels the myth that schools can't do anything about it by urging the colleges to make this a priority.

headline:
County Elections
The best of the 'burbs
abstract: This editorial offers the newspaper’s official endorsements for county commissioners, as well as their reasoning for their choices. The newspaper endorses Jim Matthews and Ruth Damsker for Montgomery County and Charles Martin and James Cawley for Bucks County. It also endorses Carol Aichele and Kathi Cozzone for Chester County and Andy Lewis, Christine Fizzano Cannon and Tom McGarrigle for Delaware County.

headline: Will Senate bill make it to Rendell?
abstract: Major differences remain between the state House and Senate on comprehensive energy legislation to satisfy Gov. Ed Rendell. The Senate on Wednesday passed its version of an energy plan by a 44-5 vote. That bill now goes to the House. Rendell said the Senate bill falls well short of what he wants. Senate Republicans say their plan, while certain to be modified in the House, gives the governor his best shot at getting something done.

headline: PHEAA to award $4M to nursing programs
abstract: The Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency Foundation has reported that 51 nursing schools in Western Pennsylvania will receive a total of $4 million for their students.  Carey Miller, spokeswoman for the organization, said it addresses the increasing nursing job vacancies cited by the US Health Resources and Services Administration as well as a lack of nursing educators.  Students use the money for books, instruments, uniforms, transportation and computer programs.

headline: PA is Largest State Purchaser of Clean Energy, Claims Governor
abstract: Since Governor Rendell took office, he has increased Pennsylvania’s percentage of renewable energy purchases to 30 percent, which makes PA the only state on the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency’s Top 25 Green Power Partnership List. Governor Rendell praised the efforts said that developing clean energy sources is crucial for protecting national security, reducing the impact on the environment and creating economic opportunities for people. Rendell’s Energy Independence Strategy, which is aimed at attracting billions in private investments for renewable energy projects, creating 13,000 new jobs and saving consumers of electricity money, is currently being considered by the General Assembly.

headline: Report: Diabetic care by police has improved
abstract: A report by monitors for the American Diabetes Association states that the Philadelphia Police Department have significantly improved the way they care for diabetic prisoners. This report comes seven years after the police force was sued by failing to give a cabaret owner who was imprisoned for over 24 hours any medical treatment for his diabetic condition. The lawsuits by over 256 diabetics resulted in a cash settlement as well as a new police policy to transfer all diabetic detainees to the main detention facility where a nurse can monitor and treat their blood sugar levels.

headline: Courting Trouble: The document granting 'power of attorney' often leads to abuse
abstract: Western Pennsylvania has notably become an infamous area for elderly people to be taking advantage of by the process of power of attorney, which allows older or extremely ill people to choose someone else to take care of any financial and property transactions.  The article cites multiple examples of this process going wrong in the areas of Pittsburgh, Erie and Upper St. Clair despite the PA General Assembly tightening the law in 1998 to disallow unlimited gifts by the power of attorney.  The most infamous case cited in the article is of Ronald Slomski, whose own mother went against his will to gift his valuables and life savings rather than giving it to his two stepdaughters.

headline: Will your vote leave paper trail?
abstract: Doug Smith, Erie County's Clerk of Elections, and Sharon Drayer, supervisor of Erie County's voter registration office, travel to Butler today to discuss the upcoming May 15 primary and the controversy over a bill in Congress that would require all voting machines to produce a paper record.  Smith and Erie County Council Chairman Fiore Leone believes paper ballots are needed for these new machines and estimates that adding printers to the new touch machines will cost $400,000.

headline: Phila. health agency in disarray
abstract: Philadelphia City Controller Alan Butkovitz has publicly criticized the Philadelphia Health Department after it was discovered that it does not keep track of prescription-drug deliveries, does not remove expired medication and cannot account for more than 2,000 pieces of equipment.  In response, John F. Domzalski was appointed to replace Carmen Paris as the health commissioner of the city.  Domzalski reported that having a $7.6 million inventory without an audit is against industry standards and simply irresponsible.

headline: Pa. trims PGW's rate-hike request
abstract: Philadelphia Gas Works, which is owned by the City of Philadelphia, recently asked the PA Public Utilities Commission for the permission to increase its base rates by $100 million a year.  The Commission voted unanimously, however, to only grant a base rate increase of $25 million a year because, according to PUC Chairman Wendell Holland, the reasons for the request were unsubstantiated and cost-cutting techniques need to be developed within the company. The company, PGW, has a long-term debt of $1.2 billion and has consistently been borrowing money because of a lack of surplus cash.

headline: Ruling that eased pardons rejected
abstract: Three prisoners in PA who successfully challenged a 1997 state referendum that made it tougher to win commutations of life terms appear ineligible to pursue their claim, an appeals court said in a setback for inmates serving life terms. The 1997 constitutional amendments require a unanimous vote of the state pardons board - instead of just a majority vote - before a clemency recommendation can go to the governor for approval. A U.S. district judge said last year that the tougher rules violated the rights of inmates sentenced before the change took effect. However, the Third Circuit Court of Appeals in Philadelphia ruled Monday that neither the three inmates nor the advocacy groups that joined the suit proved they were directly harmed by the tougher standard.

headline: Crime issue is visceral but elusive
abstract: As poll after poll lists crime as the top concern of Philadelphia voters, the candidates in this spring's Democratic mayoral primary have responded with similar sets of policy prescriptions. For former City Councilman Michael Nutter, the dominant theme is anger over the 406 homicides in Philadelphia last year. For PA State Representative Dwight Evans, the dominant themes are personnel and leadership.  And for U.S. Representative Chaka Fattah, the dominant theme was help for the poor.

headline: Williams to give up seat
abstract: State Sen. Connie Williams will not seek re-election when her senate terms is completed at the end of 2008. The Democratic lawmaker, who has served in the state legislature since 1997, posted a letter on her Internet site. Reached by phone Wednesday afternoon, Williams said her decision to end her legislative career had been a gradual one.

headline: Pitt to open vaccine research laboratory
abstract: The University of Pittsburgh will open a new vaccine research laboratory today that cost $50 million to construct to attempt to fight serious diseases such as tuberculosis and influenza.  A majority of the funding for the lab came from the National Institutes of Health, which has funded 12 other similar facilities throughout the country.  Dr. Donald S. Burke, dean of Pitt's Graduate School of Public Health and director for this new Center for Vaccine Research, states that much of the research is in response to the new threat of bio-terrorism.

headline: Planned gas tax increase derailed
abstract: Drivers won't be paying an extra penny per gallon at the pump after all. After lawmakers of both parties balked, the state Insurance Department backed off a plan to add 1 cent to Pennsylvania's 31-cent gasoline tax, starting Jan. 1. The penny per gallon would have raised almost $60 million a year for the Underground Storage Tank Indemnification Fund, which pays claims related to gasoline leaks. It would have cost the average driver about $9 a year.

headline: Sheriff's records taken in probe
abstract: Washington County Sheriff Sam Romano and James D'Alessandro, his chief deputy, talked this week with two state police investigators assigned to the FBI and handed over some of the office's transportation logs. Sheriff's office solicitor Christopher Blackwell said the state police investigators, who were also present when a safe and documents were removed last week from District Attorney John C. Pettit's office at the county courthouse, arrived with a subpoena for transportation records that included "13 named individuals."

headline: Curb consumerism
abstract: This letter compliments Mayor of Camp Hill Lou Thiebelmont for hosting a successful meeting on global warming that featured PA Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Kathleen McGinty.  The author also compliments PA Governor Ed Rendell for attempting to find new alternative fuel sources, citing Philadelphia and Pittsburgh as being recognized for their concern for global warming.  However, the letter also encourages citizens to consider their own consumerism that contributes to global warming.

headline: Wows & Scowls
abstract: This editorial praises various governmental actions in the news including PA Representative William DeWeese and PA Senator Richard Kasunic's successful attempt to get $450 million from the PA Turnpike Commission to fund Phase II of the Mon-Fayette Expressway and Jacquie Albert of the Fayette County's Domestic Violence Services called attention to the disproportionate amount of funding given to other counties besides Philadelphia to domestic violence services.  The editorial also criticized the state government for making only 1 positive change to improve government integrity after the July 2005 pay raise scandal.

headline: Pitt vaccine lab opening delayed
abstract:
A University of Pittsburgh lab charged by the National Institutes of Health with developing vaccines is a year behind schedule and likely will not open until January 2008.The lab's mission is to develop vaccines to counter bioterror attacks and deadly pathogens such as dengue fever, tuberculosis and avian flu. Installing special air filters, a machine to count cells from samples and X-ray technology has contributed to the delay, Dr. Donald Burke, director of Pitt's new Center for Vaccine Research said. 
The $29 million lab is the only section of Pitt's third biomedical science tower not yet operational, said Jim Swyers, a University of Pittsburgh Medical Center spokesman.

headline: Planned power line draws heat from locals
abstract: There is a lot of opposition to Allegheny Power's proposed plan to build a 37-mile, 500-kilovolt power line through Washington and Greene counties due mostly to the use of eminent domain but health concerns and legal issues as well.  Allegheny Power has responded that 20-30 year old infrastructure is too strained with the rising use of electricity in the areas.  The biggest problem with the National Interest Electric Transmission Corridor is the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission's authority to take over land that they need to construct the power lines.

headline: Signs of Progress: Common Pleas Court Judges are Doing Their Best
abstract: This is a report to the public on the performance of Philadelphia counts during the first six months of 1982 and on the problems that continue to confront it.   The criminal case inventory has been drastically reduced.  Whereas 5,182 criminal cases were awaiting adjudication at the beginning of the year, that figure stood at 3,883.

headline: Dally wants to restore faith in aid agency
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell was infuriated at discovering the board members of the Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency wasted $900,000 on lavish retreats and golf outings.  In response to this, Rendell is considering privatizing PHEAA as he has already received a $1 billion offer from Sallie Mae.  PA Representative Craig Dally of Northampton, a PHEAA board member, agrees that the agency must be revamped but worries privatization is not the right thing to do.

headline: Your right to know ... Some things only
abstract: Only the sausage grinders in the PA House could make mincemeat out of legislation intended to bolster one of the lamest open-records laws in the nation. The bill's much-touted "flip of presumption" -- that all government records are public unless specifically exempted -- has been rendered meaningless by House "reformers." In short order they managed to stuff the legislation plum full of loopholes. In flagrant contempt of the public's right to know, there's a blanket exemption for all e-mail by public officials and employees. This, supposedly to protect constituents' personal information in communications.

headline: Pittsburgh: Smoggy, not pet friendly?
abstract: Pittsburgh was named America's most livable city, however the American Lung Association rated it the number 2 smoggiest, and the Human Society ranked it as 16 out of 25 in "compassion for animals."

headline: Plans for big new power line in Pa. worries those in its path
abstract: null

headline: State addresses prison crowding
abstract: Faced with sobering predictions about the need for new prisons, House and Senate lawmakers are moving to largely end a practice where state-sentenced prisoners are held in county prisons and allow earlier releases of nonviolent offenders from state prisons. The House Judiciary Committee approved measures Tuesday to reserve county prisons for inmates serving sentences of less than two years and establish an early release program for state prison inmates who complete treatment programs for substance abuse. The Senate Judiciary Committee plans a vote on a similar measure next week.

headline: Day of Decision in Pa.
abstract: Today's elections in Pennsylvania offer at least one foregone conclusion in the city and several brawls in the suburbs. Polls are open from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m., as voters throughout Pennsylvania select municipal and county officials, elect state appeals court judges and decide whether 67 incumbent judges, most serving on the Court of Commons Pleas bench, should be retained. Barring a miracle of Biblical proportions, Democrat Michael Nutter is likely to be elected mayor of Philadelphia. Much more suspense attends Democrats' effort to seize control of one or more of the courthouses in Philadelphia's four suburban Pennsylvania counties after years on the outside.

headline: Berks County Lenape Indians seek recognition
abstract: For various reasons, neither the state nor federal governments recognize the Lenape Nation as an official American Indian tribe. As a result, the Lenapes are not eligible for grants that would help them turn the county-owned farmhouse at 1098 County Welfare Road into a cultural center. And some tribal members believe the state refuses to officially recognize them because officials are afraid the Lenapes will open tribal casinos that the state cannot tax or regulate. They say they just want to display their artifacts, sell their arts and crafts and teach people about the Lenape history and culture.

headline: Plan to sell Aliquippa hospital brings out skeptics
abstract: Some speakers yesterday at a public hearing about the fate of troubled Aliquippa Community Hospital openly raised doubts about a plan to sell it to a group of investors. While no one outright opposed the sale to Commonwealth Medical Center Inc., skeptics demanded information about the group's strategy to make the hospital profitable and questioned whether Commonwealth -- made up of at least two major shareholders in Legacy Health Network, which is currently managing the hospital -- could succeed. Under Legacy, the hospital's debt has increased and its operating license has been downgraded four consecutive times, putting it in jeopardy.

headline: Positive for Pennsylvanians
abstract: Carl Shaffer, President of the Pennsylvania Farm Bureau, believes that reducing America’s dependency on foreign oil is important, and a key renewable energy solution is biodiesel, which is environmentally friendly and can be produced with soybeans grown in PA. However, he claims that other states are providing better incentives for their biodiesel companies, which is making it difficult for PA producers .Mr. Shafer hopes that PA will match these incentives, so PA producers can survive and eventually become self-sufficient.

headline:
State high court debates sexual consent in civil case of 11-year-old girl
Victim seeking damages for assault at Veterans Stadium lot.
abstract: According to PA law, children under the age of 13 cannot consent to sex in terms of criminal cases, but the state Supreme Court will decide whether the same rules should be applied to a civil case involving an 11-year-old girl who is seeking damages for a sexual encounter after a Phillies game. The girl accused three juvenile boys of raping her, which the boys disputed. The girl’s lawyer claims that consent laws should be extended to civil cases, whereas the defendants, including the Phillies, oppose the move.

headline: Debating state pay still worth it
abstract: PA Rep. Ron Marsico wants to introduce legislation to create a commission to advise the PA Legislature on future pay raises. Editors believe the issue of a pay raise proved so controversial in the most recent attempt the PA Governor Ed Rendell and any of the other legislators won't touch it. However, finding some sort of mechanism for pay raises, like Rendell and PA Supreme Court Chief Justice Ralph Cappy's suggestion to link them to federal compensation, is necessary.

headline: BILLS COULD BRING MILLIONS FOR RAIL LINE, FLOOD PROJECTS
abstract: Congress sent President Bush several bills that could potentially bring millions of dollars for various projects to Northeastern Pennsylvania, from funding a passenger rail line between Scranton and New York City to additional flood-mitigation projects, federal representatives for this region announced. U.S. Sens. Arlen Specter and Robert Casey Jr. announced the appropriation of nearly $3 million for flood-control projects in the area.

headline: Politicians must agree to keep CHIP working
abstract: The article is about the federal debate over what to do with the State Children’s Health Insurance Program (SCHIP), which provides funding for Pennsylvania’s CHIP program and will expire shortly. According to the Senior Vice President for Capital BlueCross, a leading CHIP insurer, the program should be renewed because it provides health insurance to nearly 165,000 PA children whose parents cannot afford it. She believes that SCHIP is a successful federal program and outlines a number of key points that she feels the federal government should keep in mind in order to come to an agreement on its future.

headline: Power grid talks sought
abstract: PA Representative Stan Saylor has publicly requested that the US Department of Energy hold a public forum in York County to discuss to the residents the proposed Mid-Atlantic Area National Corridor, which has been created to help spark the construction of power lines across the northeastern states.  PA Representative Keith Gillespie is also proposing that the DOE holds a public meeting in York County as there are proposed power lines that will travel through the county, but the DOE has not planned any additional meetings currently.

headline: State keeps shooting blanks
abstract: Bills that would limit handgun purchases to one per month (HB22) and allow cities to enact their own gun laws (HB 18) failed to make it out of the committee, despite a sound, emotional plea from Gov. Rendell. But a law that requires gun owners to report lost or stolen firearms to police (HB 29) was tabled. We see this as progress. For years the environment in Harrisburg has been intolerant to handgun-safety legislation. So a bill tabled rather than dismissed is a sign to us that a climate change is in the works.

headline: Déjŕ vu
abstract: PA Sen. James Rhoades testified in committee on behalf of his legislation to increase voter participation in setting public policy via initiative and referendum. Under this proposal, voters would affirm or reject laws passed by the legislature. Rhoades has tried to push this legislation through before, back in 1992. It failed.

headline: Biodiesel, activism power this bus tour
abstract: The recipients of the Morris K. Udall Scholarships, funded by the Morris K. Udall Foundation, arrived at the Fairmount Park Visitors Center to talk about conservation, environmentalism, and American Indian interests. The Legacy Tour, as it is named, travels in an environmentally-friendly bus, and plans to travel over 26 cities, 6 national parks, and 6 American Indian communities.  They spoke in Philadelphia about water quality and biofuels.

headline: Pressure for statewide ban grows
abstract: Smoke-free laws are in effect in 25 states, prompting hospitality and health care workers to gather outside the Capitol to urge legislation to mandate a smoking ban. PA Rep. Michael Gerber supports the measure, also backed by Scranton city officials. The PA Restaurant Association favors a  statewide smoke-free policy as well. Allegheny County's smoking ban was struck down by the Commonwealth Court. PA Governor Rendell's health care legislation includes provisions for a smoking ban.

headline: Power line hearings
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission is planning on having 6 hearings in regards to the proposed Trans-Allegheny Interstate Line by Allegheny Energy Incorporated.  This line, $1.8 billion and 240 miles, will travel from Southwestern PA to Virginia to move power from coal power plants to the East Coast.

headline: State may toughen laws on neglect
abstract: A Lackawanna County lawmaker is sponsoring legislation to toughen state sentences for anyone convicted of causing death to a care-dependent individual through sheer neglect. The measure by Rep. Jim Wansacz, D-Old Forge, directs the Pennsylvania Commission on Sentencing to adopt new sentencing guidelines for judges that would enhance penalties under existing state law. The goal is to have the punishment fit the crime. He said the Lackawanna County district attorney’s office asked for the legislation.

headline: Dem House workers suspected of using work time for politics
abstract: PA State Attorney Tom Corbett and his office are creating a grand jury to determine if bonuses paid by the four legislative caucuses were rewards for government work or illegal payments for political work to support their own parties' candidates.  The jury will be studying all of the $4 million in bonuses that was given to legislative staffers in both 2005 and 2006.  It is illegal for legislative employees or staffers to do political work while being paid by the state, although it is legal if they are paid with campaign funds.

headline: Budget crisis creates unhappy campers
abstract: The budget crisis taking place in Pennsylvania's government will close all but 4 of the 116 state parks and 2 million acres of state forest land, including Keystone State Park where the Seybert has flown in from across the country to have a family reunion.  Almost all of the 15 full-employees at Keystone will be furloughed with the 2,300 employees of the Department of Conservation and Natural Resources.  The Seybert family plans to remain in the park despite the closure, and Gil Gilbert, the park's manager, has showed optimism that PA Governor Ed Rendell and the PA Legislature can come to an agreement quickly.

headline: Pressure placed on hospitals not to make patients sicker
abstract: Nearly 2,500 people a year die in Pennsylvania from hospital acquired infections, some 90,000 nationwide. Pennsylvania hospitals reported 19,154 cases of HAIs, which resulted in hospital charges of $3.5 billion in that year. In July, Gov. Ed Rendell signed legislation that gives Pennsylvania a plan -- considered the most compre hensive in the nation -- to address hos pital acquired infections. The program includes making "quality improvement payments" to hospitals that show a 10 percent reduction by Jan. 1, 2009. The governor's plan on hospital acquired infections and Medicare's policy not to pay for many types of infections and errors will bring a missing incentive to hospital care to get it right the first time, every time.

headline: PPL negotiates rate restructuring settlement with state regulators
abstract: After a Commonwealth Court ruling last year that determined that $222 million rate increase was unfairly placed against commercial users, PPL Electric Utilities is restructuring their rates with state regulators.  The PA Public Utilities Commission has to approve the settlement that would make residential customers pay 3.8% more for electricity while commercial consumers would pay 2-5% less.  PPL, the Office of Small Business Advocate, the Office of Consumer Advocate, the PPL Industrial Customer Alliance are reworking the negotiation after the regulators and utilities challenged the court decision.

headline: State police launch recruitment Web site
abstract: The Pennsylvania State Police have created a Web site, www.patrooper.com, in order recruit more potential troopers and make the application process easier.  The site includes informational videos, eligibility requirements and how to apply.  The starting salary is $48,780 and the applicant must be at least 20 years old on the date of the application.

headline: Dem leader wants to reduce size of Pa. legislature
abstract: PA state Senator John Pippy proposed cutting the size of the Legislature two years ago. Since then, several shocks have hit the General Assembly. Pippy got some help from the No. 2 Democrat in the Senate -- the whip, Senator Michael A. O'Pake. Pippy has revised the plan to 40 Senate members and 151 members in the House. Mr. O'Pake proposed reducing the size of the Senate to 40 members and the House to 121 members. House Democratic leader H. William DeWeese opposes reducing the Legislature, saying it will have a negative effect on small towns and rural areas, many of which now have their own legislator.

headline: Construction resumes on delayed Brady's Lake dam
abstract: The state Department of Environmental Protection in 2002 said the earthen dam that formed Brady's Lake located on state gamelands in Coolbaugh Township was unsafe and would need to be breached. Public pressure caused local and state officials to find the funds to rebuild the dam and reform the lake. In 2003, Gov. Ed Rendell came to Brady's Lake to announce construction would begin to rebuild the dam. Construction fell so far behind schedule that with the project only 40 percent finished at the deadline. There has been no progress on the dam since October.

headline: Proposal will limit where smokers light up
abstract: In addition to endorsing a statewide ban on smoking in bars, restaurants and other public places, PA Governor Ed Rendell wants to pay for his overhaul of the medical system in part by increasing cigarette taxes and imposing new levies on cigars and smokeless tobacco products. State smokers now pay tobacco taxes totaling $1.35 per pack for cigarettes. Those who buy other tobacco products pay only the 6 percent state sales tax. The governor did not specify how much his proposed tax hike would be, saying details would be disclosed in his February budget address to lawmakers. The money would be used to expand health care coverage to some 900,000 uninsured Pennsylvanians.

headline: PPL plan: Phase in 35% hike
abstract: A state consumer advocate is questioning the fairness of a proposal by PPL Electric Utilities that could increase consumer electric bills 18 months earlier than necessary. On Jan. 1, 2010, rate caps holding the cost of electricity in Pennsylvania at 5.7 cents per kilowatt-hour will be dissolved, and prices will be determined by the open market. Estimates suggest an instant rate increase near 35 percent, or 2 cents per kwh. Filed Friday for approval by the state Public Utility Commission, the PPL plan would spread the increase over five years. Rates would increase 7 percent July 1, 7 percent again in 2009, and then 6 percent each summer until 2012.

headline: State's child-protection laws still need improvement
abstract: The General Assembly and PA Governor Ed Rendell should be commended for taking action to improve the administration of Pennsylvania's Megan's Law. Additional steps are needed to make our child-protection laws rank among the national leaders. Pennsylvania's General Assembly first passed a Megan's Law in 1995. In spite of several amendments since then, the commonwealth's Megan's Law program has ranked as one of the least effective in the nation. For instance, it received an "F" rating in 2005 from the nationally recognized Parents for Megan's Law organization. The Department of the Auditor General's recent performance audit revealed a series of legislative and administrative shortcomings that had contributed to the program's failed rating.

headline: Democratic Leader DeWeese's actions fall outside of what public expects from Legislature
abstract: The editorial board says PA House Majority Leader William H. DeWeese has given taxpayer-funded bonuses to some employees of the Democratic caucus. They ask "since when is the use of taxpayer's money nobody else's business?"  But they respond that they know that as long as DeWeese and other legislative leaders of both parties have been allowed to use their confidential leadership accounts to intimidate, manipulate, reward and punish. This is not a good start for a newly seated Pennsylvania Legislature pledged to reform and greater openness and accountability.

headline: County, Avoca get $51K in flood grants
abstract: Luzerne County and Avoca Borough were awarded $51,434 in state grants for flood projects. The Luzerne County Flood Protection Authority was awarded $39,000 for sluice gate repair and Avoca was awarded $12,434 to study flooding ice jams in the borough. Rendell announced nearly $500,000 in grants across the state to help local municipalities improve operations at 17 flood protection projects in 15 counties, but explained that the statewide need for such funding far exceeds what is available.

headline:
Proposed bill to help seniors ID problem care homes
Legislation would require facilities to post inspection and violation reports at their entrances.
abstract: In light of disturbing recent reports of neglect at long-term care homes in PA, Representative Mauree Gingrich proposed a bill that would require these facilities to post inspection reports and all violations at their entrances as well as on a state website. She hopes her proposal and others will help improve elder-care laws in PA.

headline: PPL reduces request for rate increase
abstract: The Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission has reported that if PPL Corporation's $77 million rate increase were to take place, it would result in an average of 5.4% for a residential consumer rather than the company's belief of 6.6%.  Also the Commission has proposed that PPL Electric should receive $49 million, and Consumer Advocate Irwin Popowski believes the hike should be lowered to $27 million.  The key debate currently, according to Popowski, is how much profit the company should earn as PPL has asked for 11.%, Popowski's office asked for 9.36% and the PUC believes it should be 10.13%.

headline: States suing over Camel ad in Rolling Stone
abstract: Camel ads coupled with illustrations promoting rock music in Rolling Stone magazine violate the tobacco industry's nine-year-old promise not to use cartoons to sell cigarettes, prosecutors in various states. Attorneys general in at least eight states planned to file lawsuits against R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. starting over the advertising for Camel cigarettes in the November edition of Rolling Stone. The section combines pages of Camel cigarette ads with pages of magazine-produced illustrations on the theme of independent rock music.

headline: Dems' early agenda OK with GOP's Platts
abstract: The Democrats may have taken over Congress, but U.S. Representative Todd Platts isn't sweating the move to the minority because the congressman is a strong backer of most of the priority issues set forth by the Democrats under House Speaker Nancy Pelosi. Platts has pushed to update ethics rules, raise the minimum wage, implement 9/11 Commission recommendations, cut subsidies to the oil industry, promote stem cell research and make college educations and prescription drugs more affordable.

headline: Fairs get funds
abstract: County fairs in Beaver, Butler, Washington and Westmoreland counties will get some of the $750,000 the state is making available to 55 projects around the state in the 2007-08 fiscal year.

headline: Reaction mostly favorable to Rendell health-care change proposals
abstract: Several major organizations, including Highmark Inc., Hospital & Health System of Pennsylvania and the Pennsylvania Medical Society generally indicated an interest in supporting the PA Governor Rendell administration to develop reforms that will make health care more efficient in the state and improve the focus on the doctor-patient relationship. Highmark echoed Mr. Rendell's statement that the lack of health insurance, especially for those with low and modest incomes, is driving the need for reform. AARP Pennsylvania said Mr. Rendell's plan will boost access to insurance coverage and improve the quality of care residents receive.

headline: Preservationists fear power lines coming to national parks
abstract: Joy Oakes of the National Parks Conservation Association is among the many preservationist that fear the US Energy Department's new proposed designation of two pieces of land in the Northeast and Southwest "national interest" energy corridors where power lines can be built regardless of any state and local opposition.  Barbara Connors, spokeswoman for the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, reported that the commission would have the final say on where the lines will be built, not the Energy Department.  The Energy Department has predicted that electricity demand will grow 39% from 2005 to 2030 in the residential sector and 63% in the commercial sector.

headline: Street: 500 more cops might not stem slay tide
abstract: While several mayoral candidates are pledging to hire 500 more police officers to reduce homicides in the city, Philadelphia Mayor Street yesterday said that such a mass hiring might not result in fewer murders. The city now has a budget for 6,624 officers - up 200 from last year, thanks to federal funding - although fewer than that number are currently on the force. The problem with that idea, Street said, is that the Police Department's analysis of homicides and shootings shows that often the victim was specifically targeted by the perpetrator.

headline:
DeSantis raises $300,000
That's 30 times what last Republican mayoral candidate collected
abstract: Republican mayoral candidate Mark DeSantis announced that his campaign will raise $300,000 by Election Day, which is quite good in comparison to previous mayoral candidates. He claimed that the contributions and number of volunteers were adding momentum to his campaign, and incumbent Mayor Luke Ravenstahl, who hasn’t released his fundraising total yet, should be very nervous. DeSantis also pledged to enact several reforms, which are described in the article.

headline: Game Preserve decision was questionable
abstract: The author is responding to a previous editorial that claimed that Judge Lawrence Brenner made the correct decision by ruling that three citizens did not have legal standing to petition against the killing of animals on General Trexler’s Game Preserve. The author is one of those three citizens, and he explains why he is upset with what he perceives are injustices of the process and the judge’s decision.

headline: Reforms pushed in elderly care
abstract: Members of the state House Aging and Older Adult Services Committee listened to testimonies from experts at the University of Scranton and are considering four main reforms for elder care laws. These reforms are in response to the tragic death of Peggy Rogers, who died a year ago due to serious neglect at her personal care home. Personal care homes are held to much less stringent standards than nursing homes, which many legislators, including the committee's chairwoman Phyllis Mundy, hope to change.

headline: Rendell energy plan required more study
abstract: PA Senator Mary Jo White writes to oppose the recent editorial in The Patriot that the PA Senate had sufficient time to look over the energy proposal from PA Governor Ed Rendell.  She feels that if PA Governor Ed Rendell wants to impose $2.1 billion in new taxes and authority to spend hundreds of millions on projects of his choosing, he should not have introduced the proposal in late March and should have made it a priority earlier than June.  She agrees with the statement of PA Senator Dominick Pileggi, who claimed that a bill of this nature requires more time.

headline: Supreme Court rules against city police union on pensions
abstract: The state Supreme Court unanimously ruled against the Pittsburgh police union in its appeal of the city's decision to stop paying the full cost of health insurance for officers retiring after Jan. 1, 2004. The ruling will affect about 100 retirees and potentially impact more than 800 still on the job when they retire, said James Malloy, president of Fraternal Order of Police Fort Pitt Lodge No. 1. During contract negotiations in 2003, an arbitrator ruled the city could cap its contribution to retirees' health premiums at the amount of the premium at the time of the officers' retirement. The retiree would be responsible for the difference if premiums increased.

headline: Details of Rendell's priorities
abstract: This article contains a list of the priorities of PA Governor Ed Rendell as the Legislature's spring session comes to a close, including spending and legislation.

headline: Governor Rendell touts volunteer efforts, declares September 29 as 'Public Lands Day'
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell has declared that September 29 to be "National Public Lands Day" to help encourage citizens to help restore and improve public lands and parks across the country.  The effort, overseen by the PA Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, will be hosted by thirteen state parks, three environmental education centers and one conservation area all listed within the article.  The National Environmental Education & Training Foundation helps manage the day's effort reports that the contributions and work done will be valued at approximately $8 million.

headline: Rendell controls reform debate
abstract: In his second inaugural address, PA Governor Ed Rendell proposed health-care reforms complicated enough to make lobbyists for the legal, medical and insurance industries scream. The second-term governor believes he can turn a smashing election victory into a mandate. Even the PA Legislature remains relatively quiet as Rendell prepares to set off on a statewide tour to sell his health-care initiatives. The editorial board writes that the federal government has all but abandoned its health-care responsibilities. So Rendell joins other frustrated governors and proposes remedies.

headline: Rendell energy proposals face long road in Senate
abstract: The PA Legislature is expected to vote on PA Governor Ed Rendell's Energy Independence Strategy, which was proposed to counter rising fuel and electricity prices and create homegrown industries.  The plan levies a tax on electricity to fund conservation efforts and alternative fuels, allows the Pennsylvania Energy Development Authority to buy, sell and trade commodities and cost a total of $850 million.  The legislation is expected to meet more scrutiny in the Republican Senate than in the Democratic House of Representatives.

headline: Task force charges 17 as 'straw buyers' of guns
abstract: Philadelphia District Attorney Lynne M. Abraham and other law enforcement officials announced that 17 people involved in the illegal purchase and trafficking of firearms in the city had been arrested by the Gun Violence Task Force. Straw buyers are people who buy guns and illegally turn them over to convicted felons, who are prohibited from purchasing firearms. Over the last 10 months, the task force has arrested 97 people and seized 168 firearms.

headline: DeWeese says he's clean in LaGrotta ghost worker case
abstract: Prosecutors accused a former Democratic state lawmaker of installing two relatives in no-show state jobs, one day after a House staff shake-up tied to a broader corruption investigation at the Legislature. Ex-Rep. Frank LaGrotta's sister and niece collected about $25,000 for work that was never performed, a grand jury found. The three were expected to be formally charged Thursday. Prosecutors also said that House Majority Leader Bill DeWeese co-signed with LaGrotta a June 2006 agreement that backdated by four months the hiring of LaGrotta's sister as an education consultant.

headline: Grants help to protect land
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell announced that that $1.4 million will be given to improve the Trexler Nature Preserve and Cedar Beach Park as well as protecting 9 acres in Lower Macungie Township from development.  The grants will be given through the Community Conservation Partnerships Program administered by the PA Department of Conservation and Natural Resources.

headline: Rendell keeps them laughing
abstract: Governor Rendell was in Wilkes-Barre drumming up support for his Prescription for Pennsylvania health care reform plan. He also credited Wilkes-Barre Mayor Tom Leighton with helping the city make great strides under his leadership. Also the Sherriff’s department is implementing increased security for today’s pre-trial motions hearing for accused double murders Hugo Selenski and Paul Weakley.

headline: Rendell says plan aids energy contracts
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell has publicly criticized the interpretation of Pennsylvania's electricity deregulation law by some Public Utility Commission members.  These members have stated that the legislation bans the signing of long-term contracts with electricity companies despite Rendell insisting otherwise. While Rendell claims this deregulation law will save $10 billion over 10 years and reduce dependence on oil imports, PA Senate Majority Leader Dominc Pileggi of Delaware County claims that this plan contains too many new taxes.

headline: US judge weighs request to remove Sprague firm from Fumo case
abstract: PA State Senator Vincent J. Fumo is attempting to keep his defense lawyers from Sprague and Sprague on his federal fraud case, whereas the Assistant US Attorney Robert Zauzmer claims that the lawyers witnessed disputed activities that come into play during the trial.  There is a 139-count federal indictment judged by US District Judge William H. Yohn Jr. where Fumo is accused of exploited $1 million of state resources and another $1 million from a nonprofit organization he controls.  Fumo remains in the PA Senate but has stepped down from leadership positions.

headline: DeWeese says staffers fired after review of documents
abstract: House Majority Leader Bill DeWeese said Friday that he acted to remove seven caucus employees following a detailed review of documents that were about to be turned over to state investigators looking into the alleged use of state workers for campaign purposes. The state attorney general's office, which is investigating whether state funds or state workers were illegally used for campaign purposes, had requested the records be turned over.

headline: Group seeking historic status for National Negro Opera home
abstract: The Young Preservationists Society of Pittsburgh asked the Pittsburgh Historic Review Commission to consider designating the former home of the National Negro Opera Company to become one of the city’s historic landmarks.

headline: Rendell launching an effort to battle chronic diseases
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell is expected to sign an order establishing a commission to care for patients with chronic diseases and diabetes, said senior policy manager Ann Torregrossa for the Governor's Office of Health Care Reform. In another directive related to the Office of Health Equity, under the PA Department of Health, an effort will be made to remove health disparities between racial groups. Rendell proposed $2 million in his budget for a Web-based registry that gives physicians more access to data about their patients.

headline: Rendell: Reregulation of Pa.'s electricity market possible
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell  has begun promoting his energy independence plan by publicly stating he is not rejecting the regulation of the energy industry.  He claims his plan will enact a 25% increase in prices spread over 3 years rather than a 170% increase all at once, which he believes will happen under the current unregulated system.  John Hanger, of the watchdog group PennFuture, says that regulation is currently not possible because the rise in prices are due to the higher cost of fuels, and the prices of these fuels cannot be regulated.

headline: Timing of upgrade draws fire
abstract: Pennsylvanians will be unable to get new guns for several days next month because the background-check system maintained by state police will be shut down for upgrades. While state police say the improvements are long overdue, the timing of the work is under fire. Some lawmakers and gun sellers say it comes at a bad time because hunters are gearing up for new seasons. Called the Pennsylvania Instant Check System, or PICS, the database will be down from 6 p.m. Sept. 2, until noon Sept. 6.

headline: DeWeese to seek Pa. table games
abstract: PA House Majority Leader Bill DeWeese announced he will introduce legislation to allow table games in PA. DeWeese aims to significantly reduce or even eliminate property taxes with the revenue generated by licensing fees for the table games. Lead co-sponsor of the legislation and member of the Gaming Oversight Committee PA Rep. Jim Wansacz expects table games to draw a larger customer base.

headline: Lessons on good works for the Parking Authority
abstract: Editorial suggesting parking authority excesses are sent to schools. Hawk eyes - from parents who are CPAs to the city controller and the Pennsylvania governor - are trying to figure out just how a steroidal agency, the Philadelphia Parking Authority, that's raked in an inflation-adjusted 54 percent increase in revenue since 2001 has given so little in return. In 2004, the parking agency agreed to send the schools all profits from meters, towing and booting - after clearing the first $25 million. So far, that's resulted in only one payment, of $4 million.

headline: Rendell plan on health care
abstract: The author of the letter to the editor feels that the federal government will eventually be compelled to address its failure to provide adequate healthcare access. However, the author gives support to Governor Rendell’s Cover All Pennsylvanians plan, which is imperfect but a step in the right direction.

headline: Residents turn out at PUC hearings to oppose utility line
abstract: As Allegheny Power is vying for approval for a 37-mile, 500-kilovolt electric transmission line through Washington and Greene counties, two administrative law judges, Michael Nemec and Mark Hoyer, from the PA Public Utility Commission heard testimonies from residents, business owners and industry experts both in support and against the proposition.
