It was discovered that Allegheny Power is offering sums of money from $100,000 to $260,000 to the 250 property owners near the proposed line to cooperate with the project despite the vocal opposition from property owners to the plan.  However, former PUC chairman Bill Shane testified that the new power lines are especially needed in the area because of the infamous power-drag in the area during summer months.

headline: Triple homicide stuns home's neighbors
abstract: Neighbors shocked by three killings in a North 13th Street apartment stood outside their houses Thursday, unaccustomed to the bustle of police investigators. Kelsee Tharp, a community college student who lives in the neighborhood, said the porch was often crowded with young people during the summer. She said she didn't notice a heavy volume of police activity, though.

headline: Does Scranton's appearance at hearing portend governor run?
abstract: Borys Krawczeniuk believes Bill Scranton's appearance before the PA House Republican Policy Committee in opposition to PA Governor Ed Rendell's proposed budget and new or higher taxes is a signal he will run for governor in 2010. Scranton served as lieutenant governor. Scranton denied plans to run. Also on the short list of candidates are PA Attorney General Tom Corbett and Patrick Meehan, a federal prosecutor who has campaigned against corruption in the Philadelphia government.

headline: No surrender
abstract: The Civil War Preservation Trust is increasingly concerned about suburban sprawl affecting and taking over Gettysburg National Military Park, the site of the Battle of Gettysburg.  The article also expresses concern that this site is listed by the trust as one of the 10 most endangered Civil War battlefields in the country and believes state and federal governments need to do more to funding these preservation efforts.

headline: Rendell revisits health plan funding sources
abstract: Consider that there are nearly 800,000 uninsured Pennsylvania adults, the overwhelming majority of whom work. The overwhelming majority of them wants health insurance, but can't afford it. And, nearly all of us are one illness away from being in the same boat. Gov. Rendell proposed a program called Cover All Pennsylvanians nearly one year ago. It has received accolades nationally as a workable solution to the problem of the uninsured. The only attack has been over one of the funding sources for the program -- a 3 percent "fair share assessment" on businesses that don't offer health insurance coverage.

headline: Shifting the time of electrical use saves cost, benefits the environment
abstract: The editorial board writes that consumers should have "smart meters" installed in every residence, apartment, store and factory. Such meters, which are used in industry, have been in existence for at least 30 years. They display the hourly price of electricity, so that consumers can turn off appliances and lights during periods of high usage, when electric prices tend to peak, and use power when usage, and prices, are usually lower. They believe we need a model that rewards conservation and in the absence of Public Utility Commission action, we urge PA Governor Ed Rendell and the General Assembly to give Pennsylvanians the tools to both save money on their electric bills and conserve energy.

headline: Troubling rise in shooting of police
abstract: Just three days after the city buried Officer Chuck Cassidy in an emotional civic funeral, the bullets were flying at police again in Grays Ferry on Saturday when officers tried to break up a fight. No officer was injured, though one gunman was wounded when police returned fire. But the latest shooting is an example of what experts say is an alarming reversal of a long decline in law-enforcement officers' being targeted and killed. Not only have more police officers been shot at or threatened with guns this year, but experts say more are being targeted in a deliberate fashion, as Cassidy was - with close shots to the head.

headline: Dredge sides disagree on change
abstract: The Pennsylvania Environmental Hearing Board added one sentence to a 76-page decision in a case about filling Hazleton mineland with material dredged from waterways, but the two sides disagree on the significance of the change. The Nov. 2 order contained 76 pages written after months of deliberation following 14 days of hearings over which Judge Bernard Labuskes Jr. presided this spring. In contrast, the amendment adds just the following sentence to the decision: "CAUSE’s appeal for the COA is dismissed."

headline: OK of historic site bills awaited
abstract: Both the US Senate and the US House of Representatives are deciding on bills to make former mill sites in the Mon Walley a 38-acre national historic area.  US Representative Mike Doyle of Forest Hills, US Senator Arlen Specter, and US Senator Bob Casey all have introduced bills that call for $75 million funding from the US Department of Interior to create a historic park that could potentially attract additional outside investment.  A study by Heritage Corporation predicts that the site could attract up to 375,000 visitors a year.

headline: Schuylkill adds $1.1 million to cover health costs
abstract: Schuylkill County commissioners voted to add $1.1 million to cover the county's hospitalization costs for employees, a move one commissioner said was needed because of poor budgeting on a rushed spending plan. The extra money will come from an end-of-year surplus in the county's general fund and won't require a tax increase next year. At the request of the county Human Services Department, the money will be transferred into a general fund set up to cover hospitalization for county employees and retirees as part of their insurance benefits packages.

headline: Shipley launches a biodiesel heating oil
abstract: Shipley Energy is unveiling BioHeat, a renewable energy fuel made with biodiesel and heating oil. Nationwide, about 100 providers offer BioHeat. PA Governor Ed Rendell is meeting with leaders in the mid-state region this week to discuss the issue of renewable and domestic energy sources.

headline: Twenty suspected dealers arrested and 12 more are charged in Hazleton area drug sting
abstract: The PA Attorney General Tom Corbett has reported that state law enforcement officers have disrupted a $31 million cocaine trafficking ring in Hazleton that had been in operation for the past 3 years under Jorge "The Don" Rivera.  The regional director of the Attorney General's Office, Frank Noonan, has stated that 12 members of the 40 that were part of the ring, although some of them have fled to their native Dominican Republic.  Mayor Lou Barletta has thanked all law enforcement involved: the Hazleton and Butler police Departments, Tom Corbett and the Luzerne County Drug Task Force.

headline: Former lawmaker appear on ethics charge
abstract: Former State Rep. Frank LaGrotta never meant to break the law when he arranged jobs in his Ellwood City district office for his sister and niece, his attorney said. Steve Collafella, LaGrotta’s attorney, said the former Democratic lawmaker from Lawrence County didn’t try to conceal those family relationships from anyone who approved the hiring in Harrisburg. Colafella said that if LaGrotta violated the state’s Ethics Act, it was unintentional.

headline: Parking Authority to be spotlighted in reality-TV show
abstract: The people who made "Dog the Bounty Hunter" and his family into cable-TV stars are turning their attention to a much tougher crowd: the ticket-writers, booters and tow-truck drivers of the Philadelphia Parking Authority.  A&E announced the Jan. 8 premiere of "Parking Wars," a 20-episode series that looks at the men and women who, depending on your point of view, either help keep our streets clear or make our lives miserable.

headline: Senate children's health insurance bill is key to compromise, reauthorization
abstract: PA's version of the State Children's Health Insurance Program (SCHIP) provides health coverage to 159,000 of the state's children who otherwise wouldn't have it. Since SCHIP became law a decade ago, it has been a nationwide and bipartisan success. But it is set to expire by Sept. 30 unless Congress reauthorizes it. President Bush has needlessly made this a political football by threatening to veto any measure that exceeds his essentially flat-line funding approach to continuing the $25-billion SCHIP program. SCHIP provides coverage for families that earn too much to qualify for Medicaid.

headline: State approves first step for power plant
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Protection has approved one of four state permits Conectiv Energy needs before it can start to build a proposed power plant in Peach Bottom Township. DEP accepted Conectiv's air-plan proposal - a first step needed by the company to build a 1,100-megawatt generation plant off Pikes Peak and Atom roads in the township. The state has yet to approve the project's site-specific permit for storage tanks, an industrial waste-water-discharge permit and a construction-storm-water permit, said John Repetz, a DEP spokesman.

headline: Warrant issued for suspect in Philly officer's slaying
abstract: Authorities issued an arrest warrant Sunday for a suspect in the slaying of a city police officer who interrupted an armed robbery at a doughnut shop. Police Commissioner Sylvester Johnson identified the suspect as 21-year-old John Lewis, also known as Jordan Lewis, and urged anyone who might know his whereabouts to contact police. He also called on Lewis to turn himself in.

headline: Dwight Evans: the GOP’s best friend?
abstract: The author of the opinion piece writes that she was very disturbed at the selection and election of PA Representative Dennis M. O’Brien of Northeast Philadelphia as PA’s new House Speaker. The recent election provided an opportunity for the Democratic Party to elect a Democrat to be the Speaker of the House replacing PA Representative John M. Perzel, a Republican who generally ran havoc on Democratic Party legislative policies and initiative for many years.  PA Representative Dwight Evans, who is in concert with PA Governor Rendell brokered a deal ousting Perzel for O’Brien. Replacing one Republican for another Republican.

headline: River Rift
abstract: For the past 12 months, a plan to add five feet of depth to a 103-mile stretch of the Delaware River has forced a wedge between the governors of Pennsylvania and New Jersey and brought important workings of the Delaware River Port Authority (DRPA) to a virtual standstill. Proponents of the Delaware River Deepening Project include the Philadelphia Regional Port Authority and the Maritime Exchange for the Delaware River and Bay, as well as DRPA Chairman and PA Governor Ed Rendell and US Senator Arlen Specter, who was instrumental in getting the initial congressional authorization for the project in 1991.

headline: Senate Roll Call-Smoking Ban
abstract: The PA Senate, voting 33-17, approved a measure to ban smoking in most indoor public places.  This article lists the Senators and how they voted on the legislation.

headline: The Private Sector:  Rendell's energy policy overlooks importance of biodiesel industry
abstract: In this letter to the editor, a citizen comments on PA Governor Ed Rendell's Energy Independence Strategy's inability to actually spur the significant biofuel economy in Pennsylvania.  While he condones Rendell's concern for the biodiesel industry, he feels that his plan will not support existing plants who run to 10% of their capability rather only build new biodiesel plants.  The author believes that out-of-state biodiesel is much cheaper because of stronger government incentives, and in order to compete, Rendell's plan must support and fund current biodiesel factories rather than build new ones.

headline: Witness: Eckenrode was dazed, worried
abstract: Moments after Rachel Kozlusky fell 23 stories from his apartment window, Kevin Eckenrode stepped into an elevator in an apparent attempt to face the unbelievable. Paulina Cummings, a resident of Pennsylvania Place Apartments on Chestnut Street in Harrisburg who lived a floor below, said she entered the elevator and found a dazed Eckenrode heading to the first floor. It will be up to that jury to try to understand whether Eckenrode's actions add up to homicide or whether his girlfriend's death was a tragic accident. Tests showed Eckenrode and Kozlusky's blood-alcohol content to both be over the legal limit.

headline: Editorial: "Reform" still needs a push in Harrisburg
abstract: This editorial explains how the PA House of Representatives have begun to pass reforming measures such as making voting records available online; however, it expresses disappointment that these reforms are only baby steps in the right direction.  PA Representative Greg Vitali of Haverford did pass a ban on legislative nonprofits that lawmakers were using to receive government money that they could spend at their own discretion.  One change that needs to be done according to this article is moving the spending power to PA Governor Ed Rendell as PA Department of Community and Economic Development Secretary Dennis Yablonsky conceded that Legislature largely controls this power.

headline: State takes legal action against Consol for cracked dam in Greene County
abstract: The PA Department of Conservation and Natural Resources filed an intent to sue Consol Energy Inc. in Allegheny County Common Pleas Court for damage to a dam that drained Duke Lake in Ryerson Station State Park. Consol operated an extraction mine near the lake. The DCNR commissioned a study to determine Consol's fault, however the results have yet to be released. The Mountain Watershed Association, Citizens Coal Council and the Center for Coalfield Justice called on the state to publicize the results.

headline: Smokeless, but not harmless
abstract: PA Governor Rendell wants to tax "spit tobacco," a product long insulated by clever marketing and effective lobbying. But behind this laudatory move is a story that involves health risks and powerful Harrisburg lobbyists. Rendell's tax proposal on "other tobacco products," if adopted, not only would help provide health insurance to uncovered youth and adults, but it also could prevent more kids succumbing to nicotine addiction, and the resulting and oral cancers. The editorial board says that even cigarette users might applaud the equity in taxing all tobacco use - not just theirs.

headline: TMI media center may leave area
abstract: Three Mile Island is asking the Nuclear Regulatory Commission for permission to move the center where it would brief reporters in the case of a plant emergency to Coatesville. Exelon, the owner of the plant, already has emergency operations centers for its other two plants stationed there. The review could take up to a year, and a local group opposes the move.

headline: Women's group urges Pittsburgh police demotions
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl is deciding whether or not to reverse three police officer promotions after meeting with police brass and representatives of 16 local women's groups, including the Allegheny County-City of Pittsburgh Women's Commission.  All three of the police officers, Commander George T. Trosky, Lieutenant Charles Rodriguez, and Sergeant Eugene Hlavac all have been charged domestic disturbances, domestic violence, or police brutality in the past.  James Malloy, president of Fraternal Order of Police Fort Pitt Lodge No. 1, threatens to sue the city if the mayor were to cancel the promotions.

headline: Ed's late dog spoke to speaker
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell's dog recently died of a tumor, but has inspired the PA House Speaker Denny O' Brien to adopt a dog, Lucky Gov, with the help of the Pennsylvania Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals.  Rendell plans to adopt another golden retriever from the Delaware Valley Golden Retriever Rescue, as they have before.

headline: The Lenape Indians
abstract: A brief history of the Lenape Indians is given.

headline: Smokers second-class citizens
abstract: In this letter to the editor, Jim Mannion complains about the tax imposed on cigarettes claiming that smokers are treated like second-class citizens.  He calls for all smokers to stand up and protest this tax because he does not consider smokers to be obtrusive or second-class in any sense.

headline: Towers of power
abstract: PPL Corporation is considering building a third nuclear reactor in Luzerne County, which would make it one of the largest facilities in the country.  It was reported that they notified the Nuclear Regulatory Commission that PPL Corp. plans to apply for a construction and operation license within the next year.  David Lochbaum of the Union of Concerned Scientists answers many of the plans' critics by claiming that additional reactors do not pose any greater security risks.

headline: A win for the babies
abstract: Women demonstrated in front of the capitol in favor of three measures, Senate Bills 34, 35, and 36, sponsored by PA Sen. Connie Williams. S.34 gives women the right to breast feed in public. S.35 gives nursing mothers who breast feed at work or lunch protection against termination or discrimination. S.36 offers tax credits to businesses that support breast feeding mothers.

headline: Election Day turnout low in most Monroe precincts
abstract: Voter apathy was front and center in last May's primaries in Monroe County. County-wide, it averaged 14 percent. Compare that to 36 percent in the general election in 2006, 22 percent in 2005. In a state where the seat of power is arguably at the municipal level, voters don't seem to be all that interested in who's running the show.

headline: Trails association project receives $358,000 state award
abstract: Michael DiBerardinis, secretary of the PA Department of Conservation and Natural Resources, presented a $358,000 grant to the Great Allegheny Passage that extends between Foxburg and Parker.  At the presentation, PA Representative Fred McIlhattan introduced the speakers including Jim Holden of the Allegheny Valley Trails Association, which is in charge of the trail.  The money is awarded to already improve upon the funds given by the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation.

headline: Smoking ban bill sent to Senate
abstract: A PA Senate committee sent a signal that a decade-old push to ban indoor smoking in public places and workplaces is gaining momentum. The Senate Public Health and Welfare Committee voted 9-2 to move a smoking ban bill to the full Senate for consideration. This is the first time the smoke-free workplace proposal has advanced beyond a House or Senate committee. It also is an indication that the statewide smoking ban in PA Governor Ed Rendell's universal health care proposal has bipartisan support in the GOP-controlled chamber.

headline: Two elements of Rendell's energy plan pass Pa. House
abstract: The PA House of Representatives easily passed two main components of PA Governor Ed Rendell's Energy Independence Strategy that give the PA Economic Development Authority the power to fund alternative energy production and boost the use of biofuels.  The Republicans in the Senate oppose these components because of more taxes, more borrowing and a lack of specifics in where the funding will be used.

headline: Belfanti: Let nonprofits Hold ‘em
abstract: State Representative Robert Belfanti Jr. announced that he would co-sponsor a law that would permit volunteer fire departments, veterans organizations and other nonprofit organizations to hold card tournaments in order to raise money. These organizations are already allowed to raise funds via raffles, bingo and other smaller games of chance, but Belfanti feels that card games are growing in popularity and will allow these organizations to increase their limited incomes.

headline: Elmer Smith… Dear Voter: It's not just candidates on the ballot
abstract: Elmer Smith looks at questions posed in this year's election for Philadelphia Mayor and City Council, not to mention the 5 candidates for the former and 25 for the latter. He believes questions trick the voter into thinking they have a say in government, when in reality, they don't. Most egregious is a proposal to stop real estate tax assessment increases. The question blames the Philadelphia Board of Revision of Taxes for the increase, when it is City Council that sets tax percentage charged.

headline: Water park proposed near Gettysburg battlefield
abstract: A few months ago, plans to build a slots casino in Gettysburg were defeated; however, there is now a proposal from Cali Entertainment to build a 200-acre indoor water park about 4 miles south of Gettysburg National Military Park. Jim Paddock, who serves on Cumberland Township’s planning commission, questions whether an amusement park is appropriate so close to the historic battlefield. David Waybright, vice chairman of the Cumberland Township Board of Supervisors, said it will be a couple of months until the board decides whether to accept the proposal.

headline: Smoking ban OK'd by Senate
abstract: The PA Senate have approved a ban on indoor smoking but have included a long list of exemptions.  PA Governor Ed Rendell, the American Cancer Association, and the American Lung Association all disapproved of the bill as the PA House of Representatives are creating their own version of a smoking ban because of the exemptions.  Furthermore, the Pennsylvania Tavern Association  also oppose the bill because of the potential advantage it gives to certain bars.

headline: Up in the air
abstract: Over 600 residents of Somerset County attended the public hearing on the proposed wind mountain farm project on Shaffer Mountain by the Spanish company Gamesa because of the potential destruction of the aesthetic beauty and hiking trails of the mountain.  The opponents, most notably Jack Buchen, who owns acres on the mountain, have proposed that Gamesa use a former strip mine a mile away that is filled with sludge.  The opponents also consider PA Governor Ed Rendell and the PA Department of Environmental Protection Secretary Kathleen McGinty enemies in this project as Rendell is trying to push through a $850 million measure that fund alternative energy companies such as Gamesa.

headline: Child welfare in the village
abstract: Two citizens express concern about a report by national experts that exposed the challenges that Philadelphia's child welfare system faces and call for the government to adjust the Department of Human Services to address the problems.  Former Mayor Street in 2000 created what the authors view as an adequate program called Division of Social Services Cares which coordinates all the history of services that an individual or family receives.  The letter views this as a positive step and sees the solution as being coordination between the city's departments with the use of technology.

headline: Ethics Board Ruling
abstract: With Mayor-elect Michael Nutter taking direct aim at Philadelphia's pay-to-play political culture, the city's independent Board of Ethics this week gave him yet another big helping hand. In a ruling issued the Ethics Board said that City Charter limits on political activity applied to appointees at numerous city boards and commissions. This follows the ethics board's strong ruling in October that curtailed politicking by members of the influential Zoning Board of Adjustment, as well as several other city panels.

headline: null
abstract: The editorial addresses a wide array of different issues, including the Pittsburgh Police Ball, the Pittsburgh Symphony and the Pittsburgh Ballet Theatre. The author agrees with Allegheny County Council President’s remarks about a county property assessment Web site and also agrees with the Seneca Valley school board for not backing down against striking teachers. The author also argues that sports franchises in Pittsburgh should be paying property taxes.

headline: Smoking ban to get first test
abstract: The Pennsylvania Senate will decide this coming week whether or not ban smoking in the state's casinos and bars in legislation proposed by PA Senator Stewart Greenleaf. The lawmakers must also work out the legal definition of a cigar bar and deciding if the government can dictate the rules of a private country club or American Legion post.  Both PA Governor Ed Rendell and the Pennsylvania Restaurant Association support bans on smoking in public buildings.

headline: $500K grant to explore Pittsburgh-Westmoreland commuter line
abstract: Efforts to start commuter rail service from Westmoreland County into Pittsburgh keep chugging along as local transit officials this week received a $500,000 state grant to study whether the project is feasible. The Westmoreland County Transit Authority is exploring a two-phase project that would offer commuter rail service between Latrobe and downtown Pittsburgh as well as from Arnold to the Strip District. The state grant will pay for the feasibility study. Transit officials have been waiting for nearly six months for the money.

headline: City Councilwoman Wonders About SEPTA Service for Disabled
abstract: SEPTA officials spoke in front of a Philadelphia City Council committee and were forced to answer questions from city councilwoman Carol Campbell, who uses a wheelchair, as to why their assistance to the disabled is so limited.

headline: Exiting lawmakers get thousands in per diems
abstract: Three departing PA state lawmakers who live within 30 miles of the capital were reimbursed a combined $37,000 for meals and lodging while on official duty going back to 2003.  Former PA Senate Majority Leader David Brightbill cashed in $17,724 in per diems before leaving office, according to legislative records cited by The Patriot-News of Harrisburg. Former PA Representatives Mark McNaughton and Peter Zug claimed per diems totaling almost $20,000 combined.

headline: $12 fee targets Pittsburgh landlords
abstract: Apartment owners in Pittsburgh next year must pay a $12 annual fee for each rental unit, under a registration program City Council adopted Thursday. The ordinance requires apartment owners to pay to register their addresses, number and types of rentals -- all information the city will keep in a confidential database. Jim Eichenlaub, director of government affairs for the Apartment Association of Metropolitan Pittsburgh, told council the ordinance is an intrusion on individual privacy and civil rights.

headline: So this is it
abstract: Edward Hoffman of Harrisburg is frustrated that President George Bush has spent $1 trillion of taxpayers' money to found an irresponsible war in Iraq while he has vetoing an expansion of the Children's Health Insurance Program that costs $35 billion over 5 years. Hoffman feels that the country should have a national health insurance program like other developed countries and criticizes the Republican party for vehemently opposing this idea.

headline: 24 percent transit fare increase approved
abstract: Westmoreland County Transit Authority board members on Thursday approved a 24 percent fare hike for most of its 23 routes, including its most popular commuter service into Pittsburgh. The long-talked-about increase is the first approved by the authority since 1992 and is expected to generate about $135,000 annually in additional revenue. No major changes were made to the fare hike proposal first introduced in September, with the heaviest increase assess to passengers riding between Irwin and Greensburg and Mt. Pleasant and Greensburg. Those fares will increase from $1.80 per trip to $3.

headline: Hearing to probe heating assistance program
abstract: Thousands of Pennsylvanians are receiving invitations this week to participate in a program to help them pay their winter heating bills, but the agency sending the invitation may need some help of its own. This morning, allegations of fraud within the Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program (LIHEAP) will be the subject of a hearing at La Roche College by the Republican Policy Committee, comprising GOP state representatives. The hearing comes in response to a report issued in June by Auditor General Jack Wagner that found "serious deficiencies" in the state Department of Public Welfare's administration of the program, which uses federal funds to provide grants to low-income households.

headline: Ex-legislator is charged in 'ghost' worker scam
abstract: Former State Rep. Frank LaGrotta kept it all in the family. First it was his sister, then his niece. He gave them jobs last year in his waning days as a Democratic lawmaker and paid them thousands in taxpayer dollars, supposedly to archive boxes of records. It wasn't even real work, according to a criminal complaint filed by the state Attorney General's Office. The three were charged yesterday in a "ghost employee" scam that prosecutors allege involves bogus documents, embarrassing e-mails, and more than $25,000 in wasted tax dollars for a clear-cut case of nepotism.

headline: A growing sense of mission at home
abstract: Marcia Gelbart writes about Philadelphia Representative Chaka Fattah and his race for mayor of Philadelphia. She writes about where he grew up, his family life and the type of education he had. She shares Chaka Fattah’s proposal to planting 100,000 new trees, and boosting funding for the arts. In Chinatown, he even promised to open a Chinese library.

headline: 'Social animals' limited by smoke in public places
abstract: A citizen of Salisbury Township writes to the editor out of frustration for what she sees as the state senators giving in to pressure from special interests.  While she encouraged PA Governor Ed Rendell in his support of a public smoking ban, she is upset that the PA Senate did not pass the ban.  She works in the hospitality industry where she is forced to interact with secondhand smoke everyday.

headline: 30 firms show interest in turnpike
abstract: The General Assembly passed a law that calls for putting tolls on I-80, however, there has been a severe backlash from PA and US legislators that could prevent the addition of tolls. In response, Governor Rendell has pursued the leasing of the turnpike, which he believes could bring in $1.5 billion a year for state road and bridge improvements. The article provides a number of key companies that submitted their qualifications for purchasing the turnpike; thought it will be several weeks until Rendell asks for monetary bids.

headline: In Turnabout, Infant Deaths Climb in South
abstract: Within the past several years the death rate has risen in Mississippi and several other states. The setbacks have raised questions about the impact of cuts in welfare and Medicaid and of poor access to doctors. In Mississippi, infant deaths among blacks rose to 17 per thousand births in 2005 from 14.2 per thousand in 2004, while those among whites rose to 6.6 per thousand from 6.1. Jamekia Brown, 22, is an example of a woman from Mississippi who has lost two children due to her lack of prenatal care.

headline: Experts: Election is about Cordaro
abstract: This election is about Bob Cordaro. After they won the 2003 election, the Republican Lackawanna County commissioner insisted his and A.J. Munchak’s victory was not about him. The victory, Mr. Cordaro said, was about ending cronyism and politics in county government and acting based on merit. Four years later, he and Mr. Munchak run the county. Political campaigns are always about incumbents’ records, but the commissioner election will stand as a referendum on one person.

headline: A Time to Act: Schools continue to struggle with new state law
abstract:
PA Governor Ed Rendell calls Act 1 a landmark bill that will deliver statewide property-tax relief and give Pennsylvanians a greater say in how their money is spent. School boards call it a headache. 
Voters must make up their minds by May 15, when they go to the polls to decide whether to raise their income taxes in exchange for lower property taxes.  Act 1 is the product of the 2006 special legislative session in Harrisburg that is changing the way school budgets are crafted and bringing the public into a process long left to elected officials and school administrators. Signed into law last summer, Act 1 will distribute an estimated $1 billion in annual slot-machine revenue to school districts for property-tax relief.

headline: State council identifies trends behind rise in health care costs
abstract: The PA Health Care Cost Containment Council released a report that concluded that health care in PA and the rest of the United States is not economically sustainable. The council identified a number of costs that are draining the health care system; though proposes no corrective measures, which is not part of its charter.

headline: 5 deck truss bridges in county called safe
abstract: Allegheny County owns five bridges similar in construction to the Interstate 35W span that collapsed last week in Minneapolis. All have been recently reconstructed or are scheduled for rehabilitation over the next six years. The quality of the deck truss bridges ranges from "poor condition" for the 56-year-old Rankin Bridge to presumably excellent for the 70-year-old Homestead Grays Bridge, which is in the finishing stages of a $35 million renovation.

headline: Judge rules for nonprofits in $10 million trust battle
abstract: Judge Robert A. Kelly of Allegheny Orphans' Court has finally ruled that 4 nonprofit organizations win a dispute over the $10 million of a trust of Rita Conrady who died last year.  Animal Friends Incorporated, the American Cancer Society, Geneva College and the Humane Society of Western Pennsylvania will each have their donations from the trust increased substantially by over hundreds of thousands of dollars.  Jefferson Regional Medical Foundation, Phipps Conservatory and Botanical Gardens and Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra will not receive any money after Judge Kelly ruled that local attorney Gregory Harbaugh did not have authority under Florida law to change the contents of Conrady's will without her express consent.

headline: Fairness key in strike issue
abstract: The author disagrees with proposals to outlaw teacher strikes by imposing economic sanctions on teachers because it would give school board members too much power. The author believes that lawmakers should pass an alternative approach to outlawing teacher strike called the last-best-offer binding arbitration. For this method, an arbitrator would choose one final proposal over the other, which the author claims will provides incentives for each side to try to compromise.

headline: Abolish all real estate taxes
abstract: A citizen writes in criticism of Rendell's use of tax dollars to build a new arena in Pittsburgh rather than reduce the school property tax reduction.  He believes the school property tax could be completely eliminated through gambling and sales tax revenue, and the elimination of this tax would allow more people to own homes, afford better health care, and afford a college tuition.

headline: Emmaus makes plans for grant - Program funded with $30,000 of state award to provide incentive for street-front projects.
abstract: Emmaus will receive a $50,000 grant from the PA Department of Community & Economic Development. It will put $30,000 towards a program that will match 50 cents of every dollar spent by chosen property owners to revive the commercial districts. The article provides more details about the program and selection process, as well as information on how the remaining $20,000 will be spent on the development of an overarching downtown plan.

headline: State lawmakers need to enable local government smoking bans . . .
abstract: Philadelphia's ban on smoking appears to be unique to that municipality, as a similar ban in Allegheny County was struck down in PA Commonwealth Court. Judge Renee Cohn Jubelirer ruled that the state's Clean Indoor Air Act pre-empts local legislation. PA Sen. Stewart Greenleaf has been trying to pass legislation against smoking for years. PA Governor Ed Rendell has endorsed a smoking ban in his Prescription for PA health care plan. Allentown City Council recently adopted a resolution asking the PA General Assembly to adopt a statewide smoking ban.

headline: Airport project funding a priority
abstract: Despite the PA Senate rejecting the proposal to fund $495 million to build a cargo airport outside Hazleton,  PA Representative Todd Eachus claims that the project can still receive state money from the 5% tax on slots revenue.  PA Senator Lisa Baker voted against the proposal because she believes the revenue from the slots tax is to be used for property tax relief.  Luzerne and Schullkill county commissioners have agreed to create a 16-member commission in order to study the logistics of the cargo airport.

headline: PACC says it made $200K
abstract: A spokesman for the PA Child Care juvenile detention center said that the facility posted a $200,000 profit in 2003, not the $1.2 million the state claims it did. The PA state Department of Public Welfare has refused to deduct administrative costs from the center’ revenue, which results in the higher profit margin it’s reporting. PA Child Care maintains that the key issue should not be the profit but whether the daily rate to treat juveniles is in line with rates charged by other providers.

headline: Feds: Intern took Civil War papers, sold them on eBay
abstract: Denning McTague, an intern at a National Archives and Records Administration site in Philadelphia last summer, has been charged with stealing and selling about 165 Civil War documents on eBay.  McTague has helped the government recover most of the items and plans to plead guilty.  US Attorney Patrick Meehan is in charge of the investigation.

headline: Act 1 to benefit some, but hurt others' wallets
abstract: According to editors, voting really matters. The proposed tax shift for school districts from property to income taxes will benefit some and hurt many. Many districts are proposing property tax increases next year. The income tax would not affect Social Security earnings or pensions. Some districts oppose the new structure as an administrative nightmare. It was proposed by the Legislature in exchange for legalizing slot machines. Renters will not receive property tax relief and will also be taxed on income. The polls will also host judicial and county council races.

headline: Lake-Lehman strike seems inevitable - While none would not lose money by accepting health co-pays deal, some would spend more of raise than others.
abstract: The Lehman School Board proposed a new contract that would ensure teachers don’t contribute more money towards health care than the pay raises they receive, which was a concern that John Holland, leader of the local teachers’ union, had over the previous proposal. The new four-year proposal offers a 2.5 percent raise each year, and the percent of the raise that would go towards health insurance varies on a wide scale depending on pay level. The rest of the article describes what determines these pay levels, how each level affects disparities in health insurance contributions, and Holland’s anger over the board breaking labor laws.

headline: State needs to evaluate solution to infections in health care facilities
abstract: No text.

headline: Alternatives to tolling I-80 aren't desirable
abstract: PA Senator Joe Scarnati is writing an opinion piece that is criticizing the PA roads and bridges, in light of a bridge collapse in Minneapolis. The Senator states that one of the main causes of the transportation funding crisis is the passage of the deferral transportation plan that was supported by PA Congressman John Peterson, because under the law PA received the lowest increase in transportation funding of any state in the country. He says that alternatives to fund the crisis have been difficult, including the initiatives by PA Governor Edward Rendell to sell the PA Turnpike to a foreign company and increasing the state gasoline tax.

headline: Patient's death leads to hearing on care for elderly
abstract: Officials from the PA Department of Public Welfare, the Lackawanna County Area Agency on Aging and the Lackawanna County district attorney's office will provide input on legislation drafted by PA Representative Phyllis Mundy.  This will occur at a public meeting after the arrest of Gregory Salko M.D. for not diagnosing breast cancer on a care-dependent elderly woman at Birch Hills Residence Healthcare Center that eventually led to her death.  The proposed legislation will enhance a penalty for neglect of a care-dependent person and amend the Older Adult Protective Services Act.

headline: Final budget slog slowed by openness
abstract: The Pennsylvania state government still has no definitive spending plan in place 5 days after the PA Governor Ed Rendell and the Senate Republicans reached a deal.  PA Representative Dwight Evans claims that the process has been lengthened because of new laws that open the legislative process and higher public scrutiny.  The recent deal allowed the Senate Republicans to stop all new taxes proposed by the Governor while Rendell won his transportation, education and some health care initiatives.

headline: Act 1: Area voters reject tax question
abstract: Voters in all 11 Luzerne county school districts rejected Act 1 in a referendum. Act 1 proposed to shift the burden of school taxes from property to income. The legislation proposed to use revenue from slots machines to make up for the difference. Unofficial results showed the referendum was rejected by 2:1 or 3:1 in every district. During a luncheon hosted by the Pennsylvania Economy League, PA School Board Association Director of Research Services Dave Davare predicted the referendum would pass by a margin of 20 to 25 percent.

headline: State budget satisfies both sides
abstract: PA Senator Vince Fumo recently regarded the compromised spending plan in the new budget is a win-win situation for both Democrats and Republicans.  While PA Governor Ed Rendell won a $750 million transportation funding proposal and increased duties for nurses in the budget, Senate President Pro Tempore Joe Scarnati was boasting about the Republicans' ability to block all seven tax hikes and halt the Energy Independence Fund that increased taxes.  The article attributes the ability compromise on the thriving state economy, which produced a $650 million surplus from last year, about $550 million more than was expected.

headline: State to release findings of cancer study
abstract: Medical experts and members from the PA Department of Health and the U.S. Agency for Toxic Substances and Disease Registry will attend a public meeting in Hazleton where the findings on the incidence of polycythemia vera, a rare form of blood cancer, will be released to the public. U.S. Senator Arlen Specter urged public meetings on the issues since many believe that the incidence rate in the area will be over four times the normal rate. In addition, community leaders are concerned over a site that was closed in 1979.

headline: An E-ZPass tax break?
abstract: Rep. Scott Conklin wants to allow drivers to deduct up to $500 from their state income tax if they use the E-ZPass system on the Pennsylvania Turnpike. E-ZPass allows drivers to prepay turnpike tolls so they can zip through payment lines on the turnpike. The money owed is then automatically deducted from the motorist's account. The bill provokes more than one comment. Why should the tax break be limited to those who travel I-80? Why shouldn't residents of our area who must drive the Mon Valley Expressway each day also be given some consideration? Then again, if a tax deduction is deserved, why not extend it to the turnpike itself?

headline: Private Sector: Communities benefit when companies, nonprofits partner
abstract: Ralph J. Papa, president of Citizens Bank of Pennsylvania, expresses his concern about the lack of support for very important small non-profit organizations throughout Allegheny County.  He cites an example of Little Sisters of the Poor, who provide health care and support services to the elderly poor.  He also references a program sponsored by Citizens Bank and WPXI-TV, Champions in Action, which provides grant money, volunteer time, media coverage, and promotional support to one organization every year.

headline: Finally, public records makeover seems likely
abstract: At long last, Pennsylvania’s 50-year-old Right-to-Know Law, the nation’s weakest freedom-of-information law, appears headed for a legitimate makeover. The state House has passed an open records law that changes the fundamental parts of the law that had made it so restrictive. The law also has been expanded to include financial records of the legislative and judicial branches, Pennsylvania’s college loan agency, community colleges and the four state-related universities. In court disputes over whether a record should be made public, the burden of proof would be on the public.

headline: Allegheny County might buy tax liens
abstract: Allegheny County is working on a deal to regain control of tax liens to make properties more attractive to potential developers. The board of the county Redevelopment Authority initially planned to vote today on whether to approve the purchase of $1 million to $2 million in liens from GLS Capital Inc., but officials are still compiling the list of liens and negotiating a price.

headline: Report fails state on higher ed costs
abstract: According to a higher-education report card by the National Center on Public Policy and Higher Education, Pennsylvania families spend a very large share of their income on public and private four-year colleges and universities.  As such, PA received a failing grade for college affordability.

headline: Boxed in: The good and the bad of the Onorato budget
abstract: The authors of the editorial give Dan Onorato credit for some of his budgetary policy but feel that he made a mistake by freezing properties at 2002 values for taxation purposes; though the PA Supreme Court may force him to change the policy. The authors believe that Onorato’s decision to impose high taxes on alcoholic drinks and car rentals and to lay off 200 county employees is unfortunate. However, there may be no other viable alternatives since Onorato has politically boxed himself into a corner, and the county can't afford meet the state's expectations and lose out on state funding for its badly needed transit system.

headline: The OT threat to our health
abstract: Thousands of nurses and other health-care workers across PA being are overworked by a practice called mandatory overtime. This policy is bad for the employees, their families and the public. The state House has passed a bill banning it - and the Senate should do the same. But many people may not know that some workers are forced by supervisors to work past their regular shifts. Nurses and other caregivers are sometimes required to keep working for several more hours - sometimes even an entire shift. If nurses refuse to stay, they can be disciplined, fired, even lose their licenses.

headline: Analysis: Haggling pops Rendell budget bubble
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell and the PA Legislature came to an agreement to end the budget impasse on Monday where none of his seven tax hikes to pay for health care and mass transit will be enacted nor will the government lease the Pennsylvania Turnpike to a private company.  Furthermore, the legislators did not accept the $850 million alternative energy fund, and instead will consider a $60 million-a-year version instead.  Where some find that the $900 million a year dedicated to improving highways and mass transit is a victory for transportation, Matthew Bouillette of the Commonwealth Foundation contends that this money will only exacerbate the inefficiencies in the Port Authority and the Southeastern Pennsylvania Transportation Authority.

headline: Rendell says he'll donate money from Hsu to charity
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell has decided to donate the $40,000 contributed to him from Norman Hsu after Hsu did not show up for a California court hearing where he is being tried with a single felony count of grand theft.  PA House Minority Leader Sam Smith has been urging Rendell to give up the money since the accusation was made.  Other prominent politicians across the country have given up their donations from Hsu as well such as US Senators Hillary Rodham Clinton, Chris Dodd, John Kerry and Patrick Kennedy.

headline: Fiscally challenged
abstract: It is unusual for challengers to raise more money than incumbents, however in this year's Pittsburgh City Council races, Councilman Jeff Koch's fundraising has fallen behind challenger Bruce Klaus'. It is difficult to identify who is doing better in the race for Councilman Len Bodack's seat, as he started with less but has more in the account at the end of this month than his challenger Patrick Dowd. There is an eight-way race for Councilwoman Twanda Carlisle's seat.

headline: Allegheny County's Onorato widens political outlook
abstract: Allegheny County Chief Executive Dan Onorato wants to have "a story to tell" about his success in this region, and he hopes to share it outside Pittsburgh. Some of the big issues facing Onorato as he begins his second term next week -- especially property assessments and local taxes -- are the ones politicians are tackling in counties across the state. Onorato again declined to say whether coming years could find him running for governor or U.S. Senate; seeking a third and final term as executive; or leaving behind politics for the private sector. However, he did not hesitate to offer statewide perspective while addressing some issues that will face Grant Street over the next four years.

headline: CVS must pay refunds in RX scam
abstract: Under Pennsylvania law, those injured in a car accident are eligible for a 20 percent discount on perscription drugs.  CVS failed to comply with the state law and, to avoid further prosecution, has agreed to issue refunds to consumers who were overcharged for pain medications.

headline: Bill would dock lawmakers' pay if budget delayed
abstract: A midstate lawmaker is preparing legislation that would give governors and legislators incentive to get state budgets completed on time: their salaries. Rep. Jerry Nailor, R-Mechanicsburg, said he is drafting a bill that would require members of the General Assembly, the governor and his Cabinet to forfeit pay if a general fund budget is not enacted by the July 1 deadline. The pay would continue to be forfeited until a budget is in place.

headline: Sturla touts asthma tracking plan
abstract: PA Rep. Mike Sturla has reintroduced legislation to create a permanent asthma tracking system in the state. The bill passed out of the House last year but died after the Senate failed to consider it before the legislative term expired. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reports asthma sufferers doubled from 1982 to 1996. PA gets federal funding to track asthma, but it is not guaranteed. The American Lung Association of Pennsylvania and the PA Society of Respiratory Care support Sturla's bill.

headline: Analysis: Private turnpike bid blurs political lines
abstract: Republicans oppose PA Governor Ed Rendell's plan to lease the Turnpike. At the federal level, President Bush is pushing for privatization of infrastructure to save costs and raise revenue for states. Labor unions, consumer advocate groups such as the PA Public Interest Research Group (PennPIRG), and truckers are worried about such arrangements. The PA Turnpike Commission opposes private leasing. The political, personal, and ideological positions taken on the issue cross lines and divide parties.

headline: State mandated employment, training program helps welfare recipients find jobs
abstract: Republican legislators claim that the welfare system in Pennsylvania is a failure in moving people off welfare and into the workforce by citing that the state is 220% below federal requirements for cash recipients to be working. or under training.  They, including PA Representative Mike Turzai, plan to introduce legislation that plans to cut funding from the PA Department of Public Welfare if the department continues to fail to meet the mandatory federal requirements.  The state currently gives money to service providers to operate training and education for welfare recipients.

headline: Former Rendell campaign manager to lead Nutter mayoral bid
abstract: Tricia Enright, who was manager of Gov. Ed Rendell's campaign in the fall, will manage Democrat Michael Nutter's campaign for Philadelphia mayor in November.  Nutter, a former city councilman, is favored over Republican Al Taubenberger in the heavily Democratic city, which has not elected a Republican mayor in decades.

headline: Amendment flurry may lead to Phila. City Charter reform
abstract: Since the 1951 Home Rule Charter in Philadelphia was passed, voters have very adamantly rejected any proposed changes, but in recent years, the Philadelphia City Council has approved 20 amendments since 2002.  In response to the "clumsy" charter, Mayor John Street has had to spend $18.4 million on the Managing Director's Office to work around the rules created in 1951.  Democratic candidate for mayor, Michael Nutter, has called the 4 recent purely symbolic amendments to the charter an abuse of the charter system; however, if elected, he does plan to make drastic changes.

headline: Budget battle triggers competing bills
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell is pressuring the PA Legislature to pass his incentives for transportation, health care and energy in the state spending plan and has no qualms about cutting into the July vacation. Rendell's biggest concern is passing a budget before going on vacation, but he is having problems passing it through Senate, which Republicans hold by an eight vote majority. The Republicans claim the biggest problems are with transportation and energy spending and cannot be addressed until the fall.

headline: Sunday forum: Up the revolution
abstract: Karen Feinstein, president of the Jewish Healthcare Foundation and the Pittsburgh Regional Health Initiative, uses the outpouring of support for US Health and Human Services Secretary Michael Leavitt's health care initiative as proof that almost all citizens are dissatisfied with the current state of affairs.  US Representative Jason Altmire, Allegheny County Chief Executive Dan Onorato, and PA Governor Ed Rendell's southwestern Pennsylvania office director Allen Kukovich all attended to support the new imitative.  Feinstein believes that to further reform citizens and the business community need to be stronger in initiating health care reform.

headline: Another I-80 toll hearing turns shouting match
abstract: Another hearing on whether Interstate 80 should become a toll road has disintegrated into a shouting match. The Tuesday night exchange of information in Bloomsburg featured U.S. Rep. Paul Kanjorski angrily shouting at a critic not to call him a liar. Harvey Eckart, of Berwick, asked if the hearings aren't "one big sham" and Wendy Lynne Lee, of Lightstreet, described the session as "propaganda."

headline: State official calls energy assistance audit misleading
abstract: PA Secretary of the Department of Public Welfare Estelle B. Richman claimed that a report by PA Auditor General Jack Wagner that said there are "serious deficiencies" in the federal Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program for the past 6 years.  While she acknowledges that any fraud is a problem, she feels that her finding of 1% of the applications as being fraudulent is not as serious as Wagner reported.  Wagner, on the other hand, found in his sample that 429 applicants in Philadelphia County alone received $162,200 in Social Security benefits using numbers of deceased people.

headline: Freshman legislative reformers didn't get it all, but left a mark
abstract: There are 50 freshman lawmakers in the PA House of Representatives have introduced the culture of reform within the Legislature by passing some but not all of their landmark changes to the way business is done.  PA Representative Tim Mahoney of South Union passed legislation that modified the Right-to-Know law and was significant in the House Speaker's Reform Commission's recommendations.  Eric Epstein, activist from the watchdog group Rock the Capital, agrees that freshman lawmakers are having unprecedented influence in making reform a priority but have not actually passed many large reforms to date.

headline: City of Pittsburgh races: Two City Council members lose their positions
abstract: Pittsburgh Councilwoman Twanda Carlisle, who faces corruption charges, and Councilman Jeff Koch lost their Democratic primary bids. Councilman Len Bodack's race against school board members Patrick Dowd is still too close to call. A third of council experienced a turnover, indicating voters are fed up with corruption. Acting controller Tony Pokora appears to have lost his post after 22 years. Michael Lamb has won the Democratic nomination for controller, a position which acts as a watchdog over Mayor Ravenstahl.

headline: Budget deal vague about local funds
abstract: PA Representative David Argall's biggest satisfaction with the new $27.3 billion state spending budget that was agreed upon by the PA Governor Ed Rendell and the PA Legislature was the lack of no new taxes.  PA Representative Tim Seip, however, was content with the agreement because of the large transportation bill that would help six deficient state bridges and 136 miles of poor roadway within his county.  Argall has claimed that the almost $1 billion dedicated to transportation will not be sufficient and that the details of where the funding will go are still vague.

headline: Superbug may strike 5 percent of hospital, nursing home patients
abstract: According to a survey done by the Association for Professionals in Infection Control and Epidemiology, 30,000 hospital patients may have a dangerous, drug-resistant staph germ  at any given time.  This number comes to about 5% oh hospital and nursing home patients, and is about 10 times greater than health officials previously estimated.  Dr. John Jernigan, from the US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, claims the survey is a welcome piece of information because it has alerted everyone that more needs to be done to prevent it.

headline: Appropriate focus on distraction
abstract: The author of the editorial cites PennDot statistics that indicate cell phone usage has played a known role in thousands of car accidents since 2002. Representative Josh Shapiro proposed a bill that prohibits hand-held cell phone usage, and Representative Eugene DePasquale has sponsored a bill that prohibits text messaging while driving. The author believes that lawmakers should combine and pass the various cell phone bills.

headline: State to unveil new legislation for assisted living facilities
abstract: PA Governor Rendell's administration proposed a bill to regulate care of seniors, meeting with industry representatives and advocacy groups in Harrisburg. The proposal attempts to divert individuals from nursing homes to personal care, however the state is lacking the organization and funding for licensing of such institutions to be administered, the PA Department of Public Welfare admits. The state wants to apply for federal approval to use Medicaid funds to support people in assisted living.

headline: From Pa. suburbs, 2 run for treasurer
abstract: Rob McCord, a venture capitalist of PA Early Stage from Montgomery County, reports raising $1.5 million in order to acquire the Democratic nomination for the PA Treasurer in 2008 against John Cordisco, county commissioner from Bucks County.  There is no incumbent to the position as Bob Casey left the post for the US Senate, and current Treasurer Robin Wiessman accepted the position under the condition she could run for reelection.  While McCord has been supported by former Treasurer Barbara Hafer and former state Speaker Robert O' Donnell, Cordisco has been supported by US Representative Bob Brady and Auditor General Jack Wagner.

headline: City schools shrinking; big cuts looming
abstract: Pittsburgh Public Schools Superintendent Mark Roosevelt proposed elimination of 203 positions and $33 million in cuts to adjust for declining enrollment. The changes are necessary to keep the district from going into a deficit, according to a report by executive director of finance Christopher Berdnik. Officials are not considering a tax increase to solve the crisis, instead focus on marketing to expand its tax base, including a proposed tax break for new residents proposed by Mayor Luke Ravenstahl.

headline: Budget impasse continues
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell and the PA Legislature, mostly Republicans, are yet to finalize the $27 billion budget as the furlough of 24,000 state workers continues for the second straight day.  The Republican lawmakers such as Representative Jim Marshall are encouraging citizens to call Rendell and ask why there is a furlough when the state has a $650 million surplus.  The spokesman for House Majority Leader Bill DeWeese reported that Democrats were committed to discussing the budget deadlock in private meetings.

headline: Suspicious arithmetic used in SCHIP piece
abstract: The author criticizes some claims from a previous column and feels that the columnist didn’t provide arguments for both sides over the issue of expanding coverage for the SCHIP program. The program would expand health care coverage but has some drawbacks.

headline: Area highways deemed lacking
abstract: The 2004 Business Climate Survey released by the Greater Johnstown Cambria County Chamber of Commerce reported that poor highway access to Greater Johnstown is costing businesses in the area more than $450 million every year.  This report is used as evidence to the PA Transportation Commission to improve both Route 46 and Route 219.  Approximately two dozen local officials from the Southern Alleghenies Planning and Development Commission recently testified to the state commission to gather input for Pennsylvania Department of Transportation's 12-year plan.

headline: Two computers stolen from welfare department
abstract: The PA Department of Public Welfare was robbed of two computers that has 1,800 Pennsylvanians' personal information such as names and Social Security numbers.  The information is, however, protected by various passwords and there is no evidence to date that shows this information has been used inappropriately.  The department building is manned by Capitol Police every night.

headline: Front-runner Clinton gets no sisterly love in Philly
abstract: Hillary Clinton, the current frontrunner to win the Democratic Presidential nomination, was ganged up on by the other Democratic candidates in a debate in Philadelphia, where she continued to avoid direct answers to questions about Social Security, Iran’s pursuit of nuclear weapons, and whether she supports giving driver’s licenses to illegal immigrants. One of the major criticisms of Clinton was that she does not represent the best chance of defeating a Republican in the upcoming election; though she also drew criticism on a number of other issues. Clinton tried to turn every issue into an anti-Bush argument, and she grew especially irritated when questioned about the driver’s license issue.

headline: City to seek sponsorship dollars
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl's administration has picked California-based The Active Network to find ways to bring advertising money and sponsorship dollars into the city's coffers. Working for other cities, the firm has landed multimillion dollar deals with beverage makers, gotten companies to build skate parks and turned stale municipal Web sites into money makers. Pittsburgh Council members have said the names of parks and the City-County Building are probably off limits to corporate marketing.

headline: Budget impasse would cut revenue
abstract: This editorial is concerned about the budget impasse taking place between PA Governor Ed Rendell and the PA Legislature.  The biggest concern for the author is the furloughing of the state workers in the Revenue Department, which, in turn, will close down the casinos.  The closing of casinos will cause the government to lose $1.7 million dollars a day to be put towards property tax relief, and the author finds this revenue too important to lose.

headline: Teacher healthcare can be statewide
abstract: This editorial addresses the renegotiation of contracts between school districts in Northeastern Pennsylvania and the teachers from the PA School Board Association with the main topic being health care coverage.  The article encourages the PA Legislature to quickly create a commission to partake in the study of a proposed statewide coverage plan that PA Governor Ed Rendell has introduced.  The author believes that a statewide plan would save redundant administrative costs and create competition between employers.

headline: Blogging for open records
abstract: Editors cite an incident in Franklin County, where a request by the Orrstown Borough Council to erect stop signs at a dangerous intersection was denied and the results of a PA Department of Transportation Study deemed "confidential" as an example of the need for transparency reform in government. PA Governor Rendell supports increased transparency. Editors urge citizens to write their state representatives.

headline: Ways to end hunger being brought to table
abstract: State food banks and other agencies plan to meet in Harrisburg with representatives of six state agencies and the PA Legislature to discuss how to fight hunger. The 481,000 Pennsylvanians listed in last year's U.S. Department of Agriculture report as struggling to feed themselves include the working poor, the disabled and those on public assistance, said Sheila Christopher, executive director of the Pennsylvania Association of Regional Food Banks. Representatives from the agriculture, education, health, aging, public welfare, and community and economic development agencies will attend the summit.

headline: Fumo team makes plea to remain his counsel
abstract: Two US Attorneys, John J. Pease and Robert A. Zauzmer, asked the US District Judge William H. Yohn, to remove Mark P. Sheppard, the lawyer representing PA State Senator Vincent J. Fumo against federal corruption charges, off the case because of his long-standing relationship with the senator.  Fumo is accused of using taxpayer and money donated to his charity, Citizens Alliance for Better Neighborhoods, for political polls, cars, and personal errands.  Yohn has allowed Sheppard and his colleagues from the Sprague & Sprague firm to remain on the case.

headline: Controller forecasts money woes within 3 years
abstract: Acting City Controller Anthony Pokora's Comprehensive Annual Financial Report of the city's economy was mixed. It noted the city's failure to address under-resourced pension funds, and rising healthcare costs, but also the city's $80 million surplus. Pokora called on a state oversight board appointed by the Legislature, and PA Governor Ed Rendell's Act 47 recovery team to address potential pitfall's in the city's budget. Pokora is running against 4 opponents in the Democratic Primary for city controller.

headline: Budget is in place, but strife lingers
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell finally signed the $27.2 billion budget 17 days after the fiscal year actually started on July 1, and there are early indications that the budgetary process in the coming years will not be any better.  Republican legislators blame Rendell for joining unrelated proposals to the budget, while Rendell blames the PA Legislature for not compromising to resolve disagreements.  Barry Kauffman, director of Common Cause Pennsylvania, has proposed that would set deadlines, impose fines and extend the previous year's budget if the budget is not made in time.

headline: Teachers could be leaders in fixing insurance mess
abstract: The author cites statistics from Governor Rendell’s Office of Health Care Reform that indicate that something is seriously wrong with Pennsylvania’s health care system. In light of rising health care costs, the author claims that teachers could all unite throughout the state under a comprehensive health plan that would give them a lot of power to influence the insurance agency, which could reduce costs up to 20 percent. The author also highlights some important parts of Rendell’s "Prescription for PA" plan, which is aimed at providing coverage for thousands of uninsured Pennsylvanians.

headline: Bridge collapse should spur Pennsylvania to be diligent in inspections, repairs
abstract: This editorial cites Pennsylvania has having the most structurally deficient bridges in the country at 6,000 and reports that 111 of them are in Lehigh and Northampton counties.  The US Department of Transportation ranks Pennsylvania as the nation's worst as 15% of the bridges are in this category.  In the wake of the bridge collapse, this article wants PA Governor Ed Rendell to order an emergency inspection of all state bridges as his counterpart, Governor Corzine of New Jersey did, also specifically after Pennsylvania Department of Transportation Secretary Allen Biehler claimed that $1 billion would be needed for road and bridge repair.

headline: $3M per year in tax breaks awaits Westinghosue
abstract: Because Westinghouse Electric Company has decided to build a new office complex in a Strategic Development Area, it will save $3 million a year in state and local taxes for 15 years while creating 1,000 jobs and making over $45 million in capital investments over 3 years.  The PA Legislature and PA Governor Ed Rendell created these development areas with tax breaks in order to attract corporate expansion and relocation projects.  Cranberry County, Butler County and Seneca Valley School District plan to approve the tax-free zone despite the loss of tax revenues.

headline: Furlough facts: What's affected
abstract: This article reports the details of the furlough of state employees as the budget impasse in the Pennsylvania state government continues through the summer.  52,000 state workers who have been deemed critical to safety and welfare will remain working and paid such as police troopers and welfare managers, but 24,000 employees from the Pennsylvania Department of Transportation and the Revenue Department among others will be furloughed without pay until the budget has been passed.  While PA Governor Ed Rendell and the PA Legislature will not be paid until the budget is passed, Rendell claims to remain optimistic the impasse will end in a day.

headline: Councilman wants study of city wage gender gap
abstract: Pittsburgh Council President Doug Shields will introduce legislation that asks Mayor Ravenstahl and the city’s personnel director to solicit firms for a study on the earnings gap that exists between men and women working for the city. He believes the study is necessary because Pittsburgh's women make 70 cents for each dollar that men earn at similar positions.

headline: Capitol crisis didn't derail talks
abstract: According to PA Senator Vince Fumo, the $27.3 billion budget finally passed in the PA Legislature almost exactly as the PA Governor Ed Rendell originally proposed despite Republicans wanting to reduce it by $300 million.  The biggest dispute over Rendell's attachment of his Energy Independence Fund to the budget was resolved, as the administration reports they will spend the summer searching for other sources of alternative energy funding rather than an energy use tax.  Republicans also won an increase in the Educational Improvement Tax Credit that encourages school choice while using $300 million of the current surplus for next year's spending.

headline: Teaching for Life: Diabetes Institute director is committed to value of education
abstract: Dr. Linda Siminerio, executive director of the University of Pittsburgh Diabetes Institute, is nationally recognized for her work in the field of diabetes, which is described in greater detail throughout the article. Her father suffered from the disease and suffered a seizure due to a lack of knowledge, which has fueled her passion to create education and management programs throughout PA. She believes that proper education can actually reduce health care costs by better informing people of the disease, and she hopes to continue with statewide and national education and treatment programs.

headline: Bypass leaves residents on wrong side of road
abstract: A group of residents who say a road maintenance agreement with the PA Department of Transportation was ignored in a bypass project brought their case to the Middle Smithfield Township Supervisors. The Federal Highway Administration says PennDOT is responsible for maintaining private roads to compensate for imminent domain takeovers, however the residents say PennDOT has reneged. Supervisors said more legal research must be completed by residents before Supervisors get involved.

headline: Arena 'Plan C' offers Penguins profits
abstract: Pittsburgh City Councilman Bill Peduto says PA state and local politicians should go beyond Plan B to offer the Penguins a share of the profits in the redevelopment of the Mellon Arena site. The land would be available for development if a new arena is built across the street, as proposed by the city and county. Detroit businessman Don Barden already has promised a $350 million redevelopment of the lower Hill District, including the Mellon Arena property, as part of his winning casino bid. But Mr. Peduto said local and state officials, in conjunction with Mr. Barden, should offer the Penguins a chance to partner in the redevelopment and share in the profits as part of the negotiations to keep the team from moving elsewhere.

headline: Giuliani to make campaign stop in Canonsburg
abstract: Rudy Giuliani, the Republican presidential candidate and current leader for Republican nomination, will stop at Sarries Candies in Canonsburg today at 3:30 PM.

headline:
County Council budget struggle possible
Proposed new taxes may cause impasse, member warns
abstract: Allegheny County Chief Executive Dan Onorato proposed his 2008 budget last month, which relied on taxing alcoholic drinks and car rentals. However, Councilman Bill Robinson, chairman of the Budget and Finance Committee, said that there was no support on the committee for the taxes, so he held off on implementing them. Mr. Robinson tried to pass a resolution that would allow spending to continue after the budget deadline because he is extremely concerned that the council might not be able to pass a budget on time, but the resolution was rejected.

headline: City schools 2008 budget almost $526 million
abstract: The Pittsburgh school board last night released a proposed 2008 general fund budget of $525.9 million, which officials said is $3.1 million less than this year's spending plan. But with revenues of $508 million, Pittsburgh Public Schools would have to take $17.9 million from its reserve fund to balance the budget. That would leave $47.4 million in the reserve fund. The budget calls for the elimination of 37 positions on top of the 203 that have been eliminated since spring.

headline: The governor hasn't addressed the high cost of home care
abstract: Ron Barth, the President of PANPHA, an association of non-profit senior services, is addressing PA Governor Ed Rendell's column on home health care where Rendell talks about rebalancing the Medicaid system.  Barth feels that more funding should be focused on nursing home care because of Pennsylvania's particularly high elderly population where certain situations do warrant nursing home care.  He also reports that Medicaid alone does not provide enough care or cover assisted living costs.

headline: Cash, credit or home equity loan
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell's proposal to the PA Legislature to lease the Turnpike is expected to generate exactly the amount needed for infrastructure and mass transit improvements. However a study estimated tolls would rise 5.5 percent for the next 50 years under a lease, and 3 percent for the remainder of the lease. The Rendell administration argues tolls will increase whether or not the Turnpike is leased, but has yet to lobby the legislature, which is calling for a balanced approach to revenue raising.

headline: Arena talks may resume soon
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell is expected to meet with Penguins owners Mario Lemieux and Ron Burkle  during a visit to Pittsburgh to discuss progress on Plan B, the funding formula he put together for a new arena. Also expected to attend are Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl and Allegheny County Chief Executive Dan Onorato. The meeting, described as very positive, began the effort of cobbling together an agreement under Plan B to build a new arena and keep the team in Pittsburgh. The Penguins also are considering an offer from Kansas City to move into the new $276 million Sprint Center next season.

headline: Global agenda seen in I-80 tolls
abstract: U.S. Rep. Phil English correctly stands against the tolling of Interstate 80 and the Department of Homeland Security's use of Chinese steel for a section of border fence with Mexico. These ill-conceived ideas are part of President Bush's Security and Prosperity Partnership and Public-Private Partnership, two free-trade-related agendas for integrating the U.S., Canada and Mexico into a North American union. The privatization of public infrastructures would allow foreign consortiums to control fees, taxes, utilities, contractors or legal issues. The state Legislature's plan to toll I-80 would endanger public institutions and the economy.

headline: County mulls whether tax will apply to casino drinks
abstract: Allegheny County officials are looking into whether a 10 percent tax on poured alcoholic drinks would apply to complimentary drinks handed out at Pittsburgh's casino.  Officials have been talking with other cities that have drink taxes as they draft the specifics of the county's newest tax. The drink tax, backed by Chief Executive Dan Onorato and enacted by County Council, will take effect Jan. 1. It will impact nearly 3,000 bars and restaurants in Allegheny County. The money will help pay for Port Authority operations. A $2-a-day rental car tax will take effect the same day.

headline:
Districts’ scores point out highs, lows in county
The level of success varies.
abstract: According to standardized test results, Schuylkill County’s public schools scored higher than the state average for grade level and subject on 48 percent of the tests, with Blue Mountain School District doing especially well. The newspaper reviewed the data from all school districts in the county as well as some school districts that are partially in the county, and a long list of results is broken down by each subject and grade level at the end of the article. Educators had mixed reviews of the federal No Child Left Behind law, which uses the test results, but many thought the tests at least do a good job identifying problem areas, and they also identified special education, low-income students and parenting as key influences over test results.

headline: Port Authority tries to get into the naming rights game
