abstract: Citizens debate in a news program over the state cutting taxpayer funded services and how the state should be using slush fund money to stop cuts in those services.

headline: iThink: The economy worries young people, too
abstract: A local high school student applying to colleges writes to explain her experience in this troubled economy.

headline: Nutter's arts efforts aim to paint a brighter future
abstract: With Mayor Nutter's campaign promise to reestablish the city Office of Arts and Culture close to being fulfilled, the challenge now is to ensure it will be an effective force not just for the cultural sector, but for the region. Just as the mayor seeks to establish a 311 number for coordinating citizen access to city services, a strong Office of Arts and Culture can efficiently coordinate access to the many cultural programs within city government. Those resources are extensive and include the Mural Arts Program, the Free Library, the Public Art program, the Atwater Kent Museum, the Philadelphia Cultural Fund, and many other programs and services.

headline: Transit ridership rose 6 percent during July
abstract: The high cost of fuel seems to have encouraged more commuters to use public transportation. The Port Authority released ridership numbers that show an increase of over 6 percent over July 2007; however, a spokesman cautioned not to take the numbers out of context, and he said the real challenge will be retaining these figures. Several riders who were interviewed also noticed an increase in ridership.

headline: Gaming board's naivete doubted
abstract: PA police commissioner Jeffrey Miller was surprised by the PA Gaming Control Board's issue of a casino license to Louis Denaples after its investigation referred perjury allegations about DeNaples to PA police. Miller's comments were made before the PA Senate Appropriations Committee, in which he asserted Gaming Chairman Tad Decker even knew of the investigation. Last month, Decker charged that PA police acted illegally by not sharing federal wiretap information on DeNaples. Miller maintains the Commission had reason to withhold a license, but did not.

headline: Girardville welcomes Bill Clinton warmly
abstract: Former President Bill Clinton appeared at the city's annual St. Patrick's Day Parade. Clinton said the event was not political, but thanked the crowd for supporting Hillary, the US Senator from New York. Clinton walked alongside Schuylkill County Democratic Chairman Ed Kleha and other officials. He visited the home of Charles A. Marquardt, Girardville Borough Council president. Clinton later toured the borough with US Rep. Tim Holden, and PA Reps. Neal Goodman and Tim Seip. Clinton dismissed recent suggestions Hillary should drop out of the race to make room for rival, US Sen. Barack Obama.

headline: State System chief salaries easily top Rendell's
abstract: Salaries for the chief executive and 14 campus presidents in PA’s state-owned university system topped $3.1 million in the past year. The 2007-08 pay levels for the presidents were finalized last month, according to information released Wednesday by the Pennsylvania State System of Higher Education. The presidents' salaries all are higher than Gov. Ed Rendell's $170,150 salary for 2008 and rank among the 50 highest in state government.

headline: Lawmaker pushes for smaller state Legislature
abstract: State Representative Mark Mustio introduced a bill that would reduce the size of the state legislature.  The bill would cut costs and increase accountability, but many legislators feel it is too drastic a solution to legislative problems that call for reform.

headline: Property-tax case goes to PA justices today
abstract: The Pennsylvania Supreme Court is set to hear arguments on the constitutionality of the state's property-tax system.  Allegheny County Solicitor Michael H. Wojcik filed a 119-page opinon with the court, asking it to reconsider the manner in which home assessments are carried out throughout the Commonwealth.  Currently, homes are assessed with a base-year program that assesses county properties all at once and fixes values for years.  But as homes appreciate, assessments decrease as a percentage of a given home's market value, creating a tax break for owners of pricier properties.

headline: States flunk on cost of college
abstract: An indpendent organization, the National Center for Public Policy and Higher Education, rated college affordabilty state to state. Forty-nine states earned an "F" while only California received a barely passing grade of "C". The study pits the net cost of higher education, such as tuition, books, fees, room and board, against median family income. Pennsylvania has the sixth most expensive net cost to attend public institutions in the entire country.

headline: Greensburg Laurels & Lances
abstract: A ruptured gasoline transmission line in Murrysville shot fuel 75 feet into the air and threatened public safety for miles around. Public safety officials, school staff and volunteers are congratulated for their quick response.

headline: Year in Review, and Financial New Year’s Resolutions
abstract: This week's Pennsylvania Newsmakers will feature the year in review and five financial resolutions for 2009.

headline: Study: Kids less likely to graduate than parents
abstract: Dropout rates haven't budged in a generation, with 1 in 4 kids still dropping out of high school.  The US is the only industrialized country to boast young people with less of a chance to complete an education than their parents.

headline: Officials, Rendell rally for funding changes
abstract: Dozens of mayors and school superintendents rallied with Gov. Ed Rendell to promote his plan to change the way public schools are funded. Tuscarora Superintendent Rebecca Erb and Mercersburg Mayor James Zeger lent their support to the plan that Rendell wants as part of the state budget that should be approved by July 1. Rendell is pushing a two-part plan to pump more money into schools, with no tax increase, and rewrite the state funding formula to send more to districts with problems such as rapid growth or blight. Basic education subsidies would increase next year by nearly 6 percent, or $291 million, as part of a six-year plan to give schools a $2.6 billion infusion of state money.

headline: Transportation funding for turnpike becomes ball of confusion
abstract: Western PA legislators, including PA Rep. Rick Geist, minority chair of the Transportation Committee, want to eliminate confusion surrounding transportation issues, including proposals to lease the PA Turnpike, toll I-80, and raise gas taxes. PA Motor Truck Association President Jim Runk plans to outline issues for local trucking companies during a regional board meeting. The confusion is due to back and forth actions of PA Gov. Ed Rendell, the Turnpike Commission, and lawmakers. The Federal Highway Administration might not even approve tolling of I-80.

headline: Home sales in steepest decline since 1995
abstract: Residential real estate in the metropolitan Pittsburgh area is seeing its steepest decline in sales activity in more than a decade, according to a report by RealSTATs.

headline: Good Day Philadelphia
abstract: A crumbling bridge on I-95 has Philadelphia Mayor Michael Nutter and PA Gov. Ed Rendell speaking out on the need for government funding of infrastructure.

headline: Statistics on merger show more savings
abstract: Consultant Donald Boyer said that merging the Center Area and Monaca school districts could yield a $5 million property tax cut in Center. The Center board has been making a practice of discussing the consolidation behind closed doors of teachers. Under Sunshine Law regulations, boards can call executive sessions to discuss specific employees or prospective employees, to discuss buying or leasing real estate, to hold labor negotiations or to consult with an attorney or other professional to discuss litigation.

headline: Tomorrow is bid day for Philadelphia Convention Center
abstract: Officials are anxiously awaiting contractor bids on a new Convention Center expansion in Center City Philadelphia.  Bids are expected to exceed the 700 million dollars of state slot-machine revenue alloted to the project.  Governor Rendell worries that the project will not be achievable if it goes beyond 790 million.

headline: Ex-teacher derides school district's racial-balance act
abstract: A former Philadelphia school teacher, Alma Crocker, criticizes the district's racial-balancing policy and urges officials to reconsider it; the policy places a cap on the number of African-American teachers who can work in a school.  Crocker sees this policy as unfair.

headline: Clearfield ethanol plant taking shape
abstract: A corn ethanol plant is being constructed in Clearfield, Pennsylvania.  The Secretary of the PA Department of Environmental Protection, John Hanger, and  Democratic state Representative Rep. Camille "Bud" George toured the facilities of Bionol Clearfield.  It is scheduled to be compeleted in late 2009 and is expected to produce 100 million gallons of ethanol a year. The plant will be the first of its kind in the state.

headline: Greensburg Laurels & Lances
abstract: A Fayette woman in Fairchance handed a .22-caliber handgun to her 10 year old son show he could show it to a friend.  The handgun was loaded and a shot hit the boy in the thigh.

headline: Bringing the slots to our neighborhoods
abstract: Majority Whip William DeWeese and PA state Representative Tim Solobay of Canonsburg, both House Democrats, propose legislation that would bring table games into Pennsylvania casino and allow licensed liquor establishments to host a small number of slot machines. Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell wants to wait until the state's 14 casinos are in operation to see the impact of the original slots law first.  DeWeese and Solobay say expansion will keep the state competitive with other gambling markets in other states.

headline: To your health
abstract: The crumbling economy seems to be bad for people's health as they put off seeing doctors for routine visits.  The state legislature recently did nothing to assist the nearly 1 million working age adults in PA without health insurance.

headline: One school's steps to PSSA success
abstract: According to newly released state date, Logan Elementary had the biggest improvements on state exams in Philadelphia and the suburbs, and it met Adequate Yearly Progress standards under the federal No Child Left Behind law. The school has disadvantages since 82 percent of its students are poor and over half enter or leave the school each year, but it developed a game plan after disappointing test results last year that led to a remarkable turnaround. Part of the plan was to free classroom teachers to work with smaller groups, allow staff to hand-pick new teachers and invite former principals and others to do surprise walk-throughs.

headline: Trolley folly
abstract: The word "delusional" comes to mind when one reviews some key operational statistics of the Port Authority of Allegheny County. The numbers regarding the South Hills trolley system that feeds into the nation's shortest subway and soon will extend to Pittsburgh's near North Shore. A "T" car costs twice as much to run than a bus and fares from the trolley system netted just 2 percent of the mass-transit agency's budget. Now there's a rationale to spend nearly half-a-billion dollars to expand a system that most likely will become even less efficacious. About the only thing that's been "developed" along the "T" line over the last 30 years is a massive taxpayer-financed garage adjacent to the South Hills Village mall.

headline: House approves bill for more bingo nights, bigger prizes
abstract: The House has approved a revamp of the state's bingo law -- a plan that supporters say is needed to help nonprofits compete with the state's glitzy new casinos. Rep. Don Walko sponsored the bill that would allow more nights of bingo per week, permit bigger payouts, lift advertising restrictions and legalize hand-held electronic bingo devices. All House members from York and Adams counties voted for it. Critics questioned whether the changes are needed and whether it's wise to allow more gambling opportunities in Pennsylvania.

headline: Good Day Philadelphia
abstract: Local news including Ron Paul ends his campaign,  Gov. Ed Rendell signs the smoking ban bill, trials for terrorists, and weather.

headline: The O'Reilly Factor
abstract: PA Gov. Ed Rendell pushed for presidential candidate Hillary Clinton this weekend. US Sen. Barack Obama put an end to any beliefs he might settle for VP to Hillary.

headline: Council reaffirms drink-tax referendum
abstract: The Pittsburgh City Council failed to strike a drink-tax referndum from the November ballot.  The ballot question was approved by the Council's Democratic majority, but Republicans opposed to the tax were unable to repeal the portion of the law under which the question was adopted.

headline: Science Center unveils expansion plan
abstract: The Carnegie Science Center plans to expand by 80,000 square feet.  Under a ten-year master plan, the center hopes to build a new home for its SportsWorks exhibition and to create an outdoor eco park.

headline: Department watchdog minds police overtime clock
abstract: Due to Philadelphia's budget woes, the city's Mayor Michael Nutter, ordered the Police Department to cut $23 million in spending by June 30. $14 million in those cuts will come from overtime.  To manage overtime, a new department has been created, called the Overtime Management Unit.  Also, 200 officer vacancies will go unfilled, saving $8 million dollars for other uses.

headline: Greensburg Laurels & Lances
abstract: A constable fires shots toward a moving car when he attempted to serve a warrant for it.  One shot entered a mobile home.

headline: Major road work targets Route 28 at Etna
abstract: Route 28 construction at Etna tops PennDot's Alleghany County based office's $300 million list. The project will rehabilitate three bridges and add more lanes.

headline: Nation's economic repairs must include homeowners
abstract: US Senator Arlen Specter writes to explain the difficulties facing homeowners across the country.  He praises Philadelphia's program to help those facing foreclosure stay in their homes.  He says that lenders need to make sure they have the staff available to work with these homeowners.

headline: Penn State loan change may be costly to PHEAA
abstract: Penn State University plans to become a direct provider of federal student loans, putting the PA Higher Education Assistance Agency in danger of losing 8 percent of its business. The Agency confirmed losses of several hundreds of thousands of dollars each year are expected. Penn State announced it was acting to protect students wishing to enroll in the Federal Family Education Loan Program, called FFELP, which includes Stafford Loans. Loans will come through the University directly from the US Department of Education, insulating students from market swings.

headline: Tunneling machine's Downtown entrance delayed until tonight
abstract: The Port Authority’s tunnel boring machine stopped functioning because a piece of equipment failed. Workers will try to make repairs and finish the digging sometime this evening.

headline: House calls for stricter financial standards for casinos
abstract: House Republicans are calling for more stringent financial requirements for casino operators who renew, transfer or apply for new gaming licenses. The Republican Policy Committee invited experts in gaming and public policy to testify during a hearing. Both were critical of the gaming board's licensing procedures and said state law should be changed to require more thorough vetting of financial qualifications. Current law allows the board too much flexibility in deciding which criteria to use, said Jake Haulk, president of the Allegheny Institute for Public Policy, and Wayne Marlin, of the consulting firm Spectrum Gaming Group.

headline: Good Day Philadelphia
abstract: Local newscast including Gov Ed Rendell supporting Hillary Clinton for the Vice Presidential nominee.

headline: Taking us for a ride
abstract: Once again, PA residents are proving to be among the most generous, if not the most generous, people in the country when it comes to treating your public servants. You spent $15.6 million last year to maintain, service, insure and fuel a fleet of 3,650 vehicles for state employees. Not only that, you allowed many of your employees to use state-issued vehicles for their personal use. How thoughtful of you. Certainly, a number of people on the public payroll travel across the Keystone State in the performance of their duties.

headline: Ex-gambling official doing legal work for two casinos
abstract: A former top ranking state gambling regulator who left his job three months ago is now a lawyer and registered lobbyist for two casinos.  Kevin Hayes says he is doing legal work but is not a lobbyist for the casinos.  The case raises questions with the state Ethics Act and how it applies to attorneys, as they are currently exempt from a one-year waiting period that applies to those appearing before the agency for which they used to work.

headline: Clouds of Confusion
abstract: Although Pennsylvania's indoor smoking ban goes into effect on Wednesday, businesses that applied for exemptions allowed under the law can let patrons smoke--at least until the PA Department of Health processes exemption applications and determines if a given establishment is legitimately exempt.  Under the law, some bars and a few types of businesses--cigar bars and tobacco shops--can apply for exemptions.

headline: City Council postpones budget votes
abstract: Yesterday, the City Council of Pittsburgh voted to delay the first of three votes on Mayor Luke Ravenstahl's proposed $438 million budget. Councilman Patrick Dowd asks for more information on how the $37.8 million dollars in "restricted funds" would be invested and how much debt would be paid down. If answeres are received by tomorrow, then he may add back the $51 million in debt service Pittsburgh had erased in its five-year plan. Details are being worked out with the Intergovernmental Cooperation Authority, which was created by the state to oversee city finances.

headline: Greensburg Laurels & Lances
abstract: City officials issued an ordinance restricting where college students can live in the city has drawn appeals from two more landlords challenging the law's constitutionality.

headline: State Lotteries Show Big Declines
abstract: An article discusses the steep decline of state lottery sales. In California they are down 10% and in Texas 4%. Nationwide sales fell about $215 million, or nearly 2%.  Lottery sales were widely considered to be recession proof.

headline: Pittsburgh Laurels & Lances
abstract: The newspaper praises US Steel who broke ground on a $1.2 billion upgrade of its Clairton Coke Works.  It slams Keith Smith, a fake minister who was once employed as the Pittsburgh police chaplain.

headline: Penn State to require course on alcohol abuse
abstract: This fall, Penn State University students will pay a new fee for campus improvements, while freshmen will be required to take an online course aimed at combating high-risk drinking. Penn State trustees authorized administrators to phase in the fee across the 84,000-student system. The money will support projects involving nonacademic, recreational and multipurpose space, administrators said. The fee will be $100 for main campus students in the 2008-2009 academic year and $200 in 2009-2010. Amounts at other Penn State locations will be set as deemed appropriate at those campuses. Meanwhile, Penn State freshmen will get a course intended to prevent alcohol abuse.

headline: Turnpike bankrolls PennDOT again
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation has gotten another cash infusion from the Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission, part of a unique "public-public partnership" created by the state Legislature. Turnpike spokesman Carl DeFebo confirmed that the turnpike electronically transferred $229.2 million to PennDOT's account yesterday. This represented the third of four payments totaling $750 million that the toll road agency is to make to PennDOT for the 2007-08 fiscal year that ends June 30. PennDOT and the Turnpike Commission have submitted a joint application to the Federal Highway Administration, seeking to toll I-80 as a pilot toll road conversion project.

headline: Indictment exposes flaws in state gaming licensure
abstract: The authors hope that the General Assembly and the PA Gaming Control Board seriously consider the grand jury’s recommendations to have greater transparency by the control board and that the control board’s Bureau of Investigation and Enforcement be placed under the jurisdiction of the state Attorney General. These sentiments come from the grand jury charges that were filed against Louis A. DeNaples regarding his lying about organized crime ties in sworn testimony before the state gaming regulators.

headline: Good Morning Jacksonville
abstract: US Sen. Hillary Clinton kicked off her campaign for the PA primary with PA Gov. Ed Rendell at her side. John McCain nows for right now, all attention is focused on democrats. Mississippi is expected to go for Obama today.

headline: Tavis Smiley Commentary
abstract: The article provides a brief commentary of the presidential election and the Democratic National Convention.

headline: LANTA gets road map to future
abstract: Walter Cherwony, a consultant hired by the Lehigh and Northampton Trasportation Authority, presented his vision of a new transit system--one that includes light-rail trains and bus rapid transit.  His plan is based on a five month study and is similar to existing transit systems in similarly-sized cities.

headline: Time to act
abstract: Legislation that would reduce the number of uninsured Pennsylvanians and force small-market insurers to adopt consumer-friendly pricing practices is under consideration in the General Assembly.  Even though the proposed reforms are affordable, they face opposition from small-market insurers--something which could induce legislators to oppose reform.  This is not the time for legislators to make excuses, however, and the citizens of PA want them to take action.

headline: Wider sidewalk, other changes would lend more inviting look
abstract: The Capitol Preservation Committee in Harrisburg announced contruction work in the park and pedestrian areas to create for more aesthetically pleasing scenery for visitors.

headline: Greensburg Laurels & Lances
abstract: A Fayette teen with dual citizenship in Saudi Arabia and the United States is being deported to Saudia Arabia due to charges of aggravated assault and terroristic threats.

headline: Mount Airy expands smoking under state exemption
abstract: Mount Airy Casino Resort was given an exemption from the Clean Indoor Air Act enacted by the Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board and was allowed to double its smoking area to 50% on the casino floor. Pennsylvania's Clean Indoor Air Act was signed into law June 13 and took effect Sept. 11. The PA Department of Revenue calculated that revenue per machine in the smoking area equals or exceeds the revenue of a machine in a non-smoking area.

headline: WHP CBS 21 Morning News
abstract: Gov Ed Rendell says that the state property tax relief bill is helping thousands of PA seniors.

headline: Penn State Wilkes-Barre students will see tuition hike
abstract: Penn State Wilkes-Barre approved tuition increases ranging from 5.2 percent to 6.46 percent, which is similar to other rate increases for universities in Luzerne County. Undergraduates will pay about $600 more for in-state and $900 more for out-of-state tuition next year.

headline: Turnpike bid races narrows
abstract: A financial consortium once thought to be the leading candidate to lease the PA Turnpike has apparently dropped out of the running. Spain-based Cintra and Australia-based Macquarie Infrastructure Group, which bought rights to the Chicago Skyway in 2005 and the Indiana Toll Road in 2006 for a total of $5.6 billion, have decided not to increase their bid for the state toll road being offered by Gov. Ed Rendell as a means of generating more funds for roads, bridges and transit.

headline: It's a dangerous fallacy
abstract: The author believes that the promises of the casino industry in PA are fraudulent. The author discusses how she believes that they spread crime and make profits on the backs of problem gamblers and addicts. She believes that Philadelphia Mayor Michael Street’s Gaming Task force estimate that Philadelphia already has as many as 9,450 pathological gamblers, so the city would spend $200 million to $430 million every year to deal with the costs of gambling addiction and this is another reason that gambling should not be allowed into the state.

headline:
GOP: Corbett will be fair
Locals not aware of any caucus crimes
abstract: PA Attorney General Tom Corbett has been investigating corruption in all four caucuses in the state Legislature, but as of now, he has only filed charges against a dozen House Democrats, including former Whip Mike Veon and current state Representative Sean Ramaley. Since Corbett is a Republican seeking re-election, some have questioned the fairness of his investigation; however, local Republicans, including state Representatives Scott Boyd and Tom Creighton, expect him to conduct a fair, nonpartisan investigation because of his gubernatorial aspirations. A grand jury has been questioning Republicans legislators and staffers, but they have denied any wrongdoing and have little idea where the investigation is headed.

headline: Teachers are threatening to strike Tuesday
abstract: An agreement between the teacher's union and the Northwest Area School District has yet to be reached. Board Member Albert Gordon said lead negotiators where largely at the end of their careers and were trying to maximize benefits. Board member Daryl Morgan tried to put things into perspective by putting salaries earned into dollars-per-day scenarios.

headline: null
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell says that Senator Joe Biden would be Barack Obama's best choice for Vice President.

headline: Scranton teachers contract may be costly
abstract: Scranton teachers accepted a new contract that would give them increased health benefits and salary increases over the next three years.  If the Scranton Area School District does not cut spending, it would have to raise property taxes by roughly 3 million dollars to pay for increased salary and benefit costs.  School district officials have not yet commented on a potential property-tax increase.

headline: Sony closing Westmoreland plant
abstract: Due to global downsizing, Sony Corporation plans close the Sony Technology Center-Pittsburgh in East Huntingdon and Hempfield, Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell announced. The plant employed 560 workers.

headline: Governor Rendell will host the governor's conference today at Independence Hall
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell will host his conference at Independence Hall in Philadelphia. Discussion will include how the economic crisis has affected state budgets.  President-elect Barack Obama and Vice President-elect Joe Biden will be in attendance. Alaska Governor Sarah Palin will be among the forty governors in attendence.

headline: Supporting cast: How Nutter's top 5 appointees have fared over the last year
abstract: Phildelphia Mayor Michael Nutters top five appointments are given updates of their performance since being sworn in.  They are: Managing Director Camille Barnett, Finance Director Rob Dubow, Police Commissioner Charles Ramsey, Redevelopment Authority Executive Director Terry Gillen and Commerce Director Andrew Altman.

headline: WHP CBS 21 News at 5
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell thinks that Barack Obama connects with PA voters.  He specifies his plans for the economy and health care.

headline: Survey: More than a quarter of region's roads rated 'poor'
abstract: Of the state-owned roads in the Pittsburgh metropolitan area, 28 percent received a rating of "poor." The Road Information Program cites that this causes motorists an average of $464 annually in vehicular maintainence. The findings are above the national average, but below conditions in Philadelphia. TRIP Executive Director William Wilkins notes that gaps in funding will make it hard to repair the roads, to which PA Transportation Sec. Allen Biehler agreed. Money from legislative initiatives passed last year is just beginning to flow for transportation.

headline: Phila. SRC to reconsider 16 charter schools
abstract: The Philadelphia School Reform Commission is meeting to vote on whether or not to recommend renewing sixteen charter schools. Documents show they will most likely recommend that 14 schools  be renewed, and two not be renewed. At the same meeting they will also honor acts of bravery by students.

headline: Turnpike bidding goes into overtime
abstract: Preliminary bids for a 75-year lease of the Pennsylvania Turnpike came in so close to one another that at least some of the bidders have been given five more days to sweeten the pot. Gov. Rendell said yesterday that the highest bid submitted by Friday's deadline and all other bids that were at least 90 percent of the highest bid qualified for the right to submit a best and final offer by the end of the week. The governor did not say how high the initial bids were or how many qualified for the additional time.

headline: Karen Heller: A toxic cargo: Slots in Phila.
abstract: The author uses humor and sarcasm to criticize Governor Ed Rendell and his support of proposals to build casinos in the Philadelphia area. According to the Saint Consulting Group, casinos are tied with landfills as the least favorable real estate projects to live near, and he believes they are unnecessary in a Philadelphia, which has a rich cultural history. He believes casinos will bring a lot of traffic and "stupid people," and he disputes claims that casinos will create many new jobs and offer entertainment other than gambling.

headline: GOP: State ripe for John McCain
abstract: The Cambria County Republican Party held a fundraising dinner for Republican presidential nominee Senator John McCain at which Karl Rove spoke. They predict that McCain has a good chance of winning the election, but he may have trouble in Pennsylvania. In Pennsylvania in 2006, Republicans lost a United States Senate seat, two state Supreme Court seats, and the majority in the state House.

headline: Teachers look to Harrisburg
abstract: Legislation, not sickouts and rallies, may be the means for teachers in the Diocese of Scranton to get their union. Michael Milz, president of the diocesan teachers union, made the announcement Friday outside Holy Redeemer High School, with 50 supporters behind him, and state Rep. Eddie Day Pashinski at his side. A proposed bill would amend the Pennsylvania Labor Relations Act to give lay teachers and employees of private, religiously affiliated schools the right to join collective bargaining units. Mr. Pashinski distributed the co-sponsorship letter for the bill.

headline: null
abstract: A former aide of PA State Senator Vincent Fumo pleaded guilty to conspiracy and obstruction of justice.  The aide also agreed to testify against Senator Fumo, who is on trial for corruption.  Senator Fumo says he is confident in his case and is anxious for his story to be told.

headline: Scarce highway dollars help Perry Countians get around
abstract: State and federal funding shortages for infrastructure and transportation projects have caused the old tensions between rural and urban residents of Pennsylvania to crop up; rural residents complain about their tax dollars funding urban mass transit programs and argue that tax dollars should be used to make improvments only in the locality where they are collected.  The logic guiding this argument is faulty, as most rural areas would not have the tax base to support the infrastructure projects they need.

headline: The Port Authority says the new contract the drivers have agreed to accept is a huge step if the right direction.
abstract: To save the Port Authority much needed funds, workers agreed to give up some health benefits when they retired.  The Authority will save $93 million over the next four years.

headline: Pennsylvania US senator Arlen Specter says he's ready for a tough re-election race in 2010.
abstract: Pennsylvania US Senator Arlen Spector is ready for a tough re-election race in 2010.

headline: Pittsburgh Laurels & Lances
abstract: Allegheny County Chief Executive Dan Onorato was sued by citizen's group FACT (Friends Against Counterproductive Taxation) because Onorato plans to use excess drink-tax receipts on non-mass-transit transportation projects, which is illegal.  Act 44 states that tax reciepts can only be used for mass public transit projects.  The case will go before a Common Pleas judge on Monday.

headline: No headline
abstract: Voting advocates want to ensure that people will be able to vote via paper ballots should electronic ballot machines fail on election day.

headline: null
abstract: Local newscast including 21 year old man is in critical condition after being shot, budget passed just in time for the fiscal deadline, and John McCain will campaign in PA today.

headline: Pitt, PSU announce tuition increases
abstract: PA students attending the University of Pittsburgh and Penn State University will have to pay up to 6 percent more for their fall tuition. Both schools said they needed to raise tuition because state funding didn’t increase nearly as much as operating costs have. Several students’ opinions about the tuition hikes are shared in the articles.

headline: Turnpike lease protects residents in tolls, taxes
abstract: The author, Jim Courtovich, argues PA has urgent transportation needs, and the best way to address those needs would be to accept the PA Transportation Partners’ $12.8 billion bid to manage the PA Turnpike. He questions state House Transportation Chairman Joe Markosek for his opposition to leasing the turnpike, and he claims the financial incentives for the deal would go much further than initial bid, considering the company would pay a significant state corporate tax and an additional $11 billion in investments for the turnpike itself. Mr. Courtovich thinks there are far too many uncertainties in the alternate plan to toll Interstate 80, leasing the turnpike would actually protect drivers from large toll increases, and overall, a private investor would be much more motivated to improve service on the turnpike.

headline: Lawmakers to take up flood relief, prevention bills
abstract: A House floor vote looms for legislation by Rep. Jim Wansacz to provide state aid for flood victims when federal relief isn’t available, and help municipalities pay for flood prevention projects. The measure is one of several approaches being considered by lawmakers to help communities rebound from the type of floods that hit Northeastern PA two years ago and also tackle a backlog of needed improvements to dams and levees. A recent report by state Auditor General Jack Wagner calls attention to unsafe conditions at old and deteriorating dams across Pennsylvania. The state would pay for the program with an annual surcharge of 20 cents on every $100 paid on homeowners’ and business owners’ property insurance policies.

headline: Gov. Rendell's appellate nominees benched
abstract: Four vacancies on Pennsylvania's appellate courts, including one on the Supreme Court, will remain unfilled for now, stuck in a partisan dispute. The Senate's majority Republicans yesterday defied Gov. Rendell and Chief Justice Ronald D. Castille and rejected four men nominated by Rendell to temporarily fill the openings. Twenty-four senators, three of them Republicans, voted in favor of the nominations, while 26, all Republicans, voted against. A two-thirds majority vote is necessary to confirm a judicial nominee. The Democratic governor has insisted that the nominees are highly qualified.

headline: Teachers, district continue negotiations
abstract: Negotiations are continuing, but Neshaminy School District teachers will return to teach without contracts because no agreement has yet been reached. In June, the Neshaminy Federation of Teachers and the school board both rejected a fact-finder’s recommended teacher labor contract, and since then, the union’s president has accused the district of limiting substantive face-to-face negotiations, which the district has denied. The biggest sources of contention are over salary increases and health care contributions; however, both sides have expressed an interest in working out a deal that’s fair for everyone.

headline: null
abstract: Governor Rendell spoke in Centre County today at the annual legislative luncheon.  He announced a an alternative-energy plan to produce celulose ethanol.  This type of ethanol can be produced from scrap wood--which Pennsylvania has an abundance of---and thus will not drive up the cost of groceries like corn-based ethanol.  The plan has bipartisan support.

headline: null
abstract: A student in Philadelphia's Strawberry Mansion section brought a gun to school.  The student made it known to friends that he was carrying a gun, and another student informed a school staff member of the incident.

headline: And new this morning, Sony plans to slash 4% of its global work force all if an effort to save $1 billion a year.
abstract: Sony Corp. and Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell, met today to discuss Sony's closing of a plant in the state due to the company trimming its workforce worldwide.  It employs more than 600 workers.

headline: It's how bomb in s looking at the national budget,
abstract: A conversation on Pennsylvania's budget woes.

headline: GOP vows to fight Rendell's planned 'competency' tests
abstract: Both House and Senate Republicans will battle against PA Governor Ed Rendell in 2009 on the Govenor's proposed high school "competency exams".  Graduation Competency Assessments would cover math, science, English and social studies.  Passing the test would allow high schoolers to receive their diploma.  Rendell's team says it test high schoolers knowledge of core subjects, Republican critics say the exam will cost $40 million and that is too expensive in this recession.

headline: null
abstract: Local newscast including primary season ends tonight, Gov. Rendell and top officials met for about two hours at the Governor's official residence trying to complete a budget trying to avoid the late budget last year, and the Save Our Homes Rally.

headline: Pre-K Counts deserves support
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell has proposed additional funding for the PreK Counts program that provides a quality preschool education to children at risk because of economic or cultural factors. Rendell's proposed budget for 2008-09 would increase funding by $12.6 million to serve an additional 1,000 children across PA. As a provider of PreK Counts classrooms in Erie and Corry, the Barber National Institute has seen the difference that this program is already making in its first year. Our initial evaluation reveals that 100 percent of the children enrolled in our PreK Counts classes have achieved progress toward the competencies and kindergarten readiness expected for their age.

headline: Turnpike lease put on hold
abstract: PA Representative Joe Markosek, chairman of the House Transportation Committee, said he’s putting a permanent hold on a proposal by Representative Dwight Evans to privatize the PA Turnpike. Governor Ed Rendell received a $12.8 billion bid to lease the turnpike for 75 years, but Markosek referred to it as a bad deal. Rendell is hoping to hear from the Federal Highway Administration sometime in September over a proposal to toll Interstate 80, but if it is rejected, over half of the state’s funding for transportation would be gone, and raising the gas tax or motorists fees could be necessary.

headline: Lawmakers urged to tighten mortgage oversight
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Banking is urging the state Legislature to pass several new laws the agency says might have saved customers of Personal Financial Management Inc. from an estimated $40 million loss. Banking Secretary Steve Kaplan said the bills that would make more mortgages subject to state law and require better disclosure.

headline: Governor’s representative reviews projects with Newport Township
abstract: After months of disappointment, Newport Township’s commissioners feel they are making progress after meeting with Michael Lombardo, director of Governor Rendell’s Northeast Regional Office. The commissioners agreed that the South Valley Parkway access road project is the highest priority, and Lombardo will go over all funding options for the township’s proposals. Other issues that were addressed were violations of the township’s pool and weed and grass ordinances, a plan for a memory walk, the hiring of two part-time police officers and new photo identification for township employees.

headline: Teachers, school board resume talks
abstract: Since neither side has formally accepted a fact-finder's recommended teacher labor contract, the Neshaminy school board and the Neshaminy Federation of Teachers will resume negotiations. Meanwhile, the report of state-appointed fact-finder John Skonier was made public. The three-year proposed deal calls for a 3 percent salary increase but no change to the health care package, under which the union does not contribute to its health care premiums. While the administration has rejected the proposal, the teachers have not accepted or rejected it. That counts as a rejection, according to the Pennsylvania Labor Relations Board.

headline: null
abstract: The Lieutenant Governor of PA, Catherine Baker Knoll, is battling cancer.  So far, the results of her treatment are encouraging.

headline: null
abstract: Fox Woods Casino is trying to relocate from its propsed location on the Delaware waterfront to the gallery at Market East.  PA Governor Ed Rendell and Philadelphia Mayor Michael Nutter are planning a press conference today to address the issue.

headline: A midstate Republican is introducing a bill that would create uniform standards for safety reports put together by Pennsylvania's school districts
abstract: Senator Jeff Piccola, a Republican whose district covers parts of Dauphine and York counties, is introducing a bill that sets uniform standards for saftey reports. The report was created by Pennsylvania's school districts. Piccola says his bill was created due to  Auditor General Jack Wagner's criticism of the PA Department of Education's yearly safety assessments.

headline: Pennsylvanians convicted of minor offenses can now have their records expunged
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell signed into law a bill that would expunge minor offenses on an individual's record if s/he has been free of arrests and prosecutions for at least 5 years.

headline: A sorry way to close 2008
abstract: An opinion piece chastises PA Supreme Court Justice, Seamus McCaffery, for being the primary leader in ruling in favor of the public is not entitled to the complete records of public officials' taxpayer-funded cell phones. Presently, telephone records show the telephone numbers blacked out.  Justice McCaffery said, "weak, perhaps non-existent public interest in favor of disclosure of the telephone numbers" as a reason to black the numbers out.
