abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell proposes to allow agencies charge citizens for recovering public documents and and redacting private information. The Office of Open Records set the maximum charge to copy documents at 25 cents.

headline: Threat to school lunch leaves a bad taste
abstract: Since 1990 the USDA has provided schools in Philadelphia with predominantly poor populations with free meals for breakfast and lunch.  Recently the city has been informed that the program is going to be shut down.  Those students in need of the free meals will have to fill out paperwork in order to get the benefits.

headline: Our view: Property tax plan deserves a thorough examination
abstract: Why, almost immediately after a Republican state lawmaker proposed legislation to eliminate school property taxes Monday, other politicians began talking about how the bill doesn't have a chance of becoming law. Paper thinks that probably had more to do with entrenched attitudes than anything in the bill itself. And Rorher, who's been tilting at PA's property tax windmill for years, says he's revised the failed bill and removed its more contentious provisions. Property taxes would be phased out over four years under Rorher's new plan, and the state's personal income tax would increase, from 3.07 to 3.92 percent. The state would begin taxing residential utilities, prescription drugs, and public transportation and advertising, among other currently exempt purchases.

headline: Key groups in sewage dispute make progress over funding
abstract: Groups such as the Pennsylvania Municipal Authorities Association and the Pennsylvania Farm Bureau are proposing the creation of a Pennsylvania Fair Share for Clean Water Plan to provide funds for state and federal mandated upgrades to reduce pollution in the Chesapeake Bay. The state Department of Environmental Resources supports creating a task force to address the issue. The editorial board agrees that a task force should be created, but also believes funding is necessary.

headline: 'Goods for Guns' program still on
abstract: Officials are hoping that armed Philadelphians find it easier to pick up a bag of groceries than a gun. To that end, state Sen. Vincent Hughes, Councilman Curtis Jones and Deputy Mayor Everett Gillison joined radio personality E. Steven Collins, Philadelphia Safety Net's Ray Jones and Solomon Jones of U.S. Rep. Chaka Fattah's office in announcing the continuation of the "Goods for Guns" program, an initiative to get guns off the street by offering vouchers to those who turn in handguns. The program, which started about 18 months ago, has accepted more than 1,900 turned in guns. A citizen who turns in a gun will receive two $50 vouchers to use at Shop-Rite and Forman Mills. Hughes and Curtis said the gun voucher/buyback program has a "no questions asked" policy.

headline: State fields complaints about fuel surcharges
abstract: The state is getting more complaints from consumers who say they are being ripped off by businesses that impose unauthorized fees or surcharges. Attorney General Tom Corbett said Tuesday that any added fee to recoup higher fuel costs must be disclosed to a consumer in advance. The total price of a product or service is a key factor in any purchase and is something that needs to be disclosed to consumers up front. Any business intending to collect an added fee for fuel or energy must disclose those charges when they advertise their prices.

headline: Local lawmakers meet, push PA energy bills
abstract: null

headline: Merger concerns: Fewer services and jobs, more debt
abstract: At the Allegheny League of Municipalities annual conference, some expressed concern that merging Allegheny County with Pittsburgh would erode basic services and diminish the influence of unions and neighborhoods in Allegheny County. Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl and Allegheny County Chief Executive Dan Onorato are asking state lawmakers to draft legislation that would require city and county voters to give separate approvals of the merger.

headline: Pedestrian crosswalk timers being installed along deadly Roosevelt Boulevard
abstract: Approximately 500 crosswalk timers are being placed on Roosevelt Boulevard in an effort to decrease fatalities on the road.  This project is part of a larger federal authorization for the Boulevard secured by U.S. Representative Allyson Schwartz.

headline: Philly Deals: Harrisburg OK needed for AIG asset exchange
abstract: The plan by federal and New York State officials to save American International Group requires the permission of insurance officials in Harrisburg.  For the company to survive, it needs to pull liquidity out of its property and casualty insurance companies--the largest of which is has its legal home in Pennsylvania.  In order for the holding company--AIG--to take liquid assets out of the National Union Fire Insurance Company, it must get permission from the PA Department of Insurance, which will grant AIG permission to liquidate some assets if it meets certain conditions that ensure policy holder security.

headline: State power costs could kill jobs, executive says
abstract: The Public Utilty Commision heard testimony yesterday that Pennsylvania could lose between 34,400 and 64,500 jobs over the next seven years because its electricity market functions in a way that encourages high prices, making it tough to do buisness.

headline: Stout secures $1.2 million for health center work
abstract: Pennsylvania state Senator, J. Barry Stout, of the Senate Appropriations Committee received $1.2 million dollars to upgrade the Washington County Health Center.  A year ago, he was a patient at this health center.

headline: Schools reflect communities
abstract: The city should broaden its efforts to improve the quality of its education beyond the traditional solutions of extending the school day and offering more professional development.  The commentary piece suggests that the district pay for tuition reimbursement like suburban districts afford their teachers.  The district should hold the students and parents more accountable as well.

headline: Pa. budget chief to take job in Philadelphia School District
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell's budget chief said he will leave the administration for a new job overseeing the Philadelphia School District's finances. Budget Secretary Michael Masch said he has accepted an offer to become the district's chief business officer, a newly created post, starting July 1. He has been Rendell's top budget adviser since the governor took office in 2003. His departure comes at a potentially tricky time during the state budget process. A spending plan has never been finalized before the July 1 start of the new fiscal year during Rendell's more than five years in office.

headline: Land transfer in crosshairs
abstract: PA Senator Jake Corman sponsored a bill that would include the transfer of over 1,500 acres of Rockview land to Penn State University and Benner Township. However, opponents have organized a public meeting that is planned to be held before a scheduled meeting by Corman. They hope to garner support to convince Corman and other to have a single owner of all the property, such as a state environmental agency or an environmental organization.

headline: If no immunity, Johnny Doc to take 5th at Gus Dougherty trial
abstract: Gus Dougherty pleaded not guilty last month to making illegal payments to John Dougherty in connection with the sale of a Jersey Shore condo and renovations performed at the union leader's Pennsport home. Defense attorney Eric Sitarchuk said in a court filing yesterday that Hank Hock-eimer, John Dougherty's lawyer, told Sitarchuk that the union leader would take the Fifth if he's not granted immunity. Union leader John Dougherty will take the Fifth Amendment if he is called by the defense to testify at the upcoming federal trial of electrical contractor Donald "Gus" Dougherty Jr., according to court papers.

headline: State given DeNaples FBI file
abstract: Louis DeNaples, facing charges of perjury, gave a copy of his FBI file to the PA Gaming Control Board. DeNaples acquired the file through the US Freedom of Information Act while preparing for licensing hearings before the Board regarding the application for his Mount Airy Casino Resort. A grand jury charged DeNaples with hiding mob ties from the Board and withholding the file. DeNaples denies both, saying the file was not requested until recently. The Board has since barred DeNaples from his casino. A spokesman for the Board confirmed DeNaples never denied a request for the file.

headline: Lots on tap as Pa.'s Legislative session nears end
abstract: Pennsylvania’s legislators will return from recess with a long list of issues to tackle, and many of them will want to boost their images for the upcoming election, yet they will have to overcome the House Democrats’ internal power struggle and hope state Attorney General Tom Corbett’s investigation into legislative corruption doesn’t lead to more charges. The article cites some legislative accomplishments during the current two-year session; however, there isn’t much time allotted for voting, and there is still disagreement  between the House and Senate over bills to provide increased health insurance coverage. A bill backed by Governor Rendell to revise the state’s dog law may have gained new momentum, and bills pertaining to better oversight of slot machine gambling, the Sunshine Law, property tax and leasing the PA Turnpike could become legislative priorities.

headline: Merger summit with lawmakers a success, Onorato says
abstract: Allegheny County Chief Executive Dan Onorato and Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl met with about 20 local lawmakers to include them in discussions about merging the city and county governments. It marked their first sit-down with state lawmakers from Allegheny County since the two leaders announced their support for a city-county merger after a 13-member Citizens Advisory Committee led by University of Pittsburgh Chancellor Mark A. Nordenberg released a study recommending consolidation. They have said a merger would save money by eliminating duplicate services. They also have promised that consolidation would not saddle suburbanites with Pittsburgh's debt and legacy costs, or erode municipal powers.

headline: On Warhol’s 80th birthday, what would he think?
abstract: The Andy Warhol Museum is celebrating the Pittsburgh native's birthday on Saturday.

headline: Let's reopen the discussion on health care redundancies
abstract: Some PA legislators are arguing for a return to the certificate-of-needs process for the state's health care industry.  This process requires health-care facilities to justify expenditures and is designed to prevent unnecessary serices by basing new projects and purchases on community need and not profit.  Some reformers think the certificate-of-needs process should be industry-wide, while others would like to see changes in the state's licensing standards for certain facilities along with a limited certificate-of-needs-process.

headline: States face unemployment cash crisis
abstract: Rising unemployment drains state trust funds, forcing them to borrow from Washington to continue paying claims.

headline: Pennsylvania Senate's GOP leaders to return pay raise
abstract: Senate Republican leaders will return their 2.8 percent cost of living allowance (COLA) pay raise. Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell, along with his cabinet, will pay the raise back as well.

headline: I-81 Corridor Coalition seeks designation
abstract: Officials from six states are looking for Washington to take notice of Interstate 81.  Residents and business owners who use the highway are worried at the projected increase in traffic.  A coalition was formed in order to organize an approach in dealing with the federal government's recognition of the highway.

headline: Pa. budget talks spill over into weekend
abstract: Legislative leaders met several times in closed-door talks as they continued to work toward a state budget with the Rendell administration. The House and Senate have planned rare weekend voting days but almost certainly will miss Monday's constitutional deadline to pass a fiscal blueprint for 2008-09. It will mark the sixth consecutive year that Gov. Rendell has not signed a budget bill by the July 1 start of the fiscal year. With the deadline looming, the goal of negotiators is not necessarily to have a completed budget in place on time but to reach a "gentleman's agreement" soon on the spending framework. That, the sides agree, would avoid the furloughing of 25,000 state workers and the forced closing of a number of government offices and services, as happened last year.

headline: Lawmaker sponsors bill to outlaw pigeon shoots
abstract: PA Representative Daylin Leach is one of the prime sponsors of a bill to outlaw pigeon shoots. A vote on the bill is still pending.

headline: Gun owners to rally in Harrisburg today
abstract: Gun owners, including members of Firearms Owners Against Crime, rallied in Harrisburg to protest gun restrictions being considered in the state legislature. A measure that would require gun owners to report missing or stolen guns within seventy-two hours was shot down in the state House last month. Governor Ed Rendell supports legislation that would limit the number of guns a person could purchase to one a month. Currently one can only use a gun for self-defense if they are inside their home, but gun owners want to expand this to include anywhere outside their home.

headline: State racketeers
abstract: Editors believe the PA Gaming Control Board is "gaming" the system, showing questionable judgment and lack of transparency. It is no wonder why local law enforcement might not be enthusiastic to enforce gambling laws, which seem to have double standards. State government and the well-connected can cash in from this so called "legal" gambling, but not the average joe. He would be charged with racketeering.

headline: Lou Dobbs Tonight-CNN
abstract: Lou Dobbs accuses the Bush administration of being deceitful on the issue of free trade. He blames the federal government for driving jobs overseas. PA Gov. Rendell is a guest on the show.

headline: Move afoot to repeal drink tax
abstract: Allegheny County’s debated 10 percent drink tax will face the County Council’s Republican caucus moves to repeal it and the new car rental tax. County Council members Jan Rea, R-McCandless, Matt Drozd, R-Ross, Vince Gastgeb, R-Bethel Park, and Chuck McCullough, R-Upper St. Clair, are proposing legislation to reopen the 2008 budget and repeal the drink tax and the $2-a-day car rental tax by the end of March. The move to end both levies, which were proposed to pay for the county's $30 million subsidy of the Port Authority, was spurred by the county's receipt last week of a $19.9 million payment from the state

headline: Dam Spared Again
abstract: Before the removal of the low-head Beaty Dam can occur, a permit is needed from the Army Corps of Engineers.  The Corps said a permit will be issued in 30 days and the PA Department of Environmental Protection will begin taking bids to remove the dam upon receipt of the permit.  The dam was supposed to be removed in 2006, but the discovery of an endangered mussel held up the removal.

headline: Students weigh in, ask union, district to strike deal
abstract: On Monday night, Northampton Area students demanded that the teacher's union and the school board work to avoid a strike.  The union has set a deadline for walking out if a new deal cannot be struck.  Both sides met last Wednesday and will meet again this Wednesday to discuss health care premiums, salaries and retirement benefits.

headline: A show of goodwill on Election Day
abstract: Though it seemed all the ingredients were in place for ugly partisan conflicts or flare-ups of basic human impatience, many voters reported that workers, volunteers and citizens of all affiliations embraced Election Day difficulties with a sense of civic pride in Uwchlan.

headline: Gasoline led to 'total kill' in Turtle Creek
abstract: A gas leak from Sunoco Logistics contaminated Turtle Creek for six miles.  The Pennsylvania Department of Enviornmental Protection estimated that 7,500 gallons of gasoline was spilled. Ecologists described the damage to fish as "total kill". The leak did not affect ground or drinking water.

headline: Reading City Council not crazy about tax hikes
abstract: City Council is having trouble coming up with ways to close a gap in the 2009 budget.  Raising taxes and fees have received little support thus far.  City Managing Director Ryan P. Hottenstein warned that services would have to be drastically cut.

headline:
Pa. budget talks spill over into weekend
Monday's deadline is likely to be missed. Negotiators seek a 'gentleman's agreement' that would avoid job furloughs.
abstract: While PA House Minority Leader Sam Smith and Senate Majority Leader Dominic Pileggi believe budget negotiations are going in the right direction, there are still many differences that need to be worked out, and Governor Rendell will almost certainly fail to sign a budget bill by the July 1 constitutional deadline for the sixth straight year. The negotiators aren’t necessarily trying to complete the budget on time, but they are trying to reach some sort of agreement that would prevent the closing of many government offices and services, which happened last year.

headline: Long-burning mine fire in northeast Pa. is finally contained
abstract: Officials say a coal mine fire that has been burning underground for years in Lackawanna County is now contained. A trench that surrounds the Dolph Colliery mine fire in Olyphant was finished a few weeks ago. The trench is intended to isolate the flames and keep them from spreading. Some say, however, it will take 20 to 30 years for the fire to burn itself out. Mining officials say the fire goes down 165 feet in some spots. Olyphant Councilman Jerry Tully is one who would like to see more action to put out the fire. Tully says while the fire is still burning it is keeping people from developing the land. The project has cost $11 million, and Mick Kuhns of the Office of Surface Mining says it would cost many millions more to fully extinguish the fire.

headline: Hearing in Philadelphia to focus on foster care
abstract: A hearing will be held at the request of PA Senator LeAnna Washington to discuss various issues pertaining to foster care, and Philadelphia’s new commissioner of the Department of Human Services, Anne Marie Ambrose, is scheduled to testify.

headline: State slots parlors see a dip in betting
abstract: Pennsylvania’s slots revenue dropped by a little over 1 percent last week. Mount Airy surpassed Mohegan Sun in total wagers for the first time; however Mohegan Sun generated far higher gross terminal wagers, which is considered the most important measure of performance.

headline:
Lt. Gov. Knoll battling cancer
McKees Rocks native says 'outlook is good,' will continue work
abstract: Lieutenant Governor Catherine Baker Knoll is battling cancer, but she has vowed not to miss a session in the state Senate, and she plans on continuing her jobs as chairwoman of the state Board of Pardons, the PA Emergency Management Council and the Local Government Advisory Committee. Knoll has had deep political support from the Democratic Party, especially among seniors and women, and she won her first term as lieutenant governor in 2002. As of now, she is undergoing treatment and expects a full recovery.

headline: New County Council may take another look at homestead exemption
abstract: Newly elected Pittsburgh County Councilman Chuck McCullough submitted three bills for consideration an hour after being sworn into office. The bills include a call for an increase in the county’s homestead exemption by $10,000, to $25,000, were quickly referred to the council's budget and finance committee for study. Nine council members were also sworn in and after being sworn in the members unanimously re-elected Richard Fitzgerald as council president.

headline: Preliminary I-80 toll plan to be presented today
abstract: The PA Turnpike Commission is announces possible toll-collection locations along Interstate 80.  The Commission will hold a press conference at the Capitol today.

headline: Lease turnpike to repair roads
abstract: Now that the Federal highway Administration has rejected Pennsylvania's proposal to establish tolls on Interstate 80, state legislators must realize that leasing the turnpike is a viable long-term solution to the state's infrastructure and transportation budget shortfalls.  The turnpike lease is a viable and better alternative to the I-80 toll plan and lawmakers need to embrace it.

headline: Health-policy expert lauds area’s ‘leverage for change’
abstract: Area providers said they’re motivated to improve Northeast Pennsylvania’s health care delivery system after a noted scholar’s talk and a forum by local health experts Thursday at Lackawanna College.

headline: State to receive $40 million:Audit firm agrees to settlement in insurer case
abstract: Deloitte and Touche had been accused of malpratice that played a part in the bankruptcy of Reliance Insurance Co.. The two will pay Pennsylvania $40 million dollars to settle.

headline: News 8 at 6:00pm
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell signed a bill into law that sets standards for commercial dog kennels.  The alw, Act 119 calls for a 9 member canine health board.

headline: Pa's meaningless budget deadline
abstract: It's good to know the governor and state Legislature have their priorities straight. They spent weeks arguing the merits of a statewide smoking ban; there are no merits to a smoking ban, in our view &; without reaching an agreement. That's valuable time they won't be getting back. Meanwhile, the midnight June 30 deadline for a 2008-2009 state budget looms larger with each passing day. Looking on with particular interest are thousands of state employees who could be sent home without pay at the end of the month if no budget agreement is reached. That's what happened during last year's budget stalemate, although the employees were able to recoup the money they lost for being off a day.

headline: Major change near for hunters
abstract: During the Pennsylvania Game Commission meeting, the board approved a proposal that eliminates the concurrent buck and doe season for five days in wild management units in the northeastern, southwestern, north central and south central regions of the state. The change would be in effect for three to four years so Game Commission staff can study the impact of changed season lengths on hunter success rates. Commissioner Jay Delaney of Wilkes-Barre supported the proposal, saying the agency should occasionally evaluate the deer management program. The measure gives Game Commission staff another possible tool to manage deer populations.

headline: Hearing on Philadelphia's gun-control laws postponed
abstract: Common Pleas Court Judge Jane Cutler Greenspan rescheduled the hearing after a telephone conference this week with lawyers for the city and National Rifle Association. The delay was to give lawyers for the city more time to decide if they will challenge "standing" - the legal right of the NRA to file the suit. City officials hope the lawsuit will convince the state Supreme Court to reexamine its 1996 decision in Ortiz v. Commonwealth, which invalidated a city ordinance regulating assault weapons, with the state's high court ruling that the state legislature in 1994 passed a law that specifically barred municipalities from regulating guns.

headline: State won’t prosecute Personal Financial Management
abstract: State officials will not handle the criminal prosecution in the collapse of Personal Finance Management Inc. that left more than 800 mortgage customers out a collective $40 million. Federal attorneys will be able to handle the prosecution; the US attorney’s office filed one count of mail fraud against company owner Wesley A. Snyder who has pleaded guilty. When the company and its six affiliates filed for bankruptcy liquidation in September, its borrowers discovered they had larger mortgages, at higher rates with monthly payments several hundred dollars more, than the company had promised them.

headline: Lynn Hayes
abstract: According to the announcer, the grassroots support that US Sen. Barack Obama has generated during his campaign create a tremendous campaign to the point where some very strange things would have to go wrong for US Sen. Hillary Clinton to become the Democratic Nominee for President. A lot of Obama supporters were probably very upset by comments made by PA Gov. Rendell. Similar comments were made by James Carville the first time Bob Casey ran for governor.

headline: NewMarket, Fox Chase projects advance in Philly
abstract: City Council unanimously approved, with Majority Leader Marian Tasco and Councilman Bill Green abstaining due to conflicts of interest, a lease with Fairmount Park that will allow the Fox Chase Cancer Center to begin an expansion. The Council also got a look at a proposal to build a 15 story condo tower and hotel in Society Hill. Members of the Society Hill Civic Association however, are split on their support, some noting that zoning laws prohibit any construction higher than six stories. Councilman DiCicco, whose support is critical, has introduced legislation to raise the height limit.

headline: Kanjorski and Barletta will face only each other in November
abstract: Democratic U.S. Representative Paul Kanjorski and Republican candidate Lou Barletta will not face a third-party challenger this election cycle, but Republican state Representative Sandra Major will face a third-party candidate, as she will run against Green-Party candidate Jay Sweeney for the third time.  Only one other third-party candidate is running in a local legislative race, Michael Dincher, an independent.

headline: Region assesses damage
abstract: People throughout the region assess the damage caused by Hurricane Ike's remnants.

headline: Latinos want bigger role in Nutter administration
abstract: While Philadelphia Mayor Nutter has basked in popular approval and widespread political support during his first year in office, some of the Latino popular are unhappy because they feel Latinos are not featured enough in his administartion. However, Nutter refutes these claims with evidence of ranking Latinos in various positions in city government.

headline: Learn about state's new sunshine law
abstract: An editorial explaining Pennsylvania's new Sunshine Law.

headline: Rendell hosting rally for Obama in Scranton
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell will hold a rally for Democratic presidential candidate Sen. Barack Obama in Scranton on Friday.

headline: Plan ahead
abstract: The editorial’s author is critical of the PA Legislature and the governor for their handling of the budget process. In the author’s opinion, elected officials know that they must have a balanced budget by June 30, so they should set aside the month of June for nothing other than budget negotiations. The author believes this is a simple common sense approach, and it would help avoid the politicking and late night budgetary sessions that anger the public.

headline: Mining safety measure advances
abstract: PA state Senator Richard Kausnic recalled the dread that he felt as he prepared to walk into a Somerset County fire hall in July 2002 to talk to the families of the nine miners trapped at the Quecreek Mine. The Senate Environmental Resources and Energy Committee approved legislation this week that would rewrite the state’s mine safety laws for the first time since 1961.Clemmy Allen, a United Mine Workers of America special coordinator, said that the provisions requiring communications systems that would be accessible to miners underground was one of the key features of the bill.

headline: House OKs bill to increase penalty for having gun with altered serial number
abstract: The state House passed a bill that increases the penalty for having a gun with an altered serial number. An amendment that would make it a criminal offense for gun owners to fail to report a lost or stolen gun was voted down. An amendment was passed that allows those who fear for their safety to obtain a three-month license to carry a gun, bypassing the usual waiting period.

headline: Still no expansion in store for Whole Foods after 6 years
abstract: Almost six years ago, the Whole Foods Market that opened in East Liberty had Pittsburghers marveling that the natural and organic nirvana had arrived in the Steel City. Many parking lot headaches, mid-aisle tie-ups and a few flying elbows later, some are wondering why shoppers' loyalty hasn't been rewarded with a bigger and better store. Officials of the grocery chain repeatedly have expressed interest in putting a second store here. They announced a South Hills location, but that plan fell through. They've discussed building a larger store in East Liberty, but nothing has come of that. They've discussed remodeling the existing location, but it remains pretty much the same.

headline: Mail it in: Proposal to make it easier to cast absentee ballots is worth pursuing
abstract: Imagine being able to vote from the comfort of your home. Voters in Oregon already can do that, and the House State Government Committee is looking into Pennsylvania residents being able to do the same. The Associated Press reported Chairwoman Babette Josephs said she hopes to amend the state constitution to allow Pennsylvanians to vote by absentee ballot without having to state an acceptable reason. Josephs doesn’t want to stop there. She said it could be the first step toward moving Pennsylvania to an all-mail voting system.

headline: Next U.S. census could show more poverty in Phila. Area
abstract: According to U.S. Census Bureau data, Americans enjoyed a slight increase in income last year, and the nation’s poverty rate remained about the same at 12.5 percent; however, this year, the numbers are expected to be substantially worse. Camden, where 38.2 percent of the population lived in poverty in 2007, has been especially hard hit this year, and in PA, the wealth gap between the state’s poorest and richest populations is expected to continue to grow substantially. Last year, Philadelphia was the nation’s ninth-poorest big city, and the director of Philadelphia’s Coalition Against Hunger anticipates the poverty rates to worsen this year.

headline: null
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell is appearing at Bucknell University as part of a five-day, 16-stop bus tour to announce public and private investments in local communities throughout PA.

headline: null
abstract: Lieutenant Governor Katerine Baker Knoll plans to preside over the state Senate when it returns today.  Knoll is undergoing radiation and chemotherapy treatments and is suffering from neuroendocrine cancer.

headline: City Council OKs increased fine for open container violations
abstract: Pittsburgh City Council yesterday approved quadrupling the fine for open container law violations, meaning that anyone nabbed drinking alcohol in the streets could be hit with a $200 fine.

headline: College dream eroding
abstract: The National Center for Public Policy and Higher Education submitted a report on the accessability of higher education across the United States. Pennsylvania, along with 49 other states, received a grade of "F" for affordability.  California received a "C".

headline: Ensure neighbors braced for winter
abstract: This editorial encourages people to prepare themselves and neighbors for the coming winter.  Energy assistance for the poor has been increased for this season.

headline: Q&A ABOUT THE BUDGET
abstract: Question and answer segment about the 2008 budget negotiations including dooms day scenarios if it is not passed by the July 1 deadline.

headline: Mounting Costs Slow the Push for Clean Coal
abstract: For years, scientists have had a straightforward idea for taming global warming. They want to take the carbon dioxide that spews from coal-burning power plants and pump it back into the ground. President Bush is for it, and indeed has spent years talking up the virtues of clean coal. All three candidates to succeed him favor the approach. So do many other members of Congress. Coal companies are for it. Many environmentalists favor it. Utility executives are practically begging for the technology. But it has become clear in recent months that the nation’s effort to develop the technique is lagging badly.

headline: House takes up bills aimed at Pa. prison overcrowding
abstract: Under legislation addressed by the PA House yesterday, some prisoners would qualify for early release, releasing some of the burden of overcrowding for the state's Department of Corrections. The bill includes alternatives, such as treating seriously or terminally ill prisoners at hospices or hospitals. The House has yet to vote. The recidivism program would exclude those convicted of trafficking large quantities of drugs. Rep. Kathy Manderino is a sponsor of one of the bills. PA Attorney General Tom Corbett expressed concern over some of the legislation, writing to Judiciary Chairman Tom Caltagirone.

headline: Support no more: Grants target small games
abstract: The Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board gave money to several county police departments grants to eliminate illegal slot machines in bars. The legislature legalized gambling in casinos, but in spite of lobbying by the Pennsylvania Taverns Association, a bill to legalize gambling in bars failed.

headline: Mayor Nutter's watershed moments
abstract: According to the author, Mayor Nutter’s outburst last week over the role the Department of Human Services workers played in the 2006 starvation death of a 14-year-old girl wasn’t the only time he’s gotten teary or visibly angry. While he has developed a reputation for being cool and levelheaded, the author cites some other incidents that suggest that maybe Nutter isn’t as unflappable as his reputation suggests.

headline: No residency test for city job seekers
abstract: In spite of opposition from union leaders, a bill passed in Philadelphia City Council that would end the one-year residency requirement for city jobs. Now a person must only live in Philadelphia for six months before starting work. The bill was introduced by Councilman James F. Kenney and backed by Mayor Nutter. Councilman Bill Green also introduced legislation that would eliminate Philadelphia's funding of its courts.

headline: null
abstract: House Republicans are leading a protest against Democratic leaders, whom they want to bring up to vote on an energy bill.

headline: Rendell wants health insurance reform passed
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell says that helping uninsured Pennsylvanians get health insurance is a top priority.  He would like the General Assembly to approve a plan that would provide coverage for approximately 273,000 uninsured PA residents, but support for such a proposal is lukewarm in the state Senate--making the passage of such a bill unlikely this year.

headline: Gas prices higher in Berks than some other areas
abstract: Berk county residents have noticed a trend that many communities see nationally, there gas prices are higher than most of their neighboring counties.

headline: Lehigh Valley area unemployment inches up to 6 percent, according to most recent date from Pennsylvania Department of Labor & Industry
abstract: According to a Pennsylvania Department of Labor & Industry report, Lehigh Valley-area unemployment increased to 6 percent in October. This means 7,000 more people or 38 percent are out of work in the area. That is one-third higher than the 4.5 percent report a year ago.

headline: Fumo girlfriend stands by his side
abstract: Carolyn Zinni, Vince Fumo's girlfriend is discussed in an overview of her life and how it was affected by the federal corruption charges levied against Fumo.

headline: Regional economy shows improvement
abstract: The economy in the Federal Reserve’s Fourth District, which includes Western PA, Ohio, and parts of Kentucky and West Virginia, improved slightly in the early summer; though the housing industry remains weak, and the rising cost for food and gasoline is taking its toll. Nearly all the districts reported sluggish or slowing overall consumer spending, but the 4th District fared better. Regional output by factories and employment levels remained stable in the region, which was better than many other districts.

headline: No Text
abstract: Former Vice President and presidential candidate Al Gore, who has won an Oscar and the Nobel Peace Prize, appeared on "Meet the Press" to discuss his recent call to solve the issues of global warming and the energy crisis by producing all of America’s  energy through renewable energy sources within ten years, including wind, solar, and geothermal power. While some have criticized his goal as unattainable, Gore said he believes it can and must be achieved because many leading scientists are saying the current rate of burning fossil fuels is unsustainable, and if dramatic changes aren’t made soon, there could be catastrophic environmental consequences. On the 2008 presidential campaign trail, Barack Obama will travel to Afghanistan and Iraq, and John McCain will launch his first negative television campaigning.

headline: Illegal immigration, drug trafficking on rise along I-80
abstract: Motorists traveling Interstate 80 would likely be stunned if they knew how much criminal activity was riding along the highway with them. In 2007, Rockview state police arrested 109 illegal immigrants on I-80 in Centre County. Illegal immigrants and drug runners with fistfuls of cash and packages of narcotics travel the highway, police say. And state police troopers based at Rockview are doing something about it. Armed with training through a fairly new patrol initiative, Safe Highway Initiative Through Effective Law Enforcement Detection, state police at Rockview already have set a number of records for arrests and the number of illegal immigrants taken into custody on I-80.

headline: Table games bill still faces opposition from Senate, Rendell
abstract: The debate on gambling in PA shifted, if only briefly, to craps, poker and blackjack, instead of whether the Legislature set up a flawed regulatory mechanism to vet who should win a slot-machine casino license. The Democratic-led House Gaming Oversight Committee took the first step on a bill to legalize table games at the state’s licensed slots casinos, holding a hearing on it despite heavy opposition in the Senate to expanding the state’s gambling platter. The hearing featured testimony by casino executives and racing industry officials, who said that legalizing table games would boost the revenue from slots gambling, benefiting taxpayers, the equine industry and more.

headline: Mayor of Clarion throws hat in ring
abstract: Clarion Mayor John R. Stroup is the entering the race for the 5th Congressional seat. Stoup referred to the fight against Interstate 80 tolls as one of the primary issues facing the area.

headline: no text
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell is touring PA as part of a five day bus tour to highlight the economic impact of this year’s state budget on local communities. People in Somerset took the chance to say thanks for additional funding that will allow for the completion of Route 219, and overall, $28 million has been set aside for work on 21 bridges in Somerset and Northumberland Counties. In addition, Blair County’s United Way named a new leader.

headline: null
abstract: Governor Rendell announced the distribution of state money to help with business development and bridge repair in counties throughout the state.  Both are expected to help with job creation.

headline: Arm and Hammer breaks new ground on plant
abstract: State and local officials broke ground on Tuesday at the 1.1 million square foot Arm and Hammer manufacturing plant and distribution center planned for Jackson Township.  Construction of the site will be completed by the end of 2009, and the company will begin hiring workers next year.

headline: null
abstract: Discusses Attorney General Tom Corbett's second term agenda, Philadelphia budget problems, and a tribute to US Senator Arlen Specter at the Constitution Center.

headline: Docs blast delays in the mails
abstract: The Postal Service's missing and delayed mail issues are causing major problems for testing labs in the medical diagnosis of some patients. When trying to identifyi a disease, time is critical.

headline: The row offices: Corbett, Wagner & Ellis
abstract: The Pittsburgh Tribune Review endorses Tom Corbett for attorney general, Jack Wagner for auditor general and Tom Ellis for state treasurer.

headline: Rendell Optimistic on Pennsylvania Budget
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell says he's optimistic the state can avoid another long drawn-out budget battle. Rendell met with legislative leaders to work on the new budget that is supposed to be in place by the end of this month.  He thanked them for their spirit of compromise. Rendell hopes to avoid the budget delay that led to a one-day furlough of more than twenty thousand state workers last year.

headline: no text
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell is making a 5 day, 16-stop bus tour to announce public and private investments in communities, and he is expected to be at Bucknell University. Republicans in the U.S. House are leading a protest against democratic leaders, and they want an energy bill to be voted on. In sports, Brett Favre won’t be allowed to practice with the Green Bay Packers.

headline: Inside the capitol
abstract: Sheriffs and deputy sheriffs from around the state came to the capitol to call for passage of a bill that would grant power to sheriff's departments to investigate crimes and make arrests. H. 466 is intended by PA Rep. Craig Dally to make sheriffs full partners against crime. The PA State Troopers Association opposes the bill, saying sheriffs duties should be expanded merely to serve as better security in courthouses. House Republicans also revealed legislation to help combat illegal drugs. PA Faith United Against Tobacco will hold a rally in the Capitol to call for a smoking ban.

headline: The hotel debate: Canards & consequences
abstract: Pittsburgh tourism officials say the city is not making the cut list for conventions because it's new David L. Lawrence Convention Center does not have a hotel attached. Editors do not believe forcing private hotel rooms to compete with government (taxpayer)-funded rooms. Revived talk of a publicly subsidized hotel will force private developers to think twice, editors believe.

headline: Mayor seeks audit of housing authority
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl asked city Controller Michael Lamb to review spending by the Pittsburgh Housing Authority. Lamb agreed and will conduct an audit with authority Executive Director A. Fulton Meachem Jr. Former authority chairman Patrick Ford is on paid leave from the Urban Redevelopment Authority over gifts he received from a billboard advertising executive. He claimed he was forced to resign after he questioned authority expenses.

headline: No Text
abstract: Pennsylvania’s county commissioners had agreed to make district attorney positions full-time based on an agreement that the state would help pay for the costs; however, the state reneged on the deal, so county commissioners from across the state are travelling to Harrisburg to lobby to make them pay. In other news, a job fair drew hundreds of people in Blair County today, Marine Sergeant Michael Strank, who helped raise the U.S. flag at Iwo Jima, was posthumously awarded his certificate of citizenship, and a clean coal power plant might be moving into Somerset County.

headline: Ebensburg makeover gets $1M boost
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell visited the county seat of Ebensburg to announce a 1 million dollar capital project that will bolster the downtown makeover already in progress.  Governor Rendell is on a five-day tour to announce new capital projects.

headline: Lawmaker wants House to adopt priority-bill rule
abstract: State Representative David Steil has introduced legislation that would give rank-and-file members of the PA General Assembly the ability to designate two priority bills per year, guaranteeing that they will receive a vote.  Under the plan, a priority bill will be considered at the committee level within four months, and if it is passed, it will be guaranteed a vote by the full house within 30 session days.

headline: null
abstract: Discusses Attroney General Tom Corbett's second term agenda, which will include the Bonusgate Scandal.

headline: Pitt's top leaders agree with pay freeze
abstract: University of Pittsburgh Chancellor Mark Nordenberg and his leadership team have agreed to pay freezes due to the recession. They usually would have received their raises under normal circumstances.

headline: Gaming board has opportunity to correct affected communities
abstract: Lebanon County's East Hanover Twp. is trying to convince the state gaming board to give it its share of funds from casino revenue.  Currently they receive no share of the revenue disbursed to surrounding communities.  East Hanover Twp. is host to a small portion of the grounds of Penn National Turf Club.  The township could receive up to $350,000 a year.

headline: Rendell Says Pennsylvania Added More Jobs in May
abstract: Gov. Rendell said recently that Pennsylvania’s job count rose by 2,900 in May, while the statewide unemployment rate went up just two tenths of a percent to 5.2 percent. The 2,900 new jobs reported in May marks PA's second consecutive monthly gain and our unemployment rate remains below the national rate of 5.5 percent. "With two consecutive months of net job gains, Pennsylvania is faring better than much of the nation," he said. However, Pennsylvania’s future is in the balance as we fight against the faltering national economy while families and businesses struggle to deal with the sharply rising cost of fuel and energy.

headline: No Text
abstract: Pennsylvania’s Clean and Green law gives tax discounts to landowners who only use their land for farming or keep it untouched as a forest reserve, but some of these owners have been signing contracts with energy companies to allow them to extract natural gas from their land. State Representative Dan Moul believes many people will believe that’s unfair, and a revision of the law is being considered.

headline: Lawmakers seek to boost volunteer firefighting
abstract: In PA, the number of volunteer firefighters has fallen over 50 percent over the last two decades, and as part of this year’s budget agreement, Governor Ed Rendell signed a law that will provide a $100 tax credit for volunteers. Several legislators have been pushing a package of four bills to provide incentives to help firefighting recruitment efforts, and state Senator Andrew Dinniman’s proposal would offer a $400 annual local earned-income tax credit to active members of volunteer fire and emergency medical services organizations. The package of bills has been approved by the state Senate, and it awaits action in the House, where state Representative Marguerite Quinn has also been working to increase interest in the incentives package.

headline: Wine kiosks could help make buying process more convenient
abstract: The Pennsylvania Liquor Control Board is looking for a company to provide wine kiosks, where customers could purchase wine from a vending machine. Mothers Against Drunk Driving does not support this, as they think it will make it easier for underage persons to purchase alcohol.

headline: McCain tours Pa.:The Ridge factor
abstract: Republican presidential candidate John McCain will conclude a two-day bus tour of PA today, and former Governor Tom Ridge is said to be on McCain’s list of potential running mates. According to the authors, Ridge’s pro-choice stance on abortion would conflict with McCain’s position, but a McCain-Ridge ticket could attract moderate voters from both parties. They are concerned about Ridge’s opposition to some national missile defense programs in the past, though they think he’s changed his stance, and they believe Pennsylvania’s importance in the upcoming election against Barack Obama could make Ridge the perfect choice for McCain.

headline: Nutter names Human Relations Commission chief
abstract: Mayor Nutter announced that lawyer Rue Landau would serve as the next executive director of the Philadelphia Commission on Human Relations, the agency that mediates community disputes and enforces civil-rights laws. For the last 10 years, Landau has been a senior attorney in the housing unit at Community Legal Services, representing low-income tenants facing eviction. She is a former co chair of the Liberty City Democratic Club, an influential political group promoting lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender causes in the city's Democratic Party. Landau and Nutter said they wanted to "revitalize" the commission, which has had a low profile.

headline: White: DeWeese leadership violated trust
abstract: PA state Representative Jesse White has called for House Majority Leader Bill DeWeese to resign his post.  He believes the bonusgate scandal and DeWeese's violation of the public trust could hurt the Democratic Party and its legislative agenda in the fall.

headline: It's time to mend the holes
abstract: In honor of Constitution Day, this article reflects on Pennsylvania's Constitution and argues that the document has been badly sullied by self-serving politicians who use shaky legal interpretations to undermine continuously representative democracy.  The document has been so perverted that the only way to move forward is to start fresh; citizens of PA need to hold a constitutional convention and update the state's founding document so that it does not contain loopholes and guarantees fair representation.

headline: Diversity good, but fairness vital to new judge
abstract: Joseph K. Williams III, 56, of Penn Hills will be sworn in today, taking a seat on the bench of the Allegheny County Court of Common Pleas. He will become the only black judge in the criminal division and one of only three black judges on the county's 43-member bench

headline: Turnpike tolls to increase 25 percent next month
abstract: The Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission will increase tolls 25 percent in January. The Commission needs to generate $1 billion annually for the fiscal year in 2010-11, or it would fall short of transportation needs and $500 million dollars.

headline: PhillyDeals: Stock market optimism lifts its timid head
abstract: Michael P. Ryan, head of research at UBS Financial Services Inc., of New York commented on the state of the economy as major stock market benchmarks jumped 10 percent.  He says that while the market is recovering it still may not have hit bottom.  Fidelity Investments may lay off 4,000 as a result of the weak investing climate.  Vitae Pharmaceuticals Inc. has acquired funding to work on two new drugs.  They were charged just over 10 percent interest.

headline: Showdown may delay budget again
abstract: Legislators return to the Capitol today with the prospect of a showdown over how the state should spend about $28 billion in the coming year. So far in Gov. Ed Rendell's five-plus years as governor, no budget has been completed before the July 1 start of the fiscal year. And with a one-vote Democratic majority in the House, the budget could become an election-year issue should negotiations stretch again into July. Last year's budget negotiations spilled into mid-July, wrapping up only after a one-day furlough of more than 20,000 state employees and a private meeting between the Democratic governor and Dominic Pileggi, the Senate's Republican majority leader.

headline: no text
abstract: Planes spayed pesticide over the area to try to kill mosquitoes that tested positive for the West Nile virus. According to the U.S Environmental Protection Agency, there are no adverse health effects from the pesticide. However, pregnant women, children and pets were still encouraged to stay indoors during the spaying as a precaution.

headline: Jill Porter: A plan that's just in time
abstract: Police commissioner Charles Ramsey issued his new crime strategy yesterday, which is intended to reduce violence and restore the luster of a police department mired in controversy. Commissioner Ramsey's new strategy is refreshingly simple, it relies on fundamentals and sensible solutions: put more officers on patrol, focus them where they're needed in high-crime areas, hold commanders accountable.

headline: Wine-selling vending machines would be more trouble than they're worth
abstract: The PA Liquor Control Board, which limits the sale of wine to 621 state-controlled stores, now proposes also to sell wine from as many as 100 kiosks in designated supermarkets. Selling wine from a state-run, video-monitored, security-enhanced refrigerator not only disparages wine, it increases the chances of alcohol abuse. The PLCB call for proposals attracted six kiosk companies to a meeting last month where officials answered manufacturers' questions and made known their own concerns -- among them: how to keep minors from using these kiosks and how to prevent someone with more than a .05 blood alcohol level from buying more Ripple.

headline: McCain will be in Lehigh Valley today -- but where?
abstract: U.S. Senator John McCain will visit the Lehigh Valley for the third time since winning the Republican Party’s presidential nomination, which could be a common destination for McCain if he believes he has a legitimate chance of winning PA in the upcoming election.  He is scheduled to attend a Wilkes-Barre town hall meeting, but his campaign has yet to reveal where else he will go during his visit. U.S. Senator Barack Obama, the Democratic presidential candidate, hasn’t returned to the region since the state’s primary election, when Hillary Clinton did substantially better than him in Lehigh and Northampton counties.

headline: On Day One, drink tax still not potable to many
abstract: Alleghany County’s ten percent tax on alcoholic drinks took effect and is being complained about by many of the citizens in the county. County politicians established the drink tax, plus a $2-a-day tax on car rentals, to create a regular stream of money to help pay for mass transit. They hope the drink tax will generate most of the $30 million the county spends annually to subsidize buses and the light-rail system.

headline: Lawmakers are cool to the idea of city-county merger at this point
abstract: Local lawmakers feel there are a lot of steps to be taken before a city-county merger of Pittsburgh and Allegheny county takes place.  This will make it difficult for Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl and county Chief Executive Dan Onorato to get a voter referendum regarding the merger of the city into the county on the November 2009 ballot.

headline: Feeling city's budget pain
abstract: Although Philadelphia City Council approved Mayor Nutter's first budget, the city now faces a 34 million dollar deficit and the gloomy prospect of budget cuts.  Due to the budget shortfall, the mayor will have to slow tax cuts, end some programs and possibly lay off city employees.  Some of the shortfall could also be addressed by revising the business privilege tax.

headline: Rejection of pay regulation slows down lobbyist law implementation
abstract: The Independent Regulatory Review Commission this week rejected a regulation saying lobbyists must file reports once they are paid for services continuing a decade-long odyssey to put an effective lobbying disclosure law on the books continues in Pennsylvania.

headline: Senate Republicans are now joining Democrats in paying back a cost-of-living raise they received this month.
abstract: Senate Republicans will pay back the 2.8 percent cost of living allowances (COLA) pay raises.

headline: New city ordinance combats trash from apartments
abstract: Pittsburgh City Council voted 8-1 to approve an ordinance to crack down on poorly kept rental properties.  Council raised a fine from $15 to $50 that punishes landlords that don't force tenants to bring their trash to the curb where it is easier for city trash collectors to get.  The legislation would ensure that tenants are made explicitly aware of the regulations involving municipal trash pickup.  If signed by the mayor, it would take effect Dec. 1.

headline: State budget agreement reached at deadline
abstract: PA legislators and Governor Ed Rendell agreed to a $28.2 billion budget, a 3.8 percent increase from last year, which will allocate large amounts of money to public schools, alternative energy projects, bridges, dams and water and sewer facilities. Although many details are still missing or vague, Senate Majority Leader Dominic Pileggi and others are pleased to have gotten it done before the deadline because it will prevent a partial government shutdown, which happened last year. The increase in spending left a $550 million revenue gap, but negotiators were able to avoid using the state’s "rainy day" fund by using unspent money from other programs, and $2.5 billion will be borrowed for various projects over the next few years.

headline: no text
abstract: The PA Department of Environmental Protection is launching aerial spraying over parts of suburban Philadelphia to stop the West Nile virus, and some people are concerned about the safety risks from the chemicals being sprayed. The article provides information about the symptoms of the virus, which is transmitted to humans by mosquitoes, and it offers several suggestions for how people can protect themselves from the virus on their own. There has only been one severe case of the virus in PA, but state officials are concerned about the large number of mosquitoes in the area that have been found to contain the virus.

headline: Johnson rips DN, defends himself & cop shooting
abstract: Philadelphia Police Commissioner, Sylvester Johnson, discussed in the final days of his tenure the crime statistics for the city in 2007. Violent crime, which includes homicide, rape, robbery and aggravated assault, declined 8 percent citywide in 2007 from the year before, shootings dropped 13.4 percent and homicides fell from 406 to 392.

headline: 3rd Circuit: Army not liable in recruit shooting
abstract: An insurance company sued the Army because one of its recruits used a pistol he obtained as a result of service to shoot a man while robbing him in a parking garage in Pittsburgh. However, a federal appeals court ruled the Army isn’t liable for over $1 million in medical bills for the man who was shot and paralyzed.

headline:
McCain works to win over Pennsylvania's leery conservatives
He gives assurances he's with them on picking judges, other issues.
abstract: In two months of campaigning in PA, Republican presidential candidate John McCain has focused on his appeal to independent voters in suburban Philadelphia counties, but during a two-day tour through the traditionally pro-Republican areas of York and Lancaster, he tried to address concerns from conservatives about his candidacy. At an event in York, McCain was joined by former Governor Tom Ridge and U.S. Senators Arlen Specter of PA and Joseph Lieberman of Connecticut. McCain has travelled to PA to campaign far more often than his Democratic rival, Barack Obama, who has relied heavily on his huge advantages in campaign offices throughout the state to launch more of a grassroots campaign.

headline: Opinion allows council to pay fee to lawyer
abstract: Pittsburgh Council President Doug Shields plans to push for city payment of a legal bill that sparked a bitter feud between the city's legislators and the mayor's office. At issue is a $10,706 bill submitted by attorney Hugh McGough for work on behalf of Mr. Shields and his colleagues William Peduto, Bruce Kraus and Ricky Burgess, who challenged a permit granted to Lamar Advertising for a Downtown billboard. The permit was revoked, and Lamar is now seeking a new one. Last month, the four council members sought to have the city pay the bill. The Law Department wrote an opinion saying that the invoice was a personal debt of the four members, since council never voted to hire Mr. McGough.

headline: Bridge repairs forced to span growing funding gaps
abstract: Due to price increases in structural steel and fuel, as well as state revenue shortfalls on things such as the liquid fuels tax, state officials worry that the 800 million allocated to repair Pennsylvania's 6,000 structurally-deficient bridges will not go nearly as far as planned.

headline: Officials tout local project
abstract: Several Allegheny County officials were on hand to break ground for a mixed-use brownfiled redevelopment project in South Fayette Township.  Allegheny County has been aggressive in its efforts to reclaim old industrial sites, and this reclaimation will not only be good for the environment, but will also create 2,000 new jobs and increase commercial activity in one of the fastest growing municipalities in Pennsylvania.

headline: State project predicts Luzerne County’s population will drop 9.8 percent by 2030
abstract: Despite a projected statewide population increase, Schuylkill and Luzerne counties are expected to lose thousands of people through 2030, according to Pennsylvania State Data Center estimates released last week. Meanwhile, Carbon, Monroe and other counties of the Poconos will continue to experience a dramatic population surge, according to the center.

headline: Governor Ed Rendell announced he's withholding raises of about two percent for thousands of non-union state workers…"
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell will not authorize 2 percent raises for non-union state workers to save $14.3 million dollars for an already strapped budget.

headline: County budget has unexpected holes
abstract: Some County Council members wondered what happened to the funding of a number of high profile projects in the 2009 budget.  The projects include a juvenile detention center expansion, a new county parking garage, archives building and prison rehabilitation center.  These projects should be included in the long-range capital budget.

headline: State plans for the best as receipts fall
abstract: For nearly all major tax categories, except the inheritance tax, revenue projections were down, yet Governor Rendell and state legislators are debating a budget proposal that includes an optimistic 4 percent increase in spending. The author gives them credit so far for managing a surplus, especially compared to many other states; however, he is concerned about increasing spending so much when the state of the economy remains uncertain, and he thinks it may be more wise to plan for the worst and hope for the best when passing the budget. A Harley-Davidson plant in York County is laying off many of its workers, and the author argues that if the economy gets worse and the state finds it needs more money in the future to pay for all these increases in spending, levying more taxes will be bad news for Pennsylvanians that will already be struggling financially.

headline: Officials concerned about gas drilling
abstract: Technological advances in horizontal natural gas drilling have led to drastic increases in drilling, but a practice known as "fracing" has drawn concern because it requires a large amount of water, and it uses chemicals to extract natural gas from underground, which could potentially contaminate groundwater. Because of efforts to use alternative energy sources nationwide, gas drilling companies are exempt from federal standards set by the Environmental Protection Agency; however representatives from the Delaware River Basin Commission are working to develop new regulations over the use of the Delaware River’s water. Governor Rendell’s representative at the commission said PA has already sent letters advising wastewater treatment plants to not automatically accept drilling water, and other environmental groups and agencies are pushing for restrictions on gas drilling.

headline: Jurors in Wecht case won't be anonymous
abstract: The names of the jurors who will decide the criminal case of former Allegheny County Coroner Dr. Cyril H. Wecht will not be kept secret. That was the ruling of the 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals in a challenge by local news organizations.

headline: Honoring history of sacrifice
abstract: To a stately drum cadence and the wail of bagpipes, the procession arrived at the cemetery. The 144th Memorial Day service at Boalsburg had begun. As flags fluttered steadily in the wind, dozens of Civil War re-enactors, Troop 380 Boy Scouts and community residents made the traditional walk from the Village Diamond to the burial grounds beside the Zion Lutheran Church. In front was a Marine Corps League color guard, leading the annual homage to Boalsburg’s heritage.

headline: McCord gets Democratic nod for state treasurer
abstract: Robert McFord won the Democratic nomination for state Treasurer. He defeated Bucks County Democratic Chairman John Cordisco, state Rep. Jennifer Mann of Allentown, and Dennis Morrison-Wesley. The winner of the general election will replace acting Treasurer Robin Wiessman, who Governor Ed Rendell chose to replace Bob Casey when he became a U.S. Senator. U.S. Senator Hillary Clinton won more delegates in Pennsylvania than her opponent U.S. Senator Barack Obama in the race for the Democratic presidential nomination.

headline: Opponents of drink tax form PAC, plan to target county councilwoman
abstract: Restaurateurs and bar owners in Allegheny County have formed a political action committee called the Hospitality Political Action Committee of Western Pennsylvania to fight against the 10% drink tax imposed on the area. They are campaigning against former county councilwoman Brenda Frazier, a supporter of the drink tax, who is running to be the Democratic nominee for the 21st state House district. The Pennsylvania Liquor Control Board reported that alcohol sales have gone down in Allegheny County since the tax was imposed.

headline: Bridge maintenance main focus for new manager at PennDOT
abstract: Tim Cook has been the maintenance manager for District 12 of the PA Department of Transportation for 4 months.  Cook notes that budget shortfalls, largely the result of increased fuel costs, are going to impact how many miles of roadway PennDOT can maintain.  His department is shifting its focus from reparing damage to preventive maintenance, with speacial attention to bridge maintenance.

headline: Doctors urge legislators to bring back program to reduce malpractice costs
abstract: Since April, Pennsylvania doctors have been without state subsidized malpractice insurance abatements and have been forced to shoulder the larger insurance burden without state assistance.  As a result, doctors urged legislators to renew funding for the state's malpractice insurance abatement program--Mcare--and argued that the non-renewal of the program would reduce access to healthcare and make it difficult to recruit new doctors to Pennsylvania.

headline: Road-salt concerns melt for several municipalities
abstract: The state is urging counties to join a bulk salt purchasing program so they can mitigate the rising costs of salt and be prepared for the winter season.

headline: Who use the Pennsylvania Turnpike will also feel the pinch.
abstract: The Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission will increase tolls 25 percent in January.

headline: Action News 24
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell campaigns for US presidential candidate Barack Obama.  He warns Obama supporters to ignore polls that show Obama with a large lead in an effort to encourage them to show up at the polls.

headline: State plans for the best as receipts fall
abstract: PA's state government should weather the economic downturn, as long as people keep dying. Last week, staff writer Sharon Smith reported that tax receipts in May were off projections in all major categories, except the inheritance tax. Nevertheless, Gov. Ed Rendell and the legislators continued debating an optimistic budget. Rendell's proposal includes a 4 percent increase in spending. His spokesman pointed out that Rendell is confident May is a blip. One month doesn't make a trend. Unfortunately, if you wait three or four months to see a trend, that will be well into the new fiscal year. At that point, pain might have to be spread far.

headline: Pa. 2008-09 hunting licenses go on sale Monday
abstract: PA hunting licenses for the 2008-09 seasons are going on sale. Starting at 10 a.m. Monday, resident and nonresident hunting and fur taker licenses can be purchased at The Outdoor Shop on the Pennsylvania Game Commission Web site. Licenses also are available over-the-counter at all Game Commission region offices and at the Harrisburg headquarters. Hunting and fur taker licenses also will be available from nearly 850 issuing agents around the state beginning later in June. Applicants must provide their Social Security number, a requirement mandated by Congress and state General Assembly to better enforce changes to federal and state welfare reform and child support requirements. Fees have remained unchanged since the 1999-2000 license year.

headline: Lawyer gets nom for bench
abstract: Cheltenham lawyer Andrew B. Cantor could become Montgomery County's newest judge. Gov. Ed Rendell nominated Cantor, a partner in the Blue Bell law firm of Wisler, Pearlstine, Talone, Craig, Garrity and Potash, to a vacancy created last year as a result of the death of the late Judge Toby Dickman. "Andy Cantor is a fine lawyer with a great number of years of experience and we would be thrilled to have him," said county President Judge Richard J. Hodgson, whose 21-member bench has been short-handed since Dickman's death last October. The bench will be short another judge at the end of the year when Judge William T. Nicholas steps down because he reached the mandatory retirement age of 70 this year.

headline: Mental health study focuses on Southwestern Pennsylvania troops
abstract: Researchers at Washington & Jefferson College are embarking on a three-year project to determine the behavioral health needs of troops returning from war to their rural homes. But to do that, they need to hear from National Guard and Reserve personnel and their families. Lauffer is coordinating the Washington County college's Combat Stress Intervention Program, a research project funded by the U.S. Department of Defense. The researchers are inviting family members or the significant others of National Guard or Reserve personnel who served in Operation Iraqi Freedom or Operation Enduring Freedom to share their opinions at four focus group sessions in Cambria and Fayette counties.

headline: Michelle Obama received warmly at Haverford
abstract: Michelle Obama, wife of candidate for the Democratic presidential nominee Senator Barack Obama, spoke at Haverford College, and disputed the notion that Senator Barack Obama is an elitist.

headline:
Pa.'s reverse tax-appeal tangle
$1 billion at stake for school districts over next decade.
abstract: Some school districts in PA have filed appeals over what they consider to be an underassessment of properties, which can lead to property owners paying thousands of dollars more a year in property taxes and could generate over a billion dollars in tax revenue in the next decade. The state Legislature tried to pass a law banning these types of appeals, but Governor Ed Rendell vetoed it, claiming the Legislature needs to develop a long term solution to Pennsylvania’s flawed assessment system. Some school districts believe these appeals help keep property taxes down by ensuring everyone pays their fair share, whereas critics claim they are a violation of the state constitution; however, both sides agree that Pennsylvania’s property assessment system, which allows counties to avoid reassessments for decades, needs to be changed.

headline: Districts to gain tutoring funds
abstract: 163 school districts statewide will receive funding for tutoring through PA's Education Assistance Program.  The program is designed to provide extra instruction for students who are not testing at grade level on state assessments.

headline: Student protest off the mark
abstract: The chancellor of Pennsylvania's state-owned universities recently declared all state universities non-smoking--including the outdoor areas of the campuses.  This ban prompted a protest at Clarion University.  The protest is off the mark, however, and banning smoking at state-run universities is a good idea.

headline: South Butler school talks to resume Monday
abstract: Negotiators for the school board and striking teachers in the South Butler School District will resume talks at 1:30 p.m. tomorrow in district administrative offices.

headline: The Turnpike Commission will discuss plans for a 25 percent rate hike that is set to take effect on January fourth.
abstract: The Pennsylvania Turnpike Commission will increase tolls 25 percent in January. Over the next two years, the increase will provide $2.5 billion dollars for state transportation projects.

headline: NewsChannel 33 Daybreak
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell is travelling the state on behalf of Barack Obama's get out the vote effort in the US presidential election.

headline: Tax Numbers
abstract: Here's a look at some of the state's revenues for May and how much lower they were than anticipated. It looks as if we are drinking and smoking less, aren't shopping and driving as much and businesses aren't doing quite so well: The sales tax -- $5.6 million, The personal income tax -- $97.9 million, The corporate tax -- $31.5 million, The realty transfer tax -- $1.8 million, The cigarette and malt beverage tax -- $18.2 million, The motor license fund -- $15.2 million.

headline: Plane to spray municipalities affected by West Nile virus
abstract: Several municipalities or sections of municipalities with large populations of adult mosquitoes will be sprayed with pesticides in Montgomery County due to concerns of the West Nile virus. Testing found an exceptionally high number of mosquitoes infected with West Nile in the region, which prompted the spraying, and residents are encouraged to stay indoors when planes spray the pesticides. On July 22, the county reported a woman who contracted the disease, but it was the county’s first case since 2003.

headline: Lawyers sue again over prison overcrowding in Philadelphia
abstract: A class-action lawsuit on behalf of Philadelphia prisoners has been filed against the city of Philadelphia for overcrowded prisons where often three prisoners share a cell. The case was assigned to U.S. District Judge R. Barclay Surrick, who presided over the 2006 lawsuit that focused on overcrowding.

headline: No Text
abstract: After U.S. Senator Bob Casey called for changes following the death of a sergeant, the commander in Iraq says over 80 thousand facilities will now be inspected for faulty wiring. Anyone who served in the military between 1957 and 2001 is owed money by the government from Social Security taxes that were deducted. In addition, a company in Northumberland County will receive $895,000, which it will put towards the creation of an additional 165 jobs, and the Northumberland Borough has agreed to a $2.6 million signing bonus to lease its natural gas drilling rights.

headline: Money & Politics
abstract: National newscast including speculation on the running vice president nominees including Gov. Ed Rendell for the democrats.

headline: Philadelphia Academy CEO demoted amid probe
abstract: The CEO of Philadelphia Academy Charter School, Kevin M. O'Shea, has been demoted to his former position of operations director due to allegations of financial mismanagement. The Philadelphia School Reform Commission is scheduled to vote on whether or not to authorize Philadelphia Academy and fifteen other city charter schools to continue to operate another five years.

headline: Unions rip Specter's stance on card-check bill
abstract: Buisness leaders are hailing US Senator Arlen Spector while unions are ripping into him for his decision to oppose legislation that would make it easier for unions to organize.

headline: District awaits date for mediation session
abstract: Teachers in the Saucon Valley School District are still on strike after negotiations stalled over salary increases and health insurance contributions.  The PA Department of Education is in the process of determining the union's two strike deadlines, the first of which will determine when non-binding arbitration begins and the strike ends.

headline: Pa. education board eyes college costs analysis
abstract: The State Board of Education’s higher education council held a hearing yesterday and is looking to attack the growing gulf between school costs and the ability of students and parents to pay for college.

headline: Rendell announced more budget cuts today, after state revenues have came up 660 million dollars short so far this year.
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell cut $128 million in spending due to tax revenue collections being $658 million dollars lower than expected. This will bring the state's reserve to $439 million.

headline: Bill Clinton rallies support for Obama
abstract: Bill Clinton was in Western PA to convince voters who chose Hillary Clinton during the primary that Democratic nominee Barack Obama was the one to vote for.  Democrats are expecting a victory in the race, but are warning voters not to get complacent.

headline: The blind budgeting bind
abstract: The York City School District passed a nearly $88 million budget last week, and for the first time in six years, there wasn't a tax increase. That budget is based on receiving an estimated $5.6 million increase in state funding, a nearly 16 percent jump. Problem: The state General Assembly has not yet approved a new school funding plan. If legislators rework the proposed funding plan, districts might have to tweak spending plans. At York City, if the estimated state funding is cut, the district will likely have to reopen its budget to adopt a tax increase, said Tom Foust, vice president of the school board. The district will also have to reprint thousands of property-tax bills.

headline: Private donations sought for sports complex
abstract: Allegheny Chief Executive Dan Onorato will seek private and foundation donations to help convert an industrial site along the Ohio River into a public sports complex, which would cost between $70,000 and $80,000 for environmental cleanup and could cost between $10 million and $15 million for construction of the facility. The Sports Legacy Foundation donated the land to the county’s Redevelopment Authority, and Onorato believes he will be able to raise enough money for the project.

headline: Legislators tour state prison as new county jail site mulled
abstract: If Luzerne County builds another prison, Rep. John Yudich wants it within a five-mile radius of State Correctional Institutions at Retreat in Hunlock Creek and SCI Dallas. Yudichak, Rep. Todd Eachus and Rep. Eddie Day Pashinski were part of a group that toured the Retreat facilities Thursday and looked at the prison’s recent performance. Retreat does not have room to expand, as it is nestled between a mountain and the Susquehanna River.
