The closest alternatives would be the mountain top, if it is large and flat enough, or the other side of the mountain. A county prison in Newport Township, next to Retreat, would provide a boost to the community by adding economic and job opportunities and using some of the township’s undeveloped land.

headline: Saluting the fallen
abstract: The Pennsylvania National Guard sponsored the 28th Infantry "Keystone" Division annual memorial service Sunday at the Pennsylvania Military Museum in Boalsburg. The service featured a military band concert, displays of military vehicles, and a 21-gun salute

headline: Morning briefing
abstract: National newscast including Gov. Ed Rendell supporting Hillary Clinton for the Vice Presidential nomination.

headline: Philadelphia may get hotel tax hike; no such increase foreseen here
abstract: Philadelphia may get a new taxing option that would generate an additional $7.5 million to promote the city's tourism attractions like Independence Hall and its expanded convention center. The Democrat-controlled House Finance Committee approved House Bill 2167, which would give Philadelphia City Council the authority to increase its tax on hotel/motel rooms from the current 14 percent to 15.5 percent. But don't expect a similar tax increase for Pittsburgh. The current hotel room tax generates about $90 million in Philadelphia, most of which goes to pay off debt and for general city expenses. A small slice of the 14 percent tax now goes for advertising and marketing of tourist attractions.

headline: null
abstract: Governor Rendell visited Cambria County to discuss more than 18 million in state investments that will be injected into the county's economy.  The state investment is expected to create approximately 375 jobs.

headline: null
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell ordered an immediate state hiring freeze to help maintain a balanced budget.  The plan could save the state as much as 200 million dollars and will leave approximately 500 vacant jobs unfilled.

headline: Voters gripe about polls
abstract: Township Supervisor Ron Kepler is quoted as saying the polling situation as a "complete disaster" and the problems is outlined.

headline: State DEP figures that nearly 9,000 gallons much gasoline escaped.
abstract: A gas leak in Turtle Creek kills fish and leaves some residual contamination. The Pennsylvania Department of Enviornmental Protection estimates 9,000 gallons of gasoline seeped into the creek. The leak did not affect ground or drinking water.

headline: Rendell: Governor: Vote 'yes' for water $$
abstract: Ed Rendell writes to encourage voters to approve the ballot question regarding waterways in PA.  The ballot initiative will cost $400 million if passed.  The governor says that the ballot question, if passed, would clean up the state's waterways and provide a safer and more dependable source of water and sewer service.

headline:
The blind budgeting bind
If funding is cut from the state budget, districts will have to dip into savings or reopen budgets.
abstract: The York City School District didn’t increase taxes when it passed a nearly $88 million budget that’s based on an estimated $5.6 million increase in state funding; however, the PA General Assembly still hasn’t approved the spending increase in its budget, so York and school districts across the state could be forced to revise their budgets in the future. Governor Ed Rendell proposed the largest increase in state education funding in over two decades, and while York based its budget on a larger increase, other school districts based their budgets on historical funding trends. Some property owners will receive tax relief from slot machine gambling funds, but for some districts, the tax break will be eaten up by even larger tax increases.

headline: Request for PPL to study impact on habitat reasonable
abstract: The 2005 fly ash spill in the Delaware River at Martins Creek seems like ancient history, because recurring floods have taken over as the primary preoccupation with the river. PPL Corp., the PA Department of Environmental Protection, the Delaware Riverside Conservancy and a Commonwealth Court judge revisited the consent decree resulting from the spill. The parties agreed that a $1.5 million fine against PPL would be upheld as compensation and would close the door on the investigation with one exception: The conservancy, which intervened in the court case, insisted upon a long-term study of the habitat and wildlife in the area affected by the spill along with the right to reopen the case if long-term damages are discovered.

headline: Montgomery County lawmaker seeks tougher call-records law
abstract: PA Representative Michael Vereb plans to introduce legislation to prevent cell phone companies from releasing customers’ call records without a judge’s approval. He was angry that Sprint-Nextel had apparently released the phone records of the Dauphin County district attorney and state police investigators to the defense lawyer for Joseph Sica, who is accused of committing perjury in a casino license hearing. Current law allows lawyers to obtain call records without a judge’s approval, and Vereb believes the practice could result in confidential information being released.

headline: Sunday will be Pittsburgh's banner day
abstract: If Pittsburghers don't know why their city has a street named Boulevard of the Allies, they should after Sunday afternoon. More than 1,000 active-duty servicemen and women, color guard members, foreign dignitaries and of course, veterans are expected to turn out for the rededication of the 86-year-old boulevard. Complete with bagpipers, a C-130 flyover by the 911th Airlift Wing and a 21-gun salute by the Pennsylvania National Guard's 107th Field Artillery, the 1 p.m. ceremony aims to honor all veterans but especially those who served in what many had thought would be "The War to End All Wars."

headline: Morning Express with Robin Meade
abstract: National newscast including Continental Airlines cutting 3,000 jobs and Gov. Ed Rendell supporting Hillary Clinton for the Vice Presidential nomination.

headline: Philadelphia to set up 311 system for non-emergency calls
abstract: Philadelphia's new managing director, Camille Barnett, says she plans to create a 311 system to call for non-emergency help. Barnett says she expects to have the system running by year's end. The administration of former Mayor John Street had considered building a 311 system but then rejected the idea as too costly.

headline: null
abstract: The PA Turnpike Commission announced that it is pushing to toll Interstate 80.  Local residents in Johnstown say they will take alternate routes to avoid tolls.

headline: null
abstract: In an effort to avert a budget deficit, PA Governor Ed Rendell ordered a state hiring freeze and other spending cuts that are expected to save the state 200 million dollars.  The governor is also asking state agencies to cut down on their budgets and travel expenses.

headline: Traditional hunting under assault
abstract: Traditional hunting, especially of smaller game, is under assualt from variety of ecological problems in the state and the future does not look bright.

headline: The Governor is slashing at least 128 million dollars more in state spending as pennsylvania tries to weather the global financial cris
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell cuts an extra $128 million to reduce budget spending.

headline: Sen. Pat Browne says state budget projects to have a $3 billion deficit
abstract: State Sen. Pat Browne, R-16 warned that the state's budget is facing a huge deficit in a speech to members of the Greater Pocono Chamber of Commerce.  He suggests that the state closes the gap with spending cuts rather than tax increases.

headline: There should be a price to pay for dysfunctional government
abstract: An agreement over Pennsylvania’s budget has been reached, but the authors of the editorial criticize the process in which they negotiated the budget. They say Governor Ed Rendell and the state Legislature again waited too late to begin working on the budget even though the PA Constitution sets a specific deadline, and they are frustrated that there was yet again a chance that state employees could have been temporarily laid off because of the government’s irresponsibility. They criticize the General Assembly for being too large and dysfunctional, and they are calling for legislators, the governor and the governor’s cabinet to lose two days of salary for every day the fail to pass the budget in time in the future.

headline: Show on gas leases to air
abstract: The fervor over drilling for natural gas in PA is coming to television. WPSU-TV, the Penn State University-run public broadcasting station, will sponsor a one-hour, call-in program for people with questions about the natural gas that experts believe is locked in the Marcellus Shale deposits that run deep underground from upstate New York to Virginia. Residents may call with questions or submit them online at the Web site. They will be answered by a panel that includes a lawyer specializing in mineral rights leases; a representative from the state Department of Environmental Protection, who will focus on environmental concerns in the state; an educator from Penn State Cooperative Extension experienced in exploration-process issues; and a gas industry representative.

headline: Most county judges rank 'acceptable' or better
abstract: State and federal judges in Allegheny County largely received passing marks from lawyers who appear before them, according to the county bar association's Judiciary Survey, a report card released every four years. Lawyers graded 43 of the county's 46 Common Pleas judges "acceptable" or better in four categories: impartiality, legal ability, diligence and temperament. Lawyers marked 29 judges' job performances as "good" to "excellent." Federal judges in district, magistrate and bankruptcy courts also scored well, with 18 of the 25 rated good to excellent in three or more categories.

headline: PBS to reduce "Mister Rogers' Neighborhood" feeds this fall
abstract:
PBS says it will no longer offer episodes of "Mister Rogers' Neighborhood" to its member stations each weekday, but will instead send stations just one episode per week to air starting in the fall.
PBS says it is making the decision because the show is no longer in production, and because its menu of other programming continues to expand. Pittsburgh's PBS station, WQED, says it will continue broadcasting the show five days a week even after PBS cuts back on its national feed. The Pittsburgh station has a close relationship with Family Communications Inc., the Pittsburgh corporation that the late Fred Rogers founded to produce the series.

headline: Morning News
abstract: The controversy over whether to seat the Michigan and Florida delegates continues. Democratic National Committee Chairman Howard Dean is open to a solution, but will not foot the bill. PA Gov. Rendell assumes voters may retaliate in those states in the fall elections.

headline: Property tax relief is a good goal, but it should be for all Pennsylvanians
abstract: The author is talking about how tax relief is complex process in PA and a measure that would funnel revenue from slots casinos to senior citizens and away from other Pennsylvanians passed in the PA state House. The author doesn’t think its not that senior citizens don’t need help; the state became a leader nationwide with PACE and PACENET, the prescription medicine coverage programs and hundreds of thousands of senior citizens are getting property tax and rent rebates through the Taxpayer Relief Act. Additionally, a portion of new tax-relief revenue from the slots casinos already is to be directed to about 200,000 seniors under Act 1 and PA Governor Edward Rendell and both parties opened the 2008 legislative session with a lot of interest in further cuts in school property taxes, including a plan to eliminate them entirely.

headline: null
abstract: Last month, state Attorney General Tom Corbett announced that more than a dozen lawmakers in the PA General Assembly and their aides were facing corruption charges.  Tax-payer funded bonuses were handed out to aides working on political campaigns.

headline: null
abstract: Pennsylvania legislators are considering a bill that would overhaul the state's existing dog laws and more heavily regulate large breeding facilities.  Some larger facilities--sometimes called puppy mills--are accused of confining animals to small areas and denying them proper veterinary care.

headline: Editorial: The City's Deficit
abstract: Gives Philadelphia Mayor Nutter credit for doing his level best to plug a projected $1 billion budget shortfall over five years, but also encourages him to use the oppurtunity to transform city government.

headline: Rendell also chose to freeze pay increases for more than 13 thousand state workers which were supposed to take effect next month …
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell initated a pay freeze to save money in a sagging economy and strained budget.

headline: Parkway East work to take 2 more years
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation has decided to spread the final phase of the Parkway East/I-376 rehabilitation between Churchill and the Pennsylvania Turnpike over two construction seasons.  Engineers suggest that spreading out the construction will help avoid inconvenient disruptions for drivers, particularly on weekends.

headline: Think the Economy Is Bad? Wait Till the States Cut Back
abstract: Struggling as we are with the housing bust, the credit crunch, shrinking consumption, rising unemployment and faltering business investment, we can be forgiven for thinking that all the big shoes have dropped. State and city governments have yet to shrink the economy; indeed, they have even managed to prop it up. They have quietly maintained their spending at pre-crisis levels even as they warn of numerous cutbacks forced on them by declining tax revenues. The cutbacks, however, are written into budgets for a fiscal year that begins on July 1, a month away. In the meantime the states and cities, often drawing on rainy-day savings, have carried their share of the load for the national economy.

headline: Skytop I-99 cleanup gets $57.9 million
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation has budgeted $57.9 million for the Skytop Mountain section of Interstate 99 for unfinished construction and environmental cleanup. The budget appears to be consistent with PennDOT's pledge to use money in addition to its normal funding stream to the county to clean up the acid rock drainage hazard at Skytop. Construction on I-99 was halted to stop acidic runoff from leaching from the spoil piles and fill areas into streams and ground water.

headline: Needle no's
abstract:
Pennsylvania has only one tattoo regulation, those under 18 need parental consent to get one.
Some government officials and tattoo artists want to see safety measures put in place. With more and more people getting inked, state Rep. Anthony DeLuca, D-36, said he wants regulation on sanitary tattoo practice. DeLuca, who represents Allegheny County, introduced a bill in March 2007 that would regulate tattoo shops. Dubbed House Bill 793, it was never approved and never moved,  it sat in the Committee of Health and Human Services since it was introduced. Since it wasn’t passed this legislative session, the bill died and would have to be reintroduced in order to make its way into Commonwealth law.

headline: Philadelphia in talks with group to take over Wi-Fi network
abstract: Philadelphia is in talks with a group to take over its wireless Internet network. A spokesman for Mayor Michael Nutter said negotiations are under way. But he would not say whether they involved a community organization or a company. EarthLink Inc., which built the network, is scheduled to shut it down on Thursday. Last month, the company announced that it was pulling the plug on its troubled wireless high-speed Internet network, once touted as a national model. It suffered from connection problems and didn't attract enough subscribers.

headline: MSNBC News Live
abstract: US Sen. Hillary Clinton argues that she has won Ohio, Florida, and other big states, but can she win the fall election? Announcers are unsure.

headline: Raising the standard
abstract: With little fanfare, Mayor Nutter signed into law another piece of legislation that will help shore up the financial and health discrepancies faced by some low-income workers hired to work for the city. The New Wage and Benefits Bill, signed last week, requires employers with city contracts to pay their workers up to 150 percent of the federal minimum wage and to provide health benefits equal to their full-time employees. This goes into effect next year. The bill enhances a 2005 city law that made city-supported employers pay workers 150 percent of the state minimum. Councilman W. Wilson Goode Jr. introduced both measures. This means employees whose companies have contracts with the city will get paid at least $10.88 per hour starting in July 2009.

headline: null
abstract: In the wake of the bonusgate scandal, some PA residents are calling for a constitutional convention to re-write the state constitution to include stricter ethics rules.  At a minimum, residents want a special legislative session on ethics, and if that doesn't clean things up many say they would support a constitutional convention.

headline: null
abstract: As a precautionary measure, Governor Ed Rendell ordered a hiring freeze and other state spending cuts.  The hiring freeze and spending cuts are designed prevent budget shortfalls in the future and are not expected to fill an immidiate  gap in spending.

headline: Tough times hitting animal shelters, too
abstract: As the recession forces more and more Americans to downsize, leaving their homes and struggling to pay their bills, animal welfare groups report a dramatic rise in pets given up for adoption or abandoned on the street.

headline: Governor Rendell is making more cuts to the state budget in light of revenues that continue to fall short of expectations.
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell cut $128 million in spending due to tax revenue collections being $658 million dollars lower than expected. Pay freezes to state employees will  be used and the Governor will meet with state employees to discuss cost-cutting measures.

headline: Tuition running close to inflation
abstract: Average college tuition and fees are up by as much as 6.4 percent this school year.  The College Board, however, noted that this is a rate close to that of inflation.  Experts do not expect this to continue as states scraping for cash will cut back on education funding.

headline: Timely passage of state budget a question
abstract: Area lawmakers remain hopeful of bringing home a state budget on time, but fearful of state job layoffs. Baker said the earliest the budget can be considered is June 23, the date the Democratic-controlled Appropriations Committee has designated to bring the budget measure out of committee. Although the deadline is June 30, Baker and others are unsure if a week is long enough to consider the spending plan.

headline: Soot City: Pittsburgh still has work to do on clean air
abstract: Pittsburgh is ranked as having the sootiest air in the nation. To locals and visitors alike, that's hard to believe, given the visible cleanup the former Steel City and region have achieved over decades. Fine-particle pollution that contains ash, diesel exhaust, chemicals, metals and aerosols is very damaging. In the same study, which covers 2004-06, Pittsburgh came in second to Los Angeles for the worst annual readings on this unhealthful airborne cocktail. The ALA is concerned about particle pollution because coughing and sneezing cannot keep such microscopic threats from burrowing deep within the lungs, where they can lead to breathing problems, asthma, lung cancer and even heart attacks or strokes.

headline: New Sentencing hearing for Abu-Jamal would be complicated
abstract: The US Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit ordered a new sentencing hearing for Mumia Abu-Jamal for killing Philadelphia Police Officer Daniel Faulkner in 1981. Philadelphia District Attorney Lynn Abraham says she will not accede to a life sentence, considering a petition to the US Supreme Court to seek the death penalty. Appeals will delay the hearing date, which could mean Abraham's successor inherits the case. Philadelphia Common Pleas Court Judge Benjamin Lerner said winning a new sentencing hear, as has Abu-Jamal, is difficult to do.

headline: null
abstract: Local News Cast with highlights including the Democratic Presidential Primary between Hillary Clinton and Barack Obama and a state smoking ban in the state legislature.

headline: Murphy touts interaction with community
abstract: Former City Council President Kevin Murphy is running for the position of state representative of the 113th Legislative District. His stepfather, Joseph Kluck, ran for a state representative seat and lost.

headline: Reading schools taxpayers to get biggest break from slots revenue, Mifflin’s least
abstract: The state Department of Education released estimates of how much property tax relief homeowners can expect to receive. Gambling revenue will be used by school districts to reduce property taxes. However, state law requires districts to reduce the assessed value of each property to a point that matches the savings amount.

headline: null
abstract: Some lawmakers are calling for a state constitutional convention, arguing that the government is broken and the only way to fix it is to let the people decide.  All of this comes in the wake of the bonusgate scandal, in which some Democratic members of the legislature gave staffers taxpayer-funded bonuses to do campaign work.

headline: Union Fighting PA University Outdoor Smoking Ban
abstract: In an effort to negotiate changes to Pennsylvania's new indoor smoking ban, a state employee union has filed a demand to bargain with the State System of Higher Education.  The union wishes to challenges the decision of the state system's chancellor to ban smoking on all 14 state-owned college campuses.

headline: Off target: America's gun-buying spree makes no sense
abstract: Paints the current trend of increased gun ownership and purchasing of ammunition after the election of Barak Obama to the presidency as unfounded.

headline: David Cohen: Dynamo in demand
abstract: David L. Cohen will chair the University of Pennsylvania's board of trustees, beginning in November.  He is known for civic duty, belonging to many organizations such as, the  American Red Cross and Jewish Federation.

headline: Who cares what they're wearing, as long as they aren't trying to persuade others at polling place?
abstract: The editorial expresses support for allowing voters to wear politically explicit clothing in polling places.  They dismiss the notion that allowing such conduct will snowball into intimidation and be bad for the atmosphere of the polling place.  Polling supervisors should keep their duties limited to keeping the voting machines running instead of policing people's clothing.

headline: Superintendent resigns in Penn Hills, board lays off dozens of teachers
abstract: The superintendent of the troubled Penn Hills School District unexpectedly resigned just before last night's scheduled school board meeting, at which dozens of teachers and two principals were furloughed. The resignation of Patricia Gennari met with scattered applause from the crowd of about 100 people who attended the meeting. Assistant Superintendent Joseph Carroll will become acting superintendent July 1, said school board President Erin Vecchio. Board members did not ask for Dr. Gennari's resignation, according to district Solicitor Craig Alexander. And none of the board members, he said, have talked to her since she gave written notice just before the meeting.

headline: Wages of Pa. workers stagnant as economy struggles, new study finds
abstract: According to a report by the Keystone Research Center in Harrisburg, the year-old national economic crisis caused by increasing mortgage foreclosures, falling home prices and severely stressed financial institutions has already damaged the economy in PA. The report, The State of Working PA 2008, is being released early because of the upcoming Democratic and Republican national conventions, and it found since December 2007, 4,500 jobs have been lost in PA. However, problems have been present in the state’s economy for quite some time, considering the average income for the majority of Pennsylvanians has been falling, while the income for the wealthiest has increased since 2001, and the only real bright spot in the state’s economy, rising housing prices, has disappeared as prices on homes are now steadily declining.

headline: State watching so beetle doesn't bug trees
abstract: T PA Department of Agriculture will monitor Luzerne County and two others considered to be at high risk from a wood-boring beetle. There is no proven way to eradicate the beetle, so the state's efforts are focused on trying to contain and slow its spread. A separate monitoring effort will be undertaken by the PA Department of Conservation and Natural Resources and the US Department of Agriculture. Butler, Allegheny, Beaver and Lawrence have been quarantined from moving ash logs and products since discovery of the beetle last June.

headline: New year's guns: Philadelphia bystanders should not become victims
abstract: The author talks about how for the past two years people in Philadelphia have rung in the New Year by firing their guns into the air, and how in the beginning of 2007 a man fleeing neighborhood gunfire was shot by a pursuing police officer who mistook him for the shooter. The author believes that this is an example of how the officers cannot use their guns recklessly and how change needs to be made in the police department.

headline: null
abstract: Local news including lifeguards being cut from state parks and Gov. Ed Rendell saying Obama will beat McCain in November.

headline: N/A
abstract: A discussion between the radio host and guest about the political battle between US Sens. Obama and Clinton for President. The guest believes Obama needs to go on the offense more about Hillary. He has to try and win in PA, although it will be difficult with PA Governor Ed Rendell's support for Clinton. Obama has won more states, but they are smaller and not all are likely to go democratic in the presidential election.

headline:
Rendell, lawmakers spar over property tax appeals
Some municipalities, school districts doing 'spot reassessments' to collect more.
abstract: Some school districts and local governments have used "spot reassessments" to appeal assessments they believe are too low in order to collect more money in local taxes, but critics of the practice claim new homeowners and business owners are surprised to learn that their property taxes are substantially higher than they had anticipated. The PA Legislature overwhelmingly supported legislation to end the practice of spot reassessments in most PA counties, but Governor Ed Rendell surprisingly vetoed two bills, claiming local governments should have the same rights to appeal assessment values as taxpayers. While local school districts, including Blue Mountain, argue spot reassessments are necessary, state Representative Tim Seip, a sponsor of the legislation, believes they are unfair, and the Legislature will search for a compromise this fall, but it could also consider overriding Rendell’s veto.

headline: null
abstract: PA Turnpike Officials have released details for a proposal to put tolls along Interstate 80.  Plans for tolling Interstate 80 must first be approved by state and federal lawmakers.

headline: Senate panel approves convention bills
abstract: Although a state Senate committee approved three bills that call for a constitutional convention, experts say it is unlikely that a bill approving a constitutional convention will pass both chambers of the Pennsylvania General Assembly.  Given the General Assembly's unwillingness to pass reforms for greater governmental transparency, as well as its reluctance to ban bonuses for state emmployees, it is unlikely that legislators will pass a bill that could lead to even greater political reform.

headline: null
abstract: Discusses a ceremony honoring US Senator Arlen Spector in Philadelphia.

headline: Fumo corruption trial hears saga of bulldozer
abstract: Former State Senator Vince Fumo is accused of using Citizens Alliance For Better Neighboorhoods as a personal bank by a testifier in Fumo's corruption trial.

headline: A boneheaded decision of free school meals
abstract: Sydelle Zove, an advocacy & communications manager for the Greater Philadelphia Coalition Against Hunger writes to lament the inconsistency of the USDA's study that finds that a nutritious breakfast helps students perform better in school with their recent decision to cut a breakfast program in the Philadelphia schools which is open to all students regardless of socio-economic status.

headline: Taxpayers to have a say on school projects
abstract: For the first time, Allegheny County will hold a referendum mandated by the 2006 taxpayer relief law, which requires that if a school district wants to raise taxes beyond the rate of an inflation index, it must have a referendum to let the public decide. The Allegheny Valley School District has budgeted enough to make necessary repairs at Springdale Junior-Senior High School, but it will hold the referendum to seek the public’s approval to raise the property tax rate to fund $9 million in additional improvements, including the construction of a new building. The Allegheny Valley Citizens Against a New School is against the additional improvements, and Superintendant Gabriel Ziccarelli is unsure about how the rest of the public will vote.

headline: ACLU backfire
abstract: The authors of the editorial praise the American Civil Liberties Union of Nevada for going against the national chapter’s position on the Second Amendment’s right to bear arms. They believe the Nevada ACLU correctly followed a recent U.S. Supreme Court decision that found the Second Amendment is an individual right, not a collective right. They also feel that the Nevada chapter’s executive director, Gary Peck, would be a good candidate to succeed Nadine Strossen, who is retiring as president of the national ACLU.

headline: State: Remove wood, metal from site
abstract: After finding over 100 tons of unpermitted material at a site being reclaimed by Hazleton Creek Properties, the PA Department of Environmental Protection ordered the company to remove it, and the state is reviewing the site, where Hazleton Creek is permitted to use regulated fill to reclaim mine pits and a former landfill under a permit. The review comes at a time when Hazleton Creek is considering making a $3 million purchase from the Hazleton Redevelopment Authority for the property, which Mayor Lou Barletta hopes is used to build an amphitheatre; however, opponents of the deal fear that giving up control of the land will not lead to the construction of an amphitheatre. Others are concerned Hazelton Creek will use the site as a landfill for construction and demolition waste, even though the company has continuously denied this.

headline: No signs that state will abolish death penalty like New Jersey
abstract: In PA there does not seem to be a move to abolish the death penalty, the PA state Supreme Court affirmed the sentence in several year-end rulings. Prosecutors in the state say that they are working to have the executions carried out. PA has 228 inmates on death rows, which is the fourth-largest number in the country, but have only executed three people since the death penalty was reinstated in 1978. The US Supreme Court will be hearing arguments on whether lethal injection is a form of cruel and unusual punishment later in the month.

headline: null
abstract: Local newscast Gov Ed Rendell supporting Hillary Clinton for the Vice Presidential nominee.

headline: n/a
abstract: An announcer discusses the campaign. In his opinion, Clinton is not going to bring the kind of change PA needs. Clinton alluded to PA Governor Rendell, whose endorsement she received, during her kickoff speech in Scranton.

headline: Safe and Sound votes to disband itself
abstract: The nonprofit agency Philadelphia Safe and Sound was run by former Philadelphia Mayor John Street's wife, Naomi Post Street. When Mayor Nutter took office after Street, he cut $21 million from Philadelphia Safe and Sound's budget and requested that the Department of Welfare conduct a study on the management and financial practices of the organization. The Philadelphia Board of Directors voted to cease operations.

headline: null
abstract: State Representative Jerry Nailor is calling for the PA Department of Transportation to consider  upgrading the york-split along Interstate 83 immediately.  Representative Nailor says trafiic congestion makes the york-split dangerous.

headline: Freeman bill advances out of Senate committee
abstract: A bill proposed by state Representative Bob Freeman was approved by the Senate Economic and Recreational Development Committee and will be sent to the full Senate for consideration.  The bill is designed to continue the state's Elm Street program beyond its 2011 deadline and will provide up to five years of financial assistance for municipalities to hire a manager who will establish a plan for neighborhood revitalization.

headline: null
abstract: Mentions Governor Rendell as a prospective canidate for Secretary of Transportation in the Obama administartion.

headline: Pileggi leads GOP move to give up pay hike
abstract: Delaware County state Senator Joe Pileggi is returing his 2.8 percent cost of lliving allowance (COLA) raise to the state and urges other Republicans to do so as well.

headline: It's not anti-drunks, it's anti-drinks
abstract: Sarah Longwell, the managing director of the American Beverage Institute in Washington, D.C. writes to explain the ABI's position regarding steps designed to crack down on drunk driving.  She says that the Institute is not against mandating interlocks for repeat and high-BAC offenders, but thinks that such measures should be up to a judge's discretion, not mandatory for first time offenders.

headline: Teachers, board meet in bid to settle pact
abstract: The Annville-Cleona teachers and school board members sat down to settle the long-running teachers’ contract dispute. The 120 teachers in the Annville-Cleona School District have gone without a contract since Aug. 31, 2006. Teachers staged a four-day walkout in May and threatened another one at the beginning of the 2007-08 school year.

headline: Discriminating lot
abstract: Constitutions for democratic governments have two principal purposes. They establish government structure. And, as in the Bill of Rights, they establish liberty by prohibiting the government from engaging in certain conduct. Restricting rights and establishing classes of citizenship are not appropriate purposes for a democratic constitution. Yet in Harrisburg this week, the Senate is likely to vote on a state constitutional amendment that would prohibit what fear-mongering politicians call same-sex marriages, but what other states have defined as civil unions. Senators behind this political exercise are acting well beyond their portfolio as civic officials. The amendment should be rejected.

headline: Treat new hunting rules as an experiment
abstract: The PA Game Commission is scheduled to vote on a proposal to limit deer hunting in an expanded Wildlife Management Unit 5C to shotguns, muzzleloaders and bows and arrows. Also, the Game Commission would allow hunters to bait deer on private property in order to lure the animals within shotgun range. The author thinks that there should be modification and a trial period to determine whether the proposed regulations enable the Game Commission to effectively depend on hunters to keep the deep populations in check.

headline: No Text
abstract: Colonel Jeffrey Miller will leave the PA State Police to become the National Football League’s director of strategic security in the middle of August. In addition, Pitchers Jordan Zimmerman and Bobby Brownlie and outfielder Mike Daniels will represent the Harrisburg Senators in the upcoming all-star game for the Eastern League.

headline: null
abstract: Local newscast including  Gov Ed Rendell supporting Hillary Clinton for the Vice Presidential nominee.

headline: N/A
abstract: Hillary Clinton and Barack Obama will be campaiging hard in PA for the next 7 weeks leading up to the state's primary. However, while US Sen. Bob Casey has yet to announce an endorsement, PA Governor Ed Rendell has been more vocal, calling Hillary the best qualified candidate.

headline: School districts, county wrestle over $1.7 million
abstract: Monroe County's solicitor, John Dunn, sent a letter to East Stroudsburg and Pleasant Valley school districts telling them they owed the county's Tax Claim Bureau its 5 percent commission on late taxes from 2002-2006. The dispute between the school districts and the county is over two conflicting tax laws.

headline: COUNTERPOINT: What should Pennsylvania do about rising electric rates?
abstract: With energy rates on the rise, it is time to move away from a regulated market for energy provision and open up the market to competition.  Competition will provide more options, more innovation and better prices than a regulated market, and it will reward companies that operate safely and efficiently with more business.

headline: Students arrested after brawl with cops at W. Phila. School
abstract: At least 20 students from Sayre High School were arrested yesterday after a student and a number of his late-arriving classmates pushed past security--engendering a brawl between students and police.

headline: Rendell says health care proposal should connect with national plan
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell said Monday that his proposal to expand state health care to thousands of uninsured adults would serve as a "perfect bridge" to a national health insurance program fostered by President-elect Obama and a Democratic Congress.

headline: State payment delay could close schools at youth detention center
abstract: Due to a delay of state payments, the schools in Loysville Youth Detention Center in Perry County may have to close due to upaid costs. The Pennsylvania Department of Education has not been able to pay the school district and still owes the district $33,000 from last year.

headline: Rendell mixes urgency and humor in speech to local Obama supporters
abstract: PA Gov Ed Rendell is travelling the state stumping for Democratic presidential candidate Barack Obama and warning voters not to let their guard down.  While Obama leads in most polling, Rendell is stressing the need to be vigilant.  Rendell defended some of Obama's proposed policies including his plan for cutting taxes.  He is looking forward to the Democrats crushing their opponents as a way to send the message to Republican strategist Karl Rove that "a campaign of distortion and untruth" does not work in Pennsylvania.

headline: temple educator Heidi A. Ramirez confirmed to Philadelphia Reform Commission
abstract: PA Governor Rendell's nominee to the Philadelphia School Reform Commission was confirmed by the PA Senate. She is the first Latina to serve on the board. Philadelphia Mayor Michael Nutter had recommended Ramirez for the position. The Commission was established by the law leading to the state takeover of the schools in December 2001.

headline: Erie same-sex couples consider Calif. Marriages
abstract: 68,000 same-sex couples from out-of-state are expected to travel to California in the next three years to be married; however, the state of PA and most other states will not recognize the marriages, and the couples don’t receive federal marriage benefits. Californians will vote to amend the state’s constitution in November, which 27 states have already done, and the PA Senate has considered an amendment, but it has not yet been passed. PA for Marriage is pushing for the amendment, which its spokeswoman believes would pass, and the article provides the opinions of some same-sex couples from Erie who are considering getting married in California.

headline: U.S. Steel gets OK for project to reduce pollutants
abstract: The Allegheny County Health Department granted U.S. Steel Corporation a permit to make $1.1 billion in pollution-reducing upgrades at its coke-making plant in Clairton, PA. According to the American Lung Association, the region has the worst air quality in the nation. The plant plans to replace older batteries with more efficient ones that should improve the air quality.

headline: No Text
abstract: Fires caused by unattended burning cigarettes kill between 700 and 900 people every year and caused a bowling center in Dauphin County to burn down last year. In order to prevent future fires, Governor Rendell signed a law requiring all stores in PA to sell only fire safe cigarettes by April, which fire fighters hope will result in less fires caused by cigarettes.

headline: null
abstract: Local newscast including  Gov. Ed Rendell signs the smoking ban bill, York County Neighborhood vandalized, and weather.

headline: N/A
abstract: Larry King interviews a guest on the likelihood of either US Sen. Hillary Clinton or US Sen. Barack Obama winning the primary. Hillary is favored in the PA polls, but the numbers are old. She does however, have the support of PA Governor Ed Rendell. She may be able to make the argument that she is winning in the gritty industrial states that will count in November. If she does, the vote will have to go to the super delegates, and possibly, to court.

headline: School property tax elimination: What's next for Pennsylvania?
abstract: As gas and food prices continue to climb, PA Representative Sam Rohrer, the author of this piece, believes that increasing property taxes are driving people out of their homes, including hundreds of seniors, and he advocates getting rid of property taxes entirely. According to Rohrer, gambling revenue has failed to provide adequate property tax relief, and all other attempts at reform will not be able to help homeowners deal with the heavy burden of property taxes, so the only solution is the School Property Tax Elimination Act, which would amend the state’s constitution to completely phase out all property taxes in a responsible manner. He says that if Governor Ed Rendell and the state Legislature don’t pass the bill, there will be more and more foreclosures in the future, and he urges the public to support the bill.

headline: Lawmakers on vacation
abstract: One good thing has come out of the Bonusgate scandal.  It has shown us that law makers do not need all of the staff they currently have and that we need to reduce the size of the legislature and its staff.  It is the perfect time to enact these and other reforms.

headline: Debate debacle leads to sanctions at Pitt
abstract: An obscenity-laced shouting match between Pitt's debate coach, Shanara Reid-Brinkley, and Fort Hays debate coach, Bill Shannon, has led to one faculty member being fired and another being suspended from coaching.  In response to a shouting match which saw one coach mooning the other, Fort Hays fired Bill Shannon and the University of Pittsburgh suspended Shanara Reid-Brinkley from coaching the university's debate team.

headline: Lobbyist disclosure rules bogged down in wrangling
abstract: Regulations governing Pennsylvania's two-year-old lobbyist disclosure law are bogged down in a dispute over how soon lobbyists and their employers must register with the state and report how much they spend trying to influence state government.

headline: PUC approvals help electricity customers
abstract: The Pennsylvania Public Utilties Commission allowed changes for local energy utlities that will lower rates for some customers, raise rates for others and give some customers more control over the rates they pay. The PUC has expanded programs for both electricity and gas to make paying easier for more customers.

headline: DEP: Vote ‘yes’ for water treatment
abstract: The head of the state Department of Envrironmental Protection is telling voters to vote in favor of the plan to issue $400 million in bonds for a water infrastructure project.  While the project will create 12,000 state jobs, it will also prevent water and sewer issues from spiraling into a major public health crisis.

headline: Test our grads
abstract: A proposal for statewide graduation requirements has sparked a vigorous debate. On the one hand, we in PA owe our children an education that will prepare them for life in our modern global world, and a high school diploma ought to signal that we have provided a high school education that meets that obligation. Right now, we administer the PA System of School Assessment to help assure that every student makes progress toward adequate preparation for life and that every school is meeting federal and state standards. The new proposal would give school districts a number of options of to assure that students have achieved the level of education envisioned by state standards. One option would be to replace existing final exams in courses with graduate competency assessments.

headline: Gays form no 'united front' for a Democratic candidate
abstract: The article discusses the differences between the gay and lesbian community in terms of who they support in Democratic primary. The gay community is split between Senator Barack Obama and Senator Hillary Clinton, while the lesbian community solidly supports Senator Hillary Clinton.

headline: Water-treatment projects receive state funding
abstract: In Somerset County, two grants were announced by PA Sen. John Wozniak to conservations groups dedicated to reclaiming waterways damaged by abandoned mine drainage. The funding is part of the state's Growing Greener program. The money will be shared by the Clearfield Creek Watershed and the Cambria County Conservation District. Loyalhanna Watershed Association and the Juniator Clean Water Partnership are also receiving funds from the Growing Greener Program.

headline: No Text
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell is expected to sign a mine safety bill that passed the state House and Senate. It was first formulated six years ago after the Quecreek accident, and it will create a mine safety board. In other news, police arrested two juveniles for setting a fire that destroyed an owner’s shop in Pittsburgh.

headline: null
abstract: Local newscast including  Gov. Ed Rendell signs the smoking ban bill.

headline: N/A
abstract: PA is expected to play a big part in the democratic race. The state primary is April 22nd. At stake are 158 delegates. PA Governor Rendell has welcomed the focus on the outcome of the state's primary and has encouraged candidates to step up their campaigning there.

headline: Secret Budget Hearings
abstract: Mayor Nutter and City Council are trying to decide how to slice up next year's nearly $4 billion budget. But taxpayers haven't been privy to all of the discussions because some meetings took place in secret. Such closed-door meetings may be fine for a private company. But not for government when the public's business is at stake. The secret sessions clearly violate the spirit of the state's Sunshine Act. The law says the public has a right to be present at all meetings where agency business is discussed or acted upon. Closed-door sessions are restricted to personnel issues, the purchase or lease of property, and legal matters.

headline: Mayor Nutter's watershed moments
abstract: There have been several incidents throughout Philadelphia Mayor Michael Nutter's tenure that show he is not as imperturbable as his reputation suggests.  His response to Department of Human Service workers, a confrontation with the killer of Philadelphia cop, and his emotional outburst on the floor of City Council are all cited as evidence.

headline: State funds should boost local nursing education opportunities
abstract: A combination of state and private funding will benefit prospective nursing students in Northcumberland, Montour and Columbia counties.  As part of a statwide investment in nursing education, these counties will receive 750,000 dollars in state grants, as well as another 870,000 in private funding.  This funding will allow nursing education programs to expand their class sizes and hire more instructors.

headline: Sands plans to open Bethlehem casino in second quarter of 2009; other parts of project on hold
abstract: The Sands Casino project is expected to continue and the opening in the second quarter of 2009 is still expected.

headline: Montco sheriff to fight DUI center closures
abstract: Montgomery County Sheriff John Durante plans to sue state commissioners who intend to close 5 DUI centers due to no extra funds in next years  budget.  The Sheriff says closing the centers and continuing to collect the $150 dollar fee would be illegal and the money's destination would be harder to track. County solicitor Bruce Miller disagrees saying he believes the commissioners are not doing anything illegal.

headline: Road salt shortage a slippery situation
abstract: Roads may be less safe this winter as a result of the rocketing price of salt.  Some towns are deciding how to cut back their use of the pricey resource and not compromise safety.  Salt may be saved for places like road curves, intersections and grades.  Towns in the area are beginning to make their high-volume purchases of salt for the winter and some are holding on, waiting for a last minute deal.

headline: Testing students becomes very testy
abstract: Deputy superintendent for instruction, assessment and accountability for the Pittsburgh Public Schools, Linda Lane, says the tough part about preparing for the PA System of School Assessment tests is doing enough, but not too much. Director of public relations for the Bethel Park School District, Vicki Flotta, says statewide testing has overloaded kids. Districts continue to reassess the methods necessary to ensure students meet required standards.

headline: Inching toward an open records law
abstract: The author believes that state lawmakers are inching toward meaningful reform of the state's inadequate Open Records Law. On Wednesday, the Senate revised the House-amended Senate Bill 1. The author believes that the Legislature shouldn’t have separate standards for itself and other branches of the government, which they believe is one of the weaknesses of the current anemic Open Records law. They believe that the SB 1 senselessly exempts phone numbers from disclosure when they're readily available -- except when unlisted.

headline: WTAJ News at 5:30
abstract: Somerset County officials want to add warning lights and signs to make a railroad crossing safer for pedestrians. It is expected to cost about $3000 dollars. A mudslide in Allegheny County prompted officials to demolish a house and evacuate several others. PA Governor Rendell made a stop in the Johnstown region today.

headline: no text
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell is urging state legislators to approve House bill 2525, which calls for tougher laws to protect dogs from abuses at puppy mills. In other news, a Burlington County flea market reopened. There were 182 munitions buried underground as part of a top secret U.S. Army arsenal.

headline: null
abstract: Local newscast including  presidential primary results and terrorism hearing.

headline: Nanticoke to vote on contract segments
abstract: Greater Nanticoke Area School District board members are meeting to vote on the salary and health insurance segments of the Education Association union's contract.

headline: Slots to pay off in tax relief in Berks, statewide
abstract: A school real-estate tax break has arrived for Pennsylvanians: PA Governor Edward Rendell’s promise to lower property taxes through slot machine gambling will pay off when eligible taxpayers receive school tax bills in the summer. The Taxpayer Relief Act of 2006 required the raising of at least $570 million in slots revenues before money is diverted to property tax relief. State Budget Secretary Michael J. Masch said the tax relief fund had $576 million. After the $570 million threshold is reached, at least $400 million is to be released for school property-tax relief. The law also requires that $100 million is held in reserve in the Taxpayer Relief Fund each year.

headline: 'A 100-year fix'
abstract: The Department of General Services is to begin repairing a portion of the water-damaged dome on the top of the Capitol building.  The dome is leaking due to decades of water damage.

headline: Prison’s power restored
abstract: Malfunctioning generators disrupted electricity and forced an inmate lockdown at SCI Somerset on Thursday.  Officials say that the public was never at risk, although visitation was suspended and inmantes were only allowed out of their cells for meals and controlled settings.

headline: Editorial: Helping Veterans
abstract: The Obama administartion and Congress must recomit to giving veterans the best care possible and allowing the Veterans Administrations budget to be passed a year in advance is recommended.

headline: Casey: Don’t ‘scapegoat’ workers
abstract: U.S. Senator  Bob Casey believes that critics opposed to the $34 billion dollar car industry bailout are "scapegoating" the workers. He also says the word bailout is inappropriate, because the automakers must pay that money back.

headline: 300 inducted into Voter Hall of Fame
abstract: About 300 Somerset County residents who have cast ballots in each of the past 50 elections have been inducted into the Pennsylvania Voter Hall of Fame.  Harry A. VanSickle, deputy secretary for administration with the Pennsylvania Department of State, spoke along with commissioners Pamela Tokar-Ickes, John Vatavuk and Jim Marker.

headline: THE POLITICS OF CHARTER 'SCANDALS'
abstract: In a score of articles and commentaries, local papers have made the terms "charter school" and "scandal" synonymous because of the highly questionable actions of two of the city's 60 charter operators. In a nutshell, two charter operators, Philadelphia Academy's Brien Gardiner and the Laboratory Charter School's June Brown, ran good schools but also paid themselves astronomical salaries. Once their fees were made public, a media feeding frenzy ensued, along with the predictable calls for more regulation. But as a longtime observer of Philadelphia charter schools, I have to ask the powers that be - what took you so long? Everyone knew it, and many in the charter community resented it.

headline: Lawmakers urge state police to add minority troopers
abstract: Members of the PA Legislative Black Caucus called for the state trooper agency to step up efforts to recruit African Americans. In a meeting with State Police Commander Jeffrey B. Miller, caucus members said they were alarmed by an Inquirer report in December showing that the number of minority troopers had dwindled to its lowest point since the 1980s. There are now 330 minorities in the agency's ranks, or about 7 percent of the total. That's down from more than 12 percent at its peak, in the late 1990s.

headline: null
abstract: Local newscast including four 6 year olds giving police a hard time in York County, electricity prices may rise, and Gov. Ed Rendell supporitng energy conservation.

headline: No Text
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell signed a bill into law that will provide volunteer firefighters with a state income tax credit of $100. The authors of the editorial believe the legislation is unlikely to entice more volunteers, and the amount isn’t enough to reward volunteer firefighters for the amount of time they spend training and the money they save local municipalities. However, the authors do welcome the small tax break even if it isn’t very much.

headline: null
abstract: Local newscast including a conference committee of local lawmakers that spent the last six months working on the smoking ban.

headline: NBC News at 11
abstract: There is support from some for a re-vote by the Democratic National Committee to allow delegates from Michigan and Florida to be seated. Chairman Howard Dean is open to it, but will not pay for it. The cost is approximately $30 million. PA Gov. Rendell and New Jersey Gov. John Corzine have offered to help fundraise for the re-vote.

headline: SRC delays renewal of Phila. Academy Charter
abstract: The Philadelphia School Reform Commission decided to delay a vote on whether or not to renew the Philadelphia Academy Charter School's operating charter in order to give the school district's inspector time to investigate charges of financial mismanagement. The Commission already voted to close down Germantown Settlement and Renaissance, but is renewing the operating charters of thirteen other charter schools.

headline: Assisted living rule changes upset some
abstract: Last summer, the state Legislature voted to create a new assisted living category that will allow 1,474 personal care homes to shift to the new assisted living category.  This new category will help with marketing and allow homes to retain patients longer and receive increased funding.  Critics complain, however, of the high licensing fees and the costs some personal care facilities might incur to remodel their facilities to fit the new definition.

headline: Payments to ex-gaming chief Neeb frozen
abstract: After a challenge by House Republicans, the PA Treasury Department is freezing severance payments to the former PA Gaming Control Board director.  Payments to former director Anne Neeb, who resigned from the agency in June, were suspended because the gaming board did not submit Neeb's severance contract to the attorney general.  Payments will be resumed pending the outcome of the attorney general's review of the contract.

headline: New memorials honor all who donned uniform
abstract: Two new gravesites have been erected in two Aaronsburg cemeteraies for veteran's graves, who can no longer be found.

headline: Unemployment at 5.2 percent in Delco
abstract: Delaware County sees a 0.8 percent unemployment increase over the past 6 months. It is currently at a 5.2 percent unemployment rate which is 15, 100 jobless out of a total workforce of 287,500.

headline: Pennsylvania House control at stake Tuesday
abstract: This November voters will head to the polls to decide the fate of the PA House.  Currently Democrats have a small lead of 102-101 in the lower chamber.  Political winds seem to be behind Democratic candidates this election.  The article discusses the most fruitful regional strategies that are being employed by each party.

headline: U.S. losing economic war, Rendell tells teachers
abstract: PA Governor Edward Rendell warned science educators at the National Science Foundation conference that the US is losing the economic competitiveness war. He says that the decline of American students’ math and science skills, failure of the nation’s education and training system and lack of political will are all leading to this loss. Rendell’s comments come the day before the PA State Board of Education is scheduled to vote on the controversial proposal he supports that requires students in PA to pass a standardized test in order to graduate from high school.

headline: Marriage curb fails, thankfully
abstract: Republican state senators dedicated to enshrining discrimination in PA's constitution tabled a bill that would ban same-sex marriage and civil unions. But there's little doubt this GOP bigotry bid will be back. As late as Tuesday morning supporters of the constitutional amendment were looking forward to a floor vote that again would call into question the Senate's collective judgment on what legislation best serves Pennsylvanians. The bill had been sent to the floor out of the Senate Appropriations committee where York County Republican Sens. Michael Waugh and Gibson Armstrong, sadly, were among the 18 Republicans voting to approve -- property tax, mass transit, education funding and health care problems aside -- the "marriage amendment."

headline: null
abstract: Local newscast including people stealing gas from underground at gas station and Gov. Ed Rendell's bill that would change how commercial breeders in the state treat animals.

headline: no text
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell stopped in Northumberland County to award state funds for an industrial park. In other news, there was a fire at a camp for kids in Wayne County.

headline: null
abstract: Local newscast including a Lewistown man serving time for rape wants to withdraw his guilty plea and go to trial, budget update as unions plan for if the budget doesn't pass by the deadline, and community members remember officers that lost their lives in the line of duty.

headline: Nearly $15 billion flows through Congress' 'favor factory'
abstract: The practice of decorating legislation with billions of dollars in pet projects is thriving on Capitol Hill -- despite public outrage that helped flip control of Congress two years ago. More than 11,000 of those "earmarks," worth nearly $15 billion in all, were slipped last year into legislation telling the government where to spend taxpayers' money this year, keeping them at the center of Washington's culture of money, influence and politics. Now comes an election-year encore. It's a pay-to-play sandbox where perceptions of waste and abuse often obscure the good that earmarks can do.

headline: State estimates tax deductions
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell has announced that gambling revenue will finally result in lower property taxes. School districts use the gambling revenue to reduce property taxes. However, the amount homeowners will save varies by school district, with the most relief being given to those in urban areas. Governor Rendell says that the amount of property taxes savings will increase as gambling revenue increases.

headline: Petition scandal casting pall over election in Pennsylvania Commentary
abstract: State Attorney General Tom Corbett claims that leaders of the House Democratic caucus used publicly-paid subordinates to inspect third-party candidate petitions.  The inspections were used to block third-party candidates considered threats to major Democratic candidates in 2004 and 2006.  The allegation--along with others related to the Bonusgate scandal--led to 12 arrests last month and angered supporters of Ralph Nader.

headline: Report says bypass surgery deaths down in 2006
abstract: According to a new report released today, mortality rates after heart bypass surgery have continued to decline in Pennsylvania hospitals.  Readmission rates for problems like heart failure and infection have also declined.

headline: DHL cutting U.S. jobs and locations, including Upper Macungie Township facility
abstract: Overnight-delivery giant DHL is cutting 9,500 American jobs and significantly reducing its air and ground operations in the United States, a spokesman for the German company said today.

headline: Local students at higher risk for failure
abstract: A Pennsylvania Office of Child Development and Early Learning report places local counties on a scale to determine the risk of student faliure. Blair County scored a 3.29 and Clearfield County a 3.43 on the 2007-08 Program Reach and County Risk Assessment report. A preschool director says a child's learning is impacted the most at the youngest age.

headline: Rhoades’ name still on ballot; special election possible
abstract: In spite of his recent death, State Sen. James J. Rhoades will still appear on the ballot when voters head to the polls this November.  If he is reelected a special election will be necessary to pick his successor.

headline: True cost: The state must study how best to pay for education
abstract: The author believes that the PA state Legislature needs to decide how to pay for education, which at the time is estimated to cost $21.9 billion, since the state has had a long known educational funding problem. The author believes that the first step is a resolution, already approved by the state House Education Committee, that would establish a 41-member Joint Legislative Commission on Public School Finance. As proposed, the panel, that would be chosen by legislative leaders and the governor would be headed by an expert in public school funding from one of the state's universities.

headline: Pa. starts effort to document African American history
abstract: The state Historical and Museum Commission plans to spend $285,000 to document African-American history in Pennsylvania. It is funded by a grant from the group Preserve America.

headline: null
abstract: National broadcast including gas prices, Gov. Ed Rendell's 75 year lease of the turnpike, and the new Indiana Jones film.

headline: no text
abstract: In light of the recent incident where two owners of a Berks County kennel shot and killed dozens of dogs to avoid taking them to the veterinarian, Governor Ed Rendell is trying to gain support for a bill to put tighter controls on kennels throughout PA.

headline: null
abstract: Local newscast including a prediction that this year will be another bad year for insects, renovations in the area supported by Gov. Rendell and the federal government.

headline: New season opens for stadium boxes
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Nutter gave tickets to the Phillies opening game to fifteen members of his staff. The Federal Bureau of Investigation investigated Former Mayor John Street under suspicion selling those seats in order to raise campaign money.

headline: State House tackles property taxes
abstract: PA state House members debated the change in the way that public schools are funded in PA; completely eliminating the $10 billion raised annually in school property taxes and replacing it with a higher personal income tax rate and sales taxes on many professional services. It is unlikely that PA Governor Edward Rendell would sign the bill because he is counting on slots casinos to help lower property taxes but does not believe that property taxes should be completely eliminated from the funding.

headline: null
abstract: A Lancaster family wins the powerball jack pot without purchasing a ticket.  They got the ticket for free.

headline: Strike proves costly for many
abstract: The Soudertown Area School District strike is proving costly to students, teacher and parents.  According to estimates, the average teacher could lose as much as 3,000 dollars, while the cost of childcare is increasing dramatically for those parents scrambling to find alternate child-care arrangements.  Both sides are scheduled to move to non-binding arbitration on Wednesday, but teachers may strike again in the spring if no agreement is reached.

headline: Speaker at Berks County Community Foundation meeting says schools stuck in 1980s
abstract: The problem with American schools is that most are stuck in the 1980s, an internationally known education expert told about 230 attendees at the Berks County Community Foundation annual meeting in the Sheraton Reading Hotel, Wyomissing, on Monday night.

headline: City to hand out fewer pink slips than expected today
abstract: Due to Philadelphia Mayor Michael Nutter's budget cuts, 145 city workers will be layed off today. This number is significantly less than the proposed 220 fulltime positions eliminated, 600 unfilled positions and 2,000 seasonal or part time jobs.

headline: Editorial: At Last, The Parade
abstract: For the first time in 25 years the best place on Earth will be standing along Broad and Market Streets in Philadelphia as the city celebrates its first sports championship in decades.

headline: Turn to community colleges.
abstract: The columnist discusses the importance of community colleges and criticizes Governor Ed Rendell's fiscal budget, which allots community colleges a 3% increase in operating support but no new capital dollars.

headline: Pittsburgh to recognize unmarried partners
abstract:
Pittsburgh will recognize long-term commitments of unmarried partners, allowing both gay and straight couples to share employee benefits. The bill passed yesterday in a 7-1 vote, bringing cheers from the audience. Under the new law, two city residents who are not too closely related to be married under state law are eligible to show evidence of their relationship. A $25 fee makes the registration official. 
Employers could use the registration to grant shared benefits, though there is no obligation.

newspaper: Allegheny County Council targets power outages
headline: Allegheny County Council targets power outages
abstract: Because of three days of storms that caused about 22,200 power outages in the North Hills, Allegheny County Council members urged the Public Utility Commission to investigate the frequency of Duquesne Light power outages. Jim burn, who chairs the council’s Public Safety Committee, said the committee is hoping to meet with Duquesne Power next week to discuss what the company is doing to prevent power outages similar to the one last August, when 90,000 customers lost power. Duquesne Power officials claim they haven’t received an increase in customer complaints, and while the average length of time for each outage has increased since 2004, the frequency of outages has decreased.

headline: no text
abstract: It could take months to get the man accused of raping a four-year old girl in July extradited from Kansas back to Clearfield County, and State College police are investigating an attempted burglary that ended in gunshots. Governor Ed Rendell was in Centre County to push his proposal to use Pennsylvania’s forest to create cellulose ethanol for fuel. Cellulose ethanol could be made with scrap wood, which PA has a lot of, and U.S. Representative John Peterson supports the proposal.

headline: null
abstract: Local newscast including Brown pleads guilty to third degree murder, several firefighters evaluated for heat exhaustion, state Senator Vincent Fumo fainted at the State Capitol, and Penn Dot tries to keep driver from hitting trees.

headline: New This Morning
abstract: PA Gov. Rendell has offered to help fundraise for a revote to determine whether to seat Florida and Michigan delegates. It is an ongoing controversy.

headline: State law may take cash from districts
abstract: Although there are a few exceptions, Senate Bill 1247, sponsored by state Senator James Rhoades, and House Bill 1438, sponsored by state Representative Tim Seip, would essentially prohibit tax authorities from issuing "spot appeals"  in Third through Eighth Class counties. Spot appeals are often used by school districts to appeal assessments of properties that sell for more than their assessed values. The bills were passed in response to citizens who complained about receiving dramatic property tax increases due to spot appeals, and if the bills are approved by Governor Rendell, school districts, including Weatherly Area and Tamaqua Area School Districts, could be forced to make up thousands of dollars in lost revenue.

headline: null
abstract: Governor Rendell announces that the Erie Art Museum will receive a 1.5 million dollar grant from the state to facilitate museum expansion.

headline: Regional police force study would be worthwhile
abstract: Penn Township and the Duncannon and Marysville boroughs should take the PA Department of Commuunity and Economic Development up on its offer to pay for a study that would look at combining police forces.  Marysville and Penn Township are facing major growth spurts and all three communities struggle to provide police coverage--a problem a regional force would ameliorate.  The communities have nothing to lose by taking part in the study and much to gain if it works out.

headline: New Jersey transit czar calls for stimulus
abstract: New Jersey state Transportation Commissioner Kris Kolluri is following the lead of many other state officals nationwide and calling for a national econoimic stimulus package that includes money for highway projects.

headline: Councilman wants to cancel raises for 9 legislators
abstract: Pittsburgh Councilman Ricky Burgess proposed that he will cancel the 2.5 percent raises that the city's nine legislators, like all non-union employees would have received in Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl's 2009 budget. Burgess says that government must make sacrifices in this economy.

headline: Study finds county has fewer older workers than Pa. average
abstract: The article discusses the demographics of the area's worker population.  It focuses mostly on workers over the age of 55.

headline: Two board members deride city schools' proposed code of conduct
abstract: The Pittsburgh school board is considering legislation which would require members to submit to stricter rules on confidentiality, clearing constituent complaints with Superintendent Mark Roosevelt before making them public. It would also require members to accept the will of the majority once decisions have been made, effectively silencing member Mark Brentley Sr.'s continuing criticism of a 2006 round of school closing. Member Thomas Sumpter believes the proposal is in accord with core beliefs adopted from and provided by the PA School Boards Association.

headline: State amendment would ban 'counterfeit' marriage
abstract: The columnist believes people should support Senate Bill 1250. If passed by both houses of the legislature and approved by referendum, it would ban gay marriage as well as civil unions in Pennsylvania.

headline: Allegheny County Council targets power outages
abstract: Reacting to weekend storms, Allegheny County Council members said they don't want to see neighbors end up in the dark. Councilman Matt Drozd urged the Public Utility Commission to investigate the frequency of Duquesne Light power outages in the North Hills after observing what he believed to be increased outages. Officials in North Hills communities including McCandless, Shaler, Ross and West View said they have not received complaints about service. Duquesne Light spokesman Joseph Vallarian said there has not been an increase in formal complaints. Jim Burn who chairs the council's Public Safety Committee, said the committee hopes to meet with Duquesne Light to discuss what the utility company is doing to prevent a repeat of August's utility woes.

headline: No Text
abstract: Johnstown police said there are some promising leads and evidence, and they are confident that arrests are coming against those who vandalized a Kernville church. Governor Ed Rendell signed an execution warrant for Robert Rega, who was convicted of killing a night watchman during a robbery at Cook Forest State Park, but prosecutors still aren’t convinced he will be executed. Richard Barger was arrested and charged with attempted murder for stabbing Ryan Morgan, and in another stabbing in Centre County, a teenage boy was stabbed twice in the back near an elementary school.

headline: null
abstract: Local newscast including budget agreement reached.

headline: News 10 Today
abstract: US Sen. Hillary Clinton and former President Bill Clinton pushed a Hillary-Obama ticket in Mississippi prior to the state's primary. Obama flatly denied any aspirations to VP rather than President. Instead, he noted that both Hillary and US Sen. John McCain supported Bush's plan to go into Iraq. Previously, US Sen. Tom Daschle and PA Gov. Rendell were guests on the show.

headline: State to investigate poll changes
abstract: The PA Human Relations Commission said it will investigate allegations of voter discrimination by the Bucks County Board of Elections. In April, the commission received a formal complaint concerning election polls moved out of the Creekside apartment complex in Bensalem. At that time, state officials said they weren't sure whether the allegations fell under the scope of their agency's charter or met conditions of timeliness. A provision of the commission's charter also stipulates that complaints be filed 180 days after the alleged discriminatory act. The polls were moved more than a year ago.

headline: null
abstract: The State Gaming Board will hear more testimony about a possible change of ownership for the north-shor casino. The Board will hear from both the public and local leaders and will decide whether to approove an ownership transfer from Don Barden to Neal Bluhm.  Barden does not have money to pay contractors and casino construction has been halted.

headline: null
abstract: The PA state House of Representative approved legislation that will improve conditions for dogs at kennels.  The bill will increase the size of cages, require annual vet checkups, and crack down on inhumane treatment.

headline: Veteran state representative seeking Rhoades' seat
abstract: Republican state Rep. David G. Argall of Tamaqua announced Monday he is running in the pending special election to fill the vacant state Senate seat in the 29th District centered in Schuylkill County.

headline: Skrepenak: County plans to lay off 66 employees
abstract: Luzerne County Commissioner Greg Skrepenak said officials are planning to lay off another 66 employees this month to address county tax revenue problems.

headline: Schools, prevention are focus of Reading's anti-gang efforts
abstract: Reading officials are looking to develop a comprehensive gang-prevention program.  Study results of the local student population have been sobering.  In-school education is expected to be a big focus of the program.  A survey of 2000 students 10-17 showed that 14% belonged to a gang and that 9% currently belong to one.  66% of students say they know a gang member.

headline: Two Mechanicsburg schools fail to meet their progress goals
abstract: Two schools in the Mechanicsburg Area School District did not meet Adequate Yearly Progress goals mandated by the federal No Child Left Behind Act. The PA Department of Education will soon release complete scores on the PA System of Schools Assessment test, and while most of the district did well, Mechanicsburg Middle School and Elmwood Elementary School failed to meet AYP targets.

headline: State police seeking more diversity
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell signed an executive order that established an Office of Diversity Management, the Governor’s Diversity Planning Council and the Governor’s Executive Diversity Council to try to promote more diversity within the state’s agencies. The state will first concentrate on promoting more diversity within the public safety sector, which encompasses a number of different agencies, and the state police will hold a recruitment event to try to attract more minority and female officers. Only 305 of the 4,414 state troopers are women and minorities, and other agencies have also been invited to the recruitment event.

headline: Allowing a choice keeps rates down
abstract: The price of electricity could increase 40 percent by 2010 as a result of deregulation of the industry, but Gibson Armstrong argues against capping rates. He argues that whether the market is regulated or unregulated, electricity prices will still increase in the future, and the competition of the open market is essential for spurring innovation, offering choice to consumers and keeping costs down.
