abstract: Local newscast including car crash, 15-year old missing after meeting someone she met on MySpace, state budget deadline looming, and crime rates have dropped in PA according to Penn State.

headline: Officials at odds over slots money
abstract: State legislators and Washington County officials disagree over how to use revenues from The Meadows Racetrack and Casino.  County Commission Chairman Larry Maggi and Commissioner Diana Irey favor using revenue to provide property tax relief, while state legislators would like to see the money used for economic and capital projects, as well as water and sewer projects.

headline: Hearing to examine life terms for minors
abstract: State lawmakers will examine why Pennsylvania sentences more juveniles to life in prison without parole than any other state or country.  The Senate Judiciary Committee will hear testimony from opponents and proponents of lifetime sentences and will analyze data from a study released by the University of San Fransisco's Center for Law and Global Justice.

headline: Paulson bails out on his bailout plan
abstract: Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson's announcement Wednesday that he is abandoning the plan to buy troubled bank assets shows that he has come to two conclusions about what was once the chief focus of his $700 billion bank bailout plan: The first is that it wouldn't work. The second is that the economists and financial experts who agitated to inject capital directly into the banking system were right all along.

headline: The holiday sprit was alive and well this afternoon at Fort Indiantown Gap in Lebanon county
abstract: In January, 6,000 National Guard soldiers will be deployed to Iraq.  That is the National Guard's largest deployment since World War II.

headline: As Pa. deadline passes, Democratic registration at all-time high
abstract: With enthusiasm skyrocketing, officials say they have received thousands of new registrations.  They also say that the edge that Democrats have in registration is only expanding.  In Philadelphia, the margin stands at 6-to-1 in favor of Democrats.

headline: PennDOT rejects Ebensburg’s efforts to retake roads, limit trucks
abstract: Borough officials from Ebensburg have been trying to gain control of the state-owned High and Center streets for almost 10 years in order to impose weight limits on trucks and force them to take detours around the borough. However, the PA Department of Transportation denied their request.

headline: Council's expansion discussed at hearing
abstract: Hospitals have been a focus of the PA Health Care Cost Containment Council, a 22-year-old agency touted as a national leader in prying out data related to cost and quality of care. The council, known as PHC4, has compared hospitals on factors such as mortality rates and the number of patients with hospital-acquired infections. Health insurers and outpatient medical facilities might soon find themselves under a similar spotlight. The law that created the council expires at the end of the month. Lawmakers must decide whether to reauthorize the independent state agency.

headline: Gas drilling may aid NEPA’s economy
abstract: The impact of natural gas drilling in Decatur, Texas can be measured in the height of its new hotels and the width of the potholes on its roads. A La Quinta Inn and a Hampton Inn are rising on the North Texas horizon as gas companies explore the Barnett Shale beneath the soil. The new rooms will house the legions of workers who run the drills, drive the trucks and support the operations of the gas companies. After seven years of gas exploration, the city’s nine hotels and a nearly finished 112-unit apartment complex are already booked.

headline: Pa. works to stop illegal gambling
abstract: Since PA is trying to get into the slot machine business county investigators have been “cracking” down on unauthorized gambling. The new enforcement approach comes after PA Governor Edward Rendell legalized gambling and asked local authorities to go after small-time operators.

abstract: Local newscast including Gov. Rendell is expected to sign the clean air act and demonstrations at Penn State.

In other news, hikers will celebrate the 60th anniversary of the first end to end hiking of the entire Northumberland trail.

abstract: Local newscast including family of murder victim respond to allegations that her boyfriend killed her, smoking ban update, Gov. Ed Rendell trying to get more school funding, and budget talks.

headline: McCain works to win over Pennsylvania's leery conservatives
abstract: Senator John McCain attempted to convince conservative voters at town-hall meetings in Pennsylvania that he will continue to embrace traditional conservative policies regarding taxes, judicial appointments and small government.  This was part of a two-day road trip to Republican strongholds in PA.

headline: Time short for reform in House
abstract: Although the PA state Senate has approved legislation that will make government more transparent and accountable, the state House of Representatives has not yet passed similar reform legislation.  State Senator Joe Scarnati, president pro tempore of the Senate, is calling on the House to approve seven bills which will increase accountability and make the legislative process more open.

headline: Changes to teacher education could strain colleges
abstract: Sweeping changes in the way Pennsylvania colleges prepare future elementary and middle school teachers are causing an outcry from university who say they will not be able to adapt to the change in the certificate process.

headline: Fifth district congressman John Peterson says his fight against tolls on interstate 80 - won't end with his retirement in January.
abstract: Congressman John Peterson will continue to oppose tolling on interstate 80.  The federal government already rejected Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell's taxing proposal, but he plans to resubmit it again next year.

headline: Hiring freeze won't affect Pa. open-records office
abstract: The Office of Open Records, recently established under the state's new open records law will not have to comply with the state's hiring freeze, says Governor Rendell.  The freeze was designed to save $200 million in costs, but the state has promised to make open records a priority.

headline: PennDOT squeezed
abstract: In light of gas that costs $4 per gallon, drivers nationwide are cutting back on driving. This has resulted in $100 million less being collected during the past fiscal year in PA from gas-tax revenues, and the same is expected to happen next fiscal year. As of now, the PA Department of Transportation hasn’t planned any cuts, and it will try to increase efficiency to make up for the lost revenue, but the revenue loss could have an impact on the new budget’s call to fix 400 deficient bridges, and it has drawn concern from state Representative John Evans and members of the road construction industry.

headline: Counties get grants to battle West Nile
abstract: PA Gov. Ed Rendell has announced the availability of $5.3 million to combat the spread of West Nile Virus. Fayette, Indiana, and Westmoreland are among those counties slotted to receive funds. The 2008-2009 budget includes over $7 million for the West Nile Virus control program.

headline: Gas prices down two cents
abstract: The Philadelphia (5-county) gas average fell 2 cents to $3.06 - same as a month ago. Pennsylvania down 3 cents to $3.07; South Jersey down 2 cents to $2.84 - same as a month ago; National down 2 cents to $2.98.

headline: Perrysville volunteers mark a century of firefighting
abstract: Perrysville Volunteer Fire Department is celebrating its 100th birthday this year, and a brief history of the company is provided in the article. For many of the company’s members, it has become a family tradition to join the fire company; however, fire-fighting training now requires a lot more hours than in the past, which discourages many younger people from joining. Several bills to provide aid to fire fighters are under consideration in the PA Legislature, and two members of the fire company expressed their appreciation towards the PA Legislature and Governor Ed Rendell for recently approving a bill to give volunteer fire fighters a $100 tax credit, but they weren’t convinced it would be enough to encourage more volunteers.

headline: PennDOT's arrogance
abstract: According to editorial, the PA Department of Transportation (PennDOT) has known about potential problems with hundreds of bridges in the Pittsburgh area for over 20 years, including a section of the Birmingham Bridge that recently dropped a foot. PennDOT announced it was reviewing 241 bridges with similar problems to the Birmingham Bridge, but they won’t release the names of all the bridges until inspections are completed. The authors believe PennDOT’s inspections could take years, and they have an obligation to identify the bridges to the public now.

Senate Republicans are encouraging a House bill to extend the subsidy to the end of 2008. The subsidy was provided through a tax increase on cigarettes and a surcharge on traffic tickets.

headline: PennDOT's arrogance
abstract: Hundreds of bridges in the Greater Pittsburgh Area could be catastrophes waiting to happen. Yet, PennDOT won't identify which ones? It was on Feb. 8 that a southbound section of Pittsburgh's Birmingham Bridge across the Monongahela River dropped nearly a foot. A rocker bearing failed. That's what bridge superstructures rest upon to accommodate temperature-related expansion and contraction. The failure caused a 60-foot bridge pier to move. It will have to be replaced. PennDOT knew of the potential problem for 20 years. Two years ago, it deemed the problem insignificant.

headline: Earll explains vote on smoking ban
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell plans to sign a bill Friday that bans smoking in workplaces and public spaces across Pennsylvania. State Sen. Jane Earll didn't vote for the bill, and said Wednesday she still opposes it. Earll  was one of nine state senators who voted against the ban. State Sen. Mary Jo White, of Franklin, R-21st Dist., also voted against it. The bill passed 41-9 and now goes to Rendell for his signature. It will take effect 90 days after he signs it. The compromise ban allows smoking in many public places, including drinking establishments where food is 20 percent or less of annual sales; private clubs; and up to 25 percent of a casino floor -- 50 percent if the casino can prove to the state that the ban is harming business.

headline: How a bill passed in the wee hours by state lawmakers 12 years ago set the stage for surging electricity rates.
abstract: Pushed by Enron and crafted behind closed doors, the 84-page measure to deregulate PA's electric industry was slipped into a bill that called only for a one-word change in the state's taxicab law. Passage by bleary-eyed lawmakers came in a last-minute vote in the middle of the night. Nearly 12 years have passed since then, and there's yet another year and a half to go before electricity deregulation takes full effect in the Lehigh Valley. Instead of going down, PPL Corp.'s rates are expected to surge an unprecedented 34 percent for homes and up to 43 percent for some businesses on Jan. 1, 2010, when a cap on what the Allentown company can charge for electricity is due to expire.

headline: Phila. Crime-fighting cameras arrive slowly
abstract: When Philadelphia Mayor John Street announced the installation of 250 digital video cameras in some of the cities most dangerous neighborhoods to deter crime, it seemed like a feasible project. Then Democratic candidate for Mayor, Michael Nutter, was an enthusiastic supporter. Yet five months later, only one camera has been installed. Philadelphia Chief Information Officer, Terry M. Phillis, assures that the project, behind schedule, can still be completed by October. Contractor Unisys Corp. said coordination with Peco and the Southeastern PA Transit Authority was underestimated.

headline: Pennsylvania bridge project list includes local spans
abstract: Delays on Interstate 81 will continue as a massive multimillion-dollar statewide bridge repair project addresses several local spans, state Department of Transportation spokeswoman Karen Dussinger said. Out of 1,400 bridges targeted for repair across PA, several local bridges will receive extensive work, including eight bridges between mile markers 192 and 195 in Lackawanna County. Traffic will be restricted to single lanes, first northbound, then southbound, through June 2009. Work has also begun on Griffin Pond Road in South Abington Township, which means traffic along Route 2109 will be diverted to a 2-mile detour along Johnson Road. That runs through the end of this summer.

headline: Even if GOP plan works, it will be inadequate
abstract: In January 2007, Gov. Ed Rendell introduced Cover All Pennsylvanians, a plan to provide health insurance coverage for the uninsured. This past March the Democratic House leadership introduced a new plan, called Pennsylvania Access to Better Care (PA ABC), to insure about 275,000 uninsured adults over the next five years. That plan passed with substantial Republican support soon after. Since March, the Senate Republican leadership has blocked consideration of this legislation. Now, in June, only weeks before the summer recess, a small group of Senate Republicans have come forward with their own proposal for providing health care for the uninsured.

headline: Latest News: Pennsylvania calls for energy strategy to be implemented
abstract: PA Gov. Rendell introduced the Energy Independence Strategy for PA to address rising oil prices. He is urging the PA General Assembly to act quickly. The PennSecurity Fuels Initiative is central to the plan, which calls for the state to produce and consume 1 billion gallons of renewable transportation fuels a year and that those fuels should be produced in state. The Governor's proposals passed overwhelmingly in the House of Representatives. The PA Senate has time to act yet, but needs to act in time to implement legislation before current price regulations expire.

headline: Philly news anchor embroiled in e-mail hacking scandal
abstract: The FBI raided the home of an evening news anchor after his fired co-anchor complained that someone might be hacking into her private e-mails and leaking them to the media, lawyers involved said Monday. Larry Mendte of KYW-TV remains off-air following the FBI raid, during which authorities removed a computer and computer-related equipment. Former co-anchor Alycia Lane, who was fired Jan. 7 after a series of embarrassing off-camera incidents, began to suspect this year that her private e-mails were being accessed and forwarded to news outlets that have covered her career and social life. Her lawyer, Paul Rosen, said Lane did not identify any potential hacking suspects. But he noted Lane was earning $700,000 a year, when she was fired.

abstract: After a bridge collapsed in Minneapolis about a year ago, Governor Ed Rendell said PA must focus on fixing bridges considered structurally deficient, and he signed a law authorizing the Department of Transportation to borrow $350 million to start making repairs on 411 bridges during the 2008-09 fiscal year. He said now is a good time to borrow because interest rates are low and construction costs are expected to rise in the future. Key projects in Lackawanna, Luzerne, Bradford, Monroe, Susquehanna and Wayne Counties are listed in the article.

France about whether Adams’ company, Rosewood Real Estate, is living up to agreements with the facility’s former operators and the state to reopen the hospital. He has acknowledge that he has not heard from the PA state Department of Health about his application for a medical license to operate a hospital.

headline: Lawmaker’s populist pricing hits a roadblock
abstract: Sen. James Rhoades is on a populist march this election year introducing resolutions to cap college tuition and urge federal action to control gas prices and require greater public disclosure about trading in energy commodities. These proposals may seem like obvious crowd-pleasers. Yet, the Rhoades resolution calling on Congress to develop a strategy to control gas prices ran into trouble last week in the Senate Environmental Resources and Energy Committee. The panel voted 6-3 to table the resolution.  Sen. Anthony Williams spoke against the resolution, saying it’s not specific enough and could give Congress political cover to take actions that he opposes, such as opening the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge to oil drilling.

abstract: University of Pittsburgh police have teamed up with the City of Pittsburgh DUI Task Force and city police to gain access to a $152,000 grant to the city to crack down on impaired driving and underage drinking. headline: Pennsylvania must repair its roads and bridges and improve its mass transit; tolling I-80 is the fairest way to get it done, argues PETER JAVSICAS
abstract: Peter Javsicas believes that investments in the maintenance of highway infrastructure as well as mass transit are extremely important. He doesn’t think that Governor Ed Rendell’s proposal to lease the PA Turnpike is a particularly attractive option for raising money, and he feels that putting tolls on Interstate 80 is the best way to raise necessary funds. Critics of the proposal to toll Interstate 80 have said that it would cause local businesses along the highway to relocate and truckers to avoid using the road; however, Javsicas doubts any of these claims would actually come true.

headline: Federal grant helps fund program for at-risk youth
abstract: U.S. Sen. Bob Casey and U.S. Rep. Mike Doyle, D-Forest Hills, announced a grant, for at-risk youth programs at East End Cooperative Ministry, at a news conference in the basement of Crossroads United Methodist Church in East Liberty. The money will be a huge chunk of the ministry's now-$700,000 budget for its Points of Healthy Youth Sustainability Engagement and Development (PHYSED) program. The grant came as part of the Commerce, Justice and Science Appropriations Bill recently approved by Congress.

headline: Natural gas line faces doubt from property owners
abstract: Al Hartman focused on the Google Earth looping video of Spectra Energy's proposed corridor for a roughly 30-mile natural gas pipeline that would run from Lancaster County through southern York County. The Hellam Township resident watched as a yellow line depicted on the aerial video passed over the Susquehanna River, curving gently as it followed existing utility rights-of way. About 65 residents, including Hartman, attended Spectra Energy's informational meeting Tuesday evening at the Hellam Township Building.

headline: Pittsburgh firefighter sues over suspension for diabetes
abstract: A Pittsburgh firefighter is going to federal court to fight what he says is his wrongful suspension for having Type I diabetes. Christopher Guzzy says in the lawsuit that he was hired in February 2006 and diagnosed with the disease in March 2007. Guzzy's doctor placed him on a month's medical leave and the city put him on indefinite suspension without pay in April 2007. Guzzy says he can perform the essential duties of his job despite the illness and wants his job back, with back pay. The city did not immediately respond to the suit filed Thursday. Type I diabetes usually begins in childhood. It is caused when a person's immune system destroys pancreatic cells that make insulin.

headline: Pike deal beats earlier transportation funding plan, Rendell says
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell insists that leasing the Pennsylvania Turnpike for $12.8 billion is a better deal than the transportation funding plan he signed into law last year. But is it good enough to persuade the Legislature to cede operational control of the turnpike, a move that would threaten hundreds of jobs? The General Assembly must approve any deal. Rendell might find backing from unusual sources and opposition from his typical allies. Abertis Infraestructuras, one of the world's largest toll road operators, offered the highest of three bids submitted for a 75-year lease. In return, the leasing company would retain the rights to all tolls and revenue from food and fuel concessions.

headline: GOP, Dem health plans differ
abstract: State Senate Republicans unveiled a health plan that is similar in some ways to a plan favored by House Democrats and Gov. Ed Rendell but strikingly different on a key issue: providing health care to more uninsured people. The Democrats' plan, which would require higher taxes, would extend affordable health insurance to small businesses and the uninsured, with subsidized coverage for people with low incomes. The GOP plan, by contrast, would enhance care available at community health centers; promote a program for hospitals and specialists to donate their services to help the uninsured; and create a high-risk insurance pool for those who cannot find coverage elsewhere. The plan, known as HealthNET PA, does not call for a tax increase.

headline: Pittsburgh's federal anti-crime funds trimmed
abstract: The U.S. Department of Justice has cut the maximum amount of anti-crime Weed and Seed money that three portions of Pittsburgh may receive this year by $200,000, according to Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl. The change reflects a 35-percent decrease in the amount Congress has allocated to such programs nationwide. In 2007, Weed and Seed had $49.36 million available; in 2008, it is expected to have $32.1 million.

headline: Venango County man honored in Harrisburg

Larry Say, a Historical and Museum Commission employee, received the 2008 Governor's Award for Excellence in the cost savings category, representing Venango County among eight other award winning regions. Say, a site maintenance foreman at the Drake Well Museum, has completed various initiatives at the local landmark, as well as Pithole City and Oil Creek State Park. His construction project, which include help in creating and designing the Oil Transportation Exhibit building and organizing a workforce from the PA Conservation Corp, have routinely been completed at reduced costs.

headline: Group: Walk in their shoes
abstract: Many Pennsylvanians are dying for health insurance. To illustrate this grim statistic, the health care coalition dumped dozens of pairs of shoes outside the Bensalem district office of state Sen. Tommy Tomlinson. The shoes represented the 188 uninsured Pennsylvanians the group says will die if the Senate doesn't take action on a bill that would expand state-subsidized health insurance. Senate Bill 1137 includes the PA Access to Basic Care program, which would provide state-sponsored insurance to nearly 273,000 adults within five years. The bill also would help doctors pay for medical-malpractice coverage and offer grants to make insurance more affordable to small businesses.

headline: Punishment lite: Former Rep. Habay should face more time
abstract: Former PA Representative Jeff Habay was convicted in 2005 of forcing state employees to do campaign work, and in 2007, he pleaded no contest to 21 other criminal counts. After spending only a week in jail, he was allowed to be confined to house arrest while awaiting an appeal of his 2005 conviction, which the state Supreme Court ultimately rejected; however, Common Pleas Judge Jeffrey Manning decided that he could serve the rest of his sentence in a halfway house or under house arrest. The authors of the editorial believe Judge Manning was far too lenient on Habay, and they feel that if someone abuses the public trust, they should go to jail, including Habay and anyone convicted in the upcoming Bonusgate scandal.

Former PA Senate Majority Leader David Brightbill said he has no regrets about his handling of the pay raise and pension controversies, which ultimately cost him when he lost his 2006 primary to current Senator Mike Folmer, and he declined to speak out about the current "bonusgate" scandal because his new lobbying position involves work with the state Legislature. Additionally, a 1930’s street care travelled from Baltimore to Lancaster.

abstract: U.S. Senator Bob Casey was chosen to address the Democratic National Convention.  At the convention,  the Democratic Party will announce its nomination of Senator Barack Obama for president.  Senator Casey's father, former PA Governor Robert P. Casey, was denied the opportunity to speak in 1992.

headline: Lost funds jeopardize repairs to 3 Berks bridges
abstract: Because the federal government rejected Pennsylvania's plan to toll Interstate 80, three Berks County bridge projects are in jeopardy.  County planners were expecting to use revenue from I-80 tolls to repair three local bridges, but now must rely on other funding sources.  Some potential sources are revenue generated from incresing the state gas tax, or revenue generated from leasing the PA Turnpike; both proposals are currently under consideration.

headline: More DEP woes for Erie Coke
abstract: Erie Coke Corp. has exceeded pollution limits eight times since June 23, when the state Department of Environmental Protection socked the company with a $6.1 million fine, DEP inspectors have said.

headline: The bailout Claus
abstract: A Christmas parody about the economic bailouts of large companies and the recession.

headline: Onorato: Port Authority may be broke by Dec. 1
abstract: County Chief Executive Dan Onorato said that the Port Authority of Allegheny County is about to lose money in 2 months if other funding doesn't appear.  The Authority is trying to negotiate a deal with its union regarding health care and pension costs.

headline: Votes near on $800 million for water, sewer projects
abstract: Experts believe PA could face up to $20 billion in spending over the next 10 to 15 years to improve how it deals with its aging water and sewage systems. The state House approved a bill sponsored by state Senator Jane Earll that would authorize $800 million in borrowing for such projects, but an amendment to include $35 million to repair hazardous dams was added, so the bill will go back to the Senate. The House also sent a bill sponsored by state Senator Raphael Musto back to the Senate that would ask voters to approve an additional $400 million in borrowing for sewer and water projects.

headline: Health-care reform deserves support
abstract: Richard McVay is responding to an earlier article titled "Health care on life support," and he believes PA Access to Basic Health Care could reverse the trend. While Ralph Pontillo, president of the Manufacturers and Business Association, is against the proposal, McVay claims his judgment may be clouded, and he believes the plan would offer an affordable health care alternative that would benefit small businesses. He says Governor Ed Rendell has provided the leadership, and he is hopeful that Republicans won’t prevent long-overdue reform.

headline: No Text
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell signed a bill to increase the development of biodiesel fuels. He eventually wants $1 billion of gas to come from renewable sources to help reduce Pennsylvania’s reliance on foreign oil. In addition, a fire could destroy thousands of California homes, and a popular hybrid car will soon be available in the U.S.

headline: Rally in Philadelphia Calls for Renewal of Ban on Assault Weapons
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell joined Philadelphia Mayor Michael Nutter, members of the General Assembly and the entire command staff of the Philadelphia P.D. to call on Congress to renew the assault weapons ban. The original legislation was enacted under the Clinton administration, but expired in 2004.

In addition, there have been problems of theft at a local pool, and an adult and a juvenile have been taken into custody; though no charges have yet been filed.

abstract: The author interviews comedian Stephen Colbert.

headline: Inmate release notification system ready
abstract: When an inmate leaves jail in Allegheny and Fayette counties, interested people can now be alerted to it automatically by phone or email. Victims groups say steps like this go a long way for piece of mind for victims, but prisoner groups say it is a broad over reach and the system is unfair.

headline: Science PSSA scores released; Bethlehem Area, Easton Area school districts rank at bottom in Northampton County
abstract: Two of Northampton's city school districts and Bethlehem Area School District's  high school students performed poorly on standardized science exams. Less than half of each district's students scored basic or below basic.

headline: Free clinics critical for health of Pennsylvanians
abstract: Senate Bill 5 would create a Community-Based Health Care Program to help fund and support health centers throughout the state.  These health centers provide a crucial safety net for the poor and uninsured.  With economic times getting tougher, it is likely that an increasing amount of people will need the services provided by these free clinics.

headline: Votes near on $800 million for water, sewer projects
abstract: Legislation that would authorize $800 million in borrowing for municipal water and sewer projects was advanced by the state House. A final House vote on the proposal, which originated in the Senate, could come as soon as today. But because the bill was amended to include $35 million to repair ''high-hazard dams,'' it must return to the Senate for further action. The plan sponsored by Sen. Jane Earll, R-Erie, would pay off the borrowing through slot machine gambling revenue. The money would be doled out by a state agency known as the Commonwealth Financing Authority.

headline:
Hershey Med’s doctors help China’s ALS treatment take 
A CLINICAL APPROACH
abstract: Doctors from the Penn State Milton S. Hershey Medical Center went to Tianjin, China to set up a clinic for patients with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis, a fatal and incurable disease that’s also known as Lou Gehrig’s disease. The clinic will be modeled after the one in Hershey, and it will provide services to add to the patient’s quality of life. The partnership between the two medical facilities will also help Hershey by providing increased research opportunities.

headline: No Text
abstract: Governor Rendell will sign an alternative fuel bill. Consumers will now be eligible for grants and rebates to weatherize their homes, and they can receive partial reimbursement for installing solar energy technology. An additional $40 million will also be available to help low income homes pay for heating during the winter.

headline: Regola releases statement following acquittal
abstract: The article provides a statement given by PA Senator Robert Regola after he was acquitted by a jury of all charges. He is disappointed with the district attorney for filing unfounded charges against him and for prolonging the tragedy of the death of Lou Farrell. After a brief amount of time with his family, he will be available to answer questions from the media.

Mechanicsburg policemen are searching for a suspect who tried to stab a woman in her home, and police in Lebanon are looking for the men who robbed a convenience store. Governor Ed Rendell named a temporary replacement for the head of the State Police, former White House Press Secretary Tony Snow died from cancer, and the nation’s largest mortgage companies are struggling financially.

headline: Flight 93 temporary memorial to be moved at crash site
abstract: The National Park Service is moving the site of the Flight 93 National Memorial across Skyline Road after failing to reach a deal with the landowner. A temporary tribute has been there since 2001. Park service officials said the actual move will begin in about two weeks, though site preparation will start sooner. By mid-August, all of the artifacts on or around the temporary memorial’s chain-link fence, benches, flags, cross, angels, large stones and shelter will be relocated to land recently acquired by Families of Flight 93.

headline: null
abstract: A state judge upheld Governor Rendell's authority to furlough state workers when a state budget is not passed on time.  State employee unions contend that furloughs could be avoided by paying state employees with un-appropriated money.  The judge ruled this was unconstitutional.

headline: null

headline: JUST SAYING NO
abstract: A survey of thousands of students across Pennsylvania found growing numbers are saying no to drugs and alcohol. Some observers said in-school, anti-drug curricula are probably a factor.

headline: Merge not: A Highmark-IBC merger would handcuff health-care reform
abstract: The writer argues that merging insurance giants, Highmark and Independence Blue Cross, is a bad deal for consumers because it leads to higher prices. The author also writes that President-elect Barack Obama says a lack of competition raises prices. The Pennsylvania Senate Banking and Insurance Committee, the House Insurance Committee and the state insurance commissioner are looking into the issue of this potential merging.

headline: In Pa., it’s ‘Walk to School Day’ this morning
abstract: Students from 225 PA schools will walk to school as a part of a program that sets out to prevent childhood obesity.  According to recent studies, less than 15 percent of students walk to school these days.

headline: Hint of Hope as Child Obesity Rate Hits Plateau
abstract: Childhood obesity appears to have hit a plateau, a potentially significant milestone in the battle against excessive weight gain among children. But the finding, based on survey data gathered from 1999 to 2006 by the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention and published in an issue of The Journal of the American Medical Association, was greeted with guarded optimism. It is not clear if the lull in childhood weight gain is permanent or even if it is the result of public anti-obesity efforts to limit junk food and increase physical activity in schools. Doctors noted that even if the trend held up, 32 percent of American schoolchildren remained overweight or obese, representing an entire generation that will be saddled with weight-related health problems as it ages.

headline: No Text
abstract: New mine safety regulations were signed into law today. They are the first major changes to the state’s mining law in 50 years, and they are in response a recent incident where nine miners were rescued at Cue Creek. In addition, eight people were already injured while running from the bulls during a festival in Pamplona, Spain.

headline: Rendell Pushes Stricter Handgun Bill During Memorial For Slain Officers
abstract: Speaking at a memorial service on Monday in Harrisburg for police officers killed in the line of duty, Gov. Ed Rendell urged lawmakers to pass gun laws giving police greater protection. The service was in memory of 703 officers killed in the line of duty, including three in the last year. Rendell pleaded with lawmakers to pass a bill requiring a mandatory minimum sentence of 20 years for anyone who fires at a police officer, regardless of whether that officer is injured.

For the first time since Governor Ed Rendell took office in 2003, the PA Department of Health will distribute federal abstinence-only funds, even though these types of programs conflict with Rendell’s philosophy. In addition, PA Senator Jeff Piccola and Representative Ron Marsico have introduced proposals to help get state budgets passed on time.

headline: Elementary School Closed By Swine Flu Reopens
abstract: The Conrad Weiser School District in Berks County reopens its closed elementary school on Thursday. The school had been closed due to a swine flu outbreak. The district posted a letter on its website about it's reopening.

The governor claims that such measures are needed to maintain a balanced budget, but Cambria County Commissioner PJ Stevens does not buy that justification--claiming that the state put quick bottom line on their budget.

headline: Zoning changes OK'd for Foxwoods casino shift
abstract: Philadelphia City Council approved zoning legislation yesterday that opens the door to a potential casino at the Gallery in Center City while community activists let their outrage be heard loud and clear.

headline: City scrambles to post contract justifications
abstract: Yesterday, Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl ordered city department heads to explain all contracts and post the contract "justification forms" online due to a promise made in September 30 requiring transparency in these matters.  All pacts with firms must be made public.

headline: Top aide implicates DeWeese in legislative scandal
abstract: A former top legislative aide this morning implicated House Majority Leader Bill DeWeese in a scheme to use taxpayer money to reward staffers for campaign work.  DeWeese has denied any wrongdoing. Michael Manzo, a former chief of staff to DeWeese, testified that DeWeese and former Democratic Whip Mike Veon, D-Beaver County, approved the money for the bonuses.

headline: Abolish school property taxes now
abstract: The state’s budget negotiations beg Gov. Ed Rendell and the Legislature to remember the lessons learned from the credit crunch fallout: If you cannot afford it, do not expect someone else to pay for it. $6.2 billion dollars is a price that taxpayers cannot afford to pay for the governor’s educational funding program. Even if state government agreed to give the governor a blank check to spend on education it would not fix the school funding crisis in Pennsylvania. Financially unstable school districts will no longer be able to force fiscally strapped homeowners to pay higher property taxes. This unconstitutional and oft-raised tax will lead to the inevitable foreclosure of countless more privately owned properties.

headline: Hospital will be blasted for arena after all
abstract: A failure to demolish the St. Francis Central Hospital via the technique of controlled collapse will result in contractor Homrich Inc. employing explosives. According to the Pittsburgh-Allegheny County Sports & Exhibition Authority, the implosion is scheduled for March 22nd. The SEA is taking down the hospital as one of 13 properties being cleared for a new $290 million arena for the Pittsburgh Penguins.

There was a gas smell coming from the top of a gas line in Knockville, but it checked out fine, and no evacuations were necessary. Governor Rendell signed the first update of Pennsylvania’s mine safety law, and West Virginia University announced a new interim president after the former president resigned.

headline:
Reporters exempt from testifying in grand jury probe
Confidential: Shield Law protects them from being forced to reveal sources
abstract: Dauphin County Judge Todd Hoover threw out subpoenas issued to 15 PA journalists, including two from the Morning Call’s staff, who were called to testify at a hearing on whether a special prosecutor should be appointed to investigate alleged violations of grand jury secrecy laws, which lawyers for Mount Airy Casino Resort owner Louis DeNaples claim occurred. DeNaples and his friend, Reverend Joseph Sica face perjury charges for allegedly lying to the PA Gaming Control Board about DeNaples’ relationship with two supposed mobsters and two men involved in a Philadelphia political corruption scandal. Hoover has until August 2 to decide whether a special prosecutor should be appointed.

headline: no text
abstract: Barack Obama is working on his speech to formally accept the Democratic presidential nomination at the party’s National Convention in Denver, Colorado, and his running mate, Joe Biden, is also working on his speech. If his health permits, U.S. Senator Ted Kennedy may make an appearance at the convention for a film tribute, and U.S. Senator Hillary Clinton may release her convention delegates soon to allow them to support Obama. PA Governor Ed Rendell and U.S. Senator Bob Casey, who are both attending the convention, shared their thoughts on the election, and Republican presidential candidate John McCain has yet to announce his running mate; though former PA Governor Tom Ridge has been mentioned as a possible candidate.

headline: In China, Philadelphia Orchestra raising money for schools
abstract: The Philadelphia Orchestra is turning its Beijing concert into a benefit whose proceeds will help rebuild the earthquake-devastated Sichuan school system. The June 2 concert, with pianist Lang Lang and conductor Christopher Eschenbach, is being recorded and broadcast by CCTV - China's largest TV network- which will feed it to Hong Kong-based Phoenix TV to broadcast it to its viewing audience. The concert will not air live, but by delay no later than June 5 on CCTV and by Phoenix no later than June 8. Potentially hundreds of millions of viewers will see and hear the orchestra. Negotiations are underway with PBS for a U.S. broadcast, said an orchestra spokeswoman.

headline: null
abstract: Billionaire Neil Bloom is seeking approval from the PA State Gaming Board to take over ownership of the Majestic Star Casino.  Work on the casino has stopped, as the current owner, Don Barden, has run out of money.  Bloom has the support of Pittsburgh mayor Luke Ravenstahl and Allegheny County Executive Dan Onorato for the take over.

headline: At Delco rally, McCain says Obama MIA on rescue plan
abstract: While Republican presidential candidate John McCain held a rally outside the Delaware County Courthouse, Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell led a Democratic Truth Squad to combat misrepresentations being made by the McCain campaign.  The Truth Squad and Governor Rendell argued that Barack Obama's tax plan was being falsely portrayed and that John McCain was not a supporter of renewable energy.

headline: Fayette hospital dispute settled
abstract: A settlement has been reached in a dispute about ownership of Brownsville General Hospital in Fayette County. Under the terms of the deal, the defendants have until Nov. 11, 2009, to pay $2 million plus interest to settle the claim. If they miss that deadline, they would be required to pay $6 million, plus interest.

headline: We're another step closer to giving billions in federal loans to the auto industry.
abstract: Congressional Democrat leaders and the White House approve of a $15 billion loan package to troubled U.S. automakers. The package could be voted on today and enacted by the weekend.

headline: Channel 4 Action News This Morning
abstract: An update on the Bonusgate scandal.

headline: Allegheny County group forms to retain drink tax
abstract: A group called Citizens Against Raising Taxes on Property will campaign to retain Allegheny County’s 10 percent drink tax. The group will battle Friends Against Counterproductive Taxation, which is made up of restaurateurs and bar owners opposed to the drink tax. A referendum will appear on the November ballot that asks voters to choose whether to replace the drink tax with higher property taxes.

headline: Hospitals stand for healing, health, hope
abstract: In the state that is home to the nation's first hospital, we want to use National Hospital Week to recognize the dedicated hospital workforce that each day provides compassionate care to our most vulnerable citizens, celebrates the gifts of new life and medical miracles, and ensures a safe haven in times of crisis. We also recognize the critical economic contributions that hospitals make to their communities and the state. The blue-and-white "H" is the universal symbol for healing, health and hope. Let's celebrate the many opportunities the "H" represents and thank the caregivers who day in and day out meet Pennsylvania patients' health care needs with compassion and caring.

headline: no text
abstract: The largest solar-energy-generating plant east of the Mississippi is being developed in Pennsylvania’s anthracite coal region in Carbon County.

headline: Ronnie Polaneczky: Nutter cites need for 'standards'
abstract: After yesterday's announcement that four Philly cops would be canned and four others severely disciplined for their part in the beating of three shooting suspects, Mayor Nutter used a word we need to hear more often: "Standards." The more the mayor talked, the more he dropped the S-bomb. "We support the police. They do the city's most dangerous work," he said. "But we have standards and expect them to adhere to them." Even if, as Police Commissioner Charles H. Ramsey noted earlier, the criminals whom cops pursue adhere to no standards at all.

U.S. Senator Hillary Clinton, Mack Warner and U.S. Senator Bob Casey of PA spoke at the convention this evening.

abstract: Misericordia University is trying a four day work week, and it is working on other fuel saving programs for students. Governor Rendell and PA legislators agreed on a $28 billion budget that increases spending by 4 percent since last year and will give millions of dollars to alternative energy projects and projects to replace and repair bridges, dams and sewer systems. Dozens of people gathered to watch the bidding for Leiby’s restaurant, which had been a landmark in Tamaqua for years.

headline: Mack Truck jobs on the move
abstract: Mack Trucks Incorporated announced plans to reduce its Lehigh Valley workforce by more than one-third over the next two years.  The company has plans to move its Allentown headquarters to North Carolina, and will offer relocation opportunities to its Allentown employees.

headline: Probe forces scrutiny of officials
abstract: State Senator Jane Clare Orie is co-sponsoring a bill that would require criminal background checks and child-abuse clearances for PIAA sports officials.  Senator Orie's legislation comes in response to a series of reports showing dozens of present and past PIAA-registered officials who maintained their licenses despite having criminal convictions for serious offenses.

headline: Her running has helped inspire the down-and-out
abstract: Highlights Anne Mahlum, who started the Back on My Feet Running group for the homeless, and will be featured as one of CNN's heros of the year.

headline: The keystone state could be losing a big employer.
abstract: Sony Corp. tells Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell that it is closing a television producing plant in western PA due to trimming its global workforce. The plant employs 650 people.

headline: ABC27 News Live at 5
abstract: An overview of the Bonusgate scandal.

headline: Barden's request to drop funding on hold
abstract: North Shore casino owner Don Barden will put on hold a request to drop $3 million in funding for Hill District redevelopment until he has met with top Pittsburgh and Allegheny County leaders to discuss the matter. Mr. Barden said he will defer his request to the Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board, in the "spirit of cooperation," until he has met with Mayor Luke Ravenstahl and county Chief Executive Dan Onorato.

headline: House to debate plan to expand health insurance
abstract: Expansion of state-subsidized health insurance for uninsured adults, Adult Basic,  is unlikely to be approved with a slim Democratic House majority, a year after PA Governor Ed Rendell introduced a plan to accomplish the goal. PA Rep. Todd Eachus, chairman of the House Democratic Policy Committee, announced he is finishing up legislation to provide low-cost health insurance to uninsured adults and small businesses. Many lawmakers oppose the new taxes required to help finance an expansion. Rendell insists on a cigarette and smokeless tobacco tax to help with funding.

headline: Pa. nuke plant neighbor OK $27.5M settlement with ARCO
abstract: Residents living near a former nuclear fuel processing plant in Armstrong County accepted $27.5 million from Atlantic Richfield Co. to settle claims the plant caused cancer, illnesses and property damage. A federal judge signed off on the agreement. Most personal injury and wrongful death claims yield settlements of $100,000. A case against Babcock & Wilcox Co. remains.

headline:
Safety moves to the forefront at The Waterfront
After two killings, authorities try to reassure workers, customers
abstract: There have been two people killed in the past two months at The Waterfront, which is an entertainment, retail and residential complex spanning portions of Homestead, Munhall and West Homestead Townships. Some workers in the area are concerned about their safety and believe there are not enough police officers patrolling the area; however, local police chiefs claim they do conduct patrols into the area, and they simply don’t have enough officers to patrol every corner. Police are still investigating the most recent murder of a young man at a Damon’s Restaurant, and the local police departments, mayors and representatives from many of the area businesses will meet to discuss new safety options.

It will include $650 million towards alternative energy to help reduce the high price of gas, and Governor Ed Rendell praised the new budget. In other news, an accident involving a tractor trailer killed a man on Interstate 81.

headline: Hat trick: The new arena secures Pittsburgh's third franchise
abstract: The Pittsburgh Penguin's new arena had its groundbreaking yesterday.  The construction of the new arena should be celebrated as one of many rich assets the city has.

headline: 'Bonusgate' charges put off
abstract: Pennsylvania Attorney General Tom Corbett announced that no additional charges will be filed in the widespread probe into corruption in the PA Legislature until after the November 4th election.  Attorney General Corbett's office is currently focusing attention on potential wrongdoing surrounding a 1.8 million dollar computer contract for the House Republican caucus.  Critics of Corbett say he should have opened both investigations simultaneously, as delaying the Republican-caucus investigation has unfairly tarnished Democrats prior to an important election.

headline: Taylor applying for $200,000 grant
abstract: The borough of Taylor is applying for a $200,000 Brownfields Cleanup Grant through the Environmental Protection Agency to pay for the removal of soil contamination and mine hazards on the Colliery property.

headline: Illinois governor Rod Blagojevich is free on his own recognizance after his arrest on political corruption charges
abstract: Prosecutors say, Blagojevich was caught on wire tap plotting to sell the former Senator and current President-elect Barack Obama's vacant seat for cash or a better job for himself in the new administration.

headline: News 8 at 12:30
abstract: Governor Rendell is expected to sign a bill today that will allow military veterans in private nursing homes to get getting prescription drugs at a discounted rate.

headline: City employees are good for city
abstract: Many Philadelphians don't realize that our public-health centers aren't staffed entirely by civil-service employees. In fact, the city Health Department relies heavily on contracting and outsourcing rather than hiring workers directly. The city pays higher salaries plus at least 10 percent more in administrative costs, to the entities employing the workers. Result? - fewer dollars available for patient care. These outside entities serve as a giant temp agency that costs the city a small fortune. It eats away at the department budget, and hurts our ability to move forward with a robust workforce and knowledge base.

headline: Issues like generic drug pricing deserve open hearings in state
abstract: The editorial board believes that chairmen of legislative committees should not be able to block proposals from being put to a vote. A bill that would allow Wal-Mart to sell generic drugs at a lower cost was proposed by state Senator Pat Vance and is being blocked by state Senator Robert Tomlinson.

headline: Parking rate hikes would come with city lease deal
abstract: Motorists who park in Harrisburg's public garages would face a $1 increase in the daily and rates if a private company is successful in leasing the facilities. Those who pay monthly rates for garage parking would see a $15 to $20 increase. Jacob Frydman, principal of the New York company seeking the lease, defended the parking fee increases as "fair and competitive" in lay out his $215 million lease offer before City Council tonight. Harrisburg's current public parking rates are $120 monthly, $18 daily, $3 for first 2 hours in garages, and 25 cents for 10 minutes at meters. Under the lease agreement, the lease company would have the right to double city parking rates twice a year.

headline: Senate staff seeks subpoenaed reporters' numbers
abstract: A lawyer seeking the sources of some PA journalists in a grand-jury leak investigation also went looking for the reporters' cell-phone numbers. He went to the state Senate's top Democrat for help. Scranton lawyer Sal Cognetti Jr. called Sen. Robert Mellow's office seeking cell numbers for "eight or nine" reporters, a spokesman for Mellow said. They are among 15 journalists who received subpoenas seeking their sources for stories about the grand-jury investigation of casino owner Louis A. DeNaples, now charged with perjury. Authorities allege he lied when, in a hearing to obtain his casino license, he denied having connections to organized crime.

abstract: Local newscast including presidential race update and Gov. Ed Rendell is talking about infrastructure in big cities.

The PA Turnpike Commission is still pushing to toll Interstate 80, and some of the proposed details have been released. One poll says that 76 percent of Pennsylvanians want a special legislative session on ethical reform in response to a dozen lawmakers and aides who are facing public corruption charges, and state Representative John Eichelberger, who proposed a solution along with two of his colleagues, said he’d be willing to support a constitutional convention to enact ethics reform.

The head of the PA Department of Environmental Protection has resigned. The Dalai Lama spoke to a crowd of thousands in the Lehigh Valley and will continue his six day teaching tour.

headline: Wife of state Sen. LaValle charged in Beaver County theft
abstract: Darla LaVelle, wife of state Senator Gerald LaValle, was charged by the state Attorney General's Office with 11 counts of theft.  She is accused of inflating her salary and pension benefits from a small Beaver County Charity--the Voluntary Action Center--which she headed for many years.

headline: Pa. seeks more pipeline power
abstract: In order to increase state oversight of natural-gas pipeline projects, Senator Andrew Dinniman introduced a resolution that amends the Natural Gas Policy Act of 1978.  The amendment requires the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission to hold public hearings in localities affected by pipeline projects at the request of area residents.  In all, the legislation is designed to give states more control than they currently have over local natural-gas projects.

headline: null
abstract: Govenor Rendell has ordered flags at half mast in honor of Catherine Baker Knoll.

headline: New developments this morning about the economic cris.
abstract: Due to Pennsylvania law, lawmakers and PA Governor, Ed Rendell cannot simply reject the automatic 2.8 percent pay raises that will be included in their checks.  The raises must be refunded separately to the State Treasury.

headline: Mornings Live
abstract: Gov Ed Rendell and First Lady gave students a lesson over video chat as a showcase of the state's new Classrooms of the Future program.

headline: City tax board holds off on full-value assessment
abstract: Members of the Philadelphia Board of Revision of Taxes said they wouldn't implement the proposed full-value assessment system until the City Council and state legislature acted to protect property owners from devastating tax increases. The Board is awaiting state legislation that would allow Philadelphia to enact special homestead exemptions, and for City Council to enact other protections to shield homeowners from extreme increases in their property assessments and tax bills. The proposed solution is: to Reassess the whole city and move all assessments to market values, with advanced software that will allow the city to continually update the data base.

headline: Pa. health care worker accused of stealing $227,000
abstract: A home health care worker from Philadelphia is accused of stealing nearly $1 million from an elderly woman she was caring for. Montgomery County prosecutors say that over 18 months Sonjia Davis talked the 88-year-old Abington woman into giving her $227,000, including money to bail out her teenage son who was in a Delaware County jail cell on drug charges. The money has not been recovered.

headline: Pennsylvania needs energy independence
abstract: According to the author the PA Legislature must address the energy problem in the state. He believes that the Energy Independence Strategy that was first proposed by PA Governor Edward Rendell will help families and businesses, while reducing dependence on foreign oil.

headline: Senate staff seeks subpoenaed reporters' numbers
abstract: Scranton lawyer Sal Cognetti Jr. called PA Senator Robert Mellow to obtain cell phone numbers of eight or nine reporters, including three from the Inquirer, who are among 15 journalists who have been subpoenaed to testify about alleged grand jury leaks in the perjury case against Louis DeNaples and Reverend Joseph Sica. The two are accused of perjury involving the licensing hearing for DeNaples’ casino, and lawyers in the case have speculated that if DeNaples’ legal team obtains the numbers, they could use them to identify the grand jury leaks. There have been several schemes to try to obtain the cell phone numbers, and the newspapers involved have criticized DeNaples, Cognetti and Mellow.

headline: null
abstract: Local newscast including presidential race update.

headline: no text
abstract: Democratic vice presidential candidate Joe Biden and former President Bill Clinton will both speak at the party’s National Convention, and Barack Obama will be on hand. PA will play a key role in the election, and Governor Ed Rendell and U.S. Senator Bob Casey both spoke last night at the convention.

headline: On the Media
abstract: Indistinguishable transcript

headline: City, white-collar union agree on 1-year pact
abstract: Philadelphia's white-collar union--District Council 47--agreed to a one-year contract that provides workers with the same health-care contributions and a bonus, but no raises.  With the exception of firefighters, all city unions have contracts now, and mayor Michael Nutter is pursuing one-year deals with unions to give the city time to examine increasing health-care costs.

headline: Missing the bus: A cross-country transit bill threatens mischief
abstract: House Bill 270--a bill that seeks to increase competition by eliminating the Allegheny Transit Authority's monopoly on service--rests upon faulty assumptions.  Mainly, the sponsors of House Bill 270 assume that private companies will be able to survive in a competitive, free-market environment; in fact, the transit authority was created because private companies could not survive in such an environment.  Also, the sopnsors simply assume that neighboring transit agencies will pick up fares in Allegheny County; there is no evidence for this assertion.

headline: null
abstract: Govenor Rendell has ordered flags at half mast in honor of Catherine Baker Knoll.

headline: Sony says the recession is to blame for the cost cutting measures and layoffs worldwide including 650 jobs in this area.
abstract: Sony officials notifyed Pennsylvania Governor, Ed Rendell, of a plant closure in Westmoreland County over the next 16 months.

headline: WTAJ News This Morning
abstract: Gov Ed Rendell is expected to sign into a law stiffening regulations for those who house animals.

headline: Committee of 70 proposes charter changes
abstract: The Philadelphia civic watchdog group Committee of Seventy is proposing city-charter changes that give the city’s police commissioner more management authority and to permit the city to hire cops willing to move in from the suburbs.

headline: Long-term care will affect every family in state
abstract: Governor Rendell and the General Assembly will negotiate the state budget. One decision that will eventually affect nearly every family is how the state funds long-term care. The Governor has proposed continued expansion of high quality, safe and affordable home and community services as an alternative to nursing homes. Our legislators must support the ongoing shift of funding to enable more people to remain in or return to their own homes. Like most states, PA is in the process of redesigning how long-term care is provided. The goal is a 50/50 split in spending--half for nursing home care and the other half for home and community services. This is a dramatic change for Pennsylvania, which relied almost exclusively on nursing homes until a decade ago.

headline: Power line ruling may be delayed until August
abstract: Allegheny Energy Inc. subsidiary Trans-Allegheny Interstate Line Co. wants to build a multistate powerline. The West Virginia Public Service Commission must approve the proposal in order for the powerline to be built. The proposal involves giving West Virginia customers a seven-year reprieve from costs associated with the powerline.

headline: Sica attorney wants charge dropped
abstract: Reverend Joseph F. Sica is asking a Dauphin County judge to dismiss the perjury charge that was put against him. Father Sica is being accused of lying about this relationship with the Kingston crime figure Russell Bufalino during testimony before a Dauphin County grand jury. The Rev. Sica was subpoenaed to testify before the grand jury, which is investigating whether Mount Airy Casino Resort owner Louis DeNaples, a close friend of Father Sica’s, lied to state gambling regulators about his own alleged ties to organized crime.

headline: null
abstract: Local newscast including rally for Governor Ed Rendell and three teenagers are facing kidnapping and battery charges.

headline: No Text
abstract: Developer Don Barton’s $780 million casino is expected to open next May, but he has until today to pay $10 million for work done in April, and he still owes even more for work done in May. Governor Ed Rendell and PA legislators agreed to a $28.2 billion budget that Rendell say’s will advance the state’s infrastructure and energy needs. The budget agreement will prevent 25,000 state employees from going unpaid, and in other news, a water pipe in Pittsburgh broke, and two people were flown to a Pittsburgh hospital following an accident.

headline: Overnight with Frank Lloyd Wright
abstract: The Duncan House is one of Frank Lloyd Wright's creations toward the end of his career for the middle class. It is one of 11 modest Usonians. This particular one is owned by a nonprofit and rented out for weekends; an architect's delight. The Duncan House was originally located in Illinois. It was moved in pieces to PA and reconstructed on the land of Tom Papinchak, who chairs the nonprofit which now runs and maintains it.

headline: Criticized cat shelter will have to shut down
abstract: Because she failed to obtain necessary occupancy permits for her animal shelter, Collen Weigt received a cease and desist order from Limerick Township.  Weigt's shelter has been the subject of several complaints, but it is being closed for permit issues--not for reasons related to conditions inside the shelter.

headline: Ebensburg Center Trustee Reappointed
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell reappointed Darkene Lutch, a Carrolltown woman, to a second, four-year term as a trustee to the Ebensburg Center.  The center's chief purpopse and task is to help the mentally challenged maintain their dignity.

headline: null
abstract: Discusses the life and death of Catherine Baker Knoll and Governor Rendell's prospective relationship with President Pro Temp of the Senate and new Lt. Gov. Joe Scarnatti.

headline: It is almost a done deal for the auto industry but will it be enough?
abstract: Congress and the White House are almost ready to vote on the $15 billion dollar loan package for troubled U.S. automakers  Republicans are skeptical of the measure.

headline: WHP CBS 21 News at 11
abstract: Gov Ed Rendell is expected to sign into law a bill that creates tougher regulations for kennels.

headline: Council considers bigger parking fines
abstract: In a bill which aims to stop commuters from parking in neighborhoods, the Pittsburgh City Council is considering raising the fines for residential parking violations. Councilman Patrick Dowd sponsored the proposal. The hikes would close a gap in funding borne by the Pittsburgh Parking Authority. Dowd says he became aware of the problem while campaigning. City Finance Director Scott Kunka says Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl is willing to collaborate, though he is not a fan of raising fees.

headline: Lower drinking age is a terrible idea
abstract: The Presidents from about 100 of America’s best-known colleges are calling for a debate on lowering the drinking age to 18, claiming the law isn’t working; however, the authors of the editorial are against the idea. According the authors, lowering the drinking age could lead to more alcohol-related crashes for the nation’s younger population, and they don’t think it would improve problems on college campuses, where 95 percent of all violent crime and 90 percent of all rapes involve someone who consumed alcohol. They argue lowering the drinking age isn’t the solution, and college presidents should instead focus on enforcing zero-tolerance policies concerning underage drinking by students on campus.

headline: Power out for 20,000 in Erie County (VIDEO)
abstract: 20,000 homes and businesses in Erie County lost power because of high winds that were in the region. These outages led to school closings and delays.

headline: Sloysylvania GOP lawmakers: Let's have an inquiry please
abstract: Several PA House Republicans want to create a bipartisan committee to investigate what the PA Gaming Control Board knew when it licensed Louis DeNaples, under criminal investigation, to own a slots parlor. State police say they notified the board, but the board says that's false. DeNaples maintains innocence. Col. Jeffrey Miller testified that board investigators tipped off police to DeNaples possible criminal connections. House Minority Leader Sam Smith supports the establishment of a committee. Republicans deny attempting to embarrass slots supporter and PA Gov., Ed Rendell.

headline: null
abstract: Local newscast including Senator Kennedy's brain tumor surgery, smoking ban update from the legislature, and a racial slur painted on a man's home.

headline: no text
abstract: During his speech at the Democratic National Convention, Pennsylvania’s U.S. Senator, Bob Casey, criticized John McCain for voting with President Bush over 90 percent of the time. PA Governor Ed Rendell also criticized McCain and told Americans to follow U.S. Senator Clinton’s advice to rally behind Obama. Meanwhile, McCain is preparing for his own party’s convention, and he is expected to announce a running mate in two days.

headline: Penguins honor Beaver County teenager with cancer
abstract: A Freedom High School athlete dealing with terminal cancer, John Challis couldn't stop grinning  last night at Mellon Arena. The teenager's recent successful at-bat in a varsity baseball game has gained national attention, and last night he was a guest of the Penguins for their National Hockey League playoff game against the Philadelphia Flyers. The Penguins brought John, his parents and younger sister to the game in a limousine. Bravo restaurant gave the family dinner before the game. The Penguins took John and his family to Mario Lemieux's suite near the end of the first period. At one point, John was holding court with Lemieux, Steelers chairman Dan Rooney and Steelers quarterback Ben Roethlisberger.

headline: State police seeking more diversity
abstract: The PA State Police are opening a new Barrack in Philadelphia with the goal of attracting more women and minority troopers.  This is part of a state wide diversity strategy that Governor Rendell initiated via executive order; all 3,500 state agencies will be affected by the order.

headline: Casino project is back on schedule
abstract: Although work on the North Shore casino was suspended for almost two months, a good-weather streak has brought development back on track.  Work was initially suspended when former majorty owner Don Barden was unable to secure permanent financing for the project, but good weather and an approved bailout by billionaire Neil Blum has put the casino back on pace to open by next August--the date set by the Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board.

abstract: Discusses the life and death of Catherine Baker Knoll.

headline: County commissioners from across the state have come together to file a class action lawsuit with the State supreme court -- asking the court to enforce a prior ruling -- ordering the state to pay for county court costs.
abstract: Area commissioners are having trouble paying local court costs due to the economy.

headline: KDKA-TV News at Six
abstract: The Bonusgate scandal is heating up as a top aide to Bill DeWeese testified that his former boss knew that the money being distributed was taxpayer money.

headline: Council reaffirms drink-tax referendum
abstract: Republicans on the Allegheny County Council failed in their effort to get rid of a referendum that will appear on the November ballot asking voters whether they’d prefer the county’s 10 percent drink tax or an increase in property taxes. Friends Against Counterproductive Taxation has collected thousands of signatures to get their own question on the ballot, and Councilman Matt Drozd proposed an ordinance to require any new taxes or increases in taxes to be voted on by the public.

headline: Medical malpractice suits decline again after reforms
abstract: The state Supreme Court released statistics showing that the number of medical malpractice suits has decreased in Pennsylvania since reforms were enacted to prevent frivolous lawsuits. The Pennsylvania Medical Society reported that there are fewer than 25,000 doctors involved in direct patient care, but Governor Ed Rendell says that the state has not lost doctors due to medical malpractice.

headline: PPL ... profits reflect a company that was wisely run.
abstract: According to the author, California’s 2000-2001 energy crisis was basically caused by deregulation that actually brought on extra regulations such as a rate freeze; however, this resulted in enormously high energy prices and a blackout for hundreds of thousands of Californians. Pennsylvania’s Ken Lay Act of 1996 also froze rate increases for companies, including the PA Power and Light Corporation. The rate caps are supposed to expire in 2010, which PA Senator Lisa Boscola has criticized; however, the author reminds people of what happened in California when utilities weren’t allowed to sell electricity at a higher price to compensate for the rising costs of fuel needed to produce the electricity.

headline: Staring Down the NRA
abstract: Common pleas judge Jane Cutler Greenspan blocked the enforcement of Philadelphia's gun control measures due to the fact that only the state legislature can institute gun control measures. However, the state legislature is heavily influenced by the National Rifle Association. The editorial board believes the state legislature should support the proposals by Philadelphia Mayor Nutter and the city council's proposals of gun control laws and stand up to the NRA.

abstract: Local newscast including smoking ban update.

headline: No Text
abstract: Even PA Attorney General Tom Corbett was surprised about some of his finding from an investigation into bonuses that were paid by state personnel with taxpayers’ dollars as rewards for campaign work. Overall, 12 people were arraigned in court, including a former and current state House member from Beaver County, and Corbett said the scandal involves well over 400 people, leaving the potential for more arrests. A clerk at a Sunoco store said about 3 dozen kids took advantage of a power outage in parts of Bloomfield to break into and rob the store.

headline: no text
abstract: The initial speaker praises Joe Biden as Barack Obama’s running mate in the upcoming election, and he talks about how Biden grew up in Scranton, PA. Biden speaks next, and he addresses Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl, Governor Ed Rendell and state Representative Dwight Evans. Biden thanks Rendell, and he also talks about his special relationship with PA.

headline: Casino loans no sure bet
abstract: Pittsburgh's casino  is having regulatory and financing problems.  Some experts say this is not the fault of the PA government or local contractors, as casinos across the US are facing financing issues.  PA casino's do have concerns beyond the credit crunch, however, as they are facing local concerns about the politicization of the gaming industry.

headline: Wagner wants school district to tighten up contracts
abstract: PA Auditor General Jack Wagner wants the state legislature to change the rules governing school superintendent contract buyouts, as well as the public disclosure of superintendent contracts.  Districts should not be allowed to hide from public view, via confidentiality clauses, expensive, taxpayer-financed contract buyouts.  Additionally, the full superintendent contract should be disclosed to the public--not just salary information.  All school districts in PA should implement these changes.

headline: The state's loss
abstract: Discusses the life and death of Catherine Baker Knoll, highlighting her career as a politican in PA.

headline: Governor rendell went to washington Tuesday to talk about money for other roads in pennsylvania.
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell met with the PA Chamber of Commerce to tell members it could cost more than 2 trillion dollars to upgrape the state's roads, bridges and power grids.

headline: WHP CBS 21 News at 5:30
abstract: The PA state police are welcoming a new commissioner today.  Colonel Frank Pawlowski was unanimously confirmed by the state senate yesterday.  He was nominated in July.

headline: County may pit taxes on ballot
abstract: The Allegheny County Council will consider placing three referendums on the November ballots, but the measures must win approval of the full council to appear on the ballot. The first would put the county’s 10 percent drink tax up against a property tax increase, whereas the second would reduce the drink tax to 0.5 percent and cut the $2-a-day rental car surcharge to 50 cents a day, and the third would eliminate the Port Authority, which would receive funding from the drink and rental car taxes. Friends Against Counterproductive Taxation is also proposing a reduction in the drink tax by 0.5 percent, but it must collect 23,300 signatures by August 5 for it to appear on the ballot, and its members are frustrated by the council.

headline: More restaurants going smoke-free
abstract: Wyoming County restaurants are going smoke free as the PA House and Senate continue to discuss a statewide smoking ban. The Wyoming County Cancer/Tobacco Partnership believes businesses will continue to trend toward choosing to go smoke free regardless of whether a ban is enacted. Margaret Harbaugh, of the United Way, agrees. Tony Delonti, of the American Lung Association, said it is unusual to have so many restaurants in a rural county prohibit smoking. PA Sen. Robert Mellow supports a ban.

headline: PPL remained neutral on shut-off law, now leads Pennsylvania in shut-offs
abstract: When the utility industry argued for greater ability to shut off service to nonpaying customers, PPL Electric Utilities was on the sidelines. The Allentown-based electricity provider was officially neutral on the Responsible Utility Customer Protection Act, and said in press releases that the current law was sufficient, and it didn’t have the collections problems of its competitors. Community advocates, meanwhile, opposed Act 201, which they considered draconian. The law made it more difficult for people with health problems, such as those on oxygen, to get a medical designation to prevent utility shut-offs. Earlier this week, when the Pennsylvania Public Utility Commission released a survey of service terminations of the state’s major utilities, PPL led the pack.

headline: State charges 29 in local meth case
abstract: Attorney General Tom Corbett claims to have discovered the oldest known methamphetamine manufacturing operation in northwestern PA. James and Ronald Frey, two brothers, are among 29 charged by drug agents. The Freys are accused of making meth at the neighboring houses and giving it away to people they knew.
