abstract: Local newscast including smoking bill update and the Presidential campaign.

headline: no text
abstract: General David Petraeus is responding to U.S. Senator Bob Casey’s push to prevent soldier electrocutions in Iraq. 15 soldiers have been electrocuted overseas while taking a shower because of faulty underground wiring. In addition, Governor Ed Rendell is in Beaver County in the fourth of 25 stops he’ll make this week to announce financial incentives that he claims will keep 30,000 Pennsylvanians working.

headline: Armstrong gets a gold star for the 2007-08 school year
abstract: The Armstrong School District made Adequate Yearly Progress toward being proficient in math and reading under the No Child Left Behind Act.  Although the school district as a whole met the standard, six schools within the district did not make Adequate Yearly Progress and were placed on the warning list.

headline: Road Salt Prices Spiking
abstract: In many states, the combination of road-salt shortages and higher prices may translate into slippery roads this winter.  Pennsylvania, a state that purchases most of its road salt during off-peak times, is bucking this national trend.  PA Department of Transportation officials say that most of the state is in good shape and will not face severe shortages during this winter season.

headline: Pa. probes database GOP used in House
abstract: A grand jury is examining whether House Republican leaders improperly used a $9 million taxpayer-funded database to improve their chances of winning elections, The Inquirer has learned.

headline: Will Pennsylvania get early voting by the next presidentail election?
abstract: The Secretary of the Commonwealth met in Washington D.C. with other state election officials about the idea of early voting and possibly moving the election day to Saturday.  It could allow more people to vote and cut down on waiting times in line.

headline: Channel 6 News at 5
abstract: Gov Ed Rendell has dedicated $150,000 to marketing efforts for Cambria County Airport.

headline: DeWeese slams plan to cut seniors' taxes
abstract: PA House Majority Leader stated that Republican Representative John Perzel’s plan to eliminate property taxes for low-to-middle income seniors is an act of political aggression and an attempt to gain political advantage. All homeowners are slated to receive slots-funded property tax cuts under legislation approved in 2004. Perzel, however, wants to use that slots money to eliminate property taxes for seniors making $40,000 a year or less.

headline: Needle no’s
abstract: PA Representative Anthony DeLuca introduced a bill that would provide greater regulation over tattoo artists by requiring them to register with the government, so the state Department of Health could impose regulations and inspect facilities. The bill has already died in committee, so it would have to be reintroduced, and while DeLuca admits he cannot think of an incident when someone got a disease through improperly disposed, used tattoo needles, he refers to his bill as "preventative." The bill would also require some other restrictions, and several tattoo artists in the article said they don’t have a problem with health inspections because they already practice safe techniques, but they want to make sure the government seeks the input of tattoo artists before adopting restrictions.

headline: Program offers financing for energy-saving projects
abstract: With rate caps for electricity bills scheduled to be removed in 2011, many PA residents and businesses have contacted the state about Governor Rendell’s Alternative Energy Investment Fund. The fund will allocate $650 million to develop alternative forms of energy, and the new programs from the fund will be administered by the state Department of Environmental Protection and the Commonwealth Financing Authority; though exact details are still not available. The fund will provide $500 million over two years in grants, loans and rebates for a variety of alternative energy programs and an additional $150 million over an eight-year time period.

headline: State looking to give "slot cops" arrest powers
abstract: Lawmakers debated the merits of arrest powers for "slots cops"  for the first time in an effort to find consensus on gambling reform bills. The state Gaming Control Board wants to give some of its agents power to detain and arrest lawbreakers on casino floors.  In an appearance, Gaming Board Chairwoman Mary DiGiacomo Colins urged lawmakers to designate enforcement agents in the Bureau of Investigations and Enforcement as peace officers with limited jurisdiction to enforce gambling laws.  The move would provide another layer of security to the state police troopers already stationed at the casinos and give BIE enhanced criminal justice credentials, thus potentially allowing the sharing of more investigative information from other law enforcement agencies.

abstract: Local newscast including state budget deadline looming and lottery tickets sales.

headline: No Text
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell and PA legislators agreed to a $28 billion budget, and while it isn’t final, it will prevent temporary layoffs of 25,000 state employees. Even though Rendell didn’t get as much as he requested for public education, he was especially proud of the $290 million in extra funding for schools, including $51 million for Philadelphia’s schools, and Philadelphia Mayor Michael Nutter was also pleased; though many people have criticized Rendell of playing favoritism with the city. In light of comments made by a retired general, presidential candidate Barack Obama said he’d never question the patriotism of his challenger, John McCain, and New Jersey Governor Jon Corzine signed the state’s $32 billion budget.

headline: Half of county's schools meet test standards
abstract: Half of Monroe County's public schools met adequate yearly progress goals mandated by No Child Left Behind legislation.

headline: null
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell says he will sign a series of prison and sentencing reforms approved by the General Assembly.  The reforms seek to reduce the number of non-violent inmantes in prison, thus cutting county costs.  Attorney General Tom Corbett is concerned with the prospect of releasing inmantes to reduce overcrowding.

headline: Our view: New lobbyist rules in best interest of the public
abstract: Criticizes the PA legislature and the Independent Regulatory Review Commission for stalling on lobbyist legislation.

headline: The struggling economy is forcing not only the federal government to make cut-backs, but state government as well.
abstract: Like President-elect Barack Obama has addressed federal government spending, Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell says state government must restrain spending as well.

headline: Bill barring mandatory overtime for nurses headed to Rendell
abstract: Legislation barring employers from forcing nurses to work overtime has made it through the legislature and is headed to Governor Ed Rendell's desk.  The bill will ensure that nurses who feel overworked will be allowed to take the necessary rest to provide their patients with the best care.

headline: Drink up: The county's alcohol tax is imperfect but needed
abstract: Both sides in Allegheny County's drink tax debate are on a real binge. What the people deserve, though, is a little sobriety. The anti-tax forces, essentially the bars and restaurants whose alcoholic drinks are now taxed at 10 percent, want to put a referendum on the ballot to kill the levy that will raise $30 million a year for mass transit. They see the tax as a business-threatening, job-killing measure that puts them at a disadvantage with competitors in neighboring counties. We heard the same thing in the 1990s about the county's 1 percent Regional Asset District sales tax, which supports municipal budgets and maintains parks, libraries and culture -- all without the predicted calamities for business. To the drink tax foes, we say pour a tall one and chill.

headline: No Text
abstract: A bill written by House Speaker Dennis O’Brien and the father of an autistic boy to require insurance companies to expand their coverage of autistic services passed the PA House, and if it passes the Senate, the governor is expected to sign it into law. As of now, 38 members of the PA Health Care Cost Containment Council are jobless because funding expired. The council helps people find the best health care options, and there are two competing bills in the state Legislature for its renewal, but they are both stuck in committee.

headline: Rather than emphasis on coal, best energy bet is solar power
abstract: Since 1986, the federal government has spent $5 billion on research and development for "clean coal," and the current Bush Administration has been especially proactive in promoting coal research, including this year’s $648 million request from the Department of Energy. However, the administration is only seeking $156 million for solar-energy research, a cut of $12 million, and the authors of the editorial claim that despite the huge amounts of money which have been spent on coal research, there is little to show for their efforts. While the authors believe coal remains an important energy source for America, they partially blame this on the government’s failure to invest in alternative energies in the 1970s, and they believe alternative energies need to be explored now, including an effort to develop solar rooftop panels.

headline: State tax breaks for volunteers benefits smaller communities
abstract: According to a legislative study, PA has lost over half of its volunteer firefighters since 1985, so the state Senate passed four separate bills to try to address the problem by offering financial incentives to volunteers. Fires are a leading cause of death among the elderly, and PA has the second highest elderly population in the nation, so the authors of the editorial believe it’s especially important to ensure the state has enough firefighters. The editorial provides details about the Senate’s bills, and the authors hope the House considers them soon after returning from their summer recess because it would cost a lot more to pay for professional firefighters than it would be to provide more incentives to enroll volunteers.

abstract: Local newscast including state budget deadline nears, Senator Vincent Fumo faints in the state capitol, and testing of sirens at Three Mile Island.

headline: no text
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell and U.S. Senator Bob Casey, both Pennsylvanians, spoke at the Democratic National convention, and they both criticized John McCain and the Republican Party.

headline: Two Mechanicsburg schools fail to meet their progress goals
abstract: Two schools in the Mechanicsburg Area School District did not meet Adequate Yearly Progress goals in the Pennsylvania System of Schools Assessment test.

headline: null
abstract: President Bush assured world leaders that the U.S. is acting quickly and decisively to stabilize markets and sure up access to credit.  To this end, his administration has approved a 700 billion dollar bailout package.

headline: State gives $2M for construction of 40th and Pine hotel
abstract: The state of Pennsylvania recently approved a $2 million loan to the Philadelphia Industrial Development Corporation for the construction of a proposed hotel complex on 40th and Pine streets. Both the hotel developers, as well as state and local officials, hope the hotel - slated to be an extended-stay facility for families of patients in area hospitals - will serve as an economic catalyst in West Philadelphia.

headline: Governor Rendell says Pennsylvania faces a projected one point six billion dollar budget deficit.
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell says the state faces a $1.6 million dollar deficit and he has a plan to fill the gap without raising taxes. It consists mostly of program cuts, using Rainy Day fund money, aniticpated federal aid and Marcellus Shale revenues.

headline: Ramaley, Perretta-Rosepink headed to trial
abstract: State Rep. Sean Ramaley and Annamarie Perretta-Rosepink, a former staffer for state Rep. Mike Veon, were ordered Wednesday to stand trial on theft, conflict of interest and criminal conspiracy charges in the so-called Bonusgate scandal.  Prosecutors say that more than $2.6 million in bonuses were paid for campaign work using taxpayer money.

headline: Editorial: Residency requirement
abstract: The Philadelphia City Council took a step towards changing the city's antiquated residency rule. A proposal eliminates the the one-year residency requirement for applicants to most city jobs. The city's police department was freed from the rule by the Civil Service Commission in February. Fire Commissioner Lloyd Ayers raised concerns about the rule for their department. The proposal, by Councilman James F. Kenney, is supported by Mayor Michael Nutter. The city's largest municipal workers' union, AFSCME District Council 33, endorse the residency reform as well.

headline: No Text
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell signed a bill into law that will require insurance companies to pay for the diagnosis and treatment of autism. The bill, sponsored by PA House Speaker Dennis O’Brien, almost didn’t pass because O’Brien and Rendell said they wouldn’t support it after many amendments were added, but it was eventually restored to its original form.

headline: Rendell attacks McCain's energy record
abstract: During his eight-minute speech to the Democratic National Convention, PA Governor Ed Rendell criticized U.S. Senator John McCain’s energy polices, and he spoke about Barack Obama’s energy plan.

headline: State tax breaks for volunteers benefits smaller communities
abstract: In less than a generation, PA has lost more than half of its volunteer firefighters. Yet fires continue to take a serious toll of death in American communities, despite better building codes and improved fire-resistant building materials. The state Senate passed four bills recently to address the volunteer dilemma. According to the U.S. Fire Administration, house fires are the sixth-leading cause of death among the elderly, something that should concern Pennsylvania, which has the second oldest population in the country. The tradition of colonial bucket brigades continues throughout America as 87 percent of local fire departments contain at least some volunteers. More than 70 percent of fire companies and departments enroll volunteers exclusively.

abstract: The PA state Gaming Board ruled that the license to build the north shore casino could be transferred to chicago millionaire Neil Bloom.  Bloom is required to keep commitments made by former owner Don Barden.

headline: null
abstract: The PA Department of State has informed all county boards of election that voters are permitted to wear campaign buttons and T-shirts to the polls.  Ultimately, however, it is up to each individual county to decide what it considers electioneering.

headline: When the governor signed this year's state budget this summer..it was balanced…
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell held a public forum addressing the $1.6 billion dollar budget deficit the state is facing.  Rendell plans to tap into a variety of sources such as program cuts, using Rainy Day fund money, using aniticpated federal aid and Marcellus Shale revenues.

headline: Franklin County area motorists continue to curb their driving
abstract: Area drivers are keeping up their economizing habits developed during the recent explosion in gas prices even as prices abate.  Some drivers feel that the price drop is going to be short lived.  Gas prices have fallen 30 cents since Memorial Day.

headline: Existence of "unofficial" take-home cars could complicate stricter city rules
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl vetoed legislation by city Councilman Ricky Burgess that would halve the number of city officials authorized to take city cars home. He will still halve the number of officials allowed to take home the cars, but said that city council can not write rules for the practice.

headline: no text
abstract: Governor Rendell’s personal chef did some cooking for the state’s health insurance program for kids’ back to school healthy eating breakfast class.

headline: Rendell orders state buildings to use conservation measures
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell ordered that thermostats be adjusted and florescent lights installed at state-owned buildings, including the Scranton State Office Building, in an effort to save energy. Mr. Rendell’s announcement came even as he expressed optimism that state lawmakers are nearing agreement on a new energy policy for Pennsylvania. Some of the actions announced by Mr. Rendell were last undertaken during the energy crisis of the 1970s. With an electric substation as a backdrop, Mr. Rendell said he wants to reduce state government’s consumption of energy 10 percent by 2010. Starting this month, the Department of General Services will raise office thermostats to 75 degrees for the summer, from the current 74 degree setting.

headline: Rendell: would OK longer caps on power prices
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell today said he is willing to extend caps on power prices, which are set to expire in wide swaths of the state beginning in 2010. Power rates are expected to soar after the expiration of the caps, which were imposed as part of the deregulation process. The Rendell administration has been working with legislators and utility officials on less radical ways to protect electricity users after the scheduled expiration of the rate caps. The governor said those efforts could have led to legislation if there was a few more weeks' time to deal with the issue before the Legislature goes into recess. Rendell also said he wants the utilities to get a reasonable return on their investments. The Legislature is expected to take up the issue again this fall.

While two local fire chiefs thought it was a good start, they don’t believe it will be enough, and they are hoping some of the other incentives are passed in the future. U.S. Senator Bob Casey and U.S. Representative Jason Altmire have proposed a reimbursement program for fuel costs for trucks and other vehicles, which could provide a boost for fire departments.

headline: Nursing home funds needed
abstract: A dispute over whether Pennsylvania adequately pays for nursing home care landed before a state Senate panel. Gov. Ed Rendell's administration is working toward "rebalancing" PA's system of caring for the elderly and disabled so that roughly equal numbers of them receive care in nursing homes and at home or in community programs. The administration says the approach will help reduce Medicaid costs to taxpayers while giving the elderly greater freedom to stay in their homes in a state that is already one of the biggest spenders on nursing home care. A nursing home coalition called Pennsylvanians for Quality Care has been lobbying heavily against a plan by Rendell that would give nursing homes the same Medicaid dollars they receive now.

headline: Saving energy for status quo
abstract: When state mandated caps on electricity rates expire in 2010 and 2011, consumer utility rates are expected to increase 35 percent. Some PA Senate Republicans favor extending the caps rather than a plan by PA Gov. Rendell to help mitigate the impact and move the state toward more renewable energy. A House bill will authorize $850 million to expand alternative energy, producing $3.5 billion in investments over the next decade. Editors believe the state government should do all it can to promote investment in diversified energy. The PA Senate should approve the bill.

headline: The Elephant in the Room: Boy Scouts could ease city woes; leave them alone
abstract: Author commends Mayor Nutter for focusing on the violence that is keeping too many Philadelphians captive in their homes. However, the first step in addressing the horrific violence in Philadelphia is to understand that it is a symptom of a broader problem: pathologically antisocial young urban males.  Rather than get bogged down in a dispute with the Boy Scouts, the city should be supporting more organizations like this. Over the last 50 years, cities have seen dramatic increases in murder, rape and other violent crimes along with skyrocketing run-ups in incarceration rates, substance abuse, illegitimacy, abortion, suicide, child abuse, absentee fathers and divorce, as well as related dramatic declines in graduation, literacy and employment.

headline: Sen. Casey seeks new hearing on power lines
abstract:
U.S. Sen. Bob Casey Jr. and senators from seven surrounding states are concerned about plans to speed construction of high-voltage transmission lines in Pennsylvania and adjacent states.
The senators are calling for a hearing before the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee on the U.S. Department of Energy’s plan to bring more electric power where it may be needed in the future. A provision of the 2005 Energy Policy Act allows the department to establish National Interest Electric Transmission Corridors. Last year, the department established two such corridors the Mid-Atlantic and the Southwest corridors.

headline: Pa. House passes health-insurance bill
abstract: A bill to provide health insurance to 270,000 uninsured Pennsylvanians passed the PA House yesterday, but faces difficulties in the Senate. The bill would establish Pennsylvania Access to Basic Care program, covering those 19 to 64 who meet income guidelines and who have gone six months without insurance. The bill helps small low-wage employers to offer workers health insurance. Rep. Karen Beyer, a Republican, supports the measure. Minority Leader Seam Smith called the bill a tax increase waiting to happen. PA Gov. Rendell has expressed general support for the program.

headline: State PUC approves Allegheny Power's new rate plan
abstract: The PA Public Utility Commission granted preliminary approval to allow Allegheny Power to purchase electricity at lower rates following the expiration of caps on power rates in 2011, which is intended to mitigate price spikes caused by the open market. Allegheny Power agreed in 2005 to begin phasing in rate increases over a five year time period in preparation for the switch to an unregulated market. However, state Representative Camille George has said that he believes Allegheny Power’s rates will increase 63 percent after the rate caps expire, and he will hold public hearings on the issue.

headline: Today's guns make talk of 2d Amendment quaint
abstract: The authors are all too familiar with how damaging handguns can be. Almost every night, medics bring us patients either lifeless or writhing in pain with multiple gunshot wounds. The effects of greater firearm lethality are seen daily in the emergency rooms across America, from big cities to rural towns. The impact of this trauma is reflected in the policy statement of our professional organizations. The American College of Surgeons and the American College of Emergency Physicians support legislative and public health efforts to prevent firearm-related injuries and deaths. This includes the enforcement of current laws against possession, purchase, sale or use of firearms.

headline: Pa. Smoking Ban
abstract: Editors do not understand the difficulty in the PA House and Senate reaching a compromise on a smoking ban. It could have something to do with Phillip Morris, which spent $250,000 influencing PA lawmakers last year. On the other side, there are the American Lung Association, the American Heart Association, and the American Cancer Society. It appears Big Tobacco is winning, but if PA wants to move into the 21st Century, it is important to enact a smoke-free law. PA Rep. Mike Gerber's proposal is clear. A state law should not preempt local legislation.

headline: States fight utility costs
abstract: PA, NJ and other mid-Atlantic state regulators are seeking some $12 billion in refunds covering alleged excess payments for electricity auctions. The complaint estimates that electricity users in the PJM Interconnection LLC region will pay about $12 billion in "unjust and unreasonable" capacity charges over the next three years. PA's share adds up to an estimated $5 billion for energy purchases during the next three years. NJ residents face overpayments of $2.3 billion. The complaint, which was filed with the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, involves auctions that were held last year and this year to set the price of electricity from June 2008 through May 2011.

headline: US vs. THEM: Does growth lead to big-city crime?
abstract: The newspaper examined crime statistics in Monroe County, and it found crime has increased with the arrival of new residents from urban and suburban areas, yet it hasn’t increased disproportionately to population growth. The article provides some findings pertaining to recent crime trends and the rate of serious crimes, and it cites evidence that the occurrence of crime within the county’s black population is substantially higher than whites. When compared to the rest of the state, Monroe County’s crime rate is right in the middle of similarly sized counties, but it is below the state’s average.

The PA Health Department described the flu activity as “widespread,” the highest level the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention uses. So far Bucks County is leading the Philadelphia region with 38 confirmed cases, and it ranked as having the fifth highest number of cases in the state. By comparison, Montgomery County and Philadelphia had 14 and 12 confirmed cases respectively.

headline: Sticker shock may hit residents
abstract: If PA residents were paying market prices for electricity instead of capped rates, their bills would be significantly higher, according to information the PA Public Utility Commission released in an effort to educate residents about the price increases that will take effect once deregulation lifts Pennsylvania’s electric price caps. The electric company that serves most of Centre County credited the PUC for providing information, but they said the numbers don’t reflect what customers will actually pay because of efforts to transition into the new market to ease the price increases. The PUC is also promoting more efficient electrical use to cut down on costs, and the PA House approved legislation that would allow meters to give customers information on their energy usage and allow customers to be charged different rates based on the time of day and demand.

Group says it supports municipalities' right to regulate efforts.

A practice known as fracing is of particular concern because it can lead to natural gas being released into the water, but representatives of the oil and gas industry claim environmentalists are overreacting. State inspectors found problems at two drilling sites in June, and oral arguments for the Supreme Court case should begin in September.

headline: The race for nonfood biofuel
abstract: Way back in 2006, when gasoline cost just $2.50 a gallon, President Bush called for home-grown biofuels to replace three-quarters of oil imports from the Persian Gulf, or about 72 billion gallons, by 2025. How to achieve that goal is still a question. Corn-based ethanol production is expected to be 12 billion to 15 billion gallons in coming years. But with gas now at $4 a gallon and critics hammering corn ethanol for helping to pump up global food prices, it is clear that the holy grail of biofuels, cellulosic ethanol, needs to make its entrance soon.

Millions of dollars in flood damage--and a potentially large home owner federal bailout--could be avoided if the 250,000 dollar funding cut were reinstated. headline: Time to pull plug on power rip-off
abstract: In about 18, electricity bills are going to increase by 37 percent. This is due to ongoing deregulation of energy generation, transmission and delivery. That process is based on the already disproved notion that market competition, rather than government rate-setting, is the best means to ensure fair rates for consumers, fair return for utility investors and development of adequate generation to meet burgeoning future demand at reasonable rates. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission has overseen an electricity pricing regimen that accomplishes none of the goals that were supposed to be met by deregulation. The new regimen has created what is, in effect, an industry cartel controlled largely by power generators.

headline:

abstract: Less than three months after leaving his position with the PA Gaming Control Board, Kevin Hayes obtained a position as a lawyer representing two casinos. According to law, regulators must wait a year before getting a position in the private industry they once regulated; however, Hayes was exempt from the law because the state Supreme Court ruled that only the court can regulate conduct of lawyers, so the law doesn’t apply to them. The authors argue the state constitution should be changed to eliminate this exemption for lawyers.

The hospital is the first in the country to offer a money-back guarantee on the daVinci-robotic- prostatectomy procedure, but not the first to offer money-back guarantees for surgery.  The guarantee is part of an overall effort to reduce hospital mistakes and comes as Medicare is phasing out rules to end payments for extra care resulting from medical mistakes.

abstract: Pa. Gov. Ed Rendell wrapped up national "Cover the Uninsured Week" with a visit to Pottsville. headline: Wind sails into the Pa. power scene

While about 70 projects are under development, there are currently nine commercial wind farms that can provide power for 78,000 households, and nationwide, there has been increasing investment in wind technology, including funding from the Department of Energy aimed at getting 20 percent of the nation’s electricity needs from wind by 2030. There are some drawbacks to wind power that environmentalists have criticized, but for the most part, it is considered a cheap, renewable energy source, and it will likely be a key component in Pennsylvania’s requirement to have 18 percent of the state’s energy come from alternative and renewable sources by 2020.

headline: Who freed the cop-killers?

Autohrs columns always ask why those in the criminal system - judges, police, lawyers, probation officers, parole boards, prison officials and elected politicians - aren't held responsible for permitting such people to roam free. Unfortunately, nothing happens - except more people are murdered. This time it was Philadelphia Police Sgt. Stephen Liczbinski, shot and killed responding to a bank robbery in Port Richmond. All three suspects in the killing - Howard Cain, Levon T. Warner, Eric Floyd - have convictions for violent felonies.

headline: Risky rescue: The public deserves answers before any bailout
abstract: The proposed 700 billion dollar Wall-Street bailout involves some very big questions, including where the money will come from and why Americans should pick up the illiquid assets in mismanaged potfolios.  Also, where will such bailouts stop?  If the government bails out Wall Street, why not the Big Three Automakers or the Newspaper Industry? headline: Rendell Plan Helps Smaller Businesses That Help Employees With Health Care
abstract: There are about 800,000 people in PA who don't have health insurance, but Gov. Ed Rendell said he has a plan to change that. Rendell announced his plan in Greensburg on Wednesday. The plan involves reimbursing small businesses for a portion of their costs if they step up and contribute to the coverage plans of their employees. Rendell's plan is called Adult Basic Care or ABC. Simply put, employees can get it for about $60 a month if their employers will chip in $150 a month. And if they do, the state will reimburse the small business for about a quarter of their costs. An additional 10-cent tax on cigarettes and a new tax on smokeless tobacco and cigars would help the state pay for the plan.

headline: Resuscitate, stat, health council
abstract: Even when politics become sickening, it’s rarely fatal. Unfortunately, a political tug of war in Harrisburg has killed an innocent bystander that happens to be one of the state government’s most valuable entities, the PA Health Care Cost Containment Council. The agency sent home its employees and closed shop Tuesday after the Legislature failed to reauthorize it by the June 30 deadline, even though the reauthorization raised hardly any opposition in the Legislature. The Senate actually passed a reauthorization bill and sent it to the House. That legislation included a provision to reauthorize MCare, a medical malpractice insurance program administered by the state. The House passed its own bill reauthorizing the Health Care Cost Containment Council but excluding MCare.

The Bush administration released $450 million in emergency relief funds on Wednesday aimed at helping needy residents pay spiraling heating bills. The Bush administration had been under pressure from Congress and the public for more LIHEAP funding given record oil prices. Pennsylvania Sen. Arlen Specter said the situation had forced many poor people to choose between eating or staying warm.

headline: Small medical suppliers' livelihood depends on new Medicare rules
abstract: Medicare’s plan to cut costs has small medical suppliers in PA and nationwide concerned that they will be locked out of a market. Of the 1,600 Pennsylvania companies that provide wheelchairs, hospital beds, walkers, diabetic supplies and other items and services to in-home patients, 80 to 90 percent of them are considered "small businesses" by the Pennsylvania Association of Medical Suppliers, a trade and lobbying group. headline: Red Cross Disaster Fund Is Depleted
abstract: The American Red Cross said that it has depleted its national disaster relief fund and is taking out loans to pay for shelters, food and other relief services across seven Midwestern states battered by floods. Officials at the charity estimated that efforts in the Midwest will cost more than $15 million and warned that the total could surpass $40 million if the Mississippi River creates floods in St. Louis later this week. Red Cross executives said the charity has raised just $3.2 million for the Midwest floods and painted a dire picture of its overall disaster relief finances. They said many donors are giving less because of rising gasoline and food prices and the collapse of the housing market.

headline: null
abstract: State Senate leaders struck a major blow for the Legislature’s accountability when they decided not to conduct a lame-duck session this fall. PA is one of just a few states that even allow voting sessions of the Legislature after the general election and before the next Legislature is sworn in, and it’s the only one that allows such sessions for routine business. In the past, lawmakers have evaded important issues before the election and returned to Harrisburg afterward to pass laws before the next General Assembly is seated. Doing so is the opposite of accountability. On some occasions, lawmakers who lost in the general election were able to vote afterward, not what the public had in mind.

abstract: The state Senate has rejected what may be the best hope for giving the rest of PA most of the protections from secondhand smoke enjoyed by Philadelphians. Well, the senators should take a breather, then make a second attempt at approving the needed public health measure they rejected. To do otherwise might set back for months or longer the long-overdue efforts to put Pennsylvania in step with its neighbors. NJ, DE and NY, as well as more than two-dozen other states, have gone mostly smoke-free. If a family member owns a computer with high-speed Internet, a Web cam and a microphone, all they have to do is schedule an appointment, and the seniors will be able to use the centers’ facilities to talk for 15 minutes. The new technology should also cut down on costs for social workers because they’ll be able to speak with seniors without having to drive to see them, and if the pilot program runs smoothly, the program could be expanded.

headline: Berks DA forms countywide drug task force
abstract: After several months of meetings with law enforcement across Berks and neighboring counties, Berks County District Attorney, John T. Adams, announced a county-wide drug task force.

headline: Refunds for Phila. Motorists clocked improperly by red-light cameras
abstract: The Philadelphia Parking Authority will give $100 refunds to 4,390 motorists ticketed this year because its red light cameras malfunctioned.  The discovery came 7 months after the fact.  The PPA expects that the cameras are now working properly.  The city has 52 cameras at 10 intersections.

headline: Smoking ban decision delayed again
abstract: A state House-Senate meeting was scheduled to discuss bills that had passed the chambers, including a bill that would ban or limit smoking in all public places in Pennsylvania, but committee Chairman Stewart Greenleaf said the meeting will be delayed. State Representative Ron Miller authored the most publicized plan, but it is criticized by anti-smoking groups as being too weak. Governor Ed Rendell supports a strong ban.

The Clearfield County and Tourism Authority sent a letter to federal transportation officials in opposition to tolling Interstate 80, and Rendell continued his economic development tour by presenting Clearfield County with $17 million for projects. Republican presidential candidate John McCain may choose former Governor Tom Ridge as his running mate in the upcoming election, and hundreds of people, including the two candidates challenging for retiring U.S. Representative John Peterson’s 5th Congressional seat, joined PA Representative Bud George and Rendell at a picnic in Clearfield.

abstract: Three rabid kittens were recently found in the area, but the cases do not appear related.  Cases have been reported in Sprigfield and Farview Townships.

headline: Party's colors OK at polls
abstract: The York County board of elections voted 2-0 to change a previous policy that banned campaign clothing and accessories from voting booths.  This change comes after the PA Department of State issued a memo stating that the wearing of campaign attire while voting does not constitute electioneering and thus should not be prohibited.  PA statute prohibits electioneering, but leaves it up to each county to define that term.

headline: Town hall meetings set on budget cuts
abstract: Mayor Nutter has set town-hall meetings to discuss his proposed budget cuts with the public. Each session will start at 7 p.m. and will feature remarks from Nutter and other city officials.

headline: Northwest teachers end strike
abstract: After a four week strike, Northwest Area teachers return to teaching before a state mandated deadline mandates them to do so.  Because of the strike, the teachers' health insurance was cancelled by the district and still needs to be paid.

headline: City’s anti-crime plan has mixed record
abstract: Cincinnatti, OH has had recent success with its new comprehensive crime-reducing program, and Pittsburgh wants to get in on the act.  A number of other cities with successful programs are discussed and plans for Pittsburgh are sorted through.

headline: Smoking ban gets on fast track
abstract: A hard-fought ban on indoor smoking in most public places is suddenly on a fast track in the General Assembly. The bill, which received the blessing of a Senate-House conference committee and was scheduled to get a final vote in the Senate today. The state House of Representatives could follow later in the day, though a vote might wait until next week because of scheduling issues. Both chambers are expected to approve the bill. A spokesman for Gov. Ed Rendell said Rendell would sign it into law as soon as possible. The law would take effect 90 days after that. Smoking would be barred in restaurants, most offices and government buildings. The measure would allow smoking in casinos -- except the two in Philadelphia -- bars, hotel rooms and private clubs.

abstract: Local newscast including Penquins are in the Stanley Cup Finals and Gov. Ed Rendell announced the top bid for leasing the PA Turnpike.

headline: $17M facelift OK'd for Parkway
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell unveiled a $17.1 million project to make a number of different improvements to the Benjamin Franklin Parkway over the next three years. The state will provide $6.45 million, the city will provide $6.4 million and the rest will be provided by several foundations. Some of the key improvements for the project are listed in the article.

headline: ‘Bonusgate’
abstract: While reform groups criticized the PA Legislature for a lack of progress on many reform bills, PA Attorney General Tom Corbett called it a "sad day for PA" as a grand jury filed charges against former state House Minority Whip Michael Veon, current state Representative Sean Ramaley and a number of legislative staffers for illegally using taxpayers’ dollars to fund campaign work. Patrick Lavelle Jr. had charges filed against him for illegally working as a "fundraiser" for Veon, and Corbett said Veon, who faces 59 charges, consistently blurred the line between legitimate political work and illegal campaign work. Corbett’s investigation has been referred to as "Bonusgate" in reference to its focus on whether legislative staffer were illegally compensated with $3.6 million in bonuses for campaign work, but he plans to file even more charges in the future due to an expanded investigation, and Governor Ed Rendell shared his thoughts.

headline: no text
abstract: PA Senator Jim Ferlo plans to introduce a bill to defederalize the PA National Guard and bring its members home from Iraq. He believes the Governor should have the power to take over control of Pennsylvania’s soldiers in the National Guard.

headline: Agency tests to see if soy can seal the deal on roads
abstract: PA Department of Transportation officials are testing a liquid soy product as a type of sealant on local roads.  Tests have gone favorably so far, and PennDOT officials hope that the soy product can become a lower-cost alternative to expensive, petroleum based asphalt.

headline: Teen driving bill may get lost in translation
abstract: Some state lawmakers want to pass legislation making it illegal for teenagers to use handheld cell phones or text messaging devices while driving.  While the aim of reducing accidents among youthful drivers is certainly laudable, there is good reason to doubt the effectiveness of the law.  The law only imposes a fine of 100 dollars, an amount that will not create a deterrent effect.  Also, given the latitude law enforcement currently gives to speeders, one wonders if police will enforce the law; lawmakers should focus their energies instead on laws that will reduce aggressive driving and speeding.

headline: 2 Phila. schools appeal loss of charters
abstract:
Two Philadelphia charter schools have appealed to the state charter-appeals board in Harrisburg decisions by the Philadelphia School Reform Commission to not renew their operating charters. 
Germantown Settlement Charter School filed its appeal Thursday. Renaissance Charter School in Mount Airy submitted its the next day, Michael Race, a spokesman for the state Department of Education, said yesterday.

headline: GOP to name Rhoades seat pick Dec. 20
abstract: A special election is set of March 3 due to a vacant seat left by Pennsylvania Senator, James Rhoades, who died in a car accident.  The Republicans will name a candidate for the 29th district seat on December 20 while the Democrats have yet to name a candidate.

headline: Economy cuts in to eating out
abstract: The effect of the economy on small businesses is discussed.  Small eateries are feeling the pinch throughout the state.

headline: Smoking ban leaves many unprotected
abstract: Passage of PA’s indoor-smoking ban deserves no celebration. It has consigned thousands of people across the state who work in bars, private clubs and casinos to exposure to secondhand smoke for the indefinite future. For one brief moment earlier this month it appeared that some lawmakers had experienced a pang of conscience when the Senate voted down a compromise of the measure that had been crafted by a House/Senate conference committee.  In fact, the action was the work of a group of Democratic senators who were upset that the measure allowed Philadelphia to keeps its tougher smoking ban but ignored similar situations by Allegheny County and Scranton.

headline: A new era for North Phila.
abstract: North Philadelphia that is decreasing rapidly and is in danger of disappearing. The phenomenon is not caused by beach erosion or by being located on a geologic transform fault. The neighborhood is being eaten away as pricey real estate development moves forward at a rapid pace. Recently, the authored toured a townhouse under construction at 24th and Brown Streets; it was selling for $700,000. Years ago, this house, located west of Broad Street in the northern sector of the city, would have been identified as North Philadelphia. But no more. Now, it's described as being in the Art Museum, Spring Garden or Fairmount areas.

headline: 10th District race was costly
abstract: The amount of money spent on campaigning in the Republican primary race between Chris Hackett and Dan Meuser rivaled that of most general elections. Meuser outspent Hacket two to one but still lost the race.

abstract: PA Senator Vince Fumo is facing charges of using over a million dollars of state and nonprofit money for personal use, and he has decided to end his 30 year career early to focus on the court case, yet he will still be paid over $6,300 a month through the end of the year even though he won’t attend legislative sessions. Governor Ed Rendell signed five bills into law today that will implement new regulations on the mortgage industry in hopes of preventing fewer foreclosures in the future. After closing last week due to a funding dispute, Rendell used an executive order to reopen the PA Health Care Cost Containment Council, but both he and Senate Majority Leader Dominic Pileggi are urging legislators to pass a bill to extend future funding for the council.

headline: PennDOT announces Route 22 traffic changes
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation announced that beginning Monday traffic switches will occur on Route 22.  The switches will occur so that road maintenance and construction can be completed.

headline: Some see harm in hallucinogenic herb
abstract: Legislation banning salvia divinorum, an age-old herb with hallucinogenic properties, has been introduced in the Pennsylvania Legislature.  The drug, which is readily available on the interent and sold in some stores, gained national attention in 2006 when it was listed as a contributing factor in the suicide of a 17 year old Delaware teenager.  Legislators worry that a tragic event might occur if the drug is not banned.

headline: Reading's handicap space rule called a violation of state law
abstract: A Reading ordinance that limits the number of handicap parking spaces to two per block violates the Pennsylvania Human Relations Act and must be changed, a city lawyer told City Council Monday night.

headline: Allotment of casino revenues slammed
abstract: State gambling laws require a portion of casino revenues to be used for economic development. The article writer argues that Allegheny County needs to strengthen criteria for what towns, community organizers and developers qualify for the $6.6 million in casino revenues.  Republicans say the agencies in charge of rewarding the money have the potential to become politicized.

headline: Specter to seek more funds for Cheyney research center
abstract: U.S. Sen. Arlen Specter will announce proposed federal funding for Cheyney University’s Urban Aquaculture Research and Education Center today.  Specter has secured more than $1 million for this project since 2003.

headline: Smoking ban proposal offered
abstract: A compromise proposal allowing Scranton to re-enact its dormant smoking ban ordinance is being offered by Sen. Robert Mellow as a way to break a deadlock on statewide smoking ban legislation. The proposed amendment by Mr. Mellow would give municipalities that already had ordinances the right to re-enact them on the same terms once a law takes effect. He plans to offer the amendment when a House-Senate conference committee meets again on June 3. The committee was created in December to resolve differences in the smoking-ban bills that both chambers offered, and submit a new bill for a yes/no floor vote.

Winning tickets was purchased at the Willow Street Turkey Hill
abstract: The 14 winners of the Powerball lottery, including the person who purchased a winning ticket at Willow Street Turkey Hill, will be able to choose between accepting a lump sum and having payments spread out over 29 years. The federal government will collect 25 percent of the winnings, and according to the PA Department of Revenue, every Powerball jackpot winner has chosen the lump sum in the past. If the 14 winners choose that option, they will each take home $2.27 million.

abstract: Election officials and voting rights groups are concerned that the more than 1 million people who lost their homes due to foreclosure in the last two years will also lose their opportunity to vote when they go to the polls.  Since most foreclosure victims are still registered at their old addresses, it is likely they will be disqualified at the polls.  Democrats fear that such disqualifications will single out poor people.

headline: Jill Porter: Axing anti-crime programs a short-sighted mistake?
abstract: This opinion piece argues that cutting anti-violence programs created by Philadelphia Mayor Street administration is a bad idea.  A curfew center is being cut that has been credited with an 83 percent drop in juvenile shootings in one police district.  Another program is the Adolescent Violence Reduction Partnership (AVRP), which targets at risk 10 to 15 year olds. Philadelphia city officials say the programs are not working, but community organizers disagree.

headline: Economy hits schools
abstract: The crumbling economy is having its effect on school districts around the state.  The loss in stock market value has led to crushing losses in pension plans and has caused schools to have trouble borrowing.  Schools are primarily funded by property taxes.

headline: State, managed-care companies spar over drug coverage
abstract: Managed-care companies that provide health insurance to Medicaid recipients are opposing efforts by the state Department of Public Welfare to assume responsibility for buying medications prescribed to Medicaid managed-care patients. The Department of Public Welfare has been attempting to assume this responsibility for two years but has been blocked by the state legislature. Public Welfare Secretary Estelle Richman renewed her push Tuesday during House and Senate committee hearings on the proposal.

abstract: In Allegheny County the Hill House Association formally rejected the agreement offered by the city of Pittsburgh and Allegheny County for the development of the new Penguins arena. and general concepts." The group said the city and county were offering an agreement with the Penguins that calls only for consideration of projects like a new grocery store and development of other community resources. The group has asked for creation of a development fund that would be administered by directors selected by the city, county and community. The proposed agreement does not address that demand. Mayor Luke Ravenstahl has said he doesn't think the community benefits agreement should include development funds, noting that other county and city agencies could provide money for revitalizing the Hill District.

headline: A political reformer's rise and fall
abstract: In the Beaver Valley, Mike Veon walked as an icon of political benevolence, dispensing grants, arranging jobs, proving that, half a state away in Harrisburg, Western Pennsylvania still held awesome powers. Now at the epicenter of a mushrooming scandal that pivots on whether that power was used to misappropriate millions in state dollars for partisan politics, a talented young reformer is sent to Harrisburg in a backlash against a legislative pay raise, rises to a pinnacle only to be undone by the things he came to change. As Democratic whip in the Pennsylvania House, Mr. Veon ostensibly was second-in-command to Majority Leader H. William DeWeese. But while Mr. DeWeese was the loquacious public face of the caucus, Mr. Veon quietly got things done.

The county commissioners are expected to approve accepting proposals to allow for drilling in 2000 acres of Moon Lake Park.  The going rates are between $2,600 and $3,200 in signing bonuses per acre and as much as 18 percent in royalties.  Drilling isn't expected to affect mountain biking trails that weave through the park.

headline: Study OK'd to probe vitamin C effect on cancer
abstract: Researchers are preparing for clinical trials examining whether high doses of vitamin C, administered intravenously, can slow the spread of non-Hodgkin's lymphoma. Thomas Jefferson University Hospital and Jefferson's Kimmel Cancer Center, along with the National Institutes of Health, plan to begin enrollment within the next few weeks of 20 non-Hodgkin's lymphoma patients who have failed standard therapy.

headline: Bill's help for cities would skip Hanover
abstract: A senator is pushing a plan to pump more state money into small cities such as York, saying they need help fighting blight and crime and paying bills. But lawmakers who represent boroughs the size of Hanover may balk at backing a plan that doesn't help their areas. Sen. John Wozniak who represents the old steel city of Johnstown, authored the plan dubbed "Renaissance Cities." It would send $100 million a year over five years to the state's 53 cities classified as third-class, plus Scranton, the only city classified as second-class A.

headline:
A political reformer's rise and fall
Mike Veon undone by the things he went to Harrisburg to change
abstract: Former PA Representative Mike Veon was voted into the state House in 1984 largely because his opponent had voted for a pay raise for House members, but his vote for pay raises contributed to his defeat in the 2006 election, and he is now at the center of an investigation into whether bonuses were handed out illegally for campaign work. Veon rose through the ranks to become the Democratic House Whip under Representative Bill DeWeese, he often worked behind the scenes to get things done, and his constituency services left a good impression with many people. Governor Ed Rendell said that Veon has done a lot of good for the state during his years of service, and many of his accomplishments are described in the article, but ultimately, a promising career that began as reformer has fallen apart due to the things he came to change.

President George W. Bush is telling Russia to end its invasion of Georgia, claiming the action is threatening Russia’s relationship with the U.S. and Europe. headline: Profitable Slots
abstract: Gaming analysts this week reported that Pennsylvania casinos are bucking the trend of casinos in Las Vegas and Atlantic City by continuing to boom in a struggling economy.The analysts say that Pennsylvania is the only East Coast state where gaming revenues are up. KQV's Earl Bugaile reports the casino in Washington County is thriving.

headline: Police arrest a Blair county man -- on charges that he threatened the governor.
abstract: A 53 year old man sends a threatening email to Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell that contain racial slurs toward Jews.

headline: Kennel’s hellish conditions no surprise to rescuers
abstract: The Pennsylvania SPCA recently raided the Almost Heaven Kennel in Upper Milford Township and found more than 800 animals living in torrid conditions.  Dozens of animals were seized and rescued by other groups.  They report the animals have severe mental trauma.

headline: To fix health care, focus on uninsured
abstract: Where does the debate to improve Pennsylvania's health-care system begin? Does it start with controlling hospital infections, helping to retain doctors and improving medical technology? Or does it start with making sure as many Pennsylvanians as possible have health insurance that's affordable? Ideally, it's all of these things. But lawmakers in Harrisburg must start somewhere. Earlier this spring, the Democratically controlled House focused on and approved legislation insuring the uninsured. Last week, the Republican-controlled Senate focused on everything and nothing. Let's look at the question as a basic economic supply-and-demand issue.

headline: Broad effort for Valley cities merits support
abstract: If you don't pay attention to the health of your heart, eventually your body weakens and dies. That anatomical reality holds true for the health of a community, too. And the heart of the Lehigh Valley for decades past has been the downtowns of its cities. There has been significant attention in recent years to the health of the downtowns of Allentown, Bethlehem and Easton. To various degrees those efforts have had measurable impacts. It's just as true that the challenges each city faces in trying to revitalize its downtown varies in complexity and severity. Each city is unique.

headline: A tense bid to sway Pa. voters
abstract: Candidates for the Democratic presidential nomination, Senator Hillary Clinton and Senator Barack Obama, debated in Philadelphia. The discussion centered on electability and who could best beat Republican nominee Senator John McCain in the general election.

Meanwhile, Governor Ed Rendell and U.S. Senator Bob Casey will speak at the Democratic National Convention for Barack Obama. There is a video circulating of a Kansas professor mooning a University of Pittsburgh professor, and despite progress in some areas, Pittsburgh’s public school district fell below goals set by the federal No Child Left Behind Act.

headline: Lots on tap as Pa.'s Legislative session nears end
abstract: Legislators will return to Harrisburg next month with a long list of things to do.  Possible items for consideration are passing tougher regulations for dog kennels, expanding heath coverage to the uninsured, encouraging energy conservation, amending the state wiretapping law and developing better oversight of slot machine gambling.

abstract: The article speculates whether Go Ed Rendell will choose to take a post in the possible Obama Administration rather than grind out the next two years being a lame-duck governor with a hostile legislature.

headline: Two reports challenge pols
abstract: Two recent reports, one involving casino revenue and one involving health, undoubtedly will gain the notice of a handful of state lawmakers who can’t quite bring themselves to enact a statewide smoking ban. Place your bets now on which report the members of a House-Senate conference committee will find more compelling. The committee is supposed to resolve differences between House and Senate versions of a smoking ban. But it has needlessly complicated a simple task as some members continue their attempt to carve out exceptions for the casino, tobacco and tavern industries. Lawmakers should stop gambling on public health and join the trend across the world by adopting a comprehensive ban on smoking in indoor public places, including casinos.

headline: 12 News at Sunrise
abstract: PA Gov. Rendell says the emergency repairs to I-95 are an example of why a massive federal commitment is needed to help repair that nation's infrastructure. A congressman says a mistake was made by the National Transportation Safety Board in not holding an interim public hearing on last year's bridge collapse.

headline: Casino's effect on South Philadelphia traffic draws city attention
abstract: Philadelphia City Council heard three proposals for traffic if Foxwoods casino is built on the city's riverfront. The Street Department's chief traffic engineer and officials of the PA Department of Transportation say they will need another month to go over the proposals, which focused only on the first phase of a parking garage construction. Ignoring later phases bother some Council members, including Council President Anna Verna. Traffic engineers hired by the city however, discounted Foxwood's proposal, saying their proposal would not alleviate traffic as much as was claimed.

headline: ABC 12 News First
abstract: PA Gov. Ed Rendell has offered to help fundraise for a re-vote by the Democratic National Committee in an effort to seat Florida and Michigan delegates at the Party's convention. Over the weekend, US Sen. Obama won the Wyoming Democratic caucuses. US Sen. Hillary Clinton picked up four. They are now separated by less than 100 delegates. Mississippi will hold its primary Tuesday.

abstract: Some state legislators have called for a constitutional convention to enact ethical reform in the PA Legislature. As House Democrats continue to defend themselves for allegedly handing out $1.8 million in illegal bonuses, and House Majority Leader Bill DeWeese uses taxpayers’ dollars on lawyers’ fees, some legislators believe a constitutional convention is the only way to reform the state’s government. As of now, the state auditor general cannot audit the state Legislature, and the state Treasurer cannot question the checks being written for bonuses or lawyer fees.

headline: Salvos fly in gaming faceoff over outside income
abstract: Legislation sponsored by Senator Vincent Fumo and Jane Orie would prevent future gaming board members from receiving outside income.  A member of the state's casino oversight board argued that the same rules should apply to legislators.

abstract: Two members of the Northeast Pennsylvania delegation won the top leadership posts in the state House on Tuesday, giving the region its greatest sway over the legislative branch in decades.

abstract: The editorial encourages prosecutors to swiftly find out whether the allegations that House Democratic Caucus members used tax dollars to fund bonuses for campaign work are true.  The newspaper slams the idea that tax dollars should go to anything but the public's benefit.

headline: Uninsured care cuts into profits
abstract: Rising levels of uncompensated care are threatening the already-thin profit margins of area hospitals, according to findings released today by the Pennsylvania Health Care Cost Containment Council. At just over 3 percent, the share of care for patients who aren’t insured or who can’t pay is highest at Hazleton General Hospital and Tyler Hospital in Wyoming County, the report states. Administrators at other institutions say their numbers also are growing.

headline: 33 county bridges eyed for repairs
abstract: The Mount Airy Road bridge is one of 33 in Lancaster County, and 1,145 statewide, that Gov. Ed Rendell announced Thursday he wants to repair or replace through his Rebuild Pennsylvania initiative Rebuild Pennsylvania, which requires the approval of the state Legislature, calls for investing an additional $200 million per year in bridge repairs over the next 10 years. Rendell did not specify where those funds would come from, although he suggested proceeds from the proposed leasing of the Pennsylvania Turnpike are a possibility.

headline: Budget living options on rise Downtown
abstract: The Pittsburgh Downtown Partnership’s “Vacant Upper Floors Initiative” is targeting 265 Downtown buildings that have empty, wasted space that could be renovated into residential space. According to a 2006 study the partnership commissioned, renovating those Golden Triangle buildings could add 750 to 1,000 residential units. The PDP estimates there are about 5,724 Downtown housing units.

headline: He's not Santa Claus
abstract: Governor Rendell traveled across PA last week distributing state money for various projects that are expected to have a positive economic impact for everyone.  If you either approve or disapprove of such spending, tell your local legislators, but do not willingly accept state money now and voice disapproval when the bill comes due at tax time.

headline: Rendell Wants Disaster Relief from Feds After Montco Fire
abstract: After last Friday's fire in Pottstown, a fire that damaged three apartment buildings and left 50 people homeless, Governor Rendell is asking the federal government to declare Montgomery County, PA a disaster area.  Such a declaration would make available low-interest loans to eligible renters and businesses damaged in the fire.
