headline: Firefighters sue Phila., saying cuts jeopardize lives
abstract: Firefighters of Philadelphia sued the city twice yesterday because Philadelphia plans to eliminate five engines and two ladder companies on the ground to trim budget costs on January 5. Local 22 of the International Association of Firefighters says the cuts makes citizens unsafe. The State Supreme Court has made no comment on the matter.

headline: Breathalyzer interlocks (sob) will put a crimp in booze sales
abstract: The American Beverage Institute is warning lawmakers that breathalyzer interlocks for those previously convicted of DUI will cause sales at bars and restaurants to fall.  The ABI is going after what it calls ‘’modern-day prohibitionists" who look to target consumers of alcohol.

headline: A pinch on school busing - As diesel costs soar, districts cut back on rides. Two team up to find lower fuel prices.
abstract: Pennridge School District will offer fewer buses to take students home from after-school activities, and athletes from different sports may squeeze onto the same bus for away games at the same school. These are some of the changes the district plans to make in order to save on fuel costs, which are projected to rise from $520,000 last year to $900,000 this year, and the district has also taken advantage of volume discounts. Several other local school districts are exploring or have already implemented measures to cut back on fuel costs.

headline: National highway money crisis looms
abstract: The federal government is projected to run out of money for highway funding because its Highway Trust Fund is expected to have a $6 billion deficit next year, and a five-year transportation funding law is set to expire. U.S. Representative Jason Altmire criticized the Highway Trust Fund for relying on a tax that’s been unchanged since 1993, even though the price of construction materials has skyrocketed. While PA hopes to receive $97 million from one federal bill, state Representative Joe Markosek said the uncertainty of federal funding forced the state to take its own initiatives, including Governor Ed Rendell’s recent approval to borrow $365 million to repair over 400 deteriorating bridges and the state Legislature’s passing of a bill to toll Interstate 80, which still needs federal approval.

headline: no text
abstract: The governor made a stop as part of his 16 day bus tour, where he announced millions of dollars in state funds will be used to re-develop buildings in Wilkes-Barre.

headline: Casey featured in Obama commercial
abstract: Candidate for the Democratic presidential nominee, Senator Hillary Clinton, aired a commercial in Pennsylvania noting her roots in Scranton, Pennsylvania. Her opponent, Senator Barack Obama, aired a similar commercial with an endorsement from Senator Bob Casey, who is also from Scranton.

headline: One reform we don't need
abstract: The editorial board criticizes a law advocated by state Senator Joe Scarnati that would bar illegal immigrants from receiving social service benefits. Governor Ed Rendell is opposed to this law. The editorial board believes it is redundant, impractical and unenforceable .

headline: null
abstract: The PA State Department of Health is applying for 1.7 million in federal money for abstinence-only sex education.  This goes against the Health Department's philosophy on sex education and represents a reversal for the Rendell administration.  The department does not want to stand in the way of groups and schools that want to focus on abstinence-only education, however.

headline: Ravenstahl to call on panel to dispel suspicions of favoritism in contracts
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl has organized a panel of corporate executives and political allies to help him cast off suspicions that favoritism and pay-to-play politics influence how the city awards contracts.  He is planning to expose hundreds of contracts each year to greater public scrutiny and will require justification forms that explain why each company was hired.

headline: Fewer drivers means less money for roadwork
abstract: Americans, perhaps more than ever, are listening to the advice of fuel conservationists. They are consolidating personal vehicle trips, inflating tires, car pooling and buying fuel-saving vehicles.The problem is Pennsylvania wasn't fully prepared for such a positive lifestyle change and fuel tax collection is down.

headline: Ravenstahl presents donation to Pittsburgh Promise
abstract: Last night, Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl, presented a $13,500 donation to Pittsburgh Promise for college aid. City residents can add their own donations when they pay their income taxes.

headline: Channel 4 Action News This Morning
abstract: According to Gov. Ed Rendell, Lt. Gov. Knoll has been in the hospital undergoing treatment for cancer.

headline: Academic-coach positions axed in school district shake-up
abstract: Despite six years of improving test scores in math and reading, the School District of Philadelphia’s new superintendant, Arlene Ackerman, is already making some significant changes, including the elimination of 218 academic coaching positions. Some people believe academic coaches helped raise the test scores, but Ackerman said their roles were not clearly defined, and the academic coaches, often veteran teachers who mentored or trained teachers, will be able to reapply for different positions in the fall. In addition, three of the highest-ranking school officials left the district this week, Ackerman expanded the number of regions the area’s schools are grouped into, and the teachers’ union and an organization for parents aren’t surprised that some changes were made.

headline: Near-by trains to New York? Good goal
abstract: One meeting held last week in the offices of Sen. Arlen Specter deserves notice. The subject was passenger trains and the news is that renewal of service from eastern Pennsylvania to New York City may be getting closer. Joining the meeting with Republican Sen. Specter was Democratic Sen. Robert Casey Jr., officials from the Federal Transit Administration and staff from the offices of Gov. Ed Rendell, N.J. Rep. Chris Carney and Paul Kanjorski of Pennsylvania and New Jersey's state government. All came away encouraged about trains from Scranton to New York that would pass within minutes of the Lehigh Valley. The rail service, if approved, will be completed in as little as six to eight years. The project is expected to cost about $551 million.

newspaper:
Ch. 4 Action News at Noon
WTAE (ABC)
headline: no text
abstract: The PA Gaming Control Board ruled the license to build the North Shore casino could be transferred to Neil Bluhm as long as he honors all the commitments made by the previous owner, including $225 million to help build the new hockey arena and $19 million for district development and traffic improvements.

headline:
Casey pushes volunteer aid
Gas prices behind effort to raise mileage deduction
abstract: U.S. Senator Bob Casey visited the Meals on Wheels program in State College to discuss his proposal to increase how much residents can deduct as itemized expenses on their federal tax returns for miles driven on a personal vehicle for charitable work. He also expressed disappointment at the defeat of a bill in the Senate that would have more than doubled the amount of federal funds available to PA for its Low Income Energy Assistance Program.

headline: PA or D.C.? Rendell to stay in post, he says
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell says he isn't going anywhere anytime soon, even if he were to be offered a post in a Barack Obama administration. Obama, the presumptive Democratic presidential nominee, hasn't won the presidency, of course, so Rendell doesn't have a job offer yet. Still, his stature has people speculating about his future, and he keeps pledging to remain in the Governor's Residence until his term expires in January 2011. His latest pronouncement came Thursday night on WITF's "Smart Talk" program.

headline: null
abstract: With a high number of West Nile infected mosquitoes found in the region, portions of Montgomery, Bucks, Philadelphia and Delaware Counties will be sprayed with a pesticide tonight.  The pesticide will be sprayed from an airplane and will cover approximately 150 acres of the county.  Some residents are upset that no one told them about the spraying, and some have concerns for their health.

headline: Northampton County's corrections department rolls out new Web site
abstract: Northampton County corrections department launched a new web site that allows members of the public to find out if a person is still in county jail.  The web site also allows law enforcement officials to access a photo of the inmate, as well as criminal charges and fingerprints.

headline: State offer to aid Boscov's benefits region
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell offered $35 million in state-guaranteed federal loans to help retail giant Boscov's department stores exit bankruptcy and the editorial board is encouraging state help in rescuing troubled companies and innovative thinking to do so.

headline: They took their case to city hall. Now they are taking it to court.
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Michael Nutter wants to cut seven engine and ladder companies to save $10 million in an effort to close the budget deficit.  Philadelphia firefighters sued the city and their union says it compromises safety.

headline: The Last Word
abstract: According to Gov. Ed Rendell, Lt. Gov. Knoll has been in the hospital undergoing treatment for cancer.

headline: Academic-coach positions axed in school district shake-up
abstract: Despite the six years of improved student math and reading test scores announced Monday, a shake-up is under way at the School District of Philadelphia. Superintendent Arlene Ackerman, who last week completed her first month on the job, informed 218 academic coaches that their jobs were eliminated as of this Monday. "From my own investigation and looking at how we spend our resources," Ackerman said, "one of the things that was clear to me is that we have multiple layers of coaches with varying job descriptions with little or no performance criteria for how they got the jobs." In addition, three of the highest-ranking school officials left the district this week.

headline: Need for cargo airport should be examined, state official says
abstract: The state’s deputy transportation secretary for aviation raised questions about the proposal to build a cargo airport outside Hazleton at a recent meet-and-greet with representatives of the Greater Hazleton Chamber of Commerce. A study is under way to determine if the airport, planned by developer Gladstone Partners for land in East Union and Hazle townships, is worthy.

headline: no text
abstract: The people of Somerset celebrated the opening of the new municipal building, which was built at a cost of $1.4 million and will consolidate all of the borough’s vital services except public safety. Governor Ed Rendell’s bus tour came to Cambria County, where he presented a $2 million check to state Senator John Wozniak for various area improvements.

headline: Casey takes center stage
abstract: U.S. Senator Bob Casey of PA has been invited to speak at the Democratic National Convention in Denver, where Barack Obama will officially accept the party’s presidential nomination. Casey’s father, former Governor Robert Casey, has always claimed that he was never invited to speak at the event because of his opposition to the party’s pro-choice stance position on abortion. Senator Casey, who also opposes abortion, endorsed Obama in the Democratic primary, and it is unknown exactly what he will talk about in his speech.

headline: Pa. GOP to fight thinning ranks
abstract: The number of registered Republicans has declined around the time of the Presidential primary. Republican party leaders say that some Republicans are registering as Democrats to vote against either U.S. Senator Hillary Clinton or U.S. Senator Barack Obama rather than for one of them, but Democrat party leaders say that Pennsylvanians have been turning from the Republican party for long before the hotly contested election.

headline: Port Authority drivers' strike hangs over talks
abstract: A state-appointed fact finder is expected to offer possible contract resolutions for the ongoing standoff between Port of Allegheny County drivers and the Port Authority.  If both parties reject the fact finder's recommendations, a strike may ensue, but both sides hope negotiations can resume without a work stoppage.

headline: $6.6 million deal for land raises issues
abstract: The Great Valley School District used its capital reserves to purchase roughly 50 acres of land in East Whiteland Township.  Some residents are concerned with the district's use of its capital reserves to purchase the land, but the district claims that the land purchase is a capital improvement project and therefore allowed by the state Department of Education.  The district also stated that it has been using the capital reserve fund to purchase land for years.

headline: More fiscal woes
abstract: Erie's financial troubles appear to only be getting worse with more money needed to pay out in 2010, a troubled pension fund, and contracts awared to unions in 2007.

headline: State environmental regulators are working to increase fees for companies that want to drill for natural gas in the Commonwealth.
abstract: Next spring the a drilling permit for the Marcellus Shale formation will cost companies $2,600-an increase of $100 dollars. The Marcellus Shale may hold one of the largest natural gas resevoirs in the nation.

headline: WHP CBS 21 News at 6
abstract: According to Gov. Ed Rendell, Lt. Gov. Knoll has been in the hospital undergoing treatment for cancer.

headline: Ackerman releases 5-part accountability program
abstract: Philadelphia School Superintendant Arlene Ackerman unveiled a new accountability system that will be used to see how each school in the region is performing. The five assessment areas are: student achievement, school operations, class sizes and serious incidents, constituent satisfaction and school-selected indicators, which could include the percentage of students passing advanced classes, and the results will be tied to school report cards. Thanks to new state funding and policy changes at the Southeastern PA Transit Authority, the district won’t have to follow through on a proposal that would have cost 7,300 students their free weekly public transportation service to and from school.

headline: no text
abstract: A deadly crash on Interstate 83 in Cumberland County has prompted the PA Department of Transportation to take action, and it may shut down an on-ramp and install three warning lights. Four people walked away from a plane crash in Lancaster County today.

headline: no text
abstract: There was an accident between the PA Turnpike and Route 115 involving a tractor trailer carrying household cleaning products, a fire ignited at a camp for kids in Wayne County, and a mobile home in Northumberland County was destroyed by flames last night. Governor Ed Rendell was in Northumberland County as part of his 16-day bus tour to announce millions of dollars in state money to help stimulate the local economy.

headline: Castille's bully bench
abstract: Supreme Court Chief Justice Ronald Castille threatened discipline proceedings against a Lancaster lawyer who filed a lawsuit in U.S. District Court in Harrisburg on behalf of the League of Women Voters of Pennsylvania. The suit quotes anonymous legislators as saying a decision on the appeal of the state's slots law was "leveraged" with lawmakers through the 2005 pay raise for legislators, judges and executive branch employees. Lawyer Paul Rossi says he will at some point reveal the unnamed legislators quoted in the court document. Cappy was a key architect of the pay raise.

headline: PA. House votes to license massage therapists
abstract: null

headline: null
abstract: A Blair County man accused of threatening governor Ed Rendell through e-mail posted bail on Tuesday and is now home.  Vincent Stone is accused of sending a threatening message to the governor.  The email also contained racial slurs directed at the Jewish community.

headline: Souderton teachers authorize strike Tuesday
abstract: With unresolved disputes over wages and benefits, teachers in Montgomery County's Souderton Area School District voted yeaterday to strike on Tuesday if a contract agreement cannot be reached.

headline: null
abstract: The funeral for slain Philadelphia police officer Patrick McDonald was held yesterday.  Also, the Fraternal Order of Police held a tribute to Officer McDonald at its headquarters on Spring Garden Street; Philadelphia Mayor Michael Nutter was in attendance.

headline: Economy puts new spin on college costs
abstract: As parents grapple with job uncertainty, the credit crunch and dwindling investment returns, some students are expanding their shopping lists, including less prestigious, less expensive schools.

headline: Identifying Hurdles to Renewable Electricity Transmission
abstract: A report exploring the challenges and opportunities of increasing the United States renewable energy generation (clean energy) and connecting it to our nation's power grid grid via advanced electrical transmission construction.

headline: Channel 6 News at 5
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell was at a ceremony this afternoon where 23 wind turbines were being unveiled.

headline: Aiming for student proficiency in education gets high marks
abstract: The president of the Harrisburg Area Community College testified before the PA State Board of Education, saying that 55.4 percent of the entering freshman required remedial instruction in reading and that more than half of them need remedial help in math and a third required help with writing skills. The federal No Child Left Behind program, which has been both widely praised and criticized, represented recognition of the problem, and sought to bring accountability to the classroom. The PA state board is expected to adopt recommendations from the Governor's Commission on College and Career Success that would require high school students, in order to receive a diploma, to achieve proficiency on at least six of nine end-of-course examinations. These Graduation Competency Assessments would be given in English, math, science and social studies.

headline: No Text
abstract: A new report from the U.S. government ranks PA second in the nation for the number of structurally deficient bridges, and one fourth of all the nation’s bridges need repairs. Over 6,000 PA bridges are considered structurally deficient, and Governor Ed Rendell is pushing more federal funding to fix them.

headline: Nutter freezes neighborhood initiative
abstract: Senior Nutter administration officials said that they had discovered serious accounting lapses in the management of the Neighborhood Transformation Initiative, and announced that they would suspend all land-acquisition activities until a forensic audit can be done. In effect, Mayor Nutter is putting NTI - arguably former Mayor John F. Street's single largest initiative - on freeze indefinitely. Nutter has long harbored doubts about the effectiveness of NTI, a program designed to demolish neglected buildings in impoverished neighborhoods, consolidate parcels, and clear the way for redevelopment. But administration officials yesterday limited their criticism of NTI to the program's accounting problems.

headline: Challenger's hopes high in 2nd try for 56th district seat
abstract: Brian Sinclair Blasko has the support of the Westmoreland County Democratic Committee for the April 22nd primary after it was declined by incumbent state Representative James Casorio.

headline: Pa. lawmakers fill up at your expense
abstract: When Philadelphia State Rep. Robert Donatucci pulls up to the pump, it costs as much as $102 to fill his state-owned 2004 Dodge Durango, an eight-cylinder SUV. He and 72 others in PA's General Assembly continue to drive SUVs at taxpayer expense despite efforts by Harrisburg to bring more fuel-efficient vehicles to the state fleet, an Inquirer analysis shows. In many cases, they aren't paying $4 a gallon to top off their tanks on legislative business. State House and Senate members, who enjoy one of the most generous public leasing programs in the nation, have grown accustomed to critiques of what they drive.

headline: Asbury Park's Ferris wheel returns to Pennsylvania
abstract: As part of an effort to revitalize Phoenixville, PA, The Schuykill River Heritage Center is purchasing and restoring the Asbury Park Ferris wheel.  The wheel is returning to the town and foundary where it was built.

headline: null
abstract: At a tribute to fallen Philadelphia police officer Patrick McDonald, Mayor Nutter called for tougher sentencing and parole guidelines for criminals.  Tougher sentencing and parole guidelines will help ensure that criminals like Daniel Giddings--the recent parolee who killed Patrick McDonald--will not be on the streets.  Also, Governor Rendell has agreed to temporarily halt the early release of inmantes so the state's parole system can be reviewed.

headline: Natural gas companies transferring leases in NEPA with other firms
abstract:
Companies are not only signing natural gas leases with landowners in Northeastern Pennsylvania.
Leases are also being transferred between companies, and landowners have little input on such transactions, according to Pennsylvania Oil & Gas Association President Stephen Rhoads.

headline: County awaits state court reimbursements
abstract: Adams County is one of many counties in the state awaiting the results of a lawsuit against Pennsylvania for reimbursment of county positions, such as district attorney. The suit was filed by the County Commissioners Association of Pennsylvania.  The state promised to reimburse counties 65 percent of the salary for their district attorneys; the counties must make up the difference.

headline: Knoll Hospitalized
abstract: According to Gov. Ed Rendell, Lt. Gov. Knoll has been in the hospital undergoing treatment for cancer.  No prognosis was indicated.

headline: Armstrong gets a gold star for the 2007-08 school year
abstract: Armstrong School District made Adequate Yearly Progress toward being proficient in math and reading under the No Child Left Behind Act, but six schools within the district were placed on a warning list for failing to meet proficiency targets. Three AYP targets, test preparation, attendance/graduation rate and academic performance, measure whether districts and schools are making enough progress toward the goal of being 100 percent proficient by 2014. The proficiency requirements increase every year, and Larry Robb, assistant superintendant, said schools on the warning list are not failing, but some adjustments must be made.

headline: no text
abstract: A store in Blair County closed because of high food and gas prices, and as students arrive at the University of Pittsburgh Johnstown campus, they will notice some new improvements from last year. Ridgway Township supervisors voted to give 90 days for people to begin using city water lines; however, many don’t want city water, and they hope Governor Ed Rendell’s signing of a bill last month will boost their case. The PA Department of Transportation claims the Dysart bridge in Cambria County, which collapsed last winter, is on schedule to be completed by October.

headline: PA Fresh Food Initiative, finalist in national competition
abstract: The Fresh Food Initiative is a program managed through a partnership between the PA Department of Community and Economic Development and three non-profit organizations. Through the program’s 52 projects, 3,300 jobs are expected to be created, and healthier food choices are expected to be made more readily available throughout the state. Governor Ed Rendell announced the program is a finalist in a national contest held by Harvard University.

headline: Channel 11 News
abstract: Announcers are waiting for US Sen. Hillary Clinton to exit her car. PA Gov. Rendell is surrounded by a crowd. He is there to demonstrate his support for Hillary. A few supporters of US Sen. Barack Obama can be seen in the crowd of people at the St. Patrick's Day parade.

headline: Pa. lawmakers iffy on work by AG staff
abstract: Several PA legislators from the midstate region had different reactions upon learning that some of PA Attorney General Tom Corbett’s aides were conducting campaign work for him, including his chief of staff, Brian Nutt. While Nutt has taken a leave of absence, Representative Todd Rock said it still "raises too many questions," and Senator Mike Folmer made it clear that he draws a line between his legislative work and campaigning work. Representative Eugene De-Pasquale said he can understand why state employees would want to campaign for their bosses, but he prohibits his employees from doing so, and Representative Steven Nickol commented on the past use of his former chief of staff to conduct campaign work.

headline: null
abstract: Vice-presidential candidate Joe Biden discusses his Pennsylvania roots on a campaign stop in Scranton.

headline: null
abstract: After Philadelphia police officer Patrick McDonald was killed by Daniel Giddings--a recently-paroled inmate--Governor Ed Rendell called on the state Department of Corrections to suspend the release of all convicts eligible for parole until an independent review of the parole and probation process is completed.

headline: Gaming board secrecy alarms
abstract: The Pennsylvania Gaming Control Board has met more behind closed doors than it has in public, the four-year-old agency's records show.The board charged with regulating the casino industry held 128 private meetings, called executive sessions, and 77 meetings in the open, according to board records highlighting a gap in the states sunshine and open records laws.

headline: Aliquippa hospital workers left adrift after closing
abstract: After the Commonwealth Medical Center closure in Aliquippa, more than 70 employees are left to figure out their futures on their own. The hospital will not respond to their questions and concerns.

headline: Rendell signs bill on 'straw' gun buys
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell signed a bill that would crack down on so-called straw purchases, where non-felons buy guns for felons who are not allowed to have weapons.  The law will result in more gun crime prosecutions and jail time for offenders.  The bill would increase penalties for those carrying weapons with obliterated serial numbers.

headline: At CMU, Obama targets energy and education issues
abstract: Sen. Barack Obama joined an A-list panel of business, labor and education leaders at Carnegie Mellon University in a wide-ranging conversation on the roles of energy innovation, education and infrastructure improvements as foundations of prosperity. Mr. Obama was flanked on the stage by a baker's dozen of luminaries, including G. Richard Wagoner Jr., the chairman of General Motors; a Nobel laureate, and the president of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. The assembled talent proved almost too much of a good thing as the need to include comments from so many distinguished voices on an array of complex subjects worked against the ability for any of the individuals to speak at much length or depth on any of them.

headline: No Text
abstract: According to a report by the American Association of State Highway and Transportation Officials, little has been done since the bridge that collapsed in Minneapolis, and one quarter of the nation’s bridges are structurally deficient. PA Governor Ed Rendell, who now chairs the National Governor’s Association, took advantage of the report’s release to call for serious consideration of improving the nation’s infrastructure, especially bridges. The entire infrastructure system is a mess, and the Federal Highway Administration says it would cost $140 billion just to repair bridges.

headline: Parkway visitors hope $17M spices things up
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell, Philadelphia Mayor Michael Nutter and officials from several area groups plan to announce an additional $17 million in investments for the Ben Franklin Parkway. While there were recent efforts to improve the area, some people complained that more needed to be done to make it more appealing to pedestrians. The money will be funded through the state, city and several foundations to help make various improvements to the area.

headline: Channel 11 News
abstract: PA Gov. Rendell has been traveling the nation with California Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger and New York Mayor Bloomburg promoting the need to infrastructure reinvestment. His popularity however, markedly decreases from the eastern to the western side of PA. This is interesting to note given his support for US Sen. Hillary Clinton in the Democratic presidential primary.

headline: Pa. Senate to vote on legal notice bill
abstract: State Senator Robert Wonderling is sponsoring a bill that would allow local governments to place legal notices in free community papers and end a monopoly by the established newspaper industry. Two Senate committees have endorsed the proposal, Senate Bill 428, without opposition, and the full chamber could vote on it as early as next week.

headline: House Democrats should provide records
abstract: If House Democrats and Majority Leader Bill DeWeese really support government transparency and the new Open Records Law, they should allow the taxpayers to see how 677,284 dollars of their money was spent.  That is the amount of taxpayer money the House Democratic Caucus spent on legal representation for 110 caucus employees in connection with state Attorney General Tom Corbett's investigation of the Bonusgate scandal.  Majority Leader DeWeese and his attorney will not allow the list of caucus employees receiving taxpayer-funded legal help to become public information, as they claim that releasing such information constitutes a breach attorney-client privilege.

headline: Rendell, Corzine order cuts in trying times
abstract: Due to the current economic crisis, Governors Rendell and Corzine are anticipating declining state revenues and increased demands on unemployment funds.  In response to these anticipated revenue declines, Governor Rendell has instituted a number of spending cuts to keep Pennsylvania's budget balanced.  Also, Governor Corzine is calling for 5 percent budget trims in every state department.

headline: Hospital undergoes baby boom
abstract: Holy Spirit Hospital is expanding its pregnancy-related services and accepting all women, rich and poor. The Cumberland County-based hospital expanded its Center for Women's Health to include an East Shore location at 2850 Commerce Drive in Lower Paxton Twp. One goal is to offer convenience for existing patients who live on the East Shore. But Holy Spirit, a nonprofit Catholic hospital, also hopes to draw more business.

headline: $1.8 billion lost; common sense, too
abstract: Public School Employees Retirement System gave out $845,000 in bonuses to 21 investment staff employees although the System lost $1.8 billion during the 2007-08 fiscal year.

headline: Some of the key players in Fumo corruption trial
abstract: A list of the key players in the Vince Fumo federal corruption trial.

headline: Bill would limit cyber school costs
abstract: Staunch advocates of PA's cyber charter schools would have you believe that House Bill 446, legislation aimed at correcting exorbitant costs for some of these online programs, will effectively shut down cyber schools. This is merely a scare tactic to further delay consideration of the first meaningful piece of cost-containment legislation since the adoption of Act 1 of the Special Session of 2006. The PA School Boards Association is not the only organization calling for cyber charter school funding and accountability reform. Auditor General Jack Wagner called on Gov. Ed Rendell and the General Assembly to reform the way Pennsylvania funds both brick-and-mortar charter schools and cyber charter schools.

headline: no text
abstract: Company officials and workers have reached a four-year tentative agreement at a paper mill, and it must now be approved by at least 50 percent of the union employees. The governor announced that Cambria County will receive $18 million in investments for repairing ten-area bridges. In addition, the PA Turnpike Commission is still pushing to toll Interstate 80.

headline: Pennsylvania's cities deserve attention for good of entire commonwealth
abstract: The Brookings Institution, a non-partisan think-tank in Washington, conducted a study that showed that the health of Pennsylvania's cities is vital to the economic health of the entire state. They recommended encouraging growth in  Pennsylvania's metropolitan areas, and the editorial board agrees.

headline: Chelsea campaigns
abstract: Former first daughter Chelsea Clinton came to Penn State University Park to campaign on behalf of her mother Senator Hillary Clinton, a candidate to be the Democratic nominee in the upcoming Presidential election. Clinton's opponent is Senator Barack Obama.

headline: Panel to Start Hearing on Medical Data     Bill Would Streamline Privacy Protections
abstract: In light of recent news reports that pharmacies were sending customers’ information to a company in Massachusetts, U.S. Senators Robert Bennett and James Jeffords were supposed to release a final version of a bill to prohibit the sale of an individual’s health information for profit, but it was delayed because of criticism that there were too many loopholes. The Senate Labor and Human Resources Committee will hold a hearing today on the legislation, and Senator Patrick Leahy, who proposed a similar bill, will speak at the hearing.

headline: No on Unisys sign a win for the skyline
abstract: The ruling by the Zoning Board of Adhustment to reject the proposal for a Unisys sign midway up liberty place is good news.  The sign represented a clear violation of city zoning ordinances and would have set a dangerous precedent, opening the door to numerous signs on every building and causing visual congestion.  Having such a strict policy for city planning will, in the long run, attract--not deter--business and investment in the city.

headline: Pa. lawmakers exit early, leave road work undone
abstract: PA House and Senate legislative sessions are scheduled to end this month so that lawmakers can begin re-election campaigning.  This means that legislators will go home without figuring out how to provide funding to close the state's transportation budget gap.  This is an important problem that our full-time legislators need to solve, and the best way to do that is to hold a joint session after the November 4th elections.

headline: The story of library closings
abstract: W. Wilson Goode Sr, former Philadelphia mayor, outlines the situation surrounding budget cuts to the Free Philadelphia Library and branch closing.

headline: Protect auto jobs for the long term: Johnstown has shown lost work won’t return
abstract: An editorial argues that domestic car making needs protections for the long run and that calls for restructuring, not just loans. Once union jobs are lost, the writer asserts, they are lost forever.

headline: Kennel law a legacy of slaughtered dogs
abstract: The Reading Eagle supports efforts by the state to end the state's reputation as a home for crooked pet breeders.  The new kennel law will force kennel operators to upgrade their housing for dogs and will ban the practice of shooting dogs that owners do not wish to take care of with proper veterinary care.

headline: Blue Cross: Don't blame us for costs to teachers
abstract: The 34% increase in the amount of money teachers in Scranton must pay out-of-hand is not the fault of Blue Cross, but of the school districts who negotiated the contract, Blue Cross says.

headline: No Text
abstract: Gas prices remain high, and in southeastern PA, it costs $4.15 for a gallon of regular unleaded gasoline, compared to $4.03 in Delaware and $3.995 in New Jersey. Rising fuel will cost the price of jitney rides in Atlantic City to rise, and Governor Rendell will meet with developers of two proposed Philadelphia casinos along the Delaware River because of opposition from residents and Mayor Michael Nutter.

headline: Preservationists get reprieve
abstract: A PA Commonwealth Court judge ordered that the state not touch two historic North Broad Street buildings until a full trial later in the month determines whether the state Department of General Services is obliged to honor a preservation agreement that was signed by the Convention Center and state historic commission. The Preservation Alliance of Greater Philadelphia is fighting to save the buildings.

headline: Chelsea Clinton to visit York
abstract: US Sen. Hillary Clinton's daughter Chelsea Clinton will be at York College campaigning for her mother. Chelsea has been making stops at college campuses around the nation.

headline: PENNSYLVANIA PRESENCE
abstract: PA had record voter registration before the April primary, and Democratic presidential candidate Barack Obama believes there is an opportunity to register more of the remaining 1.1 million Pennsylvanians still not registered to vote. While Obama lost the state’s Democratic primary to U.S. Senator Hillary Rodham Clinton, he has established 29 campaign offices in the state, which will help him expand his grass-roots operation and get his message out. Republican challenger John McCain only has three offices in PA, but that doesn’t mean he is giving up in the battleground state.

headline: Harrison manufacturer plans 1.2 million expansion
abstract: Metplas, a precision machinery manufacturer, is planning a more than 1 million dollar expansion this year to help meet increasing demands for its products.  The company, located in Highlands Industrial Park, recently purchased and will add 1440 square feet to its building off Route 908 and will occupy the space by the end of the year.

headline: Nutter replaces minority-hiring council
abstract: Stating its inability to help minority-owned companies, Philadelphia Mayor Michael Nutter dissolved the Minority Business Enterprise Council and replaced it with a new unit that will report directly to him.  Mayor Nutter appointed Michael Bell to head the new Economic Opportunity Office--an office whose chief task will be to help minority-owned businesses get their fair share of city contracts.

headline: Editorial: The Kimmel Center
abstract: Urging the Kimmel Center's CEO to start looking at improvements to the center in order to make it the quailty that was promised now that the Kimmel's books are balanced.

headline: Voting-machine challenge back on track
abstract: The Pennsylvania Supreme court will allow the case of testing the  legality of electronic voting systems to continue. The lawsuit says direct recording electronic voting machines (DREs) violate the state election code which requires a physical permanent record of each vote cast.  The case will be returned to the Commonwealth Court.

headline: Challenge to state authority
abstract: Residents of Conestoga Township are asking the the state Fish & Boat Commission to transfer or dismiss Jeffrey Schmidt, the officer assigned to the area.  They complain of his confrontational behavior with the public.  More than 200 signed a petition about this.  While investigators in Harrisburg research the situation, Schmidt is expected to continue working.

headline: Chester-Upland School District in distress
abstract: When the morning bells ring in the Chester-Upland School District, more students in kindergarten through eighth grade are sitting in charter-school classrooms than in all other district schools combined, according to district Superintendent Gregory Thornton. State Sen. Dominic Pileggi, a charter-school proponent, says, "It should be a wake-up call to school administrators that when parents are allowed choice, they're choosing another education provider over what the district is providing." Charter schools are offering choices to parents in the city of Chester who have long been disappointed or discouraged by the school district. But the charter schools also present a challenge to a district that is trying to reform under new leadership.

headline: no text
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell said tolling Interstate 80 isn’t his top choice, but raising the gas tax, privatizing the turnpike and tolling I-80 are all worth exploring to raise badly needed funds for road and bridge repair. The decision to allow tolling now rests with the Federal Highway Administration, and Rendell doesn’t think tolling would hit local drivers too hard. In other news, ten businesses in Huntingdon County were burglarized in two nights.

headline: Ravenstahl takes sweep campaign to streets of California-Kirkbride
abstract: Over 30 people, including Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl, took part in the city’s fourth code enforcement sweep, which took place on the streets of California-Kirkbride and discovered 113 code violations. A nonprofit company contracted by the city mows weeds on over 75 vacant lots alone in the community, and numerous households in the neighborhood have been demolished since 2000. Officials are hoping to find ways to re-plan some of this land, and there are signs of improvement and hope for the community.

headline: Citizen redistricting
abstract: In 2004, the United States Supreme Court refused to rule against blatant gerrymandering by Pennsylvanian Republicans in the drawing of congressional district lines. However, now the state legislature is trying to amend the state constitution so that congressional district lines will be determined by an independent bipartisan commission. This will require passage by both the state House and Senate, as well as approval by popular referendum.

headline: Pennsylvanians speak in one voice - their own
abstract: The editorial board discusses primary races in which Pennsylvanians nominated an unlikely candidate in the primary race. National polls indicate the Democratic nomination for President will be U.S. Senator Barack Obama, but U.S. Senator Hillary Clinton won the Pennsylvania primary. In the race for retiring Senator Roger A. Madigan’s seat, Eugene Yaw defeated state Representative Stephen W. Cappelli and Bradford County Commissioner Doug McLinko in spite of being new to politics. Former Williamsport Area School Board director Dave Huffman defeated County Commissioner Rebecca Burke and Dottie White. For the House of Representatives seat occupied by Democrat Chris Carney, Republicans chose Chris Hackett, a business owner heavily outspent by his opponent.

headline: A tribute to 80 dogs
abstract: In the wake of one of the most horrific cases of animal abuse in Pennsylvania, it is especially important that members of the General Assembly pass House Bill 2525.  The bill would finally make it illegal to abuse dogs in commercial kennels and ensure that they are not neglected or treated inhumanely.  We have gone for far too long without such legislation in place, and the end result is abuse at so-called puppy mills, the most recent of which lead to the slaughter of 80 dogs.

headline: SPCA raids 'horrific' Lehigh County kennel
abstract: Pennsylvania SPCA agents raided a Lehigh County dog kennel yesterday and discovered hundreds of animals living in unsanitary conditions.  The kennel owner, Derbe Eckhart, faces 500 counts of animal cruelty; Eckhart has been convicted of animal cruelty twice in the past but currently is licensed by the PA Department of Agriculture to run a kennel.

headline: 'Forbesburgh' better reflects city's founding, military historian argues
abstract: Highlights the last "Hinge of History" seminar last night in Pittsburgh and tells the story of Gen. John Forbes, who took present day Pittsburgh from the French for the British.

headline: Doctors going paperless
abstract: An editorial presuading doctors to use electronic prescription systems for faster and better service to patients.  But cuts in Medicare bonuses will make using computerized prescription less desirable.

headline: Phillies fans tell Nutter: No cap for Billy Penn
abstract: Phillies fans are begging Philadelphia Mayor Mike Nutter to not put a giant Phillies hat on top of the William Penn statue atop Philadelphia City Hall.  History and superstition are cited as main reasons.

headline: Citizens Bank takes some colleges off loan list
abstract: Citizens Bank has notified several community colleges in PA that it will no longer provide federal loans to students attending those schools. Community College of Allegheny County said yesterday it was told of the decision in a phone call from a bank sales representative. Financial aid staff at community colleges in Westmoreland, Beaver and Butler counties say they received the same notice, as did officials with Luzerne County Community College in northeastern PA. Citizens Bank would not discuss details, including how many colleges in all it has contacted.

headline: No Text
abstract: Governor Rendell and leaders of the PA Legislature reached a budget agreement before the deadline, so state workers will avoid being temporarily laid off. PA will not use any of its "rainy day" funds or increase taxes, but it will borrow $2.5 billion for many highway, bridge, sewer, water and energy improvement projects. Yesterday, a man robbed a Dollar General store in Clymer, and at the beginning of the article, the death penalty is discussed in a criminal case.

headline: Realtors say existing laws should be used
abstract: Housing advocates told senators that outdated state laws hamper the ability of local officials to fight blight. But an influential lobby group representing realtors said the best way to rid communities of derelict properties is by enforcing municipal building codes and state laws already on the books. The contrasting views came during a hearing before the Senate Urban Affairs and Housing Committee. The committee is looking at a measure sponsored by Sen. James Rhoades to give local officials more power to take action against owners of abandoned and derelict properties.

headline: City may soon limit campaign donations
abstract: Pittsburgh lawmakers edged closer to capping contributions to candidates who have enjoyed unrestricted campaign donations. If the bill passes a final vote, individual donors would be limited each election to giving $2,000 -- and political action committees, $5,000 -- to candidates for mayor, city controller and City Council. The legislation is modeled after federal campaign finance laws. With no limits on the size of donations to candidates running for elected office, Pittsburgh is the exception among major U.S. cities, Peduto said.

headline: Pension liabilities loom as states try to help retirees
abstract: The high price of gasoline and food is prompting many states to fatten cost-of-living increases for retired teachers and civil servants. Those raises are easing the pain of inflation for government retirees but dealing a serious blow to efforts to improve the financial health of government pension plans. Cost-of-living hikes can add billions of dollars in unfunded obligations to state and local government pensions, which cover 14 million workers and 7 million retirees. Pennsylvania is considering giving retirees their first inflation increase since 2002, at a cost of $10 billion over 20 years.

headline: Lack of loans for tuition puts students in bind
abstract: Problems in financial markets have made it difficult for some lenders to access money.  As a result, many stopped offering student loans.  To free up money for college, Pennsylvania's congressional delegation helped draft a bill that was enacted in May; the bill increased the amount that students could borrow and allowed lenders to sell their outstanding loans to the U.S. Department of Education.

headline: Gov. Rendell cuts rates on three business loan programs
abstract: Citing the effects of the national economy on Pennsylvania businesses, Governor Ed Rendell announced the lowering of interest rates on three of the state's key lending programs.  The PA Industrial Development Authority voted to lower the interest rate on its loans to 3 percent on all future projects.  The measure is designed to promote business growth.

headline: Private investment would spark growth
abstract: A visiting fellow at the Brookings Institution said greater Reading must develop walkable neighborhoods in order to survive. That would require an investment from the private sector that we would love to witness says the Reading Eagle.

headline: City Council refuses South Side liquor license
abstract: Pittsburgh City Council says the South Side area has reached its alcohol saturation limit at 53 establishments. Councilman Bruce Kraus says 63 restaurants and bars already serve alcohol and 10 must close before another alcohol license will be issued for a new establishment.

headline: Market downturn imperils foundation grants
abstract: The effect that the crumbling economy is having on philanthropic organizations is discussed.  Organizations are having trouble keeping donations flowing while watching their investments lose money precipitiously.  In the meantime, like donors, the organizations are forced to pull back on investments in the community while they try to right their ship.

headline: City schools' future uncertain as enrollment dwindles
abstract: According to the PA Department of Education, enrollment in Pittsburgh Public Schools is expected to decline drastically from 75,000 students in 1967 to 22,435 in 2016, and school district officials are trying to figure out how to deal with the problem of excess capacity in many of their schools. Enrollment has dropped because of the growing popularity of charter schools and the bad perception of the city’s public schools; however, enrollment is also a reflection of the Western PA trends of an aging population and low birth rates. The school district is beginning to offer more options in schools, but it is also meeting with the public and is considering closing some of its schools to improve efficiency.

headline: No Text
abstract: Governor Rendell signed a bill that will allow PA to invest an additional $350 million to make bridge repairs more quickly and provide an extra $15 million for airport and rail projects. He also signed a new coal mine safety bill, and the newly passed state budget will include $650 million towards alternative energy sources, which many claim will help reduce the state’s reliance on foreign oil. A bio-diesel producer explained the benefits of using biofuel, which can be derived from a soybean to fuel a car, and Patrick Meehan, Southeastern Pennsylvania’s top federal prosecutor has resigned.

headline:
Rendell signs off on mortgage fraud bills
'Cornerstone' of package requires brokers to be licensed, continue education.
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell signed a package of bills into law that will make it tougher to get away with mortgage fraud in PA, and while he praised state Senator Pat Browne for his efforts in helping pass the bills, he called for even more legislation in the future. Tougher regulations could have prevented prior cases of fraud, including Wesley Snyder, who was sentenced to 12 years in prison for fraudulent business operations that resulted in borrowers finding out they owed tens of thousands more on mortgages than they’d anticipated. Rendell acknowledged the seriousness of the mortgage crisis and directed troubled homeowners to the state Housing Finance Agency.

headline: City school district union authorizes strike
abstract: For the second straight year, a labor dispute is threatening to disrupt operations for Pittsburgh’s Public Schools. Clerical workers represented by Local 2924 of the American Federation of State, County and Municipal Employees authorized their negotiating committee to call a strike at any time. School board members expressed concern that the decision will threaten negotiations, but the union’s director said he is still committed to negotiating a contract without a strike.

headline: Perhaps Obama doesn't like parades
abstract: With US Sen. Hillary Clinton leading in the PA polls, the state no longer appears to be a priority for US Sen. Barack Obama in the Democratic presidential primary. Obama denies this. Hillary has exerted much greater effort in the western part of the state than has Obama. Pennsylvanians have every right to feel cheated, as we were once told a close fight between Hillary and Obama would make the voices of residents important. We were promised the spotlight, but unless both politicians engage in the fight, attention seems unlikely.

headline: Agency scrutiny valid exercise
abstract: Pennsylvania does not need both the PA Department of Transportation and the PA Turnpike Commission, and having both guarantees a duplication of services.  Given this,  it is especially troubling that a new law establishing tolls on Interstate 80 and increase turnpike tolls across the board would give the commission more power, not less.

headline: Two-thirds of county's sudden infant deaths are African Americans
abstract: The high incidence of Sudden Infant Death Syndrome among African Americans in Allegheny County has prompted local health officials to help the African-American community reduce the risk.  Officials have created the Infant Safe Sleep Church Outreach Committee to recruit African-American clergy to educate their congregations on preventing SIDS.

headline: null
abstract: A bridge was destroyed by a druk driver in Washington Township when he struck the bridge station.

headline: Public Schools board holds line on property tax
abstract: Pittsburgh Public Schools board allowed for a property tax freeze for the eigth year in a row. The budget was balanced by making $10.4 million in cuts and using $13.1 million from the district's surplus.

headline: Don’t bank on gaming revenue
abstract: Casino revenue has taken an expected slump due to the economy, but while the initial impact of the revenue may be seen as a windfall, residents shouldn't expect it to continue indefinitely.  Revenue from state casinos has resulted in property and wage tax relief as well as aiding public projects such as libraries.

headline: City schools' future uncertain as enrollment dwindles
abstract: The city school board cannot lock away a looming problem by closing Schenley High School. The Oakland school might be only the first the board will need to shutter or find another use for. Enrollment in Pittsburgh Public Schools is expected to plunge from about 75,000 students in 1967 to 22,435 in 2016, according to the Pennsylvania Department of Education. The problem: a declining birth rate, an exodus of families from the city and growing popularity of charter schools. As a result, students occupy only 72 percent of seats in the district's high schools, even fewer in some schools.

headline: No Text
abstract: It took a lot of work to get $35 million into the state budget towards an expansion project of route 219, but the decision wasn’t approved until the final hour. It was the only road project out of 14 seeking state funding that had federal funding to match it, and Governor  Rendell said he’d support it if were included in the budget a specific way.

headline: Rendell unveils funding plan for Chester soccer stadium
abstract: PA Governor Edward Rendell unveiled a $47 million state funding package to aid in the construction of a soccer stadium on the Chester waterfront in order to attract a Major League Soccer franchise to the Philadelphia area. Rendell and the PA state Senate Majority Leader Dominic Pileggi announced the project that also calls for a convention center, offices, apartments and townhouses, retail space and a parking garage. In the state package, $25 million goes toward the stadium and is contingent on MLS awarding a franchise. That money, combined with $30 million committed by Delaware County and the city of Chester and a potential $10 million from the Delaware River Port Authority, would go toward a planned 18,500-seat stadium on the banks of the Delaware River.

headline: City taxpayers to foot bill in billboard dispute
abstract: City taxpayers will cover an $11,000 attorney bill incurred by four Pittsburgh council members in their battle with Lamar Advertising if yesterday's first vote holds up in a final tally Tuesday. Council President Doug Shields and members William Peduto, Bruce Kraus and Ricky Burgess had hired lawyer Hugh McGough, who billed for his work on a zoning challenge to a Lamar billboard permit and a civil suit by the sign firm against five members. Councilman Patrick Dowd, who also challenged Lamar and paid a lawyer from his own pocket, said council shouldn't pay "after the fact" for an expense it never voted to authorize.

headline: Petition scandal casting pall over election in Pennsylvania Commentary - Minor parties, forced off the 2004 and 2006 ballots, are lying low this year.
abstract: 12 people connected to the PA Democratic House caucus were arrested as part of state Attorney General Tom Corbett’s public corruption investigation, and one of the allegations is that they paid subordinates to inspect petitions that blocked independent and third-party candidates from running for office in 2004 and 2006. Because of this, Carl Romanelli and Ralph Nader, who were both forced off the ballot by petition challenges, have filed motions in state court to overturn court orders that require their campaigns to pay $80,000 in legal fees. Independent and third-party candidates must obtain significantly more signatures than the two major parties to seek office, and this year, there has been little contention over access to the ballot.

headline: Last call for lighting up
abstract: The PA state Legislature approved a statewide smoking ban in June.  The law takes effect in less than two weeks and bans cigarette, cigar and pipe smoking in restaurants, office buildings, schools, sports arenas, theaters, and bus and train stations.  The law does, however, allow smoking in some bars, portions of casino floors and in some private clubs.

headline: Legislation troubles Center and Monaca school boards
abstract: With the merger of the Center Area and Monaca School Districts, Center Area will lose its ability to levy mercantile taxes, which generate over 300,000 per annum.  This has upset Center Area board members and has induced state Representative Vince Biancucci to propose legislation that lets new entities levy a mercantile tax if one of the entities involved in the merger previously had the tax.  If the legislation passes, the new combined school board will have to approve the tax.  The tax will likely be opposed by Monaca residents, as it will hurt small businesses in that region.

headline: null
abstract: Highlights Catherine Baker Knoll's funeral ceremony.

headline: Federal authorities are investigating after letters containing white powder were sent to 40 governors around the country--including Governor Rendell.
abstract: A envelope with white powder and a compact disc containing anti-war sentiments was sent to the office of Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell yesterday.  Investigators say the materials were not dangerous.

headline: Growing pains in education
abstract: Studies are showing that lower classroom sizes result in higher student achievement.  Local school officials are faced with a dilemma -- allow classroom sizes to grow or find ways to cut down on classroom size.  Local schools are already running at or above capacity and some districts have been caught off guard by the recent increase in enrollment .

headline: Civics lessons take the spotlight
abstract: As Pennsylvania's first lady watched, Captain Justice bowed and exited stage left at high speed. Rendell and the other dignitaries applauded in relief. Besides enjoying the skit, the first lady (a federal appeals court judge) visited classrooms, took part in a mock congressional hearing, and listened as students presented action plans for issues. These all showed how Ritter weaves its citizenship program into its curriculum and everyday life. The school is a pilot site for a program, developed by the California-based Center for Civic Education, that aims to prevent school violence by focusing on justice, privacy, authority and responsibility.

headline: No Text
abstract: PA Attorney General Tom Corbett’s bonus investigation has led to charges against former state Representative Mike Veon and eleven others for illegally spending taxpayers’ dollars to run political campaigns. The PA Turnpike released more details about its proposal to begin tolling Interstate 80. In addition, Governor Ed Rendell became the new chairman of the National Governor’s Association, and he says his top priority will be getting more money for improvements on the nation’s roads, bridges and railroads.

headline:
Search for building code violations shows some success in Oakland
Ravenstahl plans to expand program to other neighborhoods in city
abstract: In order to improve property conditions in Central and South Oakland, building inspectors made sweeps of the areas, and by the end of the day, they had written 140 violations. It was the third year for code sweeps in Oakland, and Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl plans to conduct another one in Oakland next month as well as more in other neighborhoods. University of Pittsburgh Chancellor Mark Nordenberg spoke at a building that had been evacuated due to safety concerns but is available again for tenants, and many believe that fines costing hundreds of thousands of dollars may have scared other building owners into compliance.

headline: City, white-collar union agree on 1-year pact
abstract: Philadelphia’s white-collar union agreed to the same one-year contract that the city’s blue-collar union agreed to three weeks ago, which includes a signing bonus and the same health-care contributions but no raises. The Fraternal Order of Police already signed a one-year deal, leaving the firefighters’ union as the only city union without a contact. Mayor Nutter is pleased with the one-year contracts because the three unions agreed to participate in a city health-care committee that will examine how to lower costs.

headline: Philadelphia Ballot Questions
abstract: The editorial board urges voters to vote "yes" on two referendums that will be on the primary election ballot in Philadelphia. One would grant Philadelphia Mayor Nutter more flexibility in hiring top-level deputies to run city departments, and the other would separate the duties of the city commerce director and city representative.

headline: null
abstract: Governor Ed Rendell visited Wilkes-Barre today to announce millions of dollars of state funding to help the local economy.  Millions in state money will be used to re-develop the stegmaier building and murray complex.

headline: Boost coverage before election
abstract: Governor Rendell and Senate Republicans could not come to an agreement on expanding health insurance coverage for low-income workers. As a result, the governor threatened to discontinue the doctors' premium program--a program that is used to help pay part of physicians' malpractice insurance premiums--if the program's surplus was not used to provide health care coverage for low-income workers.  Senate Republicans are willing to use the money to fund health clinics, however, and lawmakers and the governor should work towards a compromise proposal that incorporates elements of both plans.

headline: null
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell introduced new legislation that would provide health insurance for 250,000 uninsured Pennsylvanians.  A debate on the proposal is expected to start soon.

headline: null
abstract: Highlights a speech by Governor Rendell at Catherine Baker Knoll's memorial service.

headline: Section of the state capitol was evacuated this afternoon -- after a suspicious letter -- showed up in the governor' s mail room.
abstract: A envelope leaking with white powder was sent to the mailroom of Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell yesterday.  A section of the state Capitol building was evacuated. Investigators say the powder was not dangerous.

headline: Better foreclosure information essential as reforms are made
abstract: While $700 million was approved to help banks write off bad debt, better information information and reporting are needed as reforms are attempted.  HUD should be designated as the official data center for foreclosures.

headline: Colleges get grant from government
abstract: PA Senator Robert Casey announced the Southeastern PA Consortium for Higher Education (SEPCHE) will receive a federally funded $527,000 grant. The money was signed into law as part of the Labor, Health and Human Services and Education Appropriations Bill, will be used to support the SEPCHE Institute of Mathematics and Science, which educates teachers of grades K-12 and develops instructional materials for distribution in classrooms.

headline: No Text
abstract: PA legislators passed a law in 2005 requiring all district attorney’s in the state to be full time, with the promise that it would reimburse each county for two thirds of the cost, but due to cuts in this year’s proposed budget, the state will not be able to make those payments. While the news is disappointing for Centre County Commissioner Jon Eich, he said the county should be able to find the funds to cover the costs, but it could be difficult for less fortunate counties. The temporary memorial honoring the victims of Flight 93 will be moving shortly while a permanent site is developed, and someone stole $10,000 worth of rail tracks in Clover Township.

headline: Slots applications mailed early
abstract: The Washington County Redevelopment Authority mailed applications for the county's share of slots revenue to the PA Department of Community and Economic Development, which has final authority of approval. Revenue from The Meadow's casino is expected to reach $8 million, while next year's revenue is expected to reach $12. State legislators held the first of a series of public meetings on changing the awards process for local shares. East Washington Borough Councilman Jeff Bull told PA Sen. J. Barry Stout wants to invest in projects that retain residents.

headline: City's personnel director resigns
abstract: Acting city Personnel Director Tanya Smith resigned after she was investigated by the city's inspector general, mayoral spokesman Doug Oliver said. Oliver declined to describe the investigation or to release further details. Inspector General Amy Kurland declined to comment through a staffer. The three-member commission has the authority to appoint or remove the personnel director. Mayor Nutter announced his appointees to the Civil Service Commission last week. None of Mayor John F. Street's appointees were retained.

headline: Pittsburgh council may ban windshield fliers
abstract: Pittsburgh City Councilman Bruce Kraus wants to ban most windshield fliers because they often contain images that could be considered offensive and usually end up littering the streets.

headline: null
abstract: Governor Rendell visited Somerset County yesterday to kick off his five-day bus tour.  During the tour, Governor Rendell plans to highlight how local communities will benefit from projects included in the new PA budget.  In Somerset County, some money will be used to repair local bridges.

headline: Man says he had right to carry gun to rally
abstract: John A. Noble of Industry Pennsylvania was arrested during presidential election rally in Beaver, PA.  Noble was carrying a fully-loaded handgun that was holstered on his side.  He claims that he did not break any laws and was perfectly within his rights to carry the gun in plain sight.  Noble never tried to draw his weapon and went peacefully into police custody; Noble faces misdemeanor charges.

headline: null
abstract: The 13 billion dollar offer by an investment group wishing to lease the Pennsylvania Turnpike expired yesterday.  Governor Rendell was pushing for the lease, but his hopes may have been dashed with the offer expiration.

headline: null
abstract: Highlights Catherine Baker Knoll's funeral ceremony.

headline: Treatment promising in killing two cancers
abstract: A method discovered by Washington County native John Kanzius, targets cancer cells with nanoparticals and kills then them with radio frequency, or RF energy.  So far, the tests have been sucessful in lab animals with pancreatic and colorectal cancers.  Human trials are 2 to 2 1/2 years away.

headline: Soccer parents wince at prospect of guns at games
abstract: After a Lebanon County judge ruled that Meleanie Hain should get back her concealed gun permit, parents are trying to avoid creating an environment at soccer games where guns are permitted.  Hain had her permit revoked by the county sheriff for bringing a gun to a child's soccer game.  Parents and soccer organizers are trying to figure out ways to ban people from bringing guns to games.

headline: Communities need public libraries
abstract: The prospects are bleak for PA’s public school libraries, so goes the reading ability of our children. Nearly 40 percent of the commonwealth’s public schools are without a library. Those that still have them house aging, tattered collections. A 2007 study by the Follett Software Co. at the request of the PA Department of Education’s School Library Services Division found that the average age of library books in Bucks and Berks County public schools was 23 years. In Luzerne County, the average public school library book dates from 1978. Extensive research done over 10 years in 16 states has documented that student reading scores rise when students have access to a well-stocked school library and a librarian who teaches information literacy skills.

headline: No Text
abstract: Six people were injured when two cars had a head-on collision on route 31, and police are continuing to search for the cause of the accident. Governor Rendell will sign the state’s budget, which will allot $350 million to repair some of Pennsylvania’s worst bridges. Rendell will then go to Greene County to sign an update to the deep mine safety law.

headline: Specter to HUD leader: Explain
abstract: US Senator for Arlen Specter, Arlen Specter demanded answers from Housing and Urban Development Secretary Alphonso Jackson regarding the decision to freeze $40 million for Philadelphia public housing. Specter insinuated that the freeze was a retaliation against the Philadelphia Housing Authority for spurning a developer. PHA director Carl Greene maintinas the funding freeze is punishment for his refusal to grant at no cost, properties valued at $7 million to University Community Homes, requested by Kenny Gamble, friend of Mayor Street.

headline: Clamor for change
abstract: The author, Russ Diamond, is writing about how he believes that the “Year of Reform” in PA was not as great as it was supposed to be because there has been no movement or serious reforms coming from the PA state House or Senate. He also believes that the PA governor, Edward Rendell, has not been helping to move the reform that he talked about having on his agenda in the beginning. He says that some are predicting 2008 to be a better year of reform because it is election year for over  90% of the PA General Assembly, but he is hesitant to believe this.

headline: Pittsburgh councilman urges URA contracts review
abstract: Pittsburgh Councilman Bill Peduto wants the city’s controller to review the Urban Redevelopment Authority’s contracts to make sure it is spending money wisely. He said he became suspicious after the URA awarded a $525,000 contract to a firm whose president had donated $10,000 to Mayor Luck Ravenstahl’s campaign, even though there were two lower bidders. PA Senator Jim Ferlo, a URA board member, said he’d welcome an audit, and the URA defended the contract.

headline: null
abstract: Governor Rendell kicked off a 16-stop bus tour yesterday to highlight 642 million in state investments that will help stimulate job and economic growth.  The tour includes stops in Cambria and Somerset Counties.

headline: Lebanon schools face financial woes
abstract: Due to the state budget impasse, the Lebanon School District is going to encouter problems meeting its payroll and other obligations.  If a budget does not pass soon, the district will be forced to borrow money from itself.

headline: null
abstract: A statewide smoking ban is scheduled to go into effect.  The law was signed almost 90 days ago by Governor Rendell.  The measure bans cigarette, cigar and pipe smoking in restairants, office buildings, schools, sports arenas theaters and bus and train stations.

headline: New judge appointed, Fumo trial to resume October 20
abstract: A new federal judge, U.S. District Judge Ronald Buckwalter, was assigned to the corruption trial of former PA state Senator Vincent J. Fumo.  The new judge scheduled a hearing for next week to handle unresolved legal issues, including the prosecutorial request to exclude all of Fumo's character witnesses from the courtroom until they testify.  Senator Fumo is accused of using Senate resources for personal and political benefit.

headline: null
abstract: Highlights the life and death of Catherine Baker Knoll.

headline: Narrow interests still blow smoke
abstract: An editorial that chastizes the legislators who give in to special interests that undermine the smoking ban.  Instead creating numerous exemptions for certain establishments.

headline: Program battles lead poisoning
abstract: The Penn State Fayette County Cooperative Extension Office has made free lead testing kits available to qualifying families.  Their goal is to distribute 700 kits over the next 3 years.  Lead paint is prevalent in housing built before 1950.  Nearly half the homes in the area fall into this category.

headline: Consultant off Pittsburgh Public Schools payroll
abstract: Lynn Spampinato's contract as the Pittsburgh Public Schools administrator and consultant has ended.

headline: no text
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation and State Police announced they’re spending between $2 million and $3 million to make the area where Route 581 meets Interstate 83 safer.

headline: Specter wants HUD PHA dispute resolved
abstract: US Housing and Urban Development Secretary Alphonso Jackson cannot recall if anyone with R&B Kenny Gamble's nonprofit complained about a dispute with the Philadelphia Housing Authority when asked by US Sen. Arlen Specter. However, documents in a related federal court case reveal Jackson met with Gamble. The PHA has sued HUD, saying the department stripped the agency of its funding status for not accommodating Universal Community Homes. Records show Jackson and Gamble's office discussed reaching out to Philadelphia Mayor Street to request completion of the transaction.

headline: Clinton opens Pa. push in Scranton
abstract: US Sen. Hillary Clinton kicked off her campaign in the PA primary in Scranton, mentioning all her local ties. She refrained from attacks on US Sen. Barack Obama, her democratic rival. She refused to entertain thoughts of asking Obama to serve as Vice President should she win the party's nomination. Obama wondered how someone in second place could offer the job to someone in first. The state has 157 delegates. Clinton will need support in Northeastern PA to offset Obama's support in Philadelphia and its suburbs.

headline: Pittsburgh Laurels & Lances
abstract: The editorial board lists positive and negative recent events. The number of registered voters in Allegheny County is almost as high as its previous record when Governor Ed Rendell and Bob Casey Jr. were competing for the gubernatorial seat. Pittsburgh controller Michael Lamb is advocating that the city stay under state receivership. Pittsburgh councilman advocates "revenue sharing", which amounts to a bailout. The Pennsylvania Department of Transportation won't release inspection reports on the Birmingham Bridge.

headline: null
abstract: U.S. Senator Bob Casey is pushing to prevent U.S. soldier electrocutions in Iraq.  About 15 soldiers have lost their lives due to faulty underground wiring.

headline: Souderton Teachers On Strike, No School on Tuesday
abstract: Teachers in the Soudertown Area School District announced Monday that they are going on strike.  Negotiations between the teacher's union and the school board were not successful--citing health care and salary as the main sources of disagreement.

headline: Landlord licensing deadline extended
abstract: An ordinance passed in December set a September 30th deadline for all Pittsburgh landlords to register with the city.  This deadline has been extended until April 1st--six months past the initial deadline.  Landlords will also have to pay a 12-dollar-per-unit fee.

headline: null
abstract: Highlights Catherine Baker Knoll's funeral, plans by Governor Rendell and Senate President Pro Tempore Joe Scarnati to suspendi the raises for nonunion appointees and top staff, and loans by PA to save the retailer Boscov's.

headline: Thorns to state official for seeking federal post on the taxpayers' dime
abstract: Pennsylvania's Agriculture Secretary, Dennis Wolff, used a taxpayer funded car and fuel to travel to Washington D.C. to seek a job in President-elect Barack Obama's Cabinet.  Pennsylvania Governor, Ed Rendell, placed a ban on out of state travel to cut state budget costs.

headline: Eyewitness News at 11
abstract: Gov. Ed Rendell has called the death of PA state senator James Rhoades a tremendous loss for the state.

headline: Cost relief: It's time for the state to raise its stake in schools
abstract: For too long, quality education in PA has been overly dependent on local property taxes and ZIP codes. The Legislature has a chance this month to start solving the problem by enacting Gov. Ed Rendell's public school funding formula, a six-year plan that would restore the state's share of support to levels it hasn't seen in a long time. State subsidies would take into account both the educational needs of a district and its ability to pay. The plan has broad support -- not only from school boards and teachers, but also from pivotal groups like the PA Council of Churches, the League of Women Voters and the AFL-CIO. House Bill 2449 would bring stability to school funding by using a formula to determine how much each district should receive from the state.

headline: no text
abstract: The PA Department of Transportation is warning drivers to be on the alert because of school openings, and it is working to make the York split on Interstate 83 safer. An accident there took the life of a woman on July 21st, and PennDOT plans to shut a ramp down and post warning signs to make the road safer. In other news, presidential candidate Barack Obama has made his decision on a running mate, and he could announce his choice at any time.

headline: Stadium promises never pay
abstract: The author is discussing the proposal for a new soccer stadium in Chester, believing that it will not bring the economic benefits that are always promised with new stadiums. He believes that before Delaware County and PA use $80 million of public money for the project there should be more objective information about stadium-centered initiatives in other cities.

headline: Clinton stays alive with state win
