Innovations include a new educator evaluation system and a teacher academy that provides additional training for first-year teachers.

headline: '2nd-Most-Dangerous' City May Cut Cops
abstract: Camden may have to layoff some cops, but the chief of police is promising to maintain protection levels. At one time the city was the most dangerous per capita in the country, and some feel that the cuts will land the city back at the bottom.

headline: No new contract offers at meeting
abstract: The Neshaminy Federation of Teachers and The Neshaminy school board heard presentations from two insurance companies regarding a money-saving, self insured prescription plan suggested by the board. No agreements have been reached.

headline: Geisinger Wyoming Valley unveils new $10 million technology for improved patient care
abstract: Nurses and physicians at Geisinger Wyoming Valley Medical Center demonstrated new $10 million technology on Wednesday that they say will enhance their ability to care for critically ill patients.  The technology, known as eICU, or electronic intensive care unit, adds around-the-clock visual and voice connectivity between ICU patients in Plains Township and experts at Geisinger Medical Center in Danville through computer screens.

headline: Pol wants to boost penalties for hit-run drivers
abstract: PA Senator Michael Stack will hold a Senate Transportation Hearing in Northeast Philadelphia to discuss a bill he introduced that would increase the mandatory minimum sentence for leaving the scene of a deadly accident from 1 to 5 years.

headline: Brady's visit gives striking Temple nurses a lift
abstract: Striking members of the Pennsylvania Association of Staff Nurses and Allied Professionals, who picketed yesterday for a sixth day outside Temple University Hospital received a surprise visit from U.S. Representative Bob Brady D-PA. Brady who is a close ally of the union was there to offer his encouragement to the nurses and medical professionals at Temple who went on strike Wednesday.

headline: Millcreek Community reopens obstetrics unit a month after state closes it
abstract: The Pennsylvania Department of Health had closed Millcreek Community Hospital's obstetrics unit on April 9 citing an insufficient amount of nurses as the reason. After the hospital hired 5 extra nurses, it reopened on Monday. The hospital also increased per diem pay for nurses in the obstetrics unit, created new guidelines for staffing the unit and began the e-mailing the unit's staffing schedule and patient census to the state Health Department.

headline: Heat warnings issued for Phila. Area
abstract: The National Weather Service is advising that people take caution due to severe heat in the region.  Temperatures and humidity are expected to be very high.

headline: Medical marijuana use in Pennsylvania wins lots of support
abstract: More than 70 people attended the hearing at the University of Pittsburgh's Graduate School of Public Health to discuss PA House Bill 1393. Introduced by PA Representative Mark Cohen, D-Philadelphia would make it legal for patients with cancer, glaucoma, HIV/AIDS and other medical conditions to use the drug to relieve pain and other symptoms.

headline: Census: this region weathered recession better than others
abstract: The poverty rate increased between 2008 and 2009 in the state, metropolitan area, Allegheny County and city of Pittsburgh, but not as much as for the entire United States, according to 2009 data from the American Community Survey (ACS), a sample of households. In 2009, the poverty rate was 14.3 percent for the US, 12.5 percent for Pennsylvania, 12.3 percent for the seven-county Pittsburgh metropolitan area, 13.3 percent for Allegheny County and 23.1 percent in the city, according to the ACS.

headline: Local organizations can receive training on collections management
abstract: The Fayette County Historical Society and the Brownsville Area Revitalization Corporation (BARC) have invited museums and history-related organizations to a special training. The training is for management of historical collections. PA State Senator John Heinz will help facilitate the training.

headline: Tail-wagging time: New rules on commercial kennels will go into effect
abstract: New regulations from the state Agricultural Department were approved by the state attorney general’s office. The regulations raise the standard of care in commercial kennels by establishing acceptable levels for temperature, humidity, lighting, ventilation, cleanliness, and type of flooring. Animal shelters are not subject to the regulations because they do not breed dogs.

headline: Pitt proposes construction for more housing, research space
abstract: The University of Pittsburgh is proposing changes to its masterplan that would involve additions for more housing and research space on campus.  The city Planning Commission yesterday received the proposed revisions and is expected to vote on them in two weeks.

headline: NJ Transit plans 200 layoffs, executive pay cuts
abstract: NJ Transit plans to cut 200 jobs, salaries, and 401(k) benefit contributions in order to save $30 million in the next year. NJ Governor Chris Christie plans to cut the state's budget deficit which stands at  $2.2 billion this year. NJ transit will introduce fare hikes and service cuts.

headline: Pittsburgh considers snow emergency plan
abstract: Pittsburgh City Council on Monday heard public complaints about February snow removal, as a result Mayor Luke Ravenstahl's administration is working on a winter emergency system plan. The plan would resemble Baltimore's three-phase winter emergency system, which would lead to fines for those who do not have snow tires on during a snow emergency and as the level of emergency rises so to would the restrictions and fines.

headline: Trivedi wins 6th District nod, and Gerlach takes aim
abstract: Manan Trivedi defeated Doug Pike by 672 votes Wednesday in the Democratic primary in the Sixth Congressional District. Republican Rep. Jim Gerlach will be Trivedi's next opponent.

headline: Editorial: Racist brew leaves bad taste
abstract: Racism in the Tea Party has caused a backlash against the NAACP who have been trying to shine a light on the problem.  As more and more racist signs and sound bites are captured at Tea Party events, the problem grows.

headline: Gas drilling group wants low well tax
abstract: The Cecil-based Marcellus Shale Coalition wants state officials to reinforce their authority over natural-gas drilling operations, force some reluctant landowners to sell their gas and tax new wells at a low rate during years when they're at their costliest but also producing the most gas. Kathryn Klaber, coalition president and executive director, said such steps would promote the orderly, efficient harvesting of the gas and protect landowners who want to lease their mineral rights.

headline: Protection for vulnerable Pennsylvania adults ready to be signed into law by Gov. Ed Rendell
abstract: Abuse and neglect of adults with disabilities could be less likely to be overlooked under a bill passed today by the PA House of Representatives. The PA Senate passed the bill in July, and the Adult Protective Services Act now awaits the signature of Governor Ed Rendell.

headline: Massey on cusp of new sanction from MSHA
abstract: A mining disaster in the Upper Big Branch coal mine in West Virginia is now being investigated. The US Mine Safety and Health Administration has ordered a subsidiary of Massey Energy Co. to restore water to a piece of coal mining equipment. If the company fails to comply with this federal order, it will face sanctions for obstructing a federal investigation of a mine explosion that killed 29 miners.

headline: Health violation reports muddled
abstract: A new law will require the Allegheny County Health Department and other jurisdictions that handle their own restaurant inspections to provide copies of their inspection reports to the Pennsylvania Department of Agriculture. The law will also enable the agriculture department to charge restaurants a fee if inspectors return more than once to ensure violations have been corrected. The decision comes after the Allegheny County Health Department failed to provide detailed information on their inspection database.

headline: Seniors struggle to rebound from unemployment
abstract: As a group, older workers in the United States are finding it most difficult to rebound from unemployment.  The number of unemployed workers age 55 to 64 has nearly tripled since the recession began.

headline: Editorial: The price of prejudice
abstract: The author states that the Obama administration should receive credit for reaching a settlement with black farmers who had been systematically discriminated against by the US Department of Agriculture. The USDA rejected loans or gave fewer loaned money to black farmers, instead giving more money to white farmers. The settlement is $1.25 billion.

headline: Toomey best-funded challenger for Senate
abstract: Pat Toomey the leading Republican candidate had a good first quarter of fundraising, continuing his pace as the best-funded Senate challenger in the country.  Toomey has raised $2.3 million in the first three months of 2010 for his campaign. Figures for his Democratic rivals U.S. Senator Arlen Specter and Rep. Joe Sestak were not available Monday.

headline: Penn State, Pitt Collaboration Promoting Innovative Obesity Research
abstract: Researchers from Penn State and the University of Pittsburgh are teaming up to find new ways to prevent and treat obesity. The researchers will be taking advantage of facilities such as the University of Pittsburgh Obesity Nutrition and Research Center (Pitt ONRC) and the Penn State Institute for Diabetes and Obesity (PSIDO).

headline: Oil Stops, But Will Well Hold?
abstract: Engineers for BP are preaching cautiousness, but many are breathing a sigh of relief as images show a stoppage in the flow of oil from the broken well in the Gulf of Mexico.  Oil has flowed unabated into the Gulf for 85 days.  It was estimated to be 184 million gallons.

headline: State's new kennel law readied
abstract: The Independent Regulatory Review Commission has approved final regulations dealing with proper ventilation, humidity, lighting and flooring for commercial kennels, which breed and sell dogs to dealers and pet stores. The regulations are part of a dog protection law approved in October 2008 and signed by PA Governor Ed Rendell.

headline: Onorato's pronunciation helps cut Corbett lead; Toomey still in front
abstract: A poll released by Franklin & Marshall College in Lancaster on Tuesday still shows Republican PA Gubernatorial candidate Tom Corbett leading, it indicates Democratic candidate Dan Onorato has made up some ground over the past week. In the race for US Senate, however, GOP candidate Pat Toomey has a solid lead over Democratic candidate Joe Sestak, according to the poll.

headline: Veterans homes changes planned
abstract: PA Senators Lisa Baker and Kim Ward have received numerous complaints from veterans staying in the states' six veterans homes. The complaints concern how these homes collect money from the estates of dead patients. The PA Department of Military and Veteran Affairs is moving to clarify their system due to public discontent.

headline: Mayor: Police, fire staff to stay at same numbers
abstract: Based on a review of the proposed 2011 budget, the city will keep the same number of additions to its police and fire departments. The budgets are about $6.6 million for police and $5 million for fire. One major difference concerns money for police overtime hours. Some $330,000 had been budgeted for overtime compensation, but the proposed budget shows a $60,000 difference, with  $270,000 set aside for the expense.

headline: Another Democrat joins race for 164th District
abstract: Brian C. Eury, a longtime political consultant and Drexel Democrat, will announce his candidacy for the 164th District state legislative seat tomorrow.

headline: Union workers strike at food distribution center
abstract: Workers went on strike at the Philadelphia Regional Produce Market when contract negotiations fell through with management. The Teamsters Local 929 voted down the contract after management proposed increases in employee healthcare contributions and a tier system that would leave new workers with less pay.

headline: Fuel spill imperils Great Barrier Reef
abstract: A Chinese-owned bulk coal carrier rammed into the Great Barrier Reef Saturday and is leaking fuel, Australian government officials are hoping that it does not break apart and seriously damage the planet's largest coral reef. Peter Garrett, Australia's environmental protection minister said the federal government concerned about the impact an oil spill could have on the environmentally sensitive reef.

headline: Overuse of antibiotics spurs vicious cycle
abstract: British scientists say that doctors that over prescribe antibiotics may develop drug resistance that lasts up to a year, putting them and the population at risk when more serious treatment is needed. Researchers say that the overprescribing of antibiotics is more prevalent in the wealthy regions of the world such as Europe and the United States.

headline: Ramsey: Philadelphia police helped DEA in officers' arrests
abstract: Commissioner Charles H. Ramsey of the Philadelphia Police Department is taking credit for assisting the federal Drug Enforcement Administration in its apprehension of three Philadelphia police officers who were planning to steal heroin from a drug dealer.  Ramsey said that the department is trying to make inroads in neighborhoods where people are reluctant to trust the police.

headline: Thompson addresses area's woes during town meeting
abstract: Residents in Montoursville Thursday listened  US Representative Glenn Thompson, R-Howard, discuss some of the nation's problems such as the struggling economy and the growing deficit. Thompson said he takes a dim view of federal stimulus money, including the $26 billion federal aid package that includes some $10 billion for school districts to retrain or rehire teachers and other school personnel.

headline: 'Historic' severance tax goes before Pennsylvania House
abstract: A plan by PA House Democrats to levy a tax on natural gas faces a final vote tonight, and its prospects for passage increased substantially thanks to a new provision that shifts more revenue to environmental programs. An amendment by a Republican lawmaker boosting funding to environmental programs was approved overwhelmingly Tuesday night. At the rate of 39 cents per 1,000 cubic feet, the proposed tax would be one of the highest in the nation.

headline: External hard drive reported missing at Messiah College found
abstract: A financial aid employee at Messiah College reported a flash drive missing that contained the personal financial information of about 43,000 students and their family. The flash drive, however, never left the possession of the employee; it was simply misplaced and then found again. The employee is facing sanctions from the college for taking a flash drive off of school premises.

headline: Marcellus information online
abstract: Pennsylvania’s oil and gas industry production and compliance information is available online on the public reporting website, www.marcellusreporting.state.pa.us/ogrereports/. Under Act 15, Marcellus operators are required to report their production totals every six months.

headline: John Baer: Code Red
abstract: Although many analysts view Republican Scott Brown's victory in the Massachusetts Senate race as a referendum on the policies of President Obama and the Democratic Party, it is too soon to make this assessment.  History shows us that public-approval ratings fail to predict performance, and Brown's electoral success does not necessarily spell defeat for the president's health-care legislation.

headline:
Some interests more special than the rest
The governor wages selective war on favor-seekers.
abstract: The author states that PA Governor Rendell lambasts only those special interest groups that do not work in his favor. The author states that the governor's statements against special interests are subjective depending on whether they support him in elections through campaign contributions. He states PennFuture, teacher's unions, construction unions, and his old law firm Ballard Spahr as special interests in favor of Gov. Rendell.

headline: PSPCA to evacuate and disinfect city shelter
abstract: A rare and deadly illness struck Philadelphia's Pennsylvania SPCA (PSPCA) on West Hunting Park Avenue in June, killing six dogs. Three others were euthanized after showing signs of infection, the outbreak forced a quarantine at the animal shelter. Last week PSPCA were planning emptying to empty the shelter of dogs in an effort to eradicate the disease.

headline: 13 students had drugs at school, police say
abstract: At Lower Dauphin Middle School, thirteen students are accused of trading or selling prescription drugs and marijuana. The district spokesman, Jim Hazen, said this is not a drug ring but a case of "eighth-graders making poor decisions." Authorities are investigating whether more students were involved.

headline: Some New Jersey lawmakers uneasy that towns can override tax cap
abstract: Democrats are worried that the ability for some towns to override the state's new property tax hike cap will cause for serious inequities between poor and rich towns.  Massachusetts' experience was discussed, where some of the fears were confirmed.  Officials in MA maintain, however, that poorer towns get much more state aid than affluent towns to begin with.

headline: Youths leaving foster care get intro to college
abstract: The University of Pittsburgh-Johnstown hosted the Independent Living Youth Retreat for young people in foster care who are about to age out of the foster care system. The program was sponsored by the Pitt School of Social Work’s Pennsylvania Child Welfare Training Program and the PA Department of Public Welfare Office of Children, Youth and Families.

headline: Biden speech rallies voters at Penn State
abstract: Vice President Joe Biden and the Obama administration allies are struggling to replicate the turnout of new and younger voters that helped propel them to victory two years ago. His appearance at Pennsylvania State University underscored that effort, as he reminded a crowd of about 1,000 of better days for his party. The Biden rally was a long-distance opening act to a coast-to-coast administration push to rekindle student enthusiasm for its goals and for the election of enough Democratic candidates to ward off Republican takeovers of one or both houses of Congress.

headline: Government insists full-body scanners are safe
abstract: The US Transportation Security Administration continues to reassure the public that full body scanners at airports are safe. They report that the levels of radiation emitted are only intended to locate bombs and weapons and are far below harmful levels. Some scientists, however, contend that if a machine were to malfunction, it could be harmful.

headline: Jobless benefits: Congress should extend aid for limited time
abstract: Author is in favor of extending unemployment benefits. Cutting unemployment would force people to enroll in more costly government-aid programs. The author also provides suggestions on how to transition people off of benefits.

headline: State cuts hit regional cancer institute office in Scranton
abstract: As a result of spending cuts ordered by Governor Ed Rendell, a nonprofit institute that provides cancer research and education programs throughout Northeast Pennsylvania is losing state aid.  The cuts will eliminate $1.2 million for the Northeast Regional Cancer Institute and three sister consortiums based in Philadelphia, State College and Pittsburgh. The northeast institute's share of this amount was $300,000; the cuts were part of a budget-balancing measure.

headline: PhillyDeals: Delay of State Office Building sale costly
abstract: The PA Department of General Service's delays in selling a state office building to Bart Blatstein's Tower Investments. Has forced it to push down the price from $25.2 million to $23.4 million. The state could not sell the building because they were having trouble acquiring a replacement building.

headline: Free to hold state tradition
abstract: Freeholders who are those elected to run New Jersey's counties often are called "freeloaders," a malicious mispronunciation. Burlington County's freeholder board is one of two that have officially urged the state Legislature to change the term freeholder to county commissioner.

headline: PSU to get millions for nuclear work
abstract: As part of the U.S. Department of Energy’s initiative to promote research and development at universities, Pennsylvania State University will receive $3.2 million for nuclear energy research. This is part of a total of $38 million that will go to 42 university projects that fall within four categories. Penn State researchers will work in three areas: fuel cycle research and development, the next generation of nuclear reactors and innovative ideas.

headline: A plan to save lives and money
abstract: For those covered by new federal requirements, preventative health care is about to get a lot less expensive.  41 million Americans will benefit immediately, and 88 million by 2013 from new federal regulations that require preventative health care like vaccinations, weight counseling, and cancer screenings to be completely free of charge.

headline: Problems for the next governor? He should look to the past
abstract: Pennsylvania faces an unprecedented gap between revenue and expenses in 2011 as additional federal stimulus funding allotments dry up, the bills mount for the state pension and health care funds, and the costs of government continue to rise. The next governor could face a record deficit from $3 billion to $5 billion when he puts together his first budget next year.

headline: House OKs concussion measure for young athletes
abstract: After debating Marcellus Shale from morning to night, the PA House on Tuesday night passed the Safety in Youth Sports Act aimed at trying to prevent serious brain trauma and better monitor concussions in Pennsylvania athletes in middle and high schools. The act, a year in the making by Representative Tim Briggs, D-Montgomery County, includes provisions for concussion-trained medical professionals to release in writing any injured athlete to return to participation in their sport.

headline: Agency moves to safeguard senior center funds
abstract: Senior centers in Union and Snyder counties have not been operating under federal and state guidelines for many years. Measures intended to safeguard patients' funds, such as routine banking deposits and a two signature requirement on every check, have not been followed. Local Agencies on Aging responded by promising changes soon after the audits began.

headline: Former Cumberland County official Bruce Barclay found guilty of patronizing prostitutes, other charges
abstract: Former Cumberland County Commissioner Bruce Barclay was found guilty of unlawful use of a computer and unlawful duplication, 13 counts invasion of privacy and one count of patronizing prostitutes.

headline: Wachovia bank's $10,000 donation to Lehigh County charity will pay for 2,300 Meals on Wheels
abstract: Wachovia Bank donated $10,000 to Meals on Wheels of Lehigh County on Wednesday. The check should help pay for 2,300 meals, according to Pamela Bechtel, the group's executive director.

headline: Study urges changes in Delco health system
abstract: A study by the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health concluded that Delaware County health system needs to better prepare for emergencies and better provide outreach for health services. The study did not say whether Delaware County should adopt a County Health Department which has been debated in the past.

headline: Productivity grows 3.6 percent in first quarter
abstract: The Labor Department said Thursday that productivity grew at an annual rate of 3.6 percent in the first quarter, better than the 2.5 percent increase economists had expected. During the same period labor costs dropped more than expected, which is good for corporate profits but means household incomes continue to be squeezed, putting the economic recovery at risk.

headline: Sestak eclipses Toomey in latest Rasmussen poll
abstract: According to a new Rasmussen poll, U.S. Democratic  Representative Joseph Sestak is now leading Republican Senate candidate Pat Toomey 46 percent to 42 percent. Sestak beat 30-year incumbent U.S. Sen. Arlen Specter 54 percent to 46 percent in the Democratic primary.

headline: Pennsylvania Turnpike will charge more for paying with cash
abstract: PA Turnpike drivers will soon get a discount for using EZ Pass.  Tolls will go up for everyone, but with cash drivers paying 10% more to the EZ Pass customers paying just 3% more.  The rates take effect January 2.

headline: HACC starts looking for new president
abstract: Harrisburg Area Community College is looking to the Association of Community College Trustees for help finding a replacement for Edna V. Baehre, who left in July to take a position at Napa Valley College in California.

headline: Blight bill nears finish line in Legislature
abstract: It's been more than 15 months since Senate Bill 900 was introduced in the PA Legislature, but the anti-blight measure is finally headed for the finish line. It will likely come to a full House vote next week, possibly as early as Tuesday, and may need another Senate vote if amendments are successfully added during House deliberations. Proponents argue the bill has become increasingly necessary as unoccupied homes and old businesses literally fall apart, causing not only physical danger but also financial consequences for homeowners living nearby.

headline: Chip collection has little value
abstract: The author talks about his casino chip collection. Casino chips are likely not worth more than their face value, although rarely they can sell for a very high price. Most collectors collect for sentimental value, because the vast majority of chips will not gain in value and will not exceed their casino face value.

headline: Food pantry organizers hope stockpiles hold up in case unemployment benefits run out
abstract: Food banks, which are working frantically to meet rising demands, fear that rising numbers of Pennsylvanians running out of unemployment benefits could increase demand further. Many pantries are turning to creative solutions to their demand problems.

headline: Lonza shutting Montco plant; 140 to be idled
abstract: As part of a worldwide restructuring of the company's operations, Lonza Group Ltd. is planning to close its plant in Conshohocken, Pennsylvania.  The plant closure will result in 140 layoffs.

headline: Democrats campaign from the middle at midterm
abstract: The 2010 midterm elections may prove to be costly for congressional Democrats and it may be beneficial for a candidate to have a centrist record to avoid defeat in the election. The author cites 5 congressional delegates from Pennsylvania and one from New Jersey as centrist according to a survey from the National Journal and the Congressional Quarterly.

headline: Adolph proposal would restructure Pa. student aid agency
abstract: PA Bill Adolph, R-Springfield, and PA Sen. Sean Logan, D-Allegheny, introduced identical bills Monday that would cut the number of sitting lawmakers on the 20-member Pennsylvania Higher Education Assistance Agency board from 16 to 12. Logan said the goal is to fill those four spots with people knowledgeable about finance, banking and computer technology.

headline: 50th District incumbent turns away primary challengers
abstract: Although indicted on corruption charges, voters of the 50th Legislative District were apparently willing to overlook Democratic state Representative Bill DeWeese's troubles. DeWeese triumphed over Greene County Commissioner Pam Snyder and Tony Brnusak, president of United Mine Workers Cumberland Mine Local 2300. Now DeWeese will face Republican Richard Yeager, chairman of the Greene County Republican Committee, in the general election.

headline: When it comes to skate parks, Philadelphia gets small
abstract: In the decade since Philadelphia city officials kicked skateboarders out of the city's downtown LOVE Park, a number of small skate parks around the city have sprouted up.  The planned official downtown skate park, Paine's Park, is still in fundraising.  It is expected to be located on the Schuylkill River Trail.

headline: City in motion: It pays to plan for a smart transportation future
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl last week issued a request for proposals for firms interested in developing a 25-year plan that will coordinate the city's transportation strategy. Earlier this year, when the mayor formed the MOVEPGH task force, which includes representatives from the city's planning and public works departments, the city and county development authorities.

headline: House approves severance tax bill
abstract: The PA House voted Wednesday to levy a significant state severance tax on natural gas production and earmark a sizeable portion of revenue for local governments and environmental programs. The tax measure, approved 104-94, sets the severance tax rate at 39 cents per thousand cubic feet (mcf) of natural gas at the wellhead, a minimum floor price that would be adjusted annually if the price of natural gas rises.

headline: Bernanke: Nation on 'unacceptable' path toward long-term unemployment woes
abstract: Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke recently suggested that Congress lend a helping hand in jumpstarting the economy. He said that the US was headed into a period where many would be unemployed or underemployed, and that that is simply "unacceptable." To this end the Fed has already bought $600 billion in Treasury bonds to boost lending.

headline: Pennsylvania hunters see effects of gas-drilling operations
abstract: The increase in drilling for natural gas in the Marcellus Shale is affecting hunting grounds. Marcellus permits have seen an increase, leading to a higher level of production activity o public lands, frustrating many hunters.

headline: Phila. aiming to improve energy efficiency
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Michael Nutter has contracted with a private firm to perform energy-efficiency renovations to four of the city's major government buildings.  The renovations are much needed, as the city spent nearly 48 million dollars on electricity, heating oil, and natural gas in fiscal year 2008-09.

headline: From the ugliness at S. Phila. High, a hero emerges
abstract: Violet Sutton-Lawson, a community relations liaison at South Philadelphia High School, broke up two fights between African-American and Asian students on December 3rd, 2009. The incidents of that day have opened up a district inquiry into the violence and race-relations at the school.

headline: Rendell Unveils Education Plan, Tax Proposal to Raise Funds
abstract: As part of a five-county tour across the state of Pennsylvania, PA Governor Ed Rendell made his way to Sharon High School Monday afternoon. The focus of his speech was the state's budget and stressing the importance of education funding, proposed investments center mainly around early childhood education.

headline: 15 other Philly school administrators lack certification
abstract: After recently reporting that principal LaGreta Brown of South Philadelphia High School was found to be lacking proper certification, 15 more Philadelphia School District administrators were also found without the correct certification. Under new district policy, administrators who are not certified must get emergency certification within 30 days or be fired.

headline: Corbett retreats from comments about jobless
abstract: Attorney General Tom Corbett was forced to retreat from his comments about those on unemployment benefits during record high unemployment.  He said that those on benefits do not want to go back to work while they can still collect.  He said later that he misspoke and clarified himself.

headline: Proposed legislation would expand background checks
abstract: PA Representative Nicholas Miccarelli, R-Delaware, introduced House Bill 2464, which amends the Crimes and Offenses Code of Pennsylvania's Consolidated Statutes to provide for more stringent sentencing guidelines for individuals convicted of multiple offenses of sexual abuse of children. The bill comes after a number of arrests of alleged child predators including the case involving a first-grade teacher who operated a summer camp.

headline: Texting bans may add risk to roads
abstract: Laws banning texting while driving actually may prompt a slight increase in road crashes, the Insurance Institute for Highway Safety research released today shows. Thirty states and the District of Columbia ban texting while driving; 11 of the laws were passed this year. The assertion that those efforts are futile will be a major issue at this week's annual meeting here of the Governors Highway Safety Association (GHSA).

headline: Prison board asks DOC for interim warden
abstract: The Lackawanna County Prison Board has asked the PA Department of Corrections for assistance in prison administration. The Prison Board is seeking an interim warden to manage its jail while they seek a fulltime replacement. The DOC was originally approached by County Commissioner Mike Washo.

headline: U.S. Sen. Bob Casey Jr. pushes for a vote to extend unemployment benefits for 83,000 Pennsylvanians
abstract: Senator Bob Casey Jr. hopes congress will vote to extend emergency unemployment benefits. Officials estimate that $2 is pumped into the economy for every $1 paid in unemployment benefits.

headline: Grassroots army mobilizing behind Obama's agenda
abstract: President Obama plans to use volunteers from Organizing for Amercia (OFA)--the grassroots network that helped elect him in 2008--to push issues and legislation.  Specifically, the president plans to use OFA to mobilize support for his health-care legislation; the group has already mobilized support for the legislation by staging events across the country and signing petitions.

headline: Stop, thief! Bonusgate's banality of corruption
abstract: The author asserts that there is a disconnect between PA state legislators and the people they represent. The author cites former PA Representative Mike Veon's former aide's testimony that his state-paid campaign work benefitted constituents by re-electing legislators who can pass legislation. The author says that the "bonusgate" proceedings will lead to state ethics reform.

headline: State rules on more snow day requests
abstract: The PA Department of Education has ruled on snow day requests by seven more school districts, this time allowing only seniors or no one to skip making up the missed days. This coming after the department approved waivers for eight school districts last month, allowing them to not make up all of the days missed because of severe weather in February.

headline: After 30 Years and Party Switch, Career Curtain for Specter
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell sympathizes with Republican-turned-Democrat Senator Arlen Specter, who served 30 years in the US Senate. He was defeated by fellow Democrat Joe Sestak in the Democratic Senatorial primary. President Barack Obama promised Specter all the support he could give, but due to the anti-incumbency sentiment across the country, Obama avoided campaigning in PA.

headline: Harrah's Entertainment confirms Foxwoods talks
abstract: Las Vegas-based Harrah's Entertainment says that it is in talks regarding a role at the Foxwoods Casino project in South Philadelphia.  They were not willing to discuss anything substantive regarding the talks.

headline: Energy jobs, taxes & road salt
abstract: Growth in energy sector jobs also will give a boost to Pennsylvania’s finances. Governor Ed Rendell announced a plan last week to cut state spending in the wake of a federal funding shortfall.

headline: State officials under fire
abstract: Mike Perelman, a former York City Police captain, and his company, Institute of Terrorism Research and Response, came under fire from Governor Ed Rendell last week when several protest groups complained they had shown up on state bulletins. For nearly a year, the institute provided the state Department of Homeland Security with bulletins three times a week on possible threats to the state's citizens and infrastructure.

headline: Jobless benefits to expire
abstract: Jobless benefits for 2 million people will run dry during the holidays. US House Speaker Nanci Pelosi has promised to reintroduce a measure to extend benefits after Thanksgiving. This issue may coincide with the debate over whether to extend Bush-era tax cuts on high income individuals, which could prove difficult territory for Republicans.

headline: Griffin Pond Animal Shelter faces possible shutdown
abstract: The Griffin Pond Animal shelter is in danger of shutting down due to fewer donations and escalating costs. The shelter, which does not receive government funds, relies solely on donations and grants.

headline: Haitian Orphans Get New Chance At Life
abstract: Two sisters from Pittsburgh spearheaded an effort that brought 54 Haitian orphans to Pennsylvania.  To help facilitate the sisters' efforts, PA Governor Ed Rendell got involved in the process.  The orphans will live in group homes until they can be adopted.

headline: Spy school: When educators 'follow' a student home
abstract: The author states that schools should stop using webcams to spy on students they were issued to. This follows a Lower Merion High School student who was accused of improper behavior after school officials said he was taking drugs while they tapped into his computer's webcam.

headline: Transportation agencies deal with rejection
abstract: The Federal Highway Administration's rejection of tolls for I-80 means that PA will have to cut or find other money to pay for $312.5 million worth of highway and bridge projects and $160 million in transit projects, according to PA Department of Transportation spokesman Rich Kirkpatrick. PA Governor Ed Rendell said the rejected proposal would affect 100 bridge projects and 300 miles of planned road reconstruction and repair.

headline: Sestak eclipses Toomey in latest Rasmussen poll
abstract: According to a new Rasmussen poll, U.S. Democratic  Representative Joseph Sestak is now leading Republican Senate candidate Pat Toomey 46 percent to 42 percent. Sestak beat 30-year incumbent U.S. Sen. Arlen Specter 54 percent to 46 percent in the Democratic primary.

headline: White House sets new drilling ban
abstract: The Obama Administration has responded with a new plan after federal courts blocked his recent ban on deep-sea drilling.  The ban will last until Nov. 30.  BP has recently fitted a new cap on the broken well in the Gulf of Mexico that has been spewing oil for months.

headline: PA hopes to shame taxpayers into paying up
abstract: The PA Revenue Department said Monday it has broadened its online list of businesses and individuals who are delinquent to include not only employer withholding and sales tax, but all state liens filed since July 2009.

headline: Reading Hospital confronting shortage of primary-care physicians
abstract: Reading Hospital will receive a grant of nearly $3 million to train primary-care physicians, almost 1 percent of $320 million in grants announced by the federal government Wednesday to strengthen the health care work force. The $2.88 million grant for Reading Hospital is part of the nearly $18.1 million in grants being distributed throughout Pennsylvania. The five-year grants are part of the Affordable Care Act signed into law earlier this year by Congress.

headline: Prosecution of ACORN rests in Allegheny County
abstract: Allegheny County District Attorney Stephen A. Zappala Jr. has said that the investigation into the bankrupt community group ACORN is almost over. ACORN has been found guilty of filing numerous false voter registrations, in one case a dead person. Attorney General Tom Corbett has also requested from the Commonwealth Court that an ACORN affiliate turn over its fundraising records.

headline: Cambria residents discuss drilling
abstract: More than 45 landowners, who are mostly reliant on natural springs and private wells, attended a Cambria County Conservation  meeting to discuss concerns with possible contamination of wells where drilling is nearby. Pennsylvania is one of only two states in the nation that doesn't regulate or monitor private water wells.

headline: Pittsburgh opens arms to orphans from Haiti
abstract: Two sisters from Pittsburgh spearheaded an effort that brought 54 Haitian orphans to Pennsylvania.  To help facilitate the sisters' efforts, PA Governor Ed Rendell got involved in the process.  The orphans will live in group homes until they can be adopted.

headline: Road to stability: A distressed city needs new funding sources
abstract: Lack of city funds for road construction will leave the city with having to leave over half of its scheduled street repair unrepaired. This leaves the city with less money to give to poorer local neighborhoods for community development.

headline: Could this be the year for financial reform?
abstract: Tomorrow is the deadline for campaign contributions, and Allegheny County Democrat Dan Onorato has raised over $9 million which is triple the amount raised by the three other Democratic candidates combined. PA Senator Tony Williams D-Philadelphia has raised close to $2 million, while Jack Wagner and Joe Hoeffel trail in fundraising. All four Democrats running for governor say they support limits.

headline: Specter-Sestak Senate contest tops primary slate
abstract: An article reporting the popularity of the vote between U.S. Senate primary incumbent Arlen Specter, who switched from Republican to Democrat and Democratic rival Representative Joe Sestak. In the Republican Senate primary, former Representative Pat Toomey of the Lehigh Valley will go up against Peg Luksik of the Johnstown area.  Voting is set today from 7am to 8pm.

headline: Stalled local transit projects result in loss of federal funds
abstract: SEPTA will be losing $3.9 million in federal funds that were earmarked for the mothballed Schuylkill Valley Metro project.  The project was halted due to its steep price tag.  The Delaware River Port Authority will lose $1.7 million earmarked for ferry and cruise ship facilities.

headline: Pennsylvania Cracks Down on Tax Delinquents
abstract: The PA Revenue Department has an online list of tax delinquents, and says in addition to employer withholding and sales tax, the list will also include state liens filed since 2009.

headline: Experts favor greener drilling
abstract: Experts in the natural gas industry agree that recycling the water used to hydraulically fracture the Marcellus shale is not only cost effective but also environmentally friendly. By recycling flowback water, drillers can cut back on the amount of water they would need to take from another source to frac new wells.

headline: Rate increase planned for PWSA customers
abstract: The director of the Pittsburg Water and Sewer Authority recently said that residents could see a 13 percent hike in monthly bills. The authority has said that increased conservation efforts have resulted in decreased water use, which means less revenue. They feel that the need to meet payroll and benefits justifies the rate increase.

headline: Future of Pennsylvania bonds unclear
abstract: Outgoing Gov. Ed Rendell is encountering opposition to his plans for a $1 billion taxpayer-financed bond issue to fund a slew of construction and renovation projects ranging from prisons and bridges to hospitals and museums. Auditor General Jack Wagner took opposition to the plan, citing a multi-billion dollar deficit facing the state. Wagner’s approval is needed before the bond can be sold.

headline: Pa. should follow Jersey's lead on medical marijuana
abstract: Pennsylvania should join New Jersey and the twelve other states that have legalized medical marijuana.  Research has shown that medical marijuana alleviates pain and nausea among patients with many diseases--even when other drugs fail.  Legalizing marijuana for medical use will also provide a much needed revenue source for the state.

headline: Group opposed to pigeon shooting upset over billboard denial
abstract: An animal-rights group, Showing Animals Respect and Kindness, accused Clear Channel Outdoor of refusing to put up an anti-pigeon shooting billboard over Interstate 95 because it offends PA Attorney General Tom Corbett.

headline: Casey to hold education forum
abstract: U.S. Senator Robert Casey, D-Pa, will hold a forum about early childhood education at Morrisville High School Tuesday where he will hear from educators, a researcher and a representative from the PA Governor Ed Rendell administration about the best strategies to expand access to pre-kindergarten education.

headline: Not typical primary day
abstract: An opinion column says that change in politics is possible because voters have removed the incumbents from their seats. The biggest changes, the author argues, happened in the Democratic primaries, locally with Senators Robert Mellow and Raphael Musto and , state Representative Joe Sestak and Senator Arlen Specter statewide.

headline: Editorial: Ship safe for now
abstract: Philadelphia philanthropist H.F. "Gerry" Lenfest has pledged $5.8 million to help save the SS United States.  The money will go to storage and the purchase of the liner from Norwegian Cruise Line.  The SS United States Conservancy has dreams of seeing the ship refurbished and part of a new Delaware waterfront.

headline: Lake City woman claims $1M winning Powerball ticket
abstract: Audrey Richardson a 72-year-old Lake City woman won the Powerball, with the Power Play, which in this drawing multiplied the prize of $200,000 by five.

headline: Now showing: Public deserves US Senate debates
abstract: In a Franklin & Marshall College poll released this week, Republican Tom Corbett led Democrat Dan Onorato in the race for PA Governor by three points, but a huge 37 percent of registered voters were undecided. In the race for US Senate, the F&M poll found Republican Pat Toomey leading Democrat Joe Sestak by a larger margin of 12 points, but even here 17 percent were undecided.

headline: Senators seek probe into education rule making process
abstract: Two Republican Congressmen suspect that the US Department of Education has leaked proposed rules aimed at tightening regulation of the industry. An Education Department spokesman has said that they have acted with integrity throughout the process. The information suspected of being leaked deals with 'gainful employment rules.'

headline: Valley home sales feel weight of foreclosures
abstract: A report from RealtyTrac shows nearly one-in-seven homes sold in the Lehigh Valley region in the third quarter was in some stage of foreclosure. The 255 foreclosure sales in the Lehigh Valley area in the third quarter represented 14.8 percent of all sales.

headline: Luzerne Township prisoner sues over 75-cent cable fee
abstract: An inmate serving time for robbery has filed a lawsuit over a 75-cent fee in his monthly cable bill.  Joel Santos Maldonado, who is serving a 12-26 year sentence at the State Correctional Institute at Fayette, filed suit in Commonwealth Court arguing that the 75 cent administrative fee charged by the department of corrections interferes with the business relationship and contract between inmates and the cable provider.

headline: State tax revenue continues to lag
abstract: State revenues fell below estimates in February bringing the state $476 million behind revenue estimates for the budget year 2009-2010. PA Governor Rendell said revenue estimates could end up coming in at $525 million behind revenue estimates by the end of the year.

headline: Slow and careful on natural gas
abstract: The economic pressure for new energy sources has driven runaway growth in the drilling for natural gas in the Marcellus Shale deposits that undergird 60 percent of Pennsylvania's land mass. According to the PA Department of Environmental Protection 1,000 new wells have been drilled since 2008 and permits have been issued for more than 3,000 sites.

headline: HACC president saying goodbye
abstract: Edna Baehre, the president of Harrisburg Area Community College, is leaving the college for a new job at Napa Valley Community College. Napa Valley's former president died of a heart attack in November. The Napa Valley Community College student body is much smaller at 9,000 students compared to HACC's 22,000.

headline: Uganda blasts' fallout: A new terror worry
abstract: Al-Shabab, a new al-Qaeda linked terror group in East Africa has claimed responsibility for the bombings that killed 74 during the World Cup in Uganda.  The US State Department has declared them a terrorist organization.

headline: Uniontown delays start of school year
abstract: Dr. Charles Machesky, Uniontown Area School District superintendent, announced Monday during the regular school board meeting that due to inevitable delays in the renovation project at three of the district's schools, the first day of school for all students will be September 7.

headline: Understanding health care reform
abstract: Many of the changes to health care insurance coverage that President Barack Obama signed into law earlier this year go into effect today. The Patient Protection and Affordable Care Act was opposed by Republicans and some Democrats. Other provisions of the law go into effect in over four years.

headline: Presidential spokesman: Body scan concerns will be considered
abstract: The public outrage over "invasive" airport detection systems continues. Spokesman for US President Barak Obama, Robert Gibbs, has said that government is trying to balance security concerns and invasiveness. The Transportation Security Administration has made clear that it will not balk on its commitment to doing whatever necessary to protect air bound citizens.

headline: Income tax hike OK'd in Allentown
abstract: The council approved a 35% hike in the city’s earned income tax. Mayor Ed Pawlowski had sought a 40 percent increase but council voted to shave the proposal, saying the reduction will help soften the financial blow. Residents and nonresidents working in the city who earn $50,000 a year will see a $175 increase in their earned income tax.

headline: Mount Airy holding job fair for table games
abstract: Mount Airy Casino and Resort will hold a job fair this weekend.  The casino is looking to hire workers to staff the newly legislated table games at the casino; the casino is expected to hire about 220 workers.  Earlier this month, Governor Rendell signed a new law allowing licensed casinos to operate table games.

headline: Private road: The county is right to chart a new course on transit
abstract: The author discusses the potentials of Allegheny Executive Dan Onorato's Transportation Action Partnership that would allow private enterprises to run a transit system between downtown Pittsburgh and Oakland in exchange for long-term development leases. The author supports the proposal.

headline: Battling the Bulge: Obesity rates are rising, and fighting that trend starts with our children
abstract: According to the Advocare Children’s Medical Associates are saying the common notion that kids who are heavy young wont be heavy when they get old is not correct. They say that if kids are heavy young, they’ll be heavy in adolescence and adulthood. According to the PA Department of Health, 29 percent of school-age children in Delaware County are either overweight or obese.

headline: Centenarians have different DNA 'suite'
abstract: Scientists have discovered the "Methuselah" genes that allow carriers to live to 100, even if they practiced unhealthy lifestyles. There is no one gene that guarantees someone to live until 100, but rather it is the right combination of genes-a "suite-that allows this. These genes help protect people from the bad effects of smoking and bad diet and also delay the onset of age-related illnesses such as cancer and heart disease by up to three decades. The right suite of genes are very rare, only one person in 10,000 reaches the age of 100.

headline: Governor's old Rendell '95 PAC swells and shrinks
abstract: Gov Ed Rendell's old Philadelphia mayoral political action committee has been taking in a number of sizable contributions as of late.  The PAC started out the year with $27,000 on hand but now has received $50,000 from his gubernatorial PAC.  The recipients have been a few state representative candidates.

headline: Who should decide a defendant's mental capacity?
abstract: A bill, sponsored by state Senator Mary Jo White, R-Venango County, was passed by the state Senate last summer. Under the bill, to be considered mentally retarded, the person must score low on IQ tests, have significant limitations in adapting to society and must have been diagnosed with the disability by age 18.

headline: Obama’s Economics Chief Is Set to Leave
abstract: The White House says the departure has been long-planned, Mr. Summers who directs the president’s National Economic Council said in a brief interview that he must return to his professorship at Harvard by January to keep his tenure. Summers has guided the president through an extraordinarily tumultuous time, on matters ranging from the $787 billion economic stimulus package to the financial regulatory reform bill passed this year, to the current fight with Republicans about whether to extend Bush-era tax cuts.

headline: Reading still ranks among most dangerous cities
abstract: Reading is still one of the most dangerous American cities. Chief of Police William Heim has noted the city's improvement relative to other cities, as the city has moved  from 37th to 41th in the most dangerous rankings. Heim also said that these numbers can be misleading, because they account only for cities with over 75,000 residents and only certain types of crime.

headline: State legislators pledge to dispense with raises
abstract: A number of state legislators have pledged to either return their cost of living increases to the state or donate the funds to charity. According to the Associated Press, about 130 lawmakers have given back $190,000 to the state over the past two years.

headline: Gov. Rendell aboard Haitian orphan-rescue flight
abstract: Governor Rendell was expected to arrive in Haiti last night in an effort to rescue 61 children from that earthquake-torn country.  The children live in an orphanage run by two sisters from the Pittsburgh area.  Governor Rendell worked through the weekend with the U.S. State Department and branches of the military to help set up an airlift for the kids from the BRESMA orphanage run by Jamie and Ali McMutrie, of Ben Avon, PA.

headline: Federal grant to create electronic health records
abstract: The Governor's Office of Health Care Reform will be using a $17.1 million federal American Recovery and Reinvestment Act funds to create an electronic network of health records that would connect patients and health practitioners. The program is called the Pennsylvania Health Information Exchange.

headline: 'Pony' truss bridge may be headed for last round-up
abstract: According to Jefferson County Commissioners Paul Corbin, Jim McIntyre and Jeff Pisarcik the PA Department of Transportation has chosen not to fund replacement or repair of the 106 year-old Dobson Road Bridge which crosses over Big Run Creek in Ringgold Township. The estimated cost of replacement is in the range of $976,000 while repairs could cost about a quarter of a million dollars.

headline: Rohrer tells supporters they gave him hope
abstract: PA state Republican Representative Samuel E. Rohrer's defeat to Democratic state Attorney General Tom Corbett in the gubernatorial race is covered. Rohrer addressed more than 500 supporters gathered at the Shady Maple Smorgasbord in Lancaster County.

headline: Work to begin on YMCA branch in Pittsburgh's Hill District
abstract: Officials with the YMCA are excited about their new facility in the Hill District that should open by 2012.  The facility will be replacing a 90 building and is expected to be full of the same features and state of the art equipment that their facilities in the suburbs enjoy.  The YMCA provides valuable resources to neighborhood children and families.

headline: Pittsburgh officials don't want to be shortchanged on parking
abstract: Pittsburgh Mayor Luke Ravenstahl believes privatizing the city's parking assets should generate at least $300 million in revenue, but he is not sure how much money the city will sacrifice in the long run by doing so. Pittsburgh City Councilman Patrick Dowd along with other city council members do not want to lease the cities assets until they can asses their value first.

headline: Positive trends seen in foster care statistics
abstract: On Tuesday, a reported released by the Pennsylvania Partnerships for Children said the state is making significant progress in safely reducing the number of children living in foster care. According to the report, almost 90 percent of counties reduced their foster care placement over the past year, resulting in a nearly 12 percent drop in children living in foster care and more than 16 percent in children entering the system. Statewide, there are 10,293 children in foster care, and in 2009, the number was 12,307.

headline: Now-legal synthetic marijuana substance may soon be banned in city
abstract: A synthetic marijuana substance, which goes under the names "K2", "Spice" and "Herbal Incense," is growing in popularity. The now-legal drug has the potential for abuse. Lackawanna County District Attorney Andy Jarbola and his office are working to ban the substance.

headline: Child health, education and welfare must be viewed together
abstract: Author gives three possible directions society should take in order to ensure a broader dialogue on the issue of health, education, and welfare needs of children.

headline: Rescue mission bringing Haitian orphans to Pittsburgh
abstract: A team of medical personnel accompanied by Governor Ed Rendell and U.S. Rep. Jason Altmire was in the air and headed to Pittsburgh early today with 53 children from an orphanage in earthquake-ravaged Haiti.  The rescue mission came in response to messages last week from sisters Jamie and Ali McMutrie of Pittsburgh, who said last Tuesday's devastating earthquake endangered the health of 130 children in their care at the BRESMA orphanage in Port-au-Prince.

headline: Warden: Backlog for Westmoreland inmate counseling growing
abstract: Due to state budget cuts, the Westmoreland County Prison has accrued a backlog of inmates on the waiting list for mandatory drug and alcohol treatment. Budget cuts have led the Westmoreland County Drug and Alcohol Commission to lay off one drug and alcohol counselor.

headline: Three local lawmakers hail decision
abstract: PA Senator John R. Gordner, R-27, welcomed Tuesday's decision by the Federal Highway Administration to reject the plan to toll Interstate 80. According to Gordner the law provides that federal approval to toll interstate highways may only be granted in limited circumstances and that the plan to toll Interstate 80 did not meet these requirements.

headline: Latino leaders denounce Pennsylvania's version of Arizona immigration bill
abstract: Latino community leaders gathered at the Council of Spanish Speaking Organizations of the Lehigh Valley headquarters to decry a bill being introduced in the Pennsylvania House that is recognized as the Keystone State's version of Arizona's immigration bill. The Pennsylvania House Bill 2479 proposes criminal offenses for being in the country illegally, being an undocumented worker applying for work, any employer who fails to register and use an Internet-based system that determines an employee’s eligibility to work in the country.

headline: Balancing Act: Health-care reform may spur wellness programs
abstract: The federal health care bill will encourage even more employers to consider instituting wellness programs that gives employees incentives to take better care of their health.  Large employers have been doing this for years as a way to help control rising health care costs.

headline: One last chance: Foreclosure mediation should be mandatory in Dauphin, Cumberland
abstract: Of the many programs run by government and nonprofit entities to assist down-on-their-luck homeowners, one stands out: mandatory mediation sessions between lenders and homeowners. Philadelphia has become a national leader in foreclosure mediation. The city requires all lenders to meet at least once face to face with the homeowner in a formal mediation session before the lender can foreclose on a property.

headline: No tax increase planned in Bedford
abstract: The Bedford County budget will not raise taxes for the fifth year straight. This reluctance to raise taxes in the face of budget shortfalls will in turn result in layoffs. The shortfall is the result of programming errors dealing with the Clean and Green initiative, which offers property tax relief to those who preserve forest and farmland.

headline: Support for serving with gays shows it's time to repeal 'don't ask, don't tell'
abstract: Author uses a survey from 1949 about the integration of black and white soldiers in the military to make a case for the repeal of Don’t Ask, Don’t Tell.

headline: Haitian Orphans Arrive in Pittsburgh
abstract: A charity relief mission carrying dozens of young children from an orphanage in earthquake-ravaged Haiti has arrived in Pittsburgh.  Fifty-three children, along with Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell, were on the Air Force flight, which landed at Pittsburgh International Airport about 9:30 a.m.  The children were staying at a Port-au-Prince orphanage run by two sisters from Pittsburgh.

headline: Police warn of possible increase of scams targeting the elderly
abstract: Pittsburgh police have warned the elderly of Pittsburgh of scams targeting them. They warned that they should not open their doors to people due to increase reports of people robbing houses posed as municipal and carpet cleaners.

headline: Department of Transportation rejects tolls on I-80
abstract: The U.S. Department of Transportation rejected a plan Tuesday that would toll Interstate 80 which is a popular highway among those traveling to Pennsylvania State University. PA Governor Ed Rendell held a press conference Tuesday afternoon to contest the toll's denial, pledging to find an alternative to raise state funds.

headline: Rendell: Obama Visit for Specter 'Might Jack Up Turnout'
abstract: Pennsylvania Governor Ed Rendell would like President Barack Obama to make a visit to PA to endorse Republican turned Democratic Senator Arlen Spector because it may "jack up turnout".  The author asks would Obama's appearance really make a difference.

headline: Onorato continues attack on Corbett's comment
abstract: County Executive Dan Onorato, the Democratic candidate for governor is continuing the pressure on Attorney General Tom Corbett in light of his recent remarks regarding the unemployed.  Onorato says the remarks show that he "simply doesn't get it."  Onorato continues to trail in the polls, most recently by a 7 point margin.

headline: Most Allentown State Hospital residents, employees relocated
abstract: Allentown State Hospital announced in January it was closing, as a result 179 residents had to be relocated to other state hospitals, apartments and group homes and a majority have been. Placing the hospital's 377 employees into new jobs before it closes at the end of the year is also close to being completed.

headline: Homewood children's program not chosen for federal funding
abstract: The proposed network of educational and social services designed to boost student performance and achievement known as the Homewood Children's Village was not one of the projects selected for start-up grant funding announced by the US Department of Education on Tuesday. The one-year, $500,000 grants awarded to 21 nonprofit organizations including hospitals, charter schools and institutions of higher education are part of the federal government's Promise Neighborhoods program.

headline: City facing aid squeeze
abstract: As PA Governor Ed Rendell, US Senator Arlen Specter, and PA Representative Dwight Evans step down, Philadelphia could see some of its projects stalled during a 'new age of austerity' under Republican control at various levels of government. The city has plans to overhaul the City Hall subway station at a cost of $100 million. With revenue lags and new leadership, the project could see delays.

headline: Three rabid skunks found in Camp Hill, Lemoyne
abstract: The Department of Health has confirmed that three skunks found in Cumberland County have tested positive for rabies. The skunks were shot by police and taken to the Department of Agriculture lab for testing. The Department of Health urges people who may have come in contact with the skunks t contact the Cumberland County State Health Center.

headline: Three jurors selected in Bonusgate trial
abstract: Three jurors were selected this morning for the trial of ex-Democratic House Whip Mike Veon and three of his former aides in the Bonus gate corruption scandal.

headline: Marriage of transit, real estate development pressed
abstract: The city of Pittsburgh and Allegheny county are attempting to entice private investors to build a mass transit system in Pittsburgh in return for fare revenues. It  is part of the city's Transportation Action Partnership program to build a transit system without asking for state or federal funds.

headline: Coalport may soon see flood levee built
abstract: Coalport Borough Council Chairman Joe Laurello said last night that representatives from the PA Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) were in Coalport recently looking over the site of the proposed flood levee that is expected to be built along Clearfield Creek. Laurello said Jake Kernoschak, DEP project coordinator, said if the money doesn't start getting used soon it's liable to just go away.

headline: Officials project mild regional voter turnout
abstract: Despite tight races for PA governor and U.S. Senator and as well as a special election for a PA House seat, local leaders and election officials still predict a low turnout.

headline: Misplaced priorities: State shouldn't fund Murtha, Specter libraries
abstract: Gov Ed Rendell has authorized up to $20 million to build libraries that honor the careers of US Rep John Murtha and US Sen. Arlen Spector.  The editorial disputes the amount of economic development that could come from either of the facilities and believes that there are much more worthy places the money could go especially in light of the tight budget.

headline: Salmonella recall expands to eggs sent to 17 states
abstract: Wright County Egg of Galt, Iowa, the producer of shell eggs linked to hundreds of illnesses in a massive salmonella outbreak has expanded its recall to include eggs sent to 17 states, federal health officials said Thursday. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is working with state health departments to investigate the illnesses, so far no deaths linked to the outbreak have been reported.

headline: Groups rally for Marcellus Shale gas drilling restrictions
abstract: In the summer of 2009 after deep underground drilling for natural gas began in Susquehanna County complained  residents have said the water from their well is undrinkable. Cabot Oil & Gas Corp., which is drilling in dozens of locations in the county, insisted it didn't cause the problem. Dozens of environmental groups have rallied at the Capitol in support of several Marcellus-related bills that would address such concerns.

headline: Anti-bullying measure goes to Gov. Christie
abstract: New Jersey is set to become leader in bully prevention. Both houses overwhelmingly approved the anti-bullying "bill of rights," which some say is the nation's toughest. The new legislation would require public school districts to have bullying-prevention programs and make harassment grounds for expulsion. New Jersey Governor Chris Christie is unsure whether the measure is constitutional and has not said whether he would sign it.

headline: Rail to expand
abstract: The SEDA-COG Joint Rail Authority and Shamokin Valley Railroad will announce a million-dollar expansion to the railroad network in eastern Northumberland County. The projects will be funded through $300,000 of TIGER II funds from the Federal Railroad Administration and $700,000 of PA Capital Budget funds from PennDOT Rail Freight.

headline: A hard look at health reform
abstract: This article describes the key components of the health care reform plans under consideration in Congress.  The author provides details on both the House and Senate versions of the bill.

headline: York Republican Mansfield to run independent campaign for governor
abstract: Robert Allen Mansfield of York County said he will forego the May primary and run an independent campaign for governor in November gubernatorial election. His decision comes after he lost the Republican party nomination to PA Attorney General Tom Corbett.

headline: Counties to get signs for flood-prone roads
abstract: The Susquehanna River Basin Commission and the National Weather Service announced that five counties in southern tier New York and northern tier Pennsylvania will receive road signs alerting drivers to turn around when roads are flooded. Which was prompted by the fact that more than 50 percent of the fatalities during flood events result from people attempting to drive on flooded roadways.

headline: West Wing Briefing: What will Gibbs and Co. say about Sestak's victory?
abstract: A blog discussing what White House press secretary Robert Gibbs will say when asked questions about PA Representative Joe Sestak's victory over long time US Senator Arlen Spector in the Democratic Senator primary. President Barack Obama had publicly offered his support to Arlen Specter during the campaign. Gibbs did not answer the questions directly, but White House aides have privately said that Specter's loss does not mean anything significant.

headline: Expletive deleted? Appeals court rebukes FCC on indecency policy
abstract: A federal appeals court has found that the FCC's policy regarding indecent language and conduct on television goes too far and they have been ordered to not be as strict.  The courts favor a middle ground aimed at restraining indecent language while allowing for freedom of expression.

headline: Gov. Ed Rendell: Only 100 state employee layoffs will be necessary
abstract: PA Governor Ed Rendell said that a higher than usual rate of state employee retirements, hundreds of positions going unfilled and a statewide hiring freeze means that only about 100 state workers will likely be laid off, at a noon news conference today. Rendell said about 5,000 state employees will retire this year, 2,000 more than usual, and 600 positions that became available over the last several months will not be filled.

headline: Commissioners to vote on assisting hospital in acquiring state funding
abstract: On Tuesday during a Lycoming County commissioners work session, Susquehanna Health Chief Financial Officer Charles Santangelo asked the commissioners to consider on Thursday an application to the state for a $2.5 million Redevelopment Assistant Capital Project grant. The grant would assist Susquehanna Health in acquiring state funding to help pay for upgrades to the Williamsport Regional Medical Center. The $25 million service center, which has been up and running since May 2009, includes new boilers, heating and cooling systems and a cogeneration plant.

headline: Spectrum's walls to start tumbling
abstract: Philadelphia Mayor Michael Nutter will be present at the kick-off of the demolition of the Spectrum, an arena that has entertained Philadelphia sports fans for the last half-century. The demolition will begin with wrecking balls and span a total of five months. The kick-off ceremony will have refreshments.

headline: Every neighborhood needs a park
abstract: Commissioned by the city Parks and Recreation Department in cooperation with the City Planning Commission and produced by PennPraxis, Green2015 is a plan to add 500 acres of green public space to the city by 2015. The goal is to provide park space for residents who don't live within a half-mile of a park, and ultimately to make the city more equitable, livable, and competitive. Green2015 is funded by the William Penn Foundation and the Lenfest Foundation.
Even after a tough week, one in which Massachusetts voters replaced Ted Kennedy with a Republican, President Obama says he is not giving up on health-care reform.

headline: Milcraft Industries now owns State Office Building
abstract: Milcraft Industries have purchased a state office building in downtown Pittsburgh. The company has not yet stated what the building will be used for but renovations have started.

headline: Table games: New deal begins at Mount Airy
abstract: The PA Gaming Control Board voted to allow Mount Airy Casino Resort to operate 72 table games at the Paradise Township casino. Preparation for table games is already under way at Mount Airy, and the casino said it could be ready to introduce them by July, pending state approval.

headline: Yudichak defeats W-B Mayor Leighton in Democratic primary to succeed Sen. Musto
abstract: PA state Representative John Yudichak, who served six terms in the Legislature, defeated Wilkes-Barre Mayor Tom Leighton, by capturing 66.9% of the vote therefore winning the Democratic party's nomination for the 14th state senatorial district. This seat will replace longtime PA Senator Raphael Musto In November Yudichak will face Republican Luzerne County Commissioner Stephen A. Urban and Libertarian Betsy Summers.

headline: Fitting fines: Penalties for gas well blowout send a message
abstract: State Environmental Secretary John Hanger has issued stiff fines against those responsible for a natural gas well blowout in Clearfield County last month.  Mr. Hanger fined EOG Resources of Canonsburg $353,000 and C.C. Forbes Co. of Washington, Pa., nearly $47,000.  The accident caused 35,000 gallons of fracking fluid to spill into the atmosphere for 16 hours.  The companies are in danger of losing their license if such recklessness continues.

headline: PA bill would mandate workplace sick leave
abstract: PA Representative Marc Gergely, D-White Oak, introduced House Bill 1830, which is currently before the House Labor Relations Committee for consideration, and would provide one hour of paid sick time for every 40 hours that a person works, up to a maximum of 52 hours, and 6 1/2 days per year. Gergely says currently, 46 percent of workers in private companies in the state don't get paid sick leave, which forces many to go to work sick.

headline: Cabot: Dimock water contaminated before drilling; residents' tests show water more contaminated now
abstract: Tests of two private water wells in Dimock Township, PA showed traces of toxic chemicals in 2008 before Marcellus Shale gas drilling began nearby, according to test results made available to the Times-Tribune on Tuesday by the gas driller active in the township. A spokesman for Cabot Oil and Gas Corp. said those chemicals toluene, benzene and surfactants were not detected in 2008 in pre-drill samples taken at more than a dozen nearby water supplies.

headline: McFadden's bartender says it discouraged nonwhite customers
abstract: A part-time bartender at McFadden's Restaurant and Saloon has filed a class action federal lawsuit alleging the restaurant deliberately discourages nonwhite customers. This Temple University Law student has provided as evidence text messages between the bar manager and shift supervisor. The text messages suggest that management was worried that certain  nonwhite patrons would scare off their usual white weekend crowd.

newspaper: philly.com Blogs - by Phila Daily News staff
headline: NY Times sounds alarm on public debt crisis
abstract: Author cites an article in the New York Times which warns of an oncoming public sector crisis. The NYT article points to several factors which contribute to the debt crisis, all of which are present in Philadelphia. The article comes at a time when Governor Ed Rendell is pushing to borrow $1 billion for infrastructure spending.
Sam's club is laying off more than eleven thousand employees across the United States.

headline: County GOP chair to run for House
abstract: George Dunbar, the chairman of the Westmoreland County Republican Committee and a Penn Township commissioner, announced he will seek the seat held by veteran PA Rep. James E. Casorio Jr.

headline: Pittsburgh to add 'eyes' that never sleep
abstract: With a $2 million earmark requested by U.S. Sen. Robert Casey, Pittsburgh city officials could install 100 extra cameras. Pittsburgh currently owns 22 surveillance cameras and has access to 300 cameras owned by Port Authority, PA Department of Transportation and private businesses.

headline: Status: At Risk
abstract: An advocacy group for preserving historic sites, parks, museums and organizations places Pennsylvania in the "At Risk" category of losing such sites. They write that due to flat out elimination of heritage fund programs or huge budget cuts to the Pennsylvania Historical and Museum Commission (PHMC) leaving them with just half of their employees. When asked why the PHMC's budget was cut so heavily, PA Governor Ed Rendell responded, ".., they are not part of the state's core mission." Preservation Nation say that the Commonwealth is looking for nonprofits to fund the state's historical sites.

headline: Milk money: The complexities of keeping dairy farms alive
abstract: Pennsylvania agriculture officials are in the process of adjusting their regulation of the state's dairy industry in order to help dairy farmers after a disastrous 2009 season.  Farmers are pushing to keep more of the money that is collected by retailers and the government regulators.

headline: Port Authority sets public hearing for service cuts
abstract: The Pittsburgh Port Authority will hold a public hearing on the reductions and proposed fare increases from 8 a.m. to 8 p.m. at the David L. Lawrence Convention Center, Downtown. PA Governor Ed Rendell has asked lawmakers to convene in special session next week to deal with a statewide transportation funding crisis in the wake of the federal government's rejection of the state's plan to toll Interstate 80.

headline: Harrisburg School District residents line up to support sports, early education
abstract: Harrisburg residents had their say on the Harrisburg School District’s budget crisis Monday, and if the voice of the people means anything, school directors will be hard-pressed to close a $6.8 million budget hole by cutting early-childhood education or sports. The board took no action on any of its budget-cutting proposals Monday, tabling them until more information can be obtained and more public hearings held.
